1953-iran-coup.title: Air India Flight 182
1953-iran-coup.summary: The 1985 bombing of a Boeing 747 over the Atlantic, which John Kiriakou has attributed to the government of India in the course of arguing that state sponsorship of terrorism is not confined to the countries formally designated for it.

1953-iran-coup.title: Haroon Yenor trial
1953-iran-coup.summary: Federal terrorism prosecution in which John Kiriakou testified as a defense expert witness; Yenor, arrested in November 2024 on charges tied to an alleged plot to bomb the New York Stock Exchange and a synagogue, was acquitted on all six charges on June 30; Kiriakou's expert testimony argued the FBI supplied the idea, the bomb, the explosives, the timer, the detonation cord, and the getaway car.

1953-iran-coup.title: Myanmar's civil war, per Kiriakou
1953-iran-coup.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Myanmar as the only country in the world continuously at war without a single day of peace since World War II, its Buddhist-majority persecution of Muslims, Christians, and Hindus, his view that Aung San Suu Kyi should have her Nobel Peace Prize stripped, and his argument that the world ignores the country's atrocities because it has gems rather than oil.

1953-iran-coup.title: Sofia, Bulgaria Dead Drop
1953-iran-coup.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a CIA trip to Sofia, Bulgaria, in which he tracked down and debriefed a retired Bulgarian general — a Cold War-era trainee at Fort Polk, Louisiana — about his proximity to the 1975 assassination of CIA station chief Richard Welch in Athens.

1953-iran-coup.title: Kiriakou's money-laundering tip
1953-iran-coup.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a chief operating officer job at a boutique investment firm early in the COVID pandemic that he came to believe was an international money-laundering operation possibly backed by Iran — downloading 15,000 pages of supporting documents before an FBI agent told him the bureau would only take interest if the case involved Russia, China, terrorism, or January 6th.

1953-iran-coup.title: CIA Democrats (2016)
1953-iran-coup.summary: John Kiriakou's term for a wave of 2016-era congressional candidates with intelligence or military backgrounds who ran for office opposing Trump from the right on Russia — including former CIA officer Abigail Spanberger, who won a one-term-limited Virginia governorship, and former DIA official Elissa Slotkin, who moved from intelligence into Congress and the Senate — both of whom Kiriakou suggests are positioning for future presidential runs.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: Saddam Hussein
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: CIA cable priority levels
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: The five levels of immediacy assigned to U.S. government cable traffic, as described by John Kiriakou. From lowest to highest: Routine, Priority, Immediate, Flash, CRITIC. Most career officers will never see a CRITIC; during the Gulf War, Kiriakou''s desk was receiving multiple CRITICs a day, each one announcing a hostile missile launch.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: George Habash
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

1993-bush-assassination-plot.title: Asel al-Ghabandi
1993-bush-assassination-plot.summary: Kuwaiti resistance figure during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, a "bona fide hero" whose telephone reporting on Iraqi troop movements, roadblocks, atrocities, and the location of inspections reached the CIA every single day via NSA [call interception](/wiki/the-intercept) — Kiriakou's account of the resistance figure who best understood how to weaponize the certainty that the Americans were listening to everything.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: Barack Obama
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: Espionage Act
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: Over-classification
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: Carrying classified material out of a SCIF
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: The two lawful procedures John Kiriakou describes for removing classified documents from a secure facility — a double-enveloped, double-marked package addressed to your home agency, or a leather bag with a double lock — and his flat statement that nothing about either allows a document to be forgotten in a garage for twelve years.

2023-classified-documents-scandal.title: The pillow-talk disclosure case
2023-classified-documents-scandal.summary: A case John Kiriakou witnessed from the next desk: a CIA officer told a classified fact to a former senior officer turned CNN commentator during an affair, he repeated it on air, and the agency identified her within days. Her punishment was four weeks'' suspension without pay and a memo in her file. Kiriakou uses it as the benchmark for how far the handling of disclosures has moved — today, he says, it would be an Espionage Act prosecution and about five years in prison.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: 2026 Iran war
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: The Bab el-Mandeb
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: The strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa through which everything leaving the Suez Canal must pass — narrower than the Strait of Hormuz, in John Kiriakou's account the one genuine American national interest in Yemen, and the reason Israel has offered diplomatic recognition to Somaliland in exchange for a military base.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: Strait of Hormuz
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: Yemen
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: Decapitation strikes
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that killing an adversary's leadership does not defeat the adversary — grounded in a standing joke from his own service that the CIA had killed twenty-seven separate "number three" figures in al-Qaeda, and applied to the 2026 Iran war, where the entire political, military and scientific leadership was killed in the opening days and the fighting continued regardless.

2026-iran-war-economic-shock.title: Trump's need for glorification
2026-iran-war-economic-shock.summary: John Kiriakou''s psychological reading of why the 2026 Iran war happened — that Donald Trump "craves glorification," has pursued it by attaching his name to public landmarks, and concluded that "real glory can only come with war": becoming the president who succeeded in overthrowing the Iranian government where every predecessor since Carter had failed. Kiriakou attributes the false expectation of quick collapse to wealthy Iranian-American exiles.

2026-iran-war.title: Strait of Hormuz
2026-iran-war.summary: The shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the centre of gravity of the 2026 Iran war in John Kiriakou''s account — a strait whose only navigable deep water lies on the Iranian side of the maritime border, closed not by Iran''s aggression but, as he insists, by the American and Israeli attack that provoked it: "The Strait of Hormuz was open. We''re the ones that forced the closure."

2026-iran-war.title: Decapitation strikes
2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that killing an adversary's leadership does not defeat the adversary — grounded in a standing joke from his own service that the CIA had killed twenty-seven separate "number three" figures in al-Qaeda, and applied to the 2026 Iran war, where the entire political, military and scientific leadership was killed in the opening days and the fighting continued regardless.

2026-iran-war.title: Population decline as a national-security question
2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that demographic collapse — an emigrated Greek middle class, a shrinking Russia, and a Chinese population he believes is far smaller than claimed — is a strategic variable rather than a social one, and that some countries may not remain viable as countries without large population changes.

2026-iran-war.title: Prince Muhammad bin Naif
2026-iran-war.summary: Saudi prince and former head of Saudi intelligence; survivor of an al-Qaeda assassination attempt by a suicide bomber who concealed an explosive device internally in his own body, in approximately 2009.

2026-iran-war.title: Prison pedophile accounts
2026-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account of encountering convicted pedophiles for the first time in federal prison, drawing on advice from a psychiatrist friend and his own work running the chapel library — one of only two safe spaces in prison for inmates convicted of child sex crimes.

2026-iran-war.title: The "Soylent Green is people" cable easter egg
2026-iran-war.summary: A long-running CIA case-officer in-joke in which the line "Soylent Green is people" is hidden inside classified operational cables as a sequence of incongruously lowercase letters

2028-presidential-field.title: JD Vance
2028-presidential-field.summary: Vice president and 2028 Republican front-runner, whose Joe Rogan interview admitting the administration "mishandled the Epstein files" John Kiriakou reads not as candour but as an authorised manoeuvre — and whose passing remark that any documents tying Epstein to intelligence "wouldn't exist in 2026" Kiriakou treats as a matter-of-fact accusation that the CIA destroyed evidence.

2028-presidential-field.title: Mar-a-Lago pardon pitch
2028-presidential-field.summary: The lunch at which John Kiriakou put his pardon request directly to Donald Trump. Flown to Palm Beach by a wealthy friend who also wanted a pardon, Kiriakou delivered a prepared line as the president worked the dining room, was told to take it to Pam Bondi, and was afterwards vouched for on a speakerphone call to Trump by a political fixer who then asked him for $25,000 a month until the pardon came through.

2028-presidential-field.title: International Spy Museum
2028-presidential-field.summary: The Washington museum of espionage. John Kiriakou, who gives private tours of it, describes its room on the CIA torture program as a video loop in which only the torturers are given a voice — and in which he, the officer who exposed the program, is never mentioned.

2028-presidential-field.title: Oman
2028-presidential-field.summary: The Gulf sultanate John Kiriakou singles out as America's most durable friend in the region and its most useful channel to Iran — a country that has acted as go-between for Washington and Tehran many times, and which he argues should be approached again in place of carrier deployments and public threats.

2028-presidential-field.title: Sharia law
2028-presidential-field.summary: Islamic jurisprudence. Challenged by a viewer who equated it with executions of gay people, forced child marriage and the criminalisation of apostasy, John Kiriakou answers that those acts are largely the work of ISIS rather than of any government, and that Sharia is in substance a body of civil law covering inheritance, insurance, education, property ownership and commercial disputes.

2028-presidential-field.title: Wealth concentration
2028-presidential-field.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the present distribution of wealth is historically unprecedented and politically unsustainable — that trillionaires have never existed before, that five men hold as much as the bottom eighty per cent of the world, and that a defence budget approaching $1.5 trillion cannot be reconciled with the social spending it would have to displace.

9-11-commission.title: Omar al-Bayoumi
9-11-commission.summary: The Saudi national who housed and funded two of the 9/11 hijackers in California; John Kiriakou describes him as a Saudi intelligence officer working under a ghost job, places him at President Bush's Crawford ranch before the attacks, and says the CIA blocked the 9/11 Commission from investigating him.

9-11-commission.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
9-11-commission.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

9-11-commission.title: Israeli foreknowledge of 9/11
9-11-commission.summary: John Kiriakou's stated belief that Israeli intelligence had penetrated al-Qaeda and knew an attack was coming but withheld the warning as a policy decision, offered as his explanation for the dozens of Israelis arrested in New York in the days after the attacks.

9-11-commission.title: Saudi princes and 9/11
9-11-commission.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding three Saudi princes' personal cell numbers in Abu Zubaydah's seized diary — and how, after the CIA warned the Saudis, all three princes soon died in improbable ways, convincing him the Saudi government was involved in 9/11.

9-11-commission.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
9-11-commission.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

9-11-commission.title: Kiki Camarena case
9-11-commission.summary: 1985 abduction and murder of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena in Mexico; cited by John Kiriakou as the trigger for the 1985 U.S. statute authorizing the extraterritorial seizure of foreign nationals — the legal authority underpinning the 2026 U.S. operation that seized President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Yalta conference
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: The February 1945 Allied conference, which John Kiriakou uses as his teaching example of what a well-placed spy is worth: Stalin, told by a source inside the White House that Roosevelt was ill, insisted on a venue requiring a punishing multi-leg journey, then refused to delay the talks — and an exhausted Roosevelt, Kiriakou says, conceded Poland in order to go to bed.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Superdelegates
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: The Democratic Party's automatic-delegate system, which John Kiriakou describes as created after George McGovern's 1972 landslide loss to return nominating power to party insiders. He cites West Virginia and Wyoming in 2016, where Bernie Sanders won the vote and Hillary Clinton took every delegate, and notes the Republican Party has no equivalent — which is why an insurgent like Donald Trump could win its nomination.

9-11-plea-agreements.title: Truck and Cat in the Hat
9-11-plea-agreements.summary: An incident at FCI Loretto in which John Kiriakou, told by one prisoner that another had called him a rat, invented a slur he knew would enrage a convicted serial killer — who beat the accuser badly enough to require a helicopter medevac. Kiriakou presents it as a live application of two rules he says he learned at the CIA: let others do your dirty work, and admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Elizabeth Rouser
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: Named only in a producer/narrator voiceover on a Kiriakou interview episode, not in Kiriakou's own words; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Katherine Gun
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: UK whistleblower named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Pete Hoekstra
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: Named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Restraint Camp
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: A term for foreign-policy conservatives who favor ending forever wars and regime-change interventions; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

911-attribution-of-responsibility.title: Afghan War Logs
911-attribution-of-responsibility.summary: A 2010 WikiLeaks publication discussed on a panel Kiriakou joined; the specific lines about it in the corpus belong to other panelists, not Kiriakou.

a-middle-east-reading-list.title: Elizabeth Rouser
a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: Named only in a producer/narrator voiceover on a Kiriakou interview episode, not in Kiriakou's own words; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-middle-east-reading-list.title: Katherine Gun
a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: UK whistleblower named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-middle-east-reading-list.title: Pete Hoekstra
a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: Named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-middle-east-reading-list.title: Restraint Camp
a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: A term for foreign-policy conservatives who favor ending forever wars and regime-change interventions; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

a-middle-east-reading-list.title: Italian intelligence services
a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the Italian services as very good and very close partners of the CIA — except in the Abu Omar case, when they refused to help, were ignored, and responded by investigating the CIA and identifying twenty-one of its officers.

a-middle-east-reading-list.title: The best meal overseas
a-middle-east-reading-list.summary: Asked for the best meals he had eaten abroad, John Kiriakou named first a dish cooked by a young Pakistani in a CIA guest house in Islamabad — shaved beef, a myriad of spices, hot green chillies and rice cooked in chicken stock — followed by sushi in Tokyo and the Lenten table of Clean Monday in Greece.

aafia-siddiqui.title: The CIA divorce rate
aafia-siddiqui.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why marriages fail at the CIA at a rate he says exceeds that of any other part of the U.S. government — the impossibility of explaining a midnight departure to a spouse without a clearance, and the difficulty officers have switching off a professional habit of deception. He gives the figure variously as over 75 percent and upwards of 80 percent, and counts his own first marriage among the casualties.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Juan Guaidó
aafia-siddiqui.summary: Venezuelan opposition figure whom the United States recognized as interim president starting in 2019; John Kiriakou dismisses him as having been, in substance, nothing more than a George Washington University grad student, and says the U.S. attempt to install him — followed later by María Corina Machado — failed because Venezuelan support for Nicolás Maduro rests on loyalty to Chavista revolutionary ideology rather than to Maduro personally.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Kiriakou's Cuba trip
aafia-siddiqui.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first visit to Cuba, where his books sit in the national library and officials treated him warmly — and a Cuban vice president told him every U.S. president is 'the same,' blaming Cuba while it cannot keep the lights on. He was invited as a guest of the Havana international book fair after his first two books were translated into Spanish, and later wrote about how the U.S. embargo shapes daily life there, from a dengue-fever hospital bill he had to pay in euros to a diet dominated by squash.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Kiriakou's Iran trips
aafia-siddiqui.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his own visits to Iran and his Iranian-American partner's regular travel there — noting Tehran's status as the cosmetic-surgery capital of the Middle East, a warning to Iranian state TV viewers about American fast food rather than American generals, and his own repeated but unfulfilled invitations to visit.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Venezuelan embassy occupation (2019)
aafia-siddiqui.summary: A 2019 sit-in at the Venezuelan embassy in Washington, D.C., which John Kiriakou says he joined at the Venezuelan government's request the night the United States broke relations with Venezuela; he says he still keeps Venezuelan government property from that night at his house.

aafia-siddiqui.title: Trump cartel terrorist designation
aafia-siddiqui.summary: Donald Trump's early second-term State Department designation of drug cartels as terrorist organizations, which John Kiriakou says was understood at the time mainly as a paperwork exercise to free up agencies like the NSA and DIA to spend money on intercepting communications and training foreign nationals — but which Kiriakou says Trump has since treated as license to attack any vessel he personally deems cartel-linked.

abbottabad.title: Agent payment mechanics
abbottabad.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

abbottabad.title: Abu Zubaydah
abbottabad.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abbottabad.title: Brian Ross
abbottabad.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

abbottabad.title: Eastern District of Virginia
abbottabad.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

abbottabad.title: Guantanamo Bay
abbottabad.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

abbottabad.title: Falls Church mosque
abbottabad.summary: Large mosque on Route 7 in Falls Church, Virginia; the site at which John Kiriakou, in 1993 as a CIA Arabic-language trainee, met then-imam Anwar al-Awlaki on a class field trip; the same mosque at which the September 11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: Amir of Bahrain from 1961 until his death in 1999; per John Kiriakou, who was posted to Bahrain 1994–1996, a short, "roly poly," sweet-natured ruler who kept an open beach palace for Westerners, disliked Jordan's King Hussein, and was heartbroken by the Columbine shooting even as he privately could not grasp why he should extend more support to his own Shia majority.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: The Dilmun burial mounds
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: The ancient grave mounds standing in the Shia villages of Bahrain — ordinary ones ten or twenty feet high, royal ones fifty — which John Kiriakou took visiting friends and family to see, and which sat in the same villages the government was raiding at night during the uprising.

abdul-amir-al-jamri.title: Salman bin Hamad
abdul-amir-al-jamri.summary: The Bahraini heir presumptive who became John Kiriakou's friend during his 1994–96 posting — president of the Bahrain Center for Studies and Research and patron of the environmental association, both of which fell in Kiriakou's economic brief, and a companion on nights out at a nightclub by the naval base.

abolish-the-cia.title: Elizabeth Rouser
abolish-the-cia.summary: Named only in a producer/narrator voiceover on a Kiriakou interview episode, not in Kiriakou's own words; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

abolish-the-cia.title: Katherine Gun
abolish-the-cia.summary: UK whistleblower named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

abolish-the-cia.title: Kiriakou's serial-killer letters
abolish-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's account of writing letters, as research for a planned book, to several well-known serial killers — including David Berkowitz ("Son of Sam"), Gary Leon Ridgway (the Green River Killer), the BTK killer, the "co-ed killer," and Manson family member Tex Watson — and the uniformly evangelical, Jesus-focused responses he received instead of the interviews he wanted.

abolish-the-cia.title: Kiriakou's Pakistan-Islam economic critique
abolish-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's controversial view that Islam has held Pakistan back economically, contrasting Pakistan's stalled development since the 1960s with South Korea's — which had the same GDP as Pakistan in 1964 — and citing lost productivity from prayer breaks and holy days, resentment over partition, and spending on nuclear weapons instead of infrastructure and education.

abolish-the-cia.title: Pete Hoekstra
abolish-the-cia.summary: Named once in an unlabeled multi-speaker panel transcript; not safely attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

abolish-the-cia.title: Prison pedophile accounts
abolish-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's account of encountering convicted pedophiles for the first time in federal prison, drawing on advice from a psychiatrist friend and his own work running the chapel library — one of only two safe spaces in prison for inmates convicted of child sex crimes.

abraham-accords.title: Expulsion of Palestinians from the Gulf
abraham-accords.summary: The mass expulsion of the Palestinian professional class from the Gulf Arab states in the aftermath of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which John Kiriakou witnessed from the region and identifies as the reason Gulf governments are willing to normalise relations with Israel.

abraham-accords.title: Kiriakou prison manipulation tactics
abraham-accords.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying CIA tradecraft — including deliberate deception, forged paperwork, and manipulating other inmates into violence — to protect himself and control his environment during his federal prison sentence.

abraham-accords.title: NewsGuard
abraham-accords.summary: A media-rating organization, founded by the former head of Court TV and a former Wall Street Journal publisher, that scores news outlets 0-100 for reliability. Per John Kiriakou, NewsGuard docks any outlet that takes a position on Ukraine or Syria contrary to its preferred line, is subscribed to mostly by government entities (chiefly the Pentagon), and singled out Consortium News, the Grayzone, Antiwar.com, and ScheerPost over their criticism of U.S. policy — prompting a First Amendment lawsuit.

abraham-accords.title: King Abdullah II of Jordan
abraham-accords.summary: The Jordanian monarch whom John Kiriakou rates as knowing more about the Middle East than anyone else who leads or studies it, and as almost never wrong across twenty-five years of foreign-policy predictions. Kiriakou recounts the deathbed succession that made him king against his own expectations, and his refusal after October 7 to accept Palestinian refugees on the grounds that doing so would deliver Israel the ethnic cleansing it wanted.

abraham-accords.title: Kiriakou cameo practice
abraham-accords.summary: John Kiriakou's post-2026 use of the Cameo personalised-video service — running at roughly 25 to 30 hours a week, some 900 messages in the month of March 2026 alone, nearly 2,000 messages in total by July 2026 — that he says has produced three cases in which the person receiving the video message afterwards told him he had talked them out of committing suicide, including a 15-year-old bulimic girl to whom Kiriakou gave his personal phone number.

abraham-accords.title: Kiriakou's mother's 2008 trip to Israel
abraham-accords.summary: John Kiriakou recounts his mother's 2008 church-group trip to Israel and the West Bank, during which she was struck by the contrast between first-world Tel Aviv and a walled, mined Palestinian town, and witnessed an IDF soldier tear apart a Palestinian bus driver's novel as suspected "PLO propaganda." Kiriakou made two trips of his own to Israel in 2022, including one to cover the elections, during which he personally witnessed a fatal stabbing at Jerusalem's Iron Gate.

abraham-bolden.title: Alan Dershowitz
abraham-bolden.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

abraham-bolden.title: Dick Cheney
abraham-bolden.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

abraham-bolden.title: Donald Trump
abraham-bolden.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

abraham-bolden.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
abraham-bolden.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

abraham-bolden.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
abraham-bolden.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

abraham-bolden.title: Ross Ulbricht
abraham-bolden.summary: Founder of the online marketplace Silk Road, sentenced to life plus 75 years before being pardoned by President Trump; John Kiriakou met Ulbricht's mother and sister two weeks before the pardon and calls the length of the original sentence a sickening miscarriage of justice.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Lincoln's last turd
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: A purported piece of human waste attributed by a Pennsylvania circus-freak-show museum to Abraham Lincoln on the night of his assassination; auctioned for $5,000; subsequent DNA analysis disproved the attribution. John Kiriakou's failed bid for the artifact is the anecdote that, recirculated in early 2026, made him an internet meme figure.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Kiriakou's money-laundering tip
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a chief operating officer job at a boutique investment firm early in the COVID pandemic that he came to believe was an international money-laundering operation possibly backed by Iran — downloading 15,000 pages of supporting documents before an FBI agent told him the bureau would only take interest if the case involved Russia, China, terrorism, or January 6th.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Kiriakou on Christmas
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding Christmas so depressing since his two divorces that he does not decorate or mark it at all — and of the year he replaced it by taking his children to every station on the New York City subway system in a single day.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Joby Warrick's Washington Post resignation
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his friend Joby Warrick, a multiple Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist, resigning from the Washington Post because investigative journalism at the paper was dead — amid an 80% staff reduction since Jeff Bezos bought the paper.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: Aldrich Ames
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

abraham-lincoln-collection.title: James Comey
abraham-lincoln-collection.summary: Former FBI director indicted under the second Trump administration, whose prosecution John Kiriakou reads as a search for charges to fit a man rather than evidence of a crime — and which he expects to collapse, unlike the parallel case against John Brennan.

abraxas-corporation.title: Meeting Elon Musk in 2009
abraxas-corporation.summary: The evening in 2009 when John Kiriakou, waiting to pitch a television idea to an incoming NBC president in a Washington bar, was introduced to a friend the executive had brought along — asked him what he did for a living, and listened to him talk about Mars all night.

abraxas-corporation.title: Ted Rall
abraxas-corporation.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

abraxas-corporation.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
abraxas-corporation.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

abraxas-corporation.title: The Jordanian intelligence service
abraxas-corporation.summary: The service John Kiriakou calls one of the best in the world and arguably the best in the Middle East — good, in his account, out of necessity: half of Jordan''s population is Palestinian, Black September once fought on the steps of the palace, and the survival of the monarchy depends on having infiltrated every faction in the country.

abraxas-corporation.title: The hotel bar operation
abraxas-corporation.summary: The night a visiting foreign delegation's security detail was expected in a boutique hotel bar and every seat in it turned out to be occupied by a CIA officer — an episode John Kiriakou offers as an example of bad leadership, and which left his colleagues personally out of pocket for their espresso martinis.

abraxas-corporation.title: The Romanian silver mine
abraxas-corporation.summary: The private-intelligence assignment John Kiriakou uses to explain what commercial analysis actually buys: a mining client wanted to know who would win a Romanian municipal election, because a silver deposit lay under a village that would have to be destroyed to reach it.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: John Kiriakou
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Saddam Hussein
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

abu-nidal-disruption.title: British Bases in Cyprus
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: British sovereign bases cover 3% of Cyprus. Kiriakou, a quarter Cypriot, on the 46-year US weapons embargo almost no American knows about.

abu-nidal-disruption.title: Marty Gottesfeld
abu-nidal-disruption.summary: American hacktivist and computer security engineer, convicted for a 2014 denial-of-service attack on Boston Children's Hospital in protest of the treatment of patient Justina Pelletier; a fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou who has publicly taken up the case of Donnie Reynolds Jr.

abu-omar-rendition.title: Alec Baldwin
abu-omar-rendition.summary: Actor with whom John Kiriakou recounts a bitter falling-out — Baldwin calling him a liar over lunch at a meeting about a play in which Baldwin was to play him, later attaching to a Kiriakou TV pitch that AMC bought the next day, then quitting for HBO and killing the deal without a word.

abu-omar-rendition.title: Jennings Randolph
abu-omar-rendition.summary: Longtime U.S. Senator from West Virginia who, in a phone call John Kiriakou made to thank him as a college student, gave him the advice he says shaped his life: always do the right thing, not the expedient one.

abu-omar-rendition.title: The Los Angeles Times Iran op-ed
abu-omar-rendition.summary: An op-ed on Iranian foreign policy in Latin America that John Kiriakou was commissioned to write about six months after blowing the whistle on the torture programme. He had barely begun when the CIA general counsel''s office telephoned to warn him off the subject — a call he could not explain for fourteen years, and which he now attributes to his own wife rather than to a source inside the newspaper.

abu-omar-rendition.title: Afghanistan 2011 Kerry Trip
abu-omar-rendition.summary: John Kiriakou's 2011 trip to Afghanistan as senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee under Chairman John Kerry, where the pair sat through a briefing with 11 one-to-four-star generals presenting an optimistic account of the war — after which Kerry mused the U.S. might win, only for Kiriakou to tell him the U.S. controlled only Kabul, and that the same rosy briefing had been given every year since 2002.

abu-omar-rendition.title: CIA/FBI Budget Fearmongering
abu-omar-rendition.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the FBI, under J. Edgar Hoover, pioneered the tactic of citing a shifting parade of enemies before Congress to justify annual budget increases — communists, anarchists, gangsters, beatniks, anti-war protesters — a tactic the CIA later adopted wholesale, citing "communism" until 2001 and "terrorism" since, without needing further explanation to win budget increases.

abu-omar-rendition.title: The Office of Security arrangement
abu-omar-rendition.summary: The disclosure John Kiriakou says emerged from a 2020 custody hearing: that his wife, herself a senior CIA officer, had accompanied him to the 2007 ABC News whistleblowing interview on the instruction of the CIA''s Office of Security, and had continued to report on his activities.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: The German POW chess analogy
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: The reasoning John Kiriakou gave ABC News in December 2007 for why he had believed at the time that waterboarding was necessary: he had heard of Second World War German prisoners who, over months of playing chess with their interrogators, built enough rapport to talk, and he judged that al-Qaeda prisoners were a different order of adversary who would never be seduced into cooperating.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: The slap approval cable
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: The cable-by-cable approval chain that governed each escalation of the CIA''s enhanced interrogation techniques, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: permission for even a single open-handed slap of Abu Zubaydah came from Washington after a discussion, was granted by the deputy director for operations, and had to be reported back by cable afterwards.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Abu Zubaydah
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Waterboarding
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Brian Ross
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
abu-zubaydah-as-a-sounding-board.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Abu Zubaydah
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Senate Torture Report
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Ali Soufan
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: Espionage Act
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.title: The declination letter
abu-zubaydah-cremation-footnote.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: The two Abu Zubaydahs
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the first cousin who shared Abu Zubaydah's name, whose activities were folded into a single intelligence picture of a man Kiriakou called a terrorist Superman — and who vanished as soon as the capture reached the newspapers.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: The SpongeBob shirt
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: The bright red SpongeBob SquarePants shirt, a Christmas present from his children, that John Kiriakou happened to be wearing when Abu Zubaydah opened his one good eye and realised the Americans had him.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: Abu Zubaydah
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: The Syrian bodyguard
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: The 330-pound guard captured alongside Abu Zubaydah, whose gunshot wound John Kiriakou examined and found ringed by a dinner-plate powder burn — evidence that contradicted the official account and left Kiriakou with a question about Pakistani intentions he says he will never be able to answer.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: Buzzy Krongard
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: The executive director of the CIA — the agency's third-ranking officer — who sat on the board of Johns Hopkins Medical Center and, on learning that Abu Zubaydah had been captured wounded, had the hospital's top trauma surgeon flown to Pakistan on a CIA jet.

abu-zubaydah-diary.title: Hypersonic missiles
abu-zubaydah-diary.summary: John Kiriakou confirms that hypersonic missiles are real and that Russia, China and Iran all have them; that a weapon travelling 2,500 miles an hour cannot be defended against; and that Iran holds too few of them to do anything but make each one count.

abu-zubaydah.title: The cremation footnote
abu-zubaydah.summary: A footnote John Kiriakou cites from the declassified executive summary of the Senate torture report, stating that Abu Zubaydah will never be permitted to leave Guantanamo — despite never having joined al-Qaeda, never having pledged fealty to Osama bin Laden and never having been charged — and that on his death the CIA will cremate his body and scatter the ashes at sea.

abu-zubaydah.title: CIA versus FBI at a raid
abu-zubaydah.summary: John Kiriakou''s two-sentence account of the institutional difference between the two agencies, drawn from joint raids in Pakistan in 2002: the FBI numbers the four walls with sticky notes, photographs the inside of every drawer and collects every piece of paper, because it is building a case. The CIA breaks down the door, grabs all the men and sends them to Guantánamo.

abu-zubaydah.title: DARPA LifeLog
abu-zubaydah.summary: A Pentagon research program meant to track every email, photo, location and purchase of a person; John Kiriakou notes it was killed on February 4, 2004 — one day before Mark Zuckerberg filed the Facebook LLC.

abu-zubaydah.title: Galls.com sponsor story
abu-zubaydah.summary: John Kiriakou's account of outfitting the CIA's post-9/11 Islamabad station for terrorist-safe-house raids by ordering roughly $50,000 of tactical gear from the law-enforcement retailer galls.com on his CIA credit card, shipped to Pakistan via State Department diplomatic pouch in under a week — a story he now retells as an ad-read for the retailer, which sponsors one of his podcast appearances.

abu-zubaydah.title: Geneva Conventions
abu-zubaydah.summary: The laws of war at the center of John Kiriakou''s most-told confrontation story: finding hooded prisoners in Pakistan, he demanded of the officer in charge — "Are you seriously telling me that you have never read the Geneva Convention? It is a war crime to put hoods on them. Take the hoods off." The two reported each other to headquarters; Kiriakou got in trouble — "they didn''t give two shits about the Geneva Convention." He indicts the Bush administration''s twin dodges: that al-Qaeda fighters, as non-state actors, fell outside the Conventions'' protections, and that the techniques weren''t torture at all.

abu-zubaydah.title: Jane Harman
abu-zubaydah.summary: Former U.S. Representative from California who served as ranking member and later chair of the House Intelligence Committee. Per John Kiriakou, Harman was present in the room when congressional leadership was briefed on the CIA's enhanced interrogation program; when reporters later asked her about the program, she denied knowing about it. Kiriakou told the New York Times she had been in the room, after which Harman revised her account to say she had left early and that an aide remained as a notetaker.

access-agent.title: Jeffrey Epstein
access-agent.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

access-agent.title: MOSSAD
access-agent.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

access-agent.title: CIA record deniability
access-agent.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how senior CIA officers occasionally decide to keep an event out of the written record — illustrated by a recruited asset who committed a public murder, after which the Deputy Director for Operations told Kiriakou, on second thought, 'let's not put that in writing.'

access-agent.title: Khaled Mashal
access-agent.summary: Senior Hamas political leader; survived a 1997 Mossad poisoning attempt in Amman, Jordan; the operation's failure and the political fallout in Jordan are the canonical example, in John Kiriakou's account, of Israeli operational hostility carried out in friendly third-country territory without regard for the diplomatic consequences.

access-agent.title: Mahmoud al-Mabhouh
access-agent.summary: Senior Hamas figure assassinated by Mossad in a Dubai hotel room in January 2010; the operation has been studied by intelligence services worldwide for its tradecraft, in particular the unsolved question of how the assassination team locked the hotel-room door from the inside after killing him.

access-agent.title: Israeli non-extradition of Jews
access-agent.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Israel as a refuge that does not extradite Jewish fugitives regardless of the offence, illustrated by the case of an American lawyer who fled there after a child-abuse suit and was recovered only by an Interpol sting in Cyprus. Kiriakou uses the rule to frame a question about Jeffrey Epstein: why a man with jets and hidden billions did not flee there himself.

active-measures.title: CIA political action group
active-measures.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

active-measures.title: Italian election covert action
active-measures.summary: What John Kiriakou calls the CIA''s very first covert action: bribing Italian journalists in the 1949 election to write in favor of the Christian Democrats, who narrowly beat the Communists — a operation he says amounted to stealing the election.

active-measures.title: Jeffrey Epstein
active-measures.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

active-measures.title: John Paul II and the CIA
active-measures.summary: John Kiriakou's account that CIA old-timers took credit for helping make the Polish cardinal John Paul II pope — a political move to weaken the Soviet Union — and that his later recognition of the state of Israel was seen as a bonus for the West.

active-measures.title: Jordanian al-Qaeda detainee
active-measures.summary: The subject of John Kiriakou's first-ever interrogation in Pakistan — a Jordanian who had gone to Afghanistan to run an orphanage, joined al-Qaeda for its funding, and told the truth about his escape route because 'I'm your prisoner; what good would it do to lie?'

active-measures.title: The University of Salamanca professorship
active-measures.summary: John Kiriakou's teaching post in the graduate intelligence studies programme at the University of Salamanca, where he lectures on introductory intelligence studies and the history of terrorism, at an institution he describes as older than Spain itself.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Bureau of Prisons
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Charles Samuels
administrative-remedy-process.summary: Director of the Bureau of Prisons during Kiriakou's incarceration, and the official to whom Kiriakou publicly appealed over the heads of the Loretto staff in a letter from Loretto.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Prison Legal News
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history, co-founded by former prisoner Paul Wright, and a recurring source in Kiriakou's account of Bureau of Prisons practice.

administrative-remedy-process.title: The sentencing reform bills that died
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The bipartisan legislation John Kiriakou watched from prison — the Recidivism Reduction and Public Safety Act and the Smarter Sentencing Act, alongside a Sentencing Commission move to lower drug guidelines — which would have freed thousands and which died in the Senate without a vote.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Five per cent of the population, twenty-five per cent of the prisoners
administrative-remedy-process.summary: The statistic John Kiriakou returns to from inside prison — that the United States holds five per cent of the world''s people and a quarter of its prisoners, more per head than Russia, China or Iran — and the causes he assigns: the war on drugs, election-year lawmaking, and a Congress creating some fifty new crimes a year.

administrative-remedy-process.title: Karl Rove
administrative-remedy-process.summary: U.S. political strategist; manager of George W. Bush's 2000 and 2004 presidential campaigns; in 2008 he and John Kiriakou were hired by John Rendon to rehabilitate the reputation of an Indonesian general banned from the United States on human-rights grounds — a job Kiriakou says produced four unpublishable op-eds and nothing else.

admiral-crowe.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
admiral-crowe.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

admiral-crowe.title: The Fifth Fleet in Bahrain
admiral-crowe.summary: The United States naval presence that has been based in Bahrain since 1976 — the naval component of Central Command — and the social geography it created for John Kiriakou as a diplomat: the officers'' club for its salad bar, the enlisted club for football and cheap beer.

admiral-crowe.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
admiral-crowe.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

admiral-crowe.title: Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa
admiral-crowe.summary: Amir of Bahrain from 1961 until his death in 1999; per John Kiriakou, who was posted to Bahrain 1994–1996, a short, "roly poly," sweet-natured ruler who kept an open beach palace for Westerners, disliked Jordan's King Hussein, and was heartbroken by the Columbine shooting even as he privately could not grasp why he should extend more support to his own Shia majority.

admiral-crowe.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
admiral-crowe.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

admiral-crowe.title: Hawala system
admiral-crowe.summary: Informal, ledger-based money-transfer network used across the Middle East, South Asia, and their diasporas to move funds without involving banks; per John Kiriakou's first-person account of testing one in the UAE — handing $50 to a grocer for a 16-digit number to redeem at an Arabic bakery in Bethesda, Maryland — completely untraceable; identified by Kiriakou (later, as Chief Investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee) as one of the principal channels through which al-Qaeda moved operational money in the post-9/11 period, along with DHL.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Espionage Act
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: The Department of Education SWAT raid
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a pre-dawn armed raid on the home of a Washington Times journalist and her husband, an official at the Department of Education — carried out, he says, by the Department of Education's own armed SWAT team, which seized the reporter's notes and refused to return them. He uses the episode to point out that several civilian federal departments maintain armed tactical units, and that no other journalist covered it.

admit-nothing-deny-everything.title: Lenín Moreno
admit-nothing-deny-everything.summary: President of Ecuador during the final year of Julian Assange's asylum in the country's London embassy. John Kiriakou, speaking four days before Assange's removal, called Moreno a two-faced traitor who was trading Assange for American money, tariffs and debt relief, and dismissed the INA Papers accusations against Assange as factually untrue.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Beef jerky anomaly in the Epstein files
adnan-khashoggi.summary: A pattern John Kiriakou has flagged in the released Epstein correspondence: on the order of 1,300 to 1,500 emails discuss beef jerky — making it, teaching others to make it, freezing and storing it — and none discuss eating it. Kiriakou treats it as an unexplained code and declines to speculate about what it stands for.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Gerald Bull
adnan-khashoggi.summary: British inventor of the "big gun" — a barrel so large it had to be leaned against a mountain — first offered to Israel and rejected, then sold to Iraq under Saddam Hussein; assassinated by Mossad in Brussels once Iraqi engineers solved the cracking problem with a barrel-smoothing sleeve nicknamed "the condom," after which the Israelis also bombed the gun itself.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Population decline as a national-security question
adnan-khashoggi.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that demographic collapse — an emigrated Greek middle class, a shrinking Russia, and a Chinese population he believes is far smaller than claimed — is a strategic variable rather than a social one, and that some countries may not remain viable as countries without large population changes.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Prison pedophile accounts
adnan-khashoggi.summary: John Kiriakou's account of encountering convicted pedophiles for the first time in federal prison, drawing on advice from a psychiatrist friend and his own work running the chapel library — one of only two safe spaces in prison for inmates convicted of child sex crimes.

adnan-khashoggi.title: Roy Cohn
adnan-khashoggi.summary: Closeted McCarthy-era prosecutor and fixer, later a mentor, advisor and attorney to Donald Trump from the 1970s onward; per John Kiriakou, one of the darkest, ugliest figures in modern American history, who — while closely allied with a similarly closeted J. Edgar Hoover — was central to ruining the lives of gay men, and who died of AIDS in the 1980s alone and unloved.

adnan-khashoggi.title: The "Soylent Green is people" cable easter egg
adnan-khashoggi.summary: A long-running CIA case-officer in-joke in which the line "Soylent Green is people" is hidden inside classified operational cables as a sequence of incongruously lowercase letters

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The bomb course
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The week-long CIA explosives course at a facility in another state, where John Kiriakou learned to build a Molotov cocktail, then a detonator rig, then an ammonium nitrate bomb — his final exam, which put a van's transmission three hundred yards into the woods.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: Counterterrorist driving
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The Farm
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: Kiriakou's titanium knee
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The injury John Kiriakou took crashing a junkyard car through a roadblock in CIA training — his seat tore free of the floor and his knees hit the dashboard — which sixteen years later was diagnosed as spontaneous osteonecrosis and cost him the joint.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The operations course graduation
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.title: The operational cable
advanced-counterterrorism-operations-cou.summary: The written product of every CIA field meeting — drafted the same day, printed and handed to the instructors at the Farm, who critiqued the prose, the conduct of the meeting and what the officer had been wearing.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: CIA Training Doctrine
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: ''Our job is to break the law'' — Kiriakou on what CIA training actually teaches, why it applies only overseas, and the ethics class that never comes.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Mort Halperin
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Counterterrorism Center deaths in the line of duty
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: The colleagues John Kiriakou names as having been killed doing the work he did — Helge Boes and Mike Spann of the Counterterrorism Center, and the officer who sat beside him when he was chief of the counterintelligence branch of the Osama bin Laden group, killed with six colleagues by a suicide bomber in Afghanistan. He pairs the physical risk with a second cost he states as near-certain: that a marriage will not survive an operational tour.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Expanding the definition of terrorism
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: John Kiriakou's objection to the widening of the U.S. terrorism designation beyond groups that use violence for political ends — covering the addition of organisations loosely associated with Antifa, which he argues is not a group at all, and the designation of Latin American narco organisations, which he says should be answered with criminal charges rather than drone strikes.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: The TikTok fan edits
advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: The short-form videos made by a University of Texas sophomore, giving John Kiriakou a chipmunk voice and laser eyes, which reached Gen Z at scale and led within weeks to representation by a major talent agency and meetings about film and television.

advanced-counterterrorism-operations.title: Trump cartel terrorist designation
