advanced-counterterrorism-operations.summary: Donald Trump's early second-term State Department designation of drug cartels as terrorist organizations, which John Kiriakou says was understood at the time mainly as a paperwork exercise to free up agencies like the NSA and DIA to spend money on intercepting communications and training foreign nationals — but which Kiriakou says Trump has since treated as license to attack any vessel he personally deems cartel-linked.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: The death of investigative journalism
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the collapse of investigative reporting inside the American mainstream press — Joby Warrick's resignation from the *Washington Post*, the paper that brought down a president, and the 80 per cent of its staff Kiriakou says have gone since Jeff Bezos bought it — together with the outlets he says are doing the work instead, and his advice to a student who wants to do it anyway.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Kent State shooting
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: 2026 Iran war
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Kiriakou's 2026 viral wave
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: The sudden surge in John Kiriakou''s public recognition in the spring of 2026 — five hundred selfies in three and a half hours in Dublin, a documentary shoot in Berlin interrupted thirty-five times, strangers stopping him in Poland who spoke no English — which he attributes to an algorithm he does not understand and an audience he had not expected: men between fifteen and thirty.

advice-to-the-next-generation.title: Small-country intelligence services
advice-to-the-next-generation.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of dealing with the intelligence services of very small states — Djibouti, whose entire service he says occupied less space than his rented townhouse, and whose director''s office was half the size of his living room. His operating rule is that respect is the whole of the tradecraft: address the director as Your Excellency, and doors open that money cannot.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Fentanyl and China
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China declines to stop the flow of fentanyl into the United States for the same reason he says the United States tolerated Afghan heroin reaching Iran and Russia — because an addicted society is a weaker one. He distinguishes Chinese-made illicit fentanyl, largely produced in Mexico, from the medical fentanyl that created the addiction pathway.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Christopher Steele dossier
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: The 2016 opposition-research dossier alleging Trump-Russia ties, compiled by former MI6 officer Christopher Steele. Per John Kiriakou, who worked directly with Steele on an MI6 operation in London in the 1990s, Steele was so respected at MI6 that other officers wanted to be like him — a reputation Kiriakou says the dossier episode reduced to caricature, because in private practice there was no team of analysts to vet the raw intelligence before it reached the Clinton campaign.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Haqqani White House meeting
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: A mid-to-late-1980s White House meeting between President Ronald Reagan and a Taliban delegation, per John Kiriakou — a former boss of his served as translator. One member of that delegation, a man named Haqqani, went on to found the Haqqani network, later responsible for the capture of Bowe Bergdahl and the kidnapping, rape, and torture of a Canadian couple.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Kiki Camarena case
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: 1985 abduction and murder of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena in Mexico; cited by John Kiriakou as the trigger for the 1985 U.S. statute authorizing the extraterritorial seizure of foreign nationals — the legal authority underpinning the 2026 U.S. operation that seized President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Sergey Lavrov
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat at the UN — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador in the building despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts.

afghan-heroin-policy.title: Soviet Union
afghan-heroin-policy.summary: The superpower whose collapse framed the start of John Kiriakou's CIA career — it was "literally in the process of collapsing" when he joined in January 1990, ushering in a brief "peace dividend" era when the agency's new threats were environmental degradation and AIDS. Kiriakou cites Brzezinski's "Afghan trap" that lured the Soviets into Afghanistan, argues the U.S. abandoned the radicalized mujahideen the moment the Soviets were beaten, notes America then took "a vacation from history," and recalls that Jonathan Pollard's stolen documents were traded by Israel to the Soviets in exchange for Russian Jews.

afghan-languages.title: Edward Snowden
afghan-languages.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

afghan-languages.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
afghan-languages.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

afghan-languages.title: Fort Gordon
afghan-languages.summary: The U.S. Army installation in Georgia where NSA whistleblower Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, worked as a contractor linguist before her arrest.

afghan-languages.title: Government Accountability Project
afghan-languages.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

afghan-languages.title: Miranda Rights
afghan-languages.summary: Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, says she was never read her Miranda rights during her 2017 arrest by the FBI.

afghan-languages.title: Terry Aubry
afghan-languages.summary: Named by Kiriakou both as an FBI whistleblower who exposed racism at the bureau and as one of two Intercept journalists who sent him to prison.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: The Afghan police tribal rotation
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: The Taliban truck escort origin
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Taliban began: as a Pakistani government scheme under Benazir Bhutto to take madrasa students — talib, plural taliban — out of the religious schools and put them with Kalashnikovs aboard Pakistani trucks crossing Afghanistan to Iran, to stop mujahideen fighters from pirating the cargo.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: The Hazara leader's judo belts
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou describes from Afghanistan in about 2007: a very senior Hazara leader displayed every judo belt he had ever earned, white through black, in a large shadow box on his living room wall — and explained that he had gone to fifth dan not for sport but because Hazaras were forbidden to own weapons and he needed some way to protect himself.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: Afghan rare earth minerals
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, made days after the fall of Kabul in August 2021, that the country with real leverage in Afghanistan was China — which holds an exclusive contract to mine rare earth metals valued in a Defense Department report at one trillion dollars, and therefore has a stake in a stable long-term Afghan government even a Taliban one.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: Chinese overseas police stations
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a New York Times revelation about Chinese nationals with apparent ties to the Chinese police operating out of storefronts around Manhattan and travelling around the United States to threaten Chinese people with reprisals against relatives in Beijing — and his puzzlement that the FBI missed it.

afghan-national-police-poisoning.title: Kiriakou's speaking tours
afghan-national-police-poisoning.summary: The lecture circuit John Kiriakou described in December 2025: a tour of England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland and Northern Ireland in January and February of that year, and a nationwide American tour due to begin the following February — one strand of a workload he said he was not sure he could keep up.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.title: The Hazara leader's judo belts
afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou describes from Afghanistan in about 2007: a very senior Hazara leader displayed every judo belt he had ever earned, white through black, in a large shadow box on his living room wall — and explained that he had gone to fifth dan not for sport but because Hazaras were forbidden to own weapons and he needed some way to protect himself.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Taliban began: as a Pakistani government scheme under Benazir Bhutto to take madrasa students — talib, plural taliban — out of the religious schools and put them with Kalashnikovs aboard Pakistani trucks crossing Afghanistan to Iran, to stop mujahideen fighters from pirating the cargo.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, made days after the fall of Kabul in August 2021, that the country with real leverage in Afghanistan was China — which holds an exclusive contract to mine rare earth metals valued in a Defense Department report at one trillion dollars, and therefore has a stake in a stable long-term Afghan government even a Taliban one.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.title: Renting Afghan warlords
afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

afghan-police-tribal-rotation.title: Kiriakou's speaking tours
afghan-police-tribal-rotation.summary: The lecture circuit John Kiriakou described in December 2025: a tour of England, Wales, Scotland, Ireland and Northern Ireland in January and February of that year, and a nationwide American tour due to begin the following February — one strand of a workload he said he was not sure he could keep up.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.title: The Taliban truck escort origin
afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Taliban began: as a Pakistani government scheme under Benazir Bhutto to take madrasa students — talib, plural taliban — out of the religious schools and put them with Kalashnikovs aboard Pakistani trucks crossing Afghanistan to Iran, to stop mujahideen fighters from pirating the cargo.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou describes from Afghanistan in about 2007: a very senior Hazara leader displayed every judo belt he had ever earned, white through black, in a large shadow box on his living room wall — and explained that he had gone to fifth dan not for sport but because Hazaras were forbidden to own weapons and he needed some way to protect himself.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.title: Afghan heroin policy
afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

afghan-rare-earth-minerals.title: China's base in Djibouti
afghan-rare-earth-minerals.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

afghan-war-logs.title: Collateral Murder Video
afghan-war-logs.summary: The 2010 WikiLeaks release of gun-camera footage from a 2007 U.S. Apache helicopter attack in Baghdad; part of the trove of Iraq and Afghan war logs, Guantanamo files, and State Department cables leaked by Chelsea Manning, which John Kiriakou credits with corroborating major abuses and helping to touch off the Arab Spring.

afghan-war-logs.title: Ethan Mccord Collateral Murder
afghan-war-logs.summary: The US soldier who carried wounded children out of the street in the Collateral Murder video released by WikiLeaks.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Abu Omar rendition
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: CIA/FBI Budget Fearmongering
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the FBI, under J. Edgar Hoover, pioneered the tactic of citing a shifting parade of enemies before Congress to justify annual budget increases — communists, anarchists, gangsters, beatniks, anti-war protesters — a tactic the CIA later adopted wholesale, citing "communism" until 2001 and "terrorism" since, without needing further explanation to win budget increases.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Dick Cheney
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: The Directorate of Operations
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.title: Espionage Act
afghanistan-2011-kerry-trip.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

agent-inducements.title: Agent payment mechanics
agent-inducements.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

agent-inducements.title: Asset acquisition cycle
agent-inducements.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

agent-inducements.title: CIA cash room
agent-inducements.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

agent-inducements.title: The polygraph
agent-inducements.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

agent-inducements.title: Renting Afghan warlords
agent-inducements.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

agent-inducements.title: Scholar-in-Residence program
agent-inducements.summary: The current CIA recruitment program, in operation as of the late 2020s, under which the agency places retiring senior officers as 'CIA Scholar in Residence' professors at major American universities. Per John Kiriakou, the program serves as the agency's principal university-recruitment channel since the 1993 Equal Employment Opportunity Act forbade the older practice of having professors covertly recruit students into the CIA. Officers identified as scholars in residence are openly disclosed; the recruitment work continues, just no longer in secret.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: Agent inducements
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: The non-cash things the CIA can offer a recruited agent — a child's university place anywhere in America, treatment at a top hospital for a sick spouse, or a carefully staged personal gift — and the standing arrangements with universities and large corporations that make them possible.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: "He''s been ours since the ''70s"
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: An episode John Kiriakou uses to convey the scale of CIA penetration of foreign political classes: spotting a former prime minister at a diplomatic cocktail party, rushing back to the embassy to file for a name trace and vulnerability assessment before anyone else could approach him, and receiving a same-day instruction to cease and desist because the man had already been an agency asset for decades.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: Kiriakou's volunteer trip to Guatemala
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to Guatemala to volunteer for a couple of weeks at an orphanage, which he recounts as the closing evidence in his argument about the 1954 coup: the orphanage was ringed by a twenty-foot concrete wall, and he could barely sleep for the gunfire outside.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: The SIGINT–HUMINT balance
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to what he calls the most important question facing any incoming CIA director: how to divide investment between signals intelligence and human intelligence. His position is that signals collection cannot supply the one thing policy requires — a person in the room when a decision is taken — and that every new director says so on arrival and then drifts back toward the technology.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: The four-question torture exam
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: A final examination set by a former CIA officer teaching alongside John Kiriakou at Liberty University, consisting of four escalating questions about whether the student would torture — the terrorist, then his wife in front of him, then their children — with the last question asking the student to justify the previous three answers to God. Kiriakou describes it as the most powerful exam he has ever seen.

agent-payment-mechanics.title: Liberty University
agent-payment-mechanics.summary: Evangelical university in Lynchburg, Virginia — the largest in the world — where John Kiriakou taught for several years as an adjunct professor of intelligence studies in the Jesse Helms School of Government. He says he warned the school he disagreed with it on 95% of the issues and was hired anyway, on the dean's reasoning that "torture's not Christian"; he enjoyed the post while clashing constantly with the institution over the treatment of Middle Eastern Christians.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: CovertAction Magazine
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: The muckraking outlet "exposing covert action since 1978" — and one of John Kiriakou's three long-running syndicated column homes, alongside Consortium News and ScheerPost. Kiriakou joined its podcast arm, the CovertAction Bulletin, appearing on panels with Peter Dale Scott and Pepe Escobar, and jokes that the Pentagon's browser-plugin credibility warnings — red check marks against outlets like CovertAction — are the surest sign it's worth reading.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Hamilton 68
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: A company founded by former CIA, FBI, NSA and Director of National Intelligence officials that rates news sites as reliable or unreliable, contracting mainly with the Pentagon to flag articles on government computers with green or red check marks; John Kiriakou says it threatened Consortium News with a "Kremlin apologist" red-check designation, after which PayPal permanently suspended the outlet's account and confiscated its funds.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Jack Murphy NATO Sabotage Story
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a story reported by podcaster Jack Murphy — over a year in the making, drawing on CIA and Army intelligence sources — alleging the CIA worked through a NATO partner to conduct sabotage inside Russia, including munitions-warehouse fires and rail explosions; killed before publication after the CIA deputy director denied it on a call with the editor and blamed "rogue Ukrainians."

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Pan Quake
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: An open-source, nonprofit, carbon-neutral social media platform based in Iceland and powered by geothermal energy, incorporated with lawyers in Luxembourg; John Kiriakou was asked to serve as a brand ambassador before its Icelandic bank account was frozen at the FBI's request over the platform's association with Julian Assange supporters.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: Remains of the Day Treasury Clerk Story
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of an obscure Treasury Department clerk who, during the 1814 British burning of Washington, rescued the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Washington's military commission from the National Archives — and who, after later being deemed too difficult, was quietly transferred to the National Lighthouse Service, where out of boredom he invented the refractor light still used in American lighthouses today.

agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.title: U.S. foreign policy process
agnes-von-kurowsky-grave-story.summary: Three foreign-policy observations from John Kiriakou — the narrow legal basis for U.S. military presence abroad, which he says does not cover American special forces in Syria; the formal congressional travel-clearance process that undercuts Pentagon and White House claims of no advance knowledge of Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan trip; and the depth of U.S.-China economic interdependence that Kiriakou says makes antagonizing Beijing strategically unwise.

ahmed-chalabi.title: NewsGuard
ahmed-chalabi.summary: A media-rating organization, founded by the former head of Court TV and a former Wall Street Journal publisher, that scores news outlets 0-100 for reliability. Per John Kiriakou, NewsGuard docks any outlet that takes a position on Ukraine or Syria contrary to its preferred line, is subscribed to mostly by government entities (chiefly the Pentagon), and singled out Consortium News, the Grayzone, Antiwar.com, and ScheerPost over their criticism of U.S. policy — prompting a First Amendment lawsuit.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Patrick Bet-David
ahmed-chalabi.summary: The podcast host whom John Kiriakou described on another programme as a hardcore Zionist and a total backer of Reza Pahlavi, and who then played the clip back to him on air. Kiriakou withdrew the characterisation on the record, one of the few occasions where he has retracted a public statement about a named individual.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Yellowcake Niger forgery
ahmed-chalabi.summary: The fabricated intelligence document claiming Iraq had attempted to buy yellowcake uranium from Niger; passed to the U.S. via the British (originally from the Italians); identified by CIA analysts including John Kiriakou as a forgery on sight ("it's not even in the right font"); pulled from President George W. Bush's State of the Union draft by Colin Powell; reinserted by Vice President Dick Cheney; pulled out by the CIA again; delivered in the 2003 State of the Union address anyway.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Laura Loomer
ahmed-chalabi.summary: The American activist who publicly called John Kiriakou a Russian spy, a Russian asset and a common criminal. Kiriakou consulted a lawyer as he had over an earlier attack, was advised that she carried too little weight to be worth suing, and let it go; he reads her later reversal on Russia and Ukraine as the calculation of someone who has accepted she will never be given a government job.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Leadership profiling
ahmed-chalabi.summary: The CIA practice of producing classified psychological profiles of foreign leaders for the president, vice president, national security advisor and the secretaries of state and defense before any meeting. It was John Kiriakou's first job at the agency, where he served as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological biographer working alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and anthropologists.

ahmed-chalabi.title: Louise Mensch
ahmed-chalabi.summary: The former British parliamentarian who attacked John Kiriakou on social media, prompting the only defamation action he describes having threatened. On his lawyer's advice he demanded a retraction; Mensch retracted in full and kept a pinned apology on her account for six months.

ahmed-khatib.title: George Habash
ahmed-khatib.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

ahmed-khatib.title: PFLP
ahmed-khatib.summary: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; Palestinian armed group co-founded by George Habash and Ahmed Khatib, college roommates at the American University of Beirut. It is one of the Arab organizations John Kiriakou worked against during his Athens tour, where a semi-secret 1980s deal let the Arab groups transit Greece unmolested so long as they did not kill Greeks. Kiriakou's chance paper on Khatib made him the White House expert on the occupation governor of Kuwait in August 1990, and two of the Front's retired cadres later sat across a table from him in Jordan for a Sacha Baron Cohen shoot.

ahmed-khatib.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
ahmed-khatib.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

ahmed-khatib.title: Saddam Hussein
ahmed-khatib.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

ahmed-khatib.title: Central Intelligence Agency
ahmed-khatib.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

ahmed-khatib.title: Kuwait Liberation Day
ahmed-khatib.summary: February 1991 expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait by the U.S.-led coalition; John Kiriakou entered the country with U.S. Marines on the day of liberation; the small American flags waved by the crowds — and the post-liberation arrival of Democratic and Republican National Committee personnel ostensibly to assist the country's transition to democracy — were, per Kiriakou, the work of professional propagandist John Rendon.

ai-weiwei.title: Andres Serrano
ai-weiwei.summary: American artist; in the 1980s the creator of Piss Christ — a beaker of urine containing an inverted crucifix — which so enraged President Ronald Reagan that he cut off funding to the National Endowment for the Arts. Per John Kiriakou, also the photographer of a torture-chamber series at Tate Modern, London, in which one panel is a photograph of Kiriakou next to a panel of a U.S. military torturer.

ai-weiwei.title: Afghan heroin policy
ai-weiwei.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

ai-weiwei.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
ai-weiwei.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

ai-weiwei.title: Brian Kelley
ai-weiwei.summary: Chief of counterintelligence at the CIA; framed by FBI counterintelligence chief Robert Hanssen — the actual Soviet/Russian mole — as the source of executed agents; spent a year and a half on leave without pay, surrounded around the clock by FBI agents, while his daughter was approached and told her father would face the death penalty if he did not confess.

ai-weiwei.title: Cuban double agents
ai-weiwei.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

ai-weiwei.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
ai-weiwei.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Plus 972
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: The Israeli platform that, per a 2026 Berlin panel, has published a striking number of IDF whistleblowers as AI enters modern warfare.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: US Military Venture Capital
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the U.S. military now purchases technology using a venture-capital investment model, a shift he cites as a warning sign about how national-security institutions acquire emerging tech.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Der Spiegel
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Ethan Mccord Collateral Murder
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: The US soldier who carried wounded children out of the street in the Collateral Murder video released by WikiLeaks.

ai-whistleblower-initiative.title: Meredith Whittaker
ai-whistleblower-initiative.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Meredith Whittaker is developing a new, and by his account successful, business model for the encrypted-messaging app Signal, an alternative he cites alongside ProtonMail's compromised attempt at the same thing.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Thomas Massie
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: AIPAC
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Israeli integration into U.S. agencies
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the formal embedding of Israeli personnel inside American defense and intelligence institutions — a National Defense Authorization Act provision collocating them with the Pentagon and opening Five Eyes-style liaison with the CIA, arriving in the same weeks as a DIA all-hands warning that Israeli services were unusually aggressive in recruiting inside DIA. His argument is that the two cannot both be true: either Israel is a critical counterintelligence threat or it is a partner.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Yalta conference
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: The February 1945 Allied conference, which John Kiriakou uses as his teaching example of what a well-placed spy is worth: Stalin, told by a source inside the White House that Roosevelt was ill, insisted on a venue requiring a punishing multi-leg journey, then refused to delay the talks — and an exhausted Roosevelt, Kiriakou says, conceded Poland in order to go to bed.

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Cori Bush
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: Former U.S. Representative from St. Louis (Missouri's 1st congressional district); cited by John Kiriakou as one of the two named cases of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent for delivering a House floor speech describing the Gaza war as a "wholesale massacre of Palestinian civilians."

aipac-foreign-agent-registration.title: Jamaal Bowman
aipac-foreign-agent-registration.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

aipac.title: Alec Baldwin
aipac.summary: Actor with whom John Kiriakou recounts a bitter falling-out — Baldwin calling him a liar over lunch at a meeting about a play in which Baldwin was to play him, later attaching to a Kiriakou TV pitch that AMC bought the next day, then quitting for HBO and killing the deal without a word.

aipac.title: Alex Padilla
aipac.summary: U.S. Senator from California who was forced to the ground and handcuffed at a June 2025 press event after identifying himself as a sitting senator; per John Kiriakou, DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's claim that he failed to identify himself was false, and the White House's stated interest in prosecuting him was legally baseless because sitting senators have congressional immunity while acting in the course of their duties.

aipac.title: Glenn-Symington Act
aipac.summary: U.S. federal statute, co-authored by Senators John Glenn and Stuart Symington, that prohibits the U.S. government from providing foreign aid of any kind to any country possessing a nuclear weapons program that has not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty; per John Kiriakou, Israel is the only country in the world meeting both criteria, making the law the principal reason the U.S. government officially declines to acknowledge the Israeli nuclear program.

aipac.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
aipac.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

aipac.title: Kiriakou on wine
aipac.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing interest in wine — a subscription to Wine Spectator running a quarter of a century, a climate-controlled cellar built into his house, and an eye that has twice caught a host passing off a cheap bottle as something better.

aipac.title: Myanmar's civil war, per Kiriakou
aipac.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Myanmar as the only country in the world continuously at war without a single day of peace since World War II, its Buddhist-majority persecution of Muslims, Christians, and Hindus, his view that Aung San Suu Kyi should have her Nobel Peace Prize stripped, and his argument that the world ignores the country's atrocities because it has gems rather than oil.

air-india-flight-182.title: Muslim Brotherhood terrorist designation
air-india-flight-182.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the designation of the Muslim Brotherhood, or elements of it, as a terrorist organisation: that the group is more than a century old, has never carried out an anti-American terrorist operation, and had never been so designated by any previous administration. He distinguishes fundamentalism and hostility from terrorism.

air-india-flight-182.title: Islamofascism
air-india-flight-182.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: British Bases in Cyprus
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: British sovereign bases cover 3% of Cyprus. Kiriakou, a quarter Cypriot, on the 46-year US weapons embargo almost no American knows about.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: Aldrich Ames
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: Bojinka plot
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: 1996 Khalid Sheikh Mohammed–planned operation, prepared in a Manila, Philippines apartment, to hijack as many as fourteen Boeing 747s and crash them into buildings along the U.S. West Coast; disrupted only by accident, when a cleaning lady let herself into the apartment while the planner was out, recognized the materials laid out as a terrorist plot, and called the police — who alerted Filipino intelligence and, in turn, the CIA. The plot's architect was known to U.S. intelligence for the next six years only by the alias "Mukhtar," his true identity as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed surfacing only when Abu Zubaydah named him to FBI agent Ali Soufan in 2002.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: Founding of the CIA (1947)
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's creation under the National Security Act of 1947 — built with British MI6 help after a chaotic 1945-47 interregnum, and opposed by J. Edgar Hoover until Truman falsely promised him the new agency would be part of the FBI.

akrotiri-village-evacuation.title: Cofer Black
akrotiri-village-evacuation.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

al-julani.title: ISIS
al-julani.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

al-julani.title: Barbara Leaf
al-julani.summary: American diplomat, assistant secretary of state for the Near East, and — in John Kiriakou's description — an old friend of his. He cites her trip to Damascus, made within days of al-Julani taking power and alongside the special envoy for hostage affairs, as the moment American recognition was traded for the lifting of the ten-million-dollar bounty on the new Syrian leader.

al-julani.title: Osama bin Laden
al-julani.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

al-julani.title: Origins of al-Qaeda
al-julani.summary: John Kiriakou''s position on where al-Qaeda came from: bad American foreign policy decisions led to it indirectly, but not by design. He rejects the deliberate-creation theory on the grounds that it is unnecessary — a state willing to kill does not need to manufacture a pretext first.

al-julani.title: Syria as a regime-change template
al-julani.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the fall of Bashar al-Assad shows organic regime change is faster, cheaper and less destructive than the enforced kind — and should be studied as a model. He allows aid to local forces as legitimate policy, and notes without prompting that in Syria the CIA was supplying al-Qaeda while the Pentagon supplied a group at war with it.

al-julani.title: Kashmir
al-julani.summary: The disputed territory John Kiriakou says is front and centre for every Pakistani and largely absent from Indian minds, and on which his own sympathies lie with Pakistan — a promised 1940s referendum that never happened. He also describes the appearance that ended his participation in South Asian media: an Indian programme cut his pro-Pakistani answer, aired only his prediction that India would win a conventional war, and the death threats resumed.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Foreign aid
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy of a hundredfold increase in the American foreign-aid budget — a position he concedes puts him in "a very minuscule minority" — argued on the grounds that every dollar spent saves five or ten in refugee crises, civil wars and attacks on the United States, and that development is the only thing that empties terrorist recruiting pools. His counter-example is the Sana'a water-treatment plant, built by the European Union and rendered pointless by American and Saudi politics.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Agent payment mechanics
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Ali Soufan
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Brian Ross
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Counterterrorism Center
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.title: Renting Afghan warlords
al-qaeda-foot-soldier-profile.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

al-qaeda-software.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
al-qaeda-software.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

al-qaeda-software.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
al-qaeda-software.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

al-qaeda-software.title: Mitchell and Jessen
al-qaeda-software.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

al-qaeda-software.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
al-qaeda-software.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

al-qaeda-software.title: Zawahiri assassination
al-qaeda-software.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the drone strike that killed al-Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri — using a bladed, warhead-less missile fired as he stepped onto a balcony to smoke, deliberately chosen to avoid killing the women and children inside.

al-qaeda-software.title: The Analysis Corporation
al-qaeda-software.summary: Arlington, Virginia–based [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence); one of two companion entities (alongside Arrais Corporation) created as LLC pass-throughs for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel; John Brennan was appointed its CEO in 2005.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: China's base in Djibouti
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Irish intelligence services
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: Ireland's intelligence and law-enforcement services, which John Kiriakou toured and met with during a speaking trip to Belfast, Cork, Dublin, and Waterford. Per Kiriakou, Irish intelligence and the Garda are especially strong at anti-money-laundering investigation and counterterrorism — the latter traced, he says, to the large number of Irish militants trained by Carlos the Jackal in Libya and Lebanon during the 1970s.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Kent State shooting
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Strait of Hormuz transit fees
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's proposal to charge ships up to $2 million to transit the Strait of Hormuz, payable in yuan rather than dollars, and of the U.S. Navy's subsequent announcement that it had taken control of the strait and closed it — reversing decades of U.S. policy that the strait must remain open.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Kiriakou's 2026 viral wave
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: The sudden surge in John Kiriakou''s public recognition in the spring of 2026 — five hundred selfies in three and a half hours in Dublin, a documentary shoot in Berlin interrupted thirty-five times, strangers stopping him in Poland who spoke no English — which he attributes to an algorithm he does not understand and an audience he had not expected: men between fifteen and thirty.

al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.title: Small-country intelligence services
al-qaeda-training-manual-interrogation-t.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of dealing with the intelligence services of very small states — Djibouti, whose entire service he says occupied less space than his rented townhouse, and whose director''s office was half the size of his living room. His operating rule is that respect is the whole of the tradecraft: address the director as Your Excellency, and doors open that money cannot.

alan-dershowitz.title: Peter Mandelson
alan-dershowitz.summary: British politician; described by John Kiriakou as the former British ambassador to Washington and as someone likely to be charged with serious crimes in connection with Jeffrey Epstein.

alan-dershowitz.title: Les Wexner
alan-dershowitz.summary: Ohio billionaire retail magnate; John Kiriakou cites Vanity Fair allegations that Wexner funneled millions to Jeffrey Epstein as his 'tax advisor,' offering it as evidence for his own view that Epstein's money and access served the Israelis.

alan-dershowitz.title: Kiriakou prison manipulation tactics
alan-dershowitz.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying CIA tradecraft — including deliberate deception, forged paperwork, and manipulating other inmates into violence — to protect himself and control his environment during his federal prison sentence.

alan-dershowitz.title: Ross Ulbricht
alan-dershowitz.summary: Founder of the online marketplace Silk Road, sentenced to life plus 75 years before being pardoned by President Trump; John Kiriakou met Ulbricht's mother and sister two weeks before the pardon and calls the length of the original sentence a sickening miscarriage of justice.

alan-dershowitz.title: Abraham Bolden
alan-dershowitz.summary: The first African-American Secret Service agent assigned to a presidential detail; per John Kiriakou, he quite literally saved John F. Kennedy's life in Chicago in October 1963 and was subjected to overt racism by fellow agents, who told him to his face they would not protect Kennedy from assassination because of his civil-rights sympathies.

alan-dershowitz.title: Rhodes Jewish deportation and family rescue story
alan-dershowitz.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1944 Nazi roundup and deportation of roughly 2,000 Jewish residents of the island of Rhodes to Auschwitz, of whom only 14 survived — and of his own great-grandfather, a chauffeur, hiding his Jewish employer from the Nazis until the war's end.

albert-stubblebine.title: Lynn Buchanan
albert-stubblebine.summary: A Fort Meade-trained Army intelligence veteran of the CIA and NSA remote-viewing programs — a primary source, Kiriakou says, not a TV psychic.

albert-stubblebine.title: Russell Targ
albert-stubblebine.summary: Named in a post-produced narration segment appended to an interview featuring John Kiriakou, describing Targ as an original Stanford Research Institute scientist behind government remote-viewing protocols — not a claim made by Kiriakou himself, who elsewhere expresses skepticism that remote viewing ever worked.

albert-stubblebine.title: Project Stargate
albert-stubblebine.summary: The CIA's remote-viewing program, which Kiriakou says burned millions for decades and failed — and which he understands is being revisited.

albert-stubblebine.title: Bay Path University
albert-stubblebine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he teaches in the graduate intelligence-studies program at Bay Path University in Massachusetts, covering introduction to intelligence, the history of terrorism, and intelligence and cybersecurity.

albert-stubblebine.title: Sweat Lodge
albert-stubblebine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the federal prison where he was incarcerated had a Native American sweat lodge that was shut down after it was misused for sex rather than religious ceremony; he says he has never personally been in a sweat lodge.

albert-stubblebine.title: Mark Zuckerberg–Angela Merkel Meeting
albert-stubblebine.summary: Kiriakou on Zuckerberg flying to Berlin to help Chancellor Merkel define hate speech — and why he objects to that call being Zuckerberg's.

aldrich-ames.title: James Woolsey
aldrich-ames.summary: Director of Central Intelligence for twenty-three months at the start of the Clinton administration, forced out over his refusal to discipline anyone after the exposure of Aldrich Ames, and later chairman of Booz Allen Hamilton; John Kiriakou notes that his family attributed four years of illness before his death to Havana syndrome.

aldrich-ames.title: Jennings Randolph
aldrich-ames.summary: Longtime U.S. Senator from West Virginia who, in a phone call John Kiriakou made to thank him as a college student, gave him the advice he says shaped his life: always do the right thing, not the expedient one.

aldrich-ames.title: Sandy Grimes
aldrich-ames.summary: CIA analyst who, per John Kiriakou, was the person who actually broke the Aldrich Ames case. After a 27-year-old security officer sat on an Ames file for eighteen months without action, Grimes independently noticed that Ames made $100,000–$150,000 bank deposits within days of every trip to Mexico City — the pattern that identified him as a spy. After Ames's arrest, she submitted a hot-wash paper recommending 27 reprimands across the chain of command that had promoted a known alcoholic into the most sensitive counterintelligence position in the CIA. Director John Deutch responded with strongly worded letters for seven. Grimes resigned in 1993.

aldrich-ames.title: Steven Lalas
aldrich-ames.summary: American with top-secret clearance recruited as a spy for Greece's National Intelligence Service (EYP) in a provocative mid-1990s operation run by the country's conservative government. Per John Kiriakou, who did not know Lawless personally, the case was so sensitive that his handler reported directly to the EYP director out of fear the CIA had planted a mole inside the service. Lawless was caught, served about seven years, and was given Greek citizenship on release.

aldrich-ames.title: The Russian illegals program
aldrich-ames.summary: The Russian practice, described by John Kiriakou, of recruiting people — sometimes as children — training them abroad and inserting them into Western countries as sleepers who live ordinary lives for decades until they are activated. Kiriakou says a group of illegals was broken up by the FBI in his own Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood and traded for American spies, and that he knows a former KGB sleeper in Brooklyn who refused activation after the birth of his daughter.

aldrich-ames.title: Akrotiri Village Evacuation
aldrich-ames.summary: Kiriakou says the drone that hit Britain's Akrotiri base in Cyprus was likely an Israeli operation, staged and then falsely blamed on Iran.

alec-baldwin.title: Abu Omar rendition
alec-baldwin.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

alec-baldwin.title: AIPAC
alec-baldwin.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

alec-baldwin.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
alec-baldwin.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

alec-baldwin.title: Citizens United
alec-baldwin.summary: The Supreme Court decision John Kiriakou blames for legalizing unlimited corporate political money and for corporations having "taken over" two of the three branches of government — and which he says lets AIPAC pour tens of millions into single congressional races to defeat candidates who cross Israel.

alec-baldwin.title: Havana Syndrome
alec-baldwin.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

alec-baldwin.title: Mitchell and Jessen
alec-baldwin.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

alex-karp.title: In-Q-Tel
alex-karp.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

alex-karp.title: Palantir Technologies
alex-karp.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

alex-karp.title: Peter Thiel
alex-karp.summary: U.S. venture capitalist; co-founder of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group alongside Palantir CEO Alex Karp.

alex-karp.title: Arrais Corporation
alex-karp.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

alex-karp.title: CIA National Resources Division
alex-karp.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

alex-karp.title: Balochistan drone base
alex-karp.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

alex-padilla.title: AIPAC
alex-padilla.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

alex-padilla.title: Donald Trump
alex-padilla.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

alex-padilla.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
alex-padilla.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

alex-padilla.title: Iran 12-Day War
alex-padilla.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

alex-padilla.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
alex-padilla.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

alex-padilla.title: Israel-United States relations
alex-padilla.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

alex-station.title: Ali Mohamed
alex-station.summary: Egyptian-American former U.S. Army sergeant who trained at Fort Bragg while secretly working for Egyptian intelligence, later trained some of the 9/11 hijackers and other al-Qaeda operatives, and was arrested in connection with the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings before disappearing under the George W. Bush administration; John Kiriakou speculates he was actually a double agent working for al-Qaeda — or possibly Israeli intelligence — against his CIA handlers.

alex-station.title: Cofer Black
alex-station.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

alex-station.title: 9/11 attribution of responsibility
alex-station.summary: John Kiriakou's evolving view of who bears ultimate responsibility for the September 11 attacks — that al-Qaeda carried them out but was, in his current view, "allowed" to, amid a distracted Bush administration, an uninvestigated Saudi government, and an Israeli government he believes had a vested interest in the attacks proceeding.

alex-station.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
alex-station.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

alex-station.title: Sandy Berger
alex-station.summary: National Security Adviser under President Bill Clinton; per John Kiriakou, the official who shut down CIA case officer Bob Baer's mid-1990s plan to assassinate Saddam Hussein from northern Iraq, by calling the CIA after an NSA intercept and threatening Baer with a conspiracy charge unless he was recalled.

alex-station.title: Operation Mega
alex-station.summary: A 1997 FBI investigation into a senior U.S. government official believed to be passing highly sensitive information to Israel, opened after the NSA intercepted an Israeli intelligence communication referring to a source code-named "Mega." Per John Kiriakou, unlike similar investigations into other countries, the case never resulted in an indictment or public disclosure, and the identity of the American official was never revealed.

alexa.title: French village LSD bread experiment
alexa.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a compartmented MK-Ultra experiment in which CIA operatives broke into the only bakery of a small French village he does not name and dosed the yeast with LSD, sending the entire village on an unwitting trip.

alexa.title: Brett McGurk
alexa.summary: Senior U.S. diplomat; John Kiriakou cites reporting that McGurk was caught in a sexual encounter atop a U.S. embassy while overseeing the campaign against ISIS, offering it as an example of the adultery culture he considers a security risk.

alexa.title: OnlyFans
alexa.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

alexa.title: Diary of a CEO — January 2026 Kiriakou interview
alexa.summary: The January 2026 long-form appearance by John Kiriakou on Steven Bartlett's Diary of a CEO podcast that a University of Texas at Austin sophomore then cut into TikTok shorts — sped and slowed, with lasers added — kicking off the Gen Z discovery of Kiriakou that pushed his cameo requests past 1,900 and drew a 2:30 a.m. representation call in Dubai from the Creative Artists Agency; Kiriakou treats it as the pivot after which stories he had been telling for nineteen years finally landed.

alexa.title: FBI manufactured terrorism cases
alexa.summary: John Kiriakou's account of terrorism prosecutions in which the FBI supplies the plot, the target, the explosives and the transport, then arrests the person it recruited. His central case is the 2026 Miami trial of a mentally ill homeless man facing six counts each carrying life without parole, in which Kiriakou testified for the defence and told the court that the FBI was "clearly the criminal in this case." The defendant was acquitted on every count.

alexa.title: Kiriakou cameo practice
alexa.summary: John Kiriakou's post-2026 use of the Cameo personalised-video service — running at roughly 25 to 30 hours a week, some 900 messages in the month of March 2026 alone, nearly 2,000 messages in total by July 2026 — that he says has produced three cases in which the person receiving the video message afterwards told him he had talked them out of committing suicide, including a 15-year-old bulimic girl to whom Kiriakou gave his personal phone number.

alexander-acosta.title: David Boies
alexander-acosta.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

alexander-acosta.title: The Epstein statute of limitations
alexander-acosta.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that nobody in the United States will be prosecuted over the Jeffrey Epstein case because the five-year limitation period on the sex offences has run — a lapse he says may itself have been part of the plan, and which leaves only an improbable conspiracy theory of the cover-up as a route to charges.

alexander-acosta.title: Piers Morgan
alexander-acosta.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

alexander-acosta.title: The Trilateral Commission
alexander-acosta.summary: The body John Kiriakou says he used to dismiss as conspiracy-theory material until someone close to him attended one of its meetings and told him what was actually discussed there: arms deals — and at Davos, how to manage the global economy.

alexander-acosta.title: Alan Dershowitz
alexander-acosta.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

alexander-acosta.title: Kiriakou's acting career
alexander-acosta.summary: The film role John Kiriakou took in 2025 after Tyrel Ventura wrote a part for him — a former CIA officer running a billionaire's security detail — which he shot in Mexico for a month and which made him, at sixty-odd, a member of the Screen Actors Guild.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Jennifer Matthews
