alfreda-bikowsky.summary: CIA analyst who was made chief of base at Khost, Afghanistan without operational or security training in order to complete the tour requirement for promotion, and who was killed there with six other officers by a Jordanian double agent she had gone outside the fortified perimeter to greet with a birthday cake.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Mike Scheuer
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: Founder and chief of "Alec Station", the CIA unit dedicated to tracking Osama bin Laden in the years before September 11, 2001; per John Kiriakou — alongside his New York FBI counterpart John O'Neill — "100 percent correct" about bin Laden, and uniformly hated for it inside the agency.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Senior Intelligence Service
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: The CIA's executive rank above the General Schedule, entry to which requires a tour outside an officer's own directorate and a tour in the policy community — a box-checking requirement John Kiriakou identifies as the reason an untrained analyst was sent to run a base in Afghanistan. Its officers are career staff rather than political appointees, some with thirty or forty years in place, which is why Kiriakou describes the service as capable of simply waiting a president out — or slow-rolling him. Its officers in the Counterterrorism Center were also the authors of the torture techniques.

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Forward Operating Base Chapman Attack
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: December 30, 2009 suicide bombing at Forward Operating Base Chapman in Khost, Afghanistan, killing seven CIA officers and wounding more than a dozen others — the deadliest single day in CIA history. Per John Kiriakou, the officer who led the base was a GS-14 with zero security training, assigned to the post as a career-promotion checkbox before her required elevation to the Senior Intelligence Service. The bomber — a Jordanian national who walked into the American consulate in Istanbul claiming to be Osama bin Laden's doctor — was never polygraphed because CIA personnel 'wanted so badly for this to be true.'

alfreda-bikowsky.title: Zawahiri assassination
alfreda-bikowsky.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the drone strike that killed al-Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri — using a bladed, warhead-less missile fired as he stepped onto a balcony to smoke, deliberately chosen to avoid killing the women and children inside.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Houthis
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: The Iran-aligned movement that controls the most important parts of Yemen, described by John Kiriakou as fierce fighters who beat the Saudi military over a decade of war and who in July 2026 declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Yemen
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Bab al-Mandab
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: John Kiriakou
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: Dead Drop (podcast)
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: John Kiriakou''s narrative podcast, launched in late 2025 — a season-long, memoir-style retelling of his life in intelligence, from recruitment ("The New Recruit") through Athens ("Golden Boy") to the post-9/11 hunt ("The Hunt Begins"), with mini-episodes like "A Spy''s Guide to Sofia." Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

ali-abdullah-saleh.title: John Kerry
ali-abdullah-saleh.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Saddam Hussein
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Ahmed Chalabi
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: Uday Hussein
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Eldest son of Saddam Hussein; described by John Kiriakou as so dangerous a successor-in-waiting that Saddam's two sons-in-law — Hussein Kamel and Saddam Kamel — defected to Jordan in January 1993 specifically out of fear of him.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: CIA cable priority levels
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: The five levels of immediacy assigned to U.S. government cable traffic, as described by John Kiriakou. From lowest to highest: Routine, Priority, Immediate, Flash, CRITIC. Most career officers will never see a CRITIC; during the Gulf War, Kiriakou''s desk was receiving multiple CRITICs a day, each one announcing a hostile missile launch.

ali-hassan-al-majid.title: George Habash
ali-hassan-al-majid.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

ali-mohamed.title: Alex Station
ali-mohamed.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

ali-mohamed.title: 9/11 attribution of responsibility
ali-mohamed.summary: John Kiriakou's evolving view of who bears ultimate responsibility for the September 11 attacks — that al-Qaeda carried them out but was, in his current view, "allowed" to, amid a distracted Bush administration, an uninvestigated Saudi government, and an Israeli government he believes had a vested interest in the attacks proceeding.

ali-mohamed.title: Cofer Black
ali-mohamed.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

ali-mohamed.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
ali-mohamed.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

ali-mohamed.title: CIA liaison relationships
ali-mohamed.summary: John Kiriakou's critique of CIA intelligence-liaison relationships with foreign governments — sharply expanded after 9/11 — arguing that officers do not consider the long-term risk that disclosing sensitive operations to foreign services hands those governments leverage, including potential blackmail material, over the United States, and that no one left in Congress has the will to provide real oversight of the practice.

ali-mohamed.title: Mir Aimal Kansi CIA headquarters attack
ali-mohamed.summary: The 1993 shooting outside CIA headquarters by Pakistani gunman Mir Aimal Kansi, who killed two and wounded seven CIA-bound commuters before fleeing to Pakistan; per John Kiriakou, the CIA located Kansi months later but had to hand the arrest to the FBI, and the resulting "how the FBI got their man" Time magazine cover so enraged senior CIA officers that it shaped the agency's insistence on going it alone against al-Qaeda after 9/11.

ali-soufan.title: Abu Zubaydah
ali-soufan.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ali-soufan.title: The cremation footnote
ali-soufan.summary: A footnote John Kiriakou cites from the declassified executive summary of the Senate torture report, stating that Abu Zubaydah will never be permitted to leave Guantanamo — despite never having joined al-Qaeda, never having pledged fealty to Osama bin Laden and never having been charged — and that on his death the CIA will cremate his body and scatter the ashes at sea.

ali-soufan.title: "I''m a non-person"
ali-soufan.summary: The phrase John Kiriakou uses for his standing after prison: a former colleague was sent to deliver congratulations from a mutual friend who had risen to a senior administration post, together with the message that he could never speak to Kiriakou again. Kiriakou pairs it with the loss of his federal pension after nineteen and a half years of service, and with the fact that in eight years no other CIA officer joined him in speaking publicly.

ali-soufan.title: Robert Mueller
ali-soufan.summary: Director of the FBI in the years after September 11, 2001; per John Kiriakou, the official who, upon learning on July 31, 2002 that the CIA had won presidential approval to take primacy over Abu Zubaydah's interrogation away from the FBI's Ali Soufan, withdrew not just FBI personnel from the black site but every FBI employee from the country itself within 48 hours — "we know what these CIA guys are going to do; they're going to go completely nuts; we don't want any part of it."

ali-soufan.title: John O'Neill
ali-soufan.summary: Special Agent in Charge of the FBI's New York field office for counterterrorism; "brash, flawed" but, per John Kiriakou, "spot-on about Osama bin Laden — 100 percent correct." Mentored FBI Arabic translator Ali Soufan. The principal subject of Lawrence Wright's book The Looming Tower.

ali-soufan.title: Martha Kesler
ali-soufan.summary: Long-serving CIA Syria analyst; author of the standard-issue analytical primer "Syria: Fragile Mosaic of Power"; John Brennan''s first supervisor and the figure who first fired him from the agency, before being herself fired by Brennan when their roles inverted under George Tenet''s patronage.

allen-dulles.title: Presidents and the CIA
allen-dulles.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that some presidents actively lead the CIA while others are led around by it — citing George H.W. Bush's ongoing "love affair" with the agency after his 11-month stint as director, and Richard Nixon's close relationship with the CIA, which Kiriakou says was one of the things that brought down his presidency.

allen-dulles.title: Government Purchase of Social Media Metadata
allen-dulles.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the practice by which U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies — including the NSA and FBI — buy bulk user metadata from social media companies such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter), bypassing the warrant requirements that would otherwise apply to direct surveillance. The practice exploits a provision in platform terms of service under which users surrender ownership of their metadata to the company, which may then sell it freely.

allen-dulles.title: James Jesus Angleton
allen-dulles.summary: The CIA counterintelligence chief old-timers were 'genuinely afraid' of — and the wall of illegal files on American citizens kept in his office.

allen-dulles.title: Kiriakou's volunteer trip to Guatemala
allen-dulles.summary: A visit John Kiriakou made to Guatemala to volunteer for a couple of weeks at an orphanage, which he recounts as the closing evidence in his argument about the 1954 coup: the orphanage was ringed by a twenty-foot concrete wall, and he could barely sleep for the gunfire outside.

allen-dulles.title: Ruby Ridge
allen-dulles.summary: 1992 federal standoff in Idaho involving Randy Weaver, triggered by an allegation that Weaver had sold a shotgun with a barrel two inches shorter than the legal minimum; per John Kiriakou, FBI sniper Lon Horiuchi shot and killed Weaver's wife while she was holding her baby, and Horiuchi was never punished. Kiriakou describes Ruby Ridge as one of the events that, after his own imprisonment, caused him to fundamentally reassess his earlier acceptance of the official government account.

allen-dulles.title: The four-question torture exam
allen-dulles.summary: A final examination set by a former CIA officer teaching alongside John Kiriakou at Liberty University, consisting of four escalating questions about whether the student would torture — the terrorist, then his wife in front of him, then their children — with the last question asking the student to justify the previous three answers to God. Kiriakou describes it as the most powerful exam he has ever seen.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: The botched pitch
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: The one operation John Kiriakou describes as a failure of his career: a two-year development of a terrorist working under journalist cover, brought to the point of a recruitment pitch and destroyed at the table when his station chief seized the meeting and threatened the target instead of pitching him. The target fled screaming for police, the host government''s deputy prime minister complained to the American ambassador, and the man later described the encounter to a third intelligence service as an approach by "two caricatures of CIA men."

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Oman
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: The Gulf sultanate John Kiriakou singles out as America's most durable friend in the region and its most useful channel to Iran — a country that has acted as go-between for Washington and Tehran many times, and which he argues should be approached again in place of carrier deployments and public threats.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Sharia law
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: Islamic jurisprudence. Challenged by a viewer who equated it with executions of gay people, forced child marriage and the criminalisation of apostasy, John Kiriakou answers that those acts are largely the work of ISIS rather than of any government, and that Sharia is in substance a body of civil law covering inheritance, insurance, education, property ownership and commercial disputes.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Wealth concentration
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the present distribution of wealth is historically unprecedented and politically unsustainable — that trillionaires have never existed before, that five men hold as much as the bottom eighty per cent of the world, and that a defence budget approaching $1.5 trillion cannot be reconciled with the social spending it would have to displace.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: CIA intelligence failures
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: John Kiriakou's standing position that the CIA has missed every major world event since its founding in 1947 — the building and the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Iran hostage crisis, 9/11 — and that the remedy is therefore not more money but fewer overseas bases and actual accountability, of which he says there has been none.

amaryllis-fox-kennedy.title: Flock cameras
amaryllis-fox-kennedy.summary: Automated licence-plate reading cameras mounted on police vehicles and on poles disguised as utility poles. John Kiriakou describes them as blanket, constant surveillance and a direct assault on civil liberties, more dangerous than the public realises, and says they are the point at which Edward Snowden's predictions have already come true.

american-media-consolidation.title: The CIA and Hollywood
american-media-consolidation.summary: The CIA''s standing arrangement with the film industry, as John Kiriakou describes it: a branch inside the Office of Public Affairs whose only job is to cooperate with Hollywood studios, on the model the FBI has run since the 1950s, so that what comes out of Hollywood carries a pro-agency message. Kiriakou notes it is technically illegal for the CIA to propagandise the American public and says that is exactly what happens every time an agency-linked film is released.

american-media-consolidation.title: CIA media relations
american-media-consolidation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA shapes press coverage in the 2020s without needing an Operation Mockingbird-style infiltration program — because corporate media now recites CIA messaging willingly, most journalists simply rewrite emailed statements from the agency's Office of Public Affairs, and the CIA allegedly manipulates algorithms and backs podcasts to spread its point of view.

american-media-consolidation.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
american-media-consolidation.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

american-media-consolidation.title: Jeffrey Epstein
american-media-consolidation.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

american-media-consolidation.title: John Brennan
american-media-consolidation.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

american-media-consolidation.title: The KGB denial cables
american-media-consolidation.summary: Two occasions on which, according to John Kiriakou, the first message the CIA received after an American killing came from the KGB and said the same thing: we promise it wasn''t us. One followed the assassination of Athens station chief Richard Welch in December 1975, the other the killing of President Kennedy in November 1963. Kiriakou treats them as evidence of a standing gentleman''s agreement between the two services not to touch each other''s people — one he expects to hold even where Russian troops overrun CIA bases.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: The Iron Dome
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: The Pentagon's congressional district strategy
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: The practice John Kiriakou describes of placing defence manufacturing orders in effectively all 435 congressional districts, so that every member of Congress has constituents dependent on the defence budget — and nobody has an incentive to vote against it.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: Trump's need for glorification
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: John Kiriakou''s psychological reading of why the 2026 Iran war happened — that Donald Trump "craves glorification," has pursued it by attaching his name to public landmarks, and concluded that "real glory can only come with war": becoming the president who succeeded in overthrowing the Iranian government where every predecessor since Carter had failed. Kiriakou attributes the false expectation of quick collapse to wealthy Iranian-American exiles.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: Kiriakou's acting career
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: The film role John Kiriakou took in 2025 after Tyrel Ventura wrote a part for him — a former CIA officer running a billionaire's security detail — which he shot in Mexico for a month and which made him, at sixty-odd, a member of the Screen Actors Guild.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: U.S. diplomatic vacancies
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the mass dismissal of career U.S. ambassadors — never replaced — left the Gulf without American envoys as war with Iran loomed, so allied royals had to ask him personally whether the U.S. would attack.

american-missile-stockpiles.title: Josh Shapiro
american-missile-stockpiles.summary: Governor of Pennsylvania; veteran of the Israel Defense Forces, in which he served during his late-teen kibbutz year before returning to U.S. citizenship; cited by John Kiriakou as the principal example of the loyalty question raised by American elected officials who have served the Israeli state — a disqualification Kiriakou states in absolute terms, and one he judges to have ended Shapiro's national prospects.

american-psychological-association.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
american-psychological-association.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

american-psychological-association.title: Cold cell
american-psychological-association.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

american-psychological-association.title: Waterboarding
american-psychological-association.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

american-psychological-association.title: PTSD
american-psychological-association.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

american-psychological-association.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
american-psychological-association.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

american-psychological-association.title: Abu Zubaydah
american-psychological-association.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

american-shoes.title: The declared officer
american-shoes.summary: The CIA officer whose identity is formally disclosed to the host country's intelligence service — as John Kiriakou was in Athens, taken by his chief within days of arrival to be introduced to the head of the Greek service.

american-shoes.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
american-shoes.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

american-shoes.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
american-shoes.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

american-shoes.title: Kiriakou's Athens house
american-shoes.summary: The five-storey house in the northern Athens suburb of Kifissia that John Kiriakou found for himself after refusing the embassy's offer — no square rooms, a balcony off every one of them facing a different way, and a garden with a 200-year-old olive tree whose oil the family cooked with for two years.

american-shoes.title: The Snickers bar
american-shoes.summary: The ritual in John Kiriakou''s Athens station: when an officer made a recruitment, the boss announced it in the staff meeting, everyone applauded, and he threw the officer a Snickers bar.

american-shoes.title: The Athens carjacking
american-shoes.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: The Greek health care system
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: John Kiriakou's description of Greek health care as a two-tier system in which the private sector buys nothing but position in the queue — a procedure that takes eleven or twelve months on the public system takes one or two privately, and the care itself is the same.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Islamofascism
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Kiriakou and third parties
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy for viable third parties, and his 2016 experience touring the West with Libertarian candidate Gary Johnson — including the disorganization that convinced him the party would never break through, epitomized by a colleague who ignored an airport page thinking it was 'NSA tracking my movements.'

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Candace Owens
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

americans-and-the-word-socialism.title: CIA Arabic hiring practices
americans-and-the-word-socialism.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how few CIA officers historically spoke Arabic — he was one of only two people in the entire agency fluent in both Greek and Arabic — and of how the agency's more recent pool of Arabic speakers, dominated by Arab Christian hires who clear background checks easily, often carries an innate anti-Muslim bias that limits their operational usefulness.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Ralph Nader
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: American consumer advocate and perennial third-party presidential candidate, thanked by name by John Kiriakou at his February 2013 portrait unveiling as a steadfast supporter whose backing — through the Nader Family Foundation and personally — Kiriakou described as humbling.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Heather Kiriakou
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Government Accountability Project
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: FCI Loretto
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.title: Jesselyn Radack
americans-who-tell-the-truth-portrait.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

amir.title: Faisalabad
amir.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

amir.title: The Lahore safe house
amir.summary: The ten-bedroom house in the best neighbourhood of Lahore that the CIA bought outright for two million dollars in cash in March 2002, on a cover story invented on the spot — that its buyers were textile barons — and from whose roof the team could catch seven satellites.

amir.title: Navigating Pakistan without maps
amir.summary: The logistical problem John Kiriakou says nearly undid the Abu Zubaydah operation: in 2002 Pakistan had no maps to buy, no street signs and no addresses, so the CIA team navigated a city of twelve million by shoe advertisement, traffic policeman, British school and McDonald''s — rehearsing the route twice in the small hours before the raids.

amir.title: Site 13
amir.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

amir.title: Colonel Khaled
amir.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

amir.title: Faisalabad Hospital
amir.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

amnesty-international.title: Human Rights Watch
amnesty-international.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. In his account of his own arrest, Human Rights Watch also sits inside the fateful chain of custody: when the FBI traced a classified name found in its hands, the trail ran to journalist Matthew Cole, and Cole named Kiriakou — bringing two dozen FBI agents to his door.

amnesty-international.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
amnesty-international.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

amnesty-international.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
amnesty-international.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

amnesty-international.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
amnesty-international.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

amnesty-international.title: Mitchell and Jessen
amnesty-international.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

amnesty-international.title: Witness K case
amnesty-international.summary: Australian intelligence scandal in which a former ASIS officer known as Witness K exposed Australia's bugging of the East Timorese cabinet during oil and gas revenue negotiations; his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, describes the ASIO raids on both their homes and offices as paralleling the FBI's raid on John Kiriakou.

analysis-corporation.title: John Brennan
analysis-corporation.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

analysis-corporation.title: Arrais Corporation
analysis-corporation.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

analysis-corporation.title: Central Intelligence Agency
analysis-corporation.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

analysis-corporation.title: John Kiriakou
analysis-corporation.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

analysis-corporation.title: Al Qaeda Software
analysis-corporation.summary: A claim raised on a Kiriakou-appearance podcast that "Al-Qaeda" is also the name of a terrorist-tracking software, alongside its use as the name of the terrorist organization.

analysis-corporation.title: Private Intelligence
analysis-corporation.summary: Post-CIA commercial intelligence work performed by John Kiriakou — both operational (surveillance, bribery, dossier-building for private clients) and analytical (paid forecasts for hedge funds, mutual funds, and a global mining company). Per Kiriakou, his clients ranged from a Cypriot billionaire investigating his daughter's fiancé to the ninth-largest hedge fund in the world.

andres-serrano.title: Ai Weiwei
andres-serrano.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

andres-serrano.title: Cuban double agents
andres-serrano.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

andres-serrano.title: Robert Hanssen
andres-serrano.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

andres-serrano.title: Scholar-in-Residence program
andres-serrano.summary: The current CIA recruitment program, in operation as of the late 2020s, under which the agency places retiring senior officers as 'CIA Scholar in Residence' professors at major American universities. Per John Kiriakou, the program serves as the agency's principal university-recruitment channel since the 1993 Equal Employment Opportunity Act forbade the older practice of having professors covertly recruit students into the CIA. Officers identified as scholars in residence are openly disclosed; the recruitment work continues, just no longer in secret.

andres-serrano.title: Access Agent
andres-serrano.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

andres-serrano.title: Afghan heroin policy
andres-serrano.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

andrew-bustamante.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
andrew-bustamante.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

andrew-bustamante.title: John Kiriakou
andrew-bustamante.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

andrew-bustamante.title: Presidents and the CIA
andrew-bustamante.summary: John Kiriakou's observation that some presidents actively lead the CIA while others are led around by it — citing George H.W. Bush's ongoing "love affair" with the agency after his 11-month stint as director, and Richard Nixon's close relationship with the CIA, which Kiriakou says was one of the things that brought down his presidency.

andrew-bustamante.title: Roy Cohn
andrew-bustamante.summary: Closeted McCarthy-era prosecutor and fixer, later a mentor, advisor and attorney to Donald Trump from the 1970s onward; per John Kiriakou, one of the darkest, ugliest figures in modern American history, who — while closely allied with a similarly closeted J. Edgar Hoover — was central to ruining the lives of gay men, and who died of AIDS in the 1980s alone and unloved.

andrew-bustamante.title: UK secrecy laws
andrew-bustamante.summary: John Kiriakou's view that Britain is even harsher on whistleblowers and dissent than the United States, using the Official Secrets Act and Terrorism Act to stop people at airports and threaten arrest merely for supporting Palestinian rights.

andrew-bustamante.title: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
andrew-bustamante.summary: The scholar of Islamic philosophy under whom John Kiriakou studied Shiism as an undergraduate. Kiriakou calls him probably the most important Shia Muslim scholar in the world, notes that he is the father of Vali Nasr, and remarks that at ninety-eight he is still teaching.

andrew-feinstein.title: Meredith Whittaker
andrew-feinstein.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Meredith Whittaker is developing a new, and by his account successful, business model for the encrypted-messaging app Signal, an alternative he cites alongside ProtonMail's compromised attempt at the same thing.

andrew-feinstein.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
andrew-feinstein.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

andrew-feinstein.title: Belmarsh Prison
andrew-feinstein.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

andrew-feinstein.title: Der Spiegel
andrew-feinstein.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

andrew-feinstein.title: Ethan Mccord Collateral Murder
andrew-feinstein.summary: The US soldier who carried wounded children out of the street in the Collateral Murder video released by WikiLeaks.

andrew-feinstein.title: Plus 972
andrew-feinstein.summary: The Israeli platform that, per a 2026 Berlin panel, has published a striking number of IDF whistleblowers as AI enters modern warfare.

andrew-warren.title: Mary Margaret Graham
andrew-warren.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

andrew-warren.title: Cover stop
andrew-warren.summary: A routine, innocuous errand run in the middle of a surveillance detection route so that an intelligence officer has a plausible reason to be where he is — the 7-Eleven, the dry cleaner, the wine shop — and, in John Kiriakou's account, also a petty-expense line item that has ended CIA careers.

andrew-warren.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
andrew-warren.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

andrew-warren.title: John Kiriakou
andrew-warren.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

andrew-warren.title: Central Intelligence Agency
andrew-warren.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

andrew-warren.title: Concealment of the CIA budget
andrew-warren.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA hides its spending: there is no publicly available written CIA budget, and individual line items are distributed across unrelated federal departments under invented cover programmes — a practice he says persists unchanged, and which once repeatedly exposed the agency to Senator William Proxmire''s Golden Fleece Award.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: CovertAction Magazine
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: The muckraking outlet "exposing covert action since 1978" — and one of John Kiriakou's three long-running syndicated column homes, alongside Consortium News and ScheerPost. Kiriakou joined its podcast arm, the CovertAction Bulletin, appearing on panels with Peter Dale Scott and Pepe Escobar, and jokes that the Pentagon's browser-plugin credibility warnings — red check marks against outlets like CovertAction — are the surest sign it's worth reading.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Hamilton 68
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: A company founded by former CIA, FBI, NSA and Director of National Intelligence officials that rates news sites as reliable or unreliable, contracting mainly with the Pentagon to flag articles on government computers with green or red check marks; John Kiriakou says it threatened Consortium News with a "Kremlin apologist" red-check designation, after which PayPal permanently suspended the outlet's account and confiscated its funds.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Jack Murphy NATO Sabotage Story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a story reported by podcaster Jack Murphy — over a year in the making, drawing on CIA and Army intelligence sources — alleging the CIA worked through a NATO partner to conduct sabotage inside Russia, including munitions-warehouse fires and rail explosions; killed before publication after the CIA deputy director denied it on a call with the editor and blamed "rogue Ukrainians."

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Pan Quake
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: An open-source, nonprofit, carbon-neutral social media platform based in Iceland and powered by geothermal energy, incorporated with lawyers in Luxembourg; John Kiriakou was asked to serve as a brand ambassador before its Icelandic bank account was frozen at the FBI's request over the platform's association with Julian Assange supporters.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: Remains of the Day Treasury Clerk Story
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of an obscure Treasury Department clerk who, during the 1814 British burning of Washington, rescued the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, and Washington's military commission from the National Archives — and who, after later being deemed too difficult, was quietly transferred to the National Lighthouse Service, where out of boredom he invented the refractor light still used in American lighthouses today.

andy-warhol-encounter.title: U.S. foreign policy process
andy-warhol-encounter.summary: Three foreign-policy observations from John Kiriakou — the narrow legal basis for U.S. military presence abroad, which he says does not cover American special forces in Syria; the formal congressional travel-clearance process that undercuts Pentagon and White House claims of no advance knowledge of Nancy Pelosi's Taiwan trip; and the depth of U.S.-China economic interdependence that Kiriakou says makes antagonizing Beijing strategically unwise.

angry-birds.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
angry-birds.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

angry-birds.title: 2026 Iran war
angry-birds.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

angry-birds.title: 2028 presidential field
angry-birds.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

angry-birds.title: Abraham Accords
angry-birds.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

angry-birds.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
angry-birds.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

angry-birds.title: Andrew Bustamante
angry-birds.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

anthony-fauci.title: John Kiriakou
anthony-fauci.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

anthony-fauci.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
anthony-fauci.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

anthony-fauci.title: Church Committee
anthony-fauci.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

anthony-fauci.title: CIA Gmail account felony case
anthony-fauci.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague working the counterterrorism fusion center night shift was ordered by cable to check a terrorist suspect's Gmail account and password, did so, and was later charged with a felony for illegally accessing a computer — despite having acted only on explicit written instructions from headquarters.

anthony-fauci.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
anthony-fauci.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

anthony-fauci.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
anthony-fauci.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Germany and Israel
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Roger Waters
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: Founding member of the British rock band Pink Floyd; outspoken supporter of Palestinian human rights; anonymously paid off John Kiriakou's second mortgage during his federal prison sentence, sparing his wife and children the loss of the family home; only discovered to be the benefactor years later; subsequently a personal friend of Kiriakou and a recurring guest on his programme.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Middle East Forum
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: The publication — 'clearly an Israeli publication,' in John Kiriakou's words, and one he had never heard of before a Google alert surfaced it — that ran a piece by the political adviser to the Israeli foreign minister calling Kiriakou antisemitic and describing his writing as evidence of 'the rot' in the American intellectual left. Kiriakou took the phrase as a compliment and says the episode shows how closely Israel monitors even small independent outlets.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: October 7 attack
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.title: Max Blumenthal
antisemitism-and-anti-zionism.summary: American investigative journalist and a personal friend of John Kiriakou, whom Kiriakou calls one of the most brilliant people he has ever encountered and singles out for an ability to assemble scattered fragments into a picture 'in a way that almost no one else I know is able to do.' Kiriakou also recounts Blumenthal's arrest outside the Venezuelan embassy, where he says video showed Blumenthal was the one assaulted, and counts him among the independent journalists under the same official pressure he is.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Falls Church mosque
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Large mosque on Route 7 in Falls Church, Virginia; the site at which John Kiriakou, in 1993 as a CIA Arabic-language trainee, met then-imam Anwar al-Awlaki on a class field trip; the same mosque at which the September 11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Haqqani White House meeting
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: A mid-to-late-1980s White House meeting between President Ronald Reagan and a Taliban delegation, per John Kiriakou — a former boss of his served as translator. One member of that delegation, a man named Haqqani, went on to found the Haqqani network, later responsible for the capture of Bowe Bergdahl and the kidnapping, rape, and torture of a Canadian couple.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: OnlyFans
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Prince Muhammad bin Naif
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Saudi prince and former head of Saudi intelligence; survivor of an al-Qaeda assassination attempt by a suicide bomber who concealed an explosive device internally in his own body, in approximately 2009.

anwar-al-awlaki.title: Trump Dni Replacement
anwar-al-awlaki.summary: Trump privately asked cabinet members about replacing his Director of National Intelligence, frustrated that the DNI had protected Joe Kent.

april-glaspie.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
april-glaspie.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

april-glaspie.title: Saddam Hussein
april-glaspie.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

april-glaspie.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
april-glaspie.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

april-glaspie.title: Asel al-Ghabandi
april-glaspie.summary: Kuwaiti resistance figure during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, a "bona fide hero" whose telephone reporting on Iraqi troop movements, roadblocks, atrocities, and the location of inspections reached the CIA every single day via NSA [call interception](/wiki/the-intercept) — Kiriakou's account of the resistance figure who best understood how to weaponize the certainty that the Americans were listening to everything.

april-glaspie.title: Mort Halperin
april-glaspie.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

april-glaspie.title: Norman Schwarzkopf
april-glaspie.summary: U.S. Army general and commander of CENTCOM during the 1991 Gulf War; per John Kiriakou, the architect of the "visionary" flanking maneuver that bypassed Iraq's fortified Kuwait–Saudi border, struck from the north, and produced the Highway of Death.

aq-khan.title: ISI
aq-khan.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

aq-khan.title: Pervez Musharraf
aq-khan.summary: Pakistani general and military dictator who ruled during John Kiriakou's 2002 posting as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan. Per Kiriakou, the United States 'essentially just purchased Musharraf,' paying tens of millions in cash to the ISI and meeting him several times a week — and in return 'he would let us do whatever we wanted.' Kiriakou says Musharraf, fearing the nuclear arsenal could fall into terrorist hands, unofficially turned control of Pakistan's nuclear weapons over to the Pentagon. Musharraf later pardoned proliferator A.Q. Khan.

aq-khan.title: Composition of the Saudi military
aq-khan.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing claim that there are almost no Saudi nationals in the Saudi armed forces below the most senior ranks, and that the rank and file are Pakistanis hired from among Pakistan's poor. He treats it as a standing joke in the Gulf and as a limit on what Saudi Arabia can contribute to any war with Iran.

aq-khan.title: Mr. Fish
aq-khan.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

aq-khan.title: Tora Bora
aq-khan.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

aq-khan.title: Strategic patience
aq-khan.summary: The doctrine John Kiriakou uses to describe a state that absorbs an attack and answers with a response calibrated to be smaller than the provocation — Iran's telegraphed drone waves against Israel, and India's refusal to escalate against Pakistan, which he says kept a war from becoming a nuclear one.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: The Damascus consulate strike
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The April 2024 Israeli attack on Iran's consulate in Damascus, which John Kiriakou describes as an unambiguous violation of the Vienna Convention, and whose official Israeli explanation — that it had not occurred to anyone the world would read it as a provocation — he calls disingenuous and intended purely for domestic audiences.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: The Eastern Mediterranean gas field
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The natural gas discovered off the south-eastern coast of Cyprus and running toward Lebanon, Israel and Palestine, which John Kiriakou identifies as the real source of Greek–Turkish tension. Turkey feels excluded although none of the gas lies in its waters; and although the founding agreement acknowledged a Palestinian share, Israel decides its size — an amount Kiriakou predicts will be zero.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: Iran's 2024 drone retaliation
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's telegraphed 2024 drone strike on Israel — hundreds of slow drones, launched with advance warning to the U.S. and Jordan, nearly all shot down, which he reads as a controlled show of force and an intelligence victory that exposed the Iron Dome.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: Afghan heroin policy
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: China as mediator
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.title: The Imia crisis
arab-states-and-the-gaza-war.summary: The 1996 confrontation between Greece and Turkey over an uninhabited Aegean islet, which John Kiriakou cites as the last time the two came close to exchanging fire — a flag raised, a flag taken down, warships dispatched, and Bill Clinton telephoning both capitals to tell them to stop.

arabic-and-greek.title: Training to kill
arabic-and-greek.summary: John Kiriakou's account of arriving at the CIA's clandestine training facility expecting to learn how to recruit sources at diplomatic cocktail parties, and finding instead parachute training, resistance-to-interrogation instruction, and — as his old supervisor had warned him — training to kill people.

arabic-and-greek.title: Iraq, the training account
arabic-and-greek.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says he was given the Iraq portfolio as a new CIA analyst in 1990 — that nothing ever happened there — and the promise that once he had learned tradecraft and the house writing style he would be moved to somewhere exciting, such as Romania.

arabic-and-greek.title: The oath in the auditorium
arabic-and-greek.summary: The scene John Kiriakou returns to when asked what set him on the path to blowing the whistle: standing in the CIA''s auditorium on his first day with three hundred other new hires, right hand in the air, swearing to uphold the Constitution against all enemies foreign and domestic — and his later suspicion that he may have been the only person in the room who meant it.

arabic-and-greek.title: The concealed carry advertisements
arabic-and-greek.summary: The anecdote John Kiriakou offers about surveillance capitalism: a private telephone conversation in which a friend told him he needed a concealed carry permit, followed within the hour by a Facebook feed consisting entirely of advertisements for concealed carry classes.

arabic-and-greek.title: Reading in on the Iraq invasion
arabic-and-greek.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, when he signed six secrecy agreements and was told that the United States would invade Iraq the following March, and that the agencies opposing the war had already lost the argument.

arabic-and-greek.title: The Indonesian recruitment question
arabic-and-greek.summary: A hypothetical put to John Kiriakou and other CIA applicants during the interview process — what to do when a foreign official you have cultivated for a year turns out not to be recruitable — and the answer that Kiriakou later understood had been the point of the exercise: break into the embassy and steal the information.

arabists.title: The 189 undeclared officers
arabists.summary: A figure John Kiriakou attributes to the CIA''s director of security, given to his intake class on his first day at the agency in January 1990: against two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the embassy in Washington, the FBI counted at least 189 undeclared ones operating across the United States. He pairs it with the fact that Israeli liaison officers were barred from CIA headquarters.

arabists.title: Abraham Accords
arabists.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

arabists.title: Deuce Martinez
arabists.summary: The former CIA analyst whose business card was the basis of two of the three Espionage Act charges brought against John Kiriakou. Kiriakou scanned and emailed the card — which showed Martinez had gone to work for Mitchell and Jessen, the firm of the torture programme''s architects — to a New York Times reporter and later to an ABC News reporter. The judge threw the espionage counts out.

arabists.title: Jerrold Post
arabists.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

arabists.title: Yasser Arafat
arabists.summary: Leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization, who appears in John Kiriakou's account at the two moments he treats as decisive for the Palestinians — backing Saddam Hussein after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which cost the Palestinian middle class its standing across the Gulf, and walking out of the last Clinton-era peace talks with a divided map of Jerusalem already on the table.

arabists.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
arabists.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

arianna-huffington.title: Bureau of Prisons
arianna-huffington.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

arianna-huffington.title: Oliver Stone
arianna-huffington.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

arianna-huffington.title: FCI Loretto
arianna-huffington.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

arianna-huffington.title: Code Pink
arianna-huffington.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first saw them as a Senate staffer — a room full of pink t-shirts at a hearing he'd organized for Senator Kerry, where he was caught smiling at their chants and told to keep his opinions to himself. When he was arrested, Code Pink "was right there next to me," threw his going-away party before prison, ran the sustained call campaign that helped stop his diesel-therapy transfer, stood with him through the 2019 Venezuelan embassy siege — and after prison he volunteered as coordinator of Code Pink Congress.

arianna-huffington.title: Counterterrorism Center
arianna-huffington.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career.
