bay-path-university.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

bay-path-university.title: Ilhan Omar
bay-path-university.summary: U.S. Representative whom John Kiriakou credits with sponsoring a rewrite of the Espionage Act in two consecutive Congresses — legislation he says is dead on arrival with a Republican House because of who she is.

bay-path-university.title: Lynn Buchanan
bay-path-university.summary: A Fort Meade-trained Army intelligence veteran of the CIA and NSA remote-viewing programs — a primary source, Kiriakou says, not a TV psychic.

bay-path-university.title: Mark Zuckerberg–Angela Merkel Meeting
bay-path-university.summary: Kiriakou on Zuckerberg flying to Berlin to help Chancellor Merkel define hate speech — and why he objects to that call being Zuckerberg's.

bay-path-university.title: Sweat Lodge
bay-path-university.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the federal prison where he was incarcerated had a Native American sweat lodge that was shut down after it was misused for sex rather than religious ceremony; he says he has never personally been in a sweat lodge.

bds-movement.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bds-movement.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bds-movement.title: UK secrecy laws
bds-movement.summary: John Kiriakou's view that Britain is even harsher on whistleblowers and dissent than the United States, using the Official Secrets Act and Terrorism Act to stop people at airports and threaten arrest merely for supporting Palestinian rights.

bds-movement.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
bds-movement.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

bds-movement.title: Jeffrey Epstein
bds-movement.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

bds-movement.title: CIA and NSA exotic programs
bds-movement.summary: Two obscure U.S. intelligence programs John Kiriakou has discussed — a late-1980s FBI/Defense Department investigation into a senior NSA officer who came out as a member of the Church of Satan and was accused of ritual sacrifice (which found no evidence), and a 1990s CIA battlefield laser weapon designed to blind rather than kill enemy soldiers, shelved after lawyers determined it violated international law.

bds-movement.title: Jamaal Bowman
bds-movement.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

beirut.title: Psychiatric evacuation
beirut.summary: The CIA's practice of pulling an officer out of a posting and flying him home when he breaks down — known inside the agency as being psychovac'd — and the desk-bound evaluation period that follows before he is allowed to travel again.

beirut.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
beirut.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

beirut.title: Aldrich Ames
beirut.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

beirut.title: Sandy Grimes
beirut.summary: CIA analyst who, per John Kiriakou, was the person who actually broke the Aldrich Ames case. After a 27-year-old security officer sat on an Ames file for eighteen months without action, Grimes independently noticed that Ames made $100,000–$150,000 bank deposits within days of every trip to Mexico City — the pattern that identified him as a spy. After Ames's arrest, she submitted a hot-wash paper recommending 27 reprimands across the chain of command that had promoted a known alcoholic into the most sensitive counterintelligence position in the CIA. Director John Deutch responded with strongly worded letters for seven. Grimes resigned in 1993.

beirut.title: How Can I Keep from Singing
beirut.summary: Biography of folk singer Pete Seeger and John Kiriakou's stated favorite book. Per Kiriakou, Seeger was the most important man in his life besides his father and grandfather; the two exchanged Christmas cards for years, and Seeger rallied publicly to Kiriakou's defense during his prosecution. Kiriakou identifies Seeger's 1958 defiance of HUAC — pleading the First Amendment rather than the Fifth and going to prison for it — as the model for how he wanted to live his own life.

beirut.title: Kiriakou's father and grandfather
beirut.summary: The two men John Kiriakou names as the greatest influences on his life: a grandfather with a third-grade education who pushed his children through doctorates and handed his grandson an 11th-century gold coin dug from a Greek garden, and a father, an elementary school principal, who was twice passed over for promotion because he refused to pay the bribe the school board demanded. Kiriakou says that refusal is what made him a whistleblower.

belmarsh-prison.title: Espionage Act
belmarsh-prison.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

belmarsh-prison.title: Julian Assange
belmarsh-prison.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

belmarsh-prison.title: Wikileaks as a System
belmarsh-prison.summary: Per John Kiriakou, WikiLeaks functions less as a single leader than as a durable system — one that protected whistleblowers, helped popularize the term "whistleblower" itself, was credited with contributing to the Arab Spring, weathered pressure to become a defanged NGO, and outlasted the political fallout of its 2010 cable releases (including, in Kiriakou's account, an unintended assist to Donald Trump's election).

belmarsh-prison.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
belmarsh-prison.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

belmarsh-prison.title: Andrew Feinstein
belmarsh-prison.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

belmarsh-prison.title: Plus 972
belmarsh-prison.summary: The Israeli platform that, per a 2026 Berlin panel, has published a striking number of IDF whistleblowers as AI enters modern warfare.

below-worlds-end.title: John Kiriakou
below-worlds-end.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

below-worlds-end.title: The Farm
below-worlds-end.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

below-worlds-end.title: Asset acquisition cycle
below-worlds-end.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

below-worlds-end.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
below-worlds-end.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

below-worlds-end.title: Big Assawoman Bay NASA launch
below-worlds-end.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being taken, as a junior CIA analyst, to watch a NASA rocket launch near the village of Big Assawoman on Virginia's Eastern Shore, where he was startled to find foreign space-agency officials present unsupervised.

below-worlds-end.title: Chinese illegal fishing
below-worlds-end.summary: John Kiriakou calls Chinese overfishing one of the world's biggest under-discussed problems, citing the near-extinction of Chilean sea bass and heavy overfishing of Alaskan and Atlantic cod, and recounting personally seeing Chinese fishing vessels in Antarctica on his honeymoon.

benazir-bhutto.title: John Kiriakou
benazir-bhutto.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

benazir-bhutto.title: Abu Zubaydah
benazir-bhutto.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

benazir-bhutto.title: Central Intelligence Agency
benazir-bhutto.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

benazir-bhutto.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
benazir-bhutto.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

benazir-bhutto.title: Intelligence peddlers
benazir-bhutto.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

benazir-bhutto.title: Jose Rodriguez
benazir-bhutto.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: Israeli strike on Qatar
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: The Israeli bombing of Qatar that John Kiriakou treats as Benjamin Netanyahu's decisive overreach — an attack on a major non-NATO ally that hosts the largest air force base in the world, which Kiriakou says forced Donald Trump into a public falsehood about advance warning and then into the recognition that Israel acts in Israel's interests rather than America's.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: Kiriakou and Cenk Uygur
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: A grievance John Kiriakou carried for a decade — that Cenk Uygur had spent thirty minutes attacking him over his first letter from prison — resolved live on air in July 2026 when Uygur produced his archive, found no such segment, and both men concluded it had been mistaken identity.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: The Kite Runner rescue mission
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: 2007 covert operation in which John Kiriakou, newly departed from the CIA and working as a corporate-intelligence consultant, was hired by Paramount Studios to secretly evacuate the Afghan child actors of the film "The Kite Runner" and their extended families after real death threats over the film's content.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: Maria Butina
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: Russian gun-rights activist convicted in the United States of failing to register as a foreign agent; John Kiriakou cites her case as an example of the "process crime" of FARA violations, contrasting the severity of her 18-month solitary-confinement sentence with federal guidelines calling for 0-6 months.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: Netanyahu arrest poll
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: The 2026 survey finding that a majority of Americans — not a plurality — support the arrest of Benjamin Netanyahu, a figure John Kiriakou notes is higher than the share who supported arresting Nicolás Maduro and which, per CNN, represents a fifty-point move in American opinion over five years.

benjamin-netanyahu.title: OnlyFans
benjamin-netanyahu.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the man who owned OnlyFans — whom he describes as Ukrainian-American rather than Israeli — was a major donor and strong supporter of Israel, part of a broader claim Kiriakou makes about Israeli involvement in the porn industry.

bernie-kerik.title: Rudy Giuliani
bernie-kerik.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

bernie-kerik.title: Bruce Fein
bernie-kerik.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

bernie-kerik.title: Noelle Dunphy
bernie-kerik.summary: Former aide to Rudy Giuliani; independently corroborated to the New York Times John Kiriakou's account of Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt, after Giuliani's subsequent sexual harassment of her caused her to come forward.

bernie-kerik.title: Robert MacLean
bernie-kerik.summary: TSA whistleblower; the person to whom John Kiriakou first described Rudy Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt the same evening it occurred, and who in turn tipped the FBI (which declined interest) and then the New York Times.

bernie-kerik.title: Sebastian Gorka
bernie-kerik.summary: Former Trump administration deputy assistant; subject of John Kiriakou's second attempted pardon transaction in 2018, in which Gorka asked Kiriakou for $5,000 at a book launch at the Trump International Hotel in exchange for tweeting at the president on his behalf. Kiriakou refused.

bernie-kerik.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
bernie-kerik.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

bernie-sanders.title: Hillary Clinton
bernie-sanders.summary: Former U.S. Secretary of State and 2016 presidential candidate; John Kiriakou describes her as arguably the most neoconservative candidate Democrats could have nominated, more militarist even than her husband, and credits her — separately — with correctly describing Iran as a military dictatorship run by the IRGC rather than a genuine theocracy.

bernie-sanders.title: Bill Barr
bernie-sanders.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

bernie-sanders.title: Blueprint for Free Speech
bernie-sanders.summary: The Australian non-governmental organisation that drafts whistleblower protection legislation and markets it to governments around the world, and which hired John Kiriakou in 2015 to help write Greece's law. Its board is mostly academics and transparency activists; Kiriakou credits it with successes in Canada, Zambia, Jamaica and Ukraine, and names its founder and director as Suelette Dreyfus, whom he describes as a co-founder of WikiLeaks with Julian Assange.

bernie-sanders.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
bernie-sanders.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

bernie-sanders.title: Crypto AG
bernie-sanders.summary: The Swiss encryption-machine company revealed in February 2020 to have been secretly owned by the CIA and West German intelligence, which sold riggable ciphers to governments around the world for decades. John Kiriakou, who held senior positions at the agency, says he knew nothing about it — it was held that closely — and refuses to describe it as a scandal: nobody will be prosecuted, several people will probably win medals, and an intelligence operation is not supposed to be honest or fair.

bernie-sanders.title: Eastern District of Virginia
bernie-sanders.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

bezalel-smotrich.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bezalel-smotrich.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bezalel-smotrich.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
bezalel-smotrich.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

bezalel-smotrich.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
bezalel-smotrich.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

bezalel-smotrich.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
bezalel-smotrich.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

bezalel-smotrich.title: The 1991 Saudi plan for Gaza
bezalel-smotrich.summary: A proposal John Kiriakou says he watched Ambassador Chas Freeman float to the Saudis during his first overseas tour in 1991 — that Saudi Arabia fund a port, an airport, a desalination plant and an electrical grid in Gaza. The Saudis agreed; Israel refused outright. Kiriakou raises it because the identical arrangement resurfaced in the Israeli press more than three decades later.

bezalel-smotrich.title: John Kiriakou
bezalel-smotrich.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Below World's End
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut, filmed entirely in Mexico during October 2025; Kiriakou's performance earned him a Screen Actors Guild membership card, and Sean Penn told him after a private screening that he had unknowingly been acting throughout his entire CIA career.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Chinese illegal fishing
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: John Kiriakou calls Chinese overfishing one of the world's biggest under-discussed problems, citing the near-extinction of Chilean sea bass and heavy overfishing of Alaskan and Atlantic cod, and recounting personally seeing Chinese fishing vessels in Antarctica on his honeymoon.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Joe Weisberg
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Former CIA Counterterrorism Center officer and colleague of John Kiriakou who resigned abruptly, saying he did not have it in him to convince people to commit treason, then moved to Hollywood and created the television series The Americans.

big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.title: Mike Baker
big-assawoman-bay-nasa-launch.summary: Former CIA case officer and John Kiriakou's direct predecessor in Athens on the 17 November problem; "the real deal," in Kiriakou's phrase, until a botched surveillance operation got him expelled from Greece and forced out of the agency the same day he expected a commendation.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: Kissinger and the petrodollar
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's endorsement of the theory that Henry Kissinger deliberately structured the 1970s petrodollar to tie the U.S. to Middle Eastern oil — creating a standing rationale for policing the region, even as America exports its own fracked oil.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: CIA and FBI ties to organized crime
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's survey of documented U.S. intelligence partnerships with organized crime — the FBI securing wartime ports with the Genovese family, the CIA's Castro plots with the Trafficantes, its work with the Escobar cartel against Colombian communists, and a mob hitman deployed against the Klan.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: CIA and the UFO question
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: Permanent wartime economy
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: Steve Kappes
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: Former Deputy Director of the Central Intelligence Agency; encountered by John Kiriakou in the lobby of the Sanaa Marriott during Kiriakou's final Yemen trip as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator.

bilderberg-weapon-sales.title: Cold War
bilderberg-weapon-sales.summary: The U.S.–Soviet confrontation that built the CIA John Kiriakou joined. Kiriakou argues the Cold War was real "but also at a certain level desired" — America has always needed an ism to oppose — and that its habits never died: "The Russians thought the Cold War was over, but no one told the US." From its memoirs he draws a standing tradecraft lesson (the CIA''s best recruits were always walk-ins), and in the new Russia and China confrontations he sees a Cold War 2.0 rebuilt on the old exaggerations.

bill-barr.title: Julian Assange
bill-barr.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

bill-barr.title: Lee Zeldon
bill-barr.summary: Per Megyn Kelly's opening monologue, the EPA administrator reportedly considered by Trump as a possible replacement for Attorney General Pam Bondi.

bill-barr.title: Gail Slater
bill-barr.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the head of the DOJ antitrust unit under Pam Bondi who was stripped of authority and then fired.

bill-barr.title: LSD Mind Manipulation
bill-barr.summary: Kiriakou on the CIA dosing unwitting men with LSD in safe houses, using sex workers as bait, to find out whether the drug could unlock secrets.

bill-barr.title: Podcast Bros
bill-barr.summary: Per Sohrab Ahmari, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, podcast bros.

bill-barr.title: Todd Blanch
bill-barr.summary: Per Megyn Kelly, reading Trump's own statement live during her interview with Kiriakou, Todd Blanch was named the incoming acting Attorney General, replacing Pam Bondi.

bill-binney.title: Panquake
bill-binney.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

bill-binney.title: Russiagate
bill-binney.summary: John Kiriakou''s rebuttal of the claim that Russia swung the 2016 U.S. election: the Mueller report found no interference, the DNC emails were leaked in person rather than remotely hacked, and Russia''s roughly $50,000 in Facebook ads — half spent after the election — was trivial against billions in campaign spending.

bill-binney.title: The whistleblower support network
bill-binney.summary: The informal circle of American national security whistleblowers that John Kiriakou describes as 'something of a club' — Daniel Ellsberg, Bill Binney, Kirk Wiebe, Ed Loomis, Thomas Drake, Jesselyn Radack and others — whose members in the Washington area meet socially and without which, Kiriakou says, none of them could have got through it.

bill-binney.title: Kevin Shipp
bill-binney.summary: Former CIA officer and whistleblower whose case John Kiriakou read about in the Washington Post and who, Kiriakou says, believed he was entirely alone until Kiriakou reached out to tell him he was not — an episode Kiriakou uses to illustrate the isolation that follows a national security disclosure.

bill-binney.title: Craig Murray
bill-binney.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

bill-binney.title: The US overseas basing footprint
bill-binney.summary: John Kiriakou''s summary of the one thing he says Democrats and Republicans in Washington genuinely agree on: that the United States needs a military presence in about 110 countries and bases in about 86 of them, along with the newest nuclear weapons, the biggest ships, the best aircraft and the biggest bombs.

bill-buckley.title: Mike Spann
bill-buckley.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen alongside John Kiriakou.

bill-buckley.title: Spy films and television on screen
bill-buckley.summary: John Kiriakou's scene-by-scene verdicts on how spy films and television handle real tradecraft — what they get right (static surveillance from upper floors, hostile operational meetings, exchanges of bona fides, breaking into offices), what they invent (silent helicopters, high-speed submersibles, Batcaves, gadgets that cannot be bought), and the shows he says commit felonies on screen. He opens with why CIA officers watch them at all — *"not because they love the CIA movies, but because they love to criticize them."*

bill-buckley.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
bill-buckley.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

bill-buckley.title: Moving a satellite to Kuwait
bill-buckley.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of how thin American overhead coverage once was: after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 the United States had no satellite looking at Kuwait, and it took six months to move one that had been parked over Moscow.

bill-buckley.title: Tony Mendez
bill-buckley.summary: The CIA exfiltration specialist who got the American diplomats sheltering in the Canadian embassy out of revolutionary Tehran in 1979 by inventing a fake science-fiction film production — the operation dramatised in *Argo*. John Kiriakou calls him "a giant in the history of the CIA", says the same of his wife, and rates the operation among the greatest the agency has ever carried out.

bill-buckley.title: The Russian illegals program
bill-buckley.summary: The Russian practice, described by John Kiriakou, of recruiting people — sometimes as children — training them abroad and inserting them into Western countries as sleepers who live ordinary lives for decades until they are activated. Kiriakou says a group of illegals was broken up by the FBI in his own Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood and traded for American spies, and that he knows a former KGB sleeper in Brooklyn who refused activation after the birth of his daughter.

bill-burns.title: Avril Haines
bill-burns.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the National Security Council lawyer who decided whether names could lawfully go on John Brennan's kill list — and said yes in almost every case — before becoming CIA deputy director during the agency's hacking of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and then Director of National Intelligence. Kiriakou calls her appointment the disastrous half of a week in which Biden also named Bill Burns, and says she has never had to answer for any of it.

bill-burns.title: Donald Trump
bill-burns.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

bill-burns.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
bill-burns.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

bill-burns.title: Havana Syndrome
bill-burns.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

bill-burns.title: John Ratcliffe
bill-burns.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

bill-burns.title: Senate Torture Report
bill-burns.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

bill-casey.title: Pike Committee
bill-casey.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

bill-casey.title: Church Committee
bill-casey.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

bill-casey.title: CIA National Resources Division
bill-casey.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

bill-casey.title: Denied areas
bill-casey.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

bill-casey.title: Central Intelligence Agency
bill-casey.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

bill-casey.title: Christopher Steele dossier
bill-casey.summary: The 2016 opposition-research dossier alleging Trump-Russia ties, compiled by former MI6 officer Christopher Steele. Per John Kiriakou, who worked directly with Steele on an MI6 operation in London in the 1990s, Steele was so respected at MI6 that other officers wanted to be like him — a reputation Kiriakou says the dossier episode reduced to caricature, because in private practice there was no team of analysts to vet the raw intelligence before it reached the Clinton campaign.

bill-clinton.title: MOSSAD
bill-clinton.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

bill-clinton.title: Christopher Hitchens
bill-clinton.summary: British-American journalist and author who, at John Kiriakou's telling, argued that CIA waterboarding was 'nothing … not a big deal,' underwent a filmed waterboarding in 2008, tapped out after roughly seventeen seconds, and suffered panic attacks thereafter. Kiriakou knew him and corresponded with him — the experiment happened because Hitchens thought Kiriakou was exaggerating — and remained an admirer of the writer and an opponent of his politics on Iraq.

bill-clinton.title: Serving at the pleasure of the president
bill-clinton.summary: The employment rule John Kiriakou says he was taught in his first week at the CIA: agency employees have none of the protections of the Civil Service Act and can be dismissed at will, over a bad tie or an unwelcome line in the President''s Daily Brief. He treats the rule as long-standing and harmless in itself, because every previous president wanted unbiased analysis — and as newly dangerous when a president fires the analysts whose assessments he dislikes.

bill-clinton.title: Mack McLarty
bill-clinton.summary: U.S. political consultant and Bill Clinton's former White House Chief of Staff; founder of McLarty Associates (formerly Kissinger McLarty), at which John Kiriakou was given a private office and part-time secretary in 2008.

bill-clinton.title: Watching naval movements
bill-clinton.summary: One of the first lessons John Kiriakou says he learned at the CIA: to read American military intentions, watch naval movements — one carrier strike group means business, two means war. He used it to correctly predict the 2026 strike on Iran days in advance.

bill-clinton.title: Executive assistant to the Deputy Director for Operations
bill-clinton.summary: The job John Kiriakou held during the Iraq war, and the shape of its day: a 2:45 a.m. alarm, ten thousand overnight cables triaged down to five or ten by dawn, the deputy directors briefed at seven and the director at half past — and only then the actual work of coordinating with the State Department, the Pentagon and the vice president''s office.

bill-pulte.title: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
bill-pulte.summary: The intelligence-community layer created in 2004, which John Kiriakou argues should never have existed. He traces its origin to George Tenet's failures over 9/11 and Iraq, notes it grew from sixteen employees to roughly twenty-four thousand, and points out that most agencies nominally under it are Defense Department bodies over which it controls nothing but the budget.

bill-pulte.title: Tulsi Gabbard
bill-pulte.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

bill-pulte.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
bill-pulte.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

bill-pulte.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bill-pulte.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bill-pulte.title: Five Eyes
bill-pulte.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

bill-pulte.title: Germany and Israel
bill-pulte.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

bill-richardson.title: John Kerry
bill-richardson.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

bill-richardson.title: John Kiriakou
bill-richardson.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bill-richardson.title: Mack McLarty
bill-richardson.summary: U.S. political consultant and Bill Clinton's former White House Chief of Staff; founder of McLarty Associates (formerly Kissinger McLarty), at which John Kiriakou was given a private office and part-time secretary in 2008.

bill-richardson.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
bill-richardson.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

bill-richardson.title: Bill Clinton
bill-richardson.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

bill-richardson.title: Breaking the nuclear taboo
bill-richardson.summary: John Kiriakou's reporting that Donald Trump considered using a tactical nuclear weapon in Iran not for military necessity but to break what he regards as warfare's final taboo, freeing future presidents to use larger weapons — and the related account that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs refused him the nuclear codes.

billy-waugh.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
billy-waugh.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

billy-waugh.title: Carlos the Jackal
billy-waugh.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

billy-waugh.title: Cofer Black
billy-waugh.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

billy-waugh.title: Counterterrorism Center
billy-waugh.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

billy-waugh.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
billy-waugh.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

billy-waugh.title: Abu Zubaydah
billy-waugh.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

bin-laden-health-rumors.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
bin-laden-health-rumors.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

bin-laden-health-rumors.title: The cave myth
bin-laden-health-rumors.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

bin-laden-health-rumors.title: The asset recruitment cycle
bin-laden-health-rumors.summary: The four-step career requirement John Kiriakou says governed CIA operations before September 11 — spot, assess, develop and recruit an agent, or do not get promoted — and his description of what the fourth step actually rests on: not money, revenge or ideology, but friendship, real or believed.

bin-laden-health-rumors.title: The CIA spotter professor
bin-laden-health-rumors.summary: How John Kiriakou entered the CIA: a graduate-school professor who liked his writing style asked him to stay after class, and turned out to be an undercover officer working as a talent spotter. Kiriakou, who had been planning on Capitol Hill or the foreign service, says he had given the agency no thought at all until it approached him.

bin-laden-health-rumors.title: The Benghazi hearings critique
bin-laden-health-rumors.summary: John Kiriakou''s complaint about the congressional inquiry into Benghazi, which he watched all the way through: he believes there is some evidence of gun running, doubts anyone will ever establish who was behind it, and objects that the hearings were not trying to find out — having devolved into a political contest that served the American people not at all.

bin-laden-health-rumors.title: The Libya policy reversal
bin-laden-health-rumors.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi: the United States had a healthy working relationship with a man who hated al-Qaeda as much as it did, and flipping sides at the last minute was a terrible policy error that left the country in anarchy. Told that destabilisation may have been the objective all along, he called that an incredibly shortsighted policy, because power vacuums drag America in and it cannot get back out.

black-box-transport.title: FCI Loretto
black-box-transport.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

black-box-transport.title: Federal prison security levels
black-box-transport.summary: The ladder of federal custody as John Kiriakou describes it — penitentiary, medium, low and minimum-security camp — the transfer rules that let long-sentence prisoners descend it, and why that placed dangerous men inside the low-security prison where he served his sentence.

black-box-transport.title: Legal mail
black-box-transport.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

black-box-transport.title: Civil confinement
black-box-transport.summary: The policy John Kiriakou proposed from inside FCI Loretto — moving sex offenders to a secure location on prison grounds after their sentences end rather than releasing them — an argument that drew public criticism and which he defends with the case of a prisoner named Cook.

black-box-transport.title: Depression in prison
black-box-transport.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

black-box-transport.title: Cook
black-box-transport.summary: The elderly Kentucky prisoner who worked with John Kiriakou in the FCI Loretto chapel, finished a 20-year child pornography sentence, and was back inside within four months facing 60 more — the case Kiriakou uses to answer critics of civil confinement.

black-cube.title: MOSSAD
black-cube.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

black-cube.title: The Cypriot billionaire's investigation
black-cube.summary: The six-week private-intelligence job John Kiriakou describes as operational rather than analytic: a Cypriot billionaire wanted to know about the man engaged to his only daughter, and Kiriakou bribed a police captain in Cyprus, ran surveillance in London, and reported back that the fiancé was a thief with drug convictions.

black-cube.title: David Boies
black-cube.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

black-cube.title: Access Agent
black-cube.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

black-cube.title: Khaled Mashal
black-cube.summary: Senior Hamas political leader; survived a 1997 Mossad poisoning attempt in Amman, Jordan; the operation's failure and the political fallout in Jordan are the canonical example, in John Kiriakou's account, of Israeli operational hostility carried out in friendly third-country territory without regard for the diplomatic consequences.

black-cube.title: Mahmoud al-Mabhouh
black-cube.summary: Senior Hamas figure assassinated by Mossad in a Dubai hotel room in January 2010; the operation has been studied by intelligence services worldwide for its tradecraft, in particular the unsolved question of how the assassination team locked the hotel-room door from the inside after killing him.

blackmail-in-recruitment.title: Asset acquisition cycle
blackmail-in-recruitment.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

blackmail-in-recruitment.title: Church Committee
blackmail-in-recruitment.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

blackmail-in-recruitment.title: Al-Julani
blackmail-in-recruitment.summary: The former al-Qaeda commander and, per John Kiriakou, co-founder of ISIS who was installed as president of Syria and received at the White House. Kiriakou''s initial reading was that no one moves from a ten-million-dollar American bounty to a state visit in months without being a long-term CIA asset — until a senior Turkish official told him over dinner that al-Julani was Turkey''s: ''We created him from nothing and we installed him in Syria.'' Kiriakou judged that version more plausible than his own.

blackmail-in-recruitment.title: Barbara Leaf
blackmail-in-recruitment.summary: American diplomat, assistant secretary of state for the Near East, and — in John Kiriakou's description — an old friend of his. He cites her trip to Damascus, made within days of al-Julani taking power and alongside the special envoy for hostage affairs, as the moment American recognition was traded for the lifting of the ten-million-dollar bounty on the new Syrian leader.

blackmail-in-recruitment.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
blackmail-in-recruitment.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

blackmail-in-recruitment.title: ISIS
blackmail-in-recruitment.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

blackwater.title: Cofer Black
blackwater.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

blackwater.title: Erik Prince
blackwater.summary: Founder of Blackwater; CIA non-official-cover officer with a 201 file; identified publicly by Leon Panetta in front of the House Intelligence Committee; lives in Dubai outside U.S. jurisdiction; in popular culture invoked, alongside Elon Musk, as the composite figure for the billionaire in the Tyrell Vanto film featuring John Kiriakou.

blackwater.title: Executive Order 12333
blackwater.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

blackwater.title: Title 10 vs Title 50
blackwater.summary: The U.S. legal-code distinction governing which kinds of armed action fall under military authority (Title 10) and which fall under intelligence authority (Title 50); the operative legal frame for the post-9/11 question of whether CIA contractors can lawfully kill in the agency's name, addressed in the 2025 Ninth Circuit ruling in the Abu Zubaydah contractor case.

blackwater.title: Global Response Staff
blackwater.summary: The CIA's protective-security program for case officers operating in high-threat environments; run for the agency by Blackwater; especially active in Baghdad's Green Zone during the Iraq War, where movement between fixed locations was treated as life-threatening.

blackwater.title: Ninth Circuit contractor ruling (2025)
blackwater.summary: Approximately July 2025 U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruling, in a case brought by Abu Zubaydah against CIA contractors who had tortured him, holding that contractors operating under a written CIA contract are legally protected as agents of the agency; extends Executive Order 12333 authority to contractor operations including the Blackwater assassination program; received almost no U.S. media coverage.

blue-the-guard.title: Kiriakou's FOIA request from prison
blue-the-guard.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed on himself six weeks into his sentence at FCI Loretto — despite a plea agreement promising he never would — which returned 250 pages including a warden's memorandum warning staff that the incoming prisoner had access to the media.

blue-the-guard.title: FCI Loretto
blue-the-guard.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

blue-the-guard.title: Marlon Beard
blue-the-guard.summary: The career drug dealer who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto and told him to keep writing when shakedowns over the Letters from Loretto were being used to provoke the other prisoners against him — advice Kiriakou credits with making him double down.

blue-the-guard.title: The dog food memo
blue-the-guard.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

blue-the-guard.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
blue-the-guard.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

blue-the-guard.title: Cleanliness in prison
blue-the-guard.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hygiene and order at FCI Loretto — where everybody showered daily on pain of a beating, everybody was constantly cleaning, and the rules on possessions and bedmaking left almost no room for clutter.

blueprint-for-free-speech.title: Kiriakou Greek whistleblower law
blueprint-for-free-speech.summary: A whistleblower protection law John Kiriakou says he was hired by the Greek government to write in 2015, at the invitation of Greece, after which it was passed by both the European Parliament and the Greek Parliament and became law across the European Union. Per Kiriakou, the law's first courtroom use involved a whistleblower who exposed Greece's defense minister for taking bribes from Siemens; the resulting press coverage led a consortium of Greece's four wealthiest families to ask Kiriakou to run a private equity fund for them.

blueprint-for-free-speech.title: The EU whistleblower directive
blueprint-for-free-speech.summary: The European Union whistleblower protection directive, which John Kiriakou describes as a watered-down descendant of the Greek law he helped write in 2015. His objection is to its exemption: the directive does not apply to Brussels itself. He treats that as an instance of a general legislative habit rather than a European failing — Congress, he notes, routinely exempts itself from the laws it passes, including the Occupational Safety and Health Act.

blueprint-for-free-speech.title: Julian Assange
blueprint-for-free-speech.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

blueprint-for-free-speech.title: Eastern District of Virginia
blueprint-for-free-speech.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

blueprint-for-free-speech.title: Bernie Sanders
blueprint-for-free-speech.summary: United States senator from Vermont. John Kiriakou, who watched him daily from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, describes Sanders holding open breakfast in the Senate cafeteria for anyone who walked in — insisting only that they call him "Bernie" — and names him the one 2016 candidate willing to talk about shrinking the military.

blueprint-for-free-speech.title: Bill Barr
blueprint-for-free-speech.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: NSA Surveillance
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Purchased data as a warrant workaround
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: John Kiriakou's account of U.S. federal agencies buying Americans' personal data from social-media platforms and data brokers rather than seeking a warrant — a practice he describes as an ethical and legal problem likely to reach the Supreme Court, and one in which no judge is aware a case is being built.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Vault 7
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Donald Trump
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Mass Surveillance
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: Kiriakou says the NSA has dropped any pretext of protecting civil liberties, warehousing every call, text and email in the Utah desert.

bluffdale-nsa-facility.title: Balochistan drone base
bluffdale-nsa-facility.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

bob-baer.title: Sandy Berger
bob-baer.summary: National Security Adviser under President Bill Clinton; per John Kiriakou, the official who shut down CIA case officer Bob Baer's mid-1990s plan to assassinate Saddam Hussein from northern Iraq, by calling the CIA after an NSA intercept and threatening Baer with a conspiracy charge unless he was recalled.

bob-baer.title: The Reluctant Spy
bob-baer.summary: John Kiriakou''s 2009 memoir, The Reluctant Spy: My Secret Life in the CIA''s War on Terror, begun in secret months before he blew the whistle and reaching number five on the New York Times bestseller list.

bob-baer.title: Saddam Hussein
bob-baer.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

bob-baer.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
bob-baer.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

bob-baer.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
bob-baer.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

bob-baer.title: Souda Bay Vulnerability and Nasser on American Decisions
bob-baer.summary: Two observations John Kiriakou has made on U.S. Mediterranean strategy and decision-making — a U.S. military contact's warning that Souda Bay in Crete, the nearest major port able to host a U.S. aircraft carrier like the USS Gerald Ford, is a possible vulnerability; and Kiriakou's favorite quote from Gamal Abdel Nasser, that Americans never make clear-cut stupid decisions, only complicated ones.

bob-cia-hr.title: John Kiriakou
bob-cia-hr.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bob-cia-hr.title: Jerrold Post
bob-cia-hr.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

bob-cia-hr.title: CIA Political Psychology Division
bob-cia-hr.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency unit founded by Dr. Gerald Post in the 1970s to produce long-distance psychiatric evaluations of foreign leaders

bob-cia-hr.title: George Washington University
bob-cia-hr.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

bob-cia-hr.title: The polygraph
bob-cia-hr.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

bob-cia-hr.title: United Food and Commercial Workers
bob-cia-hr.summary: The huge K Street labor union where a young John Kiriakou — from a family with a long labor history — was working when Dr. Jerrold Post''s class assignment changed his life: shadow your boss for a week and write his psychological profile. Kiriakou''s boss was a mean old-school organizer whose back had been broken by scabs; halfway through the week Kiriakou called him a racist ("which he was"), and the resulting paper diagnosed the man as a sociopath and potentially dangerous. The paper is what put Kiriakou on the CIA''s radar.

bob-grenier.title: George Tenet
bob-grenier.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

bob-grenier.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
bob-grenier.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

bob-grenier.title: Abu Zubaydah
bob-grenier.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

bob-grenier.title: Jim Pavitt
bob-grenier.summary: Long-serving CIA Deputy Director for Operations during the early post-9/11 period; characterized by John Kiriakou as "a legendary officer and a really great guy"; mocked John Brennan openly within the agency for Brennan's recurring stated ambition to head his own intelligence agency.

bob-grenier.title: Matt DeHart
bob-grenier.summary: American Army veteran and whistleblower prosecuted on charges including child pornography that the Justice Department later admitted, in court, did not exist; per John Kiriakou, DeHart fled to Canada at the first sign of military trouble, was returned to the U.S., and was held without bond as a flight risk.

bob-grenier.title: Girls' madrasa raid error
bob-grenier.summary: A mistaken CIA raid, conducted the night of the Abu Zubaydah operation, on the home of an elderly Pakistani man running an unlicensed girls' madrasa — the only phone in the neighborhood, which al-Qaeda fighters had been using and the CIA had been intercepting. John Kiriakou personally apologized to the man on the president's behalf and arranged compensation.

bob-jones-frame-up.title: The rat and pedophile table
bob-jones-frame-up.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

bob-jones-frame-up.title: Shot callers
bob-jones-frame-up.summary: The trusted representatives each faction at FCI Loretto appointed to mediate disputes — a system John Kiriakou credits with keeping violence rare in a low-security prison, and which he later manipulated to have a rival banished from his own table.

bob-jones-frame-up.title: Dave Phillips
bob-jones-frame-up.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

bob-jones-frame-up.title: Legal mail
bob-jones-frame-up.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

bob-jones-frame-up.title: Letter from Loretto
bob-jones-frame-up.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

bob-jones-frame-up.title: Sarge
bob-jones-frame-up.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer John Kiriakou named in a Letter from Loretto for swearing at him and trashing his cell — conduct he later learned was not merely a Bureau of Prisons infraction but a misdemeanour crime, and one of two offences he says the letter inadvertently exposed.

bob-trout.title: FCI Loretto
bob-trout.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

bob-trout.title: Mark McDougall
bob-trout.summary: U.S. criminal defense attorney; part of John Kiriakou's defense team in the 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution; the attorney whose framing of the case — "your problem is you think this is about justice and it's not about justice; it's about mitigating damage" — Kiriakou credits as the argument that persuaded him to take the final plea deal.

bob-trout.title: Plato Cacheris
bob-trout.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

bob-trout.title: John Kiriakou
bob-trout.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

bob-trout.title: Prison racial segregation
bob-trout.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

bob-trout.title: Sharon Scranage
