Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

condoleezza-rice.title: George Tenet
condoleezza-rice.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

condoleezza-rice.title: Abu Zubaydah
condoleezza-rice.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

condoleezza-rice.title: Jeffrey Epstein
condoleezza-rice.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

condoleezza-rice.title: Dick Clarke
condoleezza-rice.summary: The White House counterterrorism chief John Kiriakou describes as the most highly respected non-ideological counterterrorism professional in government — demoted by the incoming Bush administration, ignored when he warned Condoleezza Rice that a terrible attack was coming, and, on Kiriakou's account, lied to by CIA director George Tenet about al-Qaeda operatives already inside the United States.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Church Committee
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: The encounter at the Greek ambassador's residence
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: An exchange John Kiriakou describes from a dinner a few weeks after his release from prison, in which a Democratic member of the Senate Intelligence Committee welcomed him home, was told Kiriakou had expected him to speak up, and answered that it had taken everything he had simply to keep his own security clearance. Kiriakou offers it as evidence that the intelligence oversight committees are afraid of the agencies they oversee.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: MK-Ultra
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Pike Committee
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: The buried Senate documents
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a sitting senator who could not obtain a set of documents classified in the 1970s. Long past the point where mandatory declassification should have applied, the CIA disclaimed them as not its own; they turned out to be Senate documents, which no disclosure law reaches, and no authority existed to compel their release.

congressional-intelligence-oversight.title: Anthony Fauci
congressional-intelligence-oversight.summary: American physician and public-health official whose pardon John Kiriakou condemned as "unacceptable" in a May 2026 Fox News appearance. Kiriakou''s objection is partly personal: his cousin George was, he says, the second person in Ohio to die of COVID, in very early 2020. Kiriakou confined himself to the pardon and to his own family''s loss, and made no claim of his own about the origin of the virus.

consortium-news.title: John Kiriakou
consortium-news.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

consortium-news.title: Julian Assange
consortium-news.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

consortium-news.title: Ray McGovern
consortium-news.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

consortium-news.title: Bill Binney
consortium-news.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

consortium-news.title: Espionage Act
consortium-news.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

consortium-news.title: Kiriakou on influencing Trump
consortium-news.summary: John Kiriakou's 2019 account of how to move Donald Trump on a policy question — that the president is malleable but needs to hear the same thing from three different people he respects, illustrated with an episode in which Rand Paul mentioned Kiriakou to Trump two weeks after an aide had, and Trump remembered the earlier mention. Kiriakou used the theory to argue that a pardon for Julian Assange was reachable.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: Signing with CAA
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: Suggested responses
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: The convicted felon introduction
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: The NPR walkout
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

consulting-for-royal-families.title: The underlying sadness
consulting-for-royal-families.summary: The change several people have independently reported to John Kiriakou about himself since his prosecution — an underlying sadness that was not there before — which he says he does not see in himself, considering himself a happy and well-adjusted person.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Kiriakou's legal counteroffensive
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou's announcement in February 2021 that after thirteen years of being reactive and responsive to his detractors he intended to start going after people, having connected with Harvard and Georgetown law professors — a plan he described without giving detail, saying only that things were turning around.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Phone microphone ad targeting
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a spoken telephone conversation about concealed carry permits being followed, five minutes later, by a Facebook feed in which every single advertisement was for a concealed carry class — offered as evidence for his claim that the platforms go further than they admit and listen when the phone is turned off.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Generals in national security posts
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou''s blanket objection to putting retired generals in charge of the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department or the National Security Council, resting on a single argument about how officers reach flag rank: generals became generals by saying ''yes sir'', and what a president needs is somebody who can tell him why an idea is terrible.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Heather Kiriakou
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: ''Joe Bidenopoulos''
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: The nickname John Kiriakou says Joe Biden carries in the Greek-American community — a reputation for being so pro-Greek-American that he is called Joe Bidenopoulos — which Kiriakou hoped in 2023 might give him a connection worth trying in his pursuit of a presidential pardon.

consulting-job-entrapment-offers.title: Kamala Harris
consulting-job-entrapment-offers.summary: Vice President under Joe Biden and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; per John Kiriakou, installed as the party's nominee without a competitive primary despite having failed to reach the 2020 Iowa caucus, and closed out her 2024 campaign courting the Cheney family as a symbol of American values. Kiriakou, a lifelong progressive, says her pursuit of Dick Cheney's endorsement is what decided him against voting for her.

contra-rebels.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
contra-rebels.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

contra-rebels.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
contra-rebels.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

contra-rebels.title: Dark Alliance
contra-rebels.summary: Gary Webb's seven-part San Jose Mercury News investigation reporting that cocaine reaching Los Angeles and fuelling the crack epidemic had travelled through Nicaragua with the CIA's knowledge. John Kiriakou's account stresses what Webb did and did not claim — that the agency turned a blind eye rather than ran the operation — and that three separate federal investigations later found his reporting correct.

contra-rebels.title: Domino theory
contra-rebels.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

contra-rebels.title: Iran-Contra
contra-rebels.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

contra-rebels.title: Oscar Blandón
contra-rebels.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Civil confinement
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The policy John Kiriakou proposed from inside FCI Loretto — moving sex offenders to a secure location on prison grounds after their sentences end rather than releasing them — an argument that drew public criticism and which he defends with the case of a prisoner named Cook.

cook-the-recidivist.title: FCI Loretto
cook-the-recidivist.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Federal prison security levels
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The ladder of federal custody as John Kiriakou describes it — penitentiary, medium, low and minimum-security camp — the transfer rules that let long-sentence prisoners descend it, and why that placed dangerous men inside the low-security prison where he served his sentence.

cook-the-recidivist.title: The black box
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Legal mail
cook-the-recidivist.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

cook-the-recidivist.title: Depression in prison
cook-the-recidivist.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

cori-bush.title: AIPAC
cori-bush.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cori-bush.title: Jamaal Bowman
cori-bush.summary: Former U.S. Representative from New York; cited by John Kiriakou alongside Cori Bush as the second documented case of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent House member for criticizing Israeli conduct in the Gaza war.

cori-bush.title: Josh Shapiro
cori-bush.summary: Governor of Pennsylvania; veteran of the Israel Defense Forces, in which he served during his late-teen kibbutz year before returning to U.S. citizenship; cited by John Kiriakou as the principal example of the loyalty question raised by American elected officials who have served the Israeli state — a disqualification Kiriakou states in absolute terms, and one he judges to have ended Shapiro's national prospects.

cori-bush.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
cori-bush.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

cori-bush.title: BDS movement
cori-bush.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

cori-bush.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cori-bush.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Brian Ross
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Counterterrorism Center
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Abu Zubaydah
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

corporate-competitive-intelligence.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
corporate-competitive-intelligence.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: Mark MacGann
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: The Uber whistleblower whose case John Kiriakou presented on his own programme: a 52-year-old Irishman who ran the company''s lobbying across Europe, the Middle East and Africa from 2014 to 2016, and who later handed 124,000 pages of internal documents covering 2013 to 2017 to the Guardian. Kiriakou''s account turns on one point — that the opportunity Uber marketed to low-income drivers was never what it claimed, and that the company''s leadership knew it from the beginning.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: The UPMC whistleblower case
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: A False Claims Act suit against neurosurgeons at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, alleging inflated operation counts and needlessly complex procedures. John Kiriakou — a Pittsburgh native — argues the charge is not merely fraud but deliberate endangerment of patients for profit, calls the False Claims Act 'the RICO statute of health care', and says the story deserved national coverage it never got.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: Chelsea Manning
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: Jeremy Hammond
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: The hacker held in contempt for refusing to testify against Julian Assange before a grand jury. John Kiriakou''s point about his case is administrative rather than constitutional: Hammond was pulled out of the Bureau of Prisons drug and alcohol programme two months short of completing it, forfeiting the eighteen months it would have taken off his sentence — a penalty that applied whether or not he ever agreed to testify.

corporate-whistleblower-protections.title: The OPCW Douma investigation
corporate-whistleblower-protections.summary: The chemical weapons inquiry into the alleged 2018 attack in Douma, Syria, which John Kiriakou describes as falsified rather than merely disputed: fifteen investigators objected that their analysis had been taken out of context or fabricated outright, and the false version was then used to reach a political conclusion. He credits WikiLeaks with being the only reason any of it is public — and notes that major American shows carried on repeating the original story anyway.

cory-booker.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cory-booker.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

cory-booker.title: Jonathan Pollard
cory-booker.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

cory-booker.title: MOSSAD
cory-booker.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

cory-booker.title: AIPAC
cory-booker.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

cory-booker.title: Alexa
cory-booker.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

cory-booker.title: Restraint Camp
cory-booker.summary: A term for foreign-policy conservatives who favor ending forever wars and regime-change interventions; not attributable to Kiriakou in the corpus.

counterterrorism-center.title: Geneva Conventions
counterterrorism-center.summary: The laws of war at the center of John Kiriakou''s most-told confrontation story: finding hooded prisoners in Pakistan, he demanded of the officer in charge — "Are you seriously telling me that you have never read the Geneva Convention? It is a war crime to put hoods on them. Take the hoods off." The two reported each other to headquarters; Kiriakou got in trouble — "they didn''t give two shits about the Geneva Convention." He indicts the Bush administration''s twin dodges: that al-Qaeda fighters, as non-state actors, fell outside the Conventions'' protections, and that the techniques weren''t torture at all.

counterterrorism-center.title: Mort Halperin
counterterrorism-center.summary: Former Assistant Secretary of State, Assistant Secretary of Defense, and senior director of the National Security Council; author of the law John Kiriakou was convicted of violating (the Intelligence Identities Protection Act); wrote to President Obama stating that this is not why he wrote the law and that Kiriakou should be pardoned.

counterterrorism-center.title: Corporate competitive intelligence
counterterrorism-center.summary: The private-sector discipline John Kiriakou entered on leaving the CIA in 2004: collecting human-source intelligence on rival firms for a big-four accountancy. He was the fourth CIA officer Deloitte had hired into a group that paired former intelligence collectors with corporate research analysts, and his requirements were a rival''s pricing models, its discount structure, and which of its top-producing partners were unhappy enough to be poached. All the major firms, he says, run the same operation against each other.

counterterrorism-center.title: The promotion panel
counterterrorism-center.summary: The CIA board that reviews an officer for advancement, and the one that reviewed John Kiriakou weeks after the Abu Zubaydah capture — where his refusal to be trained in the enhanced interrogation techniques was recorded as *"a shocking lack of commitment to counterterrorism"*, and he was passed over.

counterterrorism-center.title: Dead drop
counterterrorism-center.summary: The classic tradecraft technique of passing material through a hidden location rather than a meeting. Per John Kiriakou, the hard part is not the drop but everything around it — in a sophisticated counterintelligence environment, merely identifying a viable site is very difficult, and the drop itself is bracketed by surveillance detection routes and a signal mark that can turn a single document into a sixteen-hour workday. It was the only element of clandestine training he struggled with, and the only exercise he was ever criticized for.

counterterrorism-center.title: Mohamedou Ould Slahi
counterterrorism-center.summary: Mauritanian citizen, medical student in Germany at the time of his 2001 detention; held at Guantánamo Bay for fourteen years on the basis of one phone call from his cousin asking him to relay news of a family death to a second cousin who was in al-Qaeda; identified by John Kiriakou as one of the most morally significant figures of the post-9/11 period; subject of the film The Mauritanian; became a personal friend of Kiriakou's after both men were released.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The bomb course
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The week-long CIA explosives course at a facility in another state, where John Kiriakou learned to build a Molotov cocktail, then a detonator rig, then an ammonium nitrate bomb — his final exam, which put a van's transmission three hundred yards into the woods.

counterterrorist-driving.title: Kiriakou's titanium knee
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The injury John Kiriakou took crashing a junkyard car through a roadblock in CIA training — his seat tore free of the floor and his knees hit the dashboard — which sixteen years later was diagnosed as spontaneous osteonecrosis and cost him the joint.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The shooting house
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The live-fire decision course at the Farm where a trainee has about three quarters of a second to decide whether the figure at the window is a gunman or a woman holding a baby — and where John Kiriakou says he never missed, which he connects to his own account of the temperament the CIA selects for.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The Advanced Counterterrorism Operations course
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The six-week CIA course for which John Kiriakou says he was one of only about a dozen officers in the entire agency selected — and which he finished, as he puts it, just in time for 9/11.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The operations course graduation
counterterrorist-driving.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

counterterrorist-driving.title: The El Salvador hotel drill
counterterrorist-driving.summary: A night exercise at the Farm in which trainees sat alone in a mock flea-bag hotel room in El Salvador, were visited by two men announcing housekeeping, and were shot with paint pellets. All eight failed, and the lesson John Kiriakou drew from it he says he never forgot.

cover-position.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
cover-position.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

cover-position.title: Operational vehicles
cover-position.summary: The cars John Kiriakou used in the field. In the Middle East they were whatever the rental company supplied — usually a Toyota — on the reasoning that anonymity was the point; in Athens, where the threat justified it, he was issued a factory-built, level-four armoured BMW 540 that broke down constantly.

cover-position.title: Surveillance detection route
cover-position.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

cover-position.title: The botched pitch
cover-position.summary: The one operation John Kiriakou describes as a failure of his career: a two-year development of a terrorist working under journalist cover, brought to the point of a recruitment pitch and destroyed at the table when his station chief seized the meeting and threatened the target instead of pitching him. The target fled screaming for police, the host government''s deputy prime minister complained to the American ambassador, and the man later described the encounter to a third intelligence service as an approach by "two caricatures of CIA men."

cover-position.title: Commercial off-the-shelf tradecraft
cover-position.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how much CIA field equipment is simply bought rather than built. He describes the pen recorder arriving while he was in Pakistan and early GPS units in Athens being repurposed to map surveillance detection routes, and states the underlying economics: buying existing technology is far cheaper than developing it from scratch.

cover-position.title: 2028 presidential field
cover-position.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

cover-stop.title: John Kiriakou
cover-stop.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

cover-stop.title: Chief of station
cover-stop.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

cover-stop.title: Intelligence peddlers
cover-stop.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

cover-stop.title: Andrew Warren
cover-stop.summary: Former CIA officer and station chief who, per John Kiriakou, was protected and lavishly funded by his supervisor "Mary Margaret," then convicted of raping 23 women — videotaping every attack — before a post-prison religious conversion and further sexual assault convictions.

cover-stop.title: Benazir Bhutto
cover-stop.summary: Pakistani politician; twice Prime Minister of Pakistan; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as personally corrupt and married to an even more corrupt husband

cover-stop.title: Central Intelligence Agency
cover-stop.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

covert-action-program.title: No plan for day two
covert-action-program.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned early at the CIA: the United States is very good at overthrowing governments and has no idea what to do afterwards. The planning is all about day one. He lists Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Syria, Sudan and Somalia as the record, and gives three reasons the same officials keep repeating the mistake.

covert-action-program.title: Maduro Capture
covert-action-program.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

covert-action-program.title: María Corina Machado
covert-action-program.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

covert-action-program.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
covert-action-program.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

covert-action-program.title: Manuel Noriega
covert-action-program.summary: Panamanian dictator and one of the most notorious drug traffickers in the Western Hemisphere who, John Kiriakou notes, was a paid CIA source for decades before being driven from the Vatican embassy in Panama City by U.S. forces blasting death metal and captured in the 1989 invasion.

covert-action-program.title: The Libyan constitution unveiling
covert-action-program.summary: A launch event John Kiriakou attended in Washington after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi: a new Libyan constitution, commissioned by wealthy exiles from a lobbying firm, unveiled at the lobbying firm''s offices. He calls the document better than the American one — equal rights for everybody, the oil money shared — and notes that nothing whatever was done with it, because nobody in Washington had heard of the people behind it.

covertaction-magazine.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
covertaction-magazine.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

covertaction-magazine.title: Julian Assange
covertaction-magazine.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

covertaction-magazine.title: Federal plea coercion
covertaction-magazine.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

covertaction-magazine.title: Guantanamo Bay
covertaction-magazine.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

covertaction-magazine.title: Osama bin Laden
covertaction-magazine.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

covertaction-magazine.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
covertaction-magazine.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

craig-murray.title: Russiagate
craig-murray.summary: John Kiriakou''s rebuttal of the claim that Russia swung the 2016 U.S. election: the Mueller report found no interference, the DNC emails were leaked in person rather than remotely hacked, and Russia''s roughly $50,000 in Facebook ads — half spent after the election — was trivial against billions in campaign spending.

craig-murray.title: Bill Binney
craig-murray.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

craig-murray.title: Iran-Contra
craig-murray.summary: The mid-1980s scandal in which the Reagan administration secretly sold weapons to Iran and diverted the proceeds — laundered through Cyprus — to fund the Contra rebels in Nicaragua. Per John Kiriakou, Iran-Contra marks the precise end of what he calls the ''golden age'' of congressional intelligence oversight: the roughly 1975–1982 window opened by the Church and Pike Committees, when ''serious people, heavyweights'' actually held the CIA accountable. After Iran-Contra, he says, the oversight committees reverted to being ''cheerleaders'' for the agency — a posture that has held ever since.

craig-murray.title: Julian Assange
craig-murray.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

craig-murray.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
craig-murray.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

craig-murray.title: McCain-Feinstein Amendment
craig-murray.summary: 2015 amendment, sponsored by Senator John McCain, that formally and permanently banned torture by U.S. government personnel, codifying the Army Field Manual as the single interrogation standard for all agencies. Per John Kiriakou, it restored the original language of the 1946 Federal Torture Act after U.S. policy had drifted from it through post-9/11 reinterpretation — and passed, he says, in part because of his own 2007 whistleblowing.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Lie Detection
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, both a subject he addresses in his book The CIA Insider's Guide to Lying and Lie Detection and a practical skill he describes using throughout his career. Physical tells include gaze direction (down to conceal, up to construct), fidgeting, and throat-clearing; structural tells — losing the thread mid-conversation and self-contradiction — are more reliable, because the truth is stable while a lie requires maintenance and eventually collapses under its own complexity.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Asset acquisition cycle
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Diesel Therapy
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a punitive practice within the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons in which an inmate is placed into indefinite transit — moved continuously from facility to facility — for up to six months, with no access to phone, email, or pen and paper, and listed on the BOP website only as 'in transit' with no destination. Kiriakou described it as the one threat at FCI Loretto that actually frightened him.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: FCI Loretto
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

critical-analytic-thinking.title: Safe Housekeeper
critical-analytic-thinking.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person recruited by a CIA officer to rent and maintain an apartment or other premises as a safe house, using their own name and identity to conceal any CIA connection. The role itself is minimal — rent the apartment, keep it clean, keep it stocked with water — but the recruitment is itself a covert operation requiring the same persuasion and pressure techniques used to acquire any sensitive asset. Kiriakou recruited a safe housekeeper overseas and believes the pressure he applied may have caused her a nervous breakdown.

crypto-ag.title: Over-classification
crypto-ag.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

crypto-ag.title: Julian Assange
crypto-ag.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

crypto-ag.title: Encryption before the key
crypto-ag.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where encryption actually fails, offered against John McAfee''s claim that no communication can be private. Kiriakou defers to the technologists he knows — Edward Snowden, Bill Binney, Thomas Drake and Kirk Wiebe — who tell him sufficiently sophisticated encryption does work. The exposure is upstream of the cipher: if an agency can reach your machine as you type, before you hit the encryption key, the encryption never gets a chance.

crypto-ag.title: Bernie Sanders
crypto-ag.summary: United States senator from Vermont. John Kiriakou, who watched him daily from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, describes Sanders holding open breakfast in the Senate cafeteria for anyone who walked in — insisting only that they call him "Bernie" — and names him the one 2016 candidate willing to talk about shrinking the military.

crypto-ag.title: Bill Barr
crypto-ag.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

crypto-ag.title: Blueprint for Free Speech
crypto-ag.summary: The Australian non-governmental organisation that drafts whistleblower protection legislation and markets it to governments around the world, and which hired John Kiriakou in 2015 to help write Greece's law. Its board is mostly academics and transparency activists; Kiriakou credits it with successes in Canada, Zambia, Jamaica and Ukraine, and names its founder and director as Suelette Dreyfus, whom he describes as a co-founder of WikiLeaks with Julian Assange.

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Surveillance detection route
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Abu Zubaydah
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Asset acquisition cycle
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.title: Double-Agent Capture
ctc-line-of-duty-deaths.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Daniel Ortega
cuba-protests-2021.summary: The president of Nicaragua, and the case John Kiriakou contrasts with Cuba: where he read the 2021 Cuban protests as a test run, he said Nicaragua''s circumstances — a social security shortfall, a rise in the price of bread, and eight opposition party leaders arrested and imprisoned before an election — amounted to grounds for a real uprising.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Haiti
cuba-protests-2021.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Caleb Maupin
cuba-protests-2021.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
cuba-protests-2021.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

cuba-protests-2021.title: The Backstory
cuba-protests-2021.summary: The daily Radio Sputnik programme John Kiriakou co-hosted with Lee Stranahan, carried on terrestrial radio in the Washington area as well as online. It was the successor to his earlier show Loud and Clear with Brian Becker, and he described its format as two men with a beer talking about the day.

cuba-protests-2021.title: Vladimir Putin
cuba-protests-2021.summary: President of Russia. Per John Kiriakou, Putin twice raised joining NATO — floating it to Bill Clinton and later telling Barack Obama Russia would like to explore membership — and was refused both times; Kiriakou has never believed Putin wants to conquer Ukraine or Eastern Europe, argues U.S. hostility toward Russia is driven by defense contractors and a permanent wartime economy, and notes the irony that Putin was the anti-communist the U.S. itself backed in the Yeltsin era.

cuban-double-agents.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
cuban-double-agents.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

cuban-double-agents.title: MK-Ultra
cuban-double-agents.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

cuban-double-agents.title: Robert Hanssen
cuban-double-agents.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

cuban-double-agents.title: Israel's counterintelligence threat ranking
cuban-double-agents.summary: John Kiriakou's repeated point that the American intelligence community formally ranks Israel a critical counterintelligence threat — the same tier as North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba — specifically for spying on and infiltrating the US government, and that policy has responded by giving Israel more access rather than less.

cuban-double-agents.title: "He''s been ours since the ''70s"
cuban-double-agents.summary: An episode John Kiriakou uses to convey the scale of CIA penetration of foreign political classes: spotting a former prime minister at a diplomatic cocktail party, rushing back to the embassy to file for a name trace and vulnerability assessment before anyone else could approach him, and receiving a same-day instruction to cease and desist because the man had already been an agency asset for decades.

cuban-double-agents.title: Andres Serrano
cuban-double-agents.summary: American artist; in the 1980s the creator of Piss Christ — a beaker of urine containing an inverted crucifix — which so enraged President Ronald Reagan that he cut off funding to the National Endowment for the Arts. Per John Kiriakou, also the photographer of a torture-chamber series at Tate Modern, London, in which one panel is a photograph of Kiriakou next to a panel of a U.S. military torturer.

curtailment-cables.title: The bowl of dates
curtailment-cables.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

curtailment-cables.title: The rogue officer remark
curtailment-cables.summary: The answer President George W. Bush shouted to a reporter on his way to the helicopter — that if there was torture, it was the work of a rogue CIA officer — which John Kiriakou has said convinced him he was about to be made the scapegoat, and which led him to accept Brian Ross's interview offer.

curtailment-cables.title: The declination letter
curtailment-cables.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

curtailment-cables.title: Arabic and Greek
curtailment-cables.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

curtailment-cables.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
curtailment-cables.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

curtailment-cables.title: The oath in the auditorium
curtailment-cables.summary: The scene John Kiriakou returns to when asked what set him on the path to blowing the whistle: standing in the CIA''s auditorium on his first day with three hundred other new hires, right hand in the air, swearing to uphold the Constitution against all enemies foreign and domestic — and his later suspicion that he may have been the only person in the room who meant it.

curveball.title: Ahmed Chalabi
curveball.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

curveball.title: Valerie Plame
curveball.summary: Covert CIA case officer whose identity was publicly outed by the Bush administration in retaliation for her husband, former U.S. ambassador to Niger Joseph Wilson, publishing a New York Times op-ed debunking the administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium from Niger. Per John Kiriakou, Plame's CIA career ended on the day her cover was blown — she could never travel overseas under cover again; no one was prosecuted for the leak.

curveball.title: Saddam Hussein
curveball.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

curveball.title: Joseph Wilson
curveball.summary: Former U.S. Ambassador to Niger and former Deputy Chief of Mission in Baghdad; husband of covert CIA officer Valerie Plame; in 2003 traveled to Niger at CIA request to investigate the Bush administration's claim that Iraq had attempted to purchase yellowcake uranium for a nuclear weapon, found no such Iraqi approach had occurred, and published a New York Times op-ed debunking the claim — triggering the administration's retaliatory outing of his wife.

curveball.title: George W. Bush
curveball.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

curveball.title: John Kiriakou
curveball.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

custody-standoff.title: Mary Jane Stevens
custody-standoff.summary: The lawyer who represented John Kiriakou through his custody dispute — who told him to wait for Monday and go to court, was ignored, and then got the assurance from a hostile police chief that let him walk into the hearing without being arrested.

custody-standoff.title: Cofer Black
custody-standoff.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

custody-standoff.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
custody-standoff.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

custody-standoff.title: The Foreign Relations volume and the sources still alive
custody-standoff.summary: The errand that put John Kiriakou and Cofer Black in a car to the White House on the morning of 11 September 2001: three declassified cables due to be printed in a State Department history volume named CIA sources who were still living — and an obscure law requiring the United States to resettle any source it outs.

custody-standoff.title: John Kiriakou
custody-standoff.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

custody-standoff.title: The liaison class
custody-standoff.summary: The course John Kiriakou ran at the CIA for visiting officers of allied intelligence services — the setting for Cofer Black's warning weeks before 9/11, and the reason Kiriakou was in the counterterrorism chief's office to ask whether he had meant it.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: The Oman oil lease
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: A private-intelligence assignment in which an oil company that had leased a field on Oman's border with Yemen for ninety-nine years discovered al-Qaeda controlled the ground, and sent John Kiriakou to Muscat to ask whether the Omani government would clear them out.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: The Romanian silver mine
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The private-intelligence assignment John Kiriakou uses to explain what commercial analysis actually buys: a mining client wanted to know who would win a Romanian municipal election, because a silver deposit lay under a village that would have to be destroyed to reach it.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: Abraxas Corporation
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: David Boies
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

cypriot-billionaire-investigation.title: Black Cube
cypriot-billionaire-investigation.summary: Israeli [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence) staffed by former Mossad personnel; reportedly used by attorney David Boies in the Jeffrey Epstein litigation; named by John Kiriakou as a representative of the no-compunction operating posture characteristic of Israeli private and public intelligence.

cyprus-green-line.title: Kiriakou's Cypriot ancestry
cyprus-green-line.summary: The DNA result showing John Kiriakou to be 24 per cent Cypriot — his largest single ancestry — which corrected a family belief that the line came from Crete and coincided with an invitation to address a Cypriot diaspora conference.

cyprus-green-line.title: John Kerry
cyprus-green-line.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

cyprus-green-line.title: Origin of the Kiriakou name
cyprus-green-line.summary: The Kiriakou surname originates in a clerical error at a Rhodes courthouse, where John Kiriakou's great-great-grandfather, arrested for stealing a potato while starving, gave a patronymic that was written down as his family name and never corrected.

cyprus-green-line.title: Abu Zubaydah
cyprus-green-line.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

cyprus-green-line.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
cyprus-green-line.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

cyprus-green-line.title: The false volunteer
cyprus-green-line.summary: A walk-in at an American embassy who claimed access to a high-priority target, was placed under surveillance and found to be a restaurant dishwasher, and whom John Kiriakou deliberately intimidated into never approaching an American embassy again.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: Iran's 2024 drone retaliation
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Iran's telegraphed 2024 drone strike on Israel — hundreds of slow drones, launched with advance warning to the U.S. and Jordan, nearly all shot down, which he reads as a controlled show of force and an intelligence victory that exposed the Iron Dome.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: The Arab states and the Gaza war
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's country-by-country reading of how the Arab governments positioned themselves after October 2023 — the Gulf states ranked by their fear of Iran, Jordan caught between its border and its population, Egypt sealing Rafah to prevent a repeat of earlier refugee flows — and his conclusion that every one of them is calculating damage to itself first and the Palestinians second.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: China as economic threat
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: The JCPOA
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: The Iran nuclear agreement, which John Kiriakou describes as having worked for the two or three years it was in force under an inspection regime identical to the one the United Nations had used in Iraq. He treats the American withdrawal as a strategic error that also exposed a contradiction in American law, since sanctioning every country doing business with Iran would have meant sanctioning Britain, France, Germany and Japan.

damascus-consulate-strike.title: Afghan heroin policy
damascus-consulate-strike.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Julian Assange
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Der Spiegel
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: At a 2026 Berlin panel, a former Der Spiegel journalist said it took him years before he could call Julian Assange a publisher rather than an activist.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Wikileaks as a System
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Per John Kiriakou, WikiLeaks functions less as a single leader than as a durable system — one that protected whistleblowers, helped popularize the term "whistleblower" itself, was credited with contributing to the Arab Spring, weathered pressure to become a defanged NGO, and outlasted the political fallout of its 2010 cable releases (including, in Kiriakou's account, an unintended assist to Donald Trump's election).

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

daniel-domscheit-berg.title: Andrew Feinstein
daniel-domscheit-berg.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

daniel-duggan.title: Eastern State Penitentiary
daniel-duggan.summary: The Philadelphia prison where, per John Kiriakou, solitary confinement was invented in 1829 — a neo-Gothic stone penitentiary of tiny cells arranged as spokes around a central guard post, each containing a bed, a chair, a table, a chamber pot and a Bible, on the theory that a man left alone with scripture would emerge a law-abiding Christian. What happened instead, Kiriakou says, is that everybody went insane — and the practice was kept anyway, because it worked as punishment.

daniel-duggan.title: Julian Assange
daniel-duggan.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-duggan.title: Communications management unit
daniel-duggan.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

daniel-duggan.title: Solitary confinement
daniel-duggan.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

daniel-duggan.title: FCI Loretto
daniel-duggan.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

daniel-duggan.title: Assange and solitary confinement
daniel-duggan.summary: John Kiriakou's 2018 argument that Julian Assange's isolation inside the Ecuadorian embassy amounted to solitary confinement — a practice the United Nations classes as torture — and that everybody breaks under it eventually, however strong they are.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Espionage Act
daniel-ellsberg.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Julian Assange
daniel-ellsberg.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

daniel-ellsberg.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
daniel-ellsberg.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president.
