Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

daniel-ellsberg.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
daniel-ellsberg.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

daniel-ellsberg.title: John Kiriakou
daniel-ellsberg.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

daniel-ellsberg.title: Tucker Carlson 2026 FARA referral
daniel-ellsberg.summary: The March 2026 criminal referral against Tucker Carlson to the U.S. Department of Justice accusing him of treason, espionage and Foreign Agents Registration Act violations that John Kiriakou says was widely misattributed to the CIA before the pro-Israel political activist Laura Loomer publicly claimed authorship the following day; Kiriakou treats the episode as an escalation from Israeli-aligned political actors and warns Carlson to worry less about legal jeopardy than about physical safety.

daniel-hale.title: RDAP program
daniel-hale.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which can shave 12 to 18 months off a federal sentence; John Kiriakou repeatedly advises fellow whistleblowers that, combined with good behavior and a halfway house, it can turn a five-year sentence into as little as two and a half years.

daniel-hale.title: The roadblock strike
daniel-hale.summary: The drone strike Daniel Hale described at his own sentencing and that John Kiriakou retells as the reason Hale became a whistleblower: a car approaching a U.S. roadblock in Afghanistan, two girls aged six and nine visible inside, an order to fire given twice over Hale''s objection, and a father who afterwards hid his daughters'' bodies in a village dumpster for fear that special forces would take them.

daniel-hale.title: Diary of a CEO — January 2026 Kiriakou interview
daniel-hale.summary: The January 2026 long-form appearance by John Kiriakou on Steven Bartlett's Diary of a CEO podcast that a University of Texas at Austin sophomore then cut into TikTok shorts — sped and slowed, with lasers added — kicking off the Gen Z discovery of Kiriakou that pushed his cameo requests past 1,900 and drew a 2:30 a.m. representation call in Dubai from the Creative Artists Agency; Kiriakou treats it as the pivot after which stories he had been telling for nineteen years finally landed.

daniel-hale.title: National Bird
daniel-hale.summary: Award-winning documentary on the U.S. drone program featuring whistleblower Daniel Hale; John Kiriakou calls it essential viewing, noting its footage of drone operators debating on audio whether the figures in their crosshairs are children before firing.

daniel-hale.title: Phil Ochs
daniel-hale.summary: 1960s–70s protest folk singer; John Kiriakou retells a story from Pete Seeger about the night Ochs — who had fallen into depression after being unable to sing following a mugging in Africa — called Seeger just before taking his own life.

daniel-hale.title: Qasem Soleimani
daniel-hale.summary: The Iranian general killed by an American drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. John Kiriakou, speaking the following morning, called him arguably the second most important person in Iran and a potential successor to the supreme leader, relayed the Iranian comparison that killing him was worse than killing Petraeus or Mattis — 'this is like killing Pence' — and dismissed talk of de-escalation as a pipe dream.

daniel-ortega.title: The 2021 Cuba protests
daniel-ortega.summary: The July 2021 demonstrations in Cuba, which John Kiriakou declined to read as the beginning of a revolution. He called them a test run to gauge the government's reaction, objected that a New York Times line about Democrats treading lightly in Florida meant nothing anyone could act on, and noted that everything touching Cuba is too politically loaded in the United States to be discussed plainly.

daniel-ortega.title: Haiti
daniel-ortega.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

daniel-ortega.title: Caleb Maupin
daniel-ortega.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

daniel-ortega.title: The Backstory
daniel-ortega.summary: The daily Radio Sputnik programme John Kiriakou co-hosted with Lee Stranahan, carried on terrestrial radio in the Washington area as well as online. It was the successor to his earlier show Loud and Clear with Brian Becker, and he described its format as two men with a beer talking about the day.

daniel-ortega.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
daniel-ortega.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

daniel-ortega.title: Iran under sanctions: daily life
daniel-ortega.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being talked out of his own assumptions about Iran by a close friend who travels there once or twice a year and eventually started filming ordinary life — leading him to conclude that a country with no American embassy, diplomatic presence or business presence since 1979 nonetheless lacks for nothing.

dark-alliance.title: Contra rebels
dark-alliance.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

dark-alliance.title: Oscar Blandón
dark-alliance.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

dark-alliance.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
dark-alliance.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

dark-alliance.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
dark-alliance.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

dark-alliance.title: Domino theory
dark-alliance.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

dark-alliance.title: Walter Pincus
dark-alliance.summary: The Washington Post reporter who, in John Kiriakou's account of the Gary Webb affair, took the CIA's side of the cocaine story and put it on the paper's front page — wrong, and Kiriakou believes knowingly so.

darpa-lifelog.title: Abu Zubaydah
darpa-lifelog.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

darpa-lifelog.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
darpa-lifelog.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

darpa-lifelog.title: Thomas Drake
darpa-lifelog.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

darpa-lifelog.title: Walk-in
darpa-lifelog.summary: In John Kiriakou's telling, someone who walks into an embassy offering information; 95% are lunatics or liars, some are 'intelligence peddlers' or hostile 'probes,' and about 1% are 'the real McCoy' — a framework he used to see through a supposed 'walk-in' tip during the Abu Zubaydah hunt. A genuine walk-in — a witness to a terrorist assassination — was later hypnotized by CIA psychologists in a London hotel room and read back a stolen van's license plate, verifying his account.

darpa-lifelog.title: Palantir Technologies
darpa-lifelog.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

darpa-lifelog.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
darpa-lifelog.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: General Abdul Rashid Dostum
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: Northern Alliance Afghan warlord; overseer of the November–December 2001 Dasht-i-Leili massacre; characterized by John Kiriakou as a serial defector between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance and as a psychopath.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: John Kiriakou
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: John Kerry
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

dasht-i-leili-massacre.title: Qala-i-Jangi uprising
dasht-i-leili-massacre.summary: The late-November 2001 prisoner uprising at a fortress in northern Afghanistan during which CIA officer Mike Spann was killed; the event during which the American al-Qaeda figure John Walker Lindh was captured; among the first major firefights of the post-9/11 Afghan campaign.

dave-phillips.title: The shank planting incident
dave-phillips.summary: The episode at FCI Loretto in which Dave Phillips made two homemade weapons, planted them on a pedophile the group was feuding with and informed on him anonymously — a plan John Kiriakou refused to join, and which cost Phillips a transfer while leaving Kiriakou untouched.

dave-phillips.title: Seven thousand letters
dave-phillips.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

dave-phillips.title: Spotting a CIA impostor
dave-phillips.summary: John Kiriakou's method for exposing people who falsely claim to have served in the CIA — a short sequence of questions about directorate, division and leadership whose correct answers, he says, cannot be guessed by anyone who was never inside.

dave-phillips.title: Rule six: the body endures more than the brain says
dave-phillips.summary: The CIA maxim John Kiriakou carried into prison — that the human body can take much more punishment than the brain believes — which he applied first to being punched in the face and then, more importantly, to depression.

dave-phillips.title: Sarge
dave-phillips.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer John Kiriakou named in a Letter from Loretto for swearing at him and trashing his cell — conduct he later learned was not merely a Bureau of Prisons infraction but a misdemeanour crime, and one of two offences he says the letter inadvertently exposed.

dave-phillips.title: The Second Chance Act
dave-phillips.summary: The resentencing law John Kiriakou read about in The New York Times inside FCI Loretto and used to win freedom for other prisoners — most notably Mark Lanzalotti, whose petition he wrote and who was released 17 years into a 30-year sentence.

david-boies.title: Alexander Acosta and the sweetheart deal
david-boies.summary: The US attorney who gave Jeffrey Epstein his 2006 non-prosecution agreement and later said he had been ordered to — a chain of command John Kiriakou traces upward to an attorney general famous for his powerlessness, and therefore to somebody above him whom nobody has ever named.

david-boies.title: Jeffrey Epstein
david-boies.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

david-boies.title: The Epstein statute of limitations
david-boies.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that nobody in the United States will be prosecuted over the Jeffrey Epstein case because the five-year limitation period on the sex offences has run — a lapse he says may itself have been part of the plan, and which leaves only an improbable conspiracy theory of the cover-up as a route to charges.

david-boies.title: Jonathan Pollard
david-boies.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

david-boies.title: MOSSAD
david-boies.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

david-boies.title: AIPAC
david-boies.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

david-petraeus.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
david-petraeus.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

david-petraeus.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
david-petraeus.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

david-petraeus.title: John Kiriakou
david-petraeus.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

david-petraeus.title: John Brennan
david-petraeus.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

david-petraeus.title: Public safety factor
david-petraeus.summary: The Bureau of Prisons classification that barred Kiriakou from a minimum-security camp by rating him as dangerous as a murderer, applied over the objections of both his sentencing judge and the prosecutor who convicted him.

david-petraeus.title: The CIA–State Department cover agreement
david-petraeus.summary: The standing arrangement under which CIA officers serve abroad under State Department cover. As a senior investigator for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, John Kiriakou was told the agency was misusing the agreement to place officers from the torture program under diplomatic cover so that publishing their names would expose journalists to the Intelligence Identities Protection Act. His written query, sent over Senator John Kerry''s signature, came back classified above his own clearance.

david-ransom.title: John Kiriakou
david-ransom.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

david-ransom.title: John Brennan
david-ransom.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

david-ransom.title: David Rockefeller in Bahrain
david-ransom.summary: Per John Kiriakou — economic officer at the American Embassy in Bahrain, 1994–1996, and control officer for a David Rockefeller visit — Rockefeller''s award from the US-Bahrain Banking Society was a cover stop. After three days of documented public appearances, Rockefeller flew on a military plane to Baghdad to deliver a secret message to Saddam Hussein: stop violating sanctions, or the United States would take military action. Kiriakou cites the trip as a textbook case of how public figures are used as deniable back-channel intermediaries.

david-ransom.title: Abu Zubaydah
david-ransom.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

david-ransom.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
david-ransom.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

david-ransom.title: Kiriakou on Christmas
david-ransom.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding Christmas so depressing since his two divorces that he does not decorate or mark it at all — and of the year he replaced it by taking his children to every station on the New York City subway system in a single day.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: David Ransom
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Thomas Drake
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: John Kiriakou
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Gerald Bull
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: British inventor of the "big gun" — a barrel so large it had to be leaned against a mountain — first offered to Israel and rejected, then sold to Iraq under Saddam Hussein; assassinated by Mossad in Brussels once Iraqi engineers solved the cracking problem with a barrel-smoothing sleeve nicknamed "the condom," after which the Israelis also bombed the gun itself.

david-rockefeller-bahrain.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
david-rockefeller-bahrain.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

dead-drop-podcast.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
dead-drop-podcast.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

dead-drop-podcast.title: President's Daily Brief
dead-drop-podcast.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

dead-drop-podcast.title: John Kiriakou
dead-drop-podcast.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dead-drop-podcast.title: Threats against John Kiriakou
dead-drop-podcast.summary: The stalkers and death threats John Kiriakou has received since going public in 2007 — including a woman who believed he had proposed to her in code on C-SPAN and arrived at his office armed, and a caller who recited his son's home address.

dead-drop-podcast.title: Barry Eisler
dead-drop-podcast.summary: Former CIA officer turned bestselling novelist, and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou's, who describes him as one of the very few former intelligence officers to have succeeded at storytelling outside the secret world as thoroughly as he did inside it.

dead-drop-podcast.title: Greater and Lesser Tunb Islands
dead-drop-podcast.summary: Two small, largely uninhabited islands in the Persian Gulf, belonging to the emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, occupied by Iran in a 1990s incident John Kiriakou recounts as CIA analyst; Kiriakou correctly predicted the UAE would not go to war over them given Sharjah's heavy trade dependence on Iran.

dead-drop.title: Central Intelligence Agency
dead-drop.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

dead-drop.title: John Kiriakou
dead-drop.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dead-drop.title: Counterterrorism Center
dead-drop.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

dead-drop.title: Donald Trump
dead-drop.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

dead-drop.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
dead-drop.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

dead-drop.title: PricewaterhouseCoopers
dead-drop.summary: The Big Four accounting firm that keeps intersecting John Kiriakou's story — as a target of the corporate human-source intelligence he collected after leaving the CIA, as the audience of 140 partners he told his Pakistan recruitment story to ("what I did and what you do really isn't that different"), as the auditor that spent three years trying to find the Pentagon's money before giving up, and as the Greek government's book-cooking auditor in the debt crisis, never prosecuted.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Advice to the next generation
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a Gen Z viewer who said he felt helpless — that helplessness is not new, that 1968 and 1969 were worse, and that the remedy is four concrete things: run for any office at all, starting with the local water board; demonstrate; ride your elected officials and vote them out if they will not do what they are told; and write.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: 2026 Iran war
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: China's base in Djibouti
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Irish intelligence services
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: Ireland's intelligence and law-enforcement services, which John Kiriakou toured and met with during a speaking trip to Belfast, Cork, Dublin, and Waterford. Per Kiriakou, Irish intelligence and the Garda are especially strong at anti-money-laundering investigation and counterterrorism — the latter traced, he says, to the large number of Irish militants trained by Carlos the Jackal in Libya and Lebanon during the 1970s.

death-of-investigative-journalism.title: Kent State shooting
death-of-investigative-journalism.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Whistleblower psychology
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Communications management unit
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Daniel Ellsberg
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Julian Assange
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: Sigurdur Thordarson
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: The FBI's key witness against Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou as a convicted paedophile, a convicted embezzler and a self-admitted liar — one of three facts he lists, alongside the bugging of the Ecuadorian embassy and the reported plot to kidnap or kill Assange, in asking whether judges can keep such things out of their heads.

death-threats-against-kiriakou.title: CIA media relations
death-threats-against-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA shapes press coverage in the 2020s without needing an Operation Mockingbird-style infiltration program — because corporate media now recites CIA messaging willingly, most journalists simply rewrite emailed statements from the agency's Office of Public Affairs, and the CIA allegedly manipulates algorithms and backs podcasts to spread its point of view.

decapitation-strikes.title: Tulsi Gabbard
decapitation-strikes.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

decapitation-strikes.title: 2026 Iran war
decapitation-strikes.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

decapitation-strikes.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
decapitation-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

decapitation-strikes.title: American missile stockpiles
decapitation-strikes.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

decapitation-strikes.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
decapitation-strikes.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

decapitation-strikes.title: Bill Pulte
decapitation-strikes.summary: The housing developer serving as acting Director of National Intelligence after Tulsi Gabbard's resignation. John Kiriakou, relaying the assessment of people who know him, calls him smart, personally decent and completely loyal to Trump — while saying he could not find the ODNI with a map and a GPS unit, and predicting his sole function will be to fire the president's enemies.

declared-officer.title: John Kiriakou
declared-officer.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

declared-officer.title: American shoes
declared-officer.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

declared-officer.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
declared-officer.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

declared-officer.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
declared-officer.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

declared-officer.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
declared-officer.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

declared-officer.title: Admiral William Crowe
declared-officer.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

deep-state.title: National Intelligence Council
deep-state.summary: Body housed at the CIA comprising the most senior analysts drawn from across the entire intelligence community. Its officers — National Intelligence Officers (NIOs) — hold positions at the Senior Intelligence Service level and are responsible for long-range strategic analysis on specific portfolio areas, as well as the production of National Intelligence Estimates. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

deep-state.title: UC Global and the state secrets privilege
deep-state.summary: The Spanish private security company that John Kiriakou says copied the electronic devices of everyone visiting Julian Assange at the Ecuadorian embassy in London and passed the contents to the CIA. When two journalists and two attorneys sued and the case survived dismissal, the agency moved to invoke the state secrets privilege — which Kiriakou treats as proof that a plain constitutional violation can be left without any remedy at all.

deep-state.title: Brad Birkenfeld
deep-state.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

deep-state.title: Islamofascism
deep-state.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

deep-state.title: National Security Council
deep-state.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

deep-state.title: Intelligence switching in the Iran–Iraq war
deep-state.summary: John Kiriakou''s account that during the Iran–Iraq war the United States supplied top-secret overhead imagery to whichever side was losing ground, switching as the front moved — giving the Iraqis imagery when Iran advanced, and the Iranians imagery when Iraq advanced. His summary: ''So it was hideous.''

deloitte-consulting-career.title: Plato Cacheris
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: Corporate competitive intelligence
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: The private-sector discipline John Kiriakou entered on leaving the CIA in 2004: collecting human-source intelligence on rival firms for a big-four accountancy. He was the fourth CIA officer Deloitte had hired into a group that paired former intelligence collectors with corporate research analysts, and his requirements were a rival''s pricing models, its discount structure, and which of its top-producing partners were unhappy enough to be poached. All the major firms, he says, run the same operation against each other.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: The Kite Runner rescue mission
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: 2007 covert operation in which John Kiriakou, newly departed from the CIA and working as a corporate-intelligence consultant, was hired by Paramount Studios to secretly evacuate the Afghan child actors of the film "The Kite Runner" and their extended families after real death threats over the film's content.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: 2026 congressional landscape
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: John Kiriakou's read on two developments affecting the 2026 midterm landscape — the Supreme Court's disallowance of Virginia's redistricting, which he says makes a Democratic House win less certain given widespread Republican-favoring gerrymandering, and Marjorie Taylor Greene's resignation despite winning her last race with 77.5% of the vote, because she knew she could not survive another Republican primary.

deloitte-consulting-career.title: Andrew Warren
deloitte-consulting-career.summary: Former CIA officer and station chief who, per John Kiriakou, was protected and lavishly funded by his supervisor "Mary Margaret," then convicted of raping 23 women — videotaping every attack — before a post-prison religious conversion and further sexual assault convictions.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Kamala Harris
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: Vice President under Joe Biden and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; per John Kiriakou, installed as the party's nominee without a competitive primary despite having failed to reach the 2020 Iowa caucus, and closed out her 2024 campaign courting the Cheney family as a symbol of American values. Kiriakou, a lifelong progressive, says her pursuit of Dick Cheney's endorsement is what decided him against voting for her.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: MOSSAD
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Joe Biden
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: 46th President of the United States; Vice President during the first Obama term; at John Kerry's December 2009 Christmas party, recognized John Kiriakou from a 15-year-prior conversation about a mutual hometown friend, and openly told a Kiriakou colleague within Kiriakou's hearing — and across the room from Kerry — that he disliked the colleague.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: The two-party system
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of American party politics as a spent form — more Americans now call themselves independents than Democrats or Republicans, the two parties are ''two sides of the same coin,'' and ideology has displaced party as the organizing fact. He tells it partly as autobiography: a third-generation Democrat whose grandparents joined the party for Franklin Roosevelt and who left it himself.

democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.title: Israeli strike on Qatar
democratic-party-2025-approval-decline.summary: The Israeli bombing of Qatar that John Kiriakou treats as Benjamin Netanyahu's decisive overreach — an attack on a major non-NATO ally that hosts the largest air force base in the world, which Kiriakou says forced Donald Trump into a public falsehood about advance warning and then into the recognition that Israel acts in Israel's interests rather than America's.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Mike Johnson
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Speaker of the House during the fight over the Epstein files, whose procedural manoeuvres John Kiriakou reads as an attempt to let the issue die in subcommittee, and whose midterm framing of Democrats as communists Kiriakou dismisses outright.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: James Woolsey
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Director of Central Intelligence for twenty-three months at the start of the Clinton administration, forced out over his refusal to discipline anyone after the exposure of Aldrich Ames, and later chairman of Booz Allen Hamilton; John Kiriakou notes that his family attributed four years of illness before his death to Havana syndrome.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: President's Daily Brief
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Aldrich Ames
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Ali Abdullah Saleh
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: President of Yemen for decades, close to both Saudi Arabia and the United States until Yemen's 1990 Security Council vote on Kuwait, after which his country collapsed into civil war; he fled to Saudi Arabia and was killed by a bomb planted in the palace where he had taken refuge.

democratic-redistricting-collapse.title: Bab al-Mandab
democratic-redistricting-collapse.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

denied-areas.title: John Kiriakou
denied-areas.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

denied-areas.title: Central Intelligence Agency
denied-areas.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

denied-areas.title: CIA National Resources Division
denied-areas.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

denied-areas.title: Fabricated intelligence reporting
denied-areas.summary: The three things John Kiriakou says CIA case officers are caught doing — inventing intelligence outright, holding real reports back to smooth out a monthly quota, and padding cover-stop expenses — and his argument that the fabrication is driven by production targets set by bad managers.

denied-areas.title: The hotel bar operation
denied-areas.summary: The night a visiting foreign delegation's security detail was expected in a boutique hotel bar and every seat in it turned out to be occupied by a CIA officer — an episode John Kiriakou offers as an example of bad leadership, and which left his colleagues personally out of pocket for their espresso martinis.

denied-areas.title: The Jordanian intelligence service
denied-areas.summary: The service John Kiriakou calls one of the best in the world and arguably the best in the Middle East — good, in his account, out of necessity: half of Jordan''s population is Palestinian, Black September once fought on the steps of the palace, and the survival of the monarchy depends on having infiltrated every faction in the country.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Espionage Act
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Julian Assange
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Consortium News
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for since at least 2017, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra. Kiriakou's columns there have covered John Bolton's exit, the entrapment of Maria Butina, his own first tour in Saudi Arabia and the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower. He says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

department-of-education-swat-raid.title: Eastern District of Virginia
department-of-education-swat-raid.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

der-spiegel.title: Daniel Domscheit-Berg
der-spiegel.summary: A WikiLeaks associate discussed on the same panel as John Kiriakou; the anecdote about meeting him via the Chaos Computer Club was told by fellow panelist John Goetz, a Der Spiegel journalist — not by Kiriakou himself.

der-spiegel.title: Julian Assange
der-spiegel.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

der-spiegel.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
der-spiegel.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

der-spiegel.title: Andrew Feinstein
der-spiegel.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

der-spiegel.title: Belmarsh Prison
der-spiegel.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

der-spiegel.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
der-spiegel.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

deuce-martinez.title: Espionage Act
deuce-martinez.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

deuce-martinez.title: Abu Zubaydah
deuce-martinez.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

deuce-martinez.title: Abraham Accords
deuce-martinez.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

deuce-martinez.title: Ali Soufan
deuce-martinez.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

deuce-martinez.title: Arabists
deuce-martinez.summary: The label applied inside the U.S. government to diplomats and analysts who knew Arabic and Middle Eastern history, and which John Kiriakou confirms functioned as a dismissal — the assumption being that anyone who understood the region was blindly prejudiced against Israel, or antisemitic.

deuce-martinez.title: The 189 undeclared officers
deuce-martinez.summary: A figure John Kiriakou attributes to the CIA''s director of security, given to his intake class on his first day at the agency in January 1990: against two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the embassy in Washington, the FBI counted at least 189 undeclared ones operating across the United States. He pairs it with the fact that Israeli liaison officers were barred from CIA headquarters.

dewey-clarridge.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
dewey-clarridge.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

dewey-clarridge.title: Saudi nuclear program
dewey-clarridge.summary: Saudi Arabia's decades-long pursuit of uranium enrichment, nominally for nuclear power, which John Kiriakou notes was already old news when he arrived at the CIA in 1990 and which conventional wisdom has always read as a weapons programme.

dewey-clarridge.title: Jack Devine
dewey-clarridge.summary: A former CIA officer John Kiriakou worked for briefly in 2001 or 2002, and describes with real warmth as a great officer and a true believer — while flatly rejecting his insistence that the agency was never involved with cocaine. Asked to choose between Devine and a thirty-year DEA veteran who agrees with him, Kiriakou picks the DEA man.

dewey-clarridge.title: Contra rebels
dewey-clarridge.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

dewey-clarridge.title: Extraordinary Rendition
dewey-clarridge.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

dewey-clarridge.title: Pike Committee
dewey-clarridge.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

dgse.title: Candace Owens
dgse.summary: The commentator whose claims about the killing of Charlie Kirk John Kiriakou has publicly declined to accept. He credits her reach and her intelligence and rejects her method, citing an earlier occasion — a conference call he says he was on — at which she claimed irrefutable proof that the Italian government had stolen the 2020 election and that its release would return Donald Trump to office.

dgse.title: Five Eyes
dgse.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

dgse.title: Central Intelligence Agency
dgse.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

dgse.title: JFK assassination
dgse.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

dgse.title: John Ratcliffe
dgse.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

dgse.title: Asset acquisition cycle
dgse.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

dianne-feinstein.title: Bureau of Prisons
dianne-feinstein.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

dianne-feinstein.title: Senate Intelligence Committee
dianne-feinstein.summary: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence — the CIA's designated overseer, which John Kiriakou credits with the torture report's unimpeachable method (6 million contemporaneous CIA field cables) and simultaneously dismisses, along with its House counterpart, as "little more than cheerleaders for the CIA" since the mid-1980s. It sits in the official whistleblower channel he calls a proven dead end, and its own investigation was famously spied on by the very agency it oversees.

dianne-feinstein.title: Senate Torture Report
dianne-feinstein.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

dianne-feinstein.title: John Kiriakou
dianne-feinstein.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

dianne-feinstein.title: Watergate
dianne-feinstein.summary: The scandal that ended Nixon''s presidency and the standing benchmark in John Kiriakou''s vocabulary — the CIA spying on the Senate committee investigating its torture program was, to him, "a Watergate-level kind of scandal," except that this time nothing came of it. Watergate touches his own story directly: his lead defense attorney had been John Mitchell''s lawyer during Watergate. He also relays, with fascination, Danny Sheehan''s far darker theory of what the burglars were really after.

dianne-feinstein.title: Avril Haines
dianne-feinstein.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the National Security Council lawyer who decided whether names could lawfully go on John Brennan's kill list — and said yes in almost every case — before becoming CIA deputy director during the agency's hacking of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and then Director of National Intelligence. Kiriakou calls her appointment the disastrous half of a week in which Biden also named Bill Burns, and says she has never had to answer for any of it.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: John Kiriakou
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Alexa
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Daniel Hale
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Executive Order 12333
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: Family Jewels
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: The CIA's internal catalogue of its own abuses, demanded in full by the Church and Pike Committees in 1975; per John Kiriakou, MK-Ultra and its assassination programs surfaced first, 85 percent of the MK-Ultra files were shredded in defiance of a direct order, and new officers were taught that everything in the file belonged to the era before 1975.

diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.title: John McCone
diary-of-a-ceo-january-2026.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on November 22, 1963; per John Kiriakou's retelling of an account from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., responded to Bobby Kennedy Sr.'s same-day question "Tell me your people didn't do this" not with denial but with "I don't know who did it."

dick-cheney.title: George Tenet
dick-cheney.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

dick-cheney.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
dick-cheney.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

dick-cheney.title: Ross Ulbricht
dick-cheney.summary: Founder of the online marketplace Silk Road, sentenced to life plus 75 years before being pardoned by President Trump; John Kiriakou met Ulbricht's mother and sister two weeks before the pardon and calls the length of the original sentence a sickening miscarriage of justice.

dick-cheney.title: Abraham Bolden
dick-cheney.summary: The first African-American Secret Service agent assigned to a presidential detail; per John Kiriakou, he quite literally saved John F. Kennedy's life in Chicago in October 1963 and was subjected to overt racism by fellow agents, who told him to his face they would not protect Kennedy from assassination because of his civil-rights sympathies.

dick-cheney.title: Richard Perle
dick-cheney.summary: Prominent neoconservative adviser to the George W. Bush White House whom John Kiriakou credits with planting the idea of invading Iraq in Dick Cheney's mind the day after 9/11.

dick-cheney.title: National Intelligence Council
dick-cheney.summary: Body housed at the CIA comprising the most senior analysts drawn from across the entire intelligence community. Its officers — National Intelligence Officers (NIOs) — hold positions at the Senior Intelligence Service level and are responsible for long-range strategic analysis on specific portfolio areas, as well as the production of National Intelligence Estimates. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

dick-clarke.title: Cofer Black
dick-clarke.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

dick-clarke.title: Condoleezza Rice
dick-clarke.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

dick-clarke.title: Langley
dick-clarke.summary: The Virginia location of CIA headquarters and, in John Kiriakou''s usage, shorthand for the agency''s permanent power. It''s where he worked as the CIA''s lone Iraq-Kuwait analyst — told to start on Iraq "because nothing ever happened there" — where a cafeteria conversation invited him into the torture program, and the place agencies return to after apologizing to Congress, "where of course nothing ever changes." When a host suggested the real government of America is out in Langley and Washington''s white marble is for show, Kiriakou''s answer was: "that''s about the shape of it."

dick-clarke.title: Osama bin Laden
dick-clarke.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

dick-clarke.title: CIA language training
dick-clarke.summary: The agency''s language pipeline as John Kiriakou experienced and describes it: a full year of Arabic at nine hours a day, an optional second year at the State Department''s school, and the calculation that made his own career — that it is cheaper to teach a linguist operations than to teach an operations officer Greek and Arabic.

dick-clarke.title: The Directorate of Operations
dick-clarke.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

diesel-therapy.title: FCI Loretto
diesel-therapy.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

diesel-therapy.title: Bureau of Prisons
diesel-therapy.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

diesel-therapy.title: John Kiriakou
diesel-therapy.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

diesel-therapy.title: Letter from Loretto
diesel-therapy.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

diesel-therapy.title: Charles Samuels
diesel-therapy.summary: Director of the Bureau of Prisons during Kiriakou's incarceration, and the official to whom Kiriakou publicly appealed over the heads of the Loretto staff in a letter from Loretto.

diesel-therapy.title: This desk kills fascism
diesel-therapy.summary: The sign Kiriakou taped to the cell desk on which he wrote the letters from Loretto, borrowed from Woody Guthrie's guitar, torn down by a guard within hours and kept by Kiriakou ever since.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: The Bahrain water table
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: The prehistoric aquifer that surfaces in Bahrain — running, in John Kiriakou's telling, from the Atlantic beneath the whole of Africa — which until the 1970s gushed out of the ground in natural springs and made the island an oasis, and which overdevelopment has since dropped some thirty-five feet.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: The Gulf Daily News
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: Bahrain's English-language newspaper, and the source John Kiriakou turned to when a bomb went off at the Ministry of Labour two months into his posting — its Indian reporter, whose telephone was bugged like his own, told him a civil uprising was about to explode.

dilmun-burial-mounds.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
dilmun-burial-mounds.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

directorate-of-intelligence.title: The Directorate of Operations
