epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.title: 2026 Iran war
epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.title: Adnan Khashoggi
epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.title: AIPAC
epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.title: Les Wexner
epstein-files-beef-jerky-anomaly.summary: Ohio billionaire retail magnate; John Kiriakou cites Vanity Fair allegations that Wexner funneled millions to Jeffrey Epstein as his 'tax advisor,' offering it as evidence for his own view that Epstein's money and access served the Israelis.

epstein-files-transparency-act.title: Mike Johnson
epstein-files-transparency-act.summary: Speaker of the House during the fight over the Epstein files, whose procedural manoeuvres John Kiriakou reads as an attempt to let the issue die in subcommittee, and whose midterm framing of Democrats as communists Kiriakou dismisses outright.

epstein-files-transparency-act.title: Jeffrey Epstein
epstein-files-transparency-act.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

epstein-files-transparency-act.title: John Kiriakou
epstein-files-transparency-act.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

epstein-files-transparency-act.title: Thomas Massie
epstein-files-transparency-act.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

epstein-files-transparency-act.title: Marjorie Taylor Greene
epstein-files-transparency-act.summary: American congresswoman whom John Kiriakou, despite deep political disagreement, has repeatedly credited for breaking with her party on the Epstein files, on military aid to Israel, and on Gaza. He describes her as courageous for pressing Donald Trump to release the files unredacted, and says the pressure ultimately forced her out of Washington.

epstein-files-transparency-act.title: Nick Bryant
epstein-files-transparency-act.summary: Investigative journalist, activist and co-founder of Epstein Justice, author of The Franklin Scandal, and a repeat guest on John Kiriakou's programme, where Kiriakou describes him as knowing the Epstein case better than anybody else in America.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: Alexander Acosta and the sweetheart deal
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: The US attorney who gave Jeffrey Epstein his 2006 non-prosecution agreement and later said he had been ordered to — a chain of command John Kiriakou traces upward to an attorney general famous for his powerlessness, and therefore to somebody above him whom nobody has ever named.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: David Boies
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: The Epstein files and the Starmer government
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: John Kiriakou''s prediction that the Epstein disclosures could bring down Keir Starmer''s government, on the strength of evidence that Prince Andrew and Peter Mandelson gave Epstein classified British Ministry of Defence documents — an Official Secrets Act matter that in America would fall under the Espionage Act.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: The Trilateral Commission
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: The body John Kiriakou says he used to dismiss as conspiracy-theory material until someone close to him attended one of its meetings and told him what was actually discussed there: arms deals — and at Davos, how to manage the global economy.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: American missile stockpiles
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

epstein-statute-of-limitations.title: Jeffrey Epstein
epstein-statute-of-limitations.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

eric-holder.title: John Brennan
eric-holder.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

eric-holder.title: Brian Ross
eric-holder.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

eric-holder.title: Ali Soufan
eric-holder.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

eric-holder.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
eric-holder.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

eric-holder.title: Espionage Act
eric-holder.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

eric-holder.title: Agent payment mechanics
eric-holder.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

eric-oneill.title: Harold James Nicholson
eric-oneill.summary: Former CIA Station Chief, Singapore; the third major modern CIA mole for the Russians after Aldrich Ames and Robert Hanssen. Per John Kiriakou, Nicholson was a senior officer at the CIA Counterterrorism Center during Kiriakou's tenure there. Sentenced to 31 years and seven months in 1997. While in prison, attempted to recruit his own son to act as a courier between him and the Russian intelligence service so his espionage payments could continue to compound for his eventual release — and was caught when his son walked up to the Russian embassy in Washington under FBI surveillance.

eric-oneill.title: Robert Hanssen
eric-oneill.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

eric-oneill.title: Brian Kelley
eric-oneill.summary: Chief of counterintelligence at the CIA; framed by FBI counterintelligence chief Robert Hanssen — the actual Soviet/Russian mole — as the source of executed agents; spent a year and a half on leave without pay, surrounded around the clock by FBI agents, while his daughter was approached and told her father would face the death penalty if he did not confess.

eric-oneill.title: Cuban double agents
eric-oneill.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

eric-oneill.title: Afghan heroin policy
eric-oneill.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

eric-oneill.title: Ai Weiwei
eric-oneill.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

eric-swallwell.title: Church Committee
eric-swallwell.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

eric-swallwell.title: Mexican 9 Month Work Visas
eric-swallwell.summary: A George W. Bush-administration proposal, negotiated with Mexico in the six to eight months before 9/11, to give undocumented Mexican workers renewable nine-month U.S. work visas requiring federal income tax payment — killed by the September 11 attacks before it could be ratified.

eric-swallwell.title: Central Intelligence Agency
eric-swallwell.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

eric-swallwell.title: Jose Rodriguez
eric-swallwell.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

eric-swallwell.title: Trump
eric-swallwell.summary: Kiriakou applied for a pardon on the last day of Trump's first term — and says Trump had agreed to it, until the last-minute reversal.

erik-prince.title: Blackwater
erik-prince.summary: The private military contractor founded by Erik Prince that ran the CIA's Global Response Staff and, until shut down by Leon Panetta, a global assassination program; staffed at the board level with former CIA officers including Cofer Black as Vice President.

erik-prince.title: Cofer Black
erik-prince.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

erik-prince.title: Leon Panetta
erik-prince.summary: CIA Director under President Obama (2009–2011) and subsequent Secretary of Defense; per John Kiriakou, the official who on arrival as Director shut down the Blackwater-operated CIA worldwide assassination program — and in the course of explaining the decision to the House Intelligence Committee publicly outed Erik Prince. Also one of Kiriakou's two go-to examples (with David Petraeus) of senior intelligence figures who disclosed the identities of covert CIA officers without consequence while Kiriakou himself was prosecuted for the same statute.

erik-prince.title: Tyrell Vanto
erik-prince.summary: Hollywood screenwriter and director; son of Jesse Vanto; friend of John Kiriakou; wrote and directed the late-2025 film in which Kiriakou made his acting debut.

erik-prince.title: John Kiriakou
erik-prince.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

erik-prince.title: Jeff Fahey
erik-prince.summary: American actor; star of the Tyrell Vanto film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut in late 2025; characterized by Kiriakou as generous with his time and on-set advice.

espionage-act.title: The Department of Education SWAT raid
espionage-act.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a pre-dawn armed raid on the home of a Washington Times journalist and her husband, an official at the Department of Education — carried out, he says, by the Department of Education's own armed SWAT team, which seized the reporter's notes and refused to return them. He uses the episode to point out that several civilian federal departments maintain armed tactical units, and that no other journalist covered it.

espionage-act.title: James Comey
espionage-act.summary: Former FBI director indicted under the second Trump administration, whose prosecution John Kiriakou reads as a search for charges to fit a man rather than evidence of a crime — and which he expects to collapse, unlike the parallel case against John Brennan.

espionage-act.title: "I''m a non-person"
espionage-act.summary: The phrase John Kiriakou uses for his standing after prison: a former colleague was sent to deliver congratulations from a mutual friend who had risen to a senior administration post, together with the message that he could never speak to Kiriakou again. Kiriakou pairs it with the loss of his federal pension after nineteen and a half years of service, and with the fact that in eight years no other CIA officer joined him in speaking publicly.

espionage-act.title: The pillow-talk disclosure case
espionage-act.summary: A case John Kiriakou witnessed from the next desk: a CIA officer told a classified fact to a former senior officer turned CNN commentator during an affair, he repeated it on air, and the agency identified her within days. Her punishment was four weeks'' suspension without pay and a memo in her file. Kiriakou uses it as the benchmark for how far the handling of disclosures has moved — today, he says, it would be an Espionage Act prosecution and about five years in prison.

espionage-act.title: The roadblock strike
espionage-act.summary: The drone strike Daniel Hale described at his own sentencing and that John Kiriakou retells as the reason Hale became a whistleblower: a car approaching a U.S. roadblock in Afghanistan, two girls aged six and nine visible inside, an order to fire given twice over Hale''s objection, and a father who afterwards hid his daughters'' bodies in a village dumpster for fear that special forces would take them.

espionage-act.title: Assange plea deal
espionage-act.summary: The 2024 agreement under which Julian Assange pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit espionage, was processed in Saipan, and returned to Australia; John Kiriakou details its odd terms — a Chelsea Manning purge affidavit and a 25-year green-card ban — and the debate over whether it sets a precedent.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Andrew Feinstein
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Belmarsh Prison
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Chelsea Manning
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.title: Afghan War Logs
ethan-mccord-collateral-murder.summary: A 2010 WikiLeaks publication discussed on a panel Kiriakou joined; the specific lines about it in the corpus belong to other panelists, not Kiriakou.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Nuclear war is winnable
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The belief John Kiriakou says is held by a real faction in both Ukraine and the United States: that a nuclear exchange can be survived and won. He traces the American version to Pat Buchanan''s 1992 presidential campaign — we come out from our caves and continue the fight — and reconstructs the Ukrainian version as a bet that if Russia went nuclear, the American, British and French arsenals would answer. He calls the reasoning insanity and thinks it is nonetheless being done.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Kiriakou's Ukraine settlement prediction
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The endgame John Kiriakou forecast in June 2025 and calls deliberately unbold: Russia keeps the disputed eastern territories and Crimea, Ukraine never joins NATO but probably joins the European Union, and Moscow gets ninety per cent of what it wanted. The one demand he expects Russia to trade away is denazification, which he reads as propaganda rather than policy.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: The Panda card
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The Chinese national payment card John Kiriakou encountered in Hong Kong, where he found few places willing to take Mastercard or Visa. Asked why, he was given a one-sentence answer about routing: Visa and Mastercard transactions pass through New York, Panda card transactions pass through Shanghai, and so fall outside the reach of American sanctions. He treats it as both an instance of Chinese strategic competence and an argument that the American card duopoly is a racket.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: Operation Spiderweb
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: The Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's strategic bomber fleet in June 2025, which John Kiriakou calls a brilliant operation and — against Volodymyr Zelensky's account — one Ukraine could not have run alone. Eighteen months of preparation, drones smuggled across eleven time zones by human couriers, and command from Kyiv all required outside help, he argues; and Donald Trump's uncharacteristic public silence afterwards is his evidence that Washington was in on it.

europe-without-russian-gas.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
europe-without-russian-gas.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

evangelical-zionism.title: The Greek Orthodox Church
evangelical-zionism.summary: The church John Kiriakou was raised in and still belongs to — the institution behind his Greek fluency and his family''s immigrant history, a recurring thread in his accounts of Athens, Damascus, Bethlehem and Washington, and, in two cases, an actor in his own story: the church the FBI followed him into, and the priest who tried to get him a pardon.

evangelical-zionism.title: The Iron Dome
evangelical-zionism.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

evangelical-zionism.title: The Litani River
evangelical-zionism.summary: The largest natural water source in the Middle East, which John Kiriakou says makes southern Lebanon more valuable than oil — and the northern edge of the depopulated strip he describes Israel creating there.

evangelical-zionism.title: Abraham Accords
evangelical-zionism.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

evangelical-zionism.title: American missile stockpiles
evangelical-zionism.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

evangelical-zionism.title: Arnon Milchan
evangelical-zionism.summary: Israeli-American Hollywood producer and, per John Kiriakou, an Israeli super-spy and arms dealer for LAKAM; central to a Netanyahu corruption charge, and named in FBI documents alongside Netanyahu in the smuggling of U.S. nuclear secrets.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: Spy films and television on screen
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: John Kiriakou's scene-by-scene verdicts on how spy films and television handle real tradecraft — what they get right (static surveillance from upper floors, hostile operational meetings, exchanges of bona fides, breaking into offices), what they invent (silent helicopters, high-speed submersibles, Batcaves, gadgets that cannot be bought), and the shows he says commit felonies on screen. He opens with why CIA officers watch them at all — *"not because they love the CIA movies, but because they love to criticize them."*

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: CIA driving training
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: The counterterrorism-driving component of CIA training, in which officers are ambushed in a simulated third-country no-man's-land and must "get off the X" — get out of the kill zone. John Kiriakou's own run ended with the instructors killing his engine by remote, a robot in a van firing paintballs at him, and Kiriakou shooting out his own car windows to get an angle on the robot. "Damn it, Kiriakou. That was the last decent car we had."

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: CIA psychological evaluations
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: The recurring psychiatric screening every CIA officer undergoes — before employment, again three years after hiring, and every five years thereafter for life, with extra sessions triggered by bad behaviour overseas. Per John Kiriakou, failing one grounds an officer — a colleague who "went nuts" could not be sent on a post-9/11 mission, and Kiriakou was sent in his place.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: Bill Buckley
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: Burn Notice
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: The USA Network spy series John Kiriakou watched as a fan before he became its script adviser — a job he obtained by sitting next to its creator, Matt Nix, on a flight from Washington to Los Angeles, having previously run the show's credits in slow motion to find out who was advising it. Nobody was. By the time the plane landed Kiriakou had the job for season six.

exchange-of-bona-fides.title: Concealment devices
exchange-of-bona-fides.summary: Hollowed everyday objects — known inside the CIA as CDs — issued to officers to hide documents, equipment and, in the larger sizes, a gun. Per John Kiriakou every CIA officer has access to them, some are simply assigned with no instructions attached, and the way they are found in real life is the way they are found in *The Good Shepherd* — by an anomaly a hand can feel.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Cheney's airstrip question
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: A one-line request from Vice President Dick Cheney — what is the longest airstrip in northern Iraq made of? — that nobody in the CIA's operations directorate could answer, and that John Kiriakou eventually resolved by asking the agency librarian. The answer came back within a day, with the exact mix. The purpose was to work out whether the runway would take a transport aircraft carrying two tanks.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: AIPAC
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Bill Clinton
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: The CIA as a policy support agency
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing correction to the idea that the CIA has a foreign policy of its own: it is not a policy agency but a policy support agency, it serves at the pleasure of the president, and its officers have no civil service protections at all. Career staff can slow-roll an order they dislike until an administration ends — but in a hot war, he says, they do as they are told.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Greater Israel
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: The territorial project John Kiriakou believes the Israeli government genuinely holds: the expulsion of every Palestinian, beginning in Gaza and continuing into the West Bank, pursued on a hundred- or two-hundred-year horizon in the confidence that the United States will never push back.

executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
executive-assistant-to-the-deputy-direct.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

executive-order-12333.title: Tuesday morning kill list
executive-order-12333.summary: Weekly CIA targeting meeting instituted by John Brennan in 2009 during his service as Deputy National Security Advisor for Counterterrorism in the Obama administration; produced a written list of individuals to be killed in the following week; per John Kiriakou, the program was a source of pride within the Obama administration and was made operationally possible by the targeting-software sophistication of the period.

executive-order-12333.title: Ninth Circuit contractor ruling (2025)
executive-order-12333.summary: Approximately July 2025 U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruling, in a case brought by Abu Zubaydah against CIA contractors who had tortured him, holding that contractors operating under a written CIA contract are legally protected as agents of the agency; extends Executive Order 12333 authority to contractor operations including the Blackwater assassination program; received almost no U.S. media coverage.

executive-order-12333.title: Phil Ochs
executive-order-12333.summary: 1960s–70s protest folk singer; John Kiriakou retells a story from Pete Seeger about the night Ochs — who had fallen into depression after being unable to sing following a mugging in Africa — called Seeger just before taking his own life.

executive-order-12333.title: Project Gateway
executive-order-12333.summary: A CIA astral-projection and remote-viewing effort that John Kiriakou describes as a sub-program of MK-Ultra, launched after a fabricated source claimed the Soviets were experimenting with ESP.

executive-order-12333.title: Global Response Staff
executive-order-12333.summary: The CIA's protective-security program for case officers operating in high-threat environments; run for the agency by Blackwater; especially active in Baghdad's Green Zone during the Iraq War, where movement between fixed locations was treated as life-threatening.

executive-order-12333.title: Title 10 vs Title 50
executive-order-12333.summary: The U.S. legal-code distinction governing which kinds of armed action fall under military authority (Title 10) and which fall under intelligence authority (Title 50); the operative legal frame for the post-9/11 question of whether CIA contractors can lawfully kill in the agency's name, addressed in the 2025 Ninth Circuit ruling in the Abu Zubaydah contractor case.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Trump cartel terrorist designation
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: Donald Trump's early second-term State Department designation of drug cartels as terrorist organizations, which John Kiriakou says was understood at the time mainly as a paperwork exercise to free up agencies like the NSA and DIA to spend money on intercepting communications and training foreign nationals — but which Kiriakou says Trump has since treated as license to attack any vessel he personally deems cartel-linked.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Abu Zubaydah
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Asset acquisition cycle
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.title: Counterterrorism Center deaths in the line of duty
expanding-the-definition-of-terrorism.summary: The colleagues John Kiriakou names as having been killed doing the work he did — Helge Boes and Mike Spann of the Counterterrorism Center, and the officer who sat beside him when he was chief of the counterintelligence branch of the Osama bin Laden group, killed with six colleagues by a suicide bomber in Afghanistan. He pairs the physical risk with a second cost he states as near-certain: that a marriage will not survive an operational tour.

extraordinary-rendition.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
extraordinary-rendition.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

extraordinary-rendition.title: Abu Zubaydah
extraordinary-rendition.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

extraordinary-rendition.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
extraordinary-rendition.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

extraordinary-rendition.title: John Kiriakou
extraordinary-rendition.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

extraordinary-rendition.title: Cold cell
extraordinary-rendition.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

extraordinary-rendition.title: Maher Arar
extraordinary-rendition.summary: Canadian-Syrian political-science professor at the University of Toronto; in 2002, returning from a family visit in Tunis, was seized by the FBI at JFK at CIA request, secretly rendered to Damascus, and tortured by Syrian intelligence for eight to nine months until they concluded he was the wrong man. The U.S. denied any involvement to the Canadian government until Arar's wife produced a credit-card receipt from his return flight. He sued the U.S. and lost on national-security grounds, then sued the Canadian government and won six million dollars. Per John Kiriakou, his case is the canonical illustration of the CIA rendition program rendering the wrong person.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: MOSSAD
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: AIPAC
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: Shin Bet
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: Israel's internal security service; per John Kiriakou, one of the two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the Washington embassy, and the service whose officer, alongside a Mossad officer, he says tried to recruit him at his first CIA liaison briefing in the spring of 1990 — an approach his colleagues told him had been made to every one of them.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: Israeli training of American police
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: The practice, which John Kiriakou opposes, of Israeli police and IDF personnel training American local police departments, including at the Atlanta facility known as Cop City.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: Israeli integration into U.S. agencies
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the formal embedding of Israeli personnel inside American defense and intelligence institutions — a National Defense Authorization Act provision collocating them with the Pentagon and opening Five Eyes-style liaison with the CIA, arriving in the same weeks as a DIA all-hands warning that Israeli services were unusually aggressive in recruiting inside DIA. His argument is that the two cannot both be true: either Israel is a critical counterintelligence threat or it is a partner.

f-35-israel-avionics.title: NDAA 2027 US–Israel fusion provisions
f-35-israel-avionics.summary: Provisions in the proposed National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 and the companion intelligence authorization bill that would create a permanent Pentagon executive agent for US–Israeli military fusion and lock in permanent intelligence sharing tied to Israel's qualitative military edge. John Kiriakou describes the effect as handing over voluntarily the technology Israel previously ran spies to steal.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Donald Trump
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Major non-NATO ally status for Ukraine
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: John Kiriakou''s forecast of how the Russian demand that Ukraine never join NATO can be met without leaving Ukraine unprotected: the designation of major non-NATO ally, already held by Australia, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which he says confers essentially the same rights without the membership.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Graham–Netanyahu ICC tapes
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: Recordings of Lindsey Graham coordinating with Benjamin Netanyahu on how to discredit the International Criminal Court over its arrest warrant. On the tapes Graham lines up Senate signatories for a protest letter, jokes that he should be paid "tons of shekels," and asks Netanyahu to telephone two Democratic senators to thank them. John Kiriakou argues the conduct meets the definition of espionage his own judge applied to him.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Hague Invasion Act
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: The American statute, described by John Kiriakou as having been passed during the Obama administration, that authorises the president to use the United States military to invade the Netherlands and free an American or allied national held by the International Criminal Court — the standing legal answer to the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu might be arrested abroad.

f-35-sale-to-turkey.title: Pickaxe Mountain
f-35-sale-to-turkey.summary: The Iranian site whose ongoing excavation Benjamin Netanyahu publicised in July 2026 and which Donald Trump, in response, said he already knew about — using the exchange to tell an ally publicly not to brief the press ahead of him. John Kiriakou reads the episode as Netanyahu attempting to move American public opinion and Trump refusing to be moved.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Colonel Khaled
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Site 13
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Faisalabad
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

faisalabad-hospital.title: Mr. Fish
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

faisalabad-hospital.title: The Lahore safe house
faisalabad-hospital.summary: The ten-bedroom house in the best neighbourhood of Lahore that the CIA bought outright for two million dollars in cash in March 2002, on a cover story invented on the spot — that its buyers were textile barons — and from whose roof the team could catch seven satellites.

faisalabad-hospital.title: The toll booth plan
faisalabad-hospital.summary: John Kiriakou's first idea for catching Abu Zubaydah in 2002 — to put CIA officers dressed as Pakistanis in the toll booths of the Lahore–Faisalabad motorway and grab him as he came through — drawn from his own summer job as a toll collector on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and abandoned as, in his own words, a terrible idea.

faisalabad.title: Site 13
faisalabad.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

faisalabad.title: Amir
faisalabad.summary: The pseudonym John Kiriakou gives the Muslim, ethnically Arab domestic officer sent on temporary duty to Pakistan to help with the Abu Zubaydah hunt — the colleague who drove them into India by GPS, drank the roadside tea and had diarrhoea for six weeks, and invented the textile-baron cover story on the spot.

faisalabad.title: Colonel Khaled
faisalabad.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

faisalabad.title: Faisalabad Hospital
faisalabad.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

faisalabad.title: The Lahore safe house
faisalabad.summary: The ten-bedroom house in the best neighbourhood of Lahore that the CIA bought outright for two million dollars in cash in March 2002, on a cover story invented on the spot — that its buyers were textile barons — and from whose roof the team could catch seven satellites.

faisalabad.title: The toll booth plan
faisalabad.summary: John Kiriakou's first idea for catching Abu Zubaydah in 2002 — to put CIA officers dressed as Pakistanis in the toll booths of the Lahore–Faisalabad motorway and grab him as he came through — drawn from his own summer job as a toll collector on the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and abandoned as, in his own words, a terrible idea.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The Fox News military analyst
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

fake-cia-resumes.title: Hugh Francis Redmond
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The first CIA officer to die in the line of duty, per John Kiriakou — a Special Activities Division officer sent to Shanghai in 1946 under cover as an ice cream machine salesman, arrested by the Chinese communists in 1951, held and tortured for nineteen years, and declared a suicide by Beijing in 1970. The CIA denied he had ever worked for it until his name was declassified and added to the Wall of Honor.

fake-cia-resumes.title: Robert David Steele
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The former intelligence officer and podcaster whose death during the COVID-19 pandemic John Kiriakou was asked to explain. Kiriakou, who had appeared on his show, calls him a sweet man who died of the disease, and offers a blunt assessment of his work: he did not believe most of the conspiracy theories he promoted, but they brought him an audience.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The asset recruitment cycle
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The four-step career requirement John Kiriakou says governed CIA operations before September 11 — spot, assess, develop and recruit an agent, or do not get promoted — and his description of what the fourth step actually rests on: not money, revenge or ideology, but friendship, real or believed.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The Iran–Israel exchange assessment
fake-cia-resumes.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement — which he expects to be unpopular — that Iran came out ahead of Israel in their direct missile exchange: the Iron Dome proved fallible, Iranian targeting was selective where Israel''s was not, and the ceasefire came, in his reading, because Israel had run out of missiles.

fake-cia-resumes.title: The tier one walk-up
fake-cia-resumes.summary: The recruitment John Kiriakou calls one of the best operations of his career and credits entirely to his mentor Gust Avrakotos: an approach to an official of a tier one country — one of America''s greatest enemies — made by the simple expedient of walking right up to the man''s house, a technique Avrakotos had used himself in the 1970s.

falls-church-mosque.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
falls-church-mosque.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

falls-church-mosque.title: Yemen
falls-church-mosque.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

falls-church-mosque.title: Abbottabad
falls-church-mosque.summary: The Pakistani garrison city where Osama bin Laden was found and killed — named for a British major who was Pakistan's first military trainer, home to the Pakistani military's leadership, and in John Kiriakou's judgement the last place bin Laden could have lived unnoticed by the Pakistani state.

falls-church-mosque.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
falls-church-mosque.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

falls-church-mosque.title: Avril Haines
falls-church-mosque.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the National Security Council lawyer who decided whether names could lawfully go on John Brennan's kill list — and said yes in almost every case — before becoming CIA deputy director during the agency's hacking of the Senate Intelligence Committee, and then Director of National Intelligence. Kiriakou calls her appointment the disastrous half of a week in which Biden also named Bill Burns, and says she has never had to answer for any of it.

falls-church-mosque.title: Bab al-Mandab
falls-church-mosque.summary: The strait where the Horn of Africa nearly meets the south-western tip of the Arabian Peninsula, which John Kiriakou identifies as one of the few American national interests in Yemen and as a chokepoint whose closure would push the global economy into recession.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: Robert David Steele
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: The former intelligence officer and podcaster whose death during the COVID-19 pandemic John Kiriakou was asked to explain. Kiriakou, who had appeared on his show, calls him a sweet man who died of the disease, and offers a blunt assessment of his work: he did not believe most of the conspiracy theories he promoted, but they brought him an audience.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: The Obama recruitment thesis
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: John Kiriakou''s public explanation of what happened to Barack Obama: not that the CIA created him, but that a first-term senator with no national security experience is exactly the kind of president the agency wants, and that the first briefing several levels above top secret is enough to hook him. Kiriakou supports the reading with two quotations Obama gave to reporters, including that he never had any idea he would be so good at killing people.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: Bin Laden health rumors
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: Fake CIA résumés
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

false-flags-are-too-hard.title: The 1968 waterboarding conviction
false-flags-are-too-hard.summary: The precedent John Kiriakou uses to dispose of the argument that waterboarding was legally uncertain after 2002: a January 1968 Washington Post front page showing an American soldier waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner, an investigation ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, and the soldier''s arrest, conviction for torture and imprisonment. The law, Kiriakou points out, never changed in between.

family-jewels.title: Church Committee
family-jewels.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

family-jewels.title: MK-Ultra
family-jewels.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

family-jewels.title: Pike Committee
family-jewels.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

family-jewels.title: Project Gateway
family-jewels.summary: A CIA astral-projection and remote-viewing effort that John Kiriakou describes as a sub-program of MK-Ultra, launched after a fabricated source claimed the Soviets were experimenting with ESP.

family-jewels.title: Executive Order 12333
family-jewels.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

family-jewels.title: Alexa
family-jewels.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: John Kiriakou
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: Central Intelligence Agency
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.title: Jose Rodriguez
fbi-apologies-to-kiriakou.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: FCI Loretto
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Edward Snowden
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Bureau of Prisons
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: John Kiriakou
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

fbi-arrest-strategies.title: Barack Obama
fbi-arrest-strategies.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Alexa
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Cameo
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: The personalised-video app John Kiriakou joined in February 2026 and turned into an unexpected second career — around 2,600 videos, roughly 900 of them in his first month alone. Half are birthday messages and most of the rest are requests for CIA stories, but about two hundred have been appeals for advice or a pep talk, and three of those people later told him he had talked them out of suicide.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: CIA culture of lying
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of deception as an occupational condition at the CIA — the tradecraft of detecting it, the training that instils it, and the institutional rot he says follows when officers cannot switch it off: a deputy director who married five successive secretaries, promotion panels that traded advancement for sex, and staff psychiatrists overheard planning how to push a colleague toward resignation or suicide.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: Muslim Brotherhood terrorist designation
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to the designation of the Muslim Brotherhood, or elements of it, as a terrorist organisation: that the group is more than a century old, has never carried out an anti-American terrorist operation, and had never been so designated by any previous administration. He distinguishes fundamentalism and hostility from terrorism.

fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.title: The assassination approval process
fbi-manufactured-terrorism-cases.summary: Why John Kiriakou thinks arranging the death of a foreign leader is far harder for the CIA than the public assumes. It is not the 1960s: there is congressional oversight, and before any proposal reaches the president''s signature it must clear layers of lawyers at the Justice Department''s Office of Legal Counsel, the National Security Council and the agency''s own General Counsel. Pressuring a leader into flight, he notes, is both easier and more legal.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Peter Strzok
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: Senior FBI counterintelligence officer who, per John Kiriakou, oversaw the FBI operation that included a fake Japanese-diplomat sting designed to induce Kiriakou to commit espionage, and who personally placed Kiriakou in handcuffs when he was arrested on January 12, 2012. Kiriakou did not learn Strzok's identity until 2017, when a Washington Post reporter called to ask for comment on Strzok's firing.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Jim Bamford
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: The author John Kiriakou credits with having written the definitive book on the NSA and with first making Americans aware of the surveillance state. Kiriakou highlights Bamford''s 2023 book Spy Fail for a claim he says should have been front-page news and was not: that the FBI lost ten of its Chinese sources because Peter Strzok''s counterintelligence unit had a Chinese mole inside it.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: COINTELPRO
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: The FBI programme of warrantless surveillance and disruption directed at Americans, and one of the four abuses John Kiriakou names when explaining what the Church Committee actually investigated. He treats it as the historical benchmark for what a real congressional inquiry into the security agencies looks like — and, through the campaign against Martin Luther King, as proof that the state will destroy a citizen it considers a threat.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: David Petraeus
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Leon Panetta
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: CIA Director under President Obama (2009–2011) and subsequent Secretary of Defense; per John Kiriakou, the official who on arrival as Director shut down the Blackwater-operated CIA worldwide assassination program — and in the course of explaining the decision to the House Intelligence Committee publicly outed Erik Prince. Also one of Kiriakou's two go-to examples (with David Petraeus) of senior intelligence figures who disclosed the identities of covert CIA officers without consequence while Kiriakou himself was prosecuted for the same statute.

fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.title: Vault 7
fbi-raid-on-kiriakou-s-home.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

fbi.title: Central Intelligence Agency
fbi.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

fbi.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
fbi.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

fbi.title: John Brennan
fbi.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

fbi.title: NSA
fbi.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

fbi.title: The Taliban spokesman setup
fbi.summary: Kiriakou's account of a prisoner transferred into FCI Loretto for five days who presented himself as the Taliban's American spokesman, while a guard photographed the encounter from the treeline — an attempt, in his telling, to manufacture a second case against him.

fbi.title: Intelligence Agencies
fbi.summary: Kiriakou counts roughly 19 publicly known US intelligence agencies and calls the proliferation Pentagon empire-building on duplicative work.

fci-loretto.title: Kiriakou's prison designation
fci-loretto.summary: The discrepancy between the minimum-security work camp John Kiriakou was sentenced to and the low-security prison the Bureau of Prisons actually placed him in, which he cites whenever the subject of preferential designations arises.

fci-loretto.title: Kiriakou's serial-killer letters
fci-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's account of writing letters, as research for a planned book, to several well-known serial killers — including David Berkowitz ("Son of Sam"), Gary Leon Ridgway (the Green River Killer), the BTK killer, the "co-ed killer," and Manson family member Tex Watson — and the uniformly evangelical, Jesus-focused responses he received instead of the interviews he wanted.

fci-loretto.title: Louis Farrakhan
fci-loretto.summary: Leader of the Nation of Islam; per John Kiriakou, issued a perfectly timed statement during Kiriakou's imprisonment at FCI Loretto identifying him as a hero of the Muslim people for standing up for human rights — protecting Kiriakou from the prison's Muslim population at a moment when the Aryans were simultaneously protecting him under the cover story that he was a "Muslim hunter."

fci-loretto.title: Nick Bryant
fci-loretto.summary: Investigative journalist, activist and co-founder of Epstein Justice, author of The Franklin Scandal, and a repeat guest on John Kiriakou's programme, where Kiriakou describes him as knowing the Epstein case better than anybody else in America.

fci-loretto.title: Kiriakou's Pakistan-Islam economic critique
fci-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's controversial view that Islam has held Pakistan back economically, contrasting Pakistan's stalled development since the 1960s with South Korea's — which had the same GDP as Pakistan in 1964 — and citing lost productivity from prayer breaks and holy days, resentment over partition, and spending on nuclear weapons instead of infrastructure and education.

fci-loretto.title: The prison food economy
fci-loretto.summary: The underground kitchen at FCI Loretto, where meals were cooked in bin liners heated by improvised immersion elements, guards stole and resold the food they were meant to be guarding, and Kiriakou stopped going to the cafeteria for the last six to eight months of his sentence.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Espionage Act
federal-plea-coercion.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Edward Snowden
federal-plea-coercion.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Abu Zubaydah
federal-plea-coercion.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Mark Lanzotti
federal-plea-coercion.summary: John Kiriakou's best friend in prison — an Italian sentenced to triple life without parole for a first-time nonviolent meth conspiracy he was the only man to voluntarily leave; Kiriakou wrote the appeal that won his release, and he is now the top-selling realtor on the Jersey Shore.

federal-plea-coercion.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
federal-plea-coercion.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

federal-plea-coercion.title: CovertAction Magazine
federal-plea-coercion.summary: The muckraking outlet "exposing covert action since 1978" — and one of John Kiriakou's three long-running syndicated column homes, alongside Consortium News and ScheerPost. Kiriakou joined its podcast arm, the CovertAction Bulletin, appearing on panels with Peter Dale Scott and Pepe Escobar, and jokes that the Pentagon's browser-plugin credibility warnings — red check marks against outlets like CovertAction — are the surest sign it's worth reading.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: FCI Loretto
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Chomo
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: The black box
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Civil confinement
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The policy John Kiriakou proposed from inside FCI Loretto — moving sex offenders to a secure location on prison grounds after their sentences end rather than releasing them — an argument that drew public criticism and which he defends with the case of a prisoner named Cook.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Cook
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The elderly Kentucky prisoner who worked with John Kiriakou in the FCI Loretto chapel, finished a 20-year child pornography sentence, and was back inside within four months facing 60 more — the case Kiriakou uses to answer critics of civil confinement.

federal-prison-security-levels.title: Truck
federal-prison-security-levels.summary: The convicted serial killer at FCI Loretto who sought John Kiriakou's approval, claimed to have run guns to Angolan rebels in a shrimp boat, and beat a prisoner unconscious after Kiriakou told him the man had called him a pedophile.
