federal-torture-act.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
federal-torture-act.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

federal-torture-act.title: Espionage Act
federal-torture-act.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

federal-torture-act.title: Waterboarding
federal-torture-act.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

federal-torture-act.title: Jeffrey Sterling
federal-torture-act.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

federal-torture-act.title: Abu Zubaydah
federal-torture-act.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

federal-torture-act.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
federal-torture-act.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. felix-rodriguez.title: Donald Trump
felix-rodriguez.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

felix-rodriguez.title: Jeffrey Epstein
felix-rodriguez.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

felix-rodriguez.title: JFK assassination
felix-rodriguez.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

felix-rodriguez.title: Bill Clinton
felix-rodriguez.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

felix-rodriguez.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
felix-rodriguez.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

felix-rodriguez.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
felix-rodriguez.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

fentanyl-and-china.title: Afghan heroin policy
fentanyl-and-china.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

fentanyl-and-china.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
fentanyl-and-china.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

fentanyl-and-china.title: John Kerry
fentanyl-and-china.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

fentanyl-and-china.title: The West Africa cocaine route
fentanyl-and-china.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where cocaine transiting Venezuela actually goes: not north to the United States but east to West Africa, onto camels along an old Tuareg track to Morocco, and by boat to Spain. The drugs, he says, are meant for Western Europe — and are not Venezuelan to begin with, but Colombian and Ecuadorian.

fentanyl-and-china.title: Contra rebels
fentanyl-and-china.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

fentanyl-and-china.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
fentanyl-and-china.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

field-loadout.title: CIA–Big Tech revolving door
field-loadout.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the traffic between the CIA and the major technology companies — "they work hand in glove" — illustrated by a supervisor who resigned five years short of his thirty-year pension for a Microsoft job paying eight times his government salary. The exchange, he argues, benefits both sides and is for that reason dangerous: the agency gains access to the most advanced companies in the world, and the companies gain a direct channel into the intelligence community.

field-loadout.title: CIA feeder schools
field-loadout.summary: John Kiriakou's correction to the assumption that Georgetown is the CIA's principal university pipeline — George Washington University, he says, sends more people to the agency than Georgetown does, the first applied intelligence master's programme in the country was at Mercyhurst College in Erie, Pennsylvania, and he himself teaches intelligence studies to a largely American cohort at the University of Salamanca in Spain, many of whom end up at the CIA.

field-loadout.title: FCI Loretto
field-loadout.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

field-loadout.title: Osama bin Laden
field-loadout.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

fifth-fleet.title: Admiral William Crowe
fifth-fleet.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

fifth-fleet.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
fifth-fleet.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

fifth-fleet.title: The Gulf Daily News
fifth-fleet.summary: Bahrain's English-language newspaper, and the source John Kiriakou turned to when a bomb went off at the Ministry of Labour two months into his posting — its Indian reporter, whose telephone was bugged like his own, told him a civil uprising was about to explode.

fifth-fleet.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
fifth-fleet.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

fifth-fleet.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
fifth-fleet.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

fifth-fleet.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
fifth-fleet.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: The Snickers bar
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The ritual in John Kiriakou''s Athens station: when an officer made a recruitment, the boss announced it in the staff meeting, everyone applauded, and he threw the officer a Snickers bar.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: American shoes
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: Intelligence peddlers
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: John Kiriakou
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

first-recruitment-in-athens.title: The Athens carjacking
first-recruitment-in-athens.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

fisa-court.title: Eastern District of Virginia
fisa-court.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

fisa-court.title: Julian Assange
fisa-court.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

fisa-court.title: Section 702
fisa-court.summary: Section of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act under which the U.S. government conducts warrantless electronic surveillance; per John Kiriakou the principal post-9/11 mechanism by which the CIA, NSA, and FBI surveil American citizens; renewed by Congress every two years over the objection of a small bipartisan minority; the subject of an estimated 200,000+ illegal FBI database queries — per the Brennan Center for Justice, including ~78,000 misused queries over a two-year window; the disclosure that Edward Snowden made public in summer 2013.

fisa-court.title: Access Agent
fisa-court.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

fisa-court.title: Bill Clinton
fisa-court.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

fisa-court.title: Bill Richardson
fisa-court.summary: U.S. Congressman, Ambassador to the United Nations, Secretary of Energy, and Governor of New Mexico; became friends with John Kiriakou at McClarty Associates; promised Secretary of State in exchange for endorsing Barack Obama in the 2008 Democratic primary; ultimately offered Commerce instead, then CIA director informally, before withdrawing his Commerce nomination.

fisa.title: Central Intelligence Agency
fisa.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

fisa.title: John Kiriakou
fisa.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

fisa.title: John Brennan
fisa.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

fisa.title: Patriot Act
fisa.summary: U.S. law passed after the September 11 attacks that vastly expanded domestic surveillance authority. Per John Kiriakou, the Patriot Act ''opened up everything'' — and he disputes the common belief that 9/11 was required to pass it: ''You underestimate Congress. They didn''t need a catastrophe — they would just pass it because they can.'' He ties it to NSA bulk-collection programs that vacuum up every phone call, text, email, and piece of metadata from Americans, in violation of the NSA''s own charter.

fisa.title: Tulsi Gabbard
fisa.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

fisa.title: SPLC 2025 indictment
fisa.summary: Federal criminal case unveiled by FBI director Kash Patel and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche against the Southern Poverty Law Center on multiple felony counts, described by John Kiriakou as concerning alleged payments to the Ku Klux Klan and Nazi groups and alleged money laundering; Kiriakou judges the charges are of the documentary kind that either happened or did not and that they could bring an end to an organisation whose 2024 balance sheet showed assets of roughly $786 to $822 million.

five-eyes.title: MOSSAD
five-eyes.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

five-eyes.title: John Kiriakou
five-eyes.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

five-eyes.title: George Tenet
five-eyes.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

five-eyes.title: Abu Zubaydah
five-eyes.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

five-eyes.title: Mount Weather
five-eyes.summary: U.S. government continuity-of-government underground facility on the Virginia–West Virginia line

five-eyes.title: French intelligence (DGSE)
five-eyes.summary: The French foreign intelligence service; characterized as exceptionally talented, exceptionally aggressive, and routinely lethal in the conduct of its operations

flock-cameras.title: Mass Surveillance
flock-cameras.summary: Kiriakou says the NSA has dropped any pretext of protecting civil liberties, warehousing every call, text and email in the Utah desert.

flock-cameras.title: John Kiriakou
flock-cameras.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

flock-cameras.title: 2028 presidential field
flock-cameras.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

flock-cameras.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
flock-cameras.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

flock-cameras.title: Andrew Bustamante
flock-cameras.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

flock-cameras.title: Phone microphone ad targeting
flock-cameras.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a spoken telephone conversation about concealed carry permits being followed, five minutes later, by a Facebook feed in which every single advertisement was for a concealed carry class — offered as evidence for his claim that the platforms go further than they admit and listen when the phone is turned off.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: The Iran–Israel exchange assessment
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement — which he expects to be unpopular — that Iran came out ahead of Israel in their direct missile exchange: the Iron Dome proved fallible, Iranian targeting was selective where Israel''s was not, and the ceasefire came, in his reading, because Israel had run out of missiles.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: The Syria chemical attack correction
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou's public retraction of what he wrote about the August 2013 chemical attack near Damascus. Asked about the passage in his book on Iran, he said he had written it before United Nations whistleblowers came forward to say they did not believe it was a Syrian government attack, and thanked the questioner for the chance to correct it.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: CIA attention to West Africa
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: Fake CIA résumés
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
forcing-iran-toward-a-bomb.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

foreign-aid.title: The al-Qaeda foot soldier
foreign-aid.summary: What John Kiriakou says he learned from interviewing captured al-Qaeda fighters — not the leaders but the eighteen-, nineteen- and twenty-year-olds, who told essentially the same story: an isolated village, illiteracy, no job skills, a poor relationship with their father, an age at which they wanted to marry, and no father willing to give them a daughter. The local imam offered $300 a month to go to Afghanistan, and $500 to their parents if they were martyred.

foreign-aid.title: The Sanaa sewer project
foreign-aid.summary: The example John Kiriakou uses for what patient foreign assistance looks like: on a visit to Yemen around 2000 he called on the Dutch ambassador and the Italian defence attaché, who were proud because their governments had just finished building a sewer system and water treatment facility for the capital — a project that had taken about fifteen years.

foreign-aid.title: CIA Smart TV Surveillance
foreign-aid.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA technical capability — disclosed publicly by the 2017 Vault 7 leaks — to convert a smart television's speaker system into a covert listening microphone even while the television appears to be switched off.

foreign-aid.title: Israeli foreknowledge of 9/11
foreign-aid.summary: John Kiriakou's stated belief that Israeli intelligence had penetrated al-Qaeda and knew an attack was coming but withheld the warning as a policy decision, offered as his explanation for the dozens of Israelis arrested in New York in the days after the attacks.

foreign-aid.title: Marjorie Taylor Greene
foreign-aid.summary: American congresswoman whom John Kiriakou, despite deep political disagreement, has repeatedly credited for breaking with her party on the Epstein files, on military aid to Israel, and on Gaza. He describes her as courageous for pressing Donald Trump to release the files unredacted, and says the pressure ultimately forced her out of Washington.

foreign-aid.title: Nixon's guarantee of Israeli national security
foreign-aid.summary: John Kiriakou's account that AIPAC, having begun to focus on election fundraising in the late 1960s, succeeded in getting President Nixon to guarantee Israeli national security in 1969 — a commitment he says no American president had made before.

fort-chapman.title: Jennifer Matthews
fort-chapman.summary: CIA analyst who was made chief of base at Khost, Afghanistan without operational or security training in order to complete the tour requirement for promotion, and who was killed there with six other officers by a Jordanian double agent she had gone outside the fortified perimeter to greet with a birthday cake.

fort-chapman.title: Senior Intelligence Service
fort-chapman.summary: The CIA's executive rank above the General Schedule, entry to which requires a tour outside an officer's own directorate and a tour in the policy community — a box-checking requirement John Kiriakou identifies as the reason an untrained analyst was sent to run a base in Afghanistan. Its officers are career staff rather than political appointees, some with thirty or forty years in place, which is why Kiriakou describes the service as capable of simply waiting a president out — or slow-rolling him. Its officers in the Counterterrorism Center were also the authors of the torture techniques.

fort-chapman.title: Abu Zubaydah
fort-chapman.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

fort-chapman.title: Maduro Capture
fort-chapman.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

fort-chapman.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
fort-chapman.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

fort-chapman.title: 9/11 plea agreements
fort-chapman.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.

fort-gordon.title: Miranda Rights
fort-gordon.summary: Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, says she was never read her Miranda rights during her 2017 arrest by the FBI.

fort-gordon.title: Watermark
fort-gordon.summary: Reality Winner, on Kiriakou's show, describes the printer watermark that let the NSA trace her leaked document to a specific office.

fort-gordon.title: Afghan Languages
fort-gordon.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

fort-gordon.title: Edward Snowden
fort-gordon.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

fort-gordon.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
fort-gordon.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

fort-gordon.title: Government Accountability Project
fort-gordon.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

francis-gary-powers.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
francis-gary-powers.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

francis-gary-powers.title: Vernon Walters
francis-gary-powers.summary: U.S. Army general who served as Deputy Director of the CIA, Ambassador to Germany, Ambassador to the United Nations, and as Nixon''s occasional secret envoy to foreign leaders. Per John Kiriakou — who met him at an early-career analysts'' dinner — Walters said the only time he was ever afraid for his safety was during a secret Nixon-ordered peace mission to Fidel Castro in Cuba, when it occurred to him that Castro could poison him and no one but Nixon would know he was there: ''I wouldn''t trust Nixon to call my wife.'' Then he looked at Castro and thought: ''I can take this scrawny son of a bitch.''

francis-gary-powers.title: William Donovan
francis-gary-powers.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan had President Truman's ear and insisted the new agency be independent rather than a division of the FBI; he was among the men who sat down with visiting MI6 officers in New York in 1946–47 and sketched out a centralized intelligence service on pads of paper, and he became — in Kiriakou's telling — the first director of the CIA, over the sustained opposition of J. Edgar Hoover.

francis-gary-powers.title: William and Elizabeth Friedman
francis-gary-powers.summary: American cryptologists who, per John Kiriakou, broke the Nazi Enigma encryption largely by exploiting a single known fact: every German communication ended with ''Heil Hitler'' — sometimes spelled out, sometimes abbreviated ''HH.'' Working outward from the letters H, E, I, L, T, R, they cracked the code one letter at a time. Their work led directly to the founding of the National Security Agency. Both are buried at Arlington National Cemetery.

francis-gary-powers.title: Bill Buckley
francis-gary-powers.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

francis-gary-powers.title: Carlos the Jackal
francis-gary-powers.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

frank-heart-attack.title: The glyburide incident
frank-heart-attack.summary: The episode John Kiriakou described in a Letter from Loretto of 12 September 2014: handed a bottle of glyburide by the prison pharmacy without explanation, he crashed twice and passed out on the floor — and his physician father-in-law told him the drug could have put him into heart failure.

frank-heart-attack.title: Larry
frank-heart-attack.summary: The prisoner at FCI Loretto who complained of back pain for more than a year, was given Tylenol, and progressed from a cane to a walker to a wheelchair before a chaplain forced an outside hospital referral — which found stage four cancer of the spine. He died in his bunk two weeks later.

frank-heart-attack.title: Medical care in federal prison
frank-heart-attack.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

frank-heart-attack.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
frank-heart-attack.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

frank-heart-attack.title: Paul Wright
frank-heart-attack.summary: The former prisoner who co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

frank-heart-attack.title: The chapel job
frank-heart-attack.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

frank-russo.title: Pete Calabrese
frank-russo.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

frank-russo.title: The rat and pedophile table
frank-russo.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

frank-russo.title: FCI Loretto
frank-russo.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

frank-russo.title: Jimmy Dimora
frank-russo.summary: The Cuyahoga County official convicted in the corruption case that also sent John Kiriakou's FCI Loretto bunkmate Frank Russo to prison — the man Russo testified against, and who in Kiriakou's account received a draconian sentence and will die in prison.

frank-russo.title: Mark Lanzalotti
frank-russo.summary: The prisoner John Kiriakou describes as his closest friend at FCI Loretto and one of the finest human beings he has known — a first-time non-violent drug defendant sentenced to triple life without parole for refusing to inform, the prison's foremost cook and bookie, and the man whose release Kiriakou secured by writing his Second Chance Act petition.

frank-russo.title: The stinger
frank-russo.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

frank-serpico.title: "There is almost no upside"
frank-serpico.summary: John Kiriakou''s accounting of what blowing the whistle cost him — pension, friends, freedom and finally family — set against the single thing he says is left: knowing he did the right thing. And his timeline, from the whistle in 2007 to a vindication he says took eleven years.

frank-serpico.title: The legal definition of whistleblowing
frank-serpico.summary: John Kiriakou''s insistence that whistleblowing is a legally defined act rather than a figure of speech: bringing to light evidence of waste, fraud, abuse, illegality, or threats to public health or public safety — at any level of government.

frank-serpico.title: Whistleblower psychology
frank-serpico.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

frank-serpico.title: Edward Snowden
frank-serpico.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

frank-serpico.title: Arianna Huffington
frank-serpico.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

frank-serpico.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
frank-serpico.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

freedom-of-information-act.title: George H.W. Bush
freedom-of-information-act.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

freedom-of-information-act.title: George W. Bush
freedom-of-information-act.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

freedom-of-information-act.title: Jake Tapper
freedom-of-information-act.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Tapper's visit was the head of a media wave that began with a smuggled-out letter on the Huffington Post, and it became Kiriakou's protection inside; even a guard known as a psychopath left him alone rather than find CNN parked beside his car.

freedom-of-information-act.title: Oliver Stone
freedom-of-information-act.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

freedom-of-information-act.title: The buried Senate documents
freedom-of-information-act.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a sitting senator who could not obtain a set of documents classified in the 1970s. Long past the point where mandatory declassification should have applied, the CIA disclaimed them as not its own; they turned out to be Senate documents, which no disclosure law reaches, and no authority existed to compel their release.

freedom-of-information-act.title: Thirty-year mandatory declassification
freedom-of-information-act.summary: The statutory requirement, described by John Kiriakou, that classified American documents be released after thirty years — a law he says virtually nobody knows about, and which he raises against the continued withholding of Kennedy assassination records more than sixty years on. He also describes the redaction practice that operates alongside it.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: The tier one walk-up
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: The recruitment John Kiriakou calls one of the best operations of his career and credits entirely to his mentor Gust Avrakotos: an approach to an official of a tier one country — one of America''s greatest enemies — made by the simple expedient of walking right up to the man''s house, a technique Avrakotos had used himself in the 1970s.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: CIA attention to West Africa
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: Fake CIA résumés
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.title: GeoRisk Solutions
freemasons-and-opus-dei-at-the-cia.summary: The political risk consultancy John Kiriakou founded with the dean of the University of Salamanca's intelligence studies programme, staffed with academics and a former assistant secretary of state, with offices in Salamanca and Washington and a stated business of selling cost-effective country and regional risk analysis to banks, funds and companies.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: MK-Ultra
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: Alexa
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: John Brennan
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: LSD Mind Manipulation
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: Kiriakou on the CIA dosing unwitting men with LSD in safe houses, using sex workers as bait, to find out whether the drug could unlock secrets.

french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.title: The San Francisco bacterium release
french-village-lsd-bread-experiment.summary: The MK-ULTRA experiment John Kiriakou describes in which the CIA waited for an unusually foggy day, released a bacterium across San Francisco and its public transit system to see how many people it could infect, and gave eight people a rare upper respiratory infection.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: Cofer Black
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: The liaison class
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: The course John Kiriakou ran at the CIA for visiting officers of allied intelligence services — the setting for Cofer Black's warning weeks before 9/11, and the reason Kiriakou was in the counterterrorism chief's office to ask whether he had meant it.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: John Kiriakou
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: Counterterrorism Center
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.title: The custody standoff
frus-greece-turkey-cyprus-volume.summary: The week John Kiriakou used his CIA surveillance training to find his own sons after his ex-wife hid them in breach of a custody order — ending with him carrying his eight-year-old out of a Greek Orthodox church during the consecration, a felony charge that was dropped, and a hostage-style handover at a diner on the state line.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: Chinese overseas police stations
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a New York Times revelation about Chinese nationals with apparent ties to the Chinese police operating out of storefronts around Manhattan and travelling around the United States to threaten Chinese people with reprisals against relatives in Beijing — and his puzzlement that the FBI missed it.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: The Sanaa sewer project
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: The example John Kiriakou uses for what patient foreign assistance looks like: on a visit to Yemen around 2000 he called on the Dutch ambassador and the Italian defence attaché, who were proud because their governments had just finished building a sewer system and water treatment facility for the capital — a project that had taken about fifteen years.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: The Yemen jazz radio plan
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: A scheme John Kiriakou says the American defence attaché in Sanaa described to him on his last visit to Yemen in 2011: a propaganda programme modelled on NPR that would play jazz and run call-in shows for young Yemenis. It lasted about two weeks before it shuttered, because nobody was going to listen to it.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: The Afghan police tribal rotation
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.title: CIA language training
fusha-and-the-gulf-dialect.summary: The agency''s language pipeline as John Kiriakou experienced and describes it: a full year of Arabic at nine hours a day, an optional second year at the State Department''s school, and the calculation that made his own career — that it is cheaper to teach a linguist operations than to teach an operations officer Greek and Arabic.

gail-slater.title: Pam Bondi
gail-slater.summary: Panelists alongside Kiriakou on why Trump picked Bondi for loyalty above all, and called her handling of the Epstein files a farce.

gail-slater.title: Bill Barr
gail-slater.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

gail-slater.title: Lee Zeldon
gail-slater.summary: Per Megyn Kelly's opening monologue, the EPA administrator reportedly considered by Trump as a possible replacement for Attorney General Pam Bondi.

gail-slater.title: Alexa
gail-slater.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

gail-slater.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
gail-slater.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

gail-slater.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
gail-slater.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Abu Zubaydah
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Cofer Black
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Counterterrorism Center
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

galls-com-sponsor-story.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
galls-com-sponsor-story.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

gary-johnson.title: The Libertarian Party
gary-johnson.summary: The third party a lifelong Democrat joined on release from prison, after its 2016 presidential nominee had written to him in his cell and to the Attorney General on his behalf — the party John Kiriakou says was the only one talking about whistleblowing and the security-versus-liberty trade-off, and the one whose structural problem, he was told, is that it has no benefactor.

gary-johnson.title: Oliver Stone
gary-johnson.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

gary-johnson.title: FCI Loretto
gary-johnson.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

gary-johnson.title: American missile stockpiles
gary-johnson.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

gary-johnson.title: Arianna Huffington
gary-johnson.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

gary-johnson.title: Ralph Nader
gary-johnson.summary: American consumer advocate and perennial third-party presidential candidate, thanked by name by John Kiriakou at his February 2013 portrait unveiling as a steadfast supporter whose backing — through the Nader Family Foundation and personally — Kiriakou described as humbling.

gary-schroen.title: The post-9/11 name traces
gary-schroen.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own assignment in the weeks after the September 11 attacks: with people walking into American embassies all over the world offering information on al-Qaeda, the CIA was buried under tens of thousands of names — sometimes thousands arriving in a single day — and needed, as he put it, an army of clerks to search them against its databases.

gary-schroen.title: The live satellite feed myth
gary-schroen.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat rejection of one of the most common screen conventions about American intelligence: that officers can call up a live satellite picture and watch a target walk through the streets of a city. There was no such thing then, he says, and there is no such thing now.

gary-schroen.title: Kandahar
gary-schroen.summary: The southern Afghan city and province that recurs across John Kiriakou's Afghanistan material — site of one of the two al-Qaeda training camps Abu Zubaydah founded, whose commanders were captured in the same March 2002 raids; the town Bill Clinton said he would have had to destroy, killing 300 innocents, to kill bin Laden in the 1990s; and a stop on Kiriakou's Senate-era heroin-poppy investigation, when the military helicoptered him down before refusing to let him walk the poppy fields.

gary-schroen.title: Renting Afghan warlords
gary-schroen.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

gary-schroen.title: Condoleezza Rice
gary-schroen.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

gary-schroen.title: Heather Kiriakou
gary-schroen.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Contra rebels
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The right-wing Nicaraguan insurgency armed by the Reagan administration against the Sandinista government. In John Kiriakou's account they were conservatives, right-wingers, in some cases fascists, and disgruntled military officers; they were split into a northern group the United States armed and a southern group that financed itself by selling cocaine — a distinction that became the pivot of the Gary Webb affair.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Dark Alliance
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: Gary Webb's seven-part San Jose Mercury News investigation reporting that cocaine reaching Los Angeles and fuelling the crack epidemic had travelled through Nicaragua with the CIA's knowledge. John Kiriakou's account stresses what Webb did and did not claim — that the agency turned a blind eye rather than ran the operation — and that three separate federal investigations later found his reporting correct.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Walter Pincus
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The Washington Post reporter who, in John Kiriakou's account of the Gary Webb affair, took the CIA's side of the cocaine story and put it on the paper's front page — wrong, and Kiriakou believes knowingly so.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Oscar Blandón
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The senior Contra leader whom Gary Webb's reporting identified as running the cocaine operation that moved product from Nicaragua to Los Angeles, and one of two men named in the Dark Alliance series.

gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.title: Domino theory
gary-webb-kill-the-messenger.summary: The Cold War doctrine, described by John Kiriakou as Ronald Reagan's organising obsession in Central America, holding that if one country there fell to communism the rest would fall in sequence up to the American border — the stated rationale for backing the Contra rebels against the Sandinistas.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Kompromat
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: Russian-derived term for compromising material — recordings, photographs, or documentation of an individual''s criminal, sexual, or embarrassing behavior — used to coerce cooperation or silence. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s formal policy conclusion is that kompromat doesn''t work as a recruitment tool: faced with the binary choice between confessing to a spouse and committing treason, most targets confess. The agency therefore prefers voluntary, ideologically or financially motivated recruitment.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Asset acquisition cycle
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

gay-diplomat-operation.title: John Kiriakou
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Sociopathic Tendencies
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA actively recruits for what its instructors call 'sociopathic tendencies' — not full clinical sociopathy, but the capacity to operate in legal, moral, and ethical gray areas without being paralyzed by regret. Kiriakou describes this as the trait that makes case officers effective at recruitment and adaptable in the field, and offers his own act of whistleblowing as evidence he does not possess the deeper sociopathy that, in his view, characterizes the most institutionally successful intelligence officers.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: David Boies
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

gay-diplomat-operation.title: Jeffrey Epstein
gay-diplomat-operation.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

gaza-famine.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
gaza-famine.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

gaza-famine.title: Hamas
gaza-famine.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

gaza-famine.title: Roger Waters
gaza-famine.summary: Founding member of the British rock band Pink Floyd; outspoken supporter of Palestinian human rights; anonymously paid off John Kiriakou's second mortgage during his federal prison sentence, sparing his wife and children the loss of the family home; only discovered to be the benefactor years later; subsequently a personal friend of Kiriakou and a recurring guest on his programme.

gaza-famine.title: October 7 attack
gaza-famine.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

gaza-famine.title: Christian Zionism
gaza-famine.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that American evangelical Christianity functions as an arm of Zionism, and that its support for Israel is helping extinguish the oldest Christian communities on earth — a position he says he argued directly with the evangelical students he was invited to teach, and which he grounds in the projection that Nazareth, Christian for two thousand years, may soon have no Christians left.

gaza-famine.title: Germany and Israel
gaza-famine.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

general-dostum.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
general-dostum.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

general-dostum.title: Brian Ross
general-dostum.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

general-dostum.title: John Kiriakou
general-dostum.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

general-dostum.title: Abu Zubaydah
general-dostum.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

general-dostum.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
general-dostum.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

general-dostum.title: MK-Ultra
general-dostum.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: MOSSAD
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: Abraxas Corporation
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: Central Intelligence Agency
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

general-intelligence-directorate.title: Denied areas
general-intelligence-directorate.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

general-intelligence-directorate.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
