Lawless was caught, served about seven years, and was given Greek citizenship on release.

greek-intelligence-service.title: Jerry Falwell Jr.
greek-intelligence-service.summary: Evangelical leader and former president of Liberty University; John Kiriakou recounts that Falwell personally recruited him to lecture at Liberty's Jesse Helms School of Government after his whistleblowing, with the reasoning that "torture is not Christian."

greek-intelligence-service.title: Taybeh
greek-intelligence-service.summary: The only fully Christian village in the West Bank, home to the Holy Land's oldest brewery; John Kiriakou recounts it being set on fire and its Marian festival attacked by the IDF with drones, helicopters and stun grenades.

greek-orthodox-church.title: PFLP
greek-orthodox-church.summary: Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; Palestinian armed group co-founded by George Habash and Ahmed Khatib, college roommates at the American University of Beirut. It is one of the Arab organizations John Kiriakou worked against during his Athens tour, where a semi-secret 1980s deal let the Arab groups transit Greece unmolested so long as they did not kill Greeks. Kiriakou's chance paper on Khatib made him the White House expert on the occupation governor of Kuwait in August 1990, and two of the Front's retired cadres later sat across a table from him in Jordan for a Sacha Baron Cohen shoot.

greek-orthodox-church.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
greek-orthodox-church.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

greek-orthodox-church.title: George W. Bush
greek-orthodox-church.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

greek-orthodox-church.title: Overcriminalization
greek-orthodox-church.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

greek-orthodox-church.title: Evangelical Zionism
greek-orthodox-church.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the American Christian movement that supports Israel in order to hasten the return of Christ — a belief he calls a cult rather than a religion, which he says Israeli officials knowingly exploit, and which he blames for the abandonment of the Middle East's original Christians.

greek-orthodox-church.title: Abu Zubaydah
greek-orthodox-church.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

greenland.title: China's base in Djibouti
greenland.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

greenland.title: China as economic threat
greenland.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

greenland.title: Monroe Doctrine
greenland.summary: John Kiriakou's history of the Monroe Doctrine — ignored for decades after its declaration, humiliated in the Falklands and Venezuela, and only made real by Teddy Roosevelt in 1905 — and his argument that reviving it to seize Maduro handed China a claim to Taiwan and Russia a claim to Ukraine.

greenland.title: Five Eyes
greenland.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

greenland.title: Somaliland
greenland.summary: Self-declared breakaway state in the Horn of Africa that Israel became the only country in the world to recognize as independent, gaining a military base positioned roughly 30 seconds' flight time from Yemen; John Kiriakou, who visited Somaliland while posted with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in Djibouti, describes it as a functioning city of about 100,000 unconnected to Mogadishu, al-Shabaab, or piracy.

greenland.title: Proposals to relocate the Palestinians
greenland.summary: John Kiriakou's account of recurring schemes to solve the Palestinian question by moving the population somewhere else — including a 1980s proposal to rename a barren diamond of land on the Saudi–Iraqi border "Palestine" and resettle everyone there — and his verdict that picking up an entire people and moving them is unprecedented and untenable.

grenada-invasion.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
grenada-invasion.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

grenada-invasion.title: Barry Eisler
grenada-invasion.summary: Former CIA officer turned bestselling novelist, and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou's, who describes him as one of the very few former intelligence officers to have succeeded at storytelling outside the secret world as thoroughly as he did inside it.

grenada-invasion.title: Beirut
grenada-invasion.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

grenada-invasion.title: Dead Drop (podcast)
grenada-invasion.summary: John Kiriakou''s narrative podcast, launched in late 2025 — a season-long, memoir-style retelling of his life in intelligence, from recruitment ("The New Recruit") through Athens ("Golden Boy") to the post-9/11 hunt ("The Hunt Begins"), with mini-episodes like "A Spy''s Guide to Sofia." Written by Kiriakou with Alan Katz, produced by Costard & Touchstone Productions, with Kiriakou, Katz, and Nick Mechanic as executive producers. Its stated goal: "the deepest possible perspective on the world of spying and what makes any spy tick."

grenada-invasion.title: The Directorate of Operations
grenada-invasion.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

grenada-invasion.title: Kiriakou's father and grandfather
grenada-invasion.summary: The two men John Kiriakou names as the greatest influences on his life: a grandfather with a third-grade education who pushed his children through doctorates and handed his grandson an 11th-century gold coin dug from a Greek garden, and a father, an elementary school principal, who was twice passed over for promotion because he refused to pay the bribe the school board demanded. Kiriakou says that refusal is what made him a whistleblower.

ground-branch.title: Special Activities Division
ground-branch.summary: The CIA's paramilitary arm; described by John Kiriakou as having two organizationally distinct components — the pre-9/11 SAD, a covert-action division within the Directorate of Operations, and a post-9/11 special activities group within the Counterterrorism Center, staffed largely by personnel on secondment from Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, and other special-operations units.

ground-branch.title: Abu Zubaydah
ground-branch.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ground-branch.title: Extraordinary Rendition
ground-branch.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

ground-branch.title: Blackwater
ground-branch.summary: The private military contractor founded by Erik Prince that ran the CIA's Global Response Staff and, until shut down by Leon Panetta, a global assassination program; staffed at the board level with former CIA officers including Cofer Black as Vice President.

ground-branch.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
ground-branch.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

ground-branch.title: Executive Order 12333
ground-branch.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

grs-global-response-staff.title: Blackwater
grs-global-response-staff.summary: The private military contractor founded by Erik Prince that ran the CIA's Global Response Staff and, until shut down by Leon Panetta, a global assassination program; staffed at the board level with former CIA officers including Cofer Black as Vice President.

grs-global-response-staff.title: Executive Order 12333
grs-global-response-staff.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

grs-global-response-staff.title: Ground Branch
grs-global-response-staff.summary: The land-operating component of the CIA's Special Activities Division, staffed almost entirely by former Delta Force and SEAL Team 6 operators rather than career officers; per John Kiriakou its job is to kill or kidnap anyone judged a threat to the United States, and its work is so secret that everyone in the office knew what they did and nobody mentioned it.

grs-global-response-staff.title: Special Activities Division
grs-global-response-staff.summary: The CIA's paramilitary arm; described by John Kiriakou as having two organizationally distinct components — the pre-9/11 SAD, a covert-action division within the Directorate of Operations, and a post-9/11 special activities group within the Counterterrorism Center, staffed largely by personnel on secondment from Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, and other special-operations units.

grs-global-response-staff.title: Admiral William Crowe
grs-global-response-staff.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

grs-global-response-staff.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
grs-global-response-staff.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

guantanamo-bay.title: Abu Zubaydah
guantanamo-bay.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

guantanamo-bay.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
guantanamo-bay.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

guantanamo-bay.title: Senate Torture Report
guantanamo-bay.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

guantanamo-bay.title: Hummus
guantanamo-bay.summary: The CIA's coercive 'rectal feeding' of detainees using pureed hummus — an unauthorized interrogation technique used at post-9/11 black sites, exposed in the 2014 Senate Torture Report, and the abuse for which John Kiriakou became most associated in popular culture.

guantanamo-bay.title: Strawberry Fields
guantanamo-bay.summary: The CIA's nickname for a secret black-site annex at the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base used for the post-9/11 detention and interrogation program.

guantanamo-bay.title: Salt Pit
guantanamo-bay.summary: A CIA black site north of Kabul — a former Soviet, then Taliban, dungeon the CIA took over for its post-9/11 detention programme. Gul Rahman froze to death there in a cold cell, a technique John Kiriakou considers worse than waterboarding and says killed several prisoners; he suspects others were killed off the books and never reported.

guantanamo-origin.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
guantanamo-origin.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

guantanamo-origin.title: Abu Zubaydah
guantanamo-origin.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

guantanamo-origin.title: Guantanamo Bay
guantanamo-origin.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

guantanamo-origin.title: John Kiriakou
guantanamo-origin.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

guantanamo-origin.title: Girls' madrasa raid error
guantanamo-origin.summary: A mistaken CIA raid, conducted the night of the Abu Zubaydah operation, on the home of an elderly Pakistani man running an unlicensed girls' madrasa — the only phone in the neighborhood, which al-Qaeda fighters had been using and the CIA had been intercepting. John Kiriakou personally apologized to the man on the president's behalf and arranged compensation.

guantanamo-origin.title: Jennifer Keenan
guantanamo-origin.summary: FBI agent who partnered with John Kiriakou in Islamabad on the handling of an unreliable walk-in informant who had confessed to firing a rocket at the American embassy in 1996. After the informant's leads to weapons caches in Peshawar and a safe in Multan both turned up empty, Kiriakou and Keenan decided to lure him back to the embassy and arrest him on the strength of his original confession, which carried no statute of limitations.

gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.title: 2026 Iran war
gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.title: Bill Clinton
gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.title: MOSSAD
gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.title: Netanyahu's nuclear threat to Trump
gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.summary: John Kiriakou's account, sourced to friends in the White House and the administration, that Donald Trump agreed to bomb Iran because Benjamin Netanyahu threatened to use nuclear weapons against Iran if the United States did not act. Kiriakou presents it as the reason a request every previous president refused was finally granted.

gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.title: Recruiting from the bottom
gulf-consultations-before-the-iran-war.summary: The targeting method John Kiriakou believes produced the killings of Iran''s leadership: not agents at the top of the state but destitute refugees at street level, paid a hundred dollars a month to write down when a general leaves his building and by which route. He contrasts it with the CIA''s own record in Iran, where it spent his career trying and failing to recruit inside the Ayatollah''s office, the foreign ministry and the IRGC.

gulf-daily-news.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
gulf-daily-news.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

gulf-daily-news.title: The Bahrain water table
gulf-daily-news.summary: The prehistoric aquifer that surfaces in Bahrain — running, in John Kiriakou's telling, from the Atlantic beneath the whole of Africa — which until the 1970s gushed out of the ground in natural springs and made the island an oasis, and which overdevelopment has since dropped some thirty-five feet.

gulf-daily-news.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
gulf-daily-news.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

gulf-daily-news.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
gulf-daily-news.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

gulf-daily-news.title: The Dilmun burial mounds
gulf-daily-news.summary: The ancient grave mounds standing in the Shia villages of Bahrain — ordinary ones ten or twenty feet high, royal ones fifty — which John Kiriakou took visiting friends and family to see, and which sat in the same villages the government was raiding at night during the uprising.

gulf-daily-news.title: The Fifth Fleet in Bahrain
gulf-daily-news.summary: The United States naval presence that has been based in Bahrain since 1976 — the naval component of Central Command — and the social geography it created for John Kiriakou as a diplomat: the officers'' club for its salad bar, the enlisted club for football and cheap beer.

gulf-intelligence-services.title: AIPAC
gulf-intelligence-services.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

gulf-intelligence-services.title: Israel's counterintelligence threat ranking
gulf-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou's repeated point that the American intelligence community formally ranks Israel a critical counterintelligence threat — the same tier as North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba — specifically for spying on and infiltrating the US government, and that policy has responded by giving Israel more access rather than less.

gulf-intelligence-services.title: Israeli espionage in the United States
gulf-intelligence-services.summary: The long-running Israeli intelligence effort against American targets, which John Kiriakou describes from inside the CIA: Israelis barred from the headquarters building, 187 spies identified by the FBI in 1990, a critical-threat counterintelligence ranking alongside Russia and China, and a 2026 warning that activity had intensified.

gulf-intelligence-services.title: Israeli False Flags
gulf-intelligence-services.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the Mossad has been carrying out false flag operations since the founding of the state of Israel and is "usually very good at it"; he says his first suspicion on hearing of attacks on Saudi oil fields, Azerbaijan, and Cyprus was that they were Israeli false flags, and he fears a false flag against the Al-Aqsa Mosque blamed on Iran or the Arabs.

gulf-intelligence-services.title: Israeli interception of US secure calls
gulf-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou's account of overhearing evidence, within six months of joining the CIA, that Israeli intelligence was listening to encrypted American government calls — a colleague's secure line dropped mid-conversation and two Israeli voices could be heard on the open channel discussing whether the call had ended. He treats the episode as the concrete basis for assuming that American principals are intercepted as a matter of routine.

gulf-intelligence-services.title: Israel's rightward shift
gulf-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for why Israeli politics moved sharply right over roughly two decades — that immigration from Russia, Ukraine and the United States brought in a conservatism the Israeli electorate had not seen before, displacing the socialist politics of the earlier European arrivals.

gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.title: GeoRisk Solutions
gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.summary: The political risk consultancy John Kiriakou founded with the dean of the University of Salamanca's intelligence studies programme, staffed with academics and a former assistant secretary of state, with offices in Salamanca and Washington and a stated business of selling cost-effective country and regional risk analysis to banks, funds and companies.

gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.title: The Israeli listening devices ban
gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.summary: Why Mossad and Shin Bet representatives were barred from CIA headquarters, per John Kiriakou: the gifts they brought to liaison meetings kept turning up with listening devices and batteries embedded inside, so the agency stopped admitting them and rented meeting space in Virginia instead.

gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.title: The Jerusalem harassment campaign
gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what happened to a CIA colleague and his wife during a declared two-year State Department rotation in Jerusalem: furniture rearranged after one embassy party, all three toilets in the house defecated in after another, and, before they left, the family dog''s tail cut off and bandaged. Kiriakou presents the three break-ins as routine rather than exceptional.

gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.title: The "spell your name" briefing
gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.summary: The first time John Kiriakou dealt with the Israeli services: eight weeks into his CIA career, giving the junior slot in a liaison briefing on Saddam Hussein''s state of mind, he was interrupted by a Mossad representative who asked him to spell his name and then told him he was Jewish. Kiriakou''s reply — that he was not recruitable — became one of his recurring illustrations of the liaison relationship.

gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.title: CIA attention to West Africa
gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
gulf-secret-prisons-for-hire.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

gulf-security-bargain.title: Yasser Arafat
gulf-security-bargain.summary: Leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization, who appears in John Kiriakou's account at the two moments he treats as decisive for the Palestinians — backing Saddam Hussein after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which cost the Palestinian middle class its standing across the Gulf, and walking out of the last Clinton-era peace talks with a divided map of Jerusalem already on the table.

gulf-security-bargain.title: U.S. diplomatic vacancies
gulf-security-bargain.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the mass dismissal of career U.S. ambassadors — never replaced — left the Gulf without American envoys as war with Iran loomed, so allied royals had to ask him personally whether the U.S. would attack.

gulf-security-bargain.title: 2026 Iran war
gulf-security-bargain.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

gulf-security-bargain.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
gulf-security-bargain.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

gulf-security-bargain.title: George Tenet
gulf-security-bargain.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

gulf-security-bargain.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
gulf-security-bargain.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

gust-avrakotos.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
gust-avrakotos.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

gust-avrakotos.title: Richard Welch
gust-avrakotos.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

gust-avrakotos.title: CIA sexpionage
gust-avrakotos.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the CIA''s use of sex in espionage — routine from its founding through the early 1980s, including MK-Ultra and honey-pot operations — and why the agency largely abandoned it: coercion cannot build the trust a long-term source requires. Other services never stopped.

gust-avrakotos.title: The Welch .45
gust-avrakotos.summary: The single .45 caliber pistol used by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in every confirmed assassination over the group's twenty-seven-year operational life

gust-avrakotos.title: Mike Mastrovito
gust-avrakotos.summary: Twenty-five-year Secret Service veteran; founder and first director of the Secret Service Intelligence Division; later, after a forced retirement, a CIA contractor specializing in Greek terrorism; close colleague of John Kiriakou in Athens. Started his career at the end of the Eisenhower administration, was in Dallas with President Kennedy, and was effectively removed from the Secret Service after Sara Jane Moore's 1975 attempt on President Ford — having interviewed Moore two weeks earlier on a threatening letter she had sent.

gust-avrakotos.title: Olof Palme assassination
gust-avrakotos.summary: The 1986 street murder of the Swedish prime minister, which John Kiriakou revisited step by step in Stockholm with researchers who had spent years on it. His conclusion — drawn from dozens of witness reports of two-man cars with walkie-talkies, some identified as police vehicles — is that much of the surveillance that night was carried out by people who believed they were running a practice exercise, until someone walked up and shot Palme dead.

hague-invasion-act.title: International Criminal Court
hague-invasion-act.summary: The Hague tribunal created by the Rome Statute, which has charged Benjamin Netanyahu with war crimes and crimes against humanity. John Kiriakou supports it as the necessary successor to Nuremberg, notes that neither the United States nor Israel is a signatory, and observes that a forced landing in a signatory state would oblige that country to arrest Netanyahu.

hague-invasion-act.title: Graham–Netanyahu ICC tapes
hague-invasion-act.summary: Recordings of Lindsey Graham coordinating with Benjamin Netanyahu on how to discredit the International Criminal Court over its arrest warrant. On the tapes Graham lines up Senate signatories for a protest letter, jokes that he should be paid "tons of shekels," and asks Netanyahu to telephone two Democratic senators to thank them. John Kiriakou argues the conduct meets the definition of espionage his own judge applied to him.

hague-invasion-act.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
hague-invasion-act.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

hague-invasion-act.title: Lindsey Graham
hague-invasion-act.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

hague-invasion-act.title: Donald Trump
hague-invasion-act.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

hague-invasion-act.title: Espionage Act
hague-invasion-act.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

haiti.title: The 2021 Cuba protests
haiti.summary: The July 2021 demonstrations in Cuba, which John Kiriakou declined to read as the beginning of a revolution. He called them a test run to gauge the government's reaction, objected that a New York Times line about Democrats treading lightly in Florida meant nothing anyone could act on, and noted that everything touching Cuba is too politically loaded in the United States to be discussed plainly.

haiti.title: Caleb Maupin
haiti.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

haiti.title: Daniel Ortega
haiti.summary: The president of Nicaragua, and the case John Kiriakou contrasts with Cuba: where he read the 2021 Cuban protests as a test run, he said Nicaragua''s circumstances — a social security shortfall, a rise in the price of bread, and eight opposition party leaders arrested and imprisoned before an election — amounted to grounds for a real uprising.

haiti.title: The Backstory
haiti.summary: The daily Radio Sputnik programme John Kiriakou co-hosted with Lee Stranahan, carried on terrestrial radio in the Washington area as well as online. It was the successor to his earlier show Loud and Clear with Brian Becker, and he described its format as two men with a beer talking about the day.

haiti.title: The Peace and Friendship Bridge
haiti.summary: A bridge across the narrow Pakistan–China frontier that John Kiriakou saw advertised on billboards across Pakistan while serving there, and the exchange it produced with a Pakistani general: asked why so much was being made of it, the general said the Chinese were the only friends Pakistan had who had never turned on them — and then looked at Kiriakou.

haiti.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
haiti.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

halfway-house.title: Home confinement
halfway-house.summary: The house arrest that followed John Kiriakou's release from prison — 87 days confined to the interior of his own house, telephone checks at any hour of the day or night, weekly halfway-house reporting and twice-weekly drug testing — which he describes as considerably worse than prison, and would rather have traded back for the cell. In federal sentencing arithmetic it is also one of the deductions that turns a headline number into the time actually served.

halfway-house.title: Oliver Stone
halfway-house.summary: American film director with whom John Kiriakou struck up a friendship after his release from prison. Stone optioned the rights to one chapter of Kiriakou's first book, co-developed an unmade History Channel series with him, blurbed his book on Abu Zubaydah, and was among the public figures who campaigned against the Bureau of Prisons' attempt to shut down Kiriakou's prison blog. The two disagree sharply over whether the CIA killed John F. Kennedy.

halfway-house.title: RDAP
halfway-house.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which takes a year off a federal sentence on completion — the single most valuable piece of advice John Kiriakou says he gives to people facing prison time, alongside good-conduct credit and halfway-house conversion.

halfway-house.title: Bureau of Prisons
halfway-house.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

halfway-house.title: FCI Loretto
halfway-house.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

halfway-house.title: Letter from Loretto
halfway-house.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

hamas.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
hamas.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

hamas.title: October 7 attack
hamas.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

hamas.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
hamas.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

hamas.title: Donald Trump
hamas.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

hamas.title: Famine in Gaza
hamas.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

hamas.title: Ismail Haniyeh assassination
hamas.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the killing of Hamas political bureau chief Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran, which he says Israel carried out via a bomb planted months in advance in Haniyeh's regular guesthouse and detonated remotely — an operation he contrasts with the diplomatic and airspace complications a missile strike would have entailed.

hamid-karzai.title: John Kerry
hamid-karzai.summary: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during John Kiriakou's 2009 service as the committee's senior investigator; subsequently U.S. Secretary of State; characterized by Kiriakou as a coward who buckled under CIA pressure on the Dasht-i-Leili reopening and as personally fixated on his perceived theft of the Secretary of State position by Hillary Clinton; the famously thrown medals were duplicates purchased at the post exchange.

hamid-karzai.title: Afghan heroin policy
hamid-karzai.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

hamid-karzai.title: The four requirements of a coup
hamid-karzai.summary: The checklist John Kiriakou says is taught at West Point for overthrowing a government — the presidential palace and the leader, the broadcast stations, the capital's major intersections, and the support of the military — which he uses to argue that regime change in Venezuela cannot work, because the fourth item belongs to the incumbent.

hamid-karzai.title: FBI apologies to Kiriakou
hamid-karzai.summary: John Kiriakou says three FBI agents who worked on his prosecution have written to apologize since his conviction — one saying the case was 'directed and driven by seniormost officials' while mid- and street-level personnel objected, but 'we just followed orders.'

hamid-karzai.title: Syria as a regime-change template
hamid-karzai.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the fall of Bashar al-Assad shows organic regime change is faster, cheaper and less destructive than the enforced kind — and should be studied as a model. He allows aid to local forces as legitimate policy, and notes without prompting that in Syria the CIA was supplying al-Qaeda while the Pentagon supplied a group at war with it.

hamid-karzai.title: The Taliban
hamid-karzai.summary: The Afghan movement John Kiriakou describes as loyal to nobody and, in 2001, genuinely baffled by the American invasion: its leadership held that sheltering al-Qaeda was a cultural obligation to a guest rather than an alliance, that it had never taken up arms against the United States, and that Washington was welcome to fight al-Qaeda on Afghan soil. He supported the Doha peace process but judged the Biden-era power-sharing letter an abandonment, arguing that any deal without guarantees on women, girls'' education and the vote returns the country to the 1990s.

hamilton-68.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
hamilton-68.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

hamilton-68.title: Kiriakou's personal anecdotes
hamilton-68.summary: Three personal stories John Kiriakou has told in interviews — tracking down and meeting Andy Warhol as a college senior, a Congolese vice president's remark that Americans promise democracy while the Chinese provide food, and Kiriakou's own Zelle account being suspended over Cuba-sanctions compliance after a paid article about his Cuba trip.

hamilton-68.title: Bashar al-Assad
hamilton-68.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

hamilton-68.title: Chinese spy balloon incident
hamilton-68.summary: 2023 controversy over a high-altitude balloon that crossed U.S. airspace, widely labeled in media coverage as a "Chinese spy balloon"; John Kiriakou notes no U.S. government official ever officially confirmed it was conducting espionage, and says he personally believes it was likely a weather balloon, since satellite surveillance already renders such balloons unnecessary for spying.

hamilton-68.title: CIA adultery culture
hamilton-68.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

hamilton-68.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
hamilton-68.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

haqqani-white-house-meeting.title: Afghan heroin policy
haqqani-white-house-meeting.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

haqqani-white-house-meeting.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
haqqani-white-house-meeting.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

haqqani-white-house-meeting.title: Central Intelligence Agency
haqqani-white-house-meeting.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

haqqani-white-house-meeting.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
haqqani-white-house-meeting.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

haqqani-white-house-meeting.title: Citizens United
haqqani-white-house-meeting.summary: The Supreme Court decision John Kiriakou blames for legalizing unlimited corporate political money and for corporations having "taken over" two of the three branches of government — and which he says lets AIPAC pour tens of millions into single congressional races to defeat candidates who cross Israel.

haqqani-white-house-meeting.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
haqqani-white-house-meeting.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

harold-james-nicholson.title: Eric O'Neill
harold-james-nicholson.summary: Former FBI analyst placed as Robert Hanssen's nominal assistant in the final months of the FBI's mole investigation; his role was to observe Hanssen and detect tradecraft slip-ups that would confirm Hanssen as the mole. After Hanssen's arrest, O'Neill resigned from the FBI, citing the stress of the operation. Subject of the 2007 film Breach.

harold-james-nicholson.title: Robert Hanssen
harold-james-nicholson.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

harold-james-nicholson.title: Brian Kelley
harold-james-nicholson.summary: Chief of counterintelligence at the CIA; framed by FBI counterintelligence chief Robert Hanssen — the actual Soviet/Russian mole — as the source of executed agents; spent a year and a half on leave without pay, surrounded around the clock by FBI agents, while his daughter was approached and told her father would face the death penalty if he did not confess.

harold-james-nicholson.title: Cuban double agents
harold-james-nicholson.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

harold-james-nicholson.title: Afghan heroin policy
harold-james-nicholson.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

harold-james-nicholson.title: Ai Weiwei
harold-james-nicholson.summary: Chinese contemporary artist and pro-democracy activist; designer of the Beijing Olympic Stadium; per John Kiriakou, produced a Lego portrait of him as one of 178 political prisoners in the series, with Kiriakou's panel positioned next to Martin Luther King Jr.; the work is now in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Institution.

haroon-yenor-trial.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
haroon-yenor-trial.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

haroon-yenor-trial.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
haroon-yenor-trial.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

harry-truman-israel-regret.title: Nixon's guarantee of Israeli national security
harry-truman-israel-regret.summary: John Kiriakou's account that AIPAC, having begun to focus on election fundraising in the late 1960s, succeeded in getting President Nixon to guarantee Israeli national security in 1969 — a commitment he says no American president had made before.

harry-truman-israel-regret.title: AIPAC
harry-truman-israel-regret.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

harry-truman-israel-regret.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
harry-truman-israel-regret.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

harry-truman-israel-regret.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
harry-truman-israel-regret.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

harry-truman-israel-regret.title: Israeli non-extradition of Jews
harry-truman-israel-regret.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Israel as a refuge that does not extradite Jewish fugitives regardless of the offence, illustrated by the case of an American lawyer who fled there after a child-abuse suit and was recovered only by an Interpol sting in Cyprus. Kiriakou uses the rule to frame a question about Jeffrey Epstein: why a man with jets and hidden billions did not flee there himself.

harry-truman-israel-regret.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
harry-truman-israel-regret.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

hassan-nasrallah.title: Iran 12-Day War
hassan-nasrallah.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

hassan-nasrallah.title: Hezbollah
hassan-nasrallah.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

hassan-nasrallah.title: MOSSAD
hassan-nasrallah.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

hassan-nasrallah.title: Lebanon-Israeli Conflict
hassan-nasrallah.summary: Per John Kiriakou, no Israeli government will allow Lebanon to flourish as a nation; he expects continued Israeli attacks and forced displacement of civilians, citing a statistic of up to 700,000 Lebanese internally displaced, and links the war to the "Greater Israel" rhetoric of US ambassador Mike Huckabee.

hassan-nasrallah.title: Ismail Haniyeh assassination
hassan-nasrallah.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the killing of Hamas political bureau chief Ismail Haniyeh in Tehran, which he says Israel carried out via a bomb planted months in advance in Haniyeh's regular guesthouse and detonated remotely — an operation he contrasts with the diplomatic and airspace complications a missile strike would have entailed.

hassan-nasrallah.title: Israel-United States relations
hassan-nasrallah.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

havana-syndrome.title: Jeffrey Epstein
havana-syndrome.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

havana-syndrome.title: John Kiriakou
havana-syndrome.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

havana-syndrome.title: Central Intelligence Agency
havana-syndrome.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

havana-syndrome.title: MK-Ultra
havana-syndrome.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

havana-syndrome.title: Abu Zubaydah
havana-syndrome.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

havana-syndrome.title: Bill Burns
havana-syndrome.summary: Career U.S. diplomat named CIA director in 2021, and the one senior appointment John Kiriakou has endorsed without qualification — a man he has known for thirty years, "apolitical to a fault," untouched by torture, Guantánamo or the secret prisons, and the only figure he thought had the standing to reform the agency. Kiriakou wrote an op-ed calling him "finally, an adult in the room," and says Burns ended up serving as the Biden administration's de facto Secretary of State before being drawn into the CIA's culture of drone warfare, rendition and domestic spying.

hawala-system.title: Abu Zubaydah
hawala-system.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

hawala-system.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
hawala-system.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

hawala-system.title: Admiral William Crowe
hawala-system.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

hawala-system.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
hawala-system.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

hawala-system.title: Bob Baer
hawala-system.summary: Former CIA case officer; per John Kiriakou, "pretty famous"; the subject of George Clooney's film Syriana; pulled out of northern Iraq by the Clinton White House in the 1990s after [NSA intercepted](/wiki/the-intercept) a communication revealing he was developing a network of sources to assassinate Saddam Hussein — National Security Adviser Sandy Berger called CIA and threatened him with a conspiracy charge.

hawala-system.title: Bob Trout
hawala-system.summary: Washington defense attorney, Plato Cacheris''s partner at Trout Cacheris, and one of the eleven lawyers who represented John Kiriakou: the "elegant southern gentleman" who told him, "If you were my own brother, I would beg you to take this deal."

hazara-judo-belts.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
hazara-judo-belts.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

hazara-judo-belts.title: The Afghan police tribal rotation
hazara-judo-belts.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

hazara-judo-belts.title: The Taliban truck escort origin
hazara-judo-belts.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Taliban began: as a Pakistani government scheme under Benazir Bhutto to take madrasa students — talib, plural taliban — out of the religious schools and put them with Kalashnikovs aboard Pakistani trucks crossing Afghanistan to Iran, to stop mujahideen fighters from pirating the cargo.

hazara-judo-belts.title: Afghan rare earth minerals
hazara-judo-belts.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, made days after the fall of Kabul in August 2021, that the country with real leverage in Afghanistan was China — which holds an exclusive contract to mine rare earth metals valued in a Defense Department report at one trillion dollars, and therefore has a stake in a stable long-term Afghan government even a Taliban one.

hazara-judo-belts.title: Afghan Languages
hazara-judo-belts.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

hazara-judo-belts.title: Human Rights Watch
hazara-judo-belts.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. In his account of his own arrest, Human Rights Watch also sits inside the fateful chain of custody: when the FBI traced a classified name found in its hands, the trail ran to journalist Matthew Cole, and Cole named Kiriakou — bringing two dozen FBI agents to his door.

heather-kiriakou.title: The Bolivian visa line
heather-kiriakou.summary: The CIA's interrogation of John Kiriakou's wife, then a serving senior officer, over a single sentence in a Los Angeles Times op-ed her husband had written and had already cleared through the agency's own publications review board. Told the piece was cleared, the security officer replied that one line in it was top secret — the statement that Iranians no longer needed visas to travel to Bolivia. Kiriakou had taken it off the Bolivian foreign ministry's website.

heather-kiriakou.title: The Americans Who Tell the Truth portrait
heather-kiriakou.summary: The portrait of John Kiriakou painted by Robert Shetterly for his long-running series Americans Who Tell the Truth, unveiled at Busboys and Poets in Washington on February 7, 2013 — weeks before Kiriakou reported to prison — and inscribed with the words 'Even if torture works it cannot be tolerated.'

heather-kiriakou.title: Prison as temporary duty
heather-kiriakou.summary: The frame John Kiriakou and his wife adopted in the weeks between his sentencing and his surrender: that a thirty-month sentence was to be treated as a long overseas posting. He had spent much of his CIA career deployed for months at a time, once for two years, and says the family handled the separation the way it had handled those.

heather-kiriakou.title: The IRS audits of Kiriakou
heather-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou says that within weeks of his December 2007 ABC News interview confirming CIA waterboarding he was audited by the Internal Revenue Service, and that he was audited again every single year thereafter. He places the audits alongside FBI surveillance and repeated CIA criminal referrals as part of a single pattern of retaliation that preceded his prosecution by five years.

heather-kiriakou.title: Ralph Nader
heather-kiriakou.summary: American consumer advocate and perennial third-party presidential candidate, thanked by name by John Kiriakou at his February 2013 portrait unveiling as a steadfast supporter whose backing — through the Nader Family Foundation and personally — Kiriakou described as humbling.

heather-kiriakou.title: ''Joe Bidenopoulos''
heather-kiriakou.summary: The nickname John Kiriakou says Joe Biden carries in the Greek-American community — a reputation for being so pro-Greek-American that he is called Joe Bidenopoulos — which Kiriakou hoped in 2023 might give him a connection worth trying in his pursuit of a presidential pardon.

heather-saunders.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
heather-saunders.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

heather-saunders.title: John Kiriakou
heather-saunders.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

heather-saunders.title: Stephen Saunders
heather-saunders.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

heather-saunders.title: The Welch .45
heather-saunders.summary: The single .45 caliber pistol used by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in every confirmed assassination over the group's twenty-seven-year operational life

heather-saunders.title: Mad minute
heather-saunders.summary: CIA case-officer procedure for the opening seconds of every meeting with a recruited source — confirm the source is safe, confirm a clean surveillance-detection route, and set the next meeting — so that if the door is kicked in, the operational essentials have already been taken care of.

heather-saunders.title: Richard Welch
heather-saunders.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

henry-kissinger.title: Julian Assange
henry-kissinger.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

henry-kissinger.title: George H.W. Bush
henry-kissinger.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

henry-kissinger.title: Osama bin Laden
henry-kissinger.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

henry-kissinger.title: Daniel Ellsberg
henry-kissinger.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

henry-kissinger.title: Freedom of Information Act
henry-kissinger.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

henry-kissinger.title: Zbigniew Brzezinski
henry-kissinger.summary: National security adviser to Jimmy Carter, named in John Kiriakou's account of Afghanistan as an architect of the policy of luring the Soviet Union into a war there — a policy Kiriakou says literally destroyed the country and set the conditions for the Taliban.

hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.title: Agent payment mechanics
hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.title: Cuban double agents
hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.title: Kompromat
hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.summary: Russian-derived term for compromising material — recordings, photographs, or documentation of an individual''s criminal, sexual, or embarrassing behavior — used to coerce cooperation or silence. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s formal policy conclusion is that kompromat doesn''t work as a recruitment tool: faced with the binary choice between confessing to a spouse and committing treason, most targets confess. The agency therefore prefers voluntary, ideologically or financially motivated recruitment.

hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.title: The SIGINT–HUMINT balance
hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to what he calls the most important question facing any incoming CIA director: how to divide investment between signals intelligence and human intelligence. His position is that signals collection cannot supply the one thing policy requires — a person in the room when a decision is taken — and that every new director says so on arrival and then drifts back toward the technology.

hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.title: Allen Dulles
hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.title: Church Committee
hes-been-ours-since-the-seventies.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

hezbollah.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
hezbollah.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

hezbollah.title: MOSSAD
hezbollah.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

hezbollah.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
hezbollah.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

hezbollah.title: Hassan Nasrallah
