israels-rightward-shift.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

israels-rightward-shift.title: Donald Trump
israels-rightward-shift.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

italian-election-covert-action.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
italian-election-covert-action.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

italian-election-covert-action.title: Radio and TV Martí
italian-election-covert-action.summary: U.S. government broadcasters beaming anti-communist programming at Cuba; John Kiriakou uses their accidental reach into Florida to explain why the Obama administration made it legal, in 2015, to propagandize the American people.

italian-election-covert-action.title: Operation Mockingbird
italian-election-covert-action.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

italian-election-covert-action.title: Active measures
italian-election-covert-action.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency''s clandestine propaganda arm.

italian-election-covert-action.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
italian-election-covert-action.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

italian-election-covert-action.title: John Kiriakou
italian-election-covert-action.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

italian-intelligence-services.title: "Most other countries are more moral than the CIA"
italian-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer who asked whether the United States has the most moral intelligence agency: it does not, and a hundred countries could be named whose services behave better — the disqualifying practice being the killing of people who pose no threat to the United States.

italian-intelligence-services.title: Iranian intelligence capability
italian-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Iranian intelligence as poor and always having been poor, on the ground that Iranian officers do not receive good training and are essentially on their own, with only marginal help from the Russians and the Chinese.

italian-intelligence-services.title: A Middle East reading list
italian-intelligence-services.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

italian-intelligence-services.title: Bombing the Omanis
italian-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

italian-intelligence-services.title: Bowe Bergdahl
italian-intelligence-services.summary: The American soldier who walked off his base in Afghanistan, was captured by the Haqqani network and handed to the Taliban, and was repatriated in a prisoner trade — a man John Kiriakou says was treated as a traitor although he was not one.

italian-intelligence-services.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
italian-intelligence-services.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

italians-at-loretto.title: Aryan Brotherhood
italians-at-loretto.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

italians-at-loretto.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
italians-at-loretto.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

italians-at-loretto.title: John Kiriakou
italians-at-loretto.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

italians-at-loretto.title: The prison food economy
italians-at-loretto.summary: The underground kitchen at FCI Loretto, where meals were cooked in bin liners heated by improvised immersion elements, guards stole and resold the food they were meant to be guarding, and Kiriakou stopped going to the cafeteria for the last six to eight months of his sentence.

italians-at-loretto.title: Prison tattoos
italians-at-loretto.summary: Tattoos as John Kiriakou encountered them at FCI Loretto — the swastika-necked welcoming committee on his first day, the Lady Justice piece that made him laugh and then think, the constant pressure on him to get one, and his flat refusal to take a souvenir of the place.

italians-at-loretto.title: Truck and Cat in the Hat
italians-at-loretto.summary: An incident at FCI Loretto in which John Kiriakou, told by one prisoner that another had called him a rat, invented a slur he knew would enrage a convicted serial killer — who beat the accuser badly enough to require a helicopter medevac. Kiriakou presents it as a live application of two rules he says he learned at the CIA: let others do your dirty work, and admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations.

itamar-ben-gvir.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
itamar-ben-gvir.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

itamar-ben-gvir.title: October 7 attack
itamar-ben-gvir.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

itamar-ben-gvir.title: Hamas
itamar-ben-gvir.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

itamar-ben-gvir.title: MOSSAD
itamar-ben-gvir.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

itamar-ben-gvir.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
itamar-ben-gvir.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

itamar-ben-gvir.title: Jonathan Pollard
itamar-ben-gvir.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

j-edgar-hoover.title: National Security Act of 1947
j-edgar-hoover.summary: The law that created the CIA and the National Security Council — passed, in John Kiriakou's telling, only because Harry Truman lied to J. Edgar Hoover. Hoover lobbied Capitol Hill to kill the bill until Truman promised the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the bill passed, Hoover realized he'd been duped, and ordered the FBI not to cooperate with the new agency — a freeze that lasted, incredibly, until after 9/11, when incompatible computer systems were still keeping the CIA's cables from reaching the Bureau.

j-edgar-hoover.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
j-edgar-hoover.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

j-edgar-hoover.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
j-edgar-hoover.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

j-edgar-hoover.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
j-edgar-hoover.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

j-edgar-hoover.title: William Donovan
j-edgar-hoover.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan had President Truman's ear and insisted the new agency be independent rather than a division of the FBI; he was among the men who sat down with visiting MI6 officers in New York in 1946–47 and sketched out a centralized intelligence service on pads of paper, and he became — in Kiriakou's telling — the first director of the CIA, over the sustained opposition of J. Edgar Hoover.

j-edgar-hoover.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
j-edgar-hoover.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

jack-devine.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
jack-devine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

jack-devine.title: Dewey Clarridge
jack-devine.summary: The CIA operations officer John Kiriakou calls a legendary figure and a giant of the 1980s — prosecuted over Iran-Contra, and the man who said publicly that Saudi Arabia already had nuclear weapons. Kiriakou believes him, holds that the Saudis financed the Pakistani bomb and were repaid in access to it, and believes Clarridge was also involved in the movement of cocaine into the United States.

jack-devine.title: Extraordinary Rendition
jack-devine.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA practice of seizing terrorism suspects in one country and transporting them to a third country — often a country with no due-process protections — to be held, interrogated, or tortured outside U.S. legal jurisdiction. The program operated alongside the enhanced-interrogation program and was the operational mechanism by which prisoners reached secret CIA facilities and allied torture sites in countries like Bahrain. Kiriakou himself was not in the rendition line of work but became a federal felon under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act for a single confirmation of a colleague's surname to a journalist who claimed to be writing a book on the Abu Omar rendition from Milan.

jack-devine.title: Saudi nuclear program
jack-devine.summary: Saudi Arabia's decades-long pursuit of uranium enrichment, nominally for nuclear power, which John Kiriakou notes was already old news when he arrived at the CIA in 1990 and which conventional wisdom has always read as a weapons programme.

jack-devine.title: Bob Baer
jack-devine.summary: Former CIA case officer; per John Kiriakou, "pretty famous"; the subject of George Clooney's film Syriana; pulled out of northern Iraq by the Clinton White House in the 1990s after [NSA intercepted](/wiki/the-intercept) a communication revealing he was developing a network of sources to assassinate Saddam Hussein — National Security Adviser Sandy Berger called CIA and threatened him with a conspiracy charge.

jack-devine.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
jack-devine.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.title: Special Activities Division
jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.summary: The CIA's paramilitary arm; described by John Kiriakou as having two organizationally distinct components — the pre-9/11 SAD, a covert-action division within the Directorate of Operations, and a post-9/11 special activities group within the Counterterrorism Center, staffed largely by personnel on secondment from Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, and other special-operations units.

jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.title: Kiriakou's personal anecdotes
jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.summary: Three personal stories John Kiriakou has told in interviews — tracking down and meeting Andy Warhol as a college senior, a Congolese vice president's remark that Americans promise democracy while the Chinese provide food, and Kiriakou's own Zelle account being suspended over Cuba-sanctions compliance after a paid article about his Cuba trip.

jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.title: Bashar al-Assad
jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.title: Chinese spy balloon incident
jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.summary: 2023 controversy over a high-altitude balloon that crossed U.S. airspace, widely labeled in media coverage as a "Chinese spy balloon"; John Kiriakou notes no U.S. government official ever officially confirmed it was conducting espionage, and says he personally believes it was likely a weather balloon, since satellite surveillance already renders such balloons unnecessary for spying.

jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.title: CIA adultery culture
jack-murphy-nato-sabotage-story.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

jack-teixeira.title: Chelsea Manning
jack-teixeira.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

jack-teixeira.title: Espionage Act
jack-teixeira.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

jack-teixeira.title: Julian Assange
jack-teixeira.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

jack-teixeira.title: Public-interest defense
jack-teixeira.summary: The affirmative defense the Espionage Act does not allow: John Kiriakou explains that a defendant cannot tell a jury he acted in the public interest, and that Edward Snowden''s willingness to come home hinged on getting that chance — which the Justice Department refused.

jack-teixeira.title: CIA disguise program
jack-teixeira.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's disguise and forgery specialists — including a master disguise maker recruited from a beauty academy who built him a custom bald-head mask over six weeks, and a master forger recruited off his college newspaper cartoons.

jack-teixeira.title: Donald Trump
jack-teixeira.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

jake-tapper.title: Arianna Huffington
jake-tapper.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

jake-tapper.title: Freedom of Information Act
jake-tapper.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

jake-tapper.title: Letter from Loretto
jake-tapper.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

jake-tapper.title: John Kiriakou
jake-tapper.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jake-tapper.title: Julian Assange
jake-tapper.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

jake-tapper.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
jake-tapper.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

jamaal-bowman.title: AIPAC
jamaal-bowman.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

jamaal-bowman.title: Cori Bush
jamaal-bowman.summary: Former U.S. Representative from St. Louis (Missouri's 1st congressional district); cited by John Kiriakou as one of the two named cases of AIPAC successfully primarying an incumbent for delivering a House floor speech describing the Gaza war as a "wholesale massacre of Palestinian civilians."

jamaal-bowman.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
jamaal-bowman.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

jamaal-bowman.title: BDS movement
jamaal-bowman.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

jamaal-bowman.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
jamaal-bowman.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

jamaal-bowman.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
jamaal-bowman.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

james-angleton.title: JFK assassination
james-angleton.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

james-angleton.title: MK-Ultra
james-angleton.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

james-angleton.title: Allen Dulles
james-angleton.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

james-angleton.title: James Jesus Angleton
james-angleton.summary: The CIA counterintelligence chief old-timers were 'genuinely afraid' of — and the wall of illegal files on American citizens kept in his office.

james-angleton.title: LSD Mind Manipulation
james-angleton.summary: Kiriakou on the CIA dosing unwitting men with LSD in safe houses, using sex workers as bait, to find out whether the drug could unlock secrets.

james-angleton.title: Kim Philby
james-angleton.summary: The British MI6 deputy director secretly working for the KGB — recruited in college and directed to join the service — and, in John Kiriakou's telling, James Angleton's best man and his child's godfather; his decades of betrayal broke Angleton, and he escaped from Beirut through a bathroom window to Moscow. Kiriakou ranks the Cambridge ring as damage at historic levels, above any modern comparison.

james-bond.title: George Washington University
james-bond.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

james-bond.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
james-bond.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

james-bond.title: John Kiriakou
james-bond.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

james-bond.title: Central Intelligence Agency
james-bond.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

james-bond.title: In-Q-Tel
james-bond.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

james-bond.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
james-bond.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

james-clapper.title: Espionage Act
james-clapper.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

james-clapper.title: John Brennan
james-clapper.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

james-clapper.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
james-clapper.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

james-clapper.title: Ron Wyden
james-clapper.summary: U.S. senator and the lone real challenger of the CIA on the intelligence committees; John Kiriakou faults Wyden for challenging the agency only 'by the agency's rules' — refusing to read the Senate torture report into the record, and admitting at a dinner that fighting harder would cost him his security clearance.

james-clapper.title: Langley
james-clapper.summary: The Virginia location of CIA headquarters and, in John Kiriakou''s usage, shorthand for the agency''s permanent power. It''s where he worked as the CIA''s lone Iraq-Kuwait analyst — told to start on Iraq "because nothing ever happened there" — where a cafeteria conversation invited him into the torture program, and the place agencies return to after apologizing to Congress, "where of course nothing ever changes." When a host suggested the real government of America is out in Langley and Washington''s white marble is for show, Kiriakou''s answer was: "that''s about the shape of it."

james-clapper.title: CIA political action group
james-clapper.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

james-comey.title: John Brennan
james-comey.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

james-comey.title: Espionage Act
james-comey.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

james-comey.title: Kiriakou's Abraham Lincoln collection
james-comey.summary: John Kiriakou''s private collection of Abraham Lincoln relics, assembled at auction over many years and governed by a strict standard of provenance: a blood-soaked fragment of the pillowcase Lincoln died on, wallpaper from the Petersen House death room, a swatch of Mary Todd Lincoln''s funeral dress, and wood from the gallows on which the conspirators were hanged.

james-comey.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
james-comey.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

james-comey.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
james-comey.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

james-comey.title: David Ransom
james-comey.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

james-fishback.title: AIPAC
james-fishback.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

james-fishback.title: MOSSAD
james-fishback.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

james-fishback.title: Donald Trump
james-fishback.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

james-fishback.title: Jeffrey Epstein
james-fishback.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

james-fishback.title: Ted Rall
james-fishback.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

james-fishback.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
james-fishback.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

james-jesus-angleton.title: Kim Philby
james-jesus-angleton.summary: The British MI6 deputy director secretly working for the KGB — recruited in college and directed to join the service — and, in John Kiriakou's telling, James Angleton's best man and his child's godfather; his decades of betrayal broke Angleton, and he escaped from Beirut through a bathroom window to Moscow. Kiriakou ranks the Cambridge ring as damage at historic levels, above any modern comparison.

james-jesus-angleton.title: James Angleton
james-jesus-angleton.summary: Long-serving chief of CIA counterintelligence; in John Kiriakou's account the man whose wall of files at headquarters were all dossiers on American citizens, who was best man at Kim Philby's wedding and never recovered from learning Philby was the mole, and who — per the declassified JFK files — ordered CIA officers to recruit Lee Harvey Oswald.

james-jesus-angleton.title: Allen Dulles
james-jesus-angleton.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

james-jesus-angleton.title: Alexa
james-jesus-angleton.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

james-jesus-angleton.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
james-jesus-angleton.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

james-jesus-angleton.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
james-jesus-angleton.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

james-woolsey.title: President's Daily Brief
james-woolsey.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

james-woolsey.title: Aldrich Ames
james-woolsey.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

james-woolsey.title: Bill Clinton
james-woolsey.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

james-woolsey.title: Havana Syndrome
james-woolsey.summary: Cluster of neurological symptoms — including nausea, ringing in the ears, vertigo, and traumatic brain injury — reported by American diplomatic and intelligence personnel beginning in Havana, Cuba, and subsequently at posts around the world. Per John Kiriakou, his initial skepticism gave way when a friend developed Havana Syndrome with an MRI-confirmed traumatic brain injury after a meeting outside the Russian Foreign Ministry; Kiriakou attributes the syndrome to Russian or Chinese directed-energy weapons and acknowledges the United States used a similar weapon during the operation to capture Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

james-woolsey.title: Bill Binney
james-woolsey.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

james-woolsey.title: Democratic redistricting collapse
james-woolsey.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Republicans remain competitive despite historically low approval ratings: a 1992 decision he attributes to Hillary Clinton to spend only in presidential battlegrounds, which he says ceded state legislatures and the congressional map for decades.

jane-harman.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
jane-harman.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

jane-harman.title: Senate Torture Report
jane-harman.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

jane-harman.title: Abu Zubaydah
jane-harman.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

jane-harman.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
jane-harman.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

jane-harman.title: Cold cell
jane-harman.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

jane-harman.title: Federal Torture Act
jane-harman.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Abu Zubaydah
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Federal plea coercion
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the federal justice system coerces guilty pleas by stacking charges and winning 98.2% of its cases — so that even innocent defendants take deals, as he did, told by his own attorney that the system is 'not about justice; it's about mitigating damage.'

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Athens bank fraud report
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a dream job as COO of an Athens investment firm in 2020, discovering it was an elaborate bank fraud, and being unable to get the FBI to act — an agent telling him that without 'terrorism, China, or January 6th,' they were not interested.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Barack Obama
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.title: Central Intelligence Agency
japanese-diplomat-fbi-sting.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

jared-kushner.title: Bruce Fein
jared-kushner.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

jared-kushner.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
jared-kushner.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

jared-kushner.title: Mitchell and Jessen
jared-kushner.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

jared-kushner.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
jared-kushner.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

jared-kushner.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
jared-kushner.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

jared-kushner.title: John Kiriakou
jared-kushner.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jason-leopold.title: Ken Dilanian
jason-leopold.summary: Chief national-security correspondent at NBC News and MSNBC; documented — through a Jason Leopold Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the CIA — to have sent his own articles to the CIA Office of Public Affairs for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

jason-leopold.title: John Kiriakou
jason-leopold.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jason-leopold.title: Operation Mockingbird
jason-leopold.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

jason-leopold.title: Balochistan drone base
jason-leopold.summary: Secret CIA drone surveillance base in southwestern Pakistan's Balochistan region; its location was inadvertently disclosed when investigative journalist Jason Leopold filed a Freedom of Information Act request for Pentagon aviation-fuel-delivery records and identified an outsized fuel flow to the otherwise-undocumented base.

jason-leopold.title: Tucker Carlson 2026 FARA referral
jason-leopold.summary: The March 2026 criminal referral against Tucker Carlson to the U.S. Department of Justice accusing him of treason, espionage and Foreign Agents Registration Act violations that John Kiriakou says was widely misattributed to the CIA before the pro-Israel political activist Laura Loomer publicly claimed authorship the following day; Kiriakou treats the episode as an escalation from Israeli-aligned political actors and warns Carlson to worry less about legal jeopardy than about physical safety.

jason-leopold.title: Will Hurd
jason-leopold.summary: Former CIA case officer, congressman and OpenAI board member whom John Kiriakou says he mentored at the agency; Kiriakou cites him as an example of the intelligence and tech worlds merging.

jcpoa.title: The permanent multipolar world
jcpoa.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the unipolar period following the collapse of the Soviet Union has ended permanently, and that the arrangement was not inevitable — he attributes it to American strategic choices, principally leaving the Iran nuclear agreement and choosing confrontation with China and Russia over the cooperation that was available.

jcpoa.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
jcpoa.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

jcpoa.title: China as mediator
jcpoa.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

jcpoa.title: China as economic threat
jcpoa.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

jcpoa.title: The Damascus consulate strike
jcpoa.summary: The April 2024 Israeli attack on Iran's consulate in Damascus, which John Kiriakou describes as an unambiguous violation of the Vienna Convention, and whose official Israeli explanation — that it had not occurred to anyone the world would read it as a provocation — he calls disingenuous and intended purely for domestic audiences.

jcpoa.title: Lunch with the Russian ambassador
jcpoa.summary: A meeting John Kiriakou describes in which the Russian ambassador to the United States, having read a column of his, invited him to lunch and asked whether there was anything the two countries could still cooperate on in wartime. Kiriakou's answer was three areas — narcotics, proliferation and terrorism — each with a concrete case attached.

jd-vance.title: Marco Rubio
jd-vance.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

jd-vance.title: The Republican split over the Iran war
jd-vance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the division inside the Republican Party over the 2026 war with Iran — between the voters who backed Donald Trump as the no-foreign-wars candidate and an administration Kiriakou says has reverted to the neoconservative posture of John McCain's party, with Tulsi Gabbard and J.D. Vance on one side and Marco Rubio on the other.

jd-vance.title: Tulsi Gabbard
jd-vance.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

jd-vance.title: John McCain
jd-vance.summary: Late U.S. Senator from Arizona who gave the most consequential Senate-floor defense of John Kiriakou — declaring that 'if it weren't for John Kiriakou, the American people would never have had any idea what the CIA was doing in their name' — and sponsored the McCain–Feinstein amendment banning torture.

jd-vance.title: Donald Trump
jd-vance.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

jd-vance.title: 2028 presidential field
jd-vance.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

jean-gately.title: JFK assassination
jean-gately.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

jean-gately.title: John McCone
jean-gately.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on November 22, 1963; per John Kiriakou's retelling of an account from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., responded to Bobby Kennedy Sr.'s same-day question "Tell me your people didn't do this" not with denial but with "I don't know who did it."

jean-gately.title: Gina Haspel
jean-gately.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

jean-gately.title: Jeffrey Epstein
jean-gately.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

jean-gately.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
jean-gately.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

jean-gately.title: Truman's CIA op-ed
jean-gately.summary: A 1963 Washington Post op-ed in which former President Harry Truman — who signed the CIA into being in 1947 — called it a 'damn fool mistake' that should be disbanded; John Kiriakou notes the piece ran in the morning edition and vanished from the evening one.

jeff-fahey.title: Tyrell Vanto
jeff-fahey.summary: Hollywood screenwriter and director; son of Jesse Vanto; friend of John Kiriakou; wrote and directed the late-2025 film in which Kiriakou made his acting debut.

jeff-fahey.title: Erik Prince
jeff-fahey.summary: Founder of Blackwater; CIA non-official-cover officer with a 201 file; identified publicly by Leon Panetta in front of the House Intelligence Committee; lives in Dubai outside U.S. jurisdiction; in popular culture invoked, alongside Elon Musk, as the composite figure for the billionaire in the Tyrell Vanto film featuring John Kiriakou.

jeff-fahey.title: Hummus
jeff-fahey.summary: The CIA's coercive 'rectal feeding' of detainees using pureed hummus — an unauthorized interrogation technique used at post-9/11 black sites, exposed in the 2014 Senate Torture Report, and the abuse for which John Kiriakou became most associated in popular culture.

jeff-fahey.title: John Kiriakou
jeff-fahey.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jeff-fahey.title: Lincoln's last turd
jeff-fahey.summary: A purported piece of human waste attributed by a Pennsylvania circus-freak-show museum to Abraham Lincoln on the night of his assassination; auctioned for $5,000; subsequent DNA analysis disproved the attribution. John Kiriakou's failed bid for the artifact is the anecdote that, recirculated in early 2026, made him an internet meme figure.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Kathryn Ruemmler
jeffrey-epstein.summary: Obama White House counsel whose Epstein-file emails show her repeatedly trying to introduce Jeffrey Epstein to CIA director John Brennan; John Kiriakou notes she personally received a rare CIA award from Brennan and, as the White House's top lawyer, would have been the final legal authority approving the Tuesday-morning kill list.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Mike Huckabee
jeffrey-epstein.summary: The United States ambassador to Israel under Donald Trump, and the subject of a public call for resignation from John Kiriakou after Huckabee received Jonathan Pollard at the American embassy. Kiriakou''s assessment separates two charges: Huckabee is not a traitor but an idiot who did not think the meeting was a big deal, and a former governor of a small state who still behaves as though he can set policy without the State Department or the National Security Council.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Nick Bryant
jeffrey-epstein.summary: Investigative journalist, activist and co-founder of Epstein Justice, author of The Franklin Scandal, and a repeat guest on John Kiriakou's programme, where Kiriakou describes him as knowing the Epstein case better than anybody else in America.

jeffrey-epstein.title: Somaliland
jeffrey-epstein.summary: Self-declared breakaway state in the Horn of Africa that Israel became the only country in the world to recognize as independent, gaining a military base positioned roughly 30 seconds' flight time from Yemen; John Kiriakou, who visited Somaliland while posted with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in Djibouti, describes it as a functioning city of about 100,000 unconnected to Mogadishu, al-Shabaab, or piracy.

jeffrey-epstein.title: CIA record deniability
jeffrey-epstein.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how senior CIA officers occasionally decide to keep an event out of the written record — illustrated by a recruited asset who committed a public murder, after which the Deputy Director for Operations told Kiriakou, on second thought, 'let's not put that in writing.'

jeffrey-epstein.title: Felix Rodriguez
jeffrey-epstein.summary: Cuban-American CIA officer and Bay of Pigs veteran; involved in the Vietnam War and reportedly present at the killing of Che Guevara; distinct from [Jose Rodriguez](/wiki/jose-rodriguez), the post-9/11 CIA official.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Espionage Act
jeffrey-sterling.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

jeffrey-sterling.title: PTSD
jeffrey-sterling.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Aryan Brotherhood
jeffrey-sterling.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Daniel Ellsberg
jeffrey-sterling.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Edward Snowden
jeffrey-sterling.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

jeffrey-sterling.title: Federal Torture Act
jeffrey-sterling.summary: United States statute criminalizing torture; per John Kiriakou, on the books since at least 1946, with concrete enforcement history — after World War II the United States executed Japanese soldiers convicted of waterboarding American prisoners of war, meaning waterboarding was at that time a capital offense under U.S. law. The act was effectively set aside for the CIA's enhanced interrogation program after 2002.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Tommy McHale
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: Highly decorated Port Authority of New York and New Jersey detective who worked as a terrorist hunter alongside John Kiriakou in Islamabad, Pakistan after 9/11; a survivor of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing whose best friend died on 9/11.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Bob Grenier
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Girls' madrasa raid error
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: A mistaken CIA raid, conducted the night of the Abu Zubaydah operation, on the home of an elderly Pakistani man running an unlicensed girls' madrasa — the only phone in the neighborhood, which al-Qaeda fighters had been using and the CIA had been intercepting. John Kiriakou personally apologized to the man on the president's behalf and arranged compensation.

jennifer-keenan-fbi.title: Senate Torture Report
jennifer-keenan-fbi.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

jennifer-matthews.title: Senior Intelligence Service
jennifer-matthews.summary: The CIA's executive rank above the General Schedule, entry to which requires a tour outside an officer's own directorate and a tour in the policy community — a box-checking requirement John Kiriakou identifies as the reason an untrained analyst was sent to run a base in Afghanistan. Its officers are career staff rather than political appointees, some with thirty or forty years in place, which is why Kiriakou describes the service as capable of simply waiting a president out — or slow-rolling him. Its officers in the Counterterrorism Center were also the authors of the torture techniques.

jennifer-matthews.title: Alfreda Bikowsky
jennifer-matthews.summary: Senior CIA officer who headed Alec Station and, before that, served as its chief of operations, overseeing the CIA's torture program; per John Kiriakou, "bad news from the get-go," and part of a failed attempt with Rich Blee to turn a San Diego al-Qaeda cell into double agents.

jennifer-matthews.title: Forward Operating Base Chapman Attack
jennifer-matthews.summary: December 30, 2009 suicide bombing at Forward Operating Base Chapman in Khost, Afghanistan, killing seven CIA officers and wounding more than a dozen others — the deadliest single day in CIA history. Per John Kiriakou, the officer who led the base was a GS-14 with zero security training, assigned to the post as a career-promotion checkbox before her required elevation to the Senior Intelligence Service. The bomber — a Jordanian national who walked into the American consulate in Istanbul claiming to be Osama bin Laden's doctor — was never polygraphed because CIA personnel 'wanted so badly for this to be true.'

jennifer-matthews.title: Abbottabad
jennifer-matthews.summary: The Pakistani garrison city where Osama bin Laden was found and killed — named for a British major who was Pakistan's first military trainer, home to the Pakistani military's leadership, and in John Kiriakou's judgement the last place bin Laden could have lived unnoticed by the Pakistani state.

jennifer-matthews.title: Abu Zubaydah
jennifer-matthews.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

jennifer-matthews.title: Agent payment mechanics
jennifer-matthews.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

jennings-randolph.title: Abu Omar rendition
jennings-randolph.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

jennings-randolph.title: Abu Zubaydah
jennings-randolph.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

jennings-randolph.title: Aldrich Ames
jennings-randolph.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

jennings-randolph.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
jennings-randolph.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

jennings-randolph.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
jennings-randolph.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

jennings-randolph.title: CIA National Resources Division
jennings-randolph.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

jeremy-hammond.title: RDAP
jeremy-hammond.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which takes a year off a federal sentence on completion — the single most valuable piece of advice John Kiriakou says he gives to people facing prison time, alongside good-conduct credit and halfway-house conversion.

jeremy-hammond.title: Julian Assange
jeremy-hammond.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

jeremy-hammond.title: Chelsea Manning
jeremy-hammond.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

jeremy-hammond.title: Mike Pompeo
jeremy-hammond.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

jeremy-hammond.title: Corporate whistleblower protections
jeremy-hammond.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that whistleblower law stops at the wrong boundary. Employees who report waste, fraud, abuse or illegality inside a private company are doing the very thing the word describes, and yet can be fired for it — as he says happened at Amazon. His remedy is codified statutory protection for corporate whistleblowers on the same footing as government ones.

jeremy-hammond.title: Daniel Hale
jeremy-hammond.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

jerome-post.title: John Kiriakou
jerome-post.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

jerome-post.title: Bob (CIA HR)
jerome-post.summary: Pseudonym for the CIA officer who served as director of human resources for the agency in the late 1980s and personally oversaw John Kiriakou's hiring

jerome-post.title: Stansfield Turner
jerome-post.summary: Admiral and Director of Central Intelligence under Jimmy Carter from 1977 to 1981; named by John Kiriakou as one of only two CIA directors he considers good, because he tried to rein the organization in, and remembered inside the agency for the October 1977 mass firing of Directorate of Operations officers that CIA officers call the Friday Night Massacre.

jerome-post.title: The CIA entrance examinations
jerome-post.summary: The two rounds of testing John Kiriakou sat before joining the CIA in 1990: a current-affairs multiple choice he found trivially easy, a blank fold-out map of the world, and a psychological inventory of several thousand agree-or-disagree statements that repeated the same proposition hundreds of questions apart to catch inconsistency — followed by an interview panel of a psychologist, a psychiatrist and an anthropologist.

jerome-post.title: The 189 undeclared officers
jerome-post.summary: A figure John Kiriakou attributes to the CIA''s director of security, given to his intake class on his first day at the agency in January 1990: against two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the embassy in Washington, the FBI counted at least 189 undeclared ones operating across the United States. He pairs it with the fact that Israeli liaison officers were barred from CIA headquarters.

jerome-post.title: Arabists
jerome-post.summary: The label applied inside the U.S. government to diplomats and analysts who knew Arabic and Middle Eastern history, and which John Kiriakou confirms functioned as a dismissal — the assumption being that anyone who understood the region was blindly prejudiced against Israel, or antisemitic.

jerry-falwell-jr.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
