kiriakou-titanium-knee.title: The Farm
kiriakou-titanium-knee.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

kiriakou-titanium-knee.title: The Advanced Counterterrorism Operations course
kiriakou-titanium-knee.summary: The six-week CIA course for which John Kiriakou says he was one of only about a dozen officers in the entire agency selected — and which he finished, as he puts it, just in time for 9/11.

kiriakou-titanium-knee.title: The shooting house
kiriakou-titanium-knee.summary: The live-fire decision course at the Farm where a trainee has about three quarters of a second to decide whether the figure at the window is a gunman or a woman holding a baby — and where John Kiriakou says he never missed, which he connects to his own account of the temperament the CIA selects for.

kiriakou-titanium-knee.title: The bomb course
kiriakou-titanium-knee.summary: The week-long CIA explosives course at a facility in another state, where John Kiriakou learned to build a Molotov cocktail, then a detonator rig, then an ammonium nitrate bomb — his final exam, which put a van's transmission three hundred yards into the woods.

kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.title: Greater and Lesser Tunb Islands
kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.summary: Two small, largely uninhabited islands in the Persian Gulf, belonging to the emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, occupied by Iran in a 1990s incident John Kiriakou recounts as CIA analyst; Kiriakou correctly predicted the UAE would not go to war over them given Sharjah's heavy trade dependence on Iran.

kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.title: Economic roots of terrorism
kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, drawn from interrogating young al-Qaeda fighters in Pakistan, that jihadi recruitment is driven by poverty and hopelessness rather than religion — illiterate villagers paid $300 a month who could not find the U.S. on a map and had never read the Quran.

kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.title: FBI apologies to Kiriakou
kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.summary: John Kiriakou says three FBI agents who worked on his prosecution have written to apologize since his conviction — one saying the case was 'directed and driven by seniormost officials' while mid- and street-level personnel objected, but 'we just followed orders.'

kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.title: PricewaterhouseCoopers
kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.summary: The Big Four accounting firm that keeps intersecting John Kiriakou's story — as a target of the corporate human-source intelligence he collected after leaving the CIA, as the audience of 140 partners he told his Pakistan recruitment story to ("what I did and what you do really isn't that different"), as the auditor that spent three years trying to find the Pentagon's money before giving up, and as the Greek government's book-cooking auditor in the debt crisis, never prosecuted.

kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.title: Al Qaeda Software
kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.summary: A claim raised on a Kiriakou-appearance podcast that "Al-Qaeda" is also the name of a terrorist-tracking software, alongside its use as the name of the terrorist organization.

kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.title: Amnesty International
kiriakou-transfer-to-operations.summary: The human rights organization whose 2006 torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC — and the organization whose silence during his own prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for even a one-sentence statement about his case; the director of Amnesty International USA sent him a New Yorker subscription and a letter saying they wanted nothing to do with it. "After about a year I got tired of begging."

kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.title: Kiriakou's gastrectomy
kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.summary: The experimental operation John Kiriakou paid for with a bank loan in September 2022, in which his stomach was removed to reverse an uncontrolled type 2 diabetes — a procedure he had found in a Lancet paper by a Scottish surgeon, and which cost him 55 kilos and, he says, the disease itself.

kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.title: The glyburide incident
kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.summary: The episode John Kiriakou described in a Letter from Loretto of 12 September 2014: handed a bottle of glyburide by the prison pharmacy without explanation, he crashed twice and passed out on the floor — and his physician father-in-law told him the drug could have put him into heart failure.

kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.title: Kiriakou on diet and nutrition
kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.summary: John Kiriakou''s views on eating, given to a Cypriot nutrition interviewer who challenged several of them: that the worst dietary advice he ever heard was to cut fat and cholesterol, that the American sugar lobby spent decades persuading the public that fat was the enemy, and that at his age carbohydrates are the enemy instead.

kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.title: Kiriakou's post-gastrectomy complications
kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.summary: The aftermath of John Kiriakou''s stomach removal: eighteen months of daily vomiting that turned out to be scar tissue, a diagnosis of malnutrition, and a night on his kitchen floor with a blood pressure of 80 over 52, caused by a blood clot sitting on an ulcer at the surgical site — one hour, his surgeon told him, from being too late.

kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.title: John Kiriakou
kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.title: Kiriakou on Greek and Cypriot food
kiriakou-type-2-diabetes.summary: The verdict John Kiriakou delivered on Cypriot cooking during a 2026 visit to the island — that its cheeses are more sophisticated and more distinct from one another than Greece's, where most are variations on a theme — together with his coffee positions, his conversion from frappé by a cousin in Rhodes, and his complaint about the size of the straw.

kiriakou-ufo-sighting.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
kiriakou-ufo-sighting.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a place of 50,000 people when he was growing up and about 18,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices.

kiriakou-ufo-sighting.title: CIA and the UFO question
kiriakou-ufo-sighting.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

kiriakou-ufo-sighting.title: China's base in Djibouti
kiriakou-ufo-sighting.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

kiriakou-ufo-sighting.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
kiriakou-ufo-sighting.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

kiriakou-ufo-sighting.title: Espionage Act
kiriakou-ufo-sighting.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

kiriakou-ufo-sighting.title: The orb off Yemen
kiriakou-ufo-sighting.summary: A leaked video John Kiriakou describes as the most dramatic UFO material he has seen: two F-18s following a silver orb off the coast of Yemen, given permission to fire, and a missile that hits the object and bounces off before the orb turns ninety degrees and flies on.

kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.title: The Afghan police tribal rotation
kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.title: Chinese overseas police stations
kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a New York Times revelation about Chinese nationals with apparent ties to the Chinese police operating out of storefronts around Manhattan and travelling around the United States to threaten Chinese people with reprisals against relatives in Beijing — and his puzzlement that the FBI missed it.

kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.title: Fusha and the Gulf dialect
kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own Arabic training — a first year in fusha, high standard Arabic, followed by a second year in khaleeji, the Gulf dialect — and the two consequences he reports: that Yemen is the only place where pure fusha is spoken, and that Saudis asked him why he spoke Arabic like Shakespeare.

kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.title: Iran under sanctions: daily life
kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being talked out of his own assumptions about Iran by a close friend who travels there once or twice a year and eventually started filming ordinary life — leading him to conclude that a country with no American embassy, diplomatic presence or business presence since 1979 nonetheless lacks for nothing.

kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.title: Kiriakou's public-speaking training
kiriakou-uk-speaking-tour.summary: The origin John Kiriakou gives for his manner as a speaker: a tenth-grade speech and debate class taught by Dr. Scarvel, his father''s childhood best friend, who drilled his students out of verbal fillers and pushed Kiriakou into competitive extemporaneous debate. Kiriakou credits the class with teaching him to let silence do the work of ''um''.

kiriakou-weapons-carry.title: The Athens carjacking
kiriakou-weapons-carry.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

kiriakou-weapons-carry.title: The Nordeen house
kiriakou-weapons-carry.summary: The embassy housing on Deliyani Street in Athens that John Kiriakou refused on arrival in 1998 — the house outside which the American defence attaché had been blown to pieces by 17 November, his head landing on the neighbouring roof.

kiriakou-weapons-carry.title: Beirut
kiriakou-weapons-carry.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

kiriakou-weapons-carry.title: John Kiriakou
kiriakou-weapons-carry.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

kiriakou-weapons-carry.title: The El Salvador hotel drill
kiriakou-weapons-carry.summary: A night exercise at the Farm in which trainees sat alone in a mock flea-bag hotel room in El Salvador, were visited by two men announcing housekeeping, and were shot with paint pellets. All eight failed, and the lesson John Kiriakou drew from it he says he never forgot.

kiriakou-weapons-carry.title: Psychiatric evacuation
kiriakou-weapons-carry.summary: The CIA's practice of pulling an officer out of a posting and flying him home when he breaks down — known inside the agency as being psychovac'd — and the desk-bound evaluation period that follows before he is allowed to travel again.

kiriakou-writing-process.title: Remains of the Day (book)
kiriakou-writing-process.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

kiriakou-writing-process.title: Whispers in the Dirt
kiriakou-writing-process.summary: John Kiriakou's second cemetery book — a guide to the mafia graves of New York City, and the sequel Simon & Schuster commissioned after Remains of the Day. Reporting it produced the moment he realised an inmate who had told him a body was found in a barrel in his storage unit had been telling the truth.

kiriakou-writing-process.title: Kiriakou's public-speaking training
kiriakou-writing-process.summary: The origin John Kiriakou gives for his manner as a speaker: a tenth-grade speech and debate class taught by Dr. Scarvel, his father''s childhood best friend, who drilled his students out of verbal fillers and pushed Kiriakou into competitive extemporaneous debate. Kiriakou credits the class with teaching him to let silence do the work of ''um''.

kiriakou-writing-process.title: Greek death rituals
kiriakou-writing-process.summary: The five-year grave rental, exhumation and ossuary practice of rural Greece as John Kiriakou describes it — bones washed in red wine, blessed, boxed, and eventually laid beneath the foundations of a new church, with cremation strictly forbidden. He visits the ossuary in his ancestral Rhodes village, where the records stop in the nineteenth century because the Ottomans burned everything earlier.

kiriakou-writing-process.title: Israel Boyd and the Wonder Bread story
kiriakou-writing-process.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of Israel Boyd, one of two brothers forced by their parents into the family bakery business, who went on to invent the first industrial dough mixer and dough-cutting machine, pioneer adding milk to bread dough, and build the largest bakery in America before World War I — before selling the business, whose flagship "Mrs. McGill's Delicious Bread" was renamed Wonder Bread by its buyer.

kiriakou-writing-process.title: John Kiriakou
kiriakou-writing-process.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

kite-runner-rescue-mission.title: Deloitte Consulting Career
kite-runner-rescue-mission.summary: John Kiriakou's post-CIA career at Deloitte Consulting (2004–2008), covering two corporate acquisitions he says he drove — India Tiger Analysis and, in effect, Bering Point — and ending in his effective firing weeks before his ABC News whistleblower interview aired.

kite-runner-rescue-mission.title: Abu Zubaydah
kite-runner-rescue-mission.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

kite-runner-rescue-mission.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
kite-runner-rescue-mission.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

kite-runner-rescue-mission.title: China's base in Djibouti
kite-runner-rescue-mission.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

kite-runner-rescue-mission.title: China as economic threat
kite-runner-rescue-mission.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

kite-runner-rescue-mission.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
kite-runner-rescue-mission.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

kompromat.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
kompromat.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

kompromat.title: Jeffrey Epstein
kompromat.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

kompromat.title: Gay Diplomat Operation
kompromat.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA recruitment operation he ran against a foreign diplomat who was closeted and gay. After months of cultivation under cover as a gay man, Kiriakou attempted to kiss the diplomat at his apartment and was deflated by the response: ''I am gay. I''m just not into hairy guys.'' The romantic gambit failed — but the recruitment ultimately succeeded anyway, because the diplomat had been passed over for a promotion and was angry enough at his own government to cooperate. Kiriakou cites the operation as evidence that financial motivation and personal grievance, not coercion, are the reliable drivers of recruitment.

kompromat.title: Cuban double agents
kompromat.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

kompromat.title: John Kiriakou
kompromat.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

kompromat.title: Allen Dulles
kompromat.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

kurds.title: ISIS
kurds.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

kurds.title: Saddam Hussein
kurds.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

kurds.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
kurds.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

kurds.title: George H.W. Bush
kurds.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

kurds.title: George W. Bush
kurds.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

kurds.title: Ahmed Chalabi
kurds.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

kuwait-invasion-intelligence.title: Asel al-Ghabandi
kuwait-invasion-intelligence.summary: Kuwaiti resistance figure during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, a "bona fide hero" whose telephone reporting on Iraqi troop movements, roadblocks, atrocities, and the location of inspections reached the CIA every single day via NSA [call interception](/wiki/the-intercept) — Kiriakou's account of the resistance figure who best understood how to weaponize the certainty that the Americans were listening to everything.

kuwait-invasion-intelligence.title: Collateral Murder Video
kuwait-invasion-intelligence.summary: The 2010 WikiLeaks release of gun-camera footage from a 2007 U.S. Apache helicopter attack in Baghdad; part of the trove of Iraq and Afghan war logs, Guantanamo files, and State Department cables leaked by Chelsea Manning, which John Kiriakou credits with corroborating major abuses and helping to touch off the Arab Spring.

kuwait-invasion-intelligence.title: Kuwait oil fires
kuwait-invasion-intelligence.summary: The February 1991 sabotage by retreating Iraqi forces of an estimated 600–800 Kuwaiti oil wells; per John Kiriakou's first-person account, the fires blackened the desert and blotted out the sun as far away as Riyadh, vaporized two French journalists who drove onto a sheet of melted-sand glass, and were extinguished only by an international team led by American specialist Red Adair using a Rolls-Royce jet engine to blow the flames out.

kuwait-invasion-intelligence.title: The SIGINT–HUMINT balance
kuwait-invasion-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to what he calls the most important question facing any incoming CIA director: how to divide investment between signals intelligence and human intelligence. His position is that signals collection cannot supply the one thing policy requires — a person in the room when a decision is taken — and that every new director says so on arrival and then drifts back toward the technology.

kuwait-invasion-intelligence.title: Yellowcake Niger forgery
kuwait-invasion-intelligence.summary: The fabricated intelligence document claiming Iraq had attempted to buy yellowcake uranium from Niger; passed to the U.S. via the British (originally from the Italians); identified by CIA analysts including John Kiriakou as a forgery on sight ("it's not even in the right font"); pulled from President George W. Bush's State of the Union draft by Colin Powell; reinserted by Vice President Dick Cheney; pulled out by the CIA again; delivered in the 2003 State of the Union address anyway.

kuwait-invasion-intelligence.title: Saud Nasir Al-Sabah
kuwait-invasion-intelligence.summary: Kuwaiti Ambassador to the United States in the run-up to the 1990 Iraqi invasion; per John Kiriakou, "just a lovely, lovely man, very generous with his time"; the diplomatic channel through which the CIA, working from the Kuwaiti embassy in Washington, communicated its escalating June–July 1990 warnings that Iraq was preparing to invade.

kuwait-liberation-day.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
kuwait-liberation-day.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

kuwait-liberation-day.title: Saddam Hussein
kuwait-liberation-day.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

kuwait-liberation-day.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
kuwait-liberation-day.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

kuwait-liberation-day.title: Ahmed Khatib
kuwait-liberation-day.summary: Iraqi-installed occupation governor of Kuwait announced on August 2, 1990, hours after the invasion; medical doctor trained at the American University of Beirut whose mother had been a Sudanese slave in the Kuwaiti royal household; college roommate of George Habash and co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

kuwait-liberation-day.title: Joko Widodo
kuwait-liberation-day.summary: Indonesian general; former Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of Indonesia; banned from the United States on human-rights grounds for personally killing six pro-democracy college student protesters by stabbing each in the heart in front of the others; subsequently elected Vice President of Indonesia; subject of an unsuccessful 2008 reputation-rehabilitation campaign conducted by John Rendon's firm with Karl Rove and John Kiriakou.

kuwait-liberation-day.title: National Endowment for Democracy
kuwait-liberation-day.summary: U.S. federally chartered organization characterized by John Kiriakou as a proxy for CIA propaganda — the funding vehicle by which the agency promotes pro-U.S. political leaders in foreign countries; explicitly not an operational entity in the boots-on-the-ground sense.

kuwait-oil-fires.title: Saddam Hussein
kuwait-oil-fires.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

kuwait-oil-fires.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
kuwait-oil-fires.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

kuwait-oil-fires.title: Yellowcake Niger forgery
kuwait-oil-fires.summary: The fabricated intelligence document claiming Iraq had attempted to buy yellowcake uranium from Niger; passed to the U.S. via the British (originally from the Italians); identified by CIA analysts including John Kiriakou as a forgery on sight ("it's not even in the right font"); pulled from President George W. Bush's State of the Union draft by Colin Powell; reinserted by Vice President Dick Cheney; pulled out by the CIA again; delivered in the 2003 State of the Union address anyway.

kuwait-oil-fires.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
kuwait-oil-fires.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

kuwait-oil-fires.title: Ahmed Chalabi
kuwait-oil-fires.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

kuwait-oil-fires.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
kuwait-oil-fires.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

lahore-safe-house.title: Colonel Khaled
lahore-safe-house.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

lahore-safe-house.title: Navigating Pakistan without maps
lahore-safe-house.summary: The logistical problem John Kiriakou says nearly undid the Abu Zubaydah operation: in 2002 Pakistan had no maps to buy, no street signs and no addresses, so the CIA team navigated a city of twelve million by shoe advertisement, traffic policeman, British school and McDonald''s — rehearsing the route twice in the small hours before the raids.

lahore-safe-house.title: Faisalabad
lahore-safe-house.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

lahore-safe-house.title: Amir
lahore-safe-house.summary: The pseudonym John Kiriakou gives the Muslim, ethnically Arab domestic officer sent on temporary duty to Pakistan to help with the Abu Zubaydah hunt — the colleague who drove them into India by GPS, drank the roadside tea and had diarrhoea for six weeks, and invented the textile-baron cover story on the spot.

lahore-safe-house.title: The Punjab Elite Force
lahore-safe-house.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

lahore-safe-house.title: Faisalabad Hospital
lahore-safe-house.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

langley.title: Osama bin Laden
langley.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

langley.title: Dianne Feinstein
langley.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. Per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — an unusually friendly chairwoman who exercised no real oversight, good on torture and a cheerleader for the CIA on everything else. She co-authored the 2015 McCain-Feinstein Amendment that reiterated the federal ban on torture, and she blocked Gina Haspel's promotion in 2013 before publicly warming to her in 2018.

langley.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
langley.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

langley.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
langley.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

langley.title: National Security Council
langley.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

langley.title: Dick Clarke
langley.summary: The White House counterterrorism chief John Kiriakou describes as the most highly respected non-ideological counterterrorism professional in government — demoted by the incoming Bush administration, ignored when he warned Condoleezza Rice that a terrible attack was coming, and, on Kiriakou's account, lied to by CIA director George Tenet about al-Qaeda operatives already inside the United States.

larry-devlin.title: Publications Review Board
larry-devlin.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

larry-devlin.title: John Kiriakou
larry-devlin.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

larry-devlin.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
larry-devlin.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

larry-devlin.title: John le Carré
larry-devlin.summary: British novelist and former MI6 officer, the subject of a full episode of John Kiriakou's Dead Drop podcast. Kiriakou's argument is that le Carré is the only spy novelist to have changed the business of spying itself — supplying its working vocabulary, from 'Joes' and 'lamplighters' to 'honey trap', and shaping how officers understood their own world.

larry-devlin.title: Kiriakou's shortwave listening
larry-devlin.summary: The childhood hobby John Kiriakou identifies as the reason he went to work for the CIA — a fifty-cent auction radio, a walk-in closet turned radio shack with a pinned world map, membership of the American Shortwave Listeners Club, and a verified logging of Radio Ulan Bator that put him on the cover of the club's magazine at fourteen.

larry-devlin.title: One-Time Pad
larry-devlin.summary: Cipher system in which a secret, random key — shared between sender and receiver — is used to encode a message and then destroyed so that it can never be used again. In traditional shortwave-radio tradecraft, one-time pads enabled spies to broadcast number sequences over public airwaves that only the intended recipient, holding the matching page, could decode. Per John Kiriakou, his lifelong interest in intelligence began at age nine after he picked up KGB number transmissions on a 50-cent shortwave radio.

larry-raviv.title: FCI Loretto
larry-raviv.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

larry-raviv.title: Truck
larry-raviv.summary: The convicted serial killer at FCI Loretto who sought John Kiriakou's approval, claimed to have run guns to Angolan rebels in a shrimp boat, and beat a prisoner unconscious after Kiriakou told him the man had called him a pedophile.

larry-raviv.title: Chomo
larry-raviv.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

larry-raviv.title: Clint Goswick
larry-raviv.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto; a devout Christian and Wichita Falls, Texas heating-and-air-conditioning business owner convicted of drug conspiracy and a gun charge despite never having used, possessed, manufactured, or distributed drugs.

larry-raviv.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
larry-raviv.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

larry-raviv.title: Federal prison security levels
larry-raviv.summary: The ladder of federal custody as John Kiriakou describes it — penitentiary, medium, low and minimum-security camp — the transfer rules that let long-sentence prisoners descend it, and why that placed dangerous men inside the low-security prison where he served his sentence.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Frank's heart attack
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The 65-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto, reported chest tightness for months, was given Tylenol and a request for an EKG that the regional office never approved, and collapsed in the insulin line.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: The glyburide incident
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The episode John Kiriakou described in a Letter from Loretto of 12 September 2014: handed a bottle of glyburide by the prison pharmacy without explanation, he crashed twice and passed out on the floor — and his physician father-in-law told him the drug could have put him into heart failure.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Administrative remedy process
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: The chapel job
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Medical care in federal prison
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

larry-spinal-cancer.title: Paul Wright
larry-spinal-cancer.summary: The former prisoner who co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

laura-loomer.title: Louise Mensch
laura-loomer.summary: The former British parliamentarian who attacked John Kiriakou on social media, prompting the only defamation action he describes having threatened. On his lawyer's advice he demanded a retraction; Mensch retracted in full and kept a pinned apology on her account for six months.

laura-loomer.title: Podcasters on foreign payrolls
laura-loomer.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being told by an investigative journalist he respects that four household-name podcasters were taking CIA money — an allegation she could not corroborate and would not publish. He treats it as credible and extends the logic: if the agency is paying podcasters, foreign governments will be paying them too.

laura-loomer.title: Donald Trump
laura-loomer.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

laura-loomer.title: Ahmed Chalabi
laura-loomer.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

laura-loomer.title: AIPAC
laura-loomer.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

laura-loomer.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
laura-loomer.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Colin Powell
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: U.S. Secretary of State whose 2003 UN testimony made the case for the Iraq war; John Kiriakou says the white powder in Powell's prop tube was nothing, and that Powell's own chief of staff later told him the presentation was knowingly 'sold.'

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Salt Pit
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: A CIA black site north of Kabul — a former Soviet, then Taliban, dungeon the CIA took over for its post-9/11 detention programme. Gul Rahman froze to death there in a cold cell, a technique John Kiriakou considers worse than waterboarding and says killed several prisoners; he suspects others were killed off the books and never reported.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: John Kiriakou
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Chelsea Manning
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

lawrence-wilkerson.title: Daniel Ellsberg
lawrence-wilkerson.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

leadership-profiling.title: Reza Pahlavi
leadership-profiling.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

leadership-profiling.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
leadership-profiling.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

leadership-profiling.title: Ahmed Chalabi
leadership-profiling.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

leadership-profiling.title: Saddam Hussein
leadership-profiling.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

leadership-profiling.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
leadership-profiling.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

leadership-profiling.title: Lindsey Graham
leadership-profiling.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Jesselyn Radack
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: American national-security attorney and former Justice Department ethics official who directs the whistleblower-defense practice at the Government Accountability Project. Per John Kiriakou, Radack was herself driven out of the Justice Department, had her law license threatened, and was placed on the no-fly list after blowing the whistle in the John Walker Lindh case; she went on to represent Kiriakou after his 2012 arrest and, separately, helped connect him to a path to reach Edward Snowden in 2013.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Chuck Grassley
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the only serious pro-whistleblower member of Congress — a count he says can be made on one finger. Grassley wrote the Whistleblower Protection Act and the National Security Whistleblower Protection Act, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Center's luncheon, and in Kiriakou's telling was pushed into backing the Ukraine call whistleblower because it was his own law the man had invoked.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Gina Haspel
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: Presidential call memcons
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: How a call between the president and a foreign leader is staffed and recorded, as John Kiriakou describes it. Four people are usually on the line and rarely five — not the twenty reported during the Ukraine affair — and the write-up, a memorandum of conversation or memcon, is held so tightly inside the National Security Council that a CIA analyst, he says, would never see one.

leaker-versus-whistleblower.title: The legal definition of whistleblowing
leaker-versus-whistleblower.summary: John Kiriakou''s insistence that whistleblowing is a legally defined act rather than a figure of speech: bringing to light evidence of waste, fraud, abuse, illegality, or threats to public health or public safety — at any level of government.

learned-helplessness.title: Abu Zubaydah
learned-helplessness.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

learned-helplessness.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
learned-helplessness.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

learned-helplessness.title: George W. Bush
learned-helplessness.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

learned-helplessness.title: Waterboarding
learned-helplessness.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

learned-helplessness.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
learned-helplessness.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

learned-helplessness.title: Salt Pit
learned-helplessness.summary: A CIA black site north of Kabul — a former Soviet, then Taliban, dungeon the CIA took over for its post-9/11 detention programme. Gul Rahman froze to death there in a cold cell, a technique John Kiriakou considers worse than waterboarding and says killed several prisoners; he suspects others were killed off the books and never reported.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: MOSSAD
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Iran 12-Day War
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Donald Trump
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Hezbollah
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: Lebanese Shia militant organization and political party. Per John Kiriakou, Israel''s strategic goal regarding Hezbollah is not to defeat it outright but to keep Lebanon in a state of chaos that serves Israeli interests. He cites two Israeli operations: the simultaneous pager-detonation attack that decapitated Hezbollah''s leadership, which he called ''the most incredible operation I''ve ever seen,'' and the strike that killed former leader Hassan Nasrallah by leveling an entire complex and killing roughly 300 people — which he characterized as a war crime.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Israel-United States relations
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

lebanon-israeli-conflict.title: Jonathan Pollard
lebanon-israeli-conflict.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

lee-zeldon.title: Todd Blanch
lee-zeldon.summary: Per Megyn Kelly, reading Trump's own statement live during her interview with Kiriakou, Todd Blanch was named the incoming acting Attorney General, replacing Pam Bondi.

lee-zeldon.title: Pam Bondi
lee-zeldon.summary: Panelists alongside Kiriakou on why Trump picked Bondi for loyalty above all, and called her handling of the Epstein files a farce.

lee-zeldon.title: Bill Barr
lee-zeldon.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

lee-zeldon.title: Gail Slater
lee-zeldon.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the head of the DOJ antitrust unit under Pam Bondi who was stripped of authority and then fired.

lee-zeldon.title: Alexa
lee-zeldon.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

lee-zeldon.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
lee-zeldon.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

legal-mail.title: Seven thousand letters
legal-mail.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

legal-mail.title: FCI Loretto
legal-mail.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

legal-mail.title: Sarge
legal-mail.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer John Kiriakou named in a Letter from Loretto for swearing at him and trashing his cell — conduct he later learned was not merely a Bureau of Prisons infraction but a misdemeanour crime, and one of two offences he says the letter inadvertently exposed.

legal-mail.title: Letter from Loretto
legal-mail.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

legal-mail.title: The black box
legal-mail.summary: The restraint apparatus in which John Kiriakou was moved from FCI Loretto to an outside medical appointment — handcuffs, leg irons, a waist chain and a steel box locked over the cuffs so the lock could not be picked — and the form he refused to sign because it required him to call everybody sir.

legal-mail.title: Civil confinement
legal-mail.summary: The policy John Kiriakou proposed from inside FCI Loretto — moving sex offenders to a secure location on prison grounds after their sentences end rather than releasing them — an argument that drew public criticism and which he defends with the case of a prisoner named Cook.

lenin-moreno.title: Julian Assange
lenin-moreno.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

lenin-moreno.title: The CIPA hearing in Kiriakou's case
lenin-moreno.summary: The closed pre-trial proceeding under the Classified Information Procedures Act at which John Kiriakou's defence filed seventy motions to declassify the material it needed to mount a defence, and the judge denied all seventy at once. Kiriakou describes the ruling as the moment the case ended — his lead attorney told him on the way out of the courtroom that they had just lost — and as the point at which plea negotiations began.

lenin-moreno.title: Espionage Act
lenin-moreno.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

lenin-moreno.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
lenin-moreno.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

lenin-moreno.title: Barack Obama
lenin-moreno.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

lenin-moreno.title: Bruce Fein
lenin-moreno.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

leon-panetta.title: David Petraeus
leon-panetta.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

leon-panetta.title: Espionage Act

leon-panetta.title: Abu Zubaydah
leon-panetta.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

leon-panetta.title: Thomas Drake
leon-panetta.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

leon-panetta.title: The Panetta bin Laden disclosure
leon-panetta.summary: Leon Panetta's accidental naming of the special forces ground commander of the bin Laden raid in front of a Hollywood screenwriter, which Kiriakou uses as the control case for his argument that Espionage Act enforcement is selective.

leon-panetta.title: Cofer Black
leon-panetta.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

leonie-brinkema.summary: John Kiriakou''s exposé of why U.S. records go undeclassified: the National Archives runs a 20-year-old computer with no connectivity, its head has asked for a smaller budget, and Freedom of Information Act requests face what he calls a 500-year backlog.

leonie-brinkema.title: The Panetta bin Laden disclosure

leonie-brinkema.summary: Barack Obama''s reason, as John Kiriakou reports it, for never charging Julian Assange: the Washington Post, the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and the Associated Press publish classified information every single day, so a publisher charged with espionage cannot be the only one. Kiriakou treats it as the central First Amendment question of the case, and notes that Joe Biden — who was in the room for the original argument — doubled down instead of dropping the charges.

les-wexner.title: Jeffrey Epstein
les-wexner.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

les-wexner.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
les-wexner.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

les-wexner.title: MOSSAD
les-wexner.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

les-wexner.title: Access Agent
les-wexner.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

les-wexner.title: Peter Mandelson
les-wexner.summary: British politician; described by John Kiriakou as the former British ambassador to Washington and as someone likely to be charged with serious crimes in connection with Jeffrey Epstein.

les-wexner.title: Beef jerky anomaly in the Epstein files
les-wexner.summary: A pattern John Kiriakou has flagged in the released Epstein correspondence: on the order of 1,300 to 1,500 emails discuss beef jerky — making it, teaching others to make it, freezing and storing it — and none discuss eating it. Kiriakou treats it as an unexplained code and declines to speculate about what it stands for.

letter-from-loretto.title: FCI Loretto
letter-from-loretto.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

letter-from-loretto.title: Bureau of Prisons
letter-from-loretto.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

letter-from-loretto.title: The Taliban spokesman setup
letter-from-loretto.summary: Kiriakou's account of a prisoner transferred into FCI Loretto for five days who presented himself as the Taliban's American spokesman, while a guard photographed the encounter from the treeline — an attempt, in his telling, to manufacture a second case against him.

letter-from-loretto.title: This desk kills fascism
letter-from-loretto.summary: The sign Kiriakou taped to the cell desk on which he wrote the letters from Loretto, borrowed from Woody Guthrie's guitar, torn down by a guard within hours and kept by Kiriakou ever since.

letter-from-loretto.title: Education at FCI Loretto
letter-from-loretto.summary: The classes, drug programme and good-conduct rules at FCI Loretto, which Kiriakou described in a letter from Loretto as correcting nothing — and which taught him, he wrote, how to cook methamphetamine and defraud a mortgage company.

liam-o-grady.title: Communications management unit
liam-o-grady.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

liam-o-grady.title: Daniel Hale
liam-o-grady.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

liam-o-grady.title: Espionage Act
liam-o-grady.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

liam-o-grady.title: Matthew Cole
liam-o-grady.summary: American national-security journalist whose reporting tradecraft, per John Kiriakou, has led to the federal incarceration of five whistleblowers — including Kiriakou himself. In Kiriakou's account, Cole emailed him in 2010 ostensibly researching a book on the rendition of Abu Omar, asked Kiriakou to confirm the surname of a CIA officer who appeared in Kiriakou's own first book under the alias 'John', and Kiriakou's confirmation was the act of confirming a covert officer's identity for which he was eventually prosecuted under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act.

liam-o-grady.title: Sam Adams Award
liam-o-grady.summary: The integrity-in-intelligence award John Kiriakou received in 2016 at American University, joining a laureate list that includes Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, and Sy Hersh. Named not for the founding father but for the CIA analyst who insisted the true enemy strength in Vietnam was double what General Westmoreland allowed to be reported, it is given by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity — a community Kiriakou describes as doubling as a support group for whistleblowers.

liam-o-grady.title: The Drone Papers
liam-o-grady.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

libertarian-party.title: Gary Johnson
libertarian-party.summary: The former Republican governor of New Mexico and Libertarian nominee for president who wrote to John Kiriakou in prison, wrote separately to Attorney General Eric Holder asking that he be released — a letter Kiriakou learned of only later through a Freedom of Information Act request — and telephoned him within days of his coming home.

libertarian-party.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
libertarian-party.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

libertarian-party.title: FCI Loretto

libertarian-party.title: PTSD
libertarian-party.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

libertarian-party.title: The three legal ways to enter another country
libertarian-party.summary: The test John Kiriakou applies to American military action abroad: that there are only three lawful ways for one country to move into another — with the approval of the UN Security Council, at that country''s invitation, or after being attacked by it — and that the United States, in his account, never meets any of the three.
