miranda-rights.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

miranda-rights.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
miranda-rights.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

miranda-rights.title: Government Accountability Project
miranda-rights.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

mitchell-and-jessen.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
mitchell-and-jessen.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

mitchell-and-jessen.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
mitchell-and-jessen.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

mitchell-and-jessen.title: Ticking time bomb scenario
mitchell-and-jessen.summary: The hypothetical case — an imminent attack only the captured terrorist's confession can prevent — used to justify the CIA's post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; characterized by John Kiriakou as fictional and not corresponding to any real-world case.

mitchell-and-jessen.title: Jared Kushner
mitchell-and-jessen.summary: Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser during the first Trump administration, and the first person inside the White House to open a channel on John Kiriakou's pardon. After Trump saw Kiriakou on Tucker Carlson's show, Kushner's attorney called Kiriakou's attorney Bruce Fein; the meeting that followed produced a request for a one-page paper — three-quarters of it Kiriakou's story, the last quarter an argument for how pardoning him would help Trump get re-elected — after which Kiriakou never heard back.

mitchell-and-jessen.title: Muhammad Atar
mitchell-and-jessen.summary: Nephew of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed; subjected by the CIA to the walling interrogation technique against a concrete-block wall without protective equipment, producing permanent brain damage that has prevented him from participating in his own defense.

mitchell-and-jessen.title: Ramzi bin al-Shibh
mitchell-and-jessen.summary: Alleged September 11 co-conspirator, captured in Pakistan in the summer of 2002 and taken to a secret prison rather than to trial. John Kiriakou, who is often wrongly credited with his capture, cites him as the clearest demonstration of what torture cost the United States — declared clinically insane by the Pentagon's own psychiatrist as a result of CIA sleep deprivation, and therefore untriable.

mitigating-damage.title: The sentencing remark
mitigating-damage.summary: The comment John Kiriakou says the judge made at his sentencing — that she wished she could give him the maximum, because that is what she would give him — and his reading of it as a performance for the national security reporters filling the gallery.

mitigating-damage.title: Thursday arrests
mitigating-damage.summary: The scheduling practice John Kiriakou attributes to the FBI — arresting on a Thursday so that a defendant, unable to be arraigned on a Friday, spends four nights in jail before seeing a judge — and the single sentence that he says kept him out of it.

mitigating-damage.title: Eastern District of Virginia
mitigating-damage.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

mitigating-damage.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
mitigating-damage.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

mitigating-damage.title: Espionage Act
mitigating-damage.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

mitigating-damage.title: The Loretto camp mix-up
mitigating-damage.summary: John Kiriakou's account of turning himself in at the federal work camp at Loretto, Pennsylvania as the court had ordered, being sent across the street to the prison to be processed, and then being handcuffed and walked into the prison itself — with nobody on the outside knowing where he was for five days.

mk-ultra.title: CIA and NSA exotic programs
mk-ultra.summary: Two obscure U.S. intelligence programs John Kiriakou has discussed — a late-1980s FBI/Defense Department investigation into a senior NSA officer who came out as a member of the Church of Satan and was accused of ritual sacrifice (which found no evidence), and a 1990s CIA battlefield laser weapon designed to blind rather than kill enemy soldiers, shelved after lawyers determined it violated international law.

mk-ultra.title: Sleeper Agent
mk-ultra.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person taken in early childhood, raised in a simulated version of a target country, given a false identity built from the birth record of a deceased infant, inserted into the target country, and then left dormant — sometimes for decades — until activated. Kiriakou says only Russia is known to use sleeper agents; no other country's intelligence service employs the technique. A former East German sleeper agent he interviewed on his podcast defected to the FBI after his daughter was born and a kill threat was delivered to him on the New York subway.

mk-ultra.title: The encounter at the Greek ambassador's residence
mk-ultra.summary: An exchange John Kiriakou describes from a dinner a few weeks after his release from prison, in which a Democratic member of the Senate Intelligence Committee welcomed him home, was told Kiriakou had expected him to speak up, and answered that it had taken everything he had simply to keep his own security clearance. Kiriakou offers it as evidence that the intelligence oversight committees are afraid of the agencies they oversee.

mk-ultra.title: Marble Framework
mk-ultra.summary: A CIA obfuscation tool revealed in the Vault 7 leaks; per John Kiriakou, the agency embedded snippets of Farsi and Cyrillic in the code of domestic hacking operations so that any discovery could be falsely attributed to Iran or Russia.

mk-ultra.title: Project Gateway
mk-ultra.summary: A CIA astral-projection and remote-viewing effort that John Kiriakou describes as a sub-program of MK-Ultra, launched after a fabricated source claimed the Soviets were experimenting with ESP.

mk-ultra.title: The San Francisco bacterium release
mk-ultra.summary: The MK-ULTRA experiment John Kiriakou describes in which the CIA waited for an unusually foggy day, released a bacterium across San Francisco and its public transit system to see how many people it could infect, and gave eight people a rare upper respiratory infection.

mlk-assassination.title: Martin Luther King Jr.
mlk-assassination.summary: The civil rights leader whose Letter from Birmingham Jail John Kiriakou explicitly honored in naming his own Letters from Loretto, and whose example — with Mandela and Gandhi — anchored Kiriakou''s decision to forgive his prosecutors: "I only lost two years of my life, not 35." Kiriakou''s parents marched for civil rights with King; he quotes King''s line about preaching nonviolence while his government is the world''s major purveyor of violence, and lists King''s assassination among the acts attributed to the unelected security state.

mlk-assassination.title: JFK assassination
mlk-assassination.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

mlk-assassination.title: COINTELPRO
mlk-assassination.summary: The FBI programme of warrantless surveillance and disruption directed at Americans, and one of the four abuses John Kiriakou names when explaining what the Church Committee actually investigated. He treats it as the historical benchmark for what a real congressional inquiry into the security agencies looks like — and, through the campaign against Martin Luther King, as proof that the state will destroy a citizen it considers a threat.

mlk-assassination.title: RFK Assassination
mlk-assassination.summary: Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy on June 5, 1968 in Los Angeles; per John Kiriakou, physically impossible to attribute to Sirhan Sirhan alone — Los Angeles County coroner Thomas Noguchi determined the fatal shot was fired from behind and below Kennedy's right ear at close range while Sirhan stood in front, the crime scene yielded more bullets than Sirhan's revolver could hold, and a hotel security guard named 'Caesar' was captured on video standing behind Kennedy at the moment of the shooting.

mlk-assassination.title: MK-Ultra
mlk-assassination.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

mlk-assassination.title: Peter Strzok
mlk-assassination.summary: Senior FBI counterintelligence officer who, per John Kiriakou, oversaw the FBI operation that included a fake Japanese-diplomat sting designed to induce Kiriakou to commit espionage, and who personally placed Kiriakou in handcuffs when he was arrested on January 12, 2012. Kiriakou did not learn Strzok's identity until 2017, when a Washington Post reporter called to ask for comment on Strzok's firing.

mohamed-atta-prague-claim.title: Heather Kiriakou
mohamed-atta-prague-claim.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

mohamed-atta-prague-claim.title: Ahmed Chalabi
mohamed-atta-prague-claim.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

mohamed-atta-prague-claim.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
mohamed-atta-prague-claim.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

mohamed-atta-prague-claim.title: Condoleezza Rice
mohamed-atta-prague-claim.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

mohamed-atta-prague-claim.title: Curveball
mohamed-atta-prague-claim.summary: Cryptonym for the German-handled Iraqi defector whose fabricated WMD intelligence the German BND laundered to the CIA in the run-up to the 2003 Iraq War; per John Kiriakou, in fact a dishwasher at a Shish Kebab restaurant who scraped fake reports from newspaper articles and told the Germans he was an Iraqi scientist with access to weapons of mass destruction; the Germans refused to let the CIA meet or polygraph him, and his fabricated intelligence — biological, chemical, nuclear, and long-range delivery — became one of the central pillars of the Bush administration's WMD case.

mohamed-atta-prague-claim.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
mohamed-atta-prague-claim.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

mohamedou-ould-slahi.title: Edward Snowden
mohamedou-ould-slahi.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

mohamedou-ould-slahi.title: Espionage Act
mohamedou-ould-slahi.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

mohamedou-ould-slahi.title: Khalid El-Masri
mohamedou-ould-slahi.summary: German grocery-store owner; rendered by the CIA in 2003 because his name — Khaled the Egyptian — happened to match that of a different Khaled the Egyptian whom a sister agency had reported was traveling to Albania to bomb the U.S. embassy. Tortured in Cairo to within an inch of his life. Released when Egyptian interrogators concluded he was the wrong man. Per John Kiriakou, returned to Germany with a waist-length beard and a Quran, telling a reporter: ''All I want to do is kill Americans.''

mohamedou-ould-slahi.title: Maher Arar
mohamedou-ould-slahi.summary: Canadian-Syrian political-science professor at the University of Toronto; in 2002, returning from a family visit in Tunis, was seized by the FBI at JFK at CIA request, secretly rendered to Damascus, and tortured by Syrian intelligence for eight to nine months until they concluded he was the wrong man. The U.S. denied any involvement to the Canadian government until Arar's wife produced a credit-card receipt from his return flight. He sued the U.S. and lost on national-security grounds, then sued the Canadian government and won six million dollars. Per John Kiriakou, his case is the canonical illustration of the CIA rendition program rendering the wrong person.

mohamedou-ould-slahi.title: Counterterrorism Center
mohamedou-ould-slahi.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

mohamedou-ould-slahi.title: Carlos the Jackal
mohamedou-ould-slahi.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

mohammed-atef.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
mohammed-atef.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

mohammed-atef.title: Abu Zubaydah
mohammed-atef.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

mohammed-atef.title: John Brennan
mohammed-atef.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

mohammed-atef.title: 9/11 plea agreements
mohammed-atef.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.

mohammed-atef.title: Agent payment mechanics
mohammed-atef.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

mohammed-atef.title: Bojinka plot
mohammed-atef.summary: 1996 Khalid Sheikh Mohammed–planned operation, prepared in a Manila, Philippines apartment, to hijack as many as fourteen Boeing 747s and crash them into buildings along the U.S. West Coast; disrupted only by accident, when a cleaning lady let herself into the apartment while the planner was out, recognized the materials laid out as a terrorist plot, and called the police — who alerted Filipino intelligence and, in turn, the CIA. The plot's architect was known to U.S. intelligence for the next six years only by the alias "Mukhtar," his true identity as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed surfacing only when Abu Zubaydah named him to FBI agent Ali Soufan in 2002.

mohsen-rafighdoost.title: Reza Pahlavi
mohsen-rafighdoost.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

mohsen-rafighdoost.title: Iran 12-Day War
mohsen-rafighdoost.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

mohsen-rafighdoost.title: Trump Iran Ceasefire Efforts
mohsen-rafighdoost.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Donald Trump reached out behind the scenes twice in ten days seeking a ceasefire with Iran and was rebuffed; Kiriakou also says Benjamin Netanyahu called the White House to check reports of the outreach, and that on foreign policy Netanyahu "has just as much authority as whoever happens to be president of the United States."

mohsen-rafighdoost.title: Tulsi Gabbard
mohsen-rafighdoost.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

mohsen-rafighdoost.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
mohsen-rafighdoost.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

mohsen-rafighdoost.title: Barack Obama
mohsen-rafighdoost.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

monroe-doctrine.title: Maduro Capture
monroe-doctrine.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

monroe-doctrine.title: Greenland
monroe-doctrine.summary: The Danish territory the United States has spent years talking about acquiring; John Kiriakou reports two flatly contradictory readings from his own contacts — a White House friend who says Washington is serious and will lean on a Cold War treaty to claim it is already de facto American, and a Republican friend who says the whole thing is a grenade thrown to distract the press — and warns that taking it by force would end NATO.

monroe-doctrine.title: United Fruit and the Arbenz coup
monroe-doctrine.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1954 CIA overthrow of Guatemala's President Arbenz after he nationalized the banana crop — engineered by the Dulles brothers, who sat on the board of the United Fruit Company, and followed by half a century of dictatorship.

monroe-doctrine.title: Reza Pahlavi
monroe-doctrine.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

monroe-doctrine.title: Israel's cell-phone assassinations in Iran
monroe-doctrine.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel wiped out Iran's military leadership by tracking cell phones — recruiting destitute Afghan refugees as $100-a-month spotters, and, when the generals stopped carrying phones, targeting their bodyguards' phones instead.

monroe-doctrine.title: Jeffrey Epstein
monroe-doctrine.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

moral-injury.title: John Kiriakou
moral-injury.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

moral-injury.title: FCI Loretto
moral-injury.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

moral-injury.title: Military Ethics
moral-injury.summary: The hypothetical Kiriakou puts to college audiences — and the line no CIA training class ever teaches an officer where to draw.

moral-injury.title: Asset acquisition cycle
moral-injury.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

moral-injury.title: Safe Housekeeper
moral-injury.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person recruited by a CIA officer to rent and maintain an apartment or other premises as a safe house, using their own name and identity to conceal any CIA connection. The role itself is minimal — rent the apartment, keep it clean, keep it stocked with water — but the recruitment is itself a covert operation requiring the same persuasion and pressure techniques used to acquire any sensitive asset. Kiriakou recruited a safe housekeeper overseas and believes the pressure he applied may have caused her a nervous breakdown.

moral-injury.title: Lie Detection
moral-injury.summary: Per John Kiriakou, both a subject he addresses in his book The CIA Insider's Guide to Lying and Lie Detection and a practical skill he describes using throughout his career. Physical tells include gaze direction (down to conceal, up to construct), fidgeting, and throat-clearing; structural tells — losing the thread mid-conversation and self-contradiction — are more reliable, because the truth is stable while a lie requires maintenance and eventually collapses under its own complexity.

more-moral-than-the-cia.title: The clear and present danger finding
more-moral-than-the-cia.summary: The presidential determination John Kiriakou says must precede any CIA paramilitary targeted killing — an assertion that the person concerned is a clear and present danger to the United States, to an American installation, or to an American person — and his judgement that in early 2026 that threshold had not been reached in Iran.

more-moral-than-the-cia.title: Italian intelligence services
more-moral-than-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the Italian services as very good and very close partners of the CIA — except in the Abu Omar case, when they refused to help, were ignored, and responded by investigating the CIA and identifying twenty-one of its officers.

more-moral-than-the-cia.title: Narcotics under cover
more-moral-than-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether a CIA officer under cover may take drugs when an asset offers them: yes. The rule he describes begins with qat in Yemen and extends to cocaine in Latin America, on the ground that refusing can be a matter of life and death.

more-moral-than-the-cia.title: Iranian intelligence capability
more-moral-than-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Iranian intelligence as poor and always having been poor, on the ground that Iranian officers do not receive good training and are essentially on their own, with only marginal help from the Russians and the Chinese.

more-moral-than-the-cia.title: A Middle East reading list
more-moral-than-the-cia.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

more-moral-than-the-cia.title: Bombing the Omanis
more-moral-than-the-cia.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

mormons-in-intelligence.title: Doctor Zhivago operation
mormons-in-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a joint CIA-Vatican operation to smuggle Russian-language copies of Boris Pasternak's banned Doctor Zhivago into the Soviet Union via an international book fair — an example of 'declaring victory in small increments.'

mormons-in-intelligence.title: John Paul II and the CIA
mormons-in-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou's account that CIA old-timers took credit for helping make the Polish cardinal John Paul II pope — a political move to weaken the Soviet Union — and that his later recognition of the state of Israel was seen as a bonus for the West.

mormons-in-intelligence.title: Operation Gladio
mormons-in-intelligence.summary: A CIA, MI6, Vatican and NATO operation to leave 'stay-behind' sleeper networks across Western Europe after World War II in case of a Soviet invasion; John Kiriakou, who learned of it only after leaving the CIA, notes it was made public by Italian PM Andreotti in 1990.

mormons-in-intelligence.title: The Farm
mormons-in-intelligence.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

mormons-in-intelligence.title: John Kiriakou
mormons-in-intelligence.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

mormons-in-intelligence.title: Active measures
mormons-in-intelligence.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency''s clandestine propaganda arm.

mort-halperin.title: Counterterrorism Center
mort-halperin.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

mort-halperin.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
mort-halperin.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

mort-halperin.title: April Glaspie
mort-halperin.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Iraq in the run-up to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; per John Kiriakou, delivered to Saddam Hussein — on a NODIS cable from Secretary of State James Baker — the line that the United States took no position on Arab-Arab border disputes, which Saddam is widely held to have read as a green light to invade. Kiriakou, who was in the CIA operations center the night her reporting cable came back, holds that she got a bum rap.

mort-halperin.title: Aryan Brotherhood
mort-halperin.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

mort-halperin.title: Bernie Kerik
mort-halperin.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

mort-halperin.title: Billy Waugh
mort-halperin.summary: Long-serving CIA paramilitary contractor; U.S. Army Special Forces ("Green Beret") veteran of World War II, Korea, and Vietnam; holder of approximately seventeen Purple Hearts (license plate "17 HITS"); resident of Niceville, Florida; died in his nineties.

mosaic-concept.title: MOSSAD
mosaic-concept.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

mosaic-concept.title: Mossad networks in Iran
mosaic-concept.summary: The Israeli human-intelligence penetration of Iran that John Kiriakou calls larger than anyone suspected — thousands of clandestine reporters, many of them undocumented Afghan refugees paid the equivalent of fifty or a hundred dollars a month, run in person by spymasters inside the country and compartmentalized so that rolling up one network yields nothing about the others.

mosaic-concept.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
mosaic-concept.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

mosaic-concept.title: Espionage Act
mosaic-concept.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

mosaic-concept.title: Over-classification
mosaic-concept.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

mosaic-concept.title: Sensitive but unclassified
mosaic-concept.summary: SBU — the intelligence community's name for what other agencies call controlled unclassified information. John Kiriakou stresses that it is a control and not a classification, gives gun-cleaning manuals and unreleased Commerce Department trade figures as examples, and warns that folding it under the Espionage Act would place an entire additional layer of federal employees — people with no clearances at all — inside the reach of the statute.

mossad-networks-in-iran.title: The mosaic concept
mossad-networks-in-iran.summary: The intelligence method John Kiriakou names for assembling a complete operational picture out of individually trivial fragments — one tile at a time, worthless alone, decisive together. He attributes the idea to Soviet thinking of the 1960s, cites Mossad's Iranian networks as the clearest modern demonstration, and warns that the same logic is what would let an American prosecutor charge a scholar with espionage for reading declassified documents.

mossad-networks-in-iran.title: MOSSAD
mossad-networks-in-iran.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

mossad-networks-in-iran.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
mossad-networks-in-iran.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

mossad-networks-in-iran.title: Mujahedin-e Khalq (MEK)
mossad-networks-in-iran.summary: Iranian opposition group that John Kiriakou describes as 'a quasi-communist cult' and a former U.S.-designated terrorist organization. Founded by a husband-and-wife team in the 1960s and based in northeastern Iraq, the MEK launched cross-border terrorist attacks into Iran and, per Kiriakou, attempted to murder the American ambassador and the senior U.S. general in Iran — carrying out anti-American attacks for decades. After Saddam Hussein expelled them they relocated to Paris; current leader Maryam Rajavi is widely believed to have killed or had killed her vanished husband to take over. In 2009 the MEK hired high-powered Washington lobbyists (from Howard Dean to Rudy Giuliani) to get off the terrorism list, and Kiriakou says it is now funded by Israel and used as assassins-for-hire in Tehran.

mossad-networks-in-iran.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
mossad-networks-in-iran.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

mossad-networks-in-iran.title: Bezalel Smotrich
mossad-networks-in-iran.summary: Israeli far-right minister whom John Kiriakou, alongside Itamar Ben-Gvir, blames for leaving Israel unprepared on October 7 by insisting any attack would come from the West Bank rather than Gaza.

mossad.title: Glenn-Symington Act
mossad.summary: U.S. federal statute, co-authored by Senators John Glenn and Stuart Symington, that prohibits the U.S. government from providing foreign aid of any kind to any country possessing a nuclear weapons program that has not signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty; per John Kiriakou, Israel is the only country in the world meeting both criteria, making the law the principal reason the U.S. government officially declines to acknowledge the Israeli nuclear program.

mossad.title: Hassan Nasrallah
mossad.summary: Long-serving Secretary-General of Hezbollah, killed in an Israeli strike on a complex in southern Lebanon; the strike, which killed approximately 300 people in addition to Nasrallah, decapitated Hezbollah's leadership and is characterized by John Kiriakou as a war crime under international law.

mossad.title: Sleeper Agent
mossad.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a person taken in early childhood, raised in a simulated version of a target country, given a false identity built from the birth record of a deceased infant, inserted into the target country, and then left dormant — sometimes for decades — until activated. Kiriakou says only Russia is known to use sleeper agents; no other country's intelligence service employs the technique. A former East German sleeper agent he interviewed on his podcast defected to the FBI after his daughter was born and a kill threat was delivered to him on the New York subway.

mossad.title: Trump Dni Replacement
mossad.summary: Trump privately asked cabinet members about replacing his Director of National Intelligence, frustrated that the DNI had protected Joe Kent.

mossad.title: Caspar Weinberger
mossad.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense under Ronald Reagan; John Kiriakou cites Weinberger's assessment that Jonathan Pollard's espionage caused "grave damage" — the highest category of harm — to U.S. national security.

mossad.title: Cory Booker
mossad.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he was "especially furious" with Democratic senator Cory Booker for running through the halls of Congress to get to a photo op standing behind Benjamin Netanyahu, which Kiriakou cites as an example of Democratic silence in the face of AIPAC pressure.

mount-weather.title: Five Eyes
mount-weather.summary: The intelligence-sharing partnership of the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand

mount-weather.title: The Bab el-Mandeb
mount-weather.summary: The strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa through which everything leaving the Suez Canal must pass — narrower than the Strait of Hormuz, in John Kiriakou's account the one genuine American national interest in Yemen, and the reason Israel has offered diplomatic recognition to Somaliland in exchange for a military base.

mount-weather.title: China's base in Djibouti
mount-weather.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

mount-weather.title: Guantanamo Bay
mount-weather.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

mount-weather.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
mount-weather.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

mount-weather.title: Abraham Accords
mount-weather.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: The operational cable
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The written product of every CIA field meeting — drafted the same day, printed and handed to the instructors at the Farm, who critiqued the prose, the conduct of the meeting and what the officer had been wearing.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Bill Buckley
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Mr. Fish
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Navigating Pakistan without maps
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The logistical problem John Kiriakou says nearly undid the Abu Zubaydah operation: in 2002 Pakistan had no maps to buy, no street signs and no addresses, so the CIA team navigated a city of twelve million by shoe advertisement, traffic policeman, British school and McDonald''s — rehearsing the route twice in the small hours before the raids.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Planning a surveillance detection route
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The hours of paperwork behind every CIA meeting before satellite mapping existed — photocopied road-atlas pages taped into sheets six feet across, legs and stops marked in coloured highlighter, submitted to instructors for approval and then driven in advance to check for no-left-turns and closed roads.

moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.title: Amir
moving-a-satellite-to-kuwait.summary: The pseudonym John Kiriakou gives the Muslim, ethnically Arab domestic officer sent on temporary duty to Pakistan to help with the Abu Zubaydah hunt — the colleague who drove them into India by GPS, drank the roadside tea and had diarrhoea for six weeks, and invented the textile-baron cover story on the spot.

mr-fish.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
mr-fish.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

mr-fish.title: Magic box
mr-fish.summary: An improvised cell-phone locator that two CIA tech officers built from parts bought in a Pakistani bazaar during the hunt for Abu Zubaydah. It could point toward a phone while a call was live, and did so exactly once — long enough for John Kiriakou to conclude the device was wasted time and to fly in a targeting analyst instead.

mr-fish.title: The Punjab Elite Force
mr-fish.summary: The Pakistani provincial counterterrorism unit that supplied part of the assault manpower for the Abu Zubaydah raids of March 2002 — black trousers, black t-shirts stencilled with a pistol, and, in John Kiriakou's telling, a refusal to wear body armour on the grounds that if God called them that night they would go.

mr-fish.title: Abu Zubaydah
mr-fish.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

mr-fish.title: Colonel Khaled
mr-fish.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

mr-fish.title: Pervez Musharraf
mr-fish.summary: Pakistani general and military dictator who ruled during John Kiriakou's 2002 posting as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan. Per Kiriakou, the United States 'essentially just purchased Musharraf,' paying tens of millions in cash to the ISI and meeting him several times a week — and in return 'he would let us do whatever we wanted.' Kiriakou says Musharraf, fearing the nuclear arsenal could fall into terrorist hands, unofficially turned control of Pakistan's nuclear weapons over to the Pentagon. Musharraf later pardoned proliferator A.Q. Khan.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Osama bin Laden
muammar-gaddafi.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

muammar-gaddafi.title: ISIS
muammar-gaddafi.summary: The Islamic State, in John Kiriakou''s account, is an American policy failure made flesh — created because a faction decided al-Qaeda was not radical or violent enough, founded by Baghdadi while he sat in a U.S. military prison in Iraq, armed with hardware captured from the U.S.-supplied Iraqi army, and — per an email he cites from Hillary Clinton to John Podesta — funded by the governments of Saudi Arabia and Qatar. Kiriakou repeatedly punctured the anti-ISIS coalition''s logic: ISIS operated in seven countries while the U.S. bombed two, and Turkey had no real quarrel with ISIS at all — their common enemy was the Kurds.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
muammar-gaddafi.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Ali Soufan
muammar-gaddafi.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

muammar-gaddafi.title: George W. Bush
muammar-gaddafi.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

muammar-gaddafi.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
muammar-gaddafi.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

muddling-through.title: The NATO expansion promises
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the assurances American presidents gave Russia that NATO would not expand to its borders or admit Ukraine — promises he says were made repeatedly, broken repeatedly, and, in his blunt formulation, never meant. He couples the account with an equally explicit statement that he opposes the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

muddling-through.title: The Paris rifle serial number
muddling-through.summary: The case John Kiriakou uses to argue that American weapons sent to Ukraine are leaking onto the black market: a rifle used to shoot and severely wound a policeman in Paris whose serial number, he says, matched a shipment of assault rifles the United States had sent to Ukraine some six months earlier.

muddling-through.title: CIA attention to West Africa
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

muddling-through.title: The African diplomat's remark
muddling-through.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

muddling-through.title: The Hersh publishing collapse
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Seymour Hersh's disappearance from mainstream print — from the London Review of Books in 2017, which Hersh told him was already the only outlet that would take his work, to Substack five years later. Kiriakou, who helped give Hersh an award for integrity in intelligence, presents the trajectory as a measure of how bad conditions for American journalism have become.

muddling-through.title: The secret Sahel appropriations
muddling-through.summary: John Kiriakou's complaint that the United States is quietly pumping billions of dollars into Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Conakry and Guinea-Bissau — spending he says is supposed to be a big secret, addresses a French problem rather than an American one, and which American taxpayers have a right to know about and to judge.

muhammad-atar.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
muhammad-atar.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

muhammad-atar.title: Walling
muhammad-atar.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a detainee is slammed against a wall; designed on paper to use a padded fiberboard surface and a rolled towel around the neck, but applied in practice against bare concrete-block walls without protective measures, producing in at least one case permanent brain damage.

muhammad-atar.title: Ramzi bin al-Shibh
muhammad-atar.summary: Alleged September 11 co-conspirator, captured in Pakistan in the summer of 2002 and taken to a secret prison rather than to trial. John Kiriakou, who is often wrongly credited with his capture, cites him as the clearest demonstration of what torture cost the United States — declared clinically insane by the Pentagon's own psychiatrist as a result of CIA sleep deprivation, and therefore untriable.

muhammad-atar.title: Mitchell and Jessen
muhammad-atar.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

muhammad-atar.title: Hummus
muhammad-atar.summary: The CIA's coercive 'rectal feeding' of detainees using pureed hummus — an unauthorized interrogation technique used at post-9/11 black sites, exposed in the 2014 Senate Torture Report, and the abuse for which John Kiriakou became most associated in popular culture.

muhammad-atar.title: Sleep deprivation
muhammad-atar.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

music-as-torture.title: Cold cell
music-as-torture.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

music-as-torture.title: Waterboarding
music-as-torture.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

music-as-torture.title: Sleep deprivation
music-as-torture.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

music-as-torture.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
music-as-torture.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

music-as-torture.title: Cameo
music-as-torture.summary: The personalised-video app John Kiriakou joined in February 2026 and turned into an unexpected second career — around 2,600 videos, roughly 900 of them in his first month alone. Half are birthday messages and most of the rest are requests for CIA stories, but about two hundred have been appeals for advice or a pep talk, and three of those people later told him he had talked them out of suicide.

music-as-torture.title: Israeli foreknowledge of 9/11
music-as-torture.summary: John Kiriakou's stated belief that Israeli intelligence had penetrated al-Qaeda and knew an attack was coming but withheld the warning as a policy decision, offered as his explanation for the dozens of Israelis arrested in New York in the days after the attacks.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Islamofascism
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: A term John Kiriakou says was introduced into American media around 2004 and 2005, was created by a public relations firm working for the Republican National Committee, was pushed hard into everyday usage, failed to catch on, and was quietly abandoned. He offers it as his clearest example of manufactured vocabulary intended as domestic propaganda.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Abu Zubaydah
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Bill Clinton
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

muslim-brotherhood-designation.title: Air India Flight 182
muslim-brotherhood-designation.summary: The 1985 bombing of a Boeing 747 over the Atlantic, which John Kiriakou has attributed to the government of India in the course of arguing that state sponsorship of terrorism is not confined to the countries formally designated for it.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: 1953 Iran coup
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: The U.S.- and UK-backed overthrow of Iran's democratically elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh; per John Kiriakou, the coup served British national interests rather than American ones, and the subsequent outlawing of secular political opposition under the Shah forced dissent into the mosques — producing a religious rather than secular revolution in 1979.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: AIPAC
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Barack Obama
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Below World's End
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: Film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut, filmed entirely in Mexico during October 2025; Kiriakou's performance earned him a Screen Actors Guild membership card, and Sean Penn told him after a private screening that he had unknowingly been acting throughout his entire CIA career.

myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.title: Big Assawoman Bay NASA launch
myanmar-civil-war-kiriakou-view.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being taken, as a junior CIA analyst, to watch a NASA rocket launch near the village of Big Assawoman on Virginia's Eastern Shore, where he was startled to find foreign space-agency officials present unsupervised.

narcotics-under-cover.title: Qat in Yemen
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The afternoon shrub-chewing habit of Yemen, and the special dispensation the CIA had to issue so that its officers could take part in it. John Kiriakou explains that no source could be developed in a qat-chewing country by an officer who would not chew.

narcotics-under-cover.title: "Most other countries are more moral than the CIA"
narcotics-under-cover.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer who asked whether the United States has the most moral intelligence agency: it does not, and a hundred countries could be named whose services behave better — the disqualifying practice being the killing of people who pose no threat to the United States.

narcotics-under-cover.title: Spies traded home
narcotics-under-cover.summary: What happens to intelligence officers and agents after they are exchanged and sent back, in John Kiriakou''s account: not usually execution, but a career that is irreparably damaged, because every service you would want to hide from now knows exactly who you are.

narcotics-under-cover.title: The clear and present danger finding
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The presidential determination John Kiriakou says must precede any CIA paramilitary targeted killing — an assertion that the person concerned is a clear and present danger to the United States, to an American installation, or to an American person — and his judgement that in early 2026 that threshold had not been reached in Iran.

narcotics-under-cover.title: The Islamabad guest house
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The sixteen-room guest house in Islamabad that CIA officers took over entirely during the post-9/11 deployments — a place John Kiriakou says the agency still will not let him name, which came with breakfast, dinner and laundry for about thirty-five dollars a day against a per diem of five hundred.

narcotics-under-cover.title: A Middle East reading list
narcotics-under-cover.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: Chomo
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: FCI Loretto
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: The Pisces prison gang
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: The umbrella gang every Hispanic prisoner at FCI Loretto was required to join on pain of a beating — which subordinated street rivalries like MS-13, the Norteños and the Zetas to a single inside identity and required every member to work out daily against the possibility of a race riot.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: The rat and pedophile table
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: Shot callers
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: The trusted representatives each faction at FCI Loretto appointed to mediate disputes — a system John Kiriakou credits with keeping violence rare in a low-security prison, and which he later manipulated to have a rival banished from his own table.

nation-of-islam-at-loretto.title: The stinger
nation-of-islam-at-loretto.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

national-archives-declassification.title: Espionage Act
national-archives-declassification.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

national-archives-declassification.title: Leonie Brinkema
national-archives-declassification.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

national-archives-declassification.title: Julian Assange
national-archives-declassification.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

national-archives-declassification.title: Thomas Drake
national-archives-declassification.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

national-archives-declassification.title: Classified email
national-archives-declassification.summary: John Kiriakou was serving overseas the day classified email was introduced at the CIA, and remembers his station chief saying there was no way to control it. His own illustration of what followed is a lunch invitation to his wife — a fellow senior CIA officer — marked Secret HUM 4-82, and her reply naming a deli and a time, marked the same way.

national-archives-declassification.title: Edward Snowden
national-archives-declassification.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

national-bird.title: Daniel Hale
national-bird.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

national-bird.title: The Drone Papers
national-bird.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

national-bird.title: Signature strikes
national-bird.summary: The drone-targeting doctrine, exposed by Daniel Hale's leak, under which the U.S. kills people not for who they are but for patterns of behavior or association; John Kiriakou says operators treat any male over 12 as a legitimate target on the theory that he 'could pick up a gun.'

national-bird.title: PTSD
national-bird.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

national-bird.title: Espionage Act
national-bird.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

national-bird.title: Jeffrey Sterling
national-bird.summary: Former CIA officer convicted of nine felonies, including seven counts of espionage, after giving a New York Times interview about a racial discrimination lawsuit he had filed against the CIA. Per John Kiriakou, Sterling was not accused of spying for a foreign country; his underlying case was that the CIA had passed him over for promotion and told him explicitly it was because of his race. Daniel Ellsberg asked Sterling to go to trial specifically so the constitutionality of the Espionage Act could be challenged; Sterling did, was convicted, and was sentenced by Judge Leonie Brinkema to what she described as 'Kiriakou plus 12 months.'

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: John Rendon
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: Self-described "professional propagandist"; organizer of the pre-distributed American flags waved by Kuwaiti crowds on the 1991 Kuwait Liberation Day; in 2008 hired John Kiriakou (alongside Karl Rove) to produce op-eds attempting to rehabilitate the U.S. travel ban imposed on Indonesian general Joko Widodo.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: Kuwait Liberation Day
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: February 1991 expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait by the U.S.-led coalition; John Kiriakou entered the country with U.S. Marines on the day of liberation; the small American flags waved by the crowds — and the post-liberation arrival of Democratic and Republican National Committee personnel ostensibly to assist the country's transition to democracy — were, per Kiriakou, the work of professional propagandist John Rendon.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: Operation Mockingbird
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: CIA political action group
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: The CIA's most secretive clandestine propaganda arm — successor to the Cold War 'active measures group' — which John Kiriakou says places and funds propagandists worldwide; no officer of it has been publicly identified since 1982, and he encountered its work funding the DNC's and RNC's international arms in post-war Kuwait.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: Andres Serrano
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: American artist; in the 1980s the creator of Piss Christ — a beaker of urine containing an inverted crucifix — which so enraged President Ronald Reagan that he cut off funding to the National Endowment for the Arts. Per John Kiriakou, also the photographer of a torture-chamber series at Tate Modern, London, in which one panel is a photograph of Kiriakou next to a panel of a U.S. military torturer.

national-endowment-for-democracy.title: American media consolidation
national-endowment-for-democracy.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why American news coverage is uniform: the entire national media is owned by six corporations or oligarchs, a number the Warner Brothers sale would reduce to five. He attributes the consolidation to profit rather than politics, and describes the practical consequence as an audience that turns on a cable channel believing it is being educated when it is being propagandised — with independent media the only alternative and almost nobody with the time to find it.

national-intelligence-council.title: Counterterrorism Center
national-intelligence-council.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

national-intelligence-council.title: Dick Cheney
national-intelligence-council.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it.
