Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

national-intelligence-council.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
national-intelligence-council.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

national-intelligence-council.title: Jonathan Pollard
national-intelligence-council.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

national-intelligence-council.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
national-intelligence-council.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

national-intelligence-council.title: Saddam Hussein
national-intelligence-council.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

national-security-act.title: J. Edgar Hoover
national-security-act.summary: The FBI's founding director — 48 years in the chair — whose opposition nearly strangled the CIA at birth. Per John Kiriakou, Truman lifted Hoover's objection to the National Security Act of 1947 by disingenuously assuring him the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the lie seeded the two agencies' permanent mutual hatred. Kiriakou also credits Hoover with perfecting the annual ritual the CIA later copied — scaring Congress witless and demanding budget increases — and with controlling Hollywood's FBI image so tightly that no film could be made without his approval.

national-security-act.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
national-security-act.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

national-security-act.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
national-security-act.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

national-security-act.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
national-security-act.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

national-security-act.title: Church Committee
national-security-act.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

national-security-act.title: CIA language training
national-security-act.summary: The agency''s language pipeline as John Kiriakou experienced and describes it: a full year of Arabic at nine hours a day, an optional second year at the State Department''s school, and the calculation that made his own career — that it is cheaper to teach a linguist operations than to teach an operations officer Greek and Arabic.

national-security-agency.title: Thomas Drake
national-security-agency.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

national-security-agency.title: Abu Zubaydah
national-security-agency.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

national-security-agency.title: NSA
national-security-agency.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

national-security-agency.title: NSA Surveillance
national-security-agency.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

national-security-agency.title: PTSD
national-security-agency.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

national-security-agency.title: Pegasus spyware
national-security-agency.summary: Israeli-developed phone-interception software that requires no action by the target — no link clicked, no message answered — and gives its operator the contents of the device along with live use of its camera and microphone. John Kiriakou describes it as having escaped state control: sold on commercially, routed through an American contractor and then directly by the Israelis, used against Americans, and implicated in a Greek interception scandal that he says brought down a government.

national-security-council.title: Osama bin Laden
national-security-council.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

national-security-council.title: John Bolton
national-security-council.summary: Former U.S. National Security Advisor. Per John Kiriakou, one of the most dangerous men in America and the real driver — with Elliott Abrams — of the 2019 pressure campaign against Venezuela; the signature at the National Security Council through which a covert action finding passes on its way to the president. Kiriakou predicted his 2019 departure from the Trump administration on the basis of White House chatter and Trump's premium on loyalty.

national-security-council.title: Counterterrorism Center
national-security-council.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

national-security-council.title: American Psychological Association
national-security-council.summary: The world's largest body of psychologists, which John Kiriakou cites constantly for one devastating datum — its research shows people begin to lose their minds at around day seven without sleep, and begin to die at day nine as their organs shut down. Mitchell and Jessen were nonetheless authorized to keep chained, naked prisoners awake for up to twelve days, which is why Kiriakou insists sleep deprivation was always worse than waterboarding. The organization's own role in the interrogation program later became the subject of an internal revolt and a 500-page independent report.

national-security-council.title: Donald Rumsfeld
national-security-council.summary: U.S. Secretary of Defense during the post-9/11 torture program and, per John Kiriakou, joined at the hip with Dick Cheney in pushing the Iraq war from inside the Office of the Secretary of Defense. Kiriakou recounts Rumsfeld dismissing sleep deprivation as a real technique by pointing to his own standup desk, and names him among the war criminals who would be prosecuted in any other country.

national-security-council.title: Presidential call memcons
national-security-council.summary: How a call between the president and a foreign leader is staffed and recorded, as John Kiriakou describes it. Four people are usually on the line and rarely five — not the twenty reported during the Ukraine affair — and the write-up, a memorandum of conversation or memcon, is held so tightly inside the National Security Council that a CIA analyst, he says, would never see one.

national-security-letters.title: Panquake
national-security-letters.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

national-security-letters.title: Government Purchase of Social Media Metadata
national-security-letters.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the practice by which U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies — including the NSA and FBI — buy bulk user metadata from social media companies such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter), bypassing the warrant requirements that would otherwise apply to direct surveillance. The practice exploits a provision in platform terms of service under which users surrender ownership of their metadata to the company, which may then sell it freely.

national-security-letters.title: CIA–Big Tech revolving door
national-security-letters.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the traffic between the CIA and the major technology companies — "they work hand in glove" — illustrated by a supervisor who resigned five years short of his thirty-year pension for a Microsoft job paying eight times his government salary. The exchange, he argues, benefits both sides and is for that reason dangerous: the agency gains access to the most advanced companies in the world, and the companies gain a direct channel into the intelligence community.

national-security-letters.title: Julian Assange
national-security-letters.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

national-security-letters.title: Purchased data as a warrant workaround
national-security-letters.summary: John Kiriakou's account of U.S. federal agencies buying Americans' personal data from social-media platforms and data brokers rather than seeking a warrant — a practice he describes as an ethical and legal problem likely to reach the Supreme Court, and one in which no judge is aware a case is being built.

national-security-letters.title: Bill Binney
national-security-letters.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: John Kiriakou
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: AIPAC
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

national-security-vs-civil-liberties.title: Hunter Biden Laptop
national-security-vs-civil-liberties.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the Hunter Biden laptop controversy — he saw nothing related to child sex abuse in the material but says the Biden family, particularly Hunter, has serious documented substance-abuse problems; and that the 2020 open letter in which 51 former intelligence officials called the story a Russian/KGB-style operation used deliberately hedged, CIA-trained language and was later shown (per Michael Morell's testimony) to have been solicited by the Biden campaign.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: Major non-NATO ally status for Ukraine
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou''s forecast of how the Russian demand that Ukraine never join NATO can be met without leaving Ukraine unprotected: the designation of major non-NATO ally, already held by Australia, Japan, South Korea, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which he says confers essentially the same rights without the membership.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: China as mediator
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: China as economic threat
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: F-35 sale to Turkey
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: The proposed sale of F-35 fighters to Turkey, opposed for decades by Greece and Greek-Americans who fear the aircraft would be used against Greece, and opposed by Benjamin Netanyahu for the same reason with respect to Israel. When Netanyahu raised the objection publicly in July 2026, Donald Trump answered that he does not take orders from a foreign leader about arms sales — a rebuke John Kiriakou describes as unprecedented.

nato-article-5-invoked-once.title: The Imia crisis
nato-article-5-invoked-once.summary: The 1996 confrontation between Greece and Turkey over an uninhabited Aegean islet, which John Kiriakou cites as the last time the two came close to exchanging fire — a flag raised, a flag taken down, warships dispatched, and Bill Clinton telephoning both capitals to tell them to stop.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Israel's counterintelligence threat ranking
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: John Kiriakou's repeated point that the American intelligence community formally ranks Israel a critical counterintelligence threat — the same tier as North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba — specifically for spying on and infiltrating the US government, and that policy has responded by giving Israel more access rather than less.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: MOSSAD
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Jonathan Pollard
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Veterans' benefits for IDF service
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: A bill sponsored by a Republican congressman from Pennsylvania and one from Ohio that would extend US veterans' benefits to any American who joins the Israel Defense Forces. John Kiriakou calls it an outrage and, as an American, treason.

ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
ndaa-2027-israel-fusion.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

ndaa-section-219.title: Israeli espionage in the United States
ndaa-section-219.summary: The long-running Israeli intelligence effort against American targets, which John Kiriakou describes from inside the CIA: Israelis barred from the headquarters building, 187 spies identified by the FBI in 1990, a critical-threat counterintelligence ranking alongside Russia and China, and a 2026 warning that activity had intensified.

ndaa-section-219.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
ndaa-section-219.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

ndaa-section-219.title: AIPAC
ndaa-section-219.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

ndaa-section-219.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
ndaa-section-219.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

ndaa-section-219.title: Israeli training of American police
ndaa-section-219.summary: The practice, which John Kiriakou opposes, of Israeli police and IDF personnel training American local police departments, including at the Atlanta facility known as Cop City.

ndaa-section-219.title: October 7 attack
ndaa-section-219.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Maduro Capture
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: International Criminal Court
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: The Hague tribunal created by the Rome Statute, which has charged Benjamin Netanyahu with war crimes and crimes against humanity. John Kiriakou supports it as the necessary successor to Nuremberg, notes that neither the United States nor Israel is a signatory, and observes that a forced landing in a signatory state would oblige that country to arrest Netanyahu.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Graham–Netanyahu ICC tapes
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: Recordings of Lindsey Graham coordinating with Benjamin Netanyahu on how to discredit the International Criminal Court over its arrest warrant. On the tapes Graham lines up Senate signatories for a protest letter, jokes that he should be paid "tons of shekels," and asks Netanyahu to telephone two Democratic senators to thank them. John Kiriakou argues the conduct meets the definition of espionage his own judge applied to him.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Hague Invasion Act
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: The American statute, described by John Kiriakou as having been passed during the Obama administration, that authorises the president to use the United States military to invade the Netherlands and free an American or allied national held by the International Criminal Court — the standing legal answer to the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu might be arrested abroad.

netanyahu-arrest-poll.title: Donald Trump
netanyahu-arrest-poll.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.title: 2026 Iran war
netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.title: Breaking the nuclear taboo
netanyahu-nuclear-threat-to-trump.summary: John Kiriakou's reporting that Donald Trump considered using a tactical nuclear weapon in Iran not for military necessity but to break what he regards as warfare's final taboo, freeing future presidents to use larger weapons — and the related account that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs refused him the nuclear codes.

new-castle-pennsylvania.title: George Washington University
new-castle-pennsylvania.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

new-castle-pennsylvania.title: Kiriakou's UFO sighting
new-castle-pennsylvania.summary: The object John Kiriakou and his father watched from the side of Route 60 in Amish country, western Pennsylvania, on a Friday night in 1981 — three flashes of white light, then a silent orange trapezoid hanging a couple of thousand feet up, which left at a speed he had never seen before or since.

new-castle-pennsylvania.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
new-castle-pennsylvania.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

new-castle-pennsylvania.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
new-castle-pennsylvania.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

new-castle-pennsylvania.title: The polygraph
new-castle-pennsylvania.summary: The lie-detector examination that gates entry to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou from the inside: the twenty-minute wiring-up, the psychiatrist''s advice to stare at a speck on the wall, the deliberately planted false accusation used to test a candidate''s reaction, and his contention that the machine screens out exactly the wrong people.

new-castle-pennsylvania.title: American Psychological Association
new-castle-pennsylvania.summary: The world's largest body of psychologists, which John Kiriakou cites constantly for one devastating datum — its research shows people begin to lose their minds at around day seven without sleep, and begin to die at day nine as their organs shut down. Mitchell and Jessen were nonetheless authorized to keep chained, naked prisoners awake for up to twelve days, which is why Kiriakou insists sleep deprivation was always worse than waterboarding. The organization's own role in the interrogation program later became the subject of an internal revolt and a 500-page independent report.

newsguard.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
newsguard.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

newsguard.title: Abraham Accords
newsguard.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

newsguard.title: Abu Zubaydah
newsguard.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

newsguard.title: Ahmed Chalabi
newsguard.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

newsguard.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
newsguard.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

newsguard.title: Bill Clinton
newsguard.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

nick-bryant.title: Jeffrey Epstein
nick-bryant.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

nick-bryant.title: Epstein Files Transparency Act
nick-bryant.summary: The law compelling the Justice Department to release the Epstein files by a fixed deadline, passed 419 to 1 in the House and 99 to nothing in the Senate and then, in John Kiriakou's account, simply not complied with.

nick-bryant.title: FCI Loretto
nick-bryant.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

nick-bryant.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
nick-bryant.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

nick-bryant.title: Mike Johnson
nick-bryant.summary: Speaker of the House during the fight over the Epstein files, whose procedural manoeuvres John Kiriakou reads as an attempt to let the issue die in subcommittee, and whose midterm framing of Democrats as communists Kiriakou dismisses outright.

nick-bryant.title: Bureau of Prisons
nick-bryant.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.title: Abu Zubaydah
ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.title: Executive Order 12333
ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.title: Title 10 vs Title 50
ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.summary: The U.S. legal-code distinction governing which kinds of armed action fall under military authority (Title 10) and which fall under intelligence authority (Title 50); the operative legal frame for the post-9/11 question of whether CIA contractors can lawfully kill in the agency's name, addressed in the 2025 Ninth Circuit ruling in the Abu Zubaydah contractor case.

ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.title: Blackwater
ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.summary: The private military contractor founded by Erik Prince that ran the CIA's Global Response Staff and, until shut down by Leon Panetta, a global assassination program; staffed at the board level with former CIA officers including Cofer Black as Vice President.

ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.title: Athens bank fraud report
ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.summary: John Kiriakou's account of taking a dream job as COO of an Athens investment firm in 2020, discovering it was an elaborate bank fraud, and being unable to get the FBI to act — an agent telling him that without 'terrorism, China, or January 6th,' they were not interested.

ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.title: Bill Clinton
ninth-circuit-contractor-ruling-2025.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.title: Truman's regret over Israel
nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Harry Truman called his role in the creation of the state of Israel the act of 'a damn fool' and the biggest regret of his presidency, because the situation spun out of control almost immediately.

nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.title: AIPAC
nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.title: Marjorie Taylor Greene
nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.summary: American congresswoman whom John Kiriakou, despite deep political disagreement, has repeatedly credited for breaking with her party on the Epstein files, on military aid to Israel, and on Gaza. He describes her as courageous for pressing Donald Trump to release the files unredacted, and says the pressure ultimately forced her out of Washington.

nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.title: Israeli non-extradition of Jews
nixon-israeli-security-guarantee.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of Israel as a refuge that does not extradite Jewish fugitives regardless of the offence, illustrated by the case of an American lawyer who fled there after a child-abuse suit and was recovered only by an Interpol sting in Cyprus. Kiriakou uses the rule to frame a question about Jeffrey Epstein: why a man with jets and hidden billions did not flee there himself.

no-bad-food-in-athens.title: Kiriakou on Greek and Cypriot food
no-bad-food-in-athens.summary: The verdict John Kiriakou delivered on Cypriot cooking during a 2026 visit to the island — that its cheeses are more sophisticated and more distinct from one another than Greece's, where most are variations on a theme — together with his coffee positions, his conversion from frappé by a cousin in Rhodes, and his complaint about the size of the straw.

no-bad-food-in-athens.title: John Kiriakou
no-bad-food-in-athens.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

no-bad-food-in-athens.title: Kiriakou's Athens house
no-bad-food-in-athens.summary: The five-storey house in the northern Athens suburb of Kifissia that John Kiriakou found for himself after refusing the embassy's offer — no square rooms, a balcony off every one of them facing a different way, and a garden with a 200-year-old olive tree whose oil the family cooked with for two years.

no-bad-food-in-athens.title: Kiriakou's Cypriot ancestry
no-bad-food-in-athens.summary: The DNA result showing John Kiriakou to be 24 per cent Cypriot — his largest single ancestry — which corrected a family belief that the line came from Crete and coincided with an invitation to address a Cypriot diaspora conference.

no-bad-food-in-athens.title: The declared officer
no-bad-food-in-athens.summary: The CIA officer whose identity is formally disclosed to the host country's intelligence service — as John Kiriakou was in Athens, taken by his chief within days of arrival to be introduced to the head of the Greek service.

no-bad-food-in-athens.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
no-bad-food-in-athens.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

no-bid-contracts.title: Abraxas Corporation
no-bid-contracts.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

no-bid-contracts.title: Business class after 9/11
no-bid-contracts.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

no-bid-contracts.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
no-bid-contracts.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

no-bid-contracts.title: The General Muhammad equipment gift
no-bid-contracts.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the end of the Abu Zubaydah operation in Pakistan, when headquarters told him to throw away or hand over the truckloads of equipment his station had bought — and of learning weeks later from his day-to-day Pakistani contact that the brigadier general who accepted the gift had simply taken it all himself.

no-bid-contracts.title: Prison guard hiring standards
no-bid-contracts.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what it takes to become a federal prison guard — a GED or work towards one, and no felony convictions — and his supporting anecdote that prisoners themselves regularly had to conduct mail call because the officer assigned to it could not read.

no-bid-contracts.title: Private Intelligence
no-bid-contracts.summary: Post-CIA commercial intelligence work performed by John Kiriakou — both operational (surveillance, bribery, dossier-building for private clients) and analytical (paid forecasts for hedge funds, mutual funds, and a global mining company). Per Kiriakou, his clients ranged from a Cypriot billionaire investigating his daughter's fiancé to the ninth-largest hedge fund in the world.

no-plan-for-day-two.title: The Libyan constitution unveiling
no-plan-for-day-two.summary: A launch event John Kiriakou attended in Washington after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi: a new Libyan constitution, commissioned by wealthy exiles from a lobbying firm, unveiled at the lobbying firm''s offices. He calls the document better than the American one — equal rights for everybody, the oil money shared — and notes that nothing whatever was done with it, because nobody in Washington had heard of the people behind it.

no-plan-for-day-two.title: Covert action programs
no-plan-for-day-two.summary: The most tightly held category of American intelligence activity — so tightly held, John Kiriakou says, that a serving CIA officer may not utter the phrase in public. Which is why he found it extraordinary that a president announced one on television, and doubts the announcement was straightforwardly true.

no-plan-for-day-two.title: United Fruit and the Arbenz coup
no-plan-for-day-two.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the 1954 CIA overthrow of Guatemala's President Arbenz after he nationalized the banana crop — engineered by the Dulles brothers, who sat on the board of the United Fruit Company, and followed by half a century of dictatorship.

no-plan-for-day-two.title: María Corina Machado
no-plan-for-day-two.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

no-plan-for-day-two.title: The four requirements of a coup
no-plan-for-day-two.summary: The checklist John Kiriakou says is taught at West Point for overthrowing a government — the presidential palace and the leader, the broadcast stations, the capital's major intersections, and the support of the military — which he uses to argue that regime change in Venezuela cannot work, because the fourth item belongs to the incumbent.

no-plan-for-day-two.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
no-plan-for-day-two.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

nobel-peace-prize.title: Abraham Accords
nobel-peace-prize.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

nobel-peace-prize.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
nobel-peace-prize.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

nobel-peace-prize.title: MOSSAD
nobel-peace-prize.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

nobel-peace-prize.title: Piers Morgan
nobel-peace-prize.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

nobel-peace-prize.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
nobel-peace-prize.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

nobel-peace-prize.title: Trita Parsi
nobel-peace-prize.summary: Iran scholar; in a Foreign Affairs piece published August 10, 2025, predicted a renewed Israeli–Iranian war by the end of August 2025; described by John Kiriakou as "one of the greatest Iran scholars on the planet."

noelle-dunphy.title: Rudy Giuliani
noelle-dunphy.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

noelle-dunphy.title: Counterterrorism Center
noelle-dunphy.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

noelle-dunphy.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
noelle-dunphy.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

noelle-dunphy.title: Taliban embassy raid
noelle-dunphy.summary: John Kiriakou's account of raiding the last functioning Taliban embassy, in Peshawar, in the middle of the night after 9/11 — a raid that turned up phone bills showing dozens of calls to U.S. cities that stopped on September 10 and resumed on September 16, evidence of possible sleeper cells the FBI never translated.

noelle-dunphy.title: Bernie Kerik
noelle-dunphy.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

noelle-dunphy.title: Bruce Fein
noelle-dunphy.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

non-personal-communication.title: One-Time Pad
non-personal-communication.summary: Cipher system in which a secret, random key — shared between sender and receiver — is used to encode a message and then destroyed so that it can never be used again. In traditional shortwave-radio tradecraft, one-time pads enabled spies to broadcast number sequences over public airwaves that only the intended recipient, holding the matching page, could decode. Per John Kiriakou, his lifelong interest in intelligence began at age nine after he picked up KGB number transmissions on a 50-cent shortwave radio.

non-personal-communication.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
non-personal-communication.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

non-personal-communication.title: Surveillance detection route
non-personal-communication.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

non-personal-communication.title: Double-Agent Capture
non-personal-communication.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

non-personal-communication.title: John Kiriakou
non-personal-communication.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

non-personal-communication.title: Abu Zubaydah
non-personal-communication.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

nordeen-house.title: Kiriakou's Athens house
nordeen-house.summary: The five-storey house in the northern Athens suburb of Kifissia that John Kiriakou found for himself after refusing the embassy's offer — no square rooms, a balcony off every one of them facing a different way, and a garden with a 200-year-old olive tree whose oil the family cooked with for two years.

nordeen-house.title: The Athens carjacking
nordeen-house.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

nordeen-house.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
nordeen-house.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

nordeen-house.title: John Kiriakou
nordeen-house.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

nordeen-house.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
nordeen-house.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

nordeen-house.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
nordeen-house.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.title: Bob Woodward's CIA headquarters access
nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.summary: John Kiriakou's account of watching Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward walk the halls of CIA headquarters unescorted while researching a book, after the CIA director ordered staff to cooperate with him — an episode Kiriakou cites as evidence of how close the relationship between senior CIA officials and favored journalists really is.

nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.title: Central Intelligence Agency
nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.title: MOSSAD
nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.title: Vladimir Putin
nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.summary: President of Russia. Per John Kiriakou, Putin twice raised joining NATO — floating it to Bill Clinton and later telling Barack Obama Russia would like to explore membership — and was refused both times; Kiriakou has never believed Putin wants to conquer Ukraine or Eastern Europe, argues U.S. hostility toward Russia is driven by defense contractors and a permanent wartime economy, and notes the irony that Putin was the anti-communist the U.S. itself backed in the Yeltsin era.

nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.title: Volodymyr Zelensky
nordstream-pipeline-sabotage.summary: Kiriakou says he was told not to discuss Zelensky's corruption publicly, and calls the Oval Office dressing-down of him set up in advance.

norman-schwarzkopf.title: Saddam Hussein
norman-schwarzkopf.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

norman-schwarzkopf.title: April Glaspie
norman-schwarzkopf.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Iraq in the run-up to the 1990 invasion of Kuwait; per John Kiriakou, delivered to Saddam Hussein — on a NODIS cable from Secretary of State James Baker — the line that the United States took no position on Arab-Arab border disputes, which Saddam is widely held to have read as a green light to invade. Kiriakou, who was in the CIA operations center the night her reporting cable came back, holds that she got a bum rap.

norman-schwarzkopf.title: Hussein Kamel
norman-schwarzkopf.summary: Saddam Hussein's son-in-law and Iraq's Minister of Industry and Military Industrialization; defected to Jordan in January 1993 with his brother Saddam Kamel out of fear of Uday Hussein; demanded U.S. weapons and air cover in exchange for cooperation but refused to disclose WMD locations; per John Kiriakou, the CIA burned him with a planted Arab-press leak that triggered Saddam to destroy his chemical-weapons stockpile.

norman-schwarzkopf.title: John Kiriakou
norman-schwarzkopf.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

norman-schwarzkopf.title: Kurds
norman-schwarzkopf.summary: The stateless people John Kiriakou calls generationally pro-American — he escorted visiting Kurdish delegations around Washington as a young analyst and bristled at officials who talked down to them. In his telling the Kurds were the only genuine opposition inside Saddam's Iraq, the only faction of the exile circus that ever amounted to anything (Jalal Talabani ended up president of Iraq), the victims of Saddam's chemical weapons and of a no-fly zone that forgot to ban helicopters — and the common enemy that actually united Turkey and ISIS.

norman-schwarzkopf.title: Uday Hussein
norman-schwarzkopf.summary: Eldest son of Saddam Hussein; described by John Kiriakou as so dangerous a successor-in-waiting that Saddam's two sons-in-law — Hussein Kamel and Saddam Kamel — defected to Jordan in January 1993 specifically out of fear of him.

nsa-surveillance.title: Bluffdale NSA Data Center
nsa-surveillance.summary: The NSA's purpose-built facility in the Utah desert, characterized by John Kiriakou as having storage capacity for every phone call, text message, and email of every American for the next 500 years.

nsa-surveillance.title: San Bernardino iPhone Case
nsa-surveillance.summary: The 2015–16 legal standoff in which Apple refused to unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone for the FBI, which instead paid an Israeli firm $6 million to crack it — though, per John Kiriakou, the intelligence that could have disrupted the attack never came from the phone at all.

nsa-surveillance.title: Mass Surveillance
nsa-surveillance.summary: Kiriakou says the NSA has dropped any pretext of protecting civil liberties, warehousing every call, text and email in the Utah desert.

nsa-surveillance.title: Pegasus spyware
nsa-surveillance.summary: Israeli-developed phone-interception software that requires no action by the target — no link clicked, no message answered — and gives its operator the contents of the device along with live use of its camera and microphone. John Kiriakou describes it as having escaped state control: sold on commercially, routed through an American contractor and then directly by the Israelis, used against Americans, and implicated in a Greek interception scandal that he says brought down a government.

nsa-surveillance.title: Government encryption back-door demands
nsa-surveillance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of state pressure on technology companies for access to encrypted systems — the British government's demand for a back door into Apple's operating system, which he says Apple met with a threat to leave the United Kingdom, and his prediction that the second Trump administration would make the same demand of any new platform under a counterterrorism pretext.

nsa-surveillance.title: Section 702
nsa-surveillance.summary: Section of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act under which the U.S. government conducts warrantless electronic surveillance; per John Kiriakou the principal post-9/11 mechanism by which the CIA, NSA, and FBI surveil American citizens; renewed by Congress every two years over the objection of a small bipartisan minority; the subject of an estimated 200,000+ illegal FBI database queries — per the Brennan Center for Justice, including ~78,000 misused queries over a two-year window; the disclosure that Edward Snowden made public in summer 2013.

nsa.title: FBI
nsa.summary: Kiriakou says FBI agents were sticklers for the law in a way the CIA never was — and that the bureau 'leaks like a sieve.'

nsa.title: Central Intelligence Agency
nsa.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

nsa.title: Intelligence Agencies
nsa.summary: Kiriakou counts roughly 19 publicly known US intelligence agencies and calls the proliferation Pentagon empire-building on duplicative work.

nsa.title: Thomas Drake
nsa.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

nsa.title: Yemen Diplomatic Pouch Arrest
nsa.summary: Per John Kiriakou, his most wholly negative experience with a foreign intelligence service: arrested at Sana''a Airport in Yemen in 1991, eighteen months into his CIA career, after his Riyadh station chief asked him to carry a diplomatic pouch on a long-weekend trip. Yemeni officials demanded the sealed pouch go through the X-ray machine. When the scan revealed a handheld walkie-talkie inside, someone shouted ''Jassus'' — spy — and Kiriakou was handcuffed and placed in an airport cell. The incident triggered a diplomatic chain reaction reaching the Yemeni Prime Minister before a Yemeni officer hacked open the diplomatic seal with a curved jambiya dagger to confirm the pouch contained only mail and the radio. Kiriakou spent the rest of the weekend under heavy surveillance; he later said each of his five trips to Yemen was worse than the last.

nsa.title: National Security Agency
nsa.summary: The U.S. signals-intelligence agency. John Kiriakou notes it was never created by an act of Congress and that its own charter forbids collection on Americans — a rule that, when he entered government, meant heads rolled over accidental intercepts, and which he says has since been inverted into total collection stored in Utah for 500 years.

nuclear-war-is-winnable.title: Europe without Russian gas
nuclear-war-is-winnable.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Europe needs Russia more than Russia needs Europe, made from what he has physically encountered rather than from figures. Speaking in Nottingham in 2025 he found the concert hall so cold that the audience complained, and was told by the manager that the venue could not afford to heat itself without Russian gas. He reports the same of homes in Britain, Germany and Greece, where American gas is simply too expensive to substitute.

nuclear-war-is-winnable.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
nuclear-war-is-winnable.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

nuclear-war-is-winnable.title: Operation Spiderweb
nuclear-war-is-winnable.summary: The Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's strategic bomber fleet in June 2025, which John Kiriakou calls a brilliant operation and — against Volodymyr Zelensky's account — one Ukraine could not have run alone. Eighteen months of preparation, drones smuggled across eleven time zones by human couriers, and command from Kyiv all required outside help, he argues; and Donald Trump's uncharacteristic public silence afterwards is his evidence that Washington was in on it.

nuclear-war-is-winnable.title: The Panda card
nuclear-war-is-winnable.summary: The Chinese national payment card John Kiriakou encountered in Hong Kong, where he found few places willing to take Mastercard or Visa. Asked why, he was given a one-sentence answer about routing: Visa and Mastercard transactions pass through New York, Panda card transactions pass through Shanghai, and so fall outside the reach of American sanctions. He treats it as both an instance of Chinese strategic competence and an argument that the American card duopoly is a racket.

nuclear-war-is-winnable.title: Kiriakou's Ukraine settlement prediction
nuclear-war-is-winnable.summary: The endgame John Kiriakou forecast in June 2025 and calls deliberately unbold: Russia keeps the disputed eastern territories and Crimea, Ukraine never joins NATO but probably joins the European Union, and Moscow gets ninety per cent of what it wanted. The one demand he expects Russia to trade away is denazification, which he reads as propaganda rather than policy.

nuclear-war-is-winnable.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
nuclear-war-is-winnable.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

obama-manning-commutation-decision.title: Barack Obama
obama-manning-commutation-decision.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

obama-manning-commutation-decision.title: Kiriakou pardon request
obama-manning-commutation-decision.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

obama-manning-commutation-decision.title: Chelsea Manning
obama-manning-commutation-decision.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

obama-manning-commutation-decision.title: Joe Biden
obama-manning-commutation-decision.summary: 46th President of the United States; Vice President during the first Obama term; at John Kerry's December 2009 Christmas party, recognized John Kiriakou from a 15-year-prior conversation about a mutual hometown friend, and openly told a Kiriakou colleague within Kiriakou's hearing — and across the room from Kerry — that he disliked the colleague.

obama-manning-commutation-decision.title: Julian Assange
obama-manning-commutation-decision.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

obama-manning-commutation-decision.title: Bruce Fein
obama-manning-commutation-decision.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

october-7-attack.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
october-7-attack.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

october-7-attack.title: Itamar Ben-Gvir
october-7-attack.summary: Israel's far-right Minister of National Security; John Kiriakou cites him as a convicted hate-crime felon placed in charge of security in Gaza and the West Bank over his victims, blames his insistence that any attack would come from the West Bank for diverting forces before October 7, and cites the death-penalty law passed under his portfolio for Palestinian detainees as the first reinstatement of capital punishment in Israel since it was abolished in 1956, excepting only the execution of Adolf Eichmann.

october-7-attack.title: Hamas
october-7-attack.summary: The Palestinian movement behind the October 7, 2023 attack; John Kiriakou argues that a case could be made for calling it a freedom-fighting organization dedicated to the liberation of its people rather than simply a terrorist group, notes it is labeled a terrorist organization by only a small minority of UN member states, and has ruled Gaza since Israel's 2005 withdrawal.

october-7-attack.title: AIPAC
october-7-attack.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

october-7-attack.title: Donald Trump
october-7-attack.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

october-7-attack.title: Kiriakou's mother's 2008 trip to Israel
october-7-attack.summary: John Kiriakou recounts his mother's 2008 church-group trip to Israel and the West Bank, during which she was struck by the contrast between first-world Tel Aviv and a walled, mined Palestinian town, and witnessed an IDF soldier tear apart a Palestinian bus driver's novel as suspected "PLO propaganda." Kiriakou made two trips of his own to Israel in 2022, including one to cover the elections, during which he personally witnessed a fatal stabbing at Jerusalem's Iron Gate.

office-of-leadership-analysis.title: Saddam Hussein
office-of-leadership-analysis.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

office-of-leadership-analysis.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
office-of-leadership-analysis.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

office-of-leadership-analysis.title: Abu Zubaydah
office-of-leadership-analysis.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

office-of-leadership-analysis.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
