Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

pakistan-station-2002.title: John Kiriakou
pakistan-station-2002.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

pakistan-station-2002.title: The Peace and Friendship Bridge
pakistan-station-2002.summary: A bridge across the narrow Pakistan–China frontier that John Kiriakou saw advertised on billboards across Pakistan while serving there, and the exchange it produced with a Pakistani general: asked why so much was being made of it, the general said the Chinese were the only friends Pakistan had who had never turned on them — and then looked at Kiriakou.

pakistan-without-maps.title: The Lahore safe house
pakistan-without-maps.summary: The ten-bedroom house in the best neighbourhood of Lahore that the CIA bought outright for two million dollars in cash in March 2002, on a cover story invented on the spot — that its buyers were textile barons — and from whose roof the team could catch seven satellites.

pakistan-without-maps.title: Colonel Khaled
pakistan-without-maps.summary: The ISI chief in Lahore who worked alongside John Kiriakou through the Abu Zubaydah operation — a man who had never wanted to be a soldier, who spent their first meeting drawing Kiriakou's portrait instead of taking notes, and who explained the spliced telephone wires that nearly derailed the hunt.

pakistan-without-maps.title: Amir
pakistan-without-maps.summary: The pseudonym John Kiriakou gives the Muslim, ethnically Arab domestic officer sent on temporary duty to Pakistan to help with the Abu Zubaydah hunt — the colleague who drove them into India by GPS, drank the roadside tea and had diarrhoea for six weeks, and invented the textile-baron cover story on the spot.

pakistan-without-maps.title: Faisalabad
pakistan-without-maps.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

pakistan-without-maps.title: Moving a satellite to Kuwait
pakistan-without-maps.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of how thin American overhead coverage once was: after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 the United States had no satellite looking at Kuwait, and it took six months to move one that had been parked over Moscow.

pakistan-without-maps.title: Faisalabad Hospital
pakistan-without-maps.summary: The hospital where a dying Abu Zubaydah was taken after the raid of March 2002 — open windows, animals in the corridors, mosquitoes on open wounds, and a bar of Irish Spring soap used as a pincushion for reusable syringes — which came under fire from the street while he was on the operating table.

palantir.title: In-Q-Tel
palantir.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

palantir.title: Cofer Black
palantir.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

palantir.title: Gina Haspel
palantir.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

palantir.title: CIA National Resources Division
palantir.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

palantir.title: The spy shop
palantir.summary: A London shop with a New York sister branch where, John Kiriakou says, the CIA bought a good deal of the equipment it needed, on the reasoning that a thousand-dollar purchase beat a million-dollar development programme.

palantir.title: Peter Thiel
palantir.summary: U.S. venture capitalist; co-founder of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group alongside Palantir CEO Alex Karp.

palestinians-in-the-gulf.title: Abraham Accords
palestinians-in-the-gulf.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

palestinians-in-the-gulf.title: Yasser Arafat
palestinians-in-the-gulf.summary: Leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization, who appears in John Kiriakou's account at the two moments he treats as decisive for the Palestinians — backing Saddam Hussein after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which cost the Palestinian middle class its standing across the Gulf, and walking out of the last Clinton-era peace talks with a divided map of Jerusalem already on the table.

palestinians-in-the-gulf.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
palestinians-in-the-gulf.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

palestinians-in-the-gulf.title: Lindsey Graham
palestinians-in-the-gulf.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

palestinians-in-the-gulf.title: Yemen
palestinians-in-the-gulf.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

palestinians-in-the-gulf.title: 2026 Iran war
palestinians-in-the-gulf.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

pam-bondi.title: Donald Trump
pam-bondi.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

pam-bondi.title: Kiriakou pardon request
pam-bondi.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

pam-bondi.title: Mar-a-Lago pardon pitch
pam-bondi.summary: The lunch at which John Kiriakou put his pardon request directly to Donald Trump. Flown to Palm Beach by a wealthy friend who also wanted a pardon, Kiriakou delivered a prepared line as the president worked the dining room, was told to take it to Pam Bondi, and was afterwards vouched for on a speakerphone call to Trump by a political fixer who then asked him for $25,000 a month until the pardon came through.

pam-bondi.title: Bill Barr
pam-bondi.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

pam-bondi.title: Gail Slater
pam-bondi.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the head of the DOJ antitrust unit under Pam Bondi who was stripped of authority and then fired.

pam-bondi.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
pam-bondi.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

pan-quake.title: Julian Assange
pan-quake.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

pan-quake.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
pan-quake.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

pan-quake.title: Kiriakou's personal anecdotes
pan-quake.summary: Three personal stories John Kiriakou has told in interviews — tracking down and meeting Andy Warhol as a college senior, a Congolese vice president's remark that Americans promise democracy while the Chinese provide food, and Kiriakou's own Zelle account being suspended over Cuba-sanctions compliance after a paid article about his Cuba trip.

pan-quake.title: Bashar al-Assad
pan-quake.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

pan-quake.title: Chinese spy balloon incident
pan-quake.summary: 2023 controversy over a high-altitude balloon that crossed U.S. airspace, widely labeled in media coverage as a "Chinese spy balloon"; John Kiriakou notes no U.S. government official ever officially confirmed it was conducting espionage, and says he personally believes it was likely a weather balloon, since satellite surveillance already renders such balloons unnecessary for spying.

pan-quake.title: CIA adultery culture
pan-quake.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.title: Espionage Act
panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.title: Thomas Drake
panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.title: Leon Panetta
panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.summary: CIA Director under President Obama (2009–2011) and subsequent Secretary of Defense; per John Kiriakou, the official who on arrival as Director shut down the Blackwater-operated CIA worldwide assassination program — and in the course of explaining the decision to the House Intelligence Committee publicly outed Erik Prince. Also one of Kiriakou's two go-to examples (with David Petraeus) of senior intelligence figures who disclosed the identities of covert CIA officers without consequence while Kiriakou himself was prosecuted for the same statute.

panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.title: Leonie Brinkema
panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.title: Kiriakou pardon request
panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.title: Eastern District of Virginia
panetta-bin-laden-disclosure.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

panquake.title: Julian Assange
panquake.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

panquake.title: National security letters
panquake.summary: The demand letters the FBI began sending internet service providers after 2001, which John Kiriakou describes as one of three mechanisms that between them retired the warrant requirement for obtaining Americans' personal information. The other two are the FISA process and the outright purchase of metadata from social-media companies.

panquake.title: Suzie Dawson
panquake.summary: New Zealand activist and journalist, chief executive of Talk Liberation and the driving force behind the Panquake platform. John Kiriakou, who has known her for years and serves as the platform's brand ambassador, describes her as the most dogged person he has ever known — a characterisation he traces to her defence of Julian Assange before Assange was dragged out of the Ecuadorian embassy.

panquake.title: The 2022 deplatforming
panquake.summary: The removal of John Kiriakou's radio programme from every major podcast platform after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, on the basis of his work for Sputnik News — preceded, he says, by a Washington Post article and a CSIS paper arguing that his weekly segment on American prison conditions was Russian propaganda weakening American democracy.

panquake.title: The arrest of Yves Engler
panquake.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the arrest of the Canadian activist Yves Engler in Montreal on a hate-speech charge after he criticised a prominent Canadian Zionist — five days in jail, additional harassment charges filed after he telephoned the arresting officer to request his own police reports, and suspension from Twitter and Facebook.

panquake.title: The Talk Liberation bank freeze
panquake.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the September 2022 freezing of Talk Liberation's Icelandic bank accounts — the seed funding behind the Panquake platform — on stated suspicion of money laundering and possible terrorist financing. Kiriakou, who deliberately declines to name the bank, calls the allegations nonsense, says in his personal opinion the freeze came at a government's behest, and notes the accounts were later unfrozen.

passing-time-at-loretto.title: Depression in prison
passing-time-at-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

passing-time-at-loretto.title: FCI Loretto
passing-time-at-loretto.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

passing-time-at-loretto.title: Seven thousand letters
passing-time-at-loretto.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

passing-time-at-loretto.title: The rat and pedophile table
passing-time-at-loretto.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

passing-time-at-loretto.title: The Loretto camp mix-up
passing-time-at-loretto.summary: John Kiriakou's account of turning himself in at the federal work camp at Loretto, Pennsylvania as the court had ordered, being sent across the street to the prison to be processed, and then being handcuffed and walked into the prison itself — with nobody on the outside knowing where he was for five days.

passing-time-at-loretto.title: The Pisces prison gang
passing-time-at-loretto.summary: The umbrella gang every Hispanic prisoner at FCI Loretto was required to join on pain of a beating — which subordinated street rivalries like MS-13, the Norteños and the Zetas to a single inside identity and required every member to work out daily against the possibility of a race riot.

patrick-bet-david.title: Reza Pahlavi
patrick-bet-david.summary: The exiled Iranian crown prince whom John Kiriakou dismisses as an Israeli-backed fantasy candidate to rule Iran — a man who has not lived there since his teens, supported mainly by Beverly Hills exiles, whom Kiriakou says 'wouldn't survive the walk from the plane to the terminal.'

patrick-bet-david.title: Israel-United States relations
patrick-bet-david.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

patrick-bet-david.title: Ahmed Chalabi
patrick-bet-david.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

patrick-bet-david.title: The Damascus consulate strike
patrick-bet-david.summary: The April 2024 Israeli attack on Iran's consulate in Damascus, which John Kiriakou describes as an unambiguous violation of the Vienna Convention, and whose official Israeli explanation — that it had not occurred to anyone the world would read it as a provocation — he calls disingenuous and intended purely for domestic audiences.

patrick-bet-david.title: Famine in Gaza
patrick-bet-david.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

patrick-bet-david.title: Germany and Israel
patrick-bet-david.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

patriot-act.title: John Kiriakou
patriot-act.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

patriot-act.title: FISA
patriot-act.summary: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the U.S. legal framework governing surveillance warrants for foreign-intelligence purposes. Per John Kiriakou, FISA is dangerously easy to abuse — he cites Carter Page, whose life was ruined and who was driven into bankruptcy after the Steele dossier was used to support four FISA applications against him. Kiriakou groups FISA with the Patriot Act and Section 702 as the legal architecture stripping Americans of constitutional protections, opposed by only a handful of legislators.

patriot-act.title: Edward Snowden
patriot-act.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

patriot-act.title: FCI Loretto
patriot-act.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

patriot-act.title: Central Intelligence Agency
patriot-act.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

patriot-act.title: Thin Thread
patriot-act.summary: Competing NSA programs at the center of the post-9/11 mass-surveillance turn. Per John Kiriakou, on September 11, 2001 NSA Director Michael Hayden implemented Operation Thin Thread — which 'vacuums up every phone call, every text message, every email, every bit of metadata from every American' — and reportedly called 9/11 'the greatest possible gift to NSA.' Three NSA officers (Bill Binney, Kirk Wiebe, and Ed Loomis) had built a competing program, Stellar Wind, that could collect the same data while protecting Americans' identities; Hayden chose to grab everything instead. Kiriakou says it was Tom Drake's effort to report the illegality that destroyed Drake.

paul-wright.title: Bureau of Prisons
paul-wright.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

paul-wright.title: Prison Legal News
paul-wright.summary: The longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history, co-founded by former prisoner Paul Wright, and a recurring source in Kiriakou's account of Bureau of Prisons practice.

paul-wright.title: Administrative remedy process
paul-wright.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

paul-wright.title: The prison commissary
paul-wright.summary: The federal prison store as John Kiriakou describes it: a captive market with a flat thirty per cent mark-up whose proceeds were supposed to buy library books and athletic equipment for prisoners and instead bought a large-screen television for the guards'' lounge — a diversion he established through a Freedom of Information Act request.

paul-wright.title: Medical care in federal prison
paul-wright.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

paul-wright.title: Larry
paul-wright.summary: The prisoner at FCI Loretto who complained of back pain for more than a year, was given Tylenol, and progressed from a cane to a walker to a wheelchair before a chaplain forced an outside hospital referral — which found stage four cancer of the spine. He died in his bunk two weeks later.

peace-and-friendship-bridge.title: Pakistan Station (2002)
peace-and-friendship-bridge.summary: John Kiriakou's January 2002 arrival in Islamabad to become CIA chief of counterterrorism operations — a journey via London and Kuwait with lost luggage, a warning that steered him away from the soon-to-be-bombed Marriott, a skeleton counterterrorism branch of seven CIA retirees, and the raids that followed.

peace-and-friendship-bridge.title: The Taliban
peace-and-friendship-bridge.summary: The Afghan movement John Kiriakou describes as loyal to nobody and, in 2001, genuinely baffled by the American invasion: its leadership held that sheltering al-Qaeda was a cultural obligation to a guest rather than an alliance, that it had never taken up arms against the United States, and that Washington was welcome to fight al-Qaeda on Afghan soil. He supported the Doha peace process but judged the Biden-era power-sharing letter an abandonment, arguing that any deal without guarantees on women, girls'' education and the vote returns the country to the 1990s.

peace-and-friendship-bridge.title: Haiti
peace-and-friendship-bridge.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

peace-and-friendship-bridge.title: Caleb Maupin
peace-and-friendship-bridge.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

peace-and-friendship-bridge.title: Sanctions Effectiveness
peace-and-friendship-bridge.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that U.S. sanctions have been so overused against disfavored countries that nations like China now route around them entirely, and that sanctions work only when reserved for the worst actors and imposed in concert with other countries — citing apartheid South Africa as a success and Cuba/Venezuela as failures that instead entrench nationalist narratives.

peace-and-friendship-bridge.title: The Backstory
peace-and-friendship-bridge.summary: The daily Radio Sputnik programme John Kiriakou co-hosted with Lee Stranahan, carried on terrestrial radio in the Washington area as well as online. It was the successor to his earlier show Loud and Clear with Brian Becker, and he described its format as two men with a beer talking about the day.

pegasus-spyware.title: NSA Surveillance
pegasus-spyware.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

pegasus-spyware.title: National Security Agency
pegasus-spyware.summary: The U.S. signals-intelligence agency. John Kiriakou notes it was never created by an act of Congress and that its own charter forbids collection on Americans — a rule that, when he entered government, meant heads rolled over accidental intercepts, and which he says has since been inverted into total collection stored in Utah for 500 years.

pegasus-spyware.title: San Bernardino iPhone Case
pegasus-spyware.summary: The 2015–16 legal standoff in which Apple refused to unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone for the FBI, which instead paid an Israeli firm $6 million to crack it — though, per John Kiriakou, the intelligence that could have disrupted the attack never came from the phone at all.

pegasus-spyware.title: Edward Snowden
pegasus-spyware.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

pegasus-spyware.title: F-35 avionics dispute with Israel
pegasus-spyware.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how Israel demanded F-35 fighters without the deliberately degraded avionics the U.S. installs on export models — and, refused, allegedly worked through American defense contractors to steal the technology instead.

pegasus-spyware.title: Israel's counterintelligence threat ranking
pegasus-spyware.summary: John Kiriakou's repeated point that the American intelligence community formally ranks Israel a critical counterintelligence threat — the same tier as North Korea, China, Russia, Iran and Cuba — specifically for spying on and infiltrating the US government, and that policy has responded by giving Israel more access rather than less.

pentagon-district-strategy.title: The Trilateral Commission
pentagon-district-strategy.summary: The body John Kiriakou says he used to dismiss as conspiracy-theory material until someone close to him attended one of its meetings and told him what was actually discussed there: arms deals — and at Davos, how to manage the global economy.

pentagon-district-strategy.title: American missile stockpiles
pentagon-district-strategy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

pentagon-district-strategy.title: CIA culture of lying
pentagon-district-strategy.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of deception as an occupational condition at the CIA — the tradecraft of detecting it, the training that instils it, and the institutional rot he says follows when officers cannot switch it off: a deputy director who married five successive secretaries, promotion panels that traded advancement for sex, and staff psychiatrists overheard planning how to push a colleague toward resignation or suicide.

pentagon-district-strategy.title: 2026 Iran war
pentagon-district-strategy.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

pentagon-district-strategy.title: Adnan Khashoggi
pentagon-district-strategy.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

pentagon-district-strategy.title: AIPAC
pentagon-district-strategy.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

permanent-multipolar-world.title: Lunch with the Russian ambassador
permanent-multipolar-world.summary: A meeting John Kiriakou describes in which the Russian ambassador to the United States, having read a column of his, invited him to lunch and asked whether there was anything the two countries could still cooperate on in wartime. Kiriakou's answer was three areas — narcotics, proliferation and terrorism — each with a concrete case attached.

permanent-multipolar-world.title: The pivot to Asia
permanent-multipolar-world.summary: John Kiriakou's criticism of the American realignment toward the Pacific begun under Barack Obama, which he describes as unnecessarily provocative — and his argument that the historical fear in the region runs the other way, since it was China that was invaded by Japan, and Chinese children are taught the occupation as part of their national inheritance.

permanent-multipolar-world.title: The refusal to talk to adversaries
permanent-multipolar-world.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the single worst American foreign-policy habit of the past two decades is the refusal to engage diplomatically with governments Washington disagrees with — a practice he dates to the George W. Bush administration, which he says CIA officers complained about at the time, and which has since become bipartisan.

permanent-multipolar-world.title: The JCPOA
permanent-multipolar-world.summary: The Iran nuclear agreement, which John Kiriakou describes as having worked for the two or three years it was in force under an inspection regime identical to the one the United Nations had used in Iraq. He treats the American withdrawal as a strategic error that also exposed a contradiction in American law, since sanctioning every country doing business with Iran would have meant sanctioning Britain, France, Germany and Japan.

permanent-multipolar-world.title: China as mediator
permanent-multipolar-world.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

permanent-multipolar-world.title: China as economic threat
permanent-multipolar-world.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

permanent-wartime-economy.title: MOSSAD
permanent-wartime-economy.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

permanent-wartime-economy.title: China as economic threat
permanent-wartime-economy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

permanent-wartime-economy.title: Donald Trump
permanent-wartime-economy.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

permanent-wartime-economy.title: Population decline as a national-security question
permanent-wartime-economy.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that demographic collapse — an emigrated Greek middle class, a shrinking Russia, and a Chinese population he believes is far smaller than claimed — is a strategic variable rather than a social one, and that some countries may not remain viable as countries without large population changes.

permanent-wartime-economy.title: Sara Jane Moore
permanent-wartime-economy.summary: American who attempted to assassinate President Gerald Ford in San Francisco in September 1975, two weeks after Mike Mastrovito of the Secret Service had interviewed her at her apartment regarding a threatening letter she had sent to the president. Per John Kiriakou, the case Mastrovito identified as having ended his Secret Service career.

permanent-wartime-economy.title: Secret Service
permanent-wartime-economy.summary: The U.S. agency protecting the president. John Kiriakou, who worked alongside it for 35 years, describes a culture of complacency and poor follow-up — great with guns, weak on training and follow-through — and calls the 2024 Butler rally shooting a colossal historic screw-up in which coverage of the surrounding buildings was outsourced to a county sheriff's department. He has also encountered the Service as an adversary, outside the Venezuelan embassy in Washington in 2019.

pervez-musharraf.title: A.Q. Khan
pervez-musharraf.summary: Pakistani nuclear scientist and the architect of Pakistan's bomb, who ran a black-market proliferation network that, per John Kiriakou, smuggled nuclear material and technology to North Korea and Libya. Kiriakou says the U.S. could easily have killed him — 'we knew where he lived, we knew how he spent his day' — but the Saudi government insisted the U.S. leave him alone, which Kiriakou calls a grave mistake and speculates was because the Saudis were pursuing their own nuclear capability. Khan was eventually pardoned by Pervez Musharraf, ending all investigations.

pervez-musharraf.title: ISI
pervez-musharraf.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

pervez-musharraf.title: Mr. Fish
pervez-musharraf.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

pervez-musharraf.title: Composition of the Saudi military
pervez-musharraf.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing claim that there are almost no Saudi nationals in the Saudi armed forces below the most senior ranks, and that the rank and file are Pakistanis hired from among Pakistan's poor. He treats it as a standing joke in the Gulf and as a limit on what Saudi Arabia can contribute to any war with Iran.

pervez-musharraf.title: Tora Bora
pervez-musharraf.summary: Mountainous cave complex in eastern Afghanistan that served as an al-Qaeda redoubt after the September 11 attacks. Per John Kiriakou — chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan at the time — the CIA killed al-Qaeda military-affairs chief Mohammed Atef there in October 2001, and Tora Bora was the backdrop to the hunt for the senior al-Qaeda leadership that culminated in the capture of Abu Zubaydah. Kiriakou also recounts an Egyptian al-Qaeda fighter he later recruited who survived a cruise-missile strike on a Tora Bora cave — one of only two who came out alive, his ears bleeding, describing the explosion as the most hideous sound he had ever heard.

pervez-musharraf.title: Strategic patience
pervez-musharraf.summary: The doctrine John Kiriakou uses to describe a state that absorbs an attack and answers with a response calibrated to be smaller than the provocation — Iran's telegraphed drone waves against Israel, and India's refusal to escalate against Pakistan, which he says kept a war from becoming a nuclear one.

pete-calabrese.title: The rat and pedophile table
pete-calabrese.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

pete-calabrese.title: Frank Russo
pete-calabrese.summary: The former auditor of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, who shared a bunk with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto — a corruption defendant who cooperated against Jimmy Dimora, was marked in prison as a rat, and whom Kiriakou describes as a sweetheart with a hilarious sense of humour who won everybody over anyway.

pete-calabrese.title: Mark Lanzalotti
pete-calabrese.summary: The prisoner John Kiriakou describes as his closest friend at FCI Loretto and one of the finest human beings he has known — a first-time non-violent drug defendant sentenced to triple life without parole for refusing to inform, the prison's foremost cook and bookie, and the man whose release Kiriakou secured by writing his Second Chance Act petition.

pete-calabrese.title: FCI Loretto
pete-calabrese.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

pete-calabrese.title: The stinger
pete-calabrese.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

pete-calabrese.title: Jimmy Dimora
pete-calabrese.summary: The Cuyahoga County official convicted in the corruption case that also sent John Kiriakou's FCI Loretto bunkmate Frank Russo to prison — the man Russo testified against, and who in Kiriakou's account received a draconian sentence and will die in prison.

pete-seeger.title: John Kiriakou
pete-seeger.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

pete-seeger.title: Phil Ochs
pete-seeger.summary: 1960s–70s protest folk singer; John Kiriakou retells a story from Pete Seeger about the night Ochs — who had fallen into depression after being unable to sing following a mugging in Africa — called Seeger just before taking his own life.

pete-seeger.title: John McCone
pete-seeger.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on November 22, 1963; per John Kiriakou's retelling of an account from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., responded to Bobby Kennedy Sr.'s same-day question "Tell me your people didn't do this" not with denial but with "I don't know who did it."

pete-seeger.title: How Can I Keep from Singing
pete-seeger.summary: Biography of folk singer Pete Seeger and John Kiriakou's stated favorite book. Per Kiriakou, Seeger was the most important man in his life besides his father and grandfather; the two exchanged Christmas cards for years, and Seeger rallied publicly to Kiriakou's defense during his prosecution. Kiriakou identifies Seeger's 1958 defiance of HUAC — pleading the First Amendment rather than the Fifth and going to prison for it — as the model for how he wanted to live his own life.

pete-seeger.title: Alexa
pete-seeger.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

pete-seeger.title: Asset acquisition cycle
pete-seeger.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

peter-mandelson.title: Jeffrey Epstein
peter-mandelson.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

peter-mandelson.title: MOSSAD
peter-mandelson.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

peter-mandelson.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
peter-mandelson.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

peter-mandelson.title: Les Wexner
peter-mandelson.summary: Ohio billionaire retail magnate; John Kiriakou cites Vanity Fair allegations that Wexner funneled millions to Jeffrey Epstein as his 'tax advisor,' offering it as evidence for his own view that Epstein's money and access served the Israelis.

peter-mandelson.title: Prince Andrew
peter-mandelson.summary: British royal named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, and has said that his 2026 arrest — over the alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein — is evidence that Epstein was collecting for a foreign power rather than for himself.

peter-mandelson.title: Asset acquisition cycle
peter-mandelson.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

peter-strzok.title: Church Committee
peter-strzok.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

peter-strzok.title: John Kiriakou
peter-strzok.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

peter-strzok.title: Espionage Act
peter-strzok.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

peter-strzok.title: John Brennan
peter-strzok.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

peter-strzok.title: Jim Bamford
peter-strzok.summary: The author John Kiriakou credits with having written the definitive book on the NSA and with first making Americans aware of the surveillance state. Kiriakou highlights Bamford''s 2023 book Spy Fail for a claim he says should have been front-page news and was not: that the FBI lost ten of its Chinese sources because Peter Strzok''s counterintelligence unit had a Chinese mole inside it.

peter-strzok.title: The FBI raids on Kiriakou's home
peter-strzok.summary: Twenty-two agents, eight hours, a sledgehammer hole in the kitchen wall that is still there, potted plants emptied onto the floor and every piece of electronics removed — twice, and with no charge arising from either. John Kiriakou uses the raids as the ground for his flat description of the bureau as an outlaw organization.

peter-thiel.title: Alex Karp
peter-thiel.summary: Co-founder and CEO of Palantir Technologies; subject of a biographical assessment commissioned from John Kiriakou by an unnamed interest group; characterized as militarily-industrially conservative despite a Democratic Party registration, religious, extremely patriotic, and "driven by profit."

peter-thiel.title: In-Q-Tel
peter-thiel.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

peter-thiel.title: Palantir Technologies
peter-thiel.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

peter-thiel.title: Arrais Corporation
peter-thiel.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

peter-thiel.title: CIA National Resources Division
peter-thiel.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

peter-thiel.title: Asset acquisition cycle
peter-thiel.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

petra-bank.title: Ahmed Chalabi
petra-bank.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

petra-bank.title: George Habash
petra-bank.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

petra-bank.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
petra-bank.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

petra-bank.title: Dick Cheney
petra-bank.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

petra-bank.title: Abu Zubaydah
petra-bank.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

petra-bank.title: Ali Hassan al-Majid
petra-bank.summary: Saddam Hussein cousin known as "Chemical Ali" and "the Butcher of Kurdistan"; per John Kiriakou, also briefly served as the Iraqi-installed governor of occupied Kuwait — "the Butcher of Kuwait" — and was engaged in the wholesale slaughter of Kurds in the north, Shia in the south, and Kuwaitis under occupation.

petrodollar-kissinger.title: Maduro Capture
petrodollar-kissinger.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

petrodollar-kissinger.title: Jeffrey Epstein
petrodollar-kissinger.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

petrodollar-kissinger.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
petrodollar-kissinger.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

petrodollar-kissinger.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
petrodollar-kissinger.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

petrodollar-kissinger.title: CIA and FBI ties to organized crime
petrodollar-kissinger.summary: John Kiriakou's survey of documented U.S. intelligence partnerships with organized crime — the FBI securing wartime ports with the Genovese family, the CIA's Castro plots with the Trafficantes, its work with the Escobar cartel against Colombian communists, and a mob hitman deployed against the Klan.

petrodollar-kissinger.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
petrodollar-kissinger.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

pflp.title: George Habash
pflp.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

pflp.title: Ahmed Khatib
pflp.summary: Iraqi-installed occupation governor of Kuwait announced on August 2, 1990, hours after the invasion; medical doctor trained at the American University of Beirut whose mother had been a Sudanese slave in the Kuwaiti royal household; college roommate of George Habash and co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine.

pflp.title: Abu Zubaydah
pflp.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

pflp.title: Carlos the Jackal
pflp.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

pflp.title: George W. Bush
pflp.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

pflp.title: Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
pflp.summary: Mastermind of the September 11, 2001 attacks; identified to the CIA by Abu Zubaydah, in the course of FBI interrogator Ali Soufan's rapport-based debriefing at the black site, as the man behind the kunya "Mukhtar" the agency had been hunting since at least 1996 for the Bojinka plot; per Kiriakou's relay of his self-account, radicalized by news video of an Israeli soldier with his boot on the neck of a Palestinian woman.

phil-ochs.title: Pete Seeger
phil-ochs.summary: American folk singer; John Kiriakou's personal hero alongside his father and grandfather; pleaded the First Amendment (rather than the Fifth) before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1958 and was sent to prison for it (later overturned on appeal); befriended by Kiriakou over decades of concert-going and correspondence; rallied to Kiriakou's defense after Kiriakou's 2012 arrest; the subject of Kiriakou's favorite book, How Can I Keep From Singing?

phil-ochs.title: Alexa
phil-ochs.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

phil-ochs.title: Daniel Hale
phil-ochs.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

phil-ochs.title: Executive Order 12333
phil-ochs.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

phil-ochs.title: Family Jewels
phil-ochs.summary: The CIA's internal catalogue of its own abuses, demanded in full by the Church and Pike Committees in 1975; per John Kiriakou, MK-Ultra and its assassination programs surfaced first, 85 percent of the MK-Ultra files were shredded in defiance of a direct order, and new officers were taught that everything in the file belonged to the era before 1975.

phil-ochs.title: John Kiriakou
phil-ochs.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

phone-microphone-ad-targeting.title: Consulting job entrapment offers
phone-microphone-ad-targeting.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that he receives a steady stream of emails and telephone calls offering him work — always consulting — that he reads as attempts to bait him into violating federal law, and which he says happens all the time.

phone-microphone-ad-targeting.title: Alexa
phone-microphone-ad-targeting.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

phone-microphone-ad-targeting.title: Kiriakou's legal counteroffensive
phone-microphone-ad-targeting.summary: John Kiriakou's announcement in February 2021 that after thirteen years of being reactive and responsive to his detractors he intended to start going after people, having connected with Harvard and Georgetown law professors — a plan he described without giving detail, saying only that things were turning around.

phone-microphone-ad-targeting.title: Flock cameras
phone-microphone-ad-targeting.summary: Automated licence-plate reading cameras mounted on police vehicles and on poles disguised as utility poles. John Kiriakou describes them as blanket, constant surveillance and a direct assault on civil liberties, more dangerous than the public realises, and says they are the point at which Edward Snowden's predictions have already come true.

phone-microphone-ad-targeting.title: Generals in national security posts
phone-microphone-ad-targeting.summary: John Kiriakou''s blanket objection to putting retired generals in charge of the CIA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department or the National Security Council, resting on a single argument about how officers reach flag rank: generals became generals by saying ''yes sir'', and what a president needs is somebody who can tell him why an idea is terrible.

phone-microphone-ad-targeting.title: Kamala Harris
phone-microphone-ad-targeting.summary: Vice President under Joe Biden and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; per John Kiriakou, installed as the party's nominee without a competitive primary despite having failed to reach the 2020 Iowa caucus, and closed out her 2024 campaign courting the Cheney family as a symbol of American values. Kiriakou, a lifelong progressive, says her pursuit of Dick Cheney's endorsement is what decided him against voting for her.

pick-the-man-principle.title: John Brennan
pick-the-man-principle.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

pick-the-man-principle.title: Central Intelligence Agency
pick-the-man-principle.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

pick-the-man-principle.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
pick-the-man-principle.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

pick-the-man-principle.title: George Tenet
pick-the-man-principle.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

pick-the-man-principle.title: John Kiriakou
pick-the-man-principle.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

pick-the-man-principle.title: Jose Rodriguez
pick-the-man-principle.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

pickaxe-mountain.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
pickaxe-mountain.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

pickaxe-mountain.title: Donald Trump
pickaxe-mountain.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

pickaxe-mountain.title: F-35 sale to Turkey
pickaxe-mountain.summary: The proposed sale of F-35 fighters to Turkey, opposed for decades by Greece and Greek-Americans who fear the aircraft would be used against Greece, and opposed by Benjamin Netanyahu for the same reason with respect to Israel. When Netanyahu raised the objection publicly in July 2026, Donald Trump answered that he does not take orders from a foreign leader about arms sales — a rebuke John Kiriakou describes as unprecedented.

pickaxe-mountain.title: Iran regional war (2026)
pickaxe-mountain.summary: The widening of the 2026 Iran conflict from a war between Iran on one side and the United States and Israel on the other into a regional war — Iranian missiles striking a US base in Jordan, Iranian strikes across the Gulf states, Houthi attacks on Saudi shipping and oil, and Saudi forces striking pro-Iranian militias in Iraq. John Kiriakou notes he had forecast the expansion a week earlier.

pickaxe-mountain.title: Graham–Netanyahu ICC tapes
pickaxe-mountain.summary: Recordings of Lindsey Graham coordinating with Benjamin Netanyahu on how to discredit the International Criminal Court over its arrest warrant. On the tapes Graham lines up Senate signatories for a protest letter, jokes that he should be paid "tons of shekels," and asks Netanyahu to telephone two Democratic senators to thank them. John Kiriakou argues the conduct meets the definition of espionage his own judge applied to him.

pickaxe-mountain.title: Hague Invasion Act
pickaxe-mountain.summary: The American statute, described by John Kiriakou as having been passed during the Obama administration, that authorises the president to use the United States military to invade the Netherlands and free an American or allied national held by the International Criminal Court — the standing legal answer to the possibility that Benjamin Netanyahu might be arrested abroad.

piers-morgan.title: MOSSAD
piers-morgan.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

piers-morgan.title: Jonathan Pollard
piers-morgan.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

piers-morgan.title: Jeffrey Epstein
piers-morgan.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

piers-morgan.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
piers-morgan.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

piers-morgan.title: Nobel Peace Prize
piers-morgan.summary: The prize a Swedish parliamentarian nominated John Kiriakou for in 2016 — a marker of how far world opinion had swung his way after prison. Kiriakou once believed Obama deserved his; he came to see it as unearned, and he treats Trump's foreign policy as substantially organized around wanting one too — "never underestimate Donald Trump's desire to win a Nobel Peace Prize," a White House friend told him. Netanyahu's nomination of Trump he summarized in a single unprintable phrase.

piers-morgan.title: Scott Horton
piers-morgan.summary: American antiwar journalist and interviewer whom John Kiriakou calls one of the most brilliant people he has ever engaged with on Middle East questions. The two appeared together on a Piers Morgan panel opposite Alan Dershowitz and a former Israeli intelligence chief, arguing that Israel spies actively on the United States.

pike-committee.title: Church Committee
pike-committee.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

pike-committee.title: JFK assassination
pike-committee.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

pike-committee.title: Central Intelligence Agency
pike-committee.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

pike-committee.title: Richard Helms
pike-committee.summary: CIA director who, per John Kiriakou, ordered the destruction of all MK-Ultra documents on the same day the Church Committee explicitly told him not to destroy them — and who, in Kiriakou's telling, illegally destroyed most of the agency's JFK material as well. He was held in contempt of Congress and fined a nominal sum that colleagues covered by passing a hat down the corridor to his office. Because of the destruction, only about 15% of the MK-Ultra record survives — largely financial records, from which the program had to be pieced back together.

pike-committee.title: Jeffrey Epstein
pike-committee.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

pike-committee.title: Senior Executive Service
pike-committee.summary: Highest tier of the U.S. federal civil service, above GS-1 through GS-15 pay grades; per John Kiriakou, members of the SES — and its agency-specific equivalents such as the CIA's Senior Intelligence Service — are the career officials who functionally operate the federal government across presidential administrations, serving thirty to forty years while presidents come and go every four or eight, and are protected from dismissal by the Civil Service Act.

pillow-talk-disclosure-case.title: Espionage Act
pillow-talk-disclosure-case.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

pillow-talk-disclosure-case.title: The 2023 classified documents scandal
pillow-talk-disclosure-case.summary: The run of discoveries of classified material in the private possession of Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Mike Pence, which John Kiriakou treats not as a scandal about any of them but as proof that the Espionage Act as currently applied makes almost everyone technically guilty. He rates Pence's briefing books as more highly classified than anything Julian Assange published, and says Biden's Senate-era documents are the ones that cannot be explained away.

pillow-talk-disclosure-case.title: Barack Obama
pillow-talk-disclosure-case.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

pillow-talk-disclosure-case.title: Carrying classified material out of a SCIF
pillow-talk-disclosure-case.summary: The two lawful procedures John Kiriakou describes for removing classified documents from a secure facility — a double-enveloped, double-marked package addressed to your home agency, or a leather bag with a double lock — and his flat statement that nothing about either allows a document to be forgotten in a garage for twelve years.

pillow-talk-disclosure-case.title: Over-classification
