pillow-talk-disclosure-case.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

pillow-talk-disclosure-case.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
pillow-talk-disclosure-case.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

pisces-prison-gang.title: Shot callers
pisces-prison-gang.summary: The trusted representatives each faction at FCI Loretto appointed to mediate disputes — a system John Kiriakou credits with keeping violence rare in a low-security prison, and which he later manipulated to have a rival banished from his own table.

pisces-prison-gang.title: Passing time at Loretto
pisces-prison-gang.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

pisces-prison-gang.title: FCI Loretto
pisces-prison-gang.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

pisces-prison-gang.title: The Nation of Islam at Loretto
pisces-prison-gang.summary: The largest Muslim faction at FCI Loretto — African American converts to the Nation of Islam — two of whom approached John Kiriakou on his first day to tell him that Louis Farrakhan considered him a hero of the Muslim people and that he would have no problems with them.

pisces-prison-gang.title: The rat and pedophile table
pisces-prison-gang.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

pisces-prison-gang.title: Pete Calabrese
pisces-prison-gang.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

pivot-to-asia.title: The permanent multipolar world
pivot-to-asia.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the unipolar period following the collapse of the Soviet Union has ended permanently, and that the arrangement was not inevitable — he attributes it to American strategic choices, principally leaving the Iran nuclear agreement and choosing confrontation with China and Russia over the cooperation that was available.

pivot-to-asia.title: China as economic threat
pivot-to-asia.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

pivot-to-asia.title: China as mediator
pivot-to-asia.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

pivot-to-asia.title: The JCPOA
pivot-to-asia.summary: The Iran nuclear agreement, which John Kiriakou describes as having worked for the two or three years it was in force under an inspection regime identical to the one the United Nations had used in Iraq. He treats the American withdrawal as a strategic error that also exposed a contradiction in American law, since sanctioning every country doing business with Iran would have meant sanctioning Britain, France, Germany and Japan.

pivot-to-asia.title: Lunch with the Russian ambassador
pivot-to-asia.summary: A meeting John Kiriakou describes in which the Russian ambassador to the United States, having read a column of his, invited him to lunch and asked whether there was anything the two countries could still cooperate on in wartime. Kiriakou's answer was three areas — narcotics, proliferation and terrorism — each with a concrete case attached.

pivot-to-asia.title: The refusal to talk to adversaries
pivot-to-asia.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the single worst American foreign-policy habit of the past two decades is the refusal to engage diplomatically with governments Washington disagrees with — a practice he dates to the George W. Bush administration, which he says CIA officers complained about at the time, and which has since become bipartisan.

planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.title: The hostile border crossing exercise
planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.summary: The training exercise run before dawn at a closed Dulles Airport in which CIA trainees crossed into the fictional Republic of Victoria — where John Kiriakou talked his way past a US-government-branded pen in his pocket, and the class clown ended up stripped to his underwear.

planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.title: Moving a satellite to Kuwait
planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of how thin American overhead coverage once was: after Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 the United States had no satellite looking at Kuwait, and it took six months to move one that had been parked over Moscow.

planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.title: The Farm
planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.title: Denied areas
planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.title: The Advanced Counterterrorism Operations course
planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.summary: The six-week CIA course for which John Kiriakou says he was one of only about a dozen officers in the entire agency selected — and which he finished, as he puts it, just in time for 9/11.

planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.title: Counterterrorist driving
planning-a-surveillance-detection-route.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

plato-cacheris.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
plato-cacheris.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

plato-cacheris.title: John Kiriakou
plato-cacheris.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

plato-cacheris.title: FCI Loretto
plato-cacheris.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

plato-cacheris.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
plato-cacheris.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

plato-cacheris.title: Sharon Scranage
plato-cacheris.summary: CIA secretary stationed in Ghana in the 1980s; the only other American besides John Kiriakou to have been charged under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act of 1982; revealed the names of CIA officers and sources in Ghana to a Ghanaian intelligence-service lover during pillow talk, leading to the execution of the named sources by Ghanaian authorities; sentenced to nine months in prison.

plato-cacheris.title: Mark McDougall
plato-cacheris.summary: U.S. criminal defense attorney; part of John Kiriakou's defense team in the 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution; the attorney whose framing of the case — "your problem is you think this is about justice and it's not about justice; it's about mitigating damage" — Kiriakou credits as the argument that persuaded him to take the final plea deal.

plus-972.title: Ai Whistleblower Initiative
plus-972.summary: The AI Whistleblower Initiative, working on legal protections for the wave of whistleblowers now coming out of the artificial-intelligence industry.

plus-972.title: Andrew Feinstein
plus-972.summary: Referenced on the same WikiLeaks-conference panel as John Kiriakou; the description of Feinstein's talk on the multiple factors that ended apartheid was given by another panelist putting a question to Kiriakou, not by Kiriakou himself.

plus-972.title: Belmarsh Prison
plus-972.summary: The maximum-security London prison where Julian Assange was held for years on a bail-jumping sentence John Kiriakou calls a fabrication — kept in solitary confinement alongside the worst offenders in the United Kingdom, and held past the expiry of his sentence at the request of the United States. Kiriakou corresponded with Assange there and watched the letters change.

plus-972.title: Chaos Computer Club Wikileaks
plus-972.summary: The Berlin hacker collective that shaped WikiLeaks' early years — and where a journalist first met Daniel Domscheit-Berg under a pseudonym.

plus-972.title: Chelsea Manning
plus-972.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

plus-972.title: Central Intelligence Agency
plus-972.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

podcast-bros.title: Mark Levin Iran Policy
podcast-bros.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, radio host Mark Levin was among the "outside voices" — alongside Senator Lindsey Graham — who effectively made the real policy call to invade Iran. Separately, per John Kiriakou, Levin is one of the very few prominent commentators who consistently defends Israel publicly online.

podcast-bros.title: Alexa
podcast-bros.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

podcast-bros.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
podcast-bros.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

podcast-bros.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
podcast-bros.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

podcast-bros.title: Bill Barr
podcast-bros.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

podcast-bros.title: CIA Remote Vehicle Control
podcast-bros.summary: John Kiriakou's account, corroborated by Forbes' Andy Greenberg's real-world demonstration, that the CIA can remotely take over a car's systems and cause a fatal crash disguised as an accident.

podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.title: Laura Loomer
podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.summary: The American activist who publicly called John Kiriakou a Russian spy, a Russian asset and a common criminal. Kiriakou consulted a lawyer as he had over an earlier attack, was advised that she carried too little weight to be worth suing, and let it go; he reads her later reversal on Russia and Ukraine as the calculation of someone who has accepted she will never be given a government job.

podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.title: Louise Mensch
podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.summary: The former British parliamentarian who attacked John Kiriakou on social media, prompting the only defamation action he describes having threatened. On his lawyer's advice he demanded a retraction; Mensch retracted in full and kept a pinned apology on her account for six months.

podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.title: AIPAC
podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.title: Freedom of Information Act
podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.title: Gulf intelligence services
podcasters-on-foreign-payrolls.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the intelligence services of the Gulf Cooperation Council states, which he worked with closely during his CIA career and rates uniformly excellent — highly trained, multilingual and experienced worldwide — with the Emiratis and Qataris the strongest of them and the Emiratis, in his ranking, the best of all.

polygraph.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
polygraph.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

polygraph.title: George Washington University
polygraph.summary: The Washington university where John Kiriakou took a bachelor's degree in Middle Eastern studies and began a master's in legislative affairs, and where a professor who was in fact a CIA spotter recruited him into the agency — an institution that recurs throughout his account as the place his intelligence career began, as the venue of his first CIA tests, and later as a classroom he taught in himself.

polygraph.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
polygraph.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

polygraph.title: CIA language training
polygraph.summary: The agency''s language pipeline as John Kiriakou experienced and describes it: a full year of Arabic at nine hours a day, an optional second year at the State Department''s school, and the calculation that made his own career — that it is cheaper to teach a linguist operations than to teach an operations officer Greek and Arabic.

polygraph.title: The CIA entrance examinations
polygraph.summary: The two rounds of testing John Kiriakou sat before joining the CIA in 1990: a current-affairs multiple choice he found trivially easy, a blank fold-out map of the world, and a psychological inventory of several thousand agree-or-disagree statements that repeated the same proposition hundreds of questions apart to catch inconsistency — followed by an interview panel of a psychologist, a psychiatrist and an anthropologist.

polygraph.title: New Castle, Pennsylvania
polygraph.summary: John Kiriakou's home town, an hour north of Pittsburgh on the edge of Amish country — a place of 50,000 people when he was growing up and about 18,000 now, whose decline he measures by the arrival of DEA and ATF field offices.

population-decline-analysis.title: Permanent wartime economy
population-decline-analysis.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

population-decline-analysis.title: 2026 Iran war
population-decline-analysis.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

population-decline-analysis.title: Adnan Khashoggi
population-decline-analysis.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

population-decline-analysis.title: AIPAC
population-decline-analysis.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

population-decline-analysis.title: China as economic threat
population-decline-analysis.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

population-decline-analysis.title: CIA culture of lying
population-decline-analysis.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of deception as an occupational condition at the CIA — the tradecraft of detecting it, the training that instils it, and the institutional rot he says follows when officers cannot switch it off: a deputy director who married five successive secretaries, promotion panels that traded advancement for sex, and staff psychiatrists overheard planning how to push a colleague toward resignation or suicide.

post-9-11-name-traces.title: The live satellite feed myth
post-9-11-name-traces.summary: John Kiriakou''s flat rejection of one of the most common screen conventions about American intelligence: that officers can call up a live satellite picture and watch a target walk through the streets of a city. There was no such thing then, he says, and there is no such thing now.

post-9-11-name-traces.title: Gary Schroen
post-9-11-name-traces.summary: The senior CIA officer whom John Kiriakou describes as legendary and who, with a small team of agency special operations officers, was the first CIA group into Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — going in, Kiriakou says, on something like September 12, and later writing a book about it called First In.

post-9-11-name-traces.title: Heather Kiriakou
post-9-11-name-traces.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

post-9-11-name-traces.title: Kandahar
post-9-11-name-traces.summary: The southern Afghan city and province that recurs across John Kiriakou's Afghanistan material — site of one of the two al-Qaeda training camps Abu Zubaydah founded, whose commanders were captured in the same March 2002 raids; the town Bill Clinton said he would have had to destroy, killing 300 innocents, to kill bin Laden in the 1990s; and a stop on Kiriakou's Senate-era heroin-poppy investigation, when the military helicoptered him down before refusing to let him walk the poppy fields.

post-9-11-name-traces.title: Condoleezza Rice
post-9-11-name-traces.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

post-9-11-name-traces.title: Counterterrorism Center
post-9-11-name-traces.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.title: Counterterrorism Center
post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.title: CIA cash room
post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.title: Renting Afghan warlords
post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.title: Business class after 9/11
post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.title: Agent payment mechanics
post-9-11-supplemental-appropriations.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

presidential-call-memcons.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
presidential-call-memcons.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

presidential-call-memcons.title: National Security Council
presidential-call-memcons.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Chuck Grassley
presidential-call-memcons.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the only serious pro-whistleblower member of Congress — a count he says can be made on one finger. Grassley wrote the Whistleblower Protection Act and the National Security Whistleblower Protection Act, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Center's luncheon, and in Kiriakou's telling was pushed into backing the Ukraine call whistleblower because it was his own law the man had invoked.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Gina Haspel
presidential-call-memcons.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Leaker versus whistleblower
presidential-call-memcons.summary: The fight over what the American networks would call John Kiriakou. It took his lawyers, above all Jesselyn Radack, a year of work between January 2012 and January 2013 to get CNN and MSNBC to stop introducing him as 'CIA leaker John Kiriakou'. CNN changed and Fox, he notes, never needed to; MSNBC in his account never did, and Rachel Maddow settled on a formula he quotes with some precision — a man 'who styles himself a whistleblower'.

presidential-call-memcons.title: Over-classification
presidential-call-memcons.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Allen Dulles
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Andrew Bustamante
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Barack Obama
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Bill Burns
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: Career U.S. diplomat named CIA director in 2021, and the one senior appointment John Kiriakou has endorsed without qualification — a man he has known for thirty years, "apolitical to a fault," untouched by torture, Guantánamo or the secret prisons, and the only figure he thought had the standing to reform the agency. Kiriakou wrote an op-ed calling him "finally, an adult in the room," and says Burns ended up serving as the Biden administration's de facto Secretary of State before being drawn into the CIA's culture of drone warfare, rendition and domestic spying.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Church Committee
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

presidents-and-the-cia.title: Central Intelligence Agency
presidents-and-the-cia.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

presidents-daily-brief.title: Central Intelligence Agency
presidents-daily-brief.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

presidents-daily-brief.title: John Kiriakou
presidents-daily-brief.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

presidents-daily-brief.title: Donald Trump
presidents-daily-brief.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

presidents-daily-brief.title: Counterterrorism Center
presidents-daily-brief.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

presidents-daily-brief.title: Greater and Lesser Tunb Islands
presidents-daily-brief.summary: Two small, largely uninhabited islands in the Persian Gulf, belonging to the emirate of Sharjah in the UAE, occupied by Iran in a 1990s incident John Kiriakou recounts as CIA analyst; Kiriakou correctly predicted the UAE would not go to war over them given Sharjah's heavy trade dependence on Iran.

presidents-daily-brief.title: James Woolsey
presidents-daily-brief.summary: Director of Central Intelligence for twenty-three months at the start of the Clinton administration, forced out over his refusal to discipline anyone after the exposure of Aldrich Ames, and later chairman of Booz Allen Hamilton; John Kiriakou notes that his family attributed four years of illness before his death to Havana syndrome.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: The 2022 deplatforming
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: The removal of John Kiriakou's radio programme from every major podcast platform after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, on the basis of his work for Sputnik News — preceded, he says, by a Washington Post article and a CSIS paper arguing that his weekly segment on American prison conditions was Russian propaganda weakening American democracy.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Julian Assange
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Ed Schultz
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: American broadcaster, a friend of John Kiriakou''s and later his colleague at RT, whom Kiriakou cites twice over: as a man forbidden by MSNBC to discuss Bernie Sanders during a primary, and as a dead man still being labelled a Russian government mouthpiece four years after his death.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: Panquake
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

press-tv-website-seizure.title: The state-affiliated media labels
press-tv-website-seizure.summary: The warning tags applied by social media platforms from 2020 identifying accounts as mouthpieces of foreign governments, which John Kiriakou describes checking his own account for daily. His standing example of how indiscriminate the practice became is the labelling of Ed Schultz, who had been dead for years.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: China as economic threat
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Central Intelligence Agency
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Dead drop
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: The classic tradecraft technique of passing material through a hidden location rather than a meeting. Per John Kiriakou, the hard part is not the drop but everything around it — in a sophisticated counterintelligence environment, merely identifying a viable site is very difficult, and the drop itself is bracketed by surveillance detection routes and a signal mark that can turn a single document into a sixteen-hour workday. It was the only element of clandestine training he struggled with, and the only exercise he was ever criticized for.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: Iran 12-Day War
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

pricewaterhousecoopers.title: JFK assassination
pricewaterhousecoopers.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

prince-andrew.title: MOSSAD
prince-andrew.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

prince-andrew.title: Jeffrey Epstein
prince-andrew.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

prince-andrew.title: Access Agent
prince-andrew.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

prince-andrew.title: Robert Maxwell
prince-andrew.summary: British media proprietor and father of Ghislaine Maxwell; described by John Kiriakou as "a prolific Mossad spy — that's a historic fact," and as the family channel through which the Epstein operation, in Kiriakou's phrase, was "kept all in the family."

prince-andrew.title: Bill Clinton
prince-andrew.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

prince-andrew.title: AIPAC
prince-andrew.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: Yemen
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: 2026 Iran war
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: 2026 Iran war economic shock
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: John Kiriakou''s running assessment of the economic damage from the 2026 Iran war — an oil shock he says already exceeds both 1970s shocks combined, a natural-gas shock worse than the Nord Stream destruction, and a chokepoint problem that runs through fertilizer as much as fuel, since 65% of the world''s supply must transit the Strait of Hormuz. His summary: "This is an economic slowdown of choice."

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: The al-Qaeda foot soldier
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: What John Kiriakou says he learned from interviewing captured al-Qaeda fighters — not the leaders but the eighteen-, nineteen- and twenty-year-olds, who told essentially the same story: an isolated village, illiteracy, no job skills, a poor relationship with their father, an age at which they wanted to marry, and no father willing to give them a daughter. The local imam offered $300 a month to go to Afghanistan, and $500 to their parents if they were martyred.

prince-muhammad-bin-naif.title: Ali Abdullah Saleh
prince-muhammad-bin-naif.summary: President of Yemen for decades, close to both Saudi Arabia and the United States until Yemen's 1990 Security Council vote on Kuwait, after which his country collapsed into civil war; he fled to Saudi Arabia and was killed by a bomb planted in the palace where he had taken refuge.

principals-committee-meeting.title: MOSSAD
principals-committee-meeting.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
principals-committee-meeting.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Saddam Hussein
principals-committee-meeting.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Dick Cheney
principals-committee-meeting.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Condoleezza Rice
principals-committee-meeting.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

principals-committee-meeting.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
principals-committee-meeting.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Heather Kiriakou
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: CIA crimes reports against Kiriakou
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: The referral mechanism by which the Central Intelligence Agency asked the Justice Department to investigate John Kiriakou, used not once but repeatedly — by his account after every op-ed, television interview and university speech he gave following his 2007 disclosure of the torture program. The Justice Department declined every time, and Kiriakou treats the pattern as retaliation conducted through a lawful channel.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Abu Zubaydah
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Barack Obama
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Brian Ross
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

prison-as-temporary-duty.title: Cold cell
prison-as-temporary-duty.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Cleanliness in prison
prison-cell-transfers.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hygiene and order at FCI Loretto — where everybody showered daily on pain of a beating, everybody was constantly cleaning, and the rules on possessions and bedmaking left almost no room for clutter.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Dave Phillips
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Marlon Beard
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The career drug dealer who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto and told him to keep writing when shakedowns over the Letters from Loretto were being used to provoke the other prisoners against him — advice Kiriakou credits with making him double down.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Prison nicknames
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The naming convention John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — where nearly every Black and Hispanic prisoner went by a nickname, most white prisoners did not, and the nickname rather than the legal name was what a man gave when signing up for the basketball tournament.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Spotting a CIA impostor
prison-cell-transfers.summary: John Kiriakou's method for exposing people who falsely claim to have served in the CIA — a short sequence of questions about directorate, division and leadership whose correct answers, he says, cannot be guessed by anyone who was never inside.

prison-cell-transfers.title: Sewer trout
prison-cell-transfers.summary: The name prisoners at FCI Loretto gave the fish served on Fridays — which John Kiriakou says arrived in boxes stacked illegally behind the serving line, marked Alaskan cod, product of China, and not for human consumption, feed use only.

prison-chapel-job.title: Bureau of Prisons
prison-chapel-job.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

prison-chapel-job.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
prison-chapel-job.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

prison-chapel-job.title: Private prison system
prison-chapel-job.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

prison-chapel-job.title: Solitary confinement
prison-chapel-job.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

prison-chapel-job.title: FCI Loretto
prison-chapel-job.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-chapel-job.title: Raymond Davis Lahore shooting
prison-chapel-job.summary: A 2011 incident in Lahore, Pakistan in which CIA contractor Raymond Davis shot and killed two Pakistani men who approached his car with drawn guns; per John Kiriakou, Davis stayed at the scene per CIA "getting off the X" tradecraft, and the consulate SUV sent to rescue him struck and killed an uninvolved bystander en route.

prison-cleanliness.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
prison-cleanliness.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

prison-cleanliness.title: FCI Loretto
prison-cleanliness.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-cleanliness.title: The dog food memo
prison-cleanliness.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

prison-cleanliness.title: Prison nicknames
prison-cleanliness.summary: The naming convention John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — where nearly every Black and Hispanic prisoner went by a nickname, most white prisoners did not, and the nickname rather than the legal name was what a man gave when signing up for the basketball tournament.

prison-cleanliness.title: Sewer trout
prison-cleanliness.summary: The name prisoners at FCI Loretto gave the fish served on Fridays — which John Kiriakou says arrived in boxes stacked illegally behind the serving line, marked Alaskan cod, product of China, and not for human consumption, feed use only.

prison-cleanliness.title: Blue
prison-cleanliness.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer, widely considered the most unpopular in the prison, who covered his own nameplate with masking tape so released prisoners could not find him — and who told a colleague of John Kiriakou's that he would never touch the CIA man because of the press attention.

prison-commissary.title: Bureau of Prisons
prison-commissary.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

prison-commissary.title: Arianna Huffington
prison-commissary.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

prison-commissary.title: Freedom of Information Act
prison-commissary.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

prison-commissary.title: Paul Wright
prison-commissary.summary: The former prisoner who co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

prison-commissary.title: Prison tattoos
prison-commissary.summary: Tattoos as John Kiriakou encountered them at FCI Loretto — the swastika-necked welcoming committee on his first day, the Lady Justice piece that made him laugh and then think, the constant pressure on him to get one, and his flat refusal to take a souvenir of the place.

prison-commissary.title: Jake Tapper
prison-commissary.summary: CNN anchor who drove to FCI Loretto to interview the imprisoned John Kiriakou — and who asked President Obama at a press conference why he had insisted on prosecuting a man who exposed a crime, a question Obama answered by walking away from the podium. Tapper's visit was the head of a media wave that began with a smuggled-out letter on the Huffington Post, and it became Kiriakou's protection inside; even a guard known as a psychopath left him alone rather than find CNN parked beside his car.

prison-depression.title: Passing time at Loretto
prison-depression.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

prison-depression.title: Seven thousand letters
prison-depression.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

prison-depression.title: FCI Loretto
prison-depression.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-depression.title: Rule six: the body endures more than the brain says
prison-depression.summary: The CIA maxim John Kiriakou carried into prison — that the human body can take much more punishment than the brain believes — which he applied first to being punched in the face and then, more importantly, to depression.

prison-depression.title: Dave Phillips
prison-depression.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

prison-depression.title: The shank planting incident
prison-depression.summary: The episode at FCI Loretto in which Dave Phillips made two homemade weapons, planted them on a pedophile the group was feuding with and informed on him anonymously — a plan John Kiriakou refused to join, and which cost Phillips a transfer while leaving Kiriakou untouched.

prison-foia-request.title: Blue
prison-foia-request.summary: The FCI Loretto correctional officer, widely considered the most unpopular in the prison, who covered his own nameplate with masking tape so released prisoners could not find him — and who told a colleague of John Kiriakou's that he would never touch the CIA man because of the press attention.

prison-foia-request.summary: The career drug dealer who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto and told him to keep writing when shakedowns over the Letters from Loretto were being used to provoke the other prisoners against him — advice Kiriakou credits with making him double down.

prison-foia-request.title: The stinger
prison-foia-request.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

prison-foia-request.title: Dave Phillips
prison-foia-request.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

prison-foia-request.title: The dog food memo
prison-foia-request.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

prison-food-economy.title: FCI Loretto
prison-food-economy.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-food-economy.title: The Italians at Loretto
prison-food-economy.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

prison-food-economy.title: John Kiriakou
prison-food-economy.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

prison-food-economy.title: The prison service economy
prison-food-economy.summary: The trade in goods and services at FCI Loretto as John Kiriakou describes it — used shoes resold on commission, convenience stores run out of lockers at a thirty per cent markup, a dozen bookmakers, unlicensed chiropractic, and sexual services priced in books of postage stamps.

prison-food-economy.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
prison-food-economy.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

prison-food-economy.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
prison-food-economy.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: The suicide watch protocol
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: The federal suicide watch procedure as John Kiriakou describes it from inside — a room with windows on four sides, volunteer prisoners watching in four-hour shifts around the clock, and paper sheets that cannot be knotted — which he uses to enumerate, step by step, everything that failed in the case of Jeffrey Epstein.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: Business class after 9/11
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: FCI Loretto
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-guard-hiring-standards.title: The General Muhammad equipment gift
prison-guard-hiring-standards.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the end of the Abu Zubaydah operation in Pakistan, when headquarters told him to throw away or hand over the truckloads of equipment his station had bought — and of learning weeks later from his day-to-day Pakistani contact that the brigadier general who accepted the gift had simply taken it all himself.

prison-legal-news.title: Administrative remedy process
prison-legal-news.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

prison-legal-news.title: Medical care in federal prison
prison-legal-news.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

prison-legal-news.title: Paul Wright
prison-legal-news.summary: The former prisoner who co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

prison-legal-news.title: Bureau of Prisons
prison-legal-news.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

prison-legal-news.title: Larry
prison-legal-news.summary: The prisoner at FCI Loretto who complained of back pain for more than a year, was given Tylenol, and progressed from a cane to a walker to a wheelchair before a chaplain forced an outside hospital referral — which found stage four cancer of the spine. He died in his bunk two weeks later.

prison-legal-news.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
prison-legal-news.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

prison-medical-care.title: Prison Legal News
prison-medical-care.summary: The longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history, co-founded by former prisoner Paul Wright, and a recurring source in Kiriakou's account of Bureau of Prisons practice.

prison-medical-care.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
prison-medical-care.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.
