prison-medical-care.title: Frank's heart attack
prison-medical-care.summary: The 65-year-old insulin-dependent diabetic who shared a cell with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto, reported chest tightness for months, was given Tylenol and a request for an EKG that the regional office never approved, and collapsed in the insulin line.

prison-medical-care.title: The suicide watch protocol
prison-medical-care.summary: The federal suicide watch procedure as John Kiriakou describes it from inside — a room with windows on four sides, volunteer prisoners watching in four-hour shifts around the clock, and paper sheets that cannot be knotted — which he uses to enumerate, step by step, everything that failed in the case of Jeffrey Epstein.

prison-nicknames.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
prison-nicknames.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

prison-nicknames.title: FCI Loretto
prison-nicknames.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-nicknames.title: Cleanliness in prison
prison-nicknames.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hygiene and order at FCI Loretto — where everybody showered daily on pain of a beating, everybody was constantly cleaning, and the rules on possessions and bedmaking left almost no room for clutter.

prison-nicknames.title: The dog food memo
prison-nicknames.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

prison-nicknames.title: Passing time at Loretto
prison-nicknames.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

prison-nicknames.title: Depression in prison
prison-nicknames.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: 2026 Iran war
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: Abolish the CIA
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: Adnan Khashoggi
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: AIPAC
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: CIA culture of lying
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of deception as an occupational condition at the CIA — the tradecraft of detecting it, the training that instils it, and the institutional rot he says follows when officers cannot switch it off: a deputy director who married five successive secretaries, promotion panels that traded advancement for sex, and staff psychiatrists overheard planning how to push a colleague toward resignation or suicide.

prison-pedophile-accounts.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
prison-pedophile-accounts.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: The prison visiting room
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: The room where a federal prisoner sees his family, reached through a strip-search cell — where John Kiriakou's children came to accept where their father was, where a former CIA boss turned up unannounced, and which is closed entirely to prisoners held under special administrative measures.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Solitary confinement
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Central Intelligence Agency
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

prison-phone-monitoring.title: Espionage Act
prison-phone-monitoring.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
prison-racial-segregation.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
prison-racial-segregation.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
prison-racial-segregation.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Kiriakou prison manipulation tactics
prison-racial-segregation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying CIA tradecraft — including deliberate deception, forged paperwork, and manipulating other inmates into violence — to protect himself and control his environment during his federal prison sentence.

prison-racial-segregation.title: Mark Lanzotti
prison-racial-segregation.summary: John Kiriakou's best friend in prison — an Italian sentenced to triple life without parole for a first-time nonviolent meth conspiracy he was the only man to voluntarily leave; Kiriakou wrote the appeal that won his release, and he is now the top-selling realtor on the Jersey Shore.

prison-racial-segregation.title: The Sociopath Next Door
prison-racial-segregation.summary: The book John Kiriakou reaches for when explaining why the CIA's leadership looks the way it does — sociopaths climbing over the people around them, as in any Fortune 500 company — and the source of his claim that 85 percent of American prisoners have a diagnosable mental illness.

prison-service-economy.title: FCI Loretto
prison-service-economy.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

prison-service-economy.title: John's rules for prison survival
prison-service-economy.summary: The code John Kiriakou says he wrote for himself at FCI Loretto out of his CIA training — rule one, recruit prisoners as sources using the same motivations the agency teaches; rule two, seek cover and blend in — illustrated with a plan to obtain contraband binder clips.

prison-service-economy.title: The chapel job
prison-service-economy.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

prison-service-economy.title: Ten-minute moves and the count
prison-service-economy.summary: The clock that governs a federal prison: a fixed daily timetable, movement permitted only during ten-minute windows on the hour, and five counts a day — two standing, three conducted with a flashlight in the face of a sleeping man, which John Kiriakou argues serve no purpose except sleep disruption.

prison-service-economy.title: The prison commissary
prison-service-economy.summary: The federal prison store as John Kiriakou describes it: a captive market with a flat thirty per cent mark-up whose proceeds were supposed to buy library books and athletic equipment for prisoners and instead bought a large-screen television for the guards'' lounge — a diversion he established through a Freedom of Information Act request.

prison-service-economy.title: Raymond Davis Lahore shooting
prison-service-economy.summary: A 2011 incident in Lahore, Pakistan in which CIA contractor Raymond Davis shot and killed two Pakistani men who approached his car with drawn guns; per John Kiriakou, Davis stayed at the scene per CIA "getting off the X" tradecraft, and the consulate SUV sent to rescue him struck and killed an uninvolved bystander en route.

prison-tattoos.title: The Italians at Loretto
prison-tattoos.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

prison-tattoos.title: Bureau of Prisons
prison-tattoos.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

prison-tattoos.title: Aryan Brotherhood
prison-tattoos.summary: The white prison gang that adopted John Kiriakou on his first day at FCI Loretto. Two hours in, two Aryans with swastika neck tattoos walked into his cell to check his paperwork — not a rat, not a "chomo" — and invited him to the Aryan table, which ran from hardcore Nazis at one end to merely white guys at the other. A rumor that he had been a CIA assassin earned him the nickname "the Muslim killer," which he never corrected; asked directly, he answered "we all did stuff we weren't proud of — it was wartime," and the Aryans loved it. He sat with them a year before the Italians took him in.

prison-tattoos.title: The prison commissary
prison-tattoos.summary: The federal prison store as John Kiriakou describes it: a captive market with a flat thirty per cent mark-up whose proceeds were supposed to buy library books and athletic equipment for prisoners and instead bought a large-screen television for the guards'' lounge — a diversion he established through a Freedom of Information Act request.

prison-tattoos.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
prison-tattoos.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

prison-tattoos.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

prison-visiting-room.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

prison-visiting-room.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

prison-visiting-room.title: Thomas Drake
prison-visiting-room.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

prison-visiting-room.title: Julian Assange
prison-visiting-room.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

prison-visiting-room.title: Prison phone monitoring
prison-visiting-room.summary: Kiriakou treated the recording of his prison telephone calls as an intelligence channel rather than a constraint, planting messages for staff he knew were listening — a practice that produced a confrontation with a lieutenant over the word 'Nimrod'.

prison-visiting-room.title: Correctional officers at FCI Loretto
prison-visiting-room.summary: Kiriakou's portraits of the staff at FCI Loretto — including two officers who tried to trick him into a fight, a lieutenant forced out of several prisons for harassment, and an officer whose abuse of prisoners he successfully reported.

private-intelligence.title: Arrais Corporation
private-intelligence.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

private-intelligence.title: Abraxas Corporation
private-intelligence.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

private-intelligence.title: The Analysis Corporation
private-intelligence.summary: Arlington, Virginia–based [private intelligence firm](/wiki/private-intelligence); one of two companion entities (alongside Arrais Corporation) created as LLC pass-throughs for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel; John Brennan was appointed its CEO in 2005.

private-intelligence.title: No-bid contracts
private-intelligence.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the mechanism he considers the real corruption of American national security: an officer retires on a Friday, returns Monday on a contractor badge at ten times the salary, and is fed no-bid contracts by the friends he left behind — including, in one unnamed case he describes, a tax shelter that became a multi-billion dollar company inside a decade.

private-intelligence.title: The Cypriot billionaire's investigation
private-intelligence.summary: The six-week private-intelligence job John Kiriakou describes as operational rather than analytic: a Cypriot billionaire wanted to know about the man engaged to his only daughter, and Kiriakou bribed a police captain in Cyprus, ran surveillance in London, and reported back that the fiancé was a thief with drug convictions.

private-intelligence.title: The Oman oil lease
private-intelligence.summary: A private-intelligence assignment in which an oil company that had leased a field on Oman's border with Yemen for ninety-nine years discovered al-Qaeda controlled the ground, and sent John Kiriakou to Muscat to ask whether the Omani government would clear them out.

private-prison-system.title: Overcriminalization
private-prison-system.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

private-prison-system.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
private-prison-system.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

private-prison-system.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
private-prison-system.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

private-prison-system.title: FCI Loretto
private-prison-system.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

private-prison-system.title: Counterterrorism Center
private-prison-system.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

private-prison-system.title: Donnie Reynolds Jr.
private-prison-system.summary: Tennessee businessman and antique-firearms collector serving a life-plus-75-year federal sentence at the Communications Management Unit in Terre Haute, Indiana; per John Kiriakou and Marty Gottesfeld, a scapegoat for the fallout of the ATF's Operation Fast and Furious after refusing to become an undercover cartel weapons source.

progressive-taxation.title: The Trumpcare confusion
progressive-taxation.summary: A television interview John Kiriakou says he watched, in which a woman from Arkansas wept with gratitude to President Trump because a website had insured her son's cancer treatment — and, told by the reporter that this was in fact the Affordable Care Act, insisted that Obamacare had been repealed and replaced and that what she had was Trumpcare.

progressive-taxation.title: The Speaker's office as gatekeeper
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how legislative power moved in the mid-1990s from committee chairmen and the Rules Committee into the office of the Speaker of the House, where it has stayed because no subsequent Speaker has wanted to give it back — and the member of Congress who explained the death of his own whistleblower bill in four words: ''Nancy said I couldn''t.''

progressive-taxation.title: Think tank financing
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou's warning that Washington's think tanks — more than 1,200 of them by a Washington Post count — must be read through their funding, illustrated with the case of someone close to him who controlled about $200,000 a year in donations for a Fortune 100 defence contractor and moved the money when a household-name institute proved insufficiently pro-contractor.

progressive-taxation.title: Lobbyists writing legislation
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou''s first-hand account from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: told that the committee would take part in the carbon offsets debate and protesting that he knew nothing about carbon offsets, he was told not to worry — and the next day strangers came into the office, took over most of the desks, logged on and began writing the bill.

progressive-taxation.title: Americans and the word socialism
progressive-taxation.summary: Two exchanges John Kiriakou uses to argue that the political vocabulary of the United States has stopped carrying meaning — a Thanksgiving conversation with a woman who denounced socialism and lived on Social Security, and a newspaper comment thread in which a restaurant owner taking his staff's tips was described as socialism.

progressive-taxation.title: Permanent wartime economy
progressive-taxation.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

project-gateway.title: MK-Ultra
project-gateway.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

project-gateway.title: Executive Order 12333
project-gateway.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

project-gateway.title: Family Jewels
project-gateway.summary: The CIA's internal catalogue of its own abuses, demanded in full by the Church and Pike Committees in 1975; per John Kiriakou, MK-Ultra and its assassination programs surfaced first, 85 percent of the MK-Ultra files were shredded in defiance of a direct order, and new officers were taught that everything in the file belonged to the era before 1975.

project-gateway.title: Alexa
project-gateway.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

project-gateway.title: CIA adultery culture
project-gateway.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

project-gateway.title: Daniel Hale
project-gateway.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

project-stargate.title: Russell Targ
project-stargate.summary: Named in a post-produced narration segment appended to an interview featuring John Kiriakou, describing Targ as an original Stanford Research Institute scientist behind government remote-viewing protocols — not a claim made by Kiriakou himself, who elsewhere expresses skepticism that remote viewing ever worked.

project-stargate.title: Espionage Act
project-stargate.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

project-stargate.title: Gina Haspel
project-stargate.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

project-stargate.title: Overcriminalization
project-stargate.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

project-stargate.title: Private prison system
project-stargate.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

project-stargate.title: Thomas Drake
project-stargate.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

promotion-panel.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
promotion-panel.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

promotion-panel.title: Jose Rodriguez
promotion-panel.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

promotion-panel.title: Counterterrorism Center
promotion-panel.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

promotion-panel.title: The Directorate of Operations
promotion-panel.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

promotion-panel.title: Chief of station
promotion-panel.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

promotion-panel.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
promotion-panel.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

propane-truck-ruse.title: The weapons cache map
propane-truck-ruse.summary: The single sheet of paper found inside an otherwise empty gun safe in the Middle East — a childlike map marked with an X and written directions past a palm tree and a large rock, which led John Kiriakou's team to a desert bunker packed to the ceiling with Hezbollah's arsenal.

propane-truck-ruse.title: Training foreign intelligence services
propane-truck-ruse.summary: The CIA job John Kiriakou took after returning from Athens — travelling the world to teach foreign services how to carry out counterterrorist raids, break down doors, seize people, conduct interrogations and disrupt cells — and why, he says, those countries asked the Americans rather than the Israelis or the British.

propane-truck-ruse.title: Double-Agent Capture
propane-truck-ruse.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

propane-truck-ruse.title: The Greek community of Warren, Ohio
propane-truck-ruse.summary: The Greek-American community John Kiriakou's mother and first wife both came from — overwhelmingly from the island of Chios, closely enough knit that his divorce started a fistfight in a coffee house between men who had never met him.

propane-truck-ruse.title: John Kiriakou
propane-truck-ruse.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

propane-truck-ruse.title: The Tiffany stationery letter
propane-truck-ruse.summary: The deliberately expensive note John Kiriakou wrote to his first wife on Tiffany & Co. stationery, telling her he was halving her child support on the advice of counsel — a tactic suggested by his divorce lawyer to force her to file, and which worked the next day.

proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.title: Israel's rightward shift
proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation for why Israeli politics moved sharply right over roughly two decades — that immigration from Russia, Ukraine and the United States brought in a conservatism the Israeli electorate had not seen before, displacing the socialist politics of the earlier European arrivals.

proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.title: Bashar al-Assad
proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.title: Greenland
proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.summary: The Danish territory the United States has spent years talking about acquiring; John Kiriakou reports two flatly contradictory readings from his own contacts — a White House friend who says Washington is serious and will lean on a Cold War treaty to claim it is already de facto American, and a Republican friend who says the whole thing is a grenade thrown to distract the press — and warns that taking it by force would end NATO.

proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.title: Israel-United States relations
proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S.-Israel relationship, including his own first visit to Israel as a tourist in 2022 and his characterization of Israel's willingness to destroy an entire city block to kill a single target, confident that the United States will not object.

proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.title: John Ratcliffe
proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.title: Operation Paperclip
proposals-to-relocate-the-palestinians.summary: The program by which the CIA's predecessor brought Nazi scientists to the United States after World War II; John Kiriakou notes the FBI opposed it, that the Nazis surrendered to the U.S. fearing the Soviets, and that V-2 rocket father Wernher von Braun is buried near his home in Virginia.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Julian Assange
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: The Charles Littlejohn prosecution
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: The five-year sentence handed to an IRS contractor who disclosed Donald Trump's tax returns to the New York Times, which John Kiriakou calls stunning and unjustified — the material was protected but not classified, the Biden campaign made use of it, and the sentencing judge compared the disclosure to the January 6 attack on the Capitol.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Espionage Act
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Sigurdur Thordarson
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: The FBI's key witness against Julian Assange, described by John Kiriakou as a convicted paedophile, a convicted embezzler and a self-admitted liar — one of three facts he lists, alongside the bugging of the Ecuadorian embassy and the reported plot to kidnap or kill Assange, in asking whether judges can keep such things out of their heads.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Brad Birkenfeld
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

prosecutorial-careerism.title: Chelsea Manning
prosecutorial-careerism.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

psychiatric-evacuation.title: Beirut
psychiatric-evacuation.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

psychiatric-evacuation.title: John Kiriakou
psychiatric-evacuation.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

psychiatric-evacuation.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
psychiatric-evacuation.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

psychiatric-evacuation.title: Aldrich Ames
psychiatric-evacuation.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

psychiatric-evacuation.title: Barry Eisler
psychiatric-evacuation.summary: Former CIA officer turned bestselling novelist, and a recurring guest of John Kiriakou's, who describes him as one of the very few former intelligence officers to have succeeded at storytelling outside the secret world as thoroughly as he did inside it.

psychiatric-evacuation.title: Central Intelligence Agency
psychiatric-evacuation.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

ptsd.title: Espionage Act
ptsd.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

ptsd.title: John Kiriakou
ptsd.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ptsd.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
ptsd.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

ptsd.title: Vietnam War
ptsd.summary: The war John Kiriakou grew up in the shadow of — his parents marched against it — and the deep precedent for everything he fights: entered on the Gulf of Tonkin lie, prosecuted by generals who knew for a decade they were losing (per the Pentagon Papers), studded with torture whose victims recited the Green Bay Packers'' starting lineup as "intelligence," and ended in part by Daniel Ellsberg, "the godfather of all modern national security whistleblowers." Even Robert McNamara, he notes, understood waterboarding was a bridge too far.

ptsd.title: American Psychological Association
ptsd.summary: The world's largest body of psychologists, which John Kiriakou cites constantly for one devastating datum — its research shows people begin to lose their minds at around day seven without sleep, and begin to die at day nine as their organs shut down. Mitchell and Jessen were nonetheless authorized to keep chained, naked prisoners awake for up to twelve days, which is why Kiriakou insists sleep deprivation was always worse than waterboarding. The organization's own role in the interrogation program later became the subject of an internal revolt and a 500-page independent report.

ptsd.title: The Libertarian Party
ptsd.summary: The third party a lifelong Democrat joined on release from prison, after its 2016 presidential nominee had written to him in his cell and to the Attorney General on his behalf — the party John Kiriakou says was the only one talking about whistleblowing and the security-versus-liberty trade-off, and the one whose structural problem, he was told, is that it has no benefactor.

public-interest-defense.title: Espionage Act
public-interest-defense.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

public-interest-defense.title: Edward Snowden
public-interest-defense.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

public-interest-defense.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
public-interest-defense.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

public-interest-defense.title: Jose Rodriguez
public-interest-defense.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

public-interest-defense.title: Leonie Brinkema
public-interest-defense.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

public-interest-defense.title: Jack Teixeira
public-interest-defense.summary: Massachusetts Air National Guard reservist arrested in April 2023 for leaking classified Pentagon documents to a small Discord server. John Kiriakou, discussing the case the day after Teixeira's arrest, initially suspected a covert action program rather than a genuine leak, ultimately concluded Teixeira was not a whistleblower, and predicted — correctly — that he would be charged under the Espionage Act and take a plea bargain.

public-safety-factor.title: David Petraeus
public-safety-factor.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

public-safety-factor.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
public-safety-factor.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

public-safety-factor.title: Bureau of Prisons
public-safety-factor.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

public-safety-factor.title: Administrative remedy process
public-safety-factor.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

public-safety-factor.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
public-safety-factor.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

public-safety-factor.title: Paul Wright
public-safety-factor.summary: The former prisoner who co-created Prison Legal News — the longest-running publication produced by and for current and former prisoners in American history — and whose reporting John Kiriakou draws on for the finding that the Bureau of Prisons' own grievance system increases prison violence.

publications-review-board.title: John Kiriakou
publications-review-board.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

publications-review-board.title: Heather Kiriakou
publications-review-board.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

publications-review-board.title: CIA crimes reports against Kiriakou
publications-review-board.summary: The referral mechanism by which the Central Intelligence Agency asked the Justice Department to investigate John Kiriakou, used not once but repeatedly — by his account after every op-ed, television interview and university speech he gave following his 2007 disclosure of the torture program. The Justice Department declined every time, and Kiriakou treats the pattern as retaliation conducted through a lawful channel.

publications-review-board.title: Larry Devlin
publications-review-board.summary: CIA officer and former chief of station in the Congo, whose memoir Chief of Station, Congo was published on his instruction the day after he died — never submitted to the agency's Publications Review Board. John Kiriakou cites it as an act of nerve he admits he does not have.

publications-review-board.title: The Bolivian visa line
publications-review-board.summary: The CIA's interrogation of John Kiriakou's wife, then a serving senior officer, over a single sentence in a Los Angeles Times op-ed her husband had written and had already cleared through the agency's own publications review board. Told the piece was cleared, the security officer replied that one line in it was top secret — the statement that Iranians no longer needed visas to travel to Bolivia. Kiriakou had taken it off the Bolivian foreign ministry's website.

publications-review-board.title: Abu Zubaydah
publications-review-board.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

punjab-elite-force.title: Abu Zubaydah
punjab-elite-force.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

punjab-elite-force.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
punjab-elite-force.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

punjab-elite-force.title: Site 13
punjab-elite-force.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

punjab-elite-force.title: Mr. Fish
punjab-elite-force.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

punjab-elite-force.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
punjab-elite-force.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

punjab-elite-force.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
punjab-elite-force.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

purchased-data-warrant-workaround.title: Mass Surveillance
purchased-data-warrant-workaround.summary: Kiriakou says the NSA has dropped any pretext of protecting civil liberties, warehousing every call, text and email in the Utah desert.

purchased-data-warrant-workaround.title: Bluffdale NSA Data Center
purchased-data-warrant-workaround.summary: The NSA's purpose-built facility in the Utah desert, characterized by John Kiriakou as having storage capacity for every phone call, text message, and email of every American for the next 500 years.

purchased-data-warrant-workaround.title: NSA Surveillance
purchased-data-warrant-workaround.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

purchased-data-warrant-workaround.title: Panquake
purchased-data-warrant-workaround.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

purchased-data-warrant-workaround.title: WLDragnet
purchased-data-warrant-workaround.summary: Free search tool documenting U.S. defense contractors' monitoring of social-media users by political affiliation. John Kiriakou says a search of his own name in the tool's beta showed Northrop Grumman had queried him hundreds of times, and that his attorneys used the data in separate litigation against the company.

purchased-data-warrant-workaround.title: Kiriakou on artificial intelligence
purchased-data-warrant-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou's stated experience with and objections to large language models — a ChatGPT exchange in which the system stated his degrees incorrectly, refused his correction and then cut him off, and a test in which every scholarly citation it produced for his university syllabus turned out to be fabricated. He also describes AI as the flagging layer of contemporary surveillance.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: John Walker Lindh
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: American citizen captured while fighting alongside the Taliban in late 2001, present at the Qala-i-Jangi fortress at the start of the prisoner uprising that killed CIA officer Mike Spann. In John Kiriakou's account his case matters less for what Lindh did than for what was done around him — the false claim that he had been read his rights, the destruction of the career of the Justice Department lawyer who said so, and his place on the docket of the one judge who reserves national-security cases for herself.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: Mike Spann
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen alongside John Kiriakou.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: General Abdul Rashid Dostum
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: Northern Alliance Afghan warlord; overseer of the November–December 2001 Dasht-i-Leili massacre; characterized by John Kiriakou as a serial defector between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance and as a psychopath.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

qala-i-jangi-uprising.title: The State Department cover investigation
qala-i-jangi-uprising.summary: One of the inquiries John Kiriakou opened as senior investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, on a reporter's tip that the CIA was placing some of its torturers under State Department cover in violation of the cover agreement between the two departments. He wrote to the State Department asking for clarification. Five or six weeks later a colleague told him a reply had come and had been classified above his clearance; asked what it said, the colleague summarised it as an obscenity. That was the end of the investigation.

qasem-soleimani.title: Daniel Hale
qasem-soleimani.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

qasem-soleimani.title: Mike Pompeo
qasem-soleimani.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

qasem-soleimani.title: Julian Assange
qasem-soleimani.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

qasem-soleimani.title: RDAP
qasem-soleimani.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which takes a year off a federal sentence on completion — the single most valuable piece of advice John Kiriakou says he gives to people facing prison time, alongside good-conduct credit and halfway-house conversion.

qasem-soleimani.title: Chelsea Manning
qasem-soleimani.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

qasem-soleimani.title: Corporate whistleblower protections
qasem-soleimani.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that whistleblower law stops at the wrong boundary. Employees who report waste, fraud, abuse or illegality inside a private company are doing the very thing the word describes, and yet can be fired for it — as he says happened at Amazon. His remedy is codified statutory protection for corporate whistleblowers on the same footing as government ones.

qat-in-yemen.title: Narcotics under cover
qat-in-yemen.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether a CIA officer under cover may take drugs when an asset offers them: yes. The rule he describes begins with qat in Yemen and extends to cocaine in Latin America, on the ground that refusing can be a matter of life and death.

qat-in-yemen.title: Spies traded home
qat-in-yemen.summary: What happens to intelligence officers and agents after they are exchanged and sent back, in John Kiriakou''s account: not usually execution, but a career that is irreparably damaged, because every service you would want to hide from now knows exactly who you are.

qat-in-yemen.title: The Islamabad guest house
qat-in-yemen.summary: The sixteen-room guest house in Islamabad that CIA officers took over entirely during the post-9/11 deployments — a place John Kiriakou says the agency still will not let him name, which came with breakfast, dinner and laundry for about thirty-five dollars a day against a per diem of five hundred.

qat-in-yemen.title: A Middle East reading list
qat-in-yemen.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

qat-in-yemen.title: Bombing the Omanis
qat-in-yemen.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

qat-in-yemen.title: Bowe Bergdahl
qat-in-yemen.summary: The American soldier who walked off his base in Afghanistan, was captured by the Haqqani network and handed to the Taliban, and was repatriated in a prisoner trade — a man John Kiriakou says was treated as a traitor although he was not one.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Italian election covert action
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: What John Kiriakou calls the CIA''s very first covert action: bribing Italian journalists in the 1949 election to write in favor of the Christian Democrats, who narrowly beat the Communists — a operation he says amounted to stealing the election.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Operation Mockingbird
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century program of recruiting and managing American journalists as influence assets; in John Kiriakou's account, no longer operationally necessary in the contemporary period because the U.S. media voluntarily reprints CIA-supplied material, and in at least one documented case sends articles to the agency for clearance before sending them to its own editor.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Thomas Massie
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: Republican U.S. Representative from Kentucky known for a constitutionalist voting record and consistent opposition to foreign military intervention; per John Kiriakou, a principled America-First congressman who votes with the president on the vast majority of issues, and whose opposition to U.S. funding of Israel and foreign wars is the only plausible explanation for the roughly $30 million spent by the Israel lobby to unseat him in a primary.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Tulsi Gabbard
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: Abu Zubaydah
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

radio-and-tv-marti.title: CIA animal surveillance experiments
radio-and-tv-marti.summary: Cold-War CIA efforts to turn animals into listening devices, which John Kiriakou describes as failures — including microphones and cameras mounted on pigeons trained to land on the Soviet embassy, which could reach the compound but never captured anything meaningful.

ralph-nader.title: The Americans Who Tell the Truth portrait
ralph-nader.summary: The portrait of John Kiriakou painted by Robert Shetterly for his long-running series Americans Who Tell the Truth, unveiled at Busboys and Poets in Washington on February 7, 2013 — weeks before Kiriakou reported to prison — and inscribed with the words 'Even if torture works it cannot be tolerated.'

ralph-nader.title: Heather Kiriakou
ralph-nader.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

ralph-nader.title: Gary Johnson
ralph-nader.summary: The former Republican governor of New Mexico and Libertarian nominee for president who wrote to John Kiriakou in prison, wrote separately to Attorney General Eric Holder asking that he be released — a letter Kiriakou learned of only later through a Freedom of Information Act request — and telephoned him within days of his coming home.

ralph-nader.title: Government Accountability Project
ralph-nader.summary: The Washington whistleblower-advocacy law firm and NGO, known as GAP, whose attorney Jesselyn Radack took John Kiriakou's case after his 2012 arrest and told him he was a whistleblower whether he thought so or not.

ralph-nader.title: Kiriakou and third parties
ralph-nader.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy for viable third parties, and his 2016 experience touring the West with Libertarian candidate Gary Johnson — including the disorganization that convinced him the party would never break through, epitomized by a colleague who ignored an airport page thinking it was 'NSA tracking my movements.'

ralph-nader.title: Kiriakou's daily news diet
ralph-nader.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the wide range of mainstream and alternative outlets he reads each morning to compare competing angles, the two outlets — the Associated Press and ProPublica — he singles out as exceptional, and his broader habits of media consumption, from an admitted addiction to political polling to his distrust of AI chatbots after they repeatedly fabricated his own biography.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Mitchell and Jessen
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Senate Torture Report
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Abu Zubaydah
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Ticking time bomb scenario
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: The hypothetical case — an imminent attack only the captured terrorist's confession can prevent — used to justify the CIA's post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; characterized by John Kiriakou as fictional and not corresponding to any real-world case.

ramzi-bin-al-shibh.title: Muhammad Atar
ramzi-bin-al-shibh.summary: Nephew of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed; subjected by the CIA to the walling interrogation technique against a concrete-block wall without protective equipment, producing permanent brain damage that has prevented him from participating in his own defense.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: MOSSAD
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: Ron Wyden
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: U.S. senator and the lone real challenger of the CIA on the intelligence committees; John Kiriakou faults Wyden for challenging the agency only 'by the agency's rules' — refusing to read the Senate torture report into the record, and admitting at a dinner that fighting harder would cost him his security clearance.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: CIA cash room
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

rand-paul-eric-holder.title: Trump Dni Replacement
rand-paul-eric-holder.summary: Trump privately asked cabinet members about replacing his Director of National Intelligence, frustrated that the DNI had protected Joe Kent.

rat-and-pedophile-table.title: Pete Calabrese
rat-and-pedophile-table.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

rat-and-pedophile-table.title: Frank Russo
rat-and-pedophile-table.summary: The former auditor of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, who shared a bunk with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto — a corruption defendant who cooperated against Jimmy Dimora, was marked in prison as a rat, and whom Kiriakou describes as a sweetheart with a hilarious sense of humour who won everybody over anyway.

rat-and-pedophile-table.title: Shot callers
rat-and-pedophile-table.summary: The trusted representatives each faction at FCI Loretto appointed to mediate disputes — a system John Kiriakou credits with keeping violence rare in a low-security prison, and which he later manipulated to have a rival banished from his own table.

rat-and-pedophile-table.title: The Bob Jones frame-up
rat-and-pedophile-table.summary: The operation John Kiriakou ran inside FCI Loretto against a man at his own cafeteria table — forging court papers in the prison law library from a genuine 1970s Ohio case involving a man of the same name, and using them to have him banished by the shot callers.

rat-and-pedophile-table.title: Jimmy Dimora
rat-and-pedophile-table.summary: The Cuyahoga County official convicted in the corruption case that also sent John Kiriakou's FCI Loretto bunkmate Frank Russo to prison — the man Russo testified against, and who in Kiriakou's account received a draconian sentence and will die in prison.

rat-and-pedophile-table.title: The Nation of Islam at Loretto
rat-and-pedophile-table.summary: The largest Muslim faction at FCI Loretto — African American converts to the Nation of Islam — two of whom approached John Kiriakou on his first day to tell him that Louis Farrakhan considered him a hero of the Muslim people and that he would have no problems with them.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: John's rules for prison survival
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: The code John Kiriakou says he wrote for himself at FCI Loretto out of his CIA training — rule one, recruit prisoners as sources using the same motivations the agency teaches; rule two, seek cover and blend in — illustrated with a plan to obtain contraband binder clips.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: FCI Loretto
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: The chapel job
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: The prison service economy
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: The trade in goods and services at FCI Loretto as John Kiriakou describes it — used shoes resold on commission, convenience stores run out of lockers at a thirty per cent markup, a dozen bookmakers, unlicensed chiropractic, and sexual services priced in books of postage stamps.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: Private prison system
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

ray-davis-lahore-shooting.title: Robert the arsonist
ray-davis-lahore-shooting.summary: The Australian prisoner who became John Kiriakou's roommate at FCI Loretto — convicted of burning down a Buffalo motor vehicles office over a sales tax dispute, a pathological liar who Kiriakou concluded was a clinical sociopath, and whom he says was easy to manipulate because he was an excitement junkie.

ray-mcgovern.title: Vladimir Putin
ray-mcgovern.summary: President of Russia.
