Per John Kiriakou, Putin twice raised joining NATO — floating it to Bill Clinton and later telling Barack Obama Russia would like to explore membership — and was refused both times; Kiriakou has never believed Putin wants to conquer Ukraine or Eastern Europe, argues U.S. hostility toward Russia is driven by defense contractors and a permanent wartime economy, and notes the irony that Putin was the anti-communist the U.S. itself backed in the Yeltsin era.

ray-mcgovern.title: John Kiriakou
ray-mcgovern.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ray-mcgovern.title: Sam Adams Award
ray-mcgovern.summary: The integrity-in-intelligence award John Kiriakou received in 2016 at American University, joining a laureate list that includes Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, and Sy Hersh. Named not for the founding father but for the CIA analyst who insisted the true enemy strength in Vietnam was double what General Westmoreland allowed to be reported, it is given by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity — a community Kiriakou describes as doubling as a support group for whistleblowers.

ray-mcgovern.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
ray-mcgovern.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

ray-mcgovern.title: Consortium News
ray-mcgovern.summary: Independent investigative news outlet John Kiriakou has written for since at least 2017, founded by Polk Award-winning journalist Robert Parry, who broke major stories on Iran-Contra. Kiriakou's columns there have covered John Bolton's exit, the entrapment of Maria Butina, his own first tour in Saudi Arabia and the 2019 Ukraine-call whistleblower. He says PayPal permanently shuttered the outlet's account and briefly seized its funds before backing down under public pressure, while still refusing to reinstate it.

ray-mcgovern.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
ray-mcgovern.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

rdap-program.title: Daniel Hale
rdap-program.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

rdap-program.title: Solitary confinement
rdap-program.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

rdap-program.title: Espionage Act
rdap-program.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

rdap-program.title: The Drone Papers
rdap-program.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

rdap-program.title: Home confinement
rdap-program.summary: The house arrest that followed John Kiriakou's release from prison — 87 days confined to the interior of his own house, telephone checks at any hour of the day or night, weekly halfway-house reporting and twice-weekly drug testing — which he describes as considerably worse than prison, and would rather have traded back for the cell. In federal sentencing arithmetic it is also one of the deductions that turns a headline number into the time actually served.

rdap-program.title: Julian Assange
rdap-program.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

rdap.title: Daniel Hale
rdap.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

rdap.title: Jeremy Hammond
rdap.summary: The hacker held in contempt for refusing to testify against Julian Assange before a grand jury. John Kiriakou''s point about his case is administrative rather than constitutional: Hammond was pulled out of the Bureau of Prisons drug and alcohol programme two months short of completing it, forfeiting the eighteen months it would have taken off his sentence — a penalty that applied whether or not he ever agreed to testify.

rdap.title: The halfway house
rdap.summary: The re-entry stage of a federal sentence — up to twelve months of it by law, in practice a fortnight before conversion to house arrest — which John Kiriakou was denied entirely for writing about prison conditions from inside, and which he describes as a system designed to make released prisoners fail.

rdap.title: Julian Assange
rdap.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

rdap.title: Chelsea Manning
rdap.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

rdap.title: Qasem Soleimani
rdap.summary: The Iranian general killed by an American drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020. John Kiriakou, speaking the following morning, called him arguably the second most important person in Iran and a potential successor to the supreme leader, relayed the Iranian comparison that killing him was worse than killing Petraeus or Mattis — 'this is like killing Pence' — and dismissed talk of de-escalation as a pipe dream.

reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.title: The Tehran slip
reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.summary: The moment John Kiriakou says he witnessed as note-taker in a secure video teleconference a day or two before the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when a briefing general said that if all went as planned American forces could be in Tehran by August, and CIA Director George Tenet turned off his microphone and asked Kiriakou whether the man had said Tehran or Baghdad.

reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.title: "We''re at war today"
reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.summary: The short speech John Kiriakou says Cofer Black delivered standing on his desk in the CIA's Counterterrorism Center on the morning of 11 September 2001, telling his officers that not all of them would make it home and that anyone for whom this was not enough could walk out without being thought less of. Nobody moved.

reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.title: Arabic and Greek
reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.title: Curtailment cables
reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.title: Dick Cheney
reading-in-on-the-iraq-invasion.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

recruiting-foreign-students.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
recruiting-foreign-students.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

recruiting-foreign-students.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
recruiting-foreign-students.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

recruiting-foreign-students.title: Kiriakou's Abraham Lincoln collection
recruiting-foreign-students.summary: John Kiriakou''s private collection of Abraham Lincoln relics, assembled at auction over many years and governed by a strict standard of provenance: a blood-soaked fragment of the pillowcase Lincoln died on, wallpaper from the Petersen House death room, a swatch of Mary Todd Lincoln''s funeral dress, and wood from the gallows on which the conspirators were hanged.

recruiting-foreign-students.title: Access Agent
recruiting-foreign-students.summary: CIA (and foreign intelligence service) term for a recruited asset whose value lies not in the secrets they hold directly but in their regular social access to high-value targets — politicians, executives, heads of state — who cannot themselves be recruited. Per John Kiriakou, the access agent is funded generously to maintain an environment in which the targets feel comfortable and return repeatedly; kompromat — compromising photographs or recordings — may be collected as a secondary tool. Kiriakou identifies Jeffrey Epstein as a textbook access agent, in his assessment working for Israeli intelligence.

recruiting-foreign-students.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
recruiting-foreign-students.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

recruiting-foreign-students.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
recruiting-foreign-students.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

recruiting-from-the-bottom.title: 2026 Iran war
recruiting-from-the-bottom.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

recruiting-from-the-bottom.title: MOSSAD
recruiting-from-the-bottom.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

recruiting-from-the-bottom.title: Gulf consultations before the Iran war
recruiting-from-the-bottom.summary: John Kiriakou's account of travelling in Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Doha in the weeks before the 2026 strikes on Iran, and finding that the United States had made no diplomatic case to its Gulf partners at all — in sharp contrast to the worldwide campaign that preceded the Iraq war. He told a senior Emirati royal that two carrier strike groups meant an attack was coming.

recruiting-from-the-bottom.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
recruiting-from-the-bottom.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

recruiting-from-the-bottom.title: Principals Committee Meeting (February 2003)
recruiting-from-the-bottom.summary: Senior-most interagency forum of the U.S. national security apparatus, normally chaired by the president. Per John Kiriakou — who served as notetaker for CIA Director George Tenet at the eve-of-Iraq-invasion meeting on February 19–20, 2003 — Vice President Dick Cheney chaired in place of Bush, General Tommy Franks ended his order-of-battle briefing with 'If all goes as planned, we can be in Tehran by August,' and an NSC senior director said 'When we cross that border tomorrow morning, they're going to throw flowers at us.'

recruiting-from-the-bottom.title: Bill Clinton
recruiting-from-the-bottom.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: Espionage Act
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: PTSD
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: The Reluctant Spy
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou''s 2009 memoir, The Reluctant Spy: My Secret Life in the CIA''s War on Terror, begun in secret months before he blew the whistle and reaching number five on the New York Times bestseller list.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: Shin Bet
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: Israel's internal security service; per John Kiriakou, one of the two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the Washington embassy, and the service whose officer, alongside a Mossad officer, he says tried to recruit him at his first CIA liaison briefing in the spring of 1990 — an approach his colleagues told him had been made to every one of them.

recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.title: Japanese diplomat FBI sting
recruitment-attempts-on-kiriakou.summary: John Kiriakou's account of an FBI entrapment operation in which an agent posing as a Japanese diplomat cold-pitched him for classified information over five lunches, hoping he would commit actual espionage they could charge — a scheme he discovered only in his own case discovery.

refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.title: China as mediator
refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the plausible mediator of Middle Eastern and Ukrainian conflicts, grounded in his claim that — Tibet and its border wars aside — China has no history of invading other countries, and his observation of how quickly Beijing accepted an offhand suggestion that it might mediate between Israel and Iran.

refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.title: Lunch with the Russian ambassador
refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.summary: A meeting John Kiriakou describes in which the Russian ambassador to the United States, having read a column of his, invited him to lunch and asked whether there was anything the two countries could still cooperate on in wartime. Kiriakou's answer was three areas — narcotics, proliferation and terrorism — each with a concrete case attached.

refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.title: The permanent multipolar world
refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment that the unipolar period following the collapse of the Soviet Union has ended permanently, and that the arrangement was not inevitable — he attributes it to American strategic choices, principally leaving the Iran nuclear agreement and choosing confrontation with China and Russia over the cooperation that was available.

refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.title: Afghan heroin policy
refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.title: China as economic threat
refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.title: The JCPOA
refusal-to-talk-to-adversaries.summary: The Iran nuclear agreement, which John Kiriakou describes as having worked for the two or three years it was in force under an inspection regime identical to the one the United Nations had used in Iraq. He treats the American withdrawal as a strategic error that also exposed a contradiction in American law, since sanctioning every country doing business with Iran would have meant sanctioning Britain, France, Germany and Japan.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Agnes von Kurowsky grave story
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of discovering the Washington, D.C. grave of Agnes von Kurowsky, the World War I Red Cross nurse whose four-month wartime romance with a young ambulance driver, Ernest Hemingway, made her the model for the lead female character in six of his books, including A Farewell to Arms.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Kiriakou's personal anecdotes
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: Three personal stories John Kiriakou has told in interviews — tracking down and meeting Andy Warhol as a college senior, a Congolese vice president's remark that Americans promise democracy while the Chinese provide food, and Kiriakou's own Zelle account being suspended over Cuba-sanctions compliance after a paid article about his Cuba trip.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Bashar al-Assad
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: Chinese spy balloon incident
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: 2023 controversy over a high-altitude balloon that crossed U.S. airspace, widely labeled in media coverage as a "Chinese spy balloon"; John Kiriakou notes no U.S. government official ever officially confirmed it was conducting espionage, and says he personally believes it was likely a weather balloon, since satellite surveillance already renders such balloons unnecessary for spying.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: CIA adultery culture
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
remains-of-day-treasury-clerk-story.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Kiriakou's writing process
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Israel Boyd and the Wonder Bread story
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of Israel Boyd, one of two brothers forced by their parents into the family bakery business, who went on to invent the first industrial dough mixer and dough-cutting machine, pioneer adding milk to bread dough, and build the largest bakery in America before World War I — before selling the business, whose flagship "Mrs. McGill's Delicious Bread" was renamed Wonder Bread by its buyer.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: John Kiriakou
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Gore Vidal
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: American novelist and essayist; per John Kiriakou, a Sidwell Friends/St. Albans/Phillips Exeter alumnus who enlisted after Pearl Harbor rather than attend college, wrote the controversial 1948 novel The City and the Pillar, won a National Book Award in 1993, and was buried near his one lasting partner, Howard Austen, and his boyhood best friend, James Trimble, who was killed at Iwo Jima.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Arkady Shevchenko
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: Soviet diplomat and Undersecretary General of the United Nations who secretly spied for the CIA before defecting to the United States in 1978 — described by John Kiriakou as the single most important spy the CIA ever had inside the Soviet power structure.

remains-of-the-day-book.title: Joseph B. Chambers
remains-of-the-day-book.summary: Civil War Medal of Honor recipient buried at Oak Park Cemetery in New Castle, Pennsylvania, whose grave John Kiriakou discovered as a child while looking for salamanders — sparking a lifelong interest in history.

renting-afghan-warlords.title: Agent payment mechanics
renting-afghan-warlords.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

renting-afghan-warlords.title: CIA cash room
renting-afghan-warlords.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

renting-afghan-warlords.title: Post-9/11 supplemental appropriations
renting-afghan-warlords.summary: The emergency money Congress pushed into the CIA after the September 11 attacks — a supplemental appropriation of roughly 160 per cent the day after, another at the end of the year, and a counterterrorism directorate that could not spend what it had been given.

renting-afghan-warlords.title: Counterterrorism Center
renting-afghan-warlords.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

renting-afghan-warlords.title: Gary Schroen
renting-afghan-warlords.summary: The senior CIA officer whom John Kiriakou describes as legendary and who, with a small team of agency special operations officers, was the first CIA group into Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — going in, Kiriakou says, on something like September 12, and later writing a book about it called First In.

renting-afghan-warlords.title: The Taliban
renting-afghan-warlords.summary: The Afghan movement John Kiriakou describes as loyal to nobody and, in 2001, genuinely baffled by the American invasion: its leadership held that sheltering al-Qaeda was a cultural obligation to a guest rather than an alliance, that it had never taken up arms against the United States, and that Washington was welcome to fight al-Qaeda on Afghan soil. He supported the Doha peace process but judged the Biden-era power-sharing letter an abandonment, arguing that any deal without guarantees on women, girls'' education and the vote returns the country to the 1990s.

republican-split-over-the-iran-war.title: JD Vance
republican-split-over-the-iran-war.summary: Vice president and 2028 Republican front-runner, whose Joe Rogan interview admitting the administration "mishandled the Epstein files" John Kiriakou reads not as candour but as an authorised manoeuvre — and whose passing remark that any documents tying Epstein to intelligence "wouldn't exist in 2026" Kiriakou treats as a matter-of-fact accusation that the CIA destroyed evidence.

republican-split-over-the-iran-war.title: Marco Rubio
republican-split-over-the-iran-war.summary: U.S. official whom John Kiriakou identifies as the real motivator behind pressure on Venezuela; Kiriakou argues Venezuela is not a meaningful drug threat to the U.S. and that Rubio simply wants Maduro gone.

republican-split-over-the-iran-war.title: John McCain
republican-split-over-the-iran-war.summary: Late U.S. Senator from Arizona who gave the most consequential Senate-floor defense of John Kiriakou — declaring that 'if it weren't for John Kiriakou, the American people would never have had any idea what the CIA was doing in their name' — and sponsored the McCain–Feinstein amendment banning torture.

republican-split-over-the-iran-war.title: Tulsi Gabbard
republican-split-over-the-iran-war.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

republican-split-over-the-iran-war.title: Donald Trump
republican-split-over-the-iran-war.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

republican-split-over-the-iran-war.title: Iran 12-Day War
republican-split-over-the-iran-war.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

restraint-camp.title: Cory Booker
restraint-camp.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he was "especially furious" with Democratic senator Cory Booker for running through the halls of Congress to get to a photo op standing behind Benjamin Netanyahu, which Kiriakou cites as an example of Democratic silence in the face of AIPAC pressure.

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: John Kiriakou
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Richard Welch
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Carlos the Jackal
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Stephen Saunders
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

revolutionary-organization-17-november.title: Heather Saunders
revolutionary-organization-17-november.summary: Widow of British Brigadier General Stephen Saunders, the British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November on April 22, 2000; per John Kiriakou, the person whose post-assassination Greek-television statement — "this organization is not a political organization nor is it a phantom group; it's a gang of criminals" — for the first time since 17 November's 1975 founding turned Greek public opinion against the group.

reza-pahlavi.title: Donald Trump
reza-pahlavi.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

reza-pahlavi.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
reza-pahlavi.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

reza-pahlavi.title: Iran 12-Day War
reza-pahlavi.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

reza-pahlavi.title: Leadership profiling
reza-pahlavi.summary: The CIA practice of producing classified psychological profiles of foreign leaders for the president, vice president, national security advisor and the secretaries of state and defense before any meeting. It was John Kiriakou's first job at the agency, where he served as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological biographer working alongside psychiatrists, psychologists and anthropologists.

reza-pahlavi.title: Patrick Bet-David
reza-pahlavi.summary: The podcast host whom John Kiriakou described on another programme as a hardcore Zionist and a total backer of Reza Pahlavi, and who then played the clip back to him on air. Kiriakou withdrew the characterisation on the record, one of the few occasions where he has retracted a public statement about a named individual.

reza-pahlavi.title: Mohsen Rafighdoost
reza-pahlavi.summary: Iranian journalist and political figure whom John Kiriakou identifies as a co-founder of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the propaganda voice behind the audio tapes distributed in Iran before the 1979 revolution; interviewed on the PBD Podcast, he conceded that the Shah's regime held only 3,000–3,500 political prisoners rather than the 100,000 opposition figures claimed at the time and that the Shah was, in his own judgment, a better man than Ayatollah Khomeini.

rfk-assassination.title: JFK assassination
rfk-assassination.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

rfk-assassination.title: MK-Ultra
rfk-assassination.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

rfk-assassination.title: Kent State shooting
rfk-assassination.summary: The 1970 shooting of unarmed student protesters by the Ohio National Guard; John Kiriakou says a family friend's daughter was among those killed — the closing event of a 1968–69 upheaval he treats both as the formation of his own politics and as the historical measure against which he judges the present.

rfk-assassination.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
rfk-assassination.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

rfk-assassination.title: John Brennan
rfk-assassination.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

rfk-assassination.title: Joby Warrick's Washington Post resignation
rfk-assassination.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his friend Joby Warrick, a multiple Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist, resigning from the Washington Post because investigative journalism at the paper was dead — amid an 80% staff reduction since Jeff Bezos bought the paper.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Greek death rituals
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: The five-year grave rental, exhumation and ossuary practice of rural Greece as John Kiriakou describes it — bones washed in red wine, blessed, boxed, and eventually laid beneath the foundations of a new church, with cremation strictly forbidden. He visits the ossuary in his ancestral Rhodes village, where the records stop in the nineteenth century because the Ottomans burned everything earlier.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Zakynthos Holocaust rescue
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the Greek Ionian island of Zakynthos, where the mayor and Orthodox bishop responded to a Nazi demand for a list of the island's Jews by submitting only their own two names, while residents hid every Jewish islander — making Zakynthos, per Kiriakou, the only place in Greece where no Jew died in the Holocaust.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Abraham Accords
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Alan Dershowitz
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: Arrais Corporation
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: Private intelligence firm; companion entity to The Analysis Corporation; originally an LLC pass-through for retired Senior Intelligence Service personnel from the CIA's operations side; subsequently acquired by IBM for over $1 billion.

rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.title: BDS movement
rhodes-jewish-deportation-family-story.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Israeli property acquisition in Greece and Cyprus
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israelis buying land in Greece and Cyprus at a scale he considers destabilising — entire villages rather than holiday homes, a Jewish-only village outside Paphos with a casino attached, a rejected bid for an island in the Ionian Sea, and a request to open the first Zionist high school in Cyprus.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Zakynthos Holocaust rescue
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the Greek Ionian island of Zakynthos, where the mayor and Orthodox bishop responded to a Nazi demand for a list of the island's Jews by submitting only their own two names, while residents hid every Jewish islander — making Zakynthos, per Kiriakou, the only place in Greece where no Jew died in the Holocaust.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Israel, Turkey, and NATO Article 5
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: John Kiriakou's scenario in which an Israeli attack on Turkey would oblige every NATO member, the United States included, to come to Turkey's defence — and in which the alliance would sooner dissolve than honour that obligation against Israel.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Israeli drone factories in Serbia
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: Five drone factories John Kiriakou was told the Israelis are building in Serbia — a fact relayed to him by members of a Serbian delegation who welcomed it on the grounds that Israel is effective against Islamists, and which Kiriakou treats as the same emotional play he sees used on Greeks and Cypriots.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

rhodes-jewish-deportation.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
rhodes-jewish-deportation.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

richard-helms.title: MK-Ultra
richard-helms.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

richard-helms.title: Pike Committee
richard-helms.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

richard-helms.title: Carlos the Jackal
richard-helms.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

richard-helms.title: Church Committee
richard-helms.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

richard-helms.title: Operation Midnight Climax
richard-helms.summary: Sub-project of the CIA's MK-Ultra program, conducted in San Francisco. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA rented a safe house and paid sex workers to bring men back to it, where agents dosed the men with LSD without their knowledge or consent, then observed their behavior through one-way mirrors. The operation followed an earlier phase in which the CIA had dosed its own employees; when that produced suicides, it moved to using unconsenting members of the public.

richard-helms.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
richard-helms.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

richard-perle.title: Dick Cheney
richard-perle.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

richard-perle.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
richard-perle.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

richard-perle.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
richard-perle.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

richard-perle.title: Israeli intelligence presence in the United States
richard-perle.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Israeli intelligence activity inside the United States — dozens of undeclared Mossad and Shin Bet officers identified by the FBI, a critical-threat counterintelligence classification alongside Russia, North Korea and Cuba, and a pattern of harassment and intimidation directed at declared CIA officers posted to Israel.

richard-perle.title: Donald Trump
richard-perle.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

richard-perle.title: Kamala Harris
richard-perle.summary: Vice President under Joe Biden and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee; per John Kiriakou, installed as the party's nominee without a competitive primary despite having failed to reach the 2020 Iowa caucus, and closed out her 2024 campaign courting the Cheney family as a symbol of American values. Kiriakou, a lifelong progressive, says her pursuit of Dick Cheney's endorsement is what decided him against voting for her.

richard-welch.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
richard-welch.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

richard-welch.title: Carlos the Jackal
richard-welch.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

richard-welch.title: Stephen Saunders
richard-welch.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

richard-welch.title: The Welch .45
richard-welch.summary: The single .45 caliber pistol used by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in every confirmed assassination over the group's twenty-seven-year operational life

richard-welch.title: Mike Huckabee
richard-welch.summary: The United States ambassador to Israel under Donald Trump, and the subject of a public call for resignation from John Kiriakou after Huckabee received Jonathan Pollard at the American embassy. Kiriakou''s assessment separates two charges: Huckabee is not a traitor but an idiot who did not think the meeting was a big deal, and a former governor of a small state who still behaves as though he can set policy without the State Department or the National Security Council.

richard-welch.title: The KGB denial cables
richard-welch.summary: Two occasions on which, according to John Kiriakou, the first message the CIA received after an American killing came from the KGB and said the same thing: we promise it wasn''t us. One followed the assassination of Athens station chief Richard Welch in December 1975, the other the killing of President Kennedy in November 1963. Kiriakou treats them as evidence of a standing gentleman''s agreement between the two services not to touch each other''s people — one he expects to hold even where Russian troops overrun CIA bases.

richard-wolff.title: Donald Trump
richard-wolff.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

richard-wolff.title: Trump tariffs
richard-wolff.summary: The across-the-board tariffs imposed by Donald Trump on United States trading partners, which John Kiriakou describes as having shaken up the economy faster than any president in generations — causing chaos in global stock markets, laying the groundwork for inflation and economic contraction, and producing political upheaval at home.

richard-wolff.title: China as economic threat
richard-wolff.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

richard-wolff.title: Elon Musk
richard-wolff.summary: Kiriakou met Musk by chance at a Washington hotel bar in 2009, when he was worth $1 billion and talking about Tesla, SpaceX and colonizing Mars.

richard-wolff.title: Permanent wartime economy
richard-wolff.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

richard-wolff.title: Youngstown Sheet and Tube
richard-wolff.summary: The Ohio steel producer whose closure John Kiriakou treats as the moment the economy of his hometown region ended; he remembers the day it shut and classmates weeping in the school hallways because their fathers had lost their jobs, and dates the collapse of New Castle, Pennsylvania to it.

rick-praau.title: The CIA defense
rick-praau.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what happens when a CIA asset is arrested — either the station chief privately asks the host country's intelligence service for the man's release, which he says works ninety-nine times out of a hundred, or the agency declines, leaving the defendant to argue at trial that he was acting on the CIA's behalf while the agency says nothing at all.

rick-praau.title: Bureau of Prisons
rick-praau.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

rick-praau.title: The child-trafficking misquotation
rick-praau.summary: A widely circulated claim that John Kiriakou said the CIA is involved in the sex trafficking of children. Kiriakou denies it flatly and traces it to a distorted account of a teaching hypothetical he uses in university lectures on ethics — a speech cleared by the CIA's Publications Review Board, whose video was attached to the original article by a writer who evidently had not watched it.

rick-praau.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
rick-praau.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

rick-praau.title: The 2022 deplatforming
rick-praau.summary: The removal of John Kiriakou's radio programme from every major podcast platform after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, on the basis of his work for Sputnik News — preceded, he says, by a Washington Post article and a CSIS paper arguing that his weekly segment on American prison conditions was Russian propaganda weakening American democracy.

rick-praau.title: Kiriakou pardon request
rick-praau.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

robert-david-steele.title: False flags are too hard
robert-david-steele.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

robert-david-steele.title: Fake CIA résumés
robert-david-steele.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

robert-david-steele.title: The Fox News military analyst
robert-david-steele.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

robert-david-steele.title: CIA attention to West Africa
robert-david-steele.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

robert-david-steele.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
robert-david-steele.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

robert-david-steele.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
robert-david-steele.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: JFK assassination
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: John McCone
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on November 22, 1963; per John Kiriakou's retelling of an account from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., responded to Bobby Kennedy Sr.'s same-day question "Tell me your people didn't do this" not with denial but with "I don't know who did it."

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Donald Trump
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Executive Order 12333
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Central Intelligence Agency
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

robert-f-kennedy-jr.title: Maria Butina
robert-f-kennedy-jr.summary: Russian gun-rights activist convicted in the United States of failing to register as a foreign agent; John Kiriakou cites her case as an example of the "process crime" of FARA violations, contrasting the severity of her 18-month solitary-confinement sentence with federal guidelines calling for 0-6 months.

robert-hanssen.title: Aldrich Ames
robert-hanssen.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

robert-hanssen.title: John Kiriakou
robert-hanssen.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

robert-hanssen.title: Brian Kelley
robert-hanssen.summary: Chief of counterintelligence at the CIA; framed by FBI counterintelligence chief Robert Hanssen — the actual Soviet/Russian mole — as the source of executed agents; spent a year and a half on leave without pay, surrounded around the clock by FBI agents, while his daughter was approached and told her father would face the death penalty if he did not confess.

robert-hanssen.title: Sandy Grimes
robert-hanssen.summary: CIA analyst who, per John Kiriakou, was the person who actually broke the Aldrich Ames case. After a 27-year-old security officer sat on an Ames file for eighteen months without action, Grimes independently noticed that Ames made $100,000–$150,000 bank deposits within days of every trip to Mexico City — the pattern that identified him as a spy. After Ames's arrest, she submitted a hot-wash paper recommending 27 reprimands across the chain of command that had promoted a known alcoholic into the most sensitive counterintelligence position in the CIA. Director John Deutch responded with strongly worded letters for seven. Grimes resigned in 1993.

robert-hanssen.title: Eric O'Neill
robert-hanssen.summary: Former FBI analyst placed as Robert Hanssen's nominal assistant in the final months of the FBI's mole investigation; his role was to observe Hanssen and detect tradecraft slip-ups that would confirm Hanssen as the mole. After Hanssen's arrest, O'Neill resigned from the FBI, citing the stress of the operation. Subject of the 2007 film Breach.

robert-hanssen.title: Harold James Nicholson
robert-hanssen.summary: Former CIA Station Chief, Singapore; the third major modern CIA mole for the Russians after Aldrich Ames and Robert Hanssen. Per John Kiriakou, Nicholson was a senior officer at the CIA Counterterrorism Center during Kiriakou's tenure there. Sentenced to 31 years and seven months in 1997. While in prison, attempted to recruit his own son to act as a courier between him and the Russian intelligence service so his espionage payments could continue to compound for his eventual release — and was caught when his son walked up to the Russian embassy in Washington under FBI surveillance.

robert-maclean.title: Rudy Giuliani
robert-maclean.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

robert-maclean.title: Bruce Fein
robert-maclean.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

robert-maclean.title: Sebastian Gorka
robert-maclean.summary: Former Trump administration deputy assistant; subject of John Kiriakou's second attempted pardon transaction in 2018, in which Gorka asked Kiriakou for $5,000 at a book launch at the Trump International Hotel in exchange for tweeting at the president on his behalf. Kiriakou refused.

robert-maclean.title: Bernie Kerik
robert-maclean.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

robert-maclean.title: Central Intelligence Agency
robert-maclean.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

robert-maclean.title: Noelle Dunphy
robert-maclean.summary: Former aide to Rudy Giuliani; independently corroborated to the New York Times John Kiriakou's account of Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt, after Giuliani's subsequent sexual harassment of her caused her to come forward.

robert-maxwell.title: Jeffrey Epstein
robert-maxwell.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

robert-maxwell.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
robert-maxwell.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

robert-maxwell.title: MOSSAD
robert-maxwell.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

robert-maxwell.title: John Kiriakou
robert-maxwell.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

robert-maxwell.title: Prince Andrew
robert-maxwell.summary: British royal named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, and has said that his 2026 arrest — over the alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein — is evidence that Epstein was collecting for a foreign power rather than for himself.

robert-maxwell.title: Sacha Baron Cohen
robert-maxwell.summary: British comedian and actor; per John Kiriakou, "a comedic genius" who hired Kiriakou as a Middle East script advisor for the film Bruno, and whose attempt to film in Jordan without notifying the Jordanian Intelligence Service resulted in King Abdullah II personally greeting him at the Royal Palace.

robert-mueller.title: Abu Zubaydah
robert-mueller.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

robert-mueller.title: Ali Soufan
robert-mueller.summary: FBI special agent who handled Abu Zubaydah immediately after his March 2002 capture; through patient, respectful interrogation produced the only actionable intelligence ever obtained from the detainee, including the first identification of "Mukhtar" as Khalid Sheikh Mohammed.

robert-mueller.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
robert-mueller.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

robert-mueller.title: John Brennan
robert-mueller.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

robert-mueller.title: Plato Cacheris
robert-mueller.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

robert-mueller.title: John Kiriakou
robert-mueller.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

robert-the-arsonist.title: FCI Loretto
robert-the-arsonist.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

robert-the-arsonist.title: John's rules for prison survival
robert-the-arsonist.summary: The code John Kiriakou says he wrote for himself at FCI Loretto out of his CIA training — rule one, recruit prisoners as sources using the same motivations the agency teaches; rule two, seek cover and blend in — illustrated with a plan to obtain contraband binder clips.

robert-the-arsonist.title: The prison service economy
robert-the-arsonist.summary: The trade in goods and services at FCI Loretto as John Kiriakou describes it — used shoes resold on commission, convenience stores run out of lockers at a thirty per cent markup, a dozen bookmakers, unlicensed chiropractic, and sexual services priced in books of postage stamps.

robert-the-arsonist.title: Ten-minute moves and the count
robert-the-arsonist.summary: The clock that governs a federal prison: a fixed daily timetable, movement permitted only during ten-minute windows on the hour, and five counts a day — two standing, three conducted with a flashlight in the face of a sleeping man, which John Kiriakou argues serve no purpose except sleep disruption.

robert-the-arsonist.title: Frank Russo
robert-the-arsonist.summary: The former auditor of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, who shared a bunk with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto — a corruption defendant who cooperated against Jimmy Dimora, was marked in prison as a rat, and whom Kiriakou describes as a sweetheart with a hilarious sense of humour who won everybody over anyway.

robert-the-arsonist.title: The chapel job
robert-the-arsonist.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

roger-waters.title: Shireen Abu Akleh
roger-waters.summary: Al Jazeera journalist, U.S. citizen and Greek Orthodox Christian; John Kiriakou recounts that she was shot in the face by an Israeli sniper while wearing clearly marked press gear, and that the IDF then beat pallbearers at her funeral.

roger-waters.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
roger-waters.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

roger-waters.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
roger-waters.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

roger-waters.title: Famine in Gaza
roger-waters.summary: The starvation of the civilian population of the Gaza Strip, which John Kiriakou describes as a United Nations-declared famine caused not by an absence of food but by an Israeli refusal to let food reach the people who need it; Kiriakou characterises it as a war crime, a crime against humanity and a form of genocide, attributing that characterisation to the United Nations and the International Court of Justice rather than to himself.

roger-waters.title: Germany and Israel
roger-waters.summary: John Kiriakou's account of German support for Israeli policy as an overcorrection driven by shame over the Nazi past, and of the resulting cultural blacklisting of critics of Israel in Germany — a pattern he put to Roger Waters, who described being effectively unpublishable in the German press.

roger-waters.title: October 7 attack
roger-waters.summary: John Kiriakou's analysis of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack as a policy failure, not an intelligence one — Israel was warned repeatedly, but Itamar Ben-Gvir diverted response forces to the West Bank, and Kiriakou believes Israel welcomed a pretext for overwhelming retaliation.

romanian-silver-mine.title: The Cypriot billionaire's investigation
romanian-silver-mine.summary: The six-week private-intelligence job John Kiriakou describes as operational rather than analytic: a Cypriot billionaire wanted to know about the man engaged to his only daughter, and Kiriakou bribed a police captain in Cyprus, ran surveillance in London, and reported back that the fiancé was a thief with drug convictions.

romanian-silver-mine.title: The Oman oil lease
romanian-silver-mine.summary: A private-intelligence assignment in which an oil company that had leased a field on Oman's border with Yemen for ninety-nine years discovered al-Qaeda controlled the ground, and sent John Kiriakou to Muscat to ask whether the Omani government would clear them out.

romanian-silver-mine.title: Abraxas Corporation
romanian-silver-mine.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

romanian-silver-mine.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
romanian-silver-mine.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

romanian-silver-mine.title: Concealment devices
romanian-silver-mine.summary: Hollowed everyday objects — known inside the CIA as CDs — issued to officers to hide documents, equipment and, in the larger sizes, a gun.
