Per John Kiriakou every CIA officer has access to them, some are simply assigned with no instructions attached, and the way they are found in real life is the way they are found in *The Good Shepherd* — by an anomaly a hand can feel.

romanian-silver-mine.title: David Boies
romanian-silver-mine.summary: The American litigator John Kiriakou has appeared alongside on Piers Morgan's programme, and whose observation about Alan Dershowitz — that he was not merely Epstein's attorney but his publicist — Kiriakou treats as the key distinction in the case.

romanian-twins.title: FCI Loretto
romanian-twins.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

romanian-twins.title: Chomo
romanian-twins.summary: The prison term for a child molester, which John Kiriakou first heard on his first day at FCI Loretto when two skinheads at the Aryan table put it to him as the last of three vetting questions before deciding whether he could eat with them.

romanian-twins.title: Clint Goswick
romanian-twins.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto; a devout Christian and Wichita Falls, Texas heating-and-air-conditioning business owner convicted of drug conspiracy and a gun charge despite never having used, possessed, manufactured, or distributed drugs.

romanian-twins.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
romanian-twins.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

romanian-twins.title: Federal prison security levels
romanian-twins.summary: The ladder of federal custody as John Kiriakou describes it — penitentiary, medium, low and minimum-security camp — the transfer rules that let long-sentence prisoners descend it, and why that placed dangerous men inside the low-security prison where he served his sentence.

romanian-twins.title: Larry Raviv
romanian-twins.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou, convicted of murder-for-hire after taking out a life insurance policy on his business partner to pay off a $100,000 mob gambling debt and hiring a hitman to kill him. Raviv negotiated a 20-year sentence, down from what would normally be life without parole, by testifying against the hitman, who died of a heart attack while awaiting extradition trial. Kiriakou later engineered a violent beating against Raviv after Raviv called him a "rat" for being summoned to the lieutenant's office for a Jake Tapper interview.

ron-wyden.title: Rand Paul Eric Holder
ron-wyden.summary: Rand Paul asked whether the president may kill an American on US soil without trial. Kiriakou recounts Holder''s eventual answer: yes.

ron-wyden.title: James Clapper
ron-wyden.summary: Director of National Intelligence under Obama, and in John Kiriakou's account the standing example of two arguments at once — that lying to Congress carries no consequence at the top of the intelligence community, and that career military officers make poor intelligence chiefs because they cannot tell a president no.

ron-wyden.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
ron-wyden.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

ron-wyden.title: FCI Loretto
ron-wyden.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

ron-wyden.title: John Ratcliffe
ron-wyden.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

ron-wyden.title: Julian Assange
ron-wyden.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

ross-ulbricht.title: Abraham Bolden
ross-ulbricht.summary: The first African-American Secret Service agent assigned to a presidential detail; per John Kiriakou, he quite literally saved John F. Kennedy's life in Chicago in October 1963 and was subjected to overt racism by fellow agents, who told him to his face they would not protect Kennedy from assassination because of his civil-rights sympathies.

ross-ulbricht.title: Alan Dershowitz
ross-ulbricht.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

ross-ulbricht.title: Dick Cheney
ross-ulbricht.summary: U.S. Vice President under George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou — recounting CIA Director George Tenet's memoir — Cheney intercepted the presidential finding authorizing the CIA's enhanced interrogation program in the Oval Office anteroom and took it from Tenet before Bush could sign it. Tenet later concluded the president probably never actually signed the finding and probably told the truth when he said he had no idea the program was taking place. Kiriakou characterizes Cheney as the one who actually ran foreign policy, intelligence policy, and defense policy during the Bush years.

ross-ulbricht.title: Donald Trump
ross-ulbricht.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

ross-ulbricht.title: Kill the Messenger (Gary Webb)
ross-ulbricht.summary: The 2014 film about journalist Gary Webb, on which John Kiriakou served as script advisor; when Kiriakou was arrested in January 2012, the FBI seized his electronics, including a draft of the unclassified Hollywood script, and stamped every page "top secret" despite Kiriakou having no role in writing it.

ross-ulbricht.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
ross-ulbricht.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

roy-cohn.title: Donald Trump
roy-cohn.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

roy-cohn.title: Adnan Khashoggi
roy-cohn.summary: Saudi arms dealer and Iran-Contra middleman whom John Kiriakou says was mentioned 'all the time' at the CIA — in pointed contrast to Jeffrey Epstein, whose name he never once heard there.

roy-cohn.title: Andrew Bustamante
roy-cohn.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

roy-cohn.title: Bob Woodward's CIA headquarters access
roy-cohn.summary: John Kiriakou's account of watching Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward walk the halls of CIA headquarters unescorted while researching a book, after the CIA director ordered staff to cooperate with him — an episode Kiriakou cites as evidence of how close the relationship between senior CIA officials and favored journalists really is.

roy-cohn.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
roy-cohn.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

roy-cohn.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
roy-cohn.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

ruby-ridge.title: Waco Siege
ruby-ridge.summary: 1993 federal operation against the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, led by David Koresh, resulting in the deaths of more than twenty-seven people — more than half of them children. Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague's reaction upon hearing the news was 'It's about time.' Kiriakou describes this as the kind of response he once might have shared, but which his later experiences with government abuse of power caused him to revisit.

ruby-ridge.title: Abu Zubaydah
ruby-ridge.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

ruby-ridge.title: Allen Dulles
ruby-ridge.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

ruby-ridge.title: Central Intelligence Agency
ruby-ridge.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

ruby-ridge.title: Cofer Black
ruby-ridge.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

ruby-ridge.title: Cold cell
ruby-ridge.summary: A CIA interrogation technique in which a stripped detainee is chained to a ceiling eyebolt in a cell chilled to 50°F, then doused with a bucket of ice water at hourly intervals; never authorized; documented to have killed at least two prisoners.

rudy-giuliani.title: Robert MacLean
rudy-giuliani.summary: TSA whistleblower; the person to whom John Kiriakou first described Rudy Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt the same evening it occurred, and who in turn tipped the FBI (which declined interest) and then the New York Times.

rudy-giuliani.title: Sebastian Gorka
rudy-giuliani.summary: Former Trump administration deputy assistant; subject of John Kiriakou's second attempted pardon transaction in 2018, in which Gorka asked Kiriakou for $5,000 at a book launch at the Trump International Hotel in exchange for tweeting at the president on his behalf. Kiriakou refused.

rudy-giuliani.title: Bernie Kerik
rudy-giuliani.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

rudy-giuliani.title: Bruce Fein
rudy-giuliani.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

rudy-giuliani.title: Noelle Dunphy
rudy-giuliani.summary: Former aide to Rudy Giuliani; independently corroborated to the New York Times John Kiriakou's account of Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt, after Giuliani's subsequent sexual harassment of her caused her to come forward.

rudy-giuliani.title: Central Intelligence Agency
rudy-giuliani.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

rule-six-endurance.title: Depression in prison
rule-six-endurance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

rule-six-endurance.title: Dave Phillips
rule-six-endurance.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

rule-six-endurance.title: FCI Loretto
rule-six-endurance.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

rule-six-endurance.title: Ken Schaefer
rule-six-endurance.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who told others he was inside for securities irregularities, was in fact convicted of transporting a child for sex, fled to Israel on bail, and — after John Kiriakou exposed and confronted him — offered money to prisoners to have Kiriakou attacked.

rule-six-endurance.title: Passing time at Loretto
rule-six-endurance.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

rule-six-endurance.title: Seven thousand letters
rule-six-endurance.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

running-into-former-sources.title: Sources are not traitors
running-into-former-sources.summary: Asked whether CIA officers privately regarded their recruited agents as traitors and held them in contempt, John Kiriakou answered that they did not — because the officers believed they were the good guys, and a recruited source had become one of them.

running-into-former-sources.title: The operational test
running-into-former-sources.summary: The vetting procedure John Kiriakou describes for moving a trusted source onto normal handling: put a full surveillance team on him without telling him, watch how he gets to the meeting, and then ask him to describe what he did.

running-into-former-sources.title: The density of spies in Washington
running-into-former-sources.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that there are more spies in Washington DC than anywhere else in the world, that the FBI''s counterintelligence division does nothing but try to root them out, and that the job cannot be finished short of becoming North Korea.

running-into-former-sources.title: The Greek colonel and China
running-into-former-sources.summary: The arrest of a Greek colonel assigned to NATO on charges of spying for China — a case John Kiriakou calls highly unusual not because espionage arrests are rare in Greece, but because they are almost always for Russia, and which he says shows the Chinese have begun caring about NATO communications.

running-into-former-sources.title: The anti-semite smear
running-into-former-sources.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the professional cost of saying publicly that Israel spies on the United States: Alan Dershowitz calls him names, and the political director of the Israeli foreign minister called him a noted anti-semite.

running-into-former-sources.title: The Epstein files and the Starmer government
running-into-former-sources.summary: John Kiriakou''s prediction that the Epstein disclosures could bring down Keir Starmer''s government, on the strength of evidence that Prince Andrew and Peter Mandelson gave Epstein classified British Ministry of Defence documents — an Official Secrets Act matter that in America would fall under the Espionage Act.

russell-targ.title: Project Stargate
russell-targ.summary: The CIA's remote-viewing program, which Kiriakou says burned millions for decades and failed — and which he understands is being revisited.

russell-targ.title: Albert Stubblebine
russell-targ.summary: Per John Kiriakou, General Albert "Bert" Stubblebine was among the Army Intelligence figures behind the original Project Stargate remote-viewing program; Kiriakou interviewed the program's top people and says Stubblebine, like remote viewer Lyn Buchanan, had to sign non-disclosure agreements with the NSA and CIA.

russell-targ.title: Lynn Buchanan
russell-targ.summary: A Fort Meade-trained Army intelligence veteran of the CIA and NSA remote-viewing programs — a primary source, Kiriakou says, not a TV psychic.

russell-targ.title: Bay Path University
russell-targ.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he teaches in the graduate intelligence-studies program at Bay Path University in Massachusetts, covering introduction to intelligence, the history of terrorism, and intelligence and cybersecurity.

russell-targ.title: Espionage Act
russell-targ.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

russell-targ.title: Ilhan Omar
russell-targ.summary: U.S. Representative whom John Kiriakou credits with sponsoring a rewrite of the Espionage Act in two consecutive Congresses — legislation he says is dead on arrival with a Republican House because of who she is.

russia-ukraine-war-origins.title: Donald Trump
russia-ukraine-war-origins.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

russia-ukraine-war-origins.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
russia-ukraine-war-origins.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

russia-ukraine-war-origins.title: China as economic threat
russia-ukraine-war-origins.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

russia-ukraine-war-origins.title: Zelensky action figures
russia-ukraine-war-origins.summary: The detail John Kiriakou reached for in January 2023 to describe how far American war messaging had gone: you can buy Zelensky action figures in stores now. He offered it as the marker of a ridiculousness he thought few Americans recognised, alongside his argument that the war''s real object was to bog Russia down before confronting China.

russia-ukraine-war-origins.title: Saudi-Iran diplomatic rivalry
russia-ukraine-war-origins.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the roots of Saudi-Iranian hostility — Iran's bloody 1979 infiltration of the Hajj, Saudi Arabia's suppression of its own Shia minority, and the 2023 restoration of diplomatic relations brokered, to Washington's surprise, by China.

russia-ukraine-war-origins.title: Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
russia-ukraine-war-origins.summary: The 2022 destruction of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, whose responsibility John Kiriakou treats as genuinely unresolved — citing Seymour Hersh's reporting that the CIA did it, a later Ukrainian special-forces claim of a sailboat-based operation carried out without Zelensky's knowledge, and a retired CIA colleague's private theory that Putin blew up his own pipeline to blame the Americans.

russiagate.title: Bill Binney
russiagate.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

russiagate.title: Donald Trump
russiagate.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

russiagate.title: Kiriakou's Russian media work
russiagate.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hosting a daily Sputnik radio show for seven and a half years with full contractual freedom to criticize anyone, including Putin — which he did on the morning of the Ukraine invasion — offered as a rebuttal to claims that Russian outlets are mere propaganda.

russiagate.title: Craig Murray
russiagate.summary: Former British Ambassador to Uzbekistan whom John Kiriakou cites as a whistleblower of extreme torture: during a meeting at the Uzbek intelligence service, Murray heard screaming, walked in, and saw a man being boiled in oil — reporting it cost him his career.

russiagate.title: Abu Omar rendition
russiagate.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

russiagate.title: Christopher Steele dossier
russiagate.summary: The 2016 opposition-research dossier alleging Trump-Russia ties, compiled by former MI6 officer Christopher Steele. Per John Kiriakou, who worked directly with Steele on an MI6 operation in London in the 1990s, Steele was so respected at MI6 that other officers wanted to be like him — a reputation Kiriakou says the dossier episode reduced to caricature, because in private practice there was no team of analysts to vet the raw intelligence before it reached the Clinton campaign.

russian-illegals-program.title: Spy films and television on screen
russian-illegals-program.summary: John Kiriakou's scene-by-scene verdicts on how spy films and television handle real tradecraft — what they get right (static surveillance from upper floors, hostile operational meetings, exchanges of bona fides, breaking into offices), what they invent (silent helicopters, high-speed submersibles, Batcaves, gadgets that cannot be bought), and the shows he says commit felonies on screen. He opens with why CIA officers watch them at all — *"not because they love the CIA movies, but because they love to criticize them."*

russian-illegals-program.title: Aldrich Ames
russian-illegals-program.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

russian-illegals-program.title: Bill Buckley
russian-illegals-program.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

russian-illegals-program.title: Burn Notice
russian-illegals-program.summary: The USA Network spy series John Kiriakou watched as a fan before he became its script adviser — a job he obtained by sitting next to its creator, Matt Nix, on a flight from Washington to Los Angeles, having previously run the show's credits in slow motion to find out who was advising it. Nobody was. By the time the plane landed Kiriakou had the job for season six.

russian-illegals-program.title: CIA driving training
russian-illegals-program.summary: The counterterrorism-driving component of CIA training, in which officers are ambushed in a simulated third-country no-man's-land and must "get off the X" — get out of the kill zone. John Kiriakou's own run ended with the instructors killing his engine by remote, a robot in a van firing paintballs at him, and Kiriakou shooting out his own car windows to get an angle on the robot. "Damn it, Kiriakou. That was the last decent car we had."

russian-illegals-program.title: CIA psychological evaluations
russian-illegals-program.summary: The recurring psychiatric screening every CIA officer undergoes — before employment, again three years after hiring, and every five years thereafter for life, with extra sessions triggered by bad behaviour overseas. Per John Kiriakou, failing one grounds an officer — a colleague who "went nuts" could not be sent on a post-9/11 mission, and Kiriakou was sent in his place.

sacha-baron-cohen.title: Eli Cohen
sacha-baron-cohen.summary: Israeli Mossad spy who infiltrated Damascus in the early 1960s under cover as a wealthy Syrian-Argentine businessman; per John Kiriakou, he was on the verge of being named deputy defense minister of Syria before being detected through a burst-transmission intercept and publicly hanged.

sacha-baron-cohen.title: MOSSAD
sacha-baron-cohen.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

sacha-baron-cohen.title: Jeffrey Epstein
sacha-baron-cohen.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

sacha-baron-cohen.title: Ghislaine Maxwell
sacha-baron-cohen.summary: British socialite and convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, her father Robert Maxwell was a prolific Mossad spy, and she is the likely conduit through whom Jeffrey Epstein was introduced to and recruited by Mossad.

sacha-baron-cohen.title: Robert Maxwell
sacha-baron-cohen.summary: British media proprietor and father of Ghislaine Maxwell; described by John Kiriakou as "a prolific Mossad spy — that's a historic fact," and as the family channel through which the Epstein operation, in Kiriakou's phrase, was "kept all in the family."

sacha-baron-cohen.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
sacha-baron-cohen.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

saddam-hussein-biographer.title: *Now is not the time to go wobbly*
saddam-hussein-biographer.summary: The telephone call from Margaret Thatcher to George H. W. Bush on the afternoon of the Kuwait invasion which, in John Kiriakou's account of that day inside the CIA, was what finally decided the president to expel Iraqi troops from Kuwait.

saddam-hussein-biographer.title: The Oval Office briefing of 2 August 1990
saddam-hussein-biographer.summary: The morning Iraq invaded Kuwait, a 25-year-old John Kiriakou was driven from CIA headquarters to the White House and found himself briefing President George H. W. Bush, Vice President Quayle, Brent Scowcroft and the CIA director — and answering the question *"well, now what do we do?"*

saddam-hussein-biographer.title: George Habash
saddam-hussein-biographer.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

saddam-hussein-biographer.title: William Webster
saddam-hussein-biographer.summary: Director of Central Intelligence during the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, and before that a federal judge and Director of the FBI; per John Kiriakou, "a lovely man … just a very kind, nice man" and "a giant in my mind" — the director Kiriakou first briefed at four in the morning, on fifteen minutes' notice, during the Kuwait task force, and who sat two seats away from him in the Oval Office on the morning of the invasion.

saddam-hussein-biographer.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
saddam-hussein-biographer.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

saddam-hussein-biographer.title: Saddam Hussein
saddam-hussein-biographer.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

saddam-hussein.title: John Kiriakou
saddam-hussein.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

saddam-hussein.title: Intelligence switching in the Iran–Iraq war
saddam-hussein.summary: John Kiriakou''s account that during the Iran–Iraq war the United States supplied top-secret overhead imagery to whichever side was losing ground, switching as the front moved — giving the Iraqis imagery when Iran advanced, and the Iranians imagery when Iraq advanced. His summary: ''So it was hideous.''

saddam-hussein.title: Norman Schwarzkopf
saddam-hussein.summary: U.S. Army general and commander of CENTCOM during the 1991 Gulf War; per John Kiriakou, the architect of the "visionary" flanking maneuver that bypassed Iraq's fortified Kuwait–Saudi border, struck from the north, and produced the Highway of Death.

saddam-hussein.title: Kuwait oil fires
saddam-hussein.summary: The February 1991 sabotage by retreating Iraqi forces of an estimated 600–800 Kuwaiti oil wells; per John Kiriakou's first-person account, the fires blackened the desert and blotted out the sun as far away as Riyadh, vaporized two French journalists who drove onto a sheet of melted-sand glass, and were extinguished only by an international team led by American specialist Red Adair using a Rolls-Royce jet engine to blow the flames out.

saddam-hussein.title: Abu Nidal Organization
saddam-hussein.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA destroyed the Abu Nidal Organization from within by exploiting Abu Nidal''s pathological paranoia: rather than recruiting members (impossible given the group''s extreme anti-American orientation), the agency planted false signals that various members were already cooperating with US intelligence. Members began killing each other one by one. Kiriakou: ''Next thing you know, they''ve all killed each other and the only one left is Abu Nidal.'' He also disbelieves the official heart-attack cause of Abu Nidal''s death, attributing it to a Saddam Hussein ''control'' decision.

saddam-hussein.title: Hussein Kamel
saddam-hussein.summary: Saddam Hussein's son-in-law and Iraq's Minister of Industry and Military Industrialization; defected to Jordan in January 1993 with his brother Saddam Kamel out of fear of Uday Hussein; demanded U.S. weapons and air cover in exchange for cooperation but refused to disclose WMD locations; per John Kiriakou, the CIA burned him with a planted Arab-press leak that triggered Saddam to destroy his chemical-weapons stockpile.

safe-housekeeper.title: Asset acquisition cycle
safe-housekeeper.summary: The four-step process — spot, assess, develop, recruit — taught as the first lesson of CIA case officer training

safe-housekeeper.title: John Kiriakou
safe-housekeeper.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

safe-housekeeper.title: Lie Detection
safe-housekeeper.summary: Per John Kiriakou, both a subject he addresses in his book The CIA Insider's Guide to Lying and Lie Detection and a practical skill he describes using throughout his career. Physical tells include gaze direction (down to conceal, up to construct), fidgeting, and throat-clearing; structural tells — losing the thread mid-conversation and self-contradiction — are more reliable, because the truth is stable while a lie requires maintenance and eventually collapses under its own complexity.

safe-housekeeper.title: FCI Loretto
safe-housekeeper.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

safe-housekeeper.title: Moral Injury
safe-housekeeper.summary: Psychological diagnosis John Kiriakou received from a friend — a CIA veteran, brigadier general, and psychiatrist — who identified it as the source of Kiriakou's post-divorce PTSD. The concept describes the psychological damage caused when a person you fully trust does something that violates the moral framework you were raised to believe in; the brain cannot process that such a violation has occurred, and the result is a form of PTSD. Kiriakou had no PTSD from Pakistan or his CIA career but was, in his own description, destroyed by his divorce.

safe-housekeeper.title: Critical Analytic Thinking
safe-housekeeper.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the foundational discipline of CIA analyst training and the most practically valuable skill he carried into civilian life: questioning all incoming information — including, especially, sources whose ideological positions align with one''s own — and arriving at conclusions from evidence rather than prior belief. Kiriakou cites his own COVID lab-leak conclusion, reached against his initial instinct, as an example of the method in practice.

salman-bin-hamad.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
salman-bin-hamad.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

salman-bin-hamad.title: Bahrain Prime Minister "Mr. 10 Percent"
salman-bin-hamad.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Bahrain's long-serving prime minister, the Amir's uncle, universally nicknamed "Mr. 10 Percent" for allegedly requiring a 10 percent cash cut on business deals — a cold, calculating figure Kiriakou calls "the definition of corruption," pointedly excluded from the national motto, yet credited with turning Bahrain into the Gulf's banking hub.

salman-bin-hamad.title: Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa
salman-bin-hamad.summary: Amir of Bahrain from 1961 until his death in 1999; per John Kiriakou, who was posted to Bahrain 1994–1996, a short, "roly poly," sweet-natured ruler who kept an open beach palace for Westerners, disliked Jordan's King Hussein, and was heartbroken by the Columbine shooting even as he privately could not grasp why he should extend more support to his own Shia majority.

salman-bin-hamad.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
salman-bin-hamad.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

salman-bin-hamad.title: Admiral William Crowe
salman-bin-hamad.summary: Former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff and former CENTCOM commander who had lived in Bahrain, author of the "pound for pound" formula every Bahraini and every American ambassador quotes, and the visiting dignitary John Kiriakou was assigned to escort — a week that ended with the Bahraini Prime Minister refusing to let go of Kiriakou's hand.

salman-bin-hamad.title: Bahrain Intifada (1994)
salman-bin-hamad.summary: The first Bahraini Intifada, a Shia uprising against the Sunni Al Khalifa monarchy that began roughly two months into John Kiriakou's 1994 Bahrain posting with a bombing at the Ministry of Labor, led by Abdul Amir Al-Jamri, and met by the government first with police, then armored personnel carriers and tanks, and executions.

salt-pit.title: Lawrence Wilkerson
salt-pit.summary: Retired Army colonel, chief of staff and closest friend to Secretary of State Colin Powell; John Kiriakou counts him among the most consequential military whistleblowers, cites his count of 108 deaths in military custody, and says Wilkerson confirmed on air that Powell's UN case for the Iraq war was knowingly "sold."

salt-pit.title: Learned Helplessness
salt-pit.summary: Psychological concept adapted by the CIA as the theoretical basis for its post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; per John Kiriakou, the goal of techniques including waterboarding was not primarily to elicit specific information but to render the prisoner so terrified of his captors that he would volunteer confessions on demand. In practice, applied to Abu Zubaydah, it meant a dog cage he would climb into on command, a coffin filled with cockroaches, and a towel whose mere appearance made him crumple — a programme Kiriakou says had far less to do with gathering intelligence than with ruining a man's life.

salt-pit.title: Guantanamo Bay
salt-pit.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

salt-pit.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
salt-pit.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

salt-pit.title: Gina Haspel
salt-pit.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

salt-pit.title: Langley
salt-pit.summary: The Virginia location of CIA headquarters and, in John Kiriakou''s usage, shorthand for the agency''s permanent power. It''s where he worked as the CIA''s lone Iraq-Kuwait analyst — told to start on Iraq "because nothing ever happened there" — where a cafeteria conversation invited him into the torture program, and the place agencies return to after apologizing to Congress, "where of course nothing ever changes." When a host suggested the real government of America is out in Langley and Washington''s white marble is for show, Kiriakou''s answer was: "that''s about the shape of it."

sam-adams-award.title: Vietnam War
sam-adams-award.summary: The war John Kiriakou grew up in the shadow of — his parents marched against it — and the deep precedent for everything he fights: entered on the Gulf of Tonkin lie, prosecuted by generals who knew for a decade they were losing (per the Pentagon Papers), studded with torture whose victims recited the Green Bay Packers'' starting lineup as "intelligence," and ended in part by Daniel Ellsberg, "the godfather of all modern national security whistleblowers." Even Robert McNamara, he notes, understood waterboarding was a bridge too far.

sam-adams-award.title: Ray McGovern
sam-adams-award.summary: Former senior CIA analyst turned antiwar dissident, and one of John Kiriakou's closest friends — "like a brother to me." Kiriakou began working at the CIA on the Monday after the Friday McGovern retired in January 1990, so the two never overlapped inside; they became comrades in the whistleblower world instead. McGovern coined the "MICIMATT" framing Kiriakou often borrows, went into Putin's office with Oliver Stone for a 40-minute meeting, and — per Kiriakou — believes 9/11 was a conspiracy, a view Kiriakou affectionately notes is far from his own.

sam-adams-award.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
sam-adams-award.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

sam-adams-award.title: National Security Council
sam-adams-award.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

sam-adams-award.title: Daniel Hale
sam-adams-award.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

sam-adams-award.title: Espionage Act
sam-adams-award.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

san-bernardino-iphone-case.title: NSA Surveillance
san-bernardino-iphone-case.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

san-bernardino-iphone-case.title: Central Intelligence Agency
san-bernardino-iphone-case.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

san-bernardino-iphone-case.title: MOSSAD
san-bernardino-iphone-case.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

san-bernardino-iphone-case.title: Executive Order 12333
san-bernardino-iphone-case.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

san-bernardino-iphone-case.title: Government Purchase of Social Media Metadata
san-bernardino-iphone-case.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the practice by which U.S. intelligence and law enforcement agencies — including the NSA and FBI — buy bulk user metadata from social media companies such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter), bypassing the warrant requirements that would otherwise apply to direct surveillance. The practice exploits a provision in platform terms of service under which users surrender ownership of their metadata to the company, which may then sell it freely.

san-bernardino-iphone-case.title: Pegasus spyware
san-bernardino-iphone-case.summary: Israeli-developed phone-interception software that requires no action by the target — no link clicked, no message answered — and gives its operator the contents of the device along with live use of its camera and microphone. John Kiriakou describes it as having escaped state control: sold on commercially, routed through an American contractor and then directly by the Israelis, used against Americans, and implicated in a Greek interception scandal that he says brought down a government.

sanaa-sewer-project.title: The Yemen jazz radio plan
sanaa-sewer-project.summary: A scheme John Kiriakou says the American defence attaché in Sanaa described to him on his last visit to Yemen in 2011: a propaganda programme modelled on NPR that would play jazz and run call-in shows for young Yemenis. It lasted about two weeks before it shuttered, because nobody was going to listen to it.

sanaa-sewer-project.title: Saudi aid priorities
sanaa-sewer-project.summary: John Kiriakou''s characterisation of Saudi generosity abroad as real but consistently misdirected: instead of building schools they build mosques, instead of building hospitals they send planeloads of Qurans, and instead of water treatment plants or power plants they send money for weapons, ammunition and training.

sanaa-sewer-project.title: The al-Qaeda foot soldier
sanaa-sewer-project.summary: What John Kiriakou says he learned from interviewing captured al-Qaeda fighters — not the leaders but the eighteen-, nineteen- and twenty-year-olds, who told essentially the same story: an isolated village, illiteracy, no job skills, a poor relationship with their father, an age at which they wanted to marry, and no father willing to give them a daughter. The local imam offered $300 a month to go to Afghanistan, and $500 to their parents if they were martyred.

sanaa-sewer-project.title: Foreign aid
sanaa-sewer-project.summary: John Kiriakou's advocacy of a hundredfold increase in the American foreign-aid budget — a position he concedes puts him in "a very minuscule minority" — argued on the grounds that every dollar spent saves five or ten in refugee crises, civil wars and attacks on the United States, and that development is the only thing that empties terrorist recruiting pools. His counter-example is the Sana'a water-treatment plant, built by the European Union and rendered pointless by American and Saudi politics.

sanaa-sewer-project.title: Fusha and the Gulf dialect
sanaa-sewer-project.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own Arabic training — a first year in fusha, high standard Arabic, followed by a second year in khaleeji, the Gulf dialect — and the two consequences he reports: that Yemen is the only place where pure fusha is spoken, and that Saudis asked him why he spoke Arabic like Shakespeare.

sanaa-sewer-project.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
sanaa-sewer-project.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

sanctions-effectiveness.title: Bashar al-Assad
sanctions-effectiveness.summary: President of Syria; John Kiriakou recounts warning Senator John Kerry to stop publicly calling Assad 'my dear friend' after a speech enraged Washington's Lebanese community, with Kerry citing motorcycle rides they had taken together to the Golan Heights.

sanctions-effectiveness.title: Venezuela Boat Strikes
sanctions-effectiveness.summary: September 2025 U.S. military strike on a boat in the Caribbean that killed 11 people the White House called drug traffickers; John Kiriakou calls it piracy on the high seas followed by mass murder, arguing the victims were never charged with a crime and that the boat's unusual passenger count undercuts the drug-trafficking story.

sanctions-effectiveness.title: Caleb Maupin
sanctions-effectiveness.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

sanctions-effectiveness.title: Greenland
sanctions-effectiveness.summary: The Danish territory the United States has spent years talking about acquiring; John Kiriakou reports two flatly contradictory readings from his own contacts — a White House friend who says Washington is serious and will lean on a Cold War treaty to claim it is already de facto American, and a Republican friend who says the whole thing is a grenade thrown to distract the press — and warns that taking it by force would end NATO.

sanctions-effectiveness.title: Kiriakou pardon request
sanctions-effectiveness.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

sanctions-effectiveness.title: India
sanctions-effectiveness.summary: The country John Kiriakou names as his least favourite of all the places he has worked — not, he stresses, for poverty or danger, both of which he has seen worse of, but for the caste system and "the way Indians treat one another." His illustration is an afternoon in Hyderabad when two separate restaurants refused to admit the driver he had invited to lunch.

sandy-berger.title: Bob Baer
sandy-berger.summary: Former CIA case officer; per John Kiriakou, "pretty famous"; the subject of George Clooney's film Syriana; pulled out of northern Iraq by the Clinton White House in the 1990s after [NSA intercepted](/wiki/the-intercept) a communication revealing he was developing a network of sources to assassinate Saddam Hussein — National Security Adviser Sandy Berger called CIA and threatened him with a conspiracy charge.

sandy-berger.title: George W. Bush
sandy-berger.summary: 43rd President of the United States. In John Kiriakou's telling, Bush signed the August 1, 2002 executive order that authorized the CIA torture program, spent years telling the public "we don't torture," and — days after Kiriakou's 2007 ABC interview — blamed torture on "a rogue CIA officer" while walking from the White House South Portico to Marine One, a moment Kiriakou instantly read as the White House preparing to pin the program on him. Bush also ordered the FBI removed from Abu Zubaydah's black site, flew the bin Laden family out of the country after 9/11, and loosened the assassination ban of Executive Order 12333.

sandy-berger.title: 9/11 attribution of responsibility
sandy-berger.summary: John Kiriakou's evolving view of who bears ultimate responsibility for the September 11 attacks — that al-Qaeda carried them out but was, in his current view, "allowed" to, amid a distracted Bush administration, an uninvestigated Saudi government, and an Israeli government he believes had a vested interest in the attacks proceeding.

sandy-berger.title: Abu Zubaydah
sandy-berger.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

sandy-berger.title: Alex Station
sandy-berger.summary: CIA unit that tracked Osama bin Laden beginning in 1995; per John Kiriakou, who served as chief of its counterintelligence branch, the unit kept extremely tight security around its files, limited FBI investigators' access to information about future 9/11 hijackers Khaled al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, and — under a deliberate policy of non-cooperation with the FBI — failed to watchlist participants in the Malaysia summit where al-Qaeda planned the attacks.

sandy-berger.title: Ali Mohamed
sandy-berger.summary: Egyptian-American former U.S. Army sergeant who trained at Fort Bragg while secretly working for Egyptian intelligence, later trained some of the 9/11 hijackers and other al-Qaeda operatives, and was arrested in connection with the 1998 U.S. embassy bombings before disappearing under the George W. Bush administration; John Kiriakou speculates he was actually a double agent working for al-Qaeda — or possibly Israeli intelligence — against his CIA handlers.

sandy-grimes.title: Aldrich Ames
sandy-grimes.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

sandy-grimes.title: Robert Hanssen
sandy-grimes.summary: FBI counterintelligence chief and Soviet/Russian mole; framed CIA counterintelligence chief Brian Kelley as the source of compromised assets — leading the FBI to surveil Kelly for a year and a half and threaten his family with the death penalty — before Hanssen himself was identified as the actual traitor.

sandy-grimes.title: Beirut
sandy-grimes.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

sandy-grimes.title: Central Intelligence Agency
sandy-grimes.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

sandy-grimes.title: How Can I Keep from Singing
sandy-grimes.summary: Biography of folk singer Pete Seeger and John Kiriakou's stated favorite book. Per Kiriakou, Seeger was the most important man in his life besides his father and grandfather; the two exchanged Christmas cards for years, and Seeger rallied publicly to Kiriakou's defense during his prosecution. Kiriakou identifies Seeger's 1958 defiance of HUAC — pleading the First Amendment rather than the Fifth and going to prison for it — as the model for how he wanted to live his own life.

sandy-grimes.title: John Kiriakou
sandy-grimes.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

sara-jane-moore.title: Mike Mastrovito
sara-jane-moore.summary: Twenty-five-year Secret Service veteran; founder and first director of the Secret Service Intelligence Division; later, after a forced retirement, a CIA contractor specializing in Greek terrorism; close colleague of John Kiriakou in Athens. Started his career at the end of the Eisenhower administration, was in Dallas with President Kennedy, and was effectively removed from the Secret Service after Sara Jane Moore's 1975 attempt on President Ford — having interviewed Moore two weeks earlier on a threatening letter she had sent.

sara-jane-moore.title: Secret Service
sara-jane-moore.summary: The U.S. agency protecting the president. John Kiriakou, who worked alongside it for 35 years, describes a culture of complacency and poor follow-up — great with guns, weak on training and follow-through — and calls the 2024 Butler rally shooting a colossal historic screw-up in which coverage of the surrounding buildings was outsourced to a county sheriff's department. He has also encountered the Service as an adversary, outside the Venezuelan embassy in Washington in 2019.

sara-jane-moore.title: Permanent wartime economy
sara-jane-moore.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

sara-jane-moore.title: Arnon Milchan
sara-jane-moore.summary: Israeli-American Hollywood producer and, per John Kiriakou, an Israeli super-spy and arms dealer for LAKAM; central to a Netanyahu corruption charge, and named in FBI documents alongside Netanyahu in the smuggling of U.S. nuclear secrets.

sara-jane-moore.title: BDS movement
sara-jane-moore.summary: The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel; John Kiriakou notes that some 40 U.S. states now have anti-BDS laws that can require a speaker at a publicly funded university to sign a pledge of support for Israel — which he refuses to do.

sara-jane-moore.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
sara-jane-moore.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

sarge-the-guard.title: Legal mail
sarge-the-guard.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

sarge-the-guard.title: Dave Phillips
sarge-the-guard.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

sarge-the-guard.title: Letter from Loretto
sarge-the-guard.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

sarge-the-guard.title: Seven thousand letters
sarge-the-guard.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

sarge-the-guard.title: The Bob Jones frame-up
sarge-the-guard.summary: The operation John Kiriakou ran inside FCI Loretto against a man at his own cafeteria table — forging court papers in the prison law library from a genuine 1970s Ohio case involving a man of the same name, and using them to have him banished by the shot callers.

sarge-the-guard.title: FCI Loretto
sarge-the-guard.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: Amir of Kuwait during the 1990 Iraqi invasion and the 1991 liberation; per John Kiriakou, "a very kind and decent man and a leader who genuinely loved and cared for his people"; the subject of a CIA cable Kiriakou wrote from Taif which led President George H. W. Bush to invite the Amir to Washington for "the red carpet treatment" — after which the Amir returned with renewed focus on driving the Iraqis out.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Sheikh Saad al-Abdullah
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: Crown Prince and Prime Minister of Kuwait during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, the day-to-day leader of the Kuwaiti government-in-exile in Taif — "very military," "hands-on," "the best leader Kuwait had for that situation," meeting twenty hours a day with everyone who needed to be met and simultaneously managing the Kuwaiti resistance on the ground.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Skip Gnehm
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Kuwait at the 1991 liberation; per John Kiriakou, "one of the finest men I've ever worked for anywhere in the world"; led the reopening of the U.S. embassy in Kuwait City on Liberation Day with the cable "American Embassy Kuwait City is now open for business"; famously complained that he could not stop Kuwaitis from writing pro-American graffiti on the side of the embassy.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

saud-nasir-al-sabah.title: Afghan heroin policy
saud-nasir-al-sabah.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: The Saudi fear of an election
saudi-aid-priorities.summary: The explanation a Saudi diplomat gave John Kiriakou in the late 1990s for the royal family''s opposition to democracy in the kingdom: if there were an election in Saudi Arabia, Osama bin Laden would win it — a remark Kiriakou uses to argue that the regime''s problem was not that its princes loved al-Qaeda but that it feared its own population did.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: The Sanaa sewer project
saudi-aid-priorities.summary: The example John Kiriakou uses for what patient foreign assistance looks like: on a visit to Yemen around 2000 he called on the Dutch ambassador and the Italian defence attaché, who were proud because their governments had just finished building a sewer system and water treatment facility for the capital — a project that had taken about fifteen years.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: The Yemen jazz radio plan
saudi-aid-priorities.summary: A scheme John Kiriakou says the American defence attaché in Sanaa described to him on his last visit to Yemen in 2011: a propaganda programme modelled on NPR that would play jazz and run call-in shows for young Yemenis. It lasted about two weeks before it shuttered, because nobody was going to listen to it.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: A Middle East reading list
saudi-aid-priorities.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: Abu Zubaydah
saudi-aid-priorities.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

saudi-aid-priorities.title: Economic roots of terrorism
saudi-aid-priorities.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, drawn from interrogating young al-Qaeda fighters in Pakistan, that jihadi recruitment is driven by poverty and hopelessness rather than religion — illiterate villagers paid $300 a month who could not find the U.S. on a map and had never read the Quran.

saudi-democracy-fear.title: Saudi aid priorities
saudi-democracy-fear.summary: John Kiriakou''s characterisation of Saudi generosity abroad as real but consistently misdirected: instead of building schools they build mosques, instead of building hospitals they send planeloads of Qurans, and instead of water treatment plants or power plants they send money for weapons, ammunition and training.

saudi-democracy-fear.title: Abu Zubaydah
saudi-democracy-fear.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

saudi-democracy-fear.title: Khobar Towers bombing
saudi-democracy-fear.summary: June 25, 1996 truck bombing of a U.S. military housing complex in Khobar, Saudi Arabia, that killed 19 U.S. Air Force personnel. John Kiriakou, then a CIA officer living across the water in Bahrain, felt the blast shatter his own windows and drove to the scene the next morning. He says the U.S. government worked hard to blame Iran and a small Saudi Hezbollah cell with no evidence, when the attack was in fact carried out by a radical Saudi group — a predecessor of al-Qaeda, which took credit for it.

saudi-democracy-fear.title: Omar al-Bayoumi
saudi-democracy-fear.summary: The Saudi national who housed and funded two of the 9/11 hijackers in California; John Kiriakou describes him as a Saudi intelligence officer working under a ghost job, places him at President Bush's Crawford ranch before the attacks, and says the CIA blocked the 9/11 Commission from investigating him.

saudi-democracy-fear.title: Osama bin Laden
saudi-democracy-fear.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

saudi-democracy-fear.title: Saudi-Iran diplomatic rivalry
saudi-democracy-fear.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the roots of Saudi-Iranian hostility — Iran's bloody 1979 infiltration of the Hajj, Saudi Arabia's suppression of its own Shia minority, and the 2023 restoration of diplomatic relations brokered, to Washington's surprise, by China.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Donald Trump
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Kiriakou's daily news diet
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the wide range of mainstream and alternative outlets he reads each morning to compare competing angles, the two outlets — the Associated Press and ProPublica — he singles out as exceptional, and his broader habits of media consumption, from an admitted addiction to political polling to his distrust of AI chatbots after they repeatedly fabricated his own biography.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: China as economic threat
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: Djibouti
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: The small Horn of Africa state sixteen miles across the water from Yemen that hosts the American drone base for the Yemen war — and, on the same ground with a fence down the middle, a Chinese base, in what John Kiriakou calls the worst kept secret in the world.

saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.title: George H.W. Bush
saudi-iran-diplomatic-rivalry.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

saudi-military-composition.title: 2026 Iran war
saudi-military-composition.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

saudi-military-composition.title: A.Q. Khan
saudi-military-composition.summary: Pakistani nuclear scientist and the architect of Pakistan's bomb, who ran a black-market proliferation network that, per John Kiriakou, smuggled nuclear material and technology to North Korea and Libya. Kiriakou says the U.S. could easily have killed him — 'we knew where he lived, we knew how he spent his day' — but the Saudi government insisted the U.S. leave him alone, which Kiriakou calls a grave mistake and speculates was because the Saudis were pursuing their own nuclear capability. Khan was eventually pardoned by Pervez Musharraf, ending all investigations.

saudi-military-composition.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
saudi-military-composition.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

saudi-military-composition.title: Gulf consultations before the Iran war
saudi-military-composition.summary: John Kiriakou's account of travelling in Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Doha in the weeks before the 2026 strikes on Iran, and finding that the United States had made no diplomatic case to its Gulf partners at all — in sharp contrast to the worldwide campaign that preceded the Iraq war. He told a senior Emirati royal that two carrier strike groups meant an attack was coming.

saudi-military-composition.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
saudi-military-composition.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

saudi-military-composition.title: ISI
saudi-military-composition.summary: Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence agency, the CIA''s principal counterterrorism partner during John Kiriakou''s 2002 posting. Per Kiriakou, there were effectively ''two parallel ISIs'': one made up of Sandhurst-trained, FBI-schooled professionals he calls heroes who risked their lives on counterterrorism, and another — ''people with long beards who gave you a dirty look'' — who had created Kashmiri terrorist groups like Jaish-e-Mohammed and were attacking Shia mosques and Americans. Because of this, the CIA never told the ISI the identity of high-value targets, referring to Abu Zubaydah only as ''Mr. Fish.''

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Dewey Clarridge
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: The CIA operations officer John Kiriakou calls a legendary figure and a giant of the 1980s — prosecuted over Iran-Contra, and the man who said publicly that Saudi Arabia already had nuclear weapons.
