Kiriakou believes him, holds that the Saudis financed the Pakistani bomb and were repaid in access to it, and believes Clarridge was also involved in the movement of cocaine into the United States.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Jeffrey Epstein
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Jack Devine
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: A former CIA officer John Kiriakou worked for briefly in 2001 or 2002, and describes with real warmth as a great officer and a true believer — while flatly rejecting his insistence that the agency was never involved with cocaine. Asked to choose between Devine and a thirty-year DEA veteran who agrees with him, Kiriakou picks the DEA man.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Mossad networks in Iran
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: The Israeli human-intelligence penetration of Iran that John Kiriakou calls larger than anyone suspected — thousands of clandestine reporters, many of them undocumented Afghan refugees paid the equivalent of fifty or a hundred dollars a month, run in person by spymasters inside the country and compartmentalized so that rolling up one network yields nothing about the others.

saudi-nuclear-program.title: Aldrich Ames
saudi-nuclear-program.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: Abu Zubaydah
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: George Tenet
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: Carlos the Jackal
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: Omar al-Bayoumi
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: The Saudi national who housed and funded two of the 9/11 hijackers in California; John Kiriakou describes him as a Saudi intelligence officer working under a ghost job, places him at President Bush's Crawford ranch before the attacks, and says the CIA blocked the 9/11 Commission from investigating him.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

saudi-princes-and-9-11.title: Zawahiri assassination
saudi-princes-and-9-11.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the drone strike that killed al-Qaeda's Ayman al-Zawahiri — using a bladed, warhead-less missile fired as he stepped onto a balcony to smoke, deliberately chosen to avoid killing the women and children inside.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Counterterrorism Center
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Cuban double agents
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of Cuban intelligence as one of the best services on the planet, defensive in nature and trained by the KGB, and his flat claim — repeated across several tellings — that the CIA has never recruited a Cuban who did not turn out to be working for Havana all along.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Office of Leadership Analysis
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: CIA analytic office — internally called LDA, for Leadership Development Analysis — founded by CIA psychiatrist Jerome Post, where John Kiriakou was hired at the start of his CIA career and spent his first seven and a half years as Saddam Hussein's classified psychological profiler. His first assignment, given on his first day, was covering Iraq and Kuwait, a portfolio his boss described as so quiet the office sometimes went days without a single incoming cable.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Thomas Drake
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

scholar-in-residence-program.title: Abolish the CIA
scholar-in-residence-program.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

scott-horton.title: Piers Morgan
scott-horton.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

scott-horton.title: Jonathan Pollard
scott-horton.summary: U.S. Navy civilian intelligence analyst convicted in 1985 of spying for Israel; the canonical proven case of Israeli espionage against the United States; cited by John Kiriakou in his 2024 Piers Morgan debate with a former Mossad director who denied any Israeli spying on the U.S.

scott-horton.title: Max Blumenthal
scott-horton.summary: American investigative journalist and a personal friend of John Kiriakou, whom Kiriakou calls one of the most brilliant people he has ever encountered and singles out for an ability to assemble scattered fragments into a picture 'in a way that almost no one else I know is able to do.' Kiriakou also recounts Blumenthal's arrest outside the Venezuelan embassy, where he says video showed Blumenthal was the one assaulted, and counts him among the independent journalists under the same official pressure he is.

scott-horton.title: AIPAC
scott-horton.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

scott-horton.title: MOSSAD
scott-horton.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

scott-horton.title: Trita Parsi
scott-horton.summary: Iran scholar; in a Foreign Affairs piece published August 10, 2025, predicted a renewed Israeli–Iranian war by the end of August 2025; described by John Kiriakou as "one of the greatest Iran scholars on the planet."

seal-team-six-attrition.title: Bin Laden health rumors
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: False flags are too hard
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The cave myth
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The Obama recruitment thesis
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou''s public explanation of what happened to Barack Obama: not that the CIA created him, but that a first-term senator with no national security experience is exactly the kind of president the agency wants, and that the first briefing several levels above top secret is enough to hook him. Kiriakou supports the reading with two quotations Obama gave to reporters, including that he never had any idea he would be so good at killing people.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The Taliban lobbyist in Washington
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: A story put to John Kiriakou about a Taliban delegation''s American press conference and the Washington lobbyist who represented them. Kiriakou remembered the episode and the lobbyist''s New Jersey base but not the claim about her parentage, and explained why it caused so little controversy at the time: the United States had no historical quarrel with the Taliban, and had armed and fêted some of its future members during the war against the Soviets.

seal-team-six-attrition.title: The torture memo signature
seal-team-six-attrition.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the CIA''s torture programme was authorised: a list of about ten techniques sent from headquarters through the Justice Department, the National Security Council lawyers and Condoleezza Rice to the president — who, to the surprise of the agency''s own leadership, signed it. Kiriakou recalls the deputy director saying three times in one meeting that he could not believe the president had signed the memo.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: The jury consultant''s advice
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: What John Kiriakou''s jury consultant told him about a national security trial in the Eastern District of Virginia: that in any other district in America he would say fight and win, but in that one, "buddy, you don''t have a prayer. Take the deal."

sealing-the-courtroom.title: The swimming pool substitution
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of how classified words are handled at trial: prosecutors and judge agree in advance to replace them with harmless unclassified substitutes, so that "Vault 7" becomes "swimming pool" — and the jury, told the real words are too secret for their ears, concludes the defendant must be guilty.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: Assange and the European Court of Human Rights
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: The last legal avenue John Kiriakou identified for Julian Assange in 2022 — three precedents in which the Strasbourg court refused to let Britain extradite mentally ill defendants to American solitary confinement — and the procedural trap that made it useless: Britain said the appeal need not halt the extradition.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: Julian Assange
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: Eastern District of Virginia
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

sealing-the-courtroom.title: The CIPA hearing in Kiriakou's case
sealing-the-courtroom.summary: The closed pre-trial proceeding under the Classified Information Procedures Act at which John Kiriakou's defence filed seventy motions to declassify the material it needed to mount a defence, and the judge denied all seventy at once. Kiriakou describes the ruling as the moment the case ended — his lead attorney told him on the way out of the courtroom that they had just lost — and as the point at which plea negotiations began.

sebastian-gorka.title: Rudy Giuliani
sebastian-gorka.summary: Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York and Mayor of New York City; in 2018 attempted to extort $2 million from John Kiriakou in exchange for arranging a presidential pardon from President Trump; the attempt was reported to the New York Times by Kiriakou himself and corroborated by Giuliani's then-aide Noelle Dunphy after Giuliani sexually harassed her.

sebastian-gorka.title: Bruce Fein
sebastian-gorka.summary: John Kiriakou's longtime attorney and one of his closest friends; a Harvard Law-trained constitutional scholar, former Deputy Attorney General under President Reagan and former General Counsel of the Federal Communications Commission. Fein took the call from Jared Kushner's attorney that opened Kiriakou's first pardon track, sat beside him at the 2018 Trump International Hotel meeting at which Rudy Giuliani's aide solicited $2 million for a presidential pardon, and is his co-author on a long-planned book about the CIA's record of failure.

sebastian-gorka.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
sebastian-gorka.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

sebastian-gorka.title: Robert MacLean
sebastian-gorka.summary: TSA whistleblower; the person to whom John Kiriakou first described Rudy Giuliani's 2018 $2 million pardon-extortion attempt the same evening it occurred, and who in turn tipped the FBI (which declined interest) and then the New York Times.

sebastian-gorka.title: Bernie Kerik
sebastian-gorka.summary: Former New York Police Department Commissioner; the person who, in 2018, introduced John Kiriakou to Rudy Giuliani for what became Giuliani's $2 million pardon-extortion attempt.

sebastian-gorka.title: Central Intelligence Agency
sebastian-gorka.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

second-chance-act.title: FCI Loretto
second-chance-act.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

second-chance-act.title: Mark Lanzalotti
second-chance-act.summary: The prisoner John Kiriakou describes as his closest friend at FCI Loretto and one of the finest human beings he has known — a first-time non-violent drug defendant sentenced to triple life without parole for refusing to inform, the prison's foremost cook and bookie, and the man whose release Kiriakou secured by writing his Second Chance Act petition.

second-chance-act.title: Clint Goswick
second-chance-act.summary: Fellow federal prisoner of John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto; a devout Christian and Wichita Falls, Texas heating-and-air-conditioning business owner convicted of drug conspiracy and a gun charge despite never having used, possessed, manufactured, or distributed drugs.

second-chance-act.title: Dave Phillips
second-chance-act.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

second-chance-act.title: Pete Calabrese
second-chance-act.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

second-chance-act.title: The stinger
second-chance-act.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

secret-service.title: Permanent wartime economy
secret-service.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

secret-service.title: Sara Jane Moore
secret-service.summary: American who attempted to assassinate President Gerald Ford in San Francisco in September 1975, two weeks after Mike Mastrovito of the Secret Service had interviewed her at her apartment regarding a threatening letter she had sent to the president. Per John Kiriakou, the case Mastrovito identified as having ended his Secret Service career.

secret-service.title: John Kiriakou
secret-service.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

secret-service.title: Donald Trump
secret-service.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

secret-service.title: Butler rally shooting
secret-service.summary: The July 2024 attempt on Donald Trump's life at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on which John Kiriakou takes no position as to who was responsible but argues the published facts cannot be reconciled with a competent Secret Service — and that the questions it leaves open are owed an answer for the historical record whether or not anyone alive gets one.

secret-service.title: Abraxas Corporation
secret-service.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

section-702.title: Thomas Drake
section-702.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

section-702.title: Mike Hayden
section-702.summary: Director of the National Security Agency on September 11, 2001; subsequently Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou's relay of NSA whistleblower Tom Drake, on the morning of 9/11 Hayden told NSA personnel the agency had been 'waiting for a 9/11 so that they could implement the bigger program and grab everybody's electronics' — despite the agency's founding charter forbidding it from intercepting the communications of U.S. persons.

section-702.title: NSA Surveillance
section-702.summary: ''It is part of NSA''s founding charter that it is not allowed to spy on Americans'' — Kiriakou on warrantless collection and the Bluffdale warehouse.

section-702.title: Jeffrey Epstein
section-702.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

section-702.title: San Bernardino iPhone Case
section-702.summary: The 2015–16 legal standoff in which Apple refused to unlock the San Bernardino shooter's iPhone for the FBI, which instead paid an Israeli firm $6 million to crack it — though, per John Kiriakou, the intelligence that could have disrupted the attack never came from the phone at all.

section-702.title: FISA court
section-702.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

securedrop.title: Julian Assange
securedrop.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

securedrop.title: Encryption before the key
securedrop.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where encryption actually fails, offered against John McAfee''s claim that no communication can be private. Kiriakou defers to the technologists he knows — Edward Snowden, Bill Binney, Thomas Drake and Kirk Wiebe — who tell him sufficiently sophisticated encryption does work. The exposure is upstream of the cipher: if an agency can reach your machine as you type, before you hit the encryption key, the encryption never gets a chance.

securedrop.title: Meredith Whittaker
securedrop.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Meredith Whittaker is developing a new, and by his account successful, business model for the encrypted-messaging app Signal, an alternative he cites alongside ProtonMail's compromised attempt at the same thing.

securedrop.title: Daniel Hale
securedrop.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

securedrop.title: Edward Snowden
securedrop.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

securedrop.title: Espionage Act
securedrop.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

security-finance-and-medical.title: The Faisalabad cash run
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

security-finance-and-medical.title: Arabic and Greek
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

security-finance-and-medical.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

security-finance-and-medical.title: Curtailment cables
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

security-finance-and-medical.title: The bowl of dates
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

security-finance-and-medical.title: The prostitute hypothetical
security-finance-and-medical.summary: The classroom exercise John Kiriakou uses in university lectures to demonstrate that the CIA gave its operations officers no ethical guidelines at all — a recruited terrorist source who demands a prostitute, and then the same demand for a child.

security-medical-and-finance.title: The General Muhammad equipment gift
security-medical-and-finance.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the end of the Abu Zubaydah operation in Pakistan, when headquarters told him to throw away or hand over the truckloads of equipment his station had bought — and of learning weeks later from his day-to-day Pakistani contact that the brigadier general who accepted the gift had simply taken it all himself.

security-medical-and-finance.title: Business class after 9/11
security-medical-and-finance.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

security-medical-and-finance.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
security-medical-and-finance.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

security-medical-and-finance.title: Agent payment mechanics
security-medical-and-finance.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

security-medical-and-finance.title: Abu Zubaydah
security-medical-and-finance.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

security-medical-and-finance.title: CIA cash room
security-medical-and-finance.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: The merry-go-round prank
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The dirty trick John Kiriakou played on an FCI Loretto prisoner he calls Wallace — planting a release form and a laundry bag on his bunk on a Friday evening, when no official was available to contradict them, and letting him give away his possessions and hold a farewell dinner before he was arrested for attempted escape.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: FCI Loretto
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: The astrophotographer lawyer
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The Philadelphia attorney who represented Ken Schaefer's victim and who, in John Kiriakou's account, was flown to Israel as the guest of a school he had shown his telescope to — and there asked by a government minister to make the case go away.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: Dave Phillips
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

self-destructing-terrorist-cell.title: Ken Schaefer
self-destructing-terrorist-cell.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who told others he was inside for securities irregularities, was in fact convicted of transporting a child for sex, fled to Israel on bail, and — after John Kiriakou exposed and confronted him — offered money to prisoners to have Kiriakou attacked.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: MOSSAD
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: Hawala system
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: Informal, ledger-based money-transfer network used across the Middle East, South Asia, and their diasporas to move funds without involving banks; per John Kiriakou's first-person account of testing one in the UAE — handing $50 to a grocer for a 16-digit number to redeem at an Arabic bakery in Bethesda, Maryland — completely untraceable; identified by Kiriakou (later, as Chief Investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee) as one of the principal channels through which al-Qaeda moved operational money in the post-9/11 period, along with DHL.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: Middle East Forum
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: The publication — 'clearly an Israeli publication,' in John Kiriakou's words, and one he had never heard of before a Google alert surfaced it — that ran a piece by the political adviser to the Israeli foreign minister calling Kiriakou antisemitic and describing his writing as evidence of 'the rot' in the American intellectual left. Kiriakou took the phrase as a compliment and says the episode shows how closely Israel monitors even small independent outlets.

senate-foreign-relations-committee.title: The State Department cover investigation
senate-foreign-relations-committee.summary: One of the inquiries John Kiriakou opened as senior investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, on a reporter's tip that the CIA was placing some of its torturers under State Department cover in violation of the cover agreement between the two departments. He wrote to the State Department asking for clarification. Five or six weeks later a colleague told him a reply had come and had been classified above his clearance; asked what it said, the colleague summarised it as an obscenity. That was the end of the investigation.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Dianne Feinstein
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. Per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — an unusually friendly chairwoman who exercised no real oversight, good on torture and a cheerleader for the CIA on everything else. She co-authored the 2015 McCain-Feinstein Amendment that reiterated the federal ban on torture, and she blocked Gina Haspel's promotion in 2013 before publicly warming to her in 2018.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Senate Torture Report
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Bureau of Prisons
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: Human Rights Watch
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: The organization whose 2005 report that the CIA was torturing its prisoners — two years before John Kiriakou''s ABC interview — anchors his defense that he confirmed rather than revealed the program. In his account of his own arrest, Human Rights Watch also sits inside the fateful chain of custody: when the FBI traced a classified name found in its hands, the trail ran to journalist Matthew Cole, and Cole named Kiriakou — bringing two dozen FBI agents to his door.

senate-intelligence-committee.title: John Kiriakou
senate-intelligence-committee.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

senate-torture-report.title: The cremation footnote
senate-torture-report.summary: A footnote John Kiriakou cites from the declassified executive summary of the Senate torture report, stating that Abu Zubaydah will never be permitted to leave Guantanamo — despite never having joined al-Qaeda, never having pledged fealty to Osama bin Laden and never having been charged — and that on his death the CIA will cremate his body and scatter the ashes at sea.

senate-torture-report.title: Jane Harman
senate-torture-report.summary: Former U.S. Representative from California who served as ranking member and later chair of the House Intelligence Committee. Per John Kiriakou, Harman was present in the room when congressional leadership was briefed on the CIA's enhanced interrogation program; when reporters later asked her about the program, she denied knowing about it. Kiriakou told the New York Times she had been in the room, after which Harman revised her account to say she had left early and that an aide remained as a notetaker.

senate-torture-report.title: Strawberry Fields
senate-torture-report.summary: The CIA's nickname for a secret black-site annex at the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base used for the post-9/11 detention and interrogation program.

senate-torture-report.title: Ticking time bomb scenario
senate-torture-report.summary: The hypothetical case — an imminent attack only the captured terrorist's confession can prevent — used to justify the CIA's post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; characterized by John Kiriakou as fictional and not corresponding to any real-world case.

senate-torture-report.title: Witness K case
senate-torture-report.summary: Australian intelligence scandal in which a former ASIS officer known as Witness K exposed Australia's bugging of the East Timorese cabinet during oil and gas revenue negotiations; his lawyer, Bernard Collaery, describes the ASIO raids on both their homes and offices as paralleling the FBI's raid on John Kiriakou.

senate-torture-report.title: Senate Intelligence Committee
senate-torture-report.summary: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence — the CIA's designated overseer, which John Kiriakou credits with the torture report's unimpeachable method (6 million contemporaneous CIA field cables) and simultaneously dismisses, along with its House counterpart, as "little more than cheerleaders for the CIA" since the mid-1980s. It sits in the official whistleblower channel he calls a proven dead end, and its own investigation was famously spied on by the very agency it oversees.

senior-executive-service.title: Central Intelligence Agency
senior-executive-service.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

senior-executive-service.title: Church Committee
senior-executive-service.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

senior-executive-service.title: Pike Committee
senior-executive-service.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

senior-executive-service.title: National Intelligence Council
senior-executive-service.summary: Body housed at the CIA comprising the most senior analysts drawn from across the entire intelligence community. Its officers — National Intelligence Officers (NIOs) — hold positions at the Senior Intelligence Service level and are responsible for long-range strategic analysis on specific portfolio areas, as well as the production of National Intelligence Estimates. Per John Kiriakou, learning that the NIO for Warning had held the same job for forty-two years and just received a waiver to stay until seventy was the moment he first believed in the existence of the deep state.

senior-executive-service.title: Abu Zubaydah
senior-executive-service.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

senior-executive-service.title: AIPAC
senior-executive-service.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Jennifer Matthews
senior-intelligence-service.summary: CIA analyst who was made chief of base at Khost, Afghanistan without operational or security training in order to complete the tour requirement for promotion, and who was killed there with six other officers by a Jordanian double agent she had gone outside the fortified perimeter to greet with a birthday cake.

senior-intelligence-service.title: John Brennan
senior-intelligence-service.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

senior-intelligence-service.title: National Security Council
senior-intelligence-service.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Chief of station
senior-intelligence-service.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Jose Rodriguez
senior-intelligence-service.summary: Senior CIA officer of the post-9/11 era; identified by John Kiriakou as among those responsible for crimes committed in the name of national security; described as believing himself to be a good guy.

senior-intelligence-service.title: Forward Operating Base Chapman Attack
senior-intelligence-service.summary: December 30, 2009 suicide bombing at Forward Operating Base Chapman in Khost, Afghanistan, killing seven CIA officers and wounding more than a dozen others — the deadliest single day in CIA history. Per John Kiriakou, the officer who led the base was a GS-14 with zero security training, assigned to the post as a career-promotion checkbox before her required elevation to the Senior Intelligence Service. The bomber — a Jordanian national who walked into the American consulate in Istanbul claiming to be Osama bin Laden's doctor — was never polygraphed because CIA personnel 'wanted so badly for this to be true.'

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Over-classification
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why the American government classifies far more than it can ever review: not conspiracy but incentive. At lesser agencies a classification stamp is a status marker — it puts you in the in-crowd and above the colleague who lacks access — and at the CIA everything carries a stamp by default. His complaint about press coverage of classified-document scandals is that it never reaches the underlying question of why the documents were secret at all.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Espionage Act
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Classified email
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: John Kiriakou was serving overseas the day classified email was introduced at the CIA, and remembers his station chief saying there was no way to control it. His own illustration of what followed is a lunch invitation to his wife — a fellow senior CIA officer — marked Secret HUM 4-82, and her reply naming a deli and a time, marked the same way.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: The mosaic concept
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: The intelligence method John Kiriakou names for assembling a complete operational picture out of individually trivial fragments — one tile at a time, worthless alone, decisive together. He attributes the idea to Soviet thinking of the 1960s, cites Mossad's Iranian networks as the clearest modern demonstration, and warns that the same logic is what would let an American prosecutor charge a scholar with espionage for reading declassified documents.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: The 2023 classified documents scandal
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: The run of discoveries of classified material in the private possession of Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Mike Pence, which John Kiriakou treats not as a scandal about any of them but as proof that the Espionage Act as currently applied makes almost everyone technically guilty. He rates Pence's briefing books as more highly classified than anything Julian Assange published, and says Biden's Senate-era documents are the ones that cannot be explained away.

sensitive-but-unclassified.title: Carrying classified material out of a SCIF
sensitive-but-unclassified.summary: The two lawful procedures John Kiriakou describes for removing classified documents from a secure facility — a double-enveloped, double-marked package addressed to your home agency, or a leather bag with a double lock — and his flat statement that nothing about either allows a document to be forgotten in a garage for twelve years.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Joshua Schulte
sentencing-enhancements.summary: Former CIA Directorate of Science and Technology engineer; source of the 2017 Vault 7 WikiLeaks disclosure of the agency's offensive technical capabilities; currently serving a 40-year federal sentence for espionage; maintains his innocence.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Espionage Act
sentencing-enhancements.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Brad Birkenfeld
sentencing-enhancements.summary: The UBS banking whistleblower, who was prosecuted and imprisoned before winning a $104 million settlement from the Treasury Department and spending it on the legal defence of other whistleblowers. John Kiriakou uses him as the measure of the gap between financial and national-security whistleblowing, and names him among the visitors whose devices he believes were copied at the Ecuadorian embassy in London.

sentencing-enhancements.title: The Charles Littlejohn prosecution
sentencing-enhancements.summary: The five-year sentence handed to an IRS contractor who disclosed Donald Trump's tax returns to the New York Times, which John Kiriakou calls stunning and unjustified — the material was protected but not classified, the Biden campaign made use of it, and the sentencing judge compared the disclosure to the January 6 attack on the Capitol.

sentencing-enhancements.title: Chelsea Manning
sentencing-enhancements.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

sentencing-enhancements.title: CIA adultery culture
sentencing-enhancements.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Five per cent of the population, twenty-five per cent of the prisoners
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The statistic John Kiriakou returns to from inside prison — that the United States holds five per cent of the world''s people and a quarter of its prisoners, more per head than Russia, China or Iran — and the causes he assigns: the war on drugs, election-year lawmaking, and a Congress creating some fifty new crimes a year.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Administrative remedy process
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Bureau of Prisons
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: The glyburide incident
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The episode John Kiriakou described in a Letter from Loretto of 12 September 2014: handed a bottle of glyburide by the prison pharmacy without explanation, he crashed twice and passed out on the floor — and his physician father-in-law told him the drug could have put him into heart failure.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Kiriakou on mass incarceration
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: The argument Kiriakou developed in the letters from Loretto and has repeated since: that the United States holds a quarter of the world''s prisoners with five per cent of its people, that the cause is the drug war and election-year legislating, and that reform died in the Senate without a vote.

sentencing-reform-bills.title: Medical care in federal prison
sentencing-reform-bills.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

sergey-lavrov.title: China as economic threat
sergey-lavrov.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

sergey-lavrov.title: Afghan heroin policy
sergey-lavrov.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

sergey-lavrov.title: Tony Blinken
sergey-lavrov.summary: American secretary of state under Joe Biden, and a former colleague of John Kiriakou's on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Kiriakou calls him a very nice man but holds that he owed the office to three decades of proximity to Biden rather than to being the most capable strategist the United States could have identified — an example of what he calls poor leadership.

sergey-lavrov.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
sergey-lavrov.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

sergey-lavrov.title: Permanent wartime economy
sergey-lavrov.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

sergey-lavrov.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
sergey-lavrov.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Tulsi Gabbard
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Bill Clinton
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: 2026 Iran war
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Executive Order 12333
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.title: Gulf consultations before the Iran war
serving-at-the-pleasure-of-the-president.summary: John Kiriakou's account of travelling in Kuwait, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Doha in the weeks before the 2026 strikes on Iran, and finding that the United States had made no diplomatic case to its Gulf partners at all — in sharp contrast to the worldwide campaign that preceded the Iraq war. He told a senior Emirati royal that two carrier strike groups meant an attack was coming.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Depression in prison
seven-thousand-letters.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Passing time at Loretto
seven-thousand-letters.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Dave Phillips
seven-thousand-letters.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

seven-thousand-letters.title: FCI Loretto
seven-thousand-letters.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

seven-thousand-letters.title: Legal mail
seven-thousand-letters.summary: The privileged correspondence category John Kiriakou used to smuggle the Letters from Loretto and the manuscript of his book out of prison — addressed to his attorney Jesselyn Radack and marked legal mail, which staff were forbidden to open.

seven-thousand-letters.title: The rat and pedophile table
seven-thousand-letters.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: "Ecuador is open for business"
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: The Wall Street Journal headline John Kiriakou says appeared the day after he hand-delivered a letter to Ecuador's ambassador in Washington asking that Julian Assange's internet access be restored, and which made him fear Assange was about to be used as a bargaining chip.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: Eastern District of Virginia
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: Julian Assange
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: Leonie Brinkema
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

seventy-two-denied-motions.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
seventy-two-denied-motions.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

sewer-trout.title: The dog food memo
sewer-trout.summary: The internal announcement circulated by the warden of FCI Loretto apologising for having served prisoners dog food on a taco night, which John Kiriakou cites as evidence not of the error but of how bad the ordinary food was — because nobody noticed.

sewer-trout.title: FCI Loretto
sewer-trout.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

sewer-trout.title: Cell transfers at Loretto
sewer-trout.summary: How a prisoner at FCI Loretto moved from one cell to another — a process requiring six months in place, the written agreement of the receiving cell and the signature of the counselor, which John Kiriakou describes as a guard assigned to be a designated pain in the ass.

sewer-trout.title: Cleanliness in prison
sewer-trout.summary: John Kiriakou's account of hygiene and order at FCI Loretto — where everybody showered daily on pain of a beating, everybody was constantly cleaning, and the rules on possessions and bedmaking left almost no room for clutter.

sewer-trout.title: The rat and pedophile table
sewer-trout.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

sewer-trout.title: The stinger
sewer-trout.summary: The improvised prison cooking rig John Kiriakou describes at FCI Loretto — a wall-plug faceplate wired to live current and dropped into a bucket of water — which produced restaurant-quality Italian food daily and, on one occasion, killed a correctional officer.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Saint Nectarios of Aegina
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Early-20th-century Greek Orthodox saint whom John Kiriakou identifies with more than any other and carries a photograph of in his wallet; falsely accused and driven from his post, Nectarios forgave his accusers, and posthumous miracles led to his canonization.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Sharia law
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Islamic jurisprudence. Challenged by a viewer who equated it with executions of gay people, forced child marriage and the criminalisation of apostasy, John Kiriakou answers that those acts are largely the work of ISIS rather than of any government, and that Sharia is in substance a body of civil law covering inheritance, insurance, education, property ownership and commercial disputes.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: 2028 presidential field
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Andrew Bustamante
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

seyyed-hossein-nasr.title: Angry Birds
seyyed-hossein-nasr.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

shank-planting-incident.title: Dave Phillips
shank-planting-incident.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who claimed to have been a CIA operations officer and whom John Kiriakou exposed as a fake by testing him on agency vocabulary — a possessive, risk-taking companion who planted shanks on a pedophile, was caught, and was shipped to another prison.

shank-planting-incident.title: Ken Schaefer
shank-planting-incident.summary: The FCI Loretto prisoner who told others he was inside for securities irregularities, was in fact convicted of transporting a child for sex, fled to Israel on bail, and — after John Kiriakou exposed and confronted him — offered money to prisoners to have Kiriakou attacked.

shank-planting-incident.title: Passing time at Loretto
shank-planting-incident.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

shank-planting-incident.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the condition he says everybody inside has, and the three-part regime he set against it — eating right, exercising daily and finding a distraction — which in his own case meant more than a hundred books, 7,000 letters and a book written in longhand.

shank-planting-incident.title: Seven thousand letters
shank-planting-incident.summary: The correspondence John Kiriakou conducted from FCI Loretto — 7,000 letters to 675 different people over 23 months, begun because of an unsolicited postcard of a rose that reached him four hours into his sentence.

sharia-law.title: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
sharia-law.summary: The scholar of Islamic philosophy under whom John Kiriakou studied Shiism as an undergraduate. Kiriakou calls him probably the most important Shia Muslim scholar in the world, notes that he is the father of Vali Nasr, and remarks that at ninety-eight he is still teaching.

sharia-law.title: 2028 presidential field
sharia-law.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

sharia-law.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
sharia-law.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

sharia-law.title: Andrew Bustamante
sharia-law.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

sharia-law.title: Angry Birds
sharia-law.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

sharia-law.title: CIA intelligence failures
sharia-law.summary: John Kiriakou's standing position that the CIA has missed every major world event since its founding in 1947 — the building and the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Iran hostage crisis, 9/11 — and that the remedy is therefore not more money but fewer overseas bases and actual accountability, of which he says there has been none.

sharon-scranage.title: Plato Cacheris
sharon-scranage.summary: Legendary Washington, D.C. defense attorney who served as John Kiriakou''s lead counsel in his 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution. Per Kiriakou, when discovery revealed the FBI had run a fake-diplomat sting against him, Cacheris explained the government''s posture bluntly: ''Because they have a shit case and they know it''s shit, and that''s why we''re going to trial.'' He spent most of the case urging trial, then drove to Kiriakou''s house on decision day and said ''You stupid son of a bitch — take the deal.'' Cacheris also represented FBI spy Robert Hanssen.

sharon-scranage.title: Bob Trout
sharon-scranage.summary: Washington defense attorney, Plato Cacheris''s partner at Trout Cacheris, and one of the eleven lawyers who represented John Kiriakou: the "elegant southern gentleman" who told him, "If you were my own brother, I would beg you to take this deal."

sharon-scranage.title: FCI Loretto
sharon-scranage.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

sharon-scranage.title: John Kiriakou
sharon-scranage.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

sharon-scranage.title: Mark McDougall
sharon-scranage.summary: U.S. criminal defense attorney; part of John Kiriakou's defense team in the 2012–2013 Espionage Act prosecution; the attorney whose framing of the case — "your problem is you think this is about justice and it's not about justice; it's about mitigating damage" — Kiriakou credits as the argument that persuaded him to take the final plea deal.

sharon-scranage.title: Abu Zubaydah
sharon-scranage.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: Sheikh Saad al-Abdullah
sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.summary: Crown Prince and Prime Minister of Kuwait during the 1990–91 Iraqi occupation; per John Kiriakou, the day-to-day leader of the Kuwaiti government-in-exile in Taif — "very military," "hands-on," "the best leader Kuwait had for that situation," meeting twenty hours a day with everyone who needed to be met and simultaneously managing the Kuwaiti resistance on the ground.

sheikh-jaber-al-ahmad.title: Skip Gnehm
