Kiriakou says a group of illegals was broken up by the FBI in his own Arlington, Virginia neighbourhood and traded for American spies, and that he knows a former KGB sleeper in Brooklyn who refused activation after the birth of his daughter.

spy-films-on-screen.title: Tony Mendez
spy-films-on-screen.summary: The CIA exfiltration specialist who got the American diplomats sheltering in the Canadian embassy out of revolutionary Tehran in 1979 by inventing a fake science-fiction film production — the operation dramatised in *Argo*. John Kiriakou calls him "a giant in the history of the CIA", says the same of his wife, and rates the operation among the greatest the agency has ever carried out.

st-nectarios-of-aegina.title: Greek Intelligence Service
st-nectarios-of-aegina.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

st-nectarios-of-aegina.title: John Kiriakou
st-nectarios-of-aegina.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

st-nectarios-of-aegina.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
st-nectarios-of-aegina.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

st-nectarios-of-aegina.title: Seyyed Hossein Nasr
st-nectarios-of-aegina.summary: The scholar of Islamic philosophy under whom John Kiriakou studied Shiism as an undergraduate. Kiriakou calls him probably the most important Shia Muslim scholar in the world, notes that he is the father of Vali Nasr, and remarks that at ninety-eight he is still teaching.

st-nectarios-of-aegina.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
st-nectarios-of-aegina.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

st-nectarios-of-aegina.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
st-nectarios-of-aegina.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

st-porphyrios-church-gaza.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
st-porphyrios-church-gaza.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

st-porphyrios-church-gaza.title: John Kiriakou
st-porphyrios-church-gaza.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

st-porphyrios-church-gaza.title: Taybeh
st-porphyrios-church-gaza.summary: The only fully Christian village in the West Bank, home to the Holy Land's oldest brewery; John Kiriakou recounts it being set on fire and its Marian festival attacked by the IDF with drones, helicopters and stun grenades.

st-porphyrios-church-gaza.title: Shireen Abu Akleh
st-porphyrios-church-gaza.summary: Al Jazeera journalist, U.S. citizen and Greek Orthodox Christian; John Kiriakou recounts that she was shot in the face by an Israeli sniper while wearing clearly marked press gear, and that the IDF then beat pallbearers at her funeral.

st-porphyrios-church-gaza.title: Jerry Falwell Jr.
st-porphyrios-church-gaza.summary: Evangelical leader and former president of Liberty University; John Kiriakou recounts that Falwell personally recruited him to lecture at Liberty's Jesse Helms School of Government after his whistleblowing, with the reasoning that "torture is not Christian."

st-porphyrios-church-gaza.title: King Abdullah II of Jordan
st-porphyrios-church-gaza.summary: The Jordanian monarch whom John Kiriakou rates as knowing more about the Middle East than anyone else who leads or studies it, and as almost never wrong across twenty-five years of foreign-policy predictions. Kiriakou recounts the deathbed succession that made him king against his own expectations, and his refusal after October 7 to accept Palestinian refugees on the grounds that doing so would deliver Israel the ethnic cleansing it wanted.

stansfield-turner.title: John McCone
stansfield-turner.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency on November 22, 1963; per John Kiriakou's retelling of an account from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., responded to Bobby Kennedy Sr.'s same-day question "Tell me your people didn't do this" not with denial but with "I don't know who did it."

stansfield-turner.title: Jerrold Post
stansfield-turner.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

stansfield-turner.title: Central Intelligence Agency
stansfield-turner.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

stansfield-turner.title: CIA Political Psychology Division
stansfield-turner.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency unit founded by Dr. Gerald Post in the 1970s to produce long-distance psychiatric evaluations of foreign leaders

stansfield-turner.title: Cofer Black
stansfield-turner.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

stansfield-turner.title: Colin Powell
stansfield-turner.summary: U.S. Secretary of State whose 2003 UN testimony made the case for the Iraq war; John Kiriakou says the white powder in Powell's prop tube was nothing, and that Powell's own chief of staff later told him the presentation was knowingly 'sold.'

state-department-cover-agreement.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
state-department-cover-agreement.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

state-department-cover-agreement.title: Brian Ross
state-department-cover-agreement.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

state-department-cover-agreement.title: John Kiriakou
state-department-cover-agreement.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

state-department-cover-agreement.title: Abu Zubaydah
state-department-cover-agreement.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

state-department-cover-agreement.title: David Petraeus
state-department-cover-agreement.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

state-department-cover-agreement.title: Espionage Act
state-department-cover-agreement.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

stephen-saunders.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
stephen-saunders.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

stephen-saunders.title: John Kiriakou
stephen-saunders.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

stephen-saunders.title: Carlos the Jackal
stephen-saunders.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

stephen-saunders.title: Richard Welch
stephen-saunders.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

stephen-saunders.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
stephen-saunders.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

stephen-saunders.title: Heather Saunders
stephen-saunders.summary: Widow of British Brigadier General Stephen Saunders, the British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November on April 22, 2000; per John Kiriakou, the person whose post-assassination Greek-television statement — "this organization is not a political organization nor is it a phantom group; it's a gang of criminals" — for the first time since 17 November's 1975 founding turned Greek public opinion against the group.

steve-kappes.title: Yemen
steve-kappes.summary: Country on the southern Arabian Peninsula; setting of five John Kiriakou trips between 1990 and approximately 2010, spanning the country's brief unification, its civil war, and its present condition as a high-threat operating environment for U.S. and allied diplomatic personnel.

steve-kappes.title: Abu Zubaydah
steve-kappes.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

steve-kappes.title: AIPAC
steve-kappes.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

steve-kappes.title: Barack Obama
steve-kappes.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

steve-kappes.title: Bilderberg and weapon sales
steve-kappes.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, sourced to someone he knew who attended, that elite gatherings like Bilderberg and the Shangri-La Dialogue are — beneath the talk of global issues — fundamentally 'all about weapon sales' and defense-contractor deals.

steve-kappes.title: Church Committee
steve-kappes.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

steven-lalas.title: Greek Intelligence Service
steven-lalas.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

steven-lalas.title: Aldrich Ames
steven-lalas.summary: Senior CIA officer — a GS-15 who rose to chief of counterintelligence for the Soviet branch — who spied for the KGB. Per John Kiriakou, Ames's first act of betrayal was selling the identities of two CIA agents to the Russians for $50,000 to pay off a credit-card debt; both agents were immediately executed. He ultimately caused the deaths of twelve people, accumulated $2 million, bought a house in Arlington for that amount, drove a Jaguar to work on a $70,000 salary, and built an in-ground pool with a gazebo — all while being known throughout the office as a daily drunk. A 27-year-old officer sat on the initial security file for eighteen months. Analyst Sandy Grimes ultimately caught him.

steven-lalas.title: Bahrain fishing officer demarche
steven-lalas.summary: Kiriakou's account of serving, while stationed in Bahrain, as the embassy's econ officer and by extension its fishing, banking, aviation, and environment officer — including delivering a formal U.S. demarche to Bahrain's deputy foreign minister over a U.S.-Canada dispute about whether clams legally count as fish.

steven-lalas.title: Beirut
steven-lalas.summary: The Lebanese capital John Kiriakou confirms was a genuine espionage playground — though he dates the peak to the 1950s through the mid-1970s, when Beirut was the Paris and the banking centre of the Middle East, and when, beneath the CIA, KGB and Israeli presence, "more secretly the French ran the place." He also explains why the enormous new American embassy there is about fortification rather than a regional CIA headquarters.

steven-lalas.title: Below World's End
steven-lalas.summary: Film in which John Kiriakou made his acting debut, filmed entirely in Mexico during October 2025; Kiriakou's performance earned him a Screen Actors Guild membership card, and Sean Penn told him after a private screening that he had unknowingly been acting throughout his entire CIA career.

steven-lalas.title: Big Assawoman Bay NASA launch
steven-lalas.summary: John Kiriakou's account of being taken, as a junior CIA analyst, to watch a NASA rocket launch near the village of Big Assawoman on Virginia's Eastern Shore, where he was startled to find foreign space-agency officials present unsupervised.

strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.title: Al-Qaeda training manual interrogation-resistance tactics
strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.summary: A captured al-Qaeda training manual instructing operatives on how to resist interrogation, including feigning illness — a technique John Kiriakou says he saw a detainee use, and recognized, during a capture and interrogation in Pakistan.

strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.title: China's base in Djibouti
strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.title: CIA and the UFO question
strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.summary: John Kiriakou's consistent answer that UFOs and alien technology are a Pentagon matter, not a CIA one — though he says nearly every former fighter-pilot friend of his has seen something inexplicable, sometimes emerging from the ocean.

strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.title: Guantanamo Bay
strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.title: Iran 12-Day War
strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.title: Irish intelligence services
strait-of-hormuz-transit-fees.summary: Ireland's intelligence and law-enforcement services, which John Kiriakou toured and met with during a speaking trip to Belfast, Cork, Dublin, and Waterford. Per Kiriakou, Irish intelligence and the Garda are especially strong at anti-money-laundering investigation and counterterrorism — the latter traced, he says, to the large number of Irish militants trained by Carlos the Jackal in Libya and Lebanon during the 1970s.

strait-of-hormuz.title: 2026 Iran war
strait-of-hormuz.summary: The open-ended American and Israeli war against Iran that John Kiriakou tracked week by week on his own show — a conflict he says was sold as three weeks, ran into its fifth month, achieved every decapitation objective it set, and continued anyway. His grade for it is a D, and his forecast is a Truth Social post declaring victory while nothing changes.

strait-of-hormuz.title: Lindsey Graham
strait-of-hormuz.summary: Republican senator from South Carolina who died in July 2026, and John Kiriakou's standing shorthand for the permanent war caucus — a "show horse" rather than a workhorse, a "chameleon" who "never saw a war that he didn't want to jump into with both feet," and, on posthumously released documentary footage, a man offering the US Air Force to bomb a country America was not at war with.

strait-of-hormuz.title: Abraham Accords
strait-of-hormuz.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

strait-of-hormuz.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
strait-of-hormuz.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

strait-of-hormuz.title: China's base in Djibouti
strait-of-hormuz.summary: Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, the abandoned French base the Djiboutians offered to the Americans and the Chinese took a share of — split down the middle by a chain-link fence, the only Chinese military installation outside China, and the centrepiece of John Kiriakou's argument that China is not an expansionist power.

strait-of-hormuz.title: John Kiriakou's Briefing Room
strait-of-hormuz.summary: A twice-weekly news and commentary programme launched by John Kiriakou in July 2026, presented as analysis rather than partisan opinion, and distinct from his storytelling podcast Dead Drop.

strategic-patience.title: American missile stockpiles
strategic-patience.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States has run its interceptor stocks down to the point of strategic vulnerability — that the conventional wisdom in Washington was that a round of the Iran war ended because the Patriots ran out, and that a country which cannot fight a two-front war certainly cannot do it below maximum production.

strategic-patience.title: The Iron Dome
strategic-patience.summary: Israel's air-defence system as John Kiriakou reads it — impressive against a wave of slow Iranian drones, but shown by the handful that got through, and later by Iranian ballistic missiles, to be not all it is cracked up to be; each exchange, in his account, buying Iran intelligence about the gaps.

strategic-patience.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
strategic-patience.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

strategic-patience.title: Netanyahu's nuclear threat to Trump
strategic-patience.summary: John Kiriakou's account, sourced to friends in the White House and the administration, that Donald Trump agreed to bomb Iran because Benjamin Netanyahu threatened to use nuclear weapons against Iran if the United States did not act. Kiriakou presents it as the reason a request every previous president refused was finally granted.

strategic-patience.title: Composition of the Saudi military
strategic-patience.summary: John Kiriakou's long-standing claim that there are almost no Saudi nationals in the Saudi armed forces below the most senior ranks, and that the rank and file are Pakistanis hired from among Pakistan's poor. He treats it as a standing joke in the Gulf and as a limit on what Saudi Arabia can contribute to any war with Iran.

strategic-patience.title: Antisemitism and anti-Zionism
strategic-patience.summary: The conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with hatred of Jews, which John Kiriakou describes as a worldwide confusion and, according to a young Israeli he spoke to, an explicit lesson of the Israeli school system; a subject Kiriakou says he personally struggles with.

strawberry-fields.title: Guantanamo Bay
strawberry-fields.summary: U.S. naval base in Cuba; site of CIA detention operations during the post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; briefly served by John Kiriakou as interim Chief during the summer of 2002.

strawberry-fields.title: Senate Torture Report
strawberry-fields.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

strawberry-fields.title: Hummus
strawberry-fields.summary: The CIA's coercive 'rectal feeding' of detainees using pureed hummus — an unauthorized interrogation technique used at post-9/11 black sites, exposed in the 2014 Senate Torture Report, and the abuse for which John Kiriakou became most associated in popular culture.

strawberry-fields.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
strawberry-fields.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

strawberry-fields.title: Sleep deprivation
strawberry-fields.summary: A CIA interrogation technique used against high-value detainees post-9/11; the agency was authorized to deny prisoners sleep for up to 12 days continuously; people died; at least one detainee was rendered permanently clinically insane.

strawberry-fields.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
strawberry-fields.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

suggested-responses.title: The pre-interview
suggested-responses.summary: The booking practice John Kiriakou says all the American television networks use and which he finds maddening: an invitation to appear, a quick pre-interview to establish what he thinks, and then a call a minute later saying they have decided to go a different way on the story.

suggested-responses.title: The convicted felon introduction
suggested-responses.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

suggested-responses.title: The NPR walkout
suggested-responses.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

suggested-responses.title: Consulting for royal families
suggested-responses.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

suggested-responses.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
suggested-responses.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

suggested-responses.title: Signing with CAA
suggested-responses.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

suicide-watch-protocol.title: Prison guard hiring standards
suicide-watch-protocol.summary: John Kiriakou's account of what it takes to become a federal prison guard — a GED or work towards one, and no felony convictions — and his supporting anecdote that prisoners themselves regularly had to conduct mail call because the officer assigned to it could not read.

suicide-watch-protocol.title: Medical care in federal prison
suicide-watch-protocol.summary: Kiriakou's account of health care at FCI Loretto, where a bunkmate's months of reported chest pain ended in a heart attack, a prisoner with untreated back pain was diagnosed with terminal cancer weeks before he died, and Kiriakou himself collapsed after being handed a drug nobody had explained to him.

suicide-watch-protocol.title: Bureau of Prisons
suicide-watch-protocol.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

suicide-watch-protocol.title: Business class after 9/11
suicide-watch-protocol.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of what the post-attack money did to the CIA''s habits: Cofer Black telling him to just do whatever operation he was proposing because there was so much money it could not possibly be spent, and everyone at the agency flying business class from then on, anywhere in the world.

suicide-watch-protocol.title: ''Don''t try to save the government money''
suicide-watch-protocol.summary: The instruction John Kiriakou says a CIA supervisor gave him for parking in the nine-dollar economy lot at Dulles instead of the twenty-five-dollar daily lot, and the two trips it produced: a Pittsburgh approach funded entirely by a five-dollar bill, and a $195 fattoush salad in a Dubai nightclub.

suicide-watch-protocol.title: The General Muhammad equipment gift
suicide-watch-protocol.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the end of the Abu Zubaydah operation in Pakistan, when headquarters told him to throw away or hand over the truckloads of equipment his station had bought — and of learning weeks later from his day-to-day Pakistani contact that the brigadier general who accepted the gift had simply taken it all himself.

superdelegates.title: George McGovern
superdelegates.summary: The 1972 Democratic presidential nominee, whose landslide defeat John Kiriakou identifies as the pretext for creating superdelegates. As a George Washington University sophomore in 1983, Kiriakou wrote to McGovern offering the campus theater for a campaign launch; McGovern telephoned him personally, announced his 1984 candidacy there, and afterwards took him home for tuna sandwiches made by his wife.

superdelegates.title: Tulsi Gabbard
superdelegates.summary: U.S. Director of National Intelligence; a longtime family friend of John Kiriakou's, who has known her since she was 12; Kiriakou calls her appointment "an inspired choice" despite disagreeing with her decision to join the Republican Party, and says she appears to have given up her opposition to Section 702 surveillance to secure Senate confirmation.

superdelegates.title: 9/11 plea agreements
superdelegates.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.

superdelegates.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
superdelegates.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

superdelegates.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
superdelegates.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

superdelegates.title: Iraq War Israeli tower sabotage
superdelegates.summary: Per John Kiriakou, after the U.S. rejected Israel's request to join the coalition for the Iraq War in late 2002/early 2003 — fearing the loss of Jordanian, Egyptian, and Saudi cooperation — communications towers across the western Iraqi desert began being toppled by explosives; when the New York Times asked the CIA if Israel was responsible, the agency denied any Israeli involvement.

supervised-release-travel-restrictions.title: The Virginia pardon and voting rights
supervised-release-travel-restrictions.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying to have his voting rights restored in Virginia after leaving prison and receiving, unasked, a full state pardon delivered by courier from the office of Governor Terry McAuliffe — followed by a courthouse clerk and a state employee who between them got him registered in time to vote.

supervised-release-travel-restrictions.title: The Club Fed myth
supervised-release-travel-restrictions.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing objection to the phrase ''Club Fed'' and the idea that federal prison is a soft landing for white-collar convicts: there is no such thing, he says, no golf and no gardening, only an institution designed to humiliate and emasculate and to make a man count the days.

supervised-release-travel-restrictions.title: The halfway house
supervised-release-travel-restrictions.summary: The re-entry stage of a federal sentence — up to twelve months of it by law, in practice a fortnight before conversion to house arrest — which John Kiriakou was denied entirely for writing about prison conditions from inside, and which he describes as a system designed to make released prisoners fail.

supervised-release-travel-restrictions.title: Home confinement
supervised-release-travel-restrictions.summary: The house arrest that followed John Kiriakou's release from prison — 87 days confined to the interior of his own house, telephone checks at any hour of the day or night, weekly halfway-house reporting and twice-weekly drug testing — which he describes as considerably worse than prison, and would rather have traded back for the cell. In federal sentencing arithmetic it is also one of the deductions that turns a headline number into the time actually served.

supervised-release-travel-restrictions.title: The culling of friendships
supervised-release-travel-restrictions.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of what happened to his private life after he confirmed the CIA''s torture program: friends and even family members began walking away from him before any charge was filed, a process he came to regard, oddly, as a culling exercise that dispatched phonies and left the people who genuinely loved him.

supervised-release-travel-restrictions.title: The Oz analogy
supervised-release-travel-restrictions.summary: John Kiriakou's habit of explaining federal prison social structure through the HBO drama Oz, in which rival gangs are forced to share a single unit — and his identification with the show's unaffiliated Irish character, who belonged to no faction and survived by playing them off one another.

surveillance-detection-route.title: Abu Zubaydah
surveillance-detection-route.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

surveillance-detection-route.title: The false volunteer
surveillance-detection-route.summary: A walk-in at an American embassy who claimed access to a high-priority target, was placed under surveillance and found to be a restaurant dishwasher, and whom John Kiriakou deliberately intimidated into never approaching an American embassy again.

surveillance-detection-route.title: Counterterrorism Center deaths in the line of duty
surveillance-detection-route.summary: The colleagues John Kiriakou names as having been killed doing the work he did — Helge Boes and Mike Spann of the Counterterrorism Center, and the officer who sat beside him when he was chief of the counterintelligence branch of the Osama bin Laden group, killed with six colleagues by a suicide bomber in Afghanistan. He pairs the physical risk with a second cost he states as near-certain: that a marriage will not survive an operational tour.

surveillance-detection-route.title: Non-Personal Communication
surveillance-detection-route.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a category of espionage tradecraft encompassing all methods of passing information between an officer and an agent — or between two intelligence services — that do not require the parties to meet in person. Techniques include concealment devices (e.g. hollowed-out objects no passerby would willingly touch, such as a dead rat or a used condom), signal sites and dead drops coordinated by chalk marks, and burst transmissions sent through devices hidden in false-backed drawers.

surveillance-detection-route.title: Spy films John Kiriakou considers accurate
surveillance-detection-route.summary: Kiriakou's assessment of which espionage films get it right — Argo, The Recruit and Bridge of Spies — and his flat rejection of the action genre's premises, including the hidden weapons stash.

surveillance-detection-route.title: Kiriakou's television pilots
surveillance-detection-route.summary: The eight television pilots John Kiriakou has sold over fifteen years as a hobby, beginning with Bomb Squad, a procedural about the New York City bomb squad built around a statistic that almost no bomb threat has anything to do with terrorism.

suzie-dawson.title: Julian Assange
suzie-dawson.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

suzie-dawson.title: Panquake
suzie-dawson.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

suzie-dawson.title: The Talk Liberation bank freeze
suzie-dawson.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the September 2022 freezing of Talk Liberation's Icelandic bank accounts — the seed funding behind the Panquake platform — on stated suspicion of money laundering and possible terrorist financing. Kiriakou, who deliberately declines to name the bank, calls the allegations nonsense, says in his personal opinion the freeze came at a government's behest, and notes the accounts were later unfrozen.

suzie-dawson.title: John Kiriakou
suzie-dawson.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

suzie-dawson.title: Bill Binney
suzie-dawson.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

suzie-dawson.title: Elon Musk
suzie-dawson.summary: Kiriakou met Musk by chance at a Washington hotel bar in 2009, when he was worth $1 billion and talking about Tesla, SpaceX and colonizing Mars.

sweat-lodge.title: The Reluctant Spy
sweat-lodge.summary: John Kiriakou''s 2009 memoir, The Reluctant Spy: My Secret Life in the CIA''s War on Terror, begun in secret months before he blew the whistle and reaching number five on the New York Times bestseller list.

sweat-lodge.title: Albert Stubblebine
sweat-lodge.summary: Per John Kiriakou, General Albert "Bert" Stubblebine was among the Army Intelligence figures behind the original Project Stargate remote-viewing program; Kiriakou interviewed the program's top people and says Stubblebine, like remote viewer Lyn Buchanan, had to sign non-disclosure agreements with the NSA and CIA.

sweat-lodge.title: Bay Path University
sweat-lodge.summary: Per John Kiriakou, he teaches in the graduate intelligence-studies program at Bay Path University in Massachusetts, covering introduction to intelligence, the history of terrorism, and intelligence and cybersecurity.

sweat-lodge.title: Espionage Act
sweat-lodge.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

sweat-lodge.title: Ilhan Omar
sweat-lodge.summary: U.S. Representative whom John Kiriakou credits with sponsoring a rewrite of the Espionage Act in two consecutive Congresses — legislation he says is dead on arrival with a Republican House because of who she is.

sweat-lodge.title: Lynn Buchanan
sweat-lodge.summary: A Fort Meade-trained Army intelligence veteran of the CIA and NSA remote-viewing programs — a primary source, Kiriakou says, not a TV psychic.

syria-regime-change-template.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
syria-regime-change-template.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

syria-regime-change-template.title: Al-Julani
syria-regime-change-template.summary: The former al-Qaeda commander and, per John Kiriakou, co-founder of ISIS who was installed as president of Syria and received at the White House. Kiriakou''s initial reading was that no one moves from a ten-million-dollar American bounty to a state visit in months without being a long-term CIA asset — until a senior Turkish official told him over dinner that al-Julani was Turkey''s: ''We created him from nothing and we installed him in Syria.'' Kiriakou judged that version more plausible than his own.

syria-regime-change-template.title: Hamid Karzai
syria-regime-change-template.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

syria-regime-change-template.title: The four requirements of a coup
syria-regime-change-template.summary: The checklist John Kiriakou says is taught at West Point for overthrowing a government — the presidential palace and the leader, the broadcast stations, the capital's major intersections, and the support of the military — which he uses to argue that regime change in Venezuela cannot work, because the fourth item belongs to the incumbent.

syria-regime-change-template.title: The assassination approval process
syria-regime-change-template.summary: Why John Kiriakou thinks arranging the death of a foreign leader is far harder for the CIA than the public assumes. It is not the 1960s: there is congressional oversight, and before any proposal reaches the president''s signature it must clear layers of lawyers at the Justice Department''s Office of Legal Counsel, the National Security Council and the agency''s own General Counsel. Pressuring a leader into flight, he notes, is both easier and more legal.

syria-regime-change-template.title: Maduro Capture
syria-regime-change-template.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

syrian-bodyguard.title: The SpongeBob shirt
syrian-bodyguard.summary: The bright red SpongeBob SquarePants shirt, a Christmas present from his children, that John Kiriakou happened to be wearing when Abu Zubaydah opened his one good eye and realised the Americans had him.

syrian-bodyguard.title: The two Abu Zubaydahs
syrian-bodyguard.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the first cousin who shared Abu Zubaydah's name, whose activities were folded into a single intelligence picture of a man Kiriakou called a terrorist Superman — and who vanished as soon as the capture reached the newspapers.

syrian-bodyguard.title: Abu Zubaydah
syrian-bodyguard.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

syrian-bodyguard.title: Buzzy Krongard
syrian-bodyguard.summary: The executive director of the CIA — the agency's third-ranking officer — who sat on the board of Johns Hopkins Medical Center and, on learning that Abu Zubaydah had been captured wounded, had the hospital's top trauma surgeon flown to Pakistan on a CIA jet.

syrian-bodyguard.title: Abu Zubaydah's diary
syrian-bodyguard.summary: The notebook captured with Abu Zubaydah, containing drawings and poetry, over which the CIA and the FBI came to deep disagreement — an FBI psychologist calling it the rantings of a crazy person and John Kiriakou insisting it showed creativity in a man who was not crazy at all.

taliban-embassy-raid.title: Abu Zubaydah
taliban-embassy-raid.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

taliban-embassy-raid.title: Counterterrorism Center
taliban-embassy-raid.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

taliban-embassy-raid.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
taliban-embassy-raid.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

taliban-embassy-raid.title: George H.W. Bush
taliban-embassy-raid.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

taliban-embassy-raid.title: Jerrold Post
taliban-embassy-raid.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis). Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

taliban-embassy-raid.title: Tommy McHale
taliban-embassy-raid.summary: Highly decorated Port Authority of New York and New Jersey detective who worked as a terrorist hunter alongside John Kiriakou in Islamabad, Pakistan after 9/11; a survivor of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing whose best friend died on 9/11.

taliban-spokesman-setup.title: FBI
taliban-spokesman-setup.summary: Kiriakou says FBI agents were sticklers for the law in a way the CIA never was — and that the bureau 'leaks like a sieve.'

taliban-spokesman-setup.title: FCI Loretto
taliban-spokesman-setup.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

taliban-spokesman-setup.title: Bureau of Prisons
taliban-spokesman-setup.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

taliban-spokesman-setup.title: Central Intelligence Agency
taliban-spokesman-setup.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

taliban-spokesman-setup.title: Letter from Loretto
taliban-spokesman-setup.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

taliban-spokesman-setup.title: Administrative remedy process
taliban-spokesman-setup.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

taliban-truck-escort-origin.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
taliban-truck-escort-origin.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

taliban-truck-escort-origin.title: The Afghan police tribal rotation
taliban-truck-escort-origin.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

taliban-truck-escort-origin.title: The Hazara leader's judo belts
taliban-truck-escort-origin.summary: An encounter John Kiriakou describes from Afghanistan in about 2007: a very senior Hazara leader displayed every judo belt he had ever earned, white through black, in a large shadow box on his living room wall — and explained that he had gone to fifth dan not for sport but because Hazaras were forbidden to own weapons and he needed some way to protect himself.

taliban-truck-escort-origin.title: Afghan rare earth minerals
taliban-truck-escort-origin.summary: John Kiriakou's argument, made days after the fall of Kabul in August 2021, that the country with real leverage in Afghanistan was China — which holds an exclusive contract to mine rare earth metals valued in a Defense Department report at one trillion dollars, and therefore has a stake in a stable long-term Afghan government even a Taliban one.

taliban-truck-escort-origin.title: Renting Afghan warlords
taliban-truck-escort-origin.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

taliban-truck-escort-origin.title: The ISI as two organizations
taliban-truck-escort-origin.summary: John Kiriakou''s working model of Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence during his time as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations there: one half made up of British-trained officers he calls great counterterrorism partners, and another half that created, trained, financed and armed the Taliban — a split that left him deciding case by case whom he could trust.

taliban.title: The Peace and Friendship Bridge
taliban.summary: A bridge across the narrow Pakistan–China frontier that John Kiriakou saw advertised on billboards across Pakistan while serving there, and the exchange it produced with a Pakistani general: asked why so much was being made of it, the general said the Chinese were the only friends Pakistan had who had never turned on them — and then looked at Kiriakou.

taliban.title: Hamid Karzai
taliban.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

taliban.title: Renting Afghan warlords
taliban.summary: The CIA's opening strategy in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — paying the country's warlords in cash rather than trying to buy their loyalty outright, captured in an agency saying that you cannot buy an Afghan warlord but you can certainly rent one.

taliban.title: Caleb Maupin
taliban.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

taliban.title: Haiti
taliban.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

taliban.title: Origins of al-Qaeda
taliban.summary: John Kiriakou''s position on where al-Qaeda came from: bad American foreign policy decisions led to it indirectly, but not by design. He rejects the deliberate-creation theory on the grounds that it is unnecessary — a state willing to kill does not need to manufacture a pretext first.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Panquake
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Suzie Dawson
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: New Zealand activist and journalist, chief executive of Talk Liberation and the driving force behind the Panquake platform. John Kiriakou, who has known her for years and serves as the platform's brand ambassador, describes her as the most dogged person he has ever known — a characterisation he traces to her defence of Julian Assange before Assange was dragged out of the Ecuadorian embassy.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Julian Assange
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Elon Musk
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: Kiriakou met Musk by chance at a Washington hotel bar in 2009, when he was worth $1 billion and talking about Tesla, SpaceX and colonizing Mars.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: Government encryption back-door demands
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: John Kiriakou's account of state pressure on technology companies for access to encrypted systems — the British government's demand for a back door into Apple's operating system, which he says Apple met with a threat to leave the United Kingdom, and his prediction that the second Trump administration would make the same demand of any new platform under a counterterrorism pretext.

talk-liberation-bank-freeze.title: John Kiriakou
talk-liberation-bank-freeze.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

targeting-analyst.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
targeting-analyst.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

targeting-analyst.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
targeting-analyst.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

targeting-analyst.title: Abu Zubaydah
targeting-analyst.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

targeting-analyst.title: Magic box
targeting-analyst.summary: An improvised cell-phone locator that two CIA tech officers built from parts bought in a Pakistani bazaar during the hunt for Abu Zubaydah. It could point toward a phone while a call was live, and did so exactly once — long enough for John Kiriakou to conclude the device was wasted time and to fly in a targeting analyst instead.

targeting-analyst.title: The Directorate of Science and Technology
targeting-analyst.summary: One of the CIA's four directorates, which in John Kiriakou's time was an afterthought responsible for disguises and briefcases with hidden compartments, and which he says now works with Palantir, Amazon, Nvidia and Elon Musk's companies on work closer to DARPA's than to anything the agency did in the past.

targeting-analyst.title: CIA cash room
targeting-analyst.summary: John Kiriakou's description of the rooms at large CIA stations stacked floor-to-ceiling with cash — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — from which an officer can sign out whatever an operation needs, as when he took $2 million to buy safe houses for the Abu Zubaydah capture.

taybeh.title: Church of Saint Porphyrios
taybeh.summary: The Greek Orthodox church in Gaza that John Kiriakou describes as the oldest continuously operating church in the world; per Kiriakou, Israel bombed it while 24 women and children were sheltering inside.

taybeh.title: Shireen Abu Akleh
taybeh.summary: Al Jazeera journalist, U.S. citizen and Greek Orthodox Christian; John Kiriakou recounts that she was shot in the face by an Israeli sniper while wearing clearly marked press gear, and that the IDF then beat pallbearers at her funeral.

taybeh.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
taybeh.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

taybeh.title: Greek Intelligence Service
taybeh.summary: Greece's intelligence service, with which John Kiriakou worked closely during his Athens posting; its head of surveillance called off surveillance on him after watching him make a large offering at Saint Nectarios's tomb on the island of Aegina.

taybeh.title: Jerry Falwell Jr.
taybeh.summary: Evangelical leader and former president of Liberty University; John Kiriakou recounts that Falwell personally recruited him to lecture at Liberty's Jesse Helms School of Government after his whistleblowing, with the reasoning that "torture is not Christian."

taybeh.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
taybeh.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

ted-rall.title: Abraxas Corporation
ted-rall.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

ted-rall.title: AIPAC
ted-rall.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

ted-rall.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
ted-rall.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

ted-rall.title: Publications Review Board
ted-rall.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

ted-rall.title: James Fishback
ted-rall.summary: Florida gubernatorial candidate whom Kiriakou says he never personally endorsed, despite viral claims and a since-deleted tweet posted by his assistant; Kiriakou calls Fishback's stance on Israel well-considered but distances himself from Fishback's other stated positions, including a proposed sin tax on OnlyFans creators, an immigration moratorium, and comments Kiriakou calls racist.

ted-rall.title: John Kiriakou
ted-rall.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ten-minute-moves.title: John's rules for prison survival
ten-minute-moves.summary: The code John Kiriakou says he wrote for himself at FCI Loretto out of his CIA training — rule one, recruit prisoners as sources using the same motivations the agency teaches; rule two, seek cover and blend in — illustrated with a plan to obtain contraband binder clips.

ten-minute-moves.title: FCI Loretto
ten-minute-moves.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

ten-minute-moves.title: The prison service economy
ten-minute-moves.summary: The trade in goods and services at FCI Loretto as John Kiriakou describes it — used shoes resold on commission, convenience stores run out of lockers at a thirty per cent markup, a dozen bookmakers, unlicensed chiropractic, and sexual services priced in books of postage stamps.

ten-minute-moves.title: The chapel job
ten-minute-moves.summary: The work assignment John Kiriakou was given at FCI Loretto after he volunteered to teach a class — *"if I want you to teach a class I'll ask you to teach a class"* — and was made a janitor in the chapel instead, at $1.08 a month.

ten-minute-moves.title: Robert the arsonist
ten-minute-moves.summary: The Australian prisoner who became John Kiriakou's roommate at FCI Loretto — convicted of burning down a Buffalo motor vehicles office over a sales tax dispute, a pathological liar who Kiriakou concluded was a clinical sociopath, and whom he says was easy to manipulate because he was an excitement junkie.

ten-minute-moves.title: Private prison system
ten-minute-moves.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the U.S. private prison industry as an incentive to keep beds filled and cut costs on food and medicine — illustrated by the 'sewer trout,' dog-food, and dead-rat-in-the-Kool-Aid stories from his own incarceration.

terry-aubry.title: Watermark
terry-aubry.summary: Reality Winner, on Kiriakou's show, describes the printer watermark that let the NSA trace her leaked document to a specific office.

terry-aubry.title: Afghan Languages
terry-aubry.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

terry-aubry.title: Chelsea Manning
terry-aubry.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

terry-aubry.title: CIA disguise program
terry-aubry.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's disguise and forgery specialists — including a master disguise maker recruited from a beauty academy who built him a custom bald-head mask over six weeks, and a master forger recruited off his college newspaper cartoons.

terry-aubry.title: Donald Trump
terry-aubry.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

terry-aubry.title: Edward Snowden
terry-aubry.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Why the UAE was targeted
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for the disproportionate weight of Iranian fire falling on the United Arab Emirates in 2026: not the American presence but the Emirati role at the forefront of the war against the Houthis — and a wish to bloody Emirati noses despite the thousands of Iranians living in Dubai.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Bombing the Omanis
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Iranian strikes on Gulf hotels
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the Iranian drone and missile attacks on hotels in Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Muscat during the 2026 war: not targeted killings, but deliberate strikes at the tourist economies of the Gulf states, aimed at hotels famous enough to empty the country of visitors.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Bahrain''s naturalisation policy
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: The Truth Social announcement
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to how the 2026 war was announced: at two o''clock in the morning on Truth Social, with no address from the East Room, and with a president shuttling between Washington and Mar-a-Lago rather than explaining to the country why Americans were being sent to fight.

thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.title: Hypersonic missiles
thaad-stocks-in-the-gulf.summary: John Kiriakou confirms that hypersonic missiles are real and that Russia, China and Iran all have them; that a weapon travelling 2,500 miles an hour cannot be defended against; and that Iran holds too few of them to do anything but make each one count.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: Saddam Hussein's classified biographer
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: John Kiriakou''s first job at the CIA: writing the classified biography and psychological profile of Saddam Hussein in the Office of Leadership Analysis — the desk from which he watched the agency conclude, on 30 June 1990, that Iraq would invade Kuwait, and get the scale of the invasion wrong.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: The Oval Office briefing of 2 August 1990
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: The morning Iraq invaded Kuwait, a 25-year-old John Kiriakou was driven from CIA headquarters to the White House and found himself briefing President George H. W. Bush, Vice President Quayle, Brent Scowcroft and the CIA director — and answering the question *"well, now what do we do?"*

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: George Habash
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: John Kiriakou
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

thatcher-wobbly-call.title: Abdul Amir al-Jamri
thatcher-wobbly-call.summary: The Bahraini cleric who led the Shia opposition during the 1990s uprising, and whom John Kiriakou interviewed for a human rights report in 1991 — an interview that had the Bahraini prime minister demanding, within the hour, that both American officers be expelled from the country.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Arabists
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The label applied inside the U.S. government to diplomats and analysts who knew Arabic and Middle Eastern history, and which John Kiriakou confirms functioned as a dismissal — the assumption being that anyone who understood the region was blindly prejudiced against Israel, or antisemitic.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Abraham Accords
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Deuce Martinez
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: The former CIA analyst whose business card was the basis of two of the three Espionage Act charges brought against John Kiriakou. Kiriakou scanned and emailed the card — which showed Martinez had gone to work for Mitchell and Jessen, the firm of the torture programme''s architects — to a New York Times reporter and later to an ABC News reporter. The judge threw the espionage counts out.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Jerrold Post
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: American political psychiatrist and CIA officer who recruited John Kiriakou into the agency in 1988 through the CIA's covert campus recruiting program, working undercover as a George Washington University professor; founder of the CIA's Political Psychology Division (also called the Office of Leadership Analysis).
