Held a bachelor's, master's, and PhD in psychology and a PhD in political science, all from Yale, plus an MD from Harvard, and authored a dozen books on the psychology of world leaders and terrorists. Per Kiriakou, Post identified in him not just writing talent but "sociopathic tendencies" — and, when Kiriakou later blew the whistle, called to congratulate him, telling him that reaction proved he was not a true sociopath. Died of COVID-19, approximately 2022.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Shin Bet
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: Israel's internal security service; per John Kiriakou, one of the two declared Israeli intelligence officers at the Washington embassy, and the service whose officer, alongside a Mossad officer, he says tried to recruit him at his first CIA liaison briefing in the spring of 1990 — an approach his colleagues told him had been made to every one of them.

the-189-undeclared-officers.title: Yasser Arafat
the-189-undeclared-officers.summary: Leader of the Palestine Liberation Organization, who appears in John Kiriakou's account at the two moments he treats as decisive for the Palestinians — backing Saddam Hussein after the 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which cost the Palestinian middle class its standing across the Gulf, and walking out of the last Clinton-era peace talks with a divided map of Jerusalem already on the table.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: The torture memo signature
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the CIA''s torture programme was authorised: a list of about ten techniques sent from headquarters through the Justice Department, the National Security Council lawyers and Condoleezza Rice to the president — who, to the surprise of the agency''s own leadership, signed it. Kiriakou recalls the deputy director saying three times in one meeting that he could not believe the president had signed the memo.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: The Fox News military analyst
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.title: False flags are too hard
the-1968-waterboarding-conviction.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: David Ransom
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Bahrain during the period of John Kiriakou's posting there; characterized by Kiriakou as one of the finest people he worked for in his CIA career

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: John Kiriakou
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: Chuck Grassley
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the only serious pro-whistleblower member of Congress — a count he says can be made on one finger. Grassley wrote the Whistleblower Protection Act and the National Security Whistleblower Protection Act, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Center's luncheon, and in Kiriakou's telling was pushed into backing the Ukraine call whistleblower because it was his own law the man had invoked.

the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.title: The 2007 death threats
the-1996-campaign-contribution-disclosur.summary: The immediate personal consequence of John Kiriakou''s December 2007 television appearance confirming CIA waterboarding: hundreds of pieces of hate mail, and three threats against his life that the FBI classified as credible, one of which named his children and gave his home address. On the Bureau''s advice he took his family out of the country for a week; the FBI then interviewed the senders, judged them local cranks, and told him to come home.

the-2007-death-threats.title: The Ukraine call whistleblower
the-2007-death-threats.summary: The intelligence officer whose complaint triggered Donald Trump's first impeachment, and whom John Kiriakou declines to accept as a whistleblower at all — not on partisan grounds but on procedural ones. The complaint went to the Justice Department rather than the oversight committees, and its prose, he says, is lawyers' prose rather than the uniform CIA analytic style every analyst is trained into. He is nonetheless emphatic that naming the man was indefensible.

the-2007-death-threats.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
the-2007-death-threats.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

the-2007-death-threats.title: The 1996 campaign contribution disclosure
the-2007-death-threats.summary: The whistleblower disclosure John Kiriakou made inside the CIA in 1996, sixteen years before the one that ruined him. Serving overseas, he learned of a very large illegal contribution to the Dole presidential campaign, reported it to the CIA Inspector General, and watched the system work exactly as written: the IG investigated, found the information credible, and referred it to the Federal Election Commission. He offers it as the control case against which he judges every later complaint.

the-2007-death-threats.title: Thomas Drake
the-2007-death-threats.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

the-2007-death-threats.title: Chuck Grassley
the-2007-death-threats.summary: The senior senator from Iowa, and in John Kiriakou's assessment the only serious pro-whistleblower member of Congress — a count he says can be made on one finger. Grassley wrote the Whistleblower Protection Act and the National Security Whistleblower Protection Act, speaks every year at the National Whistleblower Center's luncheon, and in Kiriakou's telling was pushed into backing the Ukraine call whistleblower because it was his own law the man had invoked.

the-2007-death-threats.title: Gina Haspel
the-2007-death-threats.summary: Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President Trump's first term; known to John Kiriakou and others at the CIA as "Bloody Gina"; per Kiriakou, flew out to the secret black site to sit in on one of the enhanced-interrogation torture sessions "just because she could," personally supervised the torture of USS Cole bombing suspect Rahim al-Nashiri, and later fed the CIA's torture tapes into an industrial document grinder after being explicitly told by White House Counsel not to destroy them.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Solitary confinement
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: The prison isolation practice the United Nations calls a form of torture; John Kiriakou, drawing on his own ten days in a six-by-sixteen-foot cell, argues that jailing depressed prisoners like Daniel Hale in solitary 'for their own safety' is precisely what drives them to suicide.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Julian Assange
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Assange and solitary confinement
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: John Kiriakou's 2018 argument that Julian Assange's isolation inside the Ecuadorian embassy amounted to solitary confinement — a practice the United Nations classes as torture — and that everybody breaks under it eventually, however strong they are.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Bernie Sanders
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: United States senator from Vermont. John Kiriakou, who watched him daily from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, describes Sanders holding open breakfast in the Senate cafeteria for anyone who walked in — insisting only that they call him "Bernie" — and names him the one 2016 candidate willing to talk about shrinking the military.

the-2020-extradition-hearing.title: Bill Barr
the-2020-extradition-hearing.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: The ISI as two organizations
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s working model of Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence during his time as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations there: one half made up of British-trained officers he calls great counterterrorism partners, and another half that created, trained, financed and armed the Taliban — a split that left him deciding case by case whom he could trust.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
the-2025-india-pakistan-clash-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: The secret Sahel appropriations
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's complaint that the United States is quietly pumping billions of dollars into Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Conakry and Guinea-Bissau — spending he says is supposed to be a big secret, addresses a French problem rather than an American one, and which American taxpayers have a right to know about and to judge.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: The Paris rifle serial number
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: The case John Kiriakou uses to argue that American weapons sent to Ukraine are leaking onto the black market: a rifle used to shoot and severely wound a policeman in Paris whose serial number, he says, matched a shipment of assault rifles the United States had sent to Ukraine some six months earlier.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: China as economic threat
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China is the real threat to the West not militarily — it has one aircraft carrier to America's two dozen and rarely invades — but economically, buying friends worldwide while the U.S. spends a trillion dollars a year on weapons.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: Muddling through
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-african-diplomats-remark.title: Permanent wartime economy
the-african-diplomats-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's thesis that since 9/11 the United States has run a permanent wartime economy so large that cutting the defense budget would trigger a depression — likening the dependency to crack addiction and warning it makes war almost inevitable.

the-anti-semite-smear.title: The Epstein files and the Starmer government
the-anti-semite-smear.summary: John Kiriakou''s prediction that the Epstein disclosures could bring down Keir Starmer''s government, on the strength of evidence that Prince Andrew and Peter Mandelson gave Epstein classified British Ministry of Defence documents — an Official Secrets Act matter that in America would fall under the Espionage Act.

the-anti-semite-smear.title: Piers Morgan
the-anti-semite-smear.summary: British broadcaster whose panel show became John Kiriakou's 2025 sparring ring — "the equivalent of a WWE Smackdown with Alan Dershowitz<Cite s="2026-06-27-deep-focus-report-john-kiriakou-on-iran-endless-wars-and-u-s-fo" t="9:18" />." Paired with Scott Horton against Dershowitz and former Mossad chief Moshe Yaalon, Kiriakou said on air that Israel spies on the United States and that Jeffrey Epstein was an Israeli access agent, drawing a chuckle from the general and the claim that spying stopped when Pollard was caught — "General, with all due respect, that's just simply not true." Morgan's producer had to instruct the polite ex-spy not to be afraid to interrupt.

the-anti-semite-smear.title: Alan Dershowitz
the-anti-semite-smear.summary: American attorney and Harvard Law professor; John Kiriakou describes debating him on Piers Morgan's show over Jeffrey Epstein, telling Dershowitz he would have wanted to see him "hanging from a tree" had he sought leniency for Epstein as an Israeli spy — and cites attorney David Boies's on-air statement that Dershowitz was far more than Epstein's lawyer, also serving as his publicist, friend, and a guest on Epstein's island.

the-anti-semite-smear.title: Bahrain''s naturalisation policy
the-anti-semite-smear.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

the-anti-semite-smear.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-anti-semite-smear.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-anti-semite-smear.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-anti-semite-smear.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.title: The Gang of Four and Gang of Eight
the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA restricts notification of its most sensitive covert operations to four or eight congressional leaders, and his verdict on the practice: because a member of an intelligence committee can be an overseer without being cleared for what is being overseen, the arrangement is not oversight but, in his word, gangsterism.

the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.title: The CIA as a paramilitary organization
the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.summary: John Kiriakou''s periodisation of the CIA''s mission — spying and analysis until Vietnam, restored after the Church and Pike hearings of 1975, and converted immediately after September 11 into a paramilitary body that he says it has remained ever since. His objection is stated without hedging: drawing up a kill list every Tuesday and dispatching officers to carry it out is not intelligence, it is murder.

the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.title: Abolish the CIA
the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-ask-forgiveness-maxim.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-asset-recruitment-cycle.title: The tier one walk-up
the-asset-recruitment-cycle.summary: The recruitment John Kiriakou calls one of the best operations of his career and credits entirely to his mentor Gust Avrakotos: an approach to an official of a tier one country — one of America''s greatest enemies — made by the simple expedient of walking right up to the man''s house, a technique Avrakotos had used himself in the 1970s.

the-asset-recruitment-cycle.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-asset-recruitment-cycle.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-asset-recruitment-cycle.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-asset-recruitment-cycle.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-asset-recruitment-cycle.title: False flags are too hard
the-asset-recruitment-cycle.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-asset-recruitment-cycle.title: Recruiting from the bottom
the-asset-recruitment-cycle.summary: The targeting method John Kiriakou believes produced the killings of Iran''s leadership: not agents at the top of the state but destitute refugees at street level, paid a hundred dollars a month to write down when a general leaves his building and by which route. He contrasts it with the CIA''s own record in Iran, where it spent his career trying and failing to recruit inside the Ayatollah''s office, the foreign ministry and the IRGC.

the-asset-recruitment-cycle.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-asset-recruitment-cycle.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-autographed-basketball.title: College tuition as an inducement
the-autographed-basketball.summary: The recruitment inducement John Kiriakou describes as among the CIA's most effective — enrolling a source's child at any American university and paying for it — and the arrangements with universities and corporations he says make it possible.

the-autographed-basketball.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-autographed-basketball.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-autographed-basketball.title: Arabic and Greek
the-autographed-basketball.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-autographed-basketball.title: The Indonesian recruitment question
the-autographed-basketball.summary: A hypothetical put to John Kiriakou and other CIA applicants during the interview process — what to do when a foreign official you have cultivated for a year turns out not to be recruitable — and the answer that Kiriakou later understood had been the point of the exercise: break into the embassy and steal the information.

the-autographed-basketball.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-autographed-basketball.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-autographed-basketball.title: Curtailment cables
the-autographed-basketball.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-backstory.title: Caleb Maupin
the-backstory.summary: American journalist and Marxist commentator, a recurring guest on John Kiriakou's radio programme The Backstory, whom Kiriakou introduces as one of the best-informed people out there. Kiriakou endorses his analysis of automation and capitalism while noting he does not agree with all of it, and proposed putting him on air opposite a libertarian economist.

the-backstory.title: Haiti
the-backstory.summary: A country John Kiriakou studied for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where he found that the seven largest merchant families — the families that run the entire Haitian economy — are white. He treats Haiti's poverty as manufactured rather than accidental, and its unrest as a story the American press declines to cover.

the-backstory.title: Abolish the CIA
the-backstory.summary: John Kiriakou's position that the CIA should be abolished because its functions are already duplicated by the other 17 U.S. intelligence agencies — analysis by the State Department, human spying by the Pentagon, technology by DARPA, NSA and the private sector.

the-backstory.title: "Admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations"
the-backstory.summary: One of the twenty life lessons John Kiriakou says the CIA taught him in training, and a slogan sold on coffee mugs and t-shirts in the headquarters gift shop — by far the most popular mug in the building. It was treated at Langley as a joke that was not quite a joke; in federal prison Kiriakou used it as an operating rule, and credits it with getting him out of an investigation into a prison-yard fight with nothing given up.

the-backstory.title: Advanced Counterterrorism Operations
the-backstory.summary: The six-week specialist course John Kiriakou flew back from Athens to attend roughly eighteen months before 9/11 as one of fourteen officers selected worldwide — high-threat operations, technical collection, and a driving syllabus built around crashing through roadblocks that left the class with whiplash. By accident of timing it meant a trained cadre was ready to deploy the moment the attacks came.

the-backstory.title: Barack Obama
the-backstory.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: The Libya policy reversal
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi: the United States had a healthy working relationship with a man who hated al-Qaeda as much as it did, and flipping sides at the last minute was a terrible policy error that left the country in anarchy. Told that destabilisation may have been the objective all along, he called that an incredibly shortsighted policy, because power vacuums drag America in and it cannot get back out.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: The September 10th country
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s formulation of what he wants back, and his ledger on the two wars: he never supported the invasion of Iraq, which he calls a war of choice and of family revenge, and he did support the war in Afghanistan until al-Qaeda was defeated in 2003, after which everything became nation building. He assigns the destruction of the pre-attack country to George W. Bush and Barack Obama equally.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-benghazi-hearings-critique.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-benghazi-hearings-critique.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: The dandelion salad
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The meal John Kiriakou assembled in the yard at FCI Loretto from foraged dandelions, commissary olive oil and sea salt, instant rice, a bouillon cube, peanuts, borrowed Sazón and a bag of chicken — which he calls the single most satisfying meal of his twenty-three months in prison.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: The Islamabad guest house
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The sixteen-room guest house in Islamabad that CIA officers took over entirely during the post-9/11 deployments — a place John Kiriakou says the agency still will not let him name, which came with breakfast, dinner and laundry for about thirty-five dollars a day against a per diem of five hundred.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: A Middle East reading list
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: Bowe Bergdahl
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: The American soldier who walked off his base in Afghanistan, was captured by the Haqqani network and handed to the Taliban, and was repatriated in a prisoner trade — a man John Kiriakou says was treated as a traitor although he was not one.

the-best-meal-overseas.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-best-meal-overseas.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Heather Kiriakou
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Publications Review Board
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: The CIA office that must clear anything a former officer publishes. John Kiriakou says everything he writes goes to it — books, articles, "even a letter to the editor of Home and Garden magazine" — and describes how the turnaround tracked his standing at the agency: his first book took 22 months to clear while the leadership hated him; his most recent six cleared in days.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: The State Department cover investigation
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: One of the inquiries John Kiriakou opened as senior investigator on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, on a reporter's tip that the CIA was placing some of its torturers under State Department cover in violation of the cover agreement between the two departments. He wrote to the State Department asking for clarification. Five or six weeks later a colleague told him a reply had come and had been classified above his clearance; asked what it said, the colleague summarised it as an obscenity. That was the end of the investigation.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: Brian Ross
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-bolivian-visa-line.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-bolivian-visa-line.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-bomb-course.title: Counterterrorist driving
the-bomb-course.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

the-bomb-course.title: The Advanced Counterterrorism Operations course
the-bomb-course.summary: The six-week CIA course for which John Kiriakou says he was one of only about a dozen officers in the entire agency selected — and which he finished, as he puts it, just in time for 9/11.

the-bomb-course.title: The operations course graduation
the-bomb-course.summary: The end of CIA field training: a graduation ceremony at which the whole class wore full disguises for the photograph, and a certificate that is itself classified and therefore cannot be displayed — it stays in the officer''s personnel file.

the-bomb-course.title: The shooting house
the-bomb-course.summary: The live-fire decision course at the Farm where a trainee has about three quarters of a second to decide whether the figure at the window is a gunman or a woman holding a baby — and where John Kiriakou says he never missed, which he connects to his own account of the temperament the CIA selects for.

the-bomb-course.title: The Farm
the-bomb-course.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

the-bomb-course.title: The hostile border crossing exercise
the-bomb-course.summary: The training exercise run before dawn at a closed Dulles Airport in which CIA trainees crossed into the fictional Republic of Victoria — where John Kiriakou talked his way past a US-government-branded pen in his pocket, and the class clown ended up stripped to his underwear.

the-botched-pitch.title: Cover position
the-botched-pitch.summary: The occupational identity under which an intelligence officer operates abroad. John Kiriakou''s account collapses the popular idea that certain embassy jobs are tell-tale: because a diplomatic mission has to do its real work every day, every position in and out of an embassy is simultaneously a genuine job and a possible cover, which is precisely what makes cover work.

the-botched-pitch.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
the-botched-pitch.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

the-botched-pitch.title: Operational vehicles
the-botched-pitch.summary: The cars John Kiriakou used in the field. In the Middle East they were whatever the rental company supplied — usually a Toyota — on the reasoning that anonymity was the point; in Athens, where the threat justified it, he was issued a factory-built, level-four armoured BMW 540 that broke down constantly.

the-botched-pitch.title: 2028 presidential field
the-botched-pitch.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

the-botched-pitch.title: Andrew Bustamante
the-botched-pitch.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

the-botched-pitch.title: Angry Birds
the-botched-pitch.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: Security, finance and medical
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-bowl-of-dates.title: The declination letter
the-bowl-of-dates.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Hypersonic missiles
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou confirms that hypersonic missiles are real and that Russia, China and Iran all have them; that a weapon travelling 2,500 miles an hour cannot be defended against; and that Iran holds too few of them to do anything but make each one count.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Dubai as Iran''s window
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iran did not hit Dubai hard during the 2026 war: the city is full of Iranian businessmen and is Iran''s outlet to the Western world and its principal means of evading sanctions.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Bahrain''s naturalisation policy
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.
