the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou''s report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.title: Why the UAE was targeted
the-bridgeton-and-the-tanker-escorts.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation for the disproportionate weight of Iranian fire falling on the United Arab Emirates in 2026: not the American presence but the Emirati role at the forefront of the war against the Houthis — and a wish to bloody Emirati noses despite the thousands of Iranians living in Dubai.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Freedom of Information Act
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Thirty-year mandatory declassification
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: The statutory requirement, described by John Kiriakou, that classified American documents be released after thirty years — a law he says virtually nobody knows about, and which he raises against the continued withholding of Kennedy assassination records more than sixty years on. He also describes the redaction practice that operates alongside it.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Podcasters on foreign payrolls
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being told by an investigative journalist he respects that four household-name podcasters were taking CIA money — an allegation she could not corroborate and would not publish. He treats it as credible and extends the logic: if the agency is paying podcasters, foreign governments will be paying them too.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: Pike Committee
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: U.S. House investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 in parallel with the Senate's Church Committee; per John Kiriakou, the two committees together were the apex — and the last genuine exercise — of congressional oversight of the CIA, staffed by heavyweights and followed by a golden age that lasted only until Iran-Contra. Their work created the permanent House and Senate intelligence committees, which Kiriakou says degraded within a decade into cheerleaders for the agency.

the-buried-senate-documents.title: The science fiction writer FOIA request
the-buried-senate-documents.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed with the CIA about a 1950s science fiction writer long rumoured to have been an undercover officer — answered only with a letter saying the agency lacked the manpower to meet its statutory ninety-day deadline. Fifteen years later, he says, he is still waiting.

the-cave-myth.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-cave-myth.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-cave-myth.title: The ISI as two organizations
the-cave-myth.summary: John Kiriakou''s working model of Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence during his time as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations there: one half made up of British-trained officers he calls great counterterrorism partners, and another half that created, trained, financed and armed the Taliban — a split that left him deciding case by case whom he could trust.

the-cave-myth.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-cave-myth.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-cave-myth.title: The Taliban lobbyist in Washington
the-cave-myth.summary: A story put to John Kiriakou about a Taliban delegation''s American press conference and the Washington lobbyist who represented them. Kiriakou remembered the episode and the lobbyist''s New Jersey base but not the claim about her parentage, and explained why it caused so little controversy at the time: the United States had no historical quarrel with the Taliban, and had armed and fêted some of its future members during the war against the Soviets.

the-cave-myth.title: The torture memo signature
the-cave-myth.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the CIA''s torture programme was authorised: a list of about ten techniques sent from headquarters through the Justice Department, the National Security Council lawyers and Condoleezza Rice to the president — who, to the surprise of the agency''s own leadership, signed it. Kiriakou recalls the deputy director saying three times in one meeting that he could not believe the president had signed the memo.

the-cave-myth.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-cave-myth.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-chain-of-command-argument.title: The Guardian smear series
the-chain-of-command-argument.summary: The run of articles about Julian Assange that John Kiriakou characterised in 2018 as a pile-on based on anonymous sources leaking intelligence-agency material, and which he read as a formal psychological operation intended to weaken Assange rather than as journalism.

the-chain-of-command-argument.title: "Ecuador is open for business"
the-chain-of-command-argument.summary: The Wall Street Journal headline John Kiriakou says appeared the day after he hand-delivered a letter to Ecuador's ambassador in Washington asking that Julian Assange's internet access be restored, and which made him fear Assange was about to be used as a bargaining chip.

the-chain-of-command-argument.title: Assange and solitary confinement
the-chain-of-command-argument.summary: John Kiriakou's 2018 argument that Julian Assange's isolation inside the Ecuadorian embassy amounted to solitary confinement — a practice the United Nations classes as torture — and that everybody breaks under it eventually, however strong they are.

the-chain-of-command-argument.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-chain-of-command-argument.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-chain-of-command-argument.title: Seventy-two denied motions
the-chain-of-command-argument.summary: The count John Kiriakou gives of the pretrial motions filed in his case and denied by Judge Leonie Brinkema — seventy-two denied and none granted — which he offers as the mechanism by which a national security defendant in the Eastern District of Virginia is prevented from mounting a defence at all.

the-chain-of-command-argument.title: The Intercept
the-chain-of-command-argument.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.title: The Gang of Four and Gang of Eight
the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA restricts notification of its most sensitive covert operations to four or eight congressional leaders, and his verdict on the practice: because a member of an intelligence committee can be an overseer without being cleared for what is being overseen, the arrangement is not oversight but, in his word, gangsterism.

the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.title: The ask-forgiveness maxim
the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.summary: The rule of thumb John Kiriakou says he was taught early in his CIA career — that it is always better to ask forgiveness than to ask permission — and which he offers as the explanation for how the agency runs legally doubtful programmes: it does what it wants, apologises if caught, and that is the end of it.

the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-cia-as-a-paramilitary-organization.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-cia-defense.title: Rick Praau
the-cia-defense.summary: Career CIA officer, chief of operations at the Counterterrorism Center and previously of the Special Activities Division, whose retirement memoir John Kiriakou reviewed critically in Covert Action Magazine. Kiriakou's objection is not to what the book contains but to what it omits — published reports that before joining the agency its author was investigated by Miami-Dade police over seven contract killings for the Medellín cartel. The surname is given here as the source transcript's auto-captions render it and may be mis-transcribed.

the-cia-defense.title: Bureau of Prisons
the-cia-defense.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

the-cia-defense.title: The child-trafficking misquotation
the-cia-defense.summary: A widely circulated claim that John Kiriakou said the CIA is involved in the sex trafficking of children. Kiriakou denies it flatly and traces it to a distorted account of a teaching hypothetical he uses in university lectures on ethics — a speech cleared by the CIA's Publications Review Board, whose video was attached to the original article by a writer who evidently had not watched it.

the-cia-defense.title: Giuliani Pardon Solicitation
the-cia-defense.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a meeting at the Trump International Hotel in Washington in which Rudy Giuliani's associate solicited $2 million in exchange for a presidential pardon — a story that subsequently appeared as a front-page New York Times article. Giuliani publicly denied ever meeting Kiriakou; Kiriakou sent the Times the photograph taken at the meeting that morning, and the paper published the story with the note that it had seen documentary proof.

the-cia-defense.title: The 2022 deplatforming
the-cia-defense.summary: The removal of John Kiriakou's radio programme from every major podcast platform after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, on the basis of his work for Sputnik News — preceded, he says, by a Washington Post article and a CSIS paper arguing that his weekly segment on American prison conditions was Russian propaganda weakening American democracy.

the-cia-defense.title: Kiriakou pardon request
the-cia-defense.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: False flags are too hard
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: Recruiting foreign students
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: The long-horizon intelligence argument for admitting foreign students to American universities — that a doctoral student in the hard sciences recruited on campus goes home to a weapons programme as an asset already in place — and John Kiriakou's view that collapsing enrolment is an operational loss nobody at the top is thinking about.

the-cia-spotter-professor.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-cia-spotter-professor.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: "Most other countries are more moral than the CIA"
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to a viewer who asked whether the United States has the most moral intelligence agency: it does not, and a hundred countries could be named whose services behave better — the disqualifying practice being the killing of people who pose no threat to the United States.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: MBS and Netanyahu asked Trump to attack Iran
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu jointly went to Donald Trump and asked him to attack Iran — a move Kiriakou finds hard to reconcile with MBS's own years of work to improve Saudi relations with Tehran.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.title: Dubai as Iran''s window
the-clear-and-present-danger-finding.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iran did not hit Dubai hard during the 2026 war: the city is full of Iranian businessmen and is Iran''s outlet to the Western world and its principal means of evading sanctions.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: The Office of Security arrangement
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The disclosure John Kiriakou says emerged from a 2020 custody hearing: that his wife, herself a senior CIA officer, had accompanied him to the 2007 ABC News whistleblowing interview on the instruction of the CIA''s Office of Security, and had continued to report on his activities.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Arabic and Greek
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Curtailment cables
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: Iraq, the training account
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says he was given the Iraq portfolio as a new CIA analyst in 1990 — that nothing ever happened there — and the promise that once he had learned tradecraft and the house writing style he would be moved to somewhere exciting, such as Romania.

the-concealed-carry-advertisements.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-concealed-carry-advertisements.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The second plane
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: John Kiriakou's account of where he was standing when United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower — in Cofer Black's outer office, mid-sentence, explaining to a secretary why a pilot could not possibly fly into the World Trade Center on so clear a day.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: "We''re at war today"
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The short speech John Kiriakou says Cofer Black delivered standing on his desk in the CIA's Counterterrorism Center on the morning of 11 September 2001, telling his officers that not all of them would make it home and that anyone for whom this was not enough could walk out without being thought less of. Nobody moved.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The honey salesman warning
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The seventy-two-year-old contractor
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The hallway conversation John Kiriakou says explained why the CIA had not sent him, an Arabic speaker, to interrogate captured al-Qaeda fighters — a returning contractor's answer that he had been in Afghanistan killing people — and the demand Kiriakou made afterwards that got him sent to Pakistan the next day.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: The Tehran slip
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The moment John Kiriakou says he witnessed as note-taker in a secure video teleconference a day or two before the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when a briefing general said that if all went as planned American forces could be in Tehran by August, and CIA Director George Tenet turned off his microphone and asked Kiriakou whether the man had said Tehran or Baghdad.

the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.title: Arabic and Greek
the-condoleezza-rice-meeting.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: Suggested responses
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: The NPR walkout
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: The pre-interview
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The booking practice John Kiriakou says all the American television networks use and which he finds maddening: an invitation to appear, a quick pre-interview to establish what he thinks, and then a call a minute later saying they have decided to go a different way on the story.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: Consulting for royal families
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-convicted-felon-introduction.title: Signing with CAA
the-convicted-felon-introduction.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Mike Pompeo
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Julian Assange
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: The chilling effect of whistleblower prosecutions
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that national-security prosecutions are not primarily about convictions but about deterrence — that the CIA cares about sending a message where the FBI cares about promotions, that his own case was meant to frighten anyone else considering disclosure, and that a New York Times reporter told him every national-security source the paper had went silent on the day of his arrest.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Authorized leaks
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou draws between the classified information Washington releases on purpose and the classified information it prosecutes people for releasing. The mechanism is the same and the legal status is identical; what differs is whether the leak flatters the leaker. His worked example is an agency leak claiming the CIA predicted the October 2023 attack on Israel three days out — a story the CIA can then piously report to the FBI, knowing the source will never be found.

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Central Intelligence Agency
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

the-counterintelligence-exemption.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-counterintelligence-exemption.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-culling-of-friendships.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-culling-of-friendships.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-culling-of-friendships.title: The Club Fed myth
the-culling-of-friendships.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing objection to the phrase ''Club Fed'' and the idea that federal prison is a soft landing for white-collar convicts: there is no such thing, he says, no golf and no gardening, only an institution designed to humiliate and emasculate and to make a man count the days.

the-culling-of-friendships.title: Supervised release travel restrictions
the-culling-of-friendships.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the years of court supervision that followed his prison term, in which a judge refused him permission to travel abroad to give paid speeches while he was expected to earn a living, and in which he had to surrender his passport on returning from every trip he was allowed to take.

the-culling-of-friendships.title: The Oz analogy
the-culling-of-friendships.summary: John Kiriakou's habit of explaining federal prison social structure through the HBO drama Oz, in which rival gangs are forced to share a single unit — and his identification with the show's unaffiliated Irish character, who belonged to no faction and survived by playing them off one another.

the-culling-of-friendships.title: The Virginia pardon and voting rights
the-culling-of-friendships.summary: John Kiriakou's account of applying to have his voting rights restored in Virginia after leaving prison and receiving, unasked, a full state pardon delivered by courier from the office of Governor Terry McAuliffe — followed by a courthouse clerk and a state employee who between them got him registered in time to vote.

the-culling-of-friendships.title: Brian Ross
the-culling-of-friendships.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-dandelion-salad.title: The best meal overseas
the-dandelion-salad.summary: Asked for the best meals he had eaten abroad, John Kiriakou named first a dish cooked by a young Pakistani in a CIA guest house in Islamabad — shaved beef, a myriad of spices, hot green chillies and rice cooked in chicken stock — followed by sushi in Tokyo and the Lenten table of Clean Monday in Greece.

the-dandelion-salad.title: The Islamabad guest house
the-dandelion-salad.summary: The sixteen-room guest house in Islamabad that CIA officers took over entirely during the post-9/11 deployments — a place John Kiriakou says the agency still will not let him name, which came with breakfast, dinner and laundry for about thirty-five dollars a day against a per diem of five hundred.

the-dandelion-salad.title: A Middle East reading list
the-dandelion-salad.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

the-dandelion-salad.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-dandelion-salad.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-dandelion-salad.title: Bowe Bergdahl
the-dandelion-salad.summary: The American soldier who walked off his base in Afghanistan, was captured by the Haqqani network and handed to the Taliban, and was repatriated in a prisoner trade — a man John Kiriakou says was treated as a traitor although he was not one.

the-dandelion-salad.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-dandelion-salad.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-declination-letter.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-declination-letter.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-declination-letter.title: The rogue officer remark
the-declination-letter.summary: The answer President George W. Bush shouted to a reporter on his way to the helicopter — that if there was torture, it was the work of a rogue CIA officer — which John Kiriakou has said convinced him he was about to be made the scapegoat, and which led him to accept Brian Ross's interview offer.

the-declination-letter.title: John Brennan
the-declination-letter.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

the-declination-letter.title: Curtailment cables
the-declination-letter.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-declination-letter.title: Arabic and Greek
the-declination-letter.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-declination-letter.title: Espionage Act
the-declination-letter.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-density-of-spies-in-washington.title: The Greek colonel and China
the-density-of-spies-in-washington.summary: The arrest of a Greek colonel assigned to NATO on charges of spying for China — a case John Kiriakou calls highly unusual not because espionage arrests are rare in Greece, but because they are almost always for Russia, and which he says shows the Chinese have begun caring about NATO communications.

the-density-of-spies-in-washington.title: The operational test
the-density-of-spies-in-washington.summary: The vetting procedure John Kiriakou describes for moving a trusted source onto normal handling: put a full surveillance team on him without telling him, watch how he gets to the meeting, and then ask him to describe what he did.

the-density-of-spies-in-washington.title: The orb off Yemen
the-density-of-spies-in-washington.summary: A leaked video John Kiriakou describes as the most dramatic UFO material he has seen: two F-18s following a silver orb off the coast of Yemen, given permission to fire, and a missile that hits the object and bounces off before the orb turns ninety degrees and flies on.

the-density-of-spies-in-washington.title: Running into former sources
the-density-of-spies-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou has twice met people he once ran as agents by accident, years after leaving the CIA — once at an airport and once in the street — and both times they came to him with a bear hug. One of them was astonished to discover he spoke English.

the-density-of-spies-in-washington.title: Sources are not traitors
the-density-of-spies-in-washington.summary: Asked whether CIA officers privately regarded their recruited agents as traitors and held them in contempt, John Kiriakou answered that they did not — because the officers believed they were the good guys, and a recruited source had become one of them.

the-density-of-spies-in-washington.title: The anti-semite smear
the-density-of-spies-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the professional cost of saying publicly that Israel spies on the United States: Alan Dershowitz calls him names, and the political director of the Israeli foreign minister called him a noted anti-semite.

the-difficulty-of-getting-out.title: MBS and Netanyahu asked Trump to attack Iran
the-difficulty-of-getting-out.summary: John Kiriakou's account that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu jointly went to Donald Trump and asked him to attack Iran — a move Kiriakou finds hard to reconcile with MBS's own years of work to improve Saudi relations with Tehran.

the-difficulty-of-getting-out.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
the-difficulty-of-getting-out.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

the-difficulty-of-getting-out.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
the-difficulty-of-getting-out.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

the-difficulty-of-getting-out.title: A Middle East reading list
the-difficulty-of-getting-out.summary: The books and the starting point John Kiriakou recommends to anyone trying to understand the modern Middle East: begin at the end of the Second World War, not five thousand years earlier, and start with The House of Saud, the Sykes-Picot Agreement and From Beirut to Jerusalem.

the-difficulty-of-getting-out.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-difficulty-of-getting-out.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-difficulty-of-getting-out.title: Bowe Bergdahl
the-difficulty-of-getting-out.summary: The American soldier who walked off his base in Afghanistan, was captured by the Haqqani network and handed to the Taliban, and was repatriated in a prisoner trade — a man John Kiriakou says was treated as a traitor although he was not one.

the-drone-papers.title: Daniel Hale
the-drone-papers.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-drone-papers.title: The Intercept
the-drone-papers.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

the-drone-papers.title: Signature strikes
the-drone-papers.summary: The drone-targeting doctrine, exposed by Daniel Hale's leak, under which the U.S. kills people not for who they are but for patterns of behavior or association; John Kiriakou says operators treat any male over 12 as a legitimate target on the theory that he 'could pick up a gun.'

the-drone-papers.title: National Bird
the-drone-papers.summary: Award-winning documentary on the U.S. drone program featuring whistleblower Daniel Hale; John Kiriakou calls it essential viewing, noting its footage of drone operators debating on audio whether the figures in their crosshairs are children before firing.

the-drone-papers.title: RDAP program
the-drone-papers.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' Residential Drug and Alcohol Program, which can shave 12 to 18 months off a federal sentence; John Kiriakou repeatedly advises fellow whistleblowers that, combined with good behavior and a halfway house, it can turn a five-year sentence into as little as two and a half years.

the-drone-papers.title: The Intercept's exposed sources
the-drone-papers.summary: John Kiriakou's charge that national security whistleblowers who take material to The Intercept end up in prison. He names Reality Winner and Terry Albury as sources whose identities the outlet exposed, says the same thing happened to Daniel Hale, and identifies the outlet's two national security reporters, Richard Esposito and Matthew Cole, as the journalists responsible for sending him to prison. His question is whether the pattern is incompetence or something worse.

the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.title: Counterterrorist driving
the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.summary: The vehicle training at the Farm — the PIT manoeuvre and how to avoid one, when to ram a roadblock and where to hit it, reversing at sixty miles an hour — conducted in a fleet of junkyard beaters the CIA bought expressly to be wrecked.

the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.title: The shooting house
the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.summary: The live-fire decision course at the Farm where a trainee has about three quarters of a second to decide whether the figure at the window is a gunman or a woman holding a baby — and where John Kiriakou says he never missed, which he connects to his own account of the temperament the CIA selects for.

the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.title: The bomb course
the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.summary: The week-long CIA explosives course at a facility in another state, where John Kiriakou learned to build a Molotov cocktail, then a detonator rig, then an ammonium nitrate bomb — his final exam, which put a van's transmission three hundred yards into the woods.

the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.title: The Farm
the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.summary: The CIA's clandestine training facility in Virginia; site of approximately 80% of all CIA operational training

the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.title: The Advanced Counterterrorism Operations course
the-el-salvador-hotel-drill.summary: The six-week CIA course for which John Kiriakou says he was one of only about a dozen officers in the entire agency selected — and which he finished, as he puts it, just in time for 9/11.

the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.title: The anti-semite smear
the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the professional cost of saying publicly that Israel spies on the United States: Alan Dershowitz calls him names, and the political director of the Israeli foreign minister called him a noted anti-semite.

the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.title: The Epstein statute of limitations
the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that nobody in the United States will be prosecuted over the Jeffrey Epstein case because the five-year limitation period on the sex offences has run — a lapse he says may itself have been part of the plan, and which leaves only an improbable conspiracy theory of the cover-up as a route to charges.

the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.title: Prince Andrew
the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.summary: British royal named repeatedly by John Kiriakou as one of the un-recruitable principals whose access made Jeffrey Epstein valuable to a foreign intelligence service. Kiriakou has asked why Andrew was never charged over conduct with minors, and has said that his 2026 arrest — over the alleged provision of classified Ministry of Defence documents to Epstein — is evidence that Epstein was collecting for a foreign power rather than for himself.

the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.title: The Greek colonel and China
the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.summary: The arrest of a Greek colonel assigned to NATO on charges of spying for China — a case John Kiriakou calls highly unusual not because espionage arrests are rare in Greece, but because they are almost always for Russia, and which he says shows the Chinese have begun caring about NATO communications.

the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.title: Peter Mandelson
the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.summary: British politician; described by John Kiriakou as the former British ambassador to Washington and as someone likely to be charged with serious crimes in connection with Jeffrey Epstein.

the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.title: Running into former sources
the-epstein-files-and-the-starmer-govern.summary: John Kiriakou has twice met people he once ran as agents by accident, years after leaving the CIA — once at an airport and once in the street — and both times they came to him with a bear hug. One of them was astonished to discover he spoke English.

the-eu-whistleblower-directive.title: Blueprint for Free Speech
the-eu-whistleblower-directive.summary: The Australian non-governmental organisation that drafts whistleblower protection legislation and markets it to governments around the world, and which hired John Kiriakou in 2015 to help write Greece's law. Its board is mostly academics and transparency activists; Kiriakou credits it with successes in Canada, Zambia, Jamaica and Ukraine, and names its founder and director as Suelette Dreyfus, whom he describes as a co-founder of WikiLeaks with Julian Assange.

the-eu-whistleblower-directive.title: Kiriakou Greek whistleblower law
the-eu-whistleblower-directive.summary: A whistleblower protection law John Kiriakou says he was hired by the Greek government to write in 2015, at the invitation of Greece, after which it was passed by both the European Parliament and the Greek Parliament and became law across the European Union. Per Kiriakou, the law's first courtroom use involved a whistleblower who exposed Greece's defense minister for taking bribes from Siemens; the resulting press coverage led a consortium of Greece's four wealthiest families to ask Kiriakou to run a private equity fund for them.

the-eu-whistleblower-directive.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-eu-whistleblower-directive.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-eu-whistleblower-directive.title: Bernie Sanders
the-eu-whistleblower-directive.summary: United States senator from Vermont. John Kiriakou, who watched him daily from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, describes Sanders holding open breakfast in the Senate cafeteria for anyone who walked in — insisting only that they call him "Bernie" — and names him the one 2016 candidate willing to talk about shrinking the military.

the-eu-whistleblower-directive.title: Bill Barr
the-eu-whistleblower-directive.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

the-eu-whistleblower-directive.title: Crypto AG
the-eu-whistleblower-directive.summary: The Swiss encryption-machine company revealed in February 2020 to have been secretly owned by the CIA and West German intelligence, which sold riggable ciphers to governments around the world for decades. John Kiriakou, who held senior positions at the agency, says he knew nothing about it — it was held that closely — and refuses to describe it as a scandal: nobody will be prosecuted, several people will probably win medals, and an intelligence operation is not supposed to be honest or fair.

the-faisalabad-cash-run.title: Security, finance and medical
the-faisalabad-cash-run.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-faisalabad-cash-run.title: Arabic and Greek
the-faisalabad-cash-run.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-faisalabad-cash-run.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-faisalabad-cash-run.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-faisalabad-cash-run.title: Curtailment cables
the-faisalabad-cash-run.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-faisalabad-cash-run.title: The bowl of dates
the-faisalabad-cash-run.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

the-faisalabad-cash-run.title: The two Tunisians
the-faisalabad-cash-run.summary: The first counterterrorist raid John Kiriakou led after arriving in Pakistan in January 2002, which produced two eighteen-year-olds from Tunisia who burst into tears when the door came down, one of them asking whether he could telephone his mother.

the-false-volunteer.title: Surveillance detection route
the-false-volunteer.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

the-false-volunteer.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-false-volunteer.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-false-volunteer.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-false-volunteer.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-false-volunteer.title: Bureau of Prisons advisory board
the-false-volunteer.summary: The advisory board John Kiriakou joined at the personal invitation of the Director of the Bureau of Prisons, who told him the president had tasked him with tearing the Bureau down and rebuilding it.

the-false-volunteer.title: The Green Line in Nicosia
the-false-volunteer.summary: The division of Nicosia between the Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-occupied north, which John Kiriakou toured in July 2026 and described as maintained through deliberate humiliation rather than any interest in settlement.

the-false-volunteer.title: Edward Snowden
the-false-volunteer.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

the-farm.title: Doing Time Like a Spy
the-farm.summary: Prison memoir by John Kiriakou, full title Doing Time Like a Spy: How the CIA Taught Me to Survive and Thrive in Prison; winner of two literary awards and reissued in a second edition by Simon and Schuster.

the-farm.title: Surveillance detection route
the-farm.summary: Tradecraft technique used by intelligence officers and assets to determine whether they are being followed before, during, or after an operational meeting

the-farm.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-farm.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-farm.title: The operational cable
the-farm.summary: The written product of every CIA field meeting — drafted the same day, printed and handed to the instructors at the Farm, who critiqued the prose, the conduct of the meeting and what the officer had been wearing.

the-farm.title: Operating Directive
the-farm.summary: The CIA's six-tier (0 through 5) intelligence priority system used to indicate the urgency with which case officers should pursue specific topics

the-farm.title: Planning a surveillance detection route
the-farm.summary: The hours of paperwork behind every CIA meeting before satellite mapping existed — photocopied road-atlas pages taped into sheets six feet across, legs and stops marked in coloured highlighter, submitted to instructors for approval and then driven in advance to check for no-left-turns and closed roads.

the-four-question-torture-exam.title: Liberty University
the-four-question-torture-exam.summary: Evangelical university in Lynchburg, Virginia — the largest in the world — where John Kiriakou taught for several years as an adjunct professor of intelligence studies in the Jesse Helms School of Government. He says he warned the school he disagreed with it on 95% of the issues and was hired anyway, on the dean's reasoning that "torture's not Christian"; he enjoyed the post while clashing constantly with the institution over the treatment of Middle Eastern Christians.

the-four-question-torture-exam.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-four-question-torture-exam.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-four-question-torture-exam.title: Agent payment mechanics
the-four-question-torture-exam.summary: How the CIA physically pays a recruited agent — cash every month, a receipt signed with any alias the agent chooses, and a polygraph regime built around the assumption that the officer handling the money is the person most likely to steal it.

the-four-question-torture-exam.title: Allen Dulles
the-four-question-torture-exam.summary: Long-serving CIA director whom John Kiriakou calls a 'monster' and a 'very dark figure in American history' — a United Fruit board member who ran the agency that overthrew Guatemala's Árbenz, who went to Truman's house to talk him out of criticising the CIA, and who stayed in touch with the men Kiriakou believes killed John F. Kennedy.

the-four-question-torture-exam.title: Church Committee
the-four-question-torture-exam.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

the-four-question-torture-exam.title: The CIA's internal social culture
the-four-question-torture-exam.summary: John Kiriakou's one-word characterisation of the agency's internal culture — "incestuous" — describing a club for every conceivable interest, actively encouraged officer-to-officer romances, and a design intent that officers should have no need of friends or activities outside the building.

the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.title: Hamid Karzai
the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.summary: The president installed in Afghanistan after the American invasion, whom John Kiriakou uses as the standing illustration of what occupation actually buys: after twenty years and more than a trillion dollars, Karzai was ''little more than the mayor of Kabul'' — and did not control all of Kabul either. The line began as a joke among Senate Foreign Relations Committee staff, and Kiriakou used it to Senator John Kerry''s face ten years into the war.

the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.title: María Corina Machado
the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.title: Maduro Capture
the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.summary: CIA-driven nighttime operation in which a team of Delta Force commandos entered Venezuela and removed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their beds. Per John Kiriakou, the key enabling intelligence — per a New York Times account he cited — came from a CIA asset inside Maduro''s presidential palace who called when Maduro went to sleep: ''He''s sound asleep. If you''re going to do it, do it now.'' At least eighty people were killed in the operation, including approximately thirty-five Cubans. Kiriakou compares it to the 1989 capture of Manuel Noriega, in which US forces blasted death metal at the Vatican Embassy until Noriega was asked to leave.

the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.title: The assassination approval process
the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.summary: Why John Kiriakou thinks arranging the death of a foreign leader is far harder for the CIA than the public assumes. It is not the 1960s: there is congressional oversight, and before any proposal reaches the president''s signature it must clear layers of lawyers at the Justice Department''s Office of Legal Counsel, the National Security Council and the agency''s own General Counsel. Pressuring a leader into flight, he notes, is both easier and more legal.

the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.title: The Mariel boatlift comparison
the-four-requirements-of-a-coup.summary: John Kiriakou''s rebuttal to the claim that Venezuela emptied its prisons and mental institutions into the United States: nothing of the kind has been shown to have happened, and the episode being described actually belongs to Cuba, which did exactly that during the Mariel boatlift.

the-fox-news-military-analyst.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-fox-news-military-analyst.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-fox-news-military-analyst.title: Hugh Francis Redmond
the-fox-news-military-analyst.summary: The first CIA officer to die in the line of duty, per John Kiriakou — a Special Activities Division officer sent to Shanghai in 1946 under cover as an ice cream machine salesman, arrested by the Chinese communists in 1951, held and tortured for nineteen years, and declared a suicide by Beijing in 1970. The CIA denied he had ever worked for it until his name was declassified and added to the Wall of Honor.

the-fox-news-military-analyst.title: Robert David Steele
the-fox-news-military-analyst.summary: The former intelligence officer and podcaster whose death during the COVID-19 pandemic John Kiriakou was asked to explain. Kiriakou, who had appeared on his show, calls him a sweet man who died of the disease, and offers a blunt assessment of his work: he did not believe most of the conspiracy theories he promoted, but they brought him an audience.

the-fox-news-military-analyst.title: The 1968 waterboarding conviction
the-fox-news-military-analyst.summary: The precedent John Kiriakou uses to dispose of the argument that waterboarding was legally uncertain after 2002: a January 1968 Washington Post front page showing an American soldier waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner, an investigation ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, and the soldier''s arrest, conviction for torture and imprisonment. The law, Kiriakou points out, never changed in between.

the-fox-news-military-analyst.title: The lawfare template
the-fox-news-military-analyst.summary: The assessment of John Kiriakou''s prosecution that he quotes most often and finds most alarming: a former United States attorney for Utah told him the Kiriakou case was the template for the Democratic Party''s policy of lawfare. Kiriakou''s gloss is that if they do not like you they can ruin your life, and there is nothing you can do to protect yourself.

the-fox-news-military-analyst.title: The science fiction writer FOIA request
the-fox-news-military-analyst.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed with the CIA about a 1950s science fiction writer long rumoured to have been an undercover officer — answered only with a letter saying the agency lacked the manpower to meet its statutory ninety-day deadline. Fifteen years later, he says, he is still waiting.

the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.title: The ask-forgiveness maxim
the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.summary: The rule of thumb John Kiriakou says he was taught early in his CIA career — that it is always better to ask forgiveness than to ask permission — and which he offers as the explanation for how the agency runs legally doubtful programmes: it does what it wants, apologises if caught, and that is the end of it.

the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.title: The CIA as a paramilitary organization
the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.summary: John Kiriakou''s periodisation of the CIA''s mission — spying and analysis until Vietnam, restored after the Church and Pike hearings of 1975, and converted immediately after September 11 into a paramilitary body that he says it has remained ever since. His objection is stated without hedging: drawing up a kill list every Tuesday and dispatching officers to carry it out is not intelligence, it is murder.

the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-gang-of-four-and-gang-of-eight.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-general-assembly-workaround.title: Ireland recognizes Palestine
the-general-assembly-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the American reaction to Ireland''s recognition of Palestine, which he says he witnessed the aftermath of while in the country: the CIA was indifferent, but the State Department was apoplectic — not about Ireland itself, but about the precedent, which Kiriakou says other European states promptly began to follow.

the-general-assembly-workaround.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-general-assembly-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-general-assembly-workaround.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-general-assembly-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-general-assembly-workaround.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-general-assembly-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-general-assembly-workaround.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-general-assembly-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-general-assembly-workaround.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
the-general-assembly-workaround.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

the-greek-colonel-and-china.title: The density of spies in Washington
the-greek-colonel-and-china.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that there are more spies in Washington DC than anywhere else in the world, that the FBI''s counterintelligence division does nothing but try to root them out, and that the job cannot be finished short of becoming North Korea.

the-greek-colonel-and-china.title: The operational test
the-greek-colonel-and-china.summary: The vetting procedure John Kiriakou describes for moving a trusted source onto normal handling: put a full surveillance team on him without telling him, watch how he gets to the meeting, and then ask him to describe what he did.

the-greek-colonel-and-china.title: Running into former sources
the-greek-colonel-and-china.summary: John Kiriakou has twice met people he once ran as agents by accident, years after leaving the CIA — once at an airport and once in the street — and both times they came to him with a bear hug. One of them was astonished to discover he spoke English.

the-greek-colonel-and-china.title: Sources are not traitors
the-greek-colonel-and-china.summary: Asked whether CIA officers privately regarded their recruited agents as traitors and held them in contempt, John Kiriakou answered that they did not — because the officers believed they were the good guys, and a recruited source had become one of them.

the-greek-colonel-and-china.title: The Epstein files and the Starmer government
the-greek-colonel-and-china.summary: John Kiriakou''s prediction that the Epstein disclosures could bring down Keir Starmer''s government, on the strength of evidence that Prince Andrew and Peter Mandelson gave Epstein classified British Ministry of Defence documents — an Official Secrets Act matter that in America would fall under the Espionage Act.

the-greek-colonel-and-china.title: The orb off Yemen
the-greek-colonel-and-china.summary: A leaked video John Kiriakou describes as the most dramatic UFO material he has seen: two F-18s following a silver orb off the coast of Yemen, given permission to fire, and a missile that hits the object and bounces off before the orb turns ninety degrees and flies on.

the-greek-turn-toward-israel.title: Ireland recognizes Palestine
the-greek-turn-toward-israel.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the American reaction to Ireland''s recognition of Palestine, which he says he witnessed the aftermath of while in the country: the CIA was indifferent, but the State Department was apoplectic — not about Ireland itself, but about the precedent, which Kiriakou says other European states promptly began to follow.

the-greek-turn-toward-israel.title: The University of Salamanca professorship
the-greek-turn-toward-israel.summary: John Kiriakou's teaching post in the graduate intelligence studies programme at the University of Salamanca, where he lectures on introductory intelligence studies and the history of terrorism, at an institution he describes as older than Spain itself.

the-greek-turn-toward-israel.title: CIA attention to West Africa
