the-guardian-smear-series.title: Assange and solitary confinement
the-guardian-smear-series.summary: John Kiriakou's 2018 argument that Julian Assange's isolation inside the Ecuadorian embassy amounted to solitary confinement — a practice the United Nations classes as torture — and that everybody breaks under it eventually, however strong they are.

the-guardian-smear-series.title: "Ecuador is open for business"
the-guardian-smear-series.summary: The Wall Street Journal headline John Kiriakou says appeared the day after he hand-delivered a letter to Ecuador's ambassador in Washington asking that Julian Assange's internet access be restored, and which made him fear Assange was about to be used as a bargaining chip.

the-guardian-smear-series.title: The chain of command argument
the-guardian-smear-series.summary: John Kiriakou's standing rejection of the advice given to new intelligence officers — that evidence of waste, fraud, abuse or illegality should be taken up the chain of command — supported by the fates of Thomas Drake, William Binney, Kirk Wiebe and Diane Roark, and by the fact that his own chain of command had created the torture programme.

the-guardian-smear-series.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-guardian-smear-series.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-guardian-smear-series.title: Julian Assange
the-guardian-smear-series.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-guardian-smear-series.title: Seventy-two denied motions
the-guardian-smear-series.summary: The count John Kiriakou gives of the pretrial motions filed in his case and denied by Judge Leonie Brinkema — seventy-two denied and none granted — which he offers as the mechanism by which a national security defendant in the Eastern District of Virginia is prevented from mounting a defence at all.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Wolf Blitzer at CIA headquarters
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: What John Kiriakou says he saw a couple of weeks into his CIA career in 1990: the CNN correspondent Wolf Blitzer walking the halls of headquarters with a camera crew and no security escort, filming a stand-up in front of an agency sign. Kiriakou offers it, alongside the Bob Woodward episode, as evidence that the supposed wall between the CIA and the American press does not exist.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Bob Woodward's CIA headquarters access
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: John Kiriakou's account of watching Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward walk the halls of CIA headquarters unescorted while researching a book, after the CIA director ordered staff to cooperate with him — an episode Kiriakou cites as evidence of how close the relationship between senior CIA officials and favored journalists really is.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Muddling through
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: The 2022 destruction of the Nord Stream gas pipelines, whose responsibility John Kiriakou treats as genuinely unresolved — citing Seymour Hersh's reporting that the CIA did it, a later Ukrainian special-forces claim of a sailboat-based operation carried out without Zelensky's knowledge, and a retired CIA colleague's private theory that Putin blew up his own pipeline to blame the Americans.

the-hersh-publishing-collapse.title: The African diplomat's remark
the-hersh-publishing-collapse.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Arabic and Greek
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Curtailment cables
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: Security, finance and medical
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: The bowl of dates
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

the-honey-salesman-warning.title: The declination letter
the-honey-salesman-warning.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-hooding-dispute.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-hooding-dispute.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-hooding-dispute.title: The martyrdom bonus
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The recruitment offer John Kiriakou says captured al-Qaeda foot soldiers described to him in Pakistan: three hundred dollars a month to go and fight the Americans in Afghanistan, and five hundred dollars paid to the fighter''s parents if he was killed.

the-hooding-dispute.title: The two Tunisians
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The first counterterrorist raid John Kiriakou led after arriving in Pakistan in January 2002, which produced two eighteen-year-olds from Tunisia who burst into tears when the door came down, one of them asking whether he could telephone his mother.

the-hooding-dispute.title: Arabic and Greek
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-hooding-dispute.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-hooding-dispute.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: The Directorate of Operations
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The CIA's clandestine service, which John Kiriakou joined from analysis because he spoke both Greek and Arabic — a culture he describes as wildly different from the analytic side, short on institutional memory and organised around the race to become a station chief.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: The Directorate of Intelligence
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The CIA's analytic cadre, where John Kiriakou spent the first seven years of his career working on Iraq before switching to operations — a culture he describes as convinced it holds the smartest people in the room, and whose function he says is duplicated across a dozen other agencies.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: Operating Directive
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The CIA's six-tier (0 through 5) intelligence priority system used to indicate the urgency with which case officers should pursue specific topics

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: President's Daily Brief
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the President's Daily Brief (PDB) is a roughly 16-page, top-secret intelligence document produced daily for the president, written in a uniform CIA house style, briefed each morning, and — in his account — used partly to gauge and flatter incoming presidents.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: John Ratcliffe
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: CIA director under Trump's second term; per John Kiriakou, a "bombthrower" he mostly disagrees with politically but supported as a needed disruptor for the agency — "a good guy, expert in what he does," though "not a visionary thinker" and, on Kiriakou's later assessment, a neocon who has outmanoeuvred Tulsi Gabbard for primacy over U.S. intelligence. Ratcliffe told the White House the CIA had no objection to pardoning Kiriakou.

the-hot-dog-lady-cable.title: National Security Council
the-hot-dog-lady-cable.summary: The White House body that, in John Kiriakou's telling, sat on the pro-war side of every fight that defined his era — gung-ho for the Iraq invasion alongside Cheney's and Rumsfeld's offices while the CIA, State Department, and Joint Chiefs opposed it; the place where an official predicted Iraqis would "throw flowers at us"; a signature stop in the approval chain for both the torture program and covert action findings; and the perch from which John Brennan, as its number two, urged the Justice Department to secretly reopen the case against Kiriakou.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Fabricated intelligence reporting
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The three things John Kiriakou says CIA case officers are caught doing — inventing intelligence outright, holding real reports back to smooth out a monthly quota, and padding cover-stop expenses — and his argument that the fabrication is driven by production targets set by bad managers.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Denied areas
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The CIA term for countries so hostile and so heavily surveilled that ordinary operational movement is impossible — the Soviet Union, Cuba, Syria, and later Russia, China, North Korea and Iran — and the reason, in John Kiriakou's account, that officers heading to one get specialist briefings, eight-hour surveillance detection routes, and that the Agency has to fall back on liaison services instead of its own sources.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Abraxas Corporation
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The private intelligence company founded in the 1990s by retired CIA operations officers as a tax pass-through and a place to smoke cigars and tell stories — which, after 9/11, made its founders, in John Kiriakou's phrase, Mega Millions rich.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: The Brüno shoot in Jordan
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The scene John Kiriakou set up for Sacha Baron Cohen in Amman — four retired Palestinian militants, found in the Damascus telephone book at the Library of Congress, shown hardcore pornography by a character they believed to be an Austrian documentary journalist — which produced no reaction at all and was cut from the film entirely.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Chief of station
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: The CIA's senior officer in a foreign country — appointed by the CIA director alone, outranking the ambassador's intelligence equities in practice, and in John Kiriakou's account the figure who sets the moral temperature of a station, from the officer who handed him his first counterterrorism assignment to the one who walks into a minister's office fifteen minutes after the human rights officer has left.

the-hotel-bar-operation.title: Concealment devices
the-hotel-bar-operation.summary: Hollowed everyday objects — known inside the CIA as CDs — issued to officers to hide documents, equipment and, in the larger sizes, a gun. Per John Kiriakou every CIA officer has access to them, some are simply assigned with no instructions attached, and the way they are found in real life is the way they are found in *The Good Shepherd* — by an anomaly a hand can feel.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: Arabic and Greek
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: Security, finance and medical
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: The autographed basketball
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: A recruitment John Kiriakou has cited as proof that an agent''s price is not always money: a source who loved the Chicago Bulls, an ordinary basketball bought from the NBA online store with a forged provenance involving Michael Jordan, and an acrylic display box.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: The prostitute hypothetical
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The classroom exercise John Kiriakou uses in university lectures to demonstrate that the CIA gave its operations officers no ethical guidelines at all — a recruited terrorist source who demands a prostitute, and then the same demand for a child.

the-indonesian-recruitment-question.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-indonesian-recruitment-question.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: The Intercept
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: Matthew Cole
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: American national-security journalist whose reporting tradecraft, per John Kiriakou, has led to the federal incarceration of five whistleblowers — including Kiriakou himself. In Kiriakou's account, Cole emailed him in 2010 ostensibly researching a book on the rendition of Abu Omar, asked Kiriakou to confirm the surname of a CIA officer who appeared in Kiriakou's own first book under the alias 'John', and Kiriakou's confirmation was the act of confirming a covert officer's identity for which he was eventually prosecuted under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: Daniel Hale
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: The Drone Papers
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: Communications management unit
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

the-intercept-source-exposures.title: Liam O'Grady
the-intercept-source-exposures.summary: The Eastern District of Virginia judge who sentenced Daniel Hale, and who in John Kiriakou''s account surprised the courtroom twice: with a sentence of 45 months rather than the far longer term expected, and with a recommendation that Hale serve it in a low-security prison where he could be treated for depression and addiction. The Bureau of Prisons ignored the recommendation and sent him to the communications management unit at Marion instead.

the-intercept.title: Matthew Cole
the-intercept.summary: American national-security journalist whose reporting tradecraft, per John Kiriakou, has led to the federal incarceration of five whistleblowers — including Kiriakou himself. In Kiriakou's account, Cole emailed him in 2010 ostensibly researching a book on the rendition of Abu Omar, asked Kiriakou to confirm the surname of a CIA officer who appeared in Kiriakou's own first book under the alias 'John', and Kiriakou's confirmation was the act of confirming a covert officer's identity for which he was eventually prosecuted under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act.

the-intercept.title: The Intercept's exposed sources
the-intercept.summary: John Kiriakou's charge that national security whistleblowers who take material to The Intercept end up in prison. He names Reality Winner and Terry Albury as sources whose identities the outlet exposed, says the same thing happened to Daniel Hale, and identifies the outlet's two national security reporters, Richard Esposito and Matthew Cole, as the journalists responsible for sending him to prison. His question is whether the pattern is incompetence or something worse.

the-intercept.title: India
the-intercept.summary: The country John Kiriakou names as his least favourite of all the places he has worked — not, he stresses, for poverty or danger, both of which he has seen worse of, but for the caste system and "the way Indians treat one another." His illustration is an afternoon in Hyderabad when two separate restaurants refused to admit the driver he had invited to lunch.

the-intercept.title: Wikileaks as a System
the-intercept.summary: Per John Kiriakou, WikiLeaks functions less as a single leader than as a durable system — one that protected whistleblowers, helped popularize the term "whistleblower" itself, was credited with contributing to the Arab Spring, weathered pressure to become a defanged NGO, and outlasted the political fallout of its 2010 cable releases (including, in Kiriakou's account, an unintended assist to Donald Trump's election).

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: The Syria chemical attack correction
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: John Kiriakou's public retraction of what he wrote about the August 2013 chemical attack near Damascus. Asked about the passage in his book on Iran, he said he had written it before United Nations whistleblowers came forward to say they did not believe it was a Syrian government attack, and thanked the questioner for the chance to correct it.

the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-iran-israel-exchange-assessment.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: The Taliban lobbyist in Washington
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: A story put to John Kiriakou about a Taliban delegation''s American press conference and the Washington lobbyist who represented them. Kiriakou remembered the episode and the lobbyist''s New Jersey base but not the claim about her parentage, and explained why it caused so little controversy at the time: the United States had no historical quarrel with the Taliban, and had armed and fêted some of its future members during the war against the Soviets.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: The 2025 India–Pakistan clash assessment
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the most recent India–Pakistan confrontation, delivered after an unusually explicit declaration of his own bias: he loved living in Pakistan, favours Pakistan on Kashmir, and judges that India accomplished nothing while Pakistan lost nothing, leaving the Pakistanis slightly ahead.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: The cave myth
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-isi-as-two-organizations.title: False flags are too hard
the-isi-as-two-organizations.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-islamabad-guest-house.title: The best meal overseas
the-islamabad-guest-house.summary: Asked for the best meals he had eaten abroad, John Kiriakou named first a dish cooked by a young Pakistani in a CIA guest house in Islamabad — shaved beef, a myriad of spices, hot green chillies and rice cooked in chicken stock — followed by sushi in Tokyo and the Lenten table of Clean Monday in Greece.

the-islamabad-guest-house.title: The dandelion salad
the-islamabad-guest-house.summary: The meal John Kiriakou assembled in the yard at FCI Loretto from foraged dandelions, commissary olive oil and sea salt, instant rice, a bouillon cube, peanuts, borrowed Sazón and a bag of chicken — which he calls the single most satisfying meal of his twenty-three months in prison.

the-islamabad-guest-house.title: Dubai as Iran''s window
the-islamabad-guest-house.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iran did not hit Dubai hard during the 2026 war: the city is full of Iranian businessmen and is Iran''s outlet to the Western world and its principal means of evading sanctions.

the-islamabad-guest-house.title: Embassy fortification after 9/11
the-islamabad-guest-house.summary: The post-2001 rebuilding of American embassies as hardened compounds, which John Kiriakou explains as a direct answer to Iranian Revolutionary Guard reconnaissance of diplomatic premises. His illustration is Doha: an embassy sitting above a grocery store in 1990, and an embassy occupying an entire city block and fortified "nine ways from Sunday" today.

the-islamabad-guest-house.title: Narcotics under cover
the-islamabad-guest-house.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether a CIA officer under cover may take drugs when an asset offers them: yes. The rule he describes begins with qat in Yemen and extends to cocaine in Latin America, on the ground that refusing can be a matter of life and death.

the-islamabad-guest-house.title: Qat in Yemen
the-islamabad-guest-house.summary: The afternoon shrub-chewing habit of Yemen, and the special dispensation the CIA had to issue so that its officers could take part in it. John Kiriakou explains that no source could be developed in a qat-chewing country by an officer who would not chew.

the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.title: The Jerusalem harassment campaign
the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what happened to a CIA colleague and his wife during a declared two-year State Department rotation in Jerusalem: furniture rearranged after one embassy party, all three toilets in the house defecated in after another, and, before they left, the family dog''s tail cut off and bandaged. Kiriakou presents the three break-ins as routine rather than exceptional.

the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.title: The "spell your name" briefing
the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.summary: The first time John Kiriakou dealt with the Israeli services: eight weeks into his CIA career, giving the junior slot in a liaison briefing on Saddam Hussein''s state of mind, he was interrupted by a Mossad representative who asked him to spell his name and then told him he was Jewish. Kiriakou''s reply — that he was not recruitable — became one of his recurring illustrations of the liaison relationship.

the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.title: Gulf secret prisons for hire
the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.summary: Asked whether the CIA knew of Gulf royals operating underground torture facilities and secret prisons, John Kiriakou answered that it did — one hundred per cent — then refused to give details, saying he would risk returning to prison. He described the arrangement instead: the United States sought out these countries precisely because they had no parliament and no free press to answer to, and paid for the use of their cells.

the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-israeli-listening-devices-ban.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-istanbul-peace-talks.title: Kiriakou's Ukraine settlement prediction
the-istanbul-peace-talks.summary: The endgame John Kiriakou forecast in June 2025 and calls deliberately unbold: Russia keeps the disputed eastern territories and Crimea, Ukraine never joins NATO but probably joins the European Union, and Moscow gets ninety per cent of what it wanted. The one demand he expects Russia to trade away is denazification, which he reads as propaganda rather than policy.

the-istanbul-peace-talks.title: Assange and the European Court of Human Rights
the-istanbul-peace-talks.summary: The last legal avenue John Kiriakou identified for Julian Assange in 2022 — three precedents in which the Strasbourg court refused to let Britain extradite mentally ill defendants to American solitary confinement — and the procedural trap that made it useless: Britain said the appeal need not halt the extradition.

the-istanbul-peace-talks.title: Russia-Ukraine war origins
the-istanbul-peace-talks.summary: John Kiriakou's account that the war began in 2014, not 2022 — rooted in broken U.S. promises that NATO would not expand to Russia's borders, the 2014 removal of a pro-Russian Ukrainian leader, and the seizure of Crimea; he says Russia is now winning and has no reason to negotiate.

the-istanbul-peace-talks.title: Sealing the courtroom
the-istanbul-peace-talks.summary: The physical measures John Kiriakou describes as accompanying a classified-information trial: plastic sheeting and duct tape over the windows so lasers cannot read the vibrations, white noise in the vestibule, and the clearing of everyone but the judge, jury, bailiff, clerk, lawyers and defendant.

the-istanbul-peace-talks.title: The jury consultant''s advice
the-istanbul-peace-talks.summary: What John Kiriakou''s jury consultant told him about a national security trial in the Eastern District of Virginia: that in any other district in America he would say fight and win, but in that one, "buddy, you don''t have a prayer. Take the deal."

the-istanbul-peace-talks.title: The swimming pool substitution
the-istanbul-peace-talks.summary: John Kiriakou''s illustration of how classified words are handled at trial: prosecutors and judge agree in advance to replace them with harmless unclassified substitutes, so that "Vault 7" becomes "swimming pool" — and the jury, told the real words are too secret for their ears, concludes the defendant must be guilty.

the-jerusalem-harassment-campaign.title: The Israeli listening devices ban
the-jerusalem-harassment-campaign.summary: Why Mossad and Shin Bet representatives were barred from CIA headquarters, per John Kiriakou: the gifts they brought to liaison meetings kept turning up with listening devices and batteries embedded inside, so the agency stopped admitting them and rented meeting space in Virginia instead.

the-jerusalem-harassment-campaign.title: The minister of Awqaf compliment
the-jerusalem-harassment-campaign.summary: The moment John Kiriakou calls the highlight of his Bahrain tour and freely describes as an ego booster: interpreting for Ambassador David Ransom''s first courtesy call on the only Bahraini cabinet member who did not speak fluent English, and being complimented on his Arabic on the way out — something he says he still thinks about thirty years later.

the-jury-consultants-advice.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-jury-consultants-advice.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-jury-consultants-advice.title: Julian Assange
the-jury-consultants-advice.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-jury-consultants-advice.title: FISA court
the-jury-consultants-advice.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance court — created under Carter, sitting atop the Justice Department, issuing warrants that are never public — which he says was abused against Carter Page as part of what he believes was John Brennan's plan to deny Trump the presidency.

the-kgb-denial-cables.title: Richard Welch
the-kgb-denial-cables.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

the-kgb-denial-cables.title: Ukraine as a proxy war
the-kgb-denial-cables.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment, given two months into the 2022 Russian invasion, that the United States was funding a proxy war it knew Ukraine could not win in order to bog Russia down — and that the outcome was already fixed, so peace talks should happen at once.

the-kgb-denial-cables.title: American media consolidation
the-kgb-denial-cables.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why American news coverage is uniform: the entire national media is owned by six corporations or oligarchs, a number the Warner Brothers sale would reduce to five. He attributes the consolidation to profit rather than politics, and describes the practical consequence as an audience that turns on a cable channel believing it is being educated when it is being propagandised — with independent media the only alternative and almost nobody with the time to find it.

the-kgb-denial-cables.title: The CIA and Hollywood
the-kgb-denial-cables.summary: The CIA''s standing arrangement with the film industry, as John Kiriakou describes it: a branch inside the Office of Public Affairs whose only job is to cooperate with Hollywood studios, on the model the FBI has run since the 1950s, so that what comes out of Hollywood carries a pro-agency message. Kiriakou notes it is technically illegal for the CIA to propagandise the American public and says that is exactly what happens every time an agency-linked film is released.

the-kgb-denial-cables.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-kgb-denial-cables.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-kgb-denial-cables.title: Jeffrey Epstein
the-kgb-denial-cables.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

the-la-times-iran-op-ed.title: The Office of Security arrangement
the-la-times-iran-op-ed.summary: The disclosure John Kiriakou says emerged from a 2020 custody hearing: that his wife, herself a senior CIA officer, had accompanied him to the 2007 ABC News whistleblowing interview on the instruction of the CIA''s Office of Security, and had continued to report on his activities.

the-la-times-iran-op-ed.title: Abu Omar rendition
the-la-times-iran-op-ed.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

the-la-times-iran-op-ed.title: Intelligence Identities Protection Act
the-la-times-iran-op-ed.summary: U.S. law enacted in 1982 that makes it a crime to knowingly disclose the identity of a covert intelligence officer; per John Kiriakou, his 2012 prosecution under the act arose from confirming a single surname of a former CIA colleague to a journalist — a confirmation that was never published. The name passed through a chain from journalist to Human Rights Watch to Guantanamo defense attorneys before reaching a judge and ultimately the FBI, which traced it back to Kiriakou.

the-la-times-iran-op-ed.title: The custody standoff
the-la-times-iran-op-ed.summary: The week John Kiriakou used his CIA surveillance training to find his own sons after his ex-wife hid them in breach of a custody order — ending with him carrying his eight-year-old out of a Greek Orthodox church during the consecration, a felony charge that was dropped, and a hostage-style handover at a diner on the state line.

the-la-times-iran-op-ed.title: The Greek community of Warren, Ohio
the-la-times-iran-op-ed.summary: The Greek-American community John Kiriakou's mother and first wife both came from — overwhelmingly from the island of Chios, closely enough knit that his divorce started a fistfight in a coffee house between men who had never met him.

the-la-times-iran-op-ed.title: Mary Jane Stevens
the-la-times-iran-op-ed.summary: The lawyer who represented John Kiriakou through his custody dispute — who told him to wait for Monday and go to court, was ignored, and then got the assurance from a hostile police chief that let him walk into the hearing without being arrested.

the-lawfare-template.title: Kiriakou pardon request
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou's public campaign for a presidential pardon from Donald Trump to restore the pension and firearm rights he lost after his 2013 felony conviction for disclosing the identity of a covert CIA officer; includes a five-second Mar-a-Lago encounter in which Trump referred him to Attorney General Pam Bondi, a Kalshi prediction-market contract that opened at roughly 19 to 20 percent odds on his being pardoned, and letters of support from Tucker Carlson, Judge Andrew Napolitano and Dr. Phil.

the-lawfare-template.title: The Fox News military analyst
the-lawfare-template.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

the-lawfare-template.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-lawfare-template.title: Espionage Act
the-lawfare-template.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-lawfare-template.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-lawfare-template.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: Frank Serpico
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: The New York police officer John Kiriakou calls one of the giants of the twentieth century and ranks with Daniel Ellsberg among its greatest whistleblowers — a man shot in the face whose police colleagues did not call an ambulance, and whom Kiriakou counts as a friend.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: "There is almost no upside"
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: John Kiriakou''s accounting of what blowing the whistle cost him — pension, friends, freedom and finally family — set against the single thing he says is left: knowing he did the right thing. And his timeline, from the whistle in 2007 to a vindication he says took eleven years.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: Leaker versus whistleblower
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: The fight over what the American networks would call John Kiriakou. It took his lawyers, above all Jesselyn Radack, a year of work between January 2012 and January 2013 to get CNN and MSNBC to stop introducing him as 'CIA leaker John Kiriakou'. CNN changed and Fox, he notes, never needed to; MSNBC in his account never did, and Rachel Maddow settled on a formula he quotes with some precision — a man 'who styles himself a whistleblower'.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: The EU whistleblower directive
the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.summary: The European Union whistleblower protection directive, which John Kiriakou describes as a watered-down descendant of the Greek law he helped write in 2015. His objection is to its exemption: the directive does not apply to Brussels itself. He treats that as an instance of a general legislative habit rather than a European failing — Congress, he notes, routinely exempts itself from the laws it passes, including the Occupational Safety and Health Act.

the-legal-definition-of-whistleblowing.title: Assange and the European Court of Human Rights

the-liaison-class.title: Cofer Black's warning to the liaison class
the-liaison-class.summary: The briefing Cofer Black gave to a class of visiting foreign liaison officers weeks before 11 September 2001 — code words about a honey salesman, a great football match and an enormous wedding — and the private exchange afterwards in which he told John Kiriakou he had been deadly serious.

the-liaison-class.title: Cofer Black
the-liaison-class.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

the-liaison-class.title: The Foreign Relations volume and the sources still alive
the-liaison-class.summary: The errand that put John Kiriakou and Cofer Black in a car to the White House on the morning of 11 September 2001: three declassified cables due to be printed in a State Department history volume named CIA sources who were still living — and an obscure law requiring the United States to resettle any source it outs.

the-liaison-class.title: John Kiriakou
the-liaison-class.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-liaison-class.title: Counterterrorism Center
the-liaison-class.summary: The CIA's Counterterrorism Center (CTC) — the unit where John Kiriakou spent the defining years of his operational career. He joined in the late 1990s as the only officer in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic, served as chief of counterintelligence in the bin Laden unit, watched the Center swell from a few hundred employees to nearly 2,000 by September 12, 2001, and it was to CTC that he walked back down in May 2002 to refuse the torture program — the moment, he says, the CIA began to turn on him.

the-liaison-class.title: The custody standoff
the-liaison-class.summary: The week John Kiriakou used his CIA surveillance training to find his own sons after his ex-wife hid them in breach of a custody order — ending with him carrying his eight-year-old out of a Greek Orthodox church during the consecration, a felony charge that was dropped, and a hostage-style handover at a diner on the state line.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: The Benghazi hearings critique
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s complaint about the congressional inquiry into Benghazi, which he watched all the way through: he believes there is some evidence of gun running, doubts anyone will ever establish who was behind it, and objects that the hearings were not trying to find out — having devolved into a political contest that served the American people not at all.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: The September 10th country
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s formulation of what he wants back, and his ledger on the two wars: he never supported the invasion of Iraq, which he calls a war of choice and of family revenge, and he did support the war in Afghanistan until al-Qaeda was defeated in 2003, after which everything became nation building. He assigns the destruction of the pre-attack country to George W. Bush and Barack Obama equally.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.
