He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-libya-policy-reversal.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-libya-policy-reversal.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: No plan for day two
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned early at the CIA: the United States is very good at overthrowing governments and has no idea what to do afterwards. The planning is all about day one. He lists Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Syria, Sudan and Somalia as the record, and gives three reasons the same officials keep repeating the mistake.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: Covert action programs
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: The most tightly held category of American intelligence activity — so tightly held, John Kiriakou says, that a serving CIA officer may not utter the phrase in public. Which is why he found it extraordinary that a president announced one on television, and doubts the announcement was straightforwardly true.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: María Corina Machado
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: The West Africa cocaine route
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of where cocaine transiting Venezuela actually goes: not north to the United States but east to West Africa, onto camels along an old Tuareg track to Morocco, and by boat to Spain. The drugs, he says, are meant for Western Europe — and are not Venezuelan to begin with, but Colombian and Ecuadorian.

the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.title: Venezuelan heavy crude and the refining bottleneck
the-libyan-constitution-unveiling.summary: John Kiriakou''s economic explanation for American pressure on Venezuela: the country''s oil is unusually high in sulfur and requires specialty refining, which for years could only be done in Houston. He says sanctions pushed India and China to build refineries capable of processing it, and that a Chinese announcement of a Caribbean refinery for Venezuelan crude left Washington with a policy it could not admit had failed.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: The post-9/11 name traces
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own assignment in the weeks after the September 11 attacks: with people walking into American embassies all over the world offering information on al-Qaeda, the CIA was buried under tens of thousands of names — sometimes thousands arriving in a single day — and needed, as he put it, an army of clerks to search them against its databases.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Gary Schroen
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: The senior CIA officer whom John Kiriakou describes as legendary and who, with a small team of agency special operations officers, was the first CIA group into Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks — going in, Kiriakou says, on something like September 12, and later writing a book about it called First In.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Kandahar
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: The southern Afghan city and province that recurs across John Kiriakou's Afghanistan material — site of one of the two al-Qaeda training camps Abu Zubaydah founded, whose commanders were captured in the same March 2002 raids; the town Bill Clinton said he would have had to destroy, killing 300 innocents, to kill bin Laden in the 1990s; and a stop on Kiriakou's Senate-era heroin-poppy investigation, when the military helicoptered him down before refusing to let him walk the poppy fields.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Condoleezza Rice
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: Heather Kiriakou
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: John Kiriakou's wife, a senior CIA analyst who — in his account — was one of the best analysts in the entire intelligence community and who lost her job at the agency for no reason other than being married to him. She sat off camera at his December 2007 ABC News interview and told him afterwards that he had said nothing classified.

the-live-satellite-feed-myth.title: The Mohamed Atta Prague claim
the-live-satellite-feed-myth.summary: Dick Cheney's televised assertion tying the September 11 hijacker Mohamed Atta to Saddam Hussein by way of a meeting with the Iraqi intelligence station chief in Prague, which John Kiriakou calls an out-and-out lie made up without a shred of supporting evidence.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: The sentencing remark
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The comment John Kiriakou says the judge made at his sentencing — that she wished she could give him the maximum, because that is what she would give him — and his reading of it as a performance for the national security reporters filling the gallery.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Passing time at Loretto
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: How prisoners at FCI Loretto filled days John Kiriakou describes as Groundhog Day — working out and watching television on a set of screens divided between factions, while Kiriakou himself read, answered mail and wrote a book.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Arabic and Greek
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-loretto-camp-mixup.title: Curtailment cables
the-loretto-camp-mixup.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: The two Tunisians
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The first counterterrorist raid John Kiriakou led after arriving in Pakistan in January 2002, which produced two eighteen-year-olds from Tunisia who burst into tears when the door came down, one of them asking whether he could telephone his mother.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: The honey salesman warning
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: The hooding dispute
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The argument John Kiriakou says he had with a subordinate at a CIA safe house in Pakistan on the night of the Abu Zubaydah raid, over hoods placed on captured prisoners; both men reported each other to headquarters, and Kiriakou was the one reprimanded.

the-martyrdom-bonus.title: Arabic and Greek
the-martyrdom-bonus.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: The Jerusalem harassment campaign
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what happened to a CIA colleague and his wife during a declared two-year State Department rotation in Jerusalem: furniture rearranged after one embassy party, all three toilets in the house defecated in after another, and, before they left, the family dog''s tail cut off and bandaged. Kiriakou presents the three break-ins as routine rather than exceptional.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: CIA language training
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: The agency''s language pipeline as John Kiriakou experienced and describes it: a full year of Arabic at nine hours a day, an optional second year at the State Department''s school, and the calculation that made his own career — that it is cheaper to teach a linguist operations than to teach an operations officer Greek and Arabic.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-minister-of-awqaf-compliment.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: Muddling through
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: The Paris rifle serial number
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: The case John Kiriakou uses to argue that American weapons sent to Ukraine are leaking onto the black market: a rifle used to shoot and severely wound a policeman in Paris whose serial number, he says, matched a shipment of assault rifles the United States had sent to Ukraine some six months earlier.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-nato-expansion-promises.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-nato-expansion-promises.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Julian Assange
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Authorized leaks
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: The distinction John Kiriakou draws between the classified information Washington releases on purpose and the classified information it prosecutes people for releasing. The mechanism is the same and the legal status is identical; what differs is whether the leak flatters the leaker. His worked example is an agency leak claiming the CIA predicted the October 2023 attack on Israel three days out — a story the CIA can then piously report to the FBI, knowing the source will never be found.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Espionage Act
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Eastern District of Virginia
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: The U.S. federal district covering northern Virginia — home to Langley, the Pentagon, DHS and much of the intelligence-contractor industry — which John Kiriakou calls 'the espionage court' because the Justice Department files the great majority of its national security prosecutions there and because, in his telling, no national-security defendant has ever won a case in it; Kiriakou, Julian Assange, Edward Snowden and Jeffrey Sterling were all charged there.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Leonie Brinkema
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: U.S. federal judge in the Eastern District of Virginia — informally the 'Espionage Court' — a Reagan appointee John Kiriakou calls "a hanging judge." Per Kiriakou, Brinkema systematically reserved all major national security cases for herself rather than allowing them to be distributed randomly among judges, and ruled in Kiriakou's case that his reason for blowing the whistle was legally irrelevant and that classified documents could not be used in his defense — effectively making it impossible to mount one.

the-new-york-times-problem.title: Mike Pompeo
the-new-york-times-problem.summary: CIA director and later Secretary of State under Trump. John Kiriakou read Pompeo's 2017 speech branding WikiLeaks a "hostile non-state intelligence service" as the groundwork for an Espionage Act case against Julian Assange in the Eastern District of Virginia — the "Espionage Court" where Kiriakou himself was prosecuted. Friends who briefed Pompeo told Kiriakou he was extraordinarily bright but wrong on Iran; Kiriakou's own verdict soured permanently when Pompeo named Gina Haspel deputy director, flirted publicly with reinstating torture, and called Chelsea Manning a traitor — a crime she was never convicted of.

the-npr-walkout.title: The pre-interview
the-npr-walkout.summary: The booking practice John Kiriakou says all the American television networks use and which he finds maddening: an invitation to appear, a quick pre-interview to establish what he thinks, and then a call a minute later saying they have decided to go a different way on the story.

the-npr-walkout.title: The convicted felon introduction
the-npr-walkout.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

the-npr-walkout.title: Suggested responses
the-npr-walkout.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-npr-walkout.title: Consulting for royal families
the-npr-walkout.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-npr-walkout.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-npr-walkout.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-npr-walkout.title: Signing with CAA
the-npr-walkout.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Arabic and Greek
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Curtailment cables
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: Iraq, the training account
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says he was given the Iraq portfolio as a new CIA analyst in 1990 — that nothing ever happened there — and the promise that once he had learned tradecraft and the house writing style he would be moved to somewhere exciting, such as Romania.

the-oath-in-the-auditorium.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-oath-in-the-auditorium.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: The September 10th country
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s formulation of what he wants back, and his ledger on the two wars: he never supported the invasion of Iraq, which he calls a war of choice and of family revenge, and he did support the war in Afghanistan until al-Qaeda was defeated in 2003, after which everything became nation building. He assigns the destruction of the pre-attack country to George W. Bush and Barack Obama equally.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: False flags are too hard
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-obama-recruitment-thesis.title: The 1968 waterboarding conviction
the-obama-recruitment-thesis.summary: The precedent John Kiriakou uses to dispose of the argument that waterboarding was legally uncertain after 2002: a January 1968 Washington Post front page showing an American soldier waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner, an investigation ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, and the soldier''s arrest, conviction for torture and imprisonment. The law, Kiriakou points out, never changed in between.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The Los Angeles Times Iran op-ed
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: An op-ed on Iranian foreign policy in Latin America that John Kiriakou was commissioned to write about six months after blowing the whistle on the torture programme. He had barely begun when the CIA general counsel''s office telephoned to warn him off the subject — a call he could not explain for fourteen years, and which he now attributes to his own wife rather than to a source inside the newspaper.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The concealed carry advertisements
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The anecdote John Kiriakou offers about surveillance capitalism: a private telephone conversation in which a friend told him he needed a concealed carry permit, followed within the hour by a Facebook feed consisting entirely of advertisements for concealed carry classes.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: Abu Omar rendition
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The CIA's kidnapping of a Milan cleric, Abu Omar, who was sent to Egypt to be tortured; John Kiriakou calls it a case that ought to be taught at the CIA as how not to run a rendition, and it is what ultimately sent him to prison, after he confirmed a former colleague's surname to a journalist claiming to be writing a book about it.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The declination letter
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: The rogue officer remark
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The answer President George W. Bush shouted to a reporter on his way to the helicopter — that if there was torture, it was the work of a rogue CIA officer — which John Kiriakou has said convinced him he was about to be made the scapegoat, and which led him to accept Brian Ross's interview offer.

the-office-of-security-arrangement.title: Arabic and Greek
the-office-of-security-arrangement.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-operational-test.title: Running into former sources
the-operational-test.summary: John Kiriakou has twice met people he once ran as agents by accident, years after leaving the CIA — once at an airport and once in the street — and both times they came to him with a bear hug. One of them was astonished to discover he spoke English.

the-operational-test.title: Sources are not traitors
the-operational-test.summary: Asked whether CIA officers privately regarded their recruited agents as traitors and held them in contempt, John Kiriakou answered that they did not — because the officers believed they were the good guys, and a recruited source had become one of them.

the-operational-test.title: The Greek colonel and China
the-operational-test.summary: The arrest of a Greek colonel assigned to NATO on charges of spying for China — a case John Kiriakou calls highly unusual not because espionage arrests are rare in Greece, but because they are almost always for Russia, and which he says shows the Chinese have begun caring about NATO communications.

the-operational-test.title: The density of spies in Washington
the-operational-test.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that there are more spies in Washington DC than anywhere else in the world, that the FBI''s counterintelligence division does nothing but try to root them out, and that the job cannot be finished short of becoming North Korea.

the-operational-test.title: Qat in Yemen
the-operational-test.summary: The afternoon shrub-chewing habit of Yemen, and the special dispensation the CIA had to issue so that its officers could take part in it. John Kiriakou explains that no source could be developed in a qat-chewing country by an officer who would not chew.

the-operational-test.title: The anti-semite smear
the-operational-test.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the professional cost of saying publicly that Israel spies on the United States: Alan Dershowitz calls him names, and the political director of the Israeli foreign minister called him a noted anti-semite.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: The density of spies in Washington
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: John Kiriakou''s claim that there are more spies in Washington DC than anywhere else in the world, that the FBI''s counterintelligence division does nothing but try to root them out, and that the job cannot be finished short of becoming North Korea.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: The Greek colonel and China
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: The arrest of a Greek colonel assigned to NATO on charges of spying for China — a case John Kiriakou calls highly unusual not because espionage arrests are rare in Greece, but because they are almost always for Russia, and which he says shows the Chinese have begun caring about NATO communications.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: Kiriakou's UFO sighting
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: The object John Kiriakou and his father watched from the side of Route 60 in Amish country, western Pennsylvania, on a Friday night in 1981 — three flashes of white light, then a silent orange trapezoid hanging a couple of thousand feet up, which left at a speed he had never seen before or since.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: Running into former sources
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: John Kiriakou has twice met people he once ran as agents by accident, years after leaving the CIA — once at an airport and once in the street — and both times they came to him with a bear hug. One of them was astonished to discover he spoke English.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: Sources are not traitors
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: Asked whether CIA officers privately regarded their recruited agents as traitors and held them in contempt, John Kiriakou answered that they did not — because the officers believed they were the good guys, and a recruited source had become one of them.

the-orb-off-yemen.title: The anti-semite smear
the-orb-off-yemen.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the professional cost of saying publicly that Israel spies on the United States: Alan Dershowitz calls him names, and the political director of the Israeli foreign minister called him a noted anti-semite.

the-oz-analogy.title: The Club Fed myth
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing objection to the phrase ''Club Fed'' and the idea that federal prison is a soft landing for white-collar convicts: there is no such thing, he says, no golf and no gardening, only an institution designed to humiliate and emasculate and to make a man count the days.

the-oz-analogy.title: Truck and Cat in the Hat
the-oz-analogy.summary: An incident at FCI Loretto in which John Kiriakou, told by one prisoner that another had called him a rat, invented a slur he knew would enrage a convicted serial killer — who beat the accuser badly enough to require a helicopter medevac. Kiriakou presents it as a live application of two rules he says he learned at the CIA: let others do your dirty work, and admit nothing, deny everything, make counter-accusations.

the-oz-analogy.title: The Italians at Loretto
the-oz-analogy.summary: The mafia contingent at FCI Loretto — men with last names like Gambino, Bonanno, Lucchese, Genovese, DeCavalcante — who adopted John Kiriakou in his second year, largely because he hated the FBI as much as they did. The cast included the boss of the Gambino family (in on a dozen-plus murder counts, the man who replaced John Gotti), Pete the Bonanno captain across the hall who asked why he sat "with those Nazi retards," and a crooked guard on the payroll delivering pork loin and fresh mozzarella. When the FBI later came to Kiriakou's door asking him to inform on Pete, his answer was "get off my property."

the-oz-analogy.title: Prison racial segregation
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

the-oz-analogy.title: Supervised release travel restrictions
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the years of court supervision that followed his prison term, in which a judge refused him permission to travel abroad to give paid speeches while he was expected to earn a living, and in which he had to surrender his passport on returning from every trip he was allowed to take.

the-oz-analogy.title: The culling of friendships
the-oz-analogy.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of what happened to his private life after he confirmed the CIA''s torture program: friends and even family members began walking away from him before any charge was filed, a process he came to regard, oddly, as a culling exercise that dispatched phonies and left the people who genuinely loved him.

the-panda-card.title: Europe without Russian gas
the-panda-card.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that Europe needs Russia more than Russia needs Europe, made from what he has physically encountered rather than from figures. Speaking in Nottingham in 2025 he found the concert hall so cold that the audience complained, and was told by the manager that the venue could not afford to heat itself without Russian gas. He reports the same of homes in Britain, Germany and Greece, where American gas is simply too expensive to substitute.

the-panda-card.title: Nuclear war is winnable
the-panda-card.summary: The belief John Kiriakou says is held by a real faction in both Ukraine and the United States: that a nuclear exchange can be survived and won. He traces the American version to Pat Buchanan''s 1992 presidential campaign — we come out from our caves and continue the fight — and reconstructs the Ukrainian version as a bet that if Russia went nuclear, the American, British and French arsenals would answer. He calls the reasoning insanity and thinks it is nonetheless being done.

the-panda-card.title: The scholar-in-residence pipeline
the-panda-card.summary: John Kiriakou's description of retired CIA operations officers taking scholar-in-residence posts at universities and teaching literature courses that function, by their own account, as a recruitment funnel — students enrol knowing the instructor is a former officer and hoping for help getting in.

the-panda-card.title: Operation Spiderweb
the-panda-card.summary: The Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's strategic bomber fleet in June 2025, which John Kiriakou calls a brilliant operation and — against Volodymyr Zelensky's account — one Ukraine could not have run alone. Eighteen months of preparation, drones smuggled across eleven time zones by human couriers, and command from Kyiv all required outside help, he argues; and Donald Trump's uncharacteristic public silence afterwards is his evidence that Washington was in on it.

the-panda-card.title: Recruiting foreign students
the-panda-card.summary: The long-horizon intelligence argument for admitting foreign students to American universities — that a doctoral student in the hard sciences recruited on campus goes home to a weapons programme as an asset already in place — and John Kiriakou's view that collapsing enrolment is an operational loss nobody at the top is thinking about.

the-panda-card.title: Ted Rall
the-panda-card.summary: American editorial cartoonist and two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist; co-host with John Kiriakou of the daily news-commentary podcast "Deprogram," launched in September 2025 and by late 2025 running every weekday morning.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The secret Sahel appropriations
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou's complaint that the United States is quietly pumping billions of dollars into Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Conakry and Guinea-Bissau — spending he says is supposed to be a big secret, addresses a French problem rather than an American one, and which American taxpayers have a right to know about and to judge.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The African diplomat's remark
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: Muddling through
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The NATO expansion promises
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the assurances American presidents gave Russia that NATO would not expand to its borders or admit Ukraine — promises he says were made repeatedly, broken repeatedly, and, in his blunt formulation, never meant. He couples the account with an equally explicit statement that he opposes the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

the-paris-rifle-serial-number.title: The Hersh publishing collapse
the-paris-rifle-serial-number.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Seymour Hersh's disappearance from mainstream print — from the London Review of Books in 2017, which Hersh told him was already the only outlet that would take his work, to Substack five years later. Kiriakou, who helped give Hersh an award for integrity in intelligence, presents the trajectory as a measure of how bad conditions for American journalism have become.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: "Don''t charge Donald Trump with espionage"
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: An opinion piece John Kiriakou wrote for Consortium News after the classified documents were found at Mar-a-Lago, arguing against an Espionage Act prosecution of Trump — and, in its subheading, against Espionage Act prosecutions of anyone else either. He uses it as the frame for his position that the statute should be scrapped and rewritten to reach only those who mean the country harm.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: Espionage Act
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: CIA adultery culture
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: John Kiriakou's recurring characterization of the CIA officer corps as riddled with adultery and casual sex — which he frames not as gossip but as a systemic counterintelligence vulnerability that makes officers easy to recruit.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: Classification compartments
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: John Kiriakou's explanation of the U.S. secrecy tiers above 'top secret' — the TS/SCI/TK/gamma clearances everyone at the CIA gets, and the additional compartments that mean even senior officials can be barred from a single cable.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: The Charles Littlejohn prosecution
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: The five-year sentence handed to an IRS contractor who disclosed Donald Trump's tax returns to the New York Times, which John Kiriakou calls stunning and unjustified — the material was protected but not classified, the Biden campaign made use of it, and the sentencing judge compared the disclosure to the January 6 attack on the Capitol.

the-pillow-talk-leak-case.title: Chelsea Manning
the-pillow-talk-leak-case.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Iraq, the training account
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The reason John Kiriakou says he was given the Iraq portfolio as a new CIA analyst in 1990 — that nothing ever happened there — and the promise that once he had learned tradecraft and the house writing style he would be moved to somewhere exciting, such as Romania.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Arabic and Greek
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: The Tehran slip
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The moment John Kiriakou says he witnessed as note-taker in a secure video teleconference a day or two before the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when a briefing general said that if all went as planned American forces could be in Tehran by August, and CIA Director George Tenet turned off his microphone and asked Kiriakou whether the man had said Tehran or Baghdad.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Training to kill
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: John Kiriakou's account of arriving at the CIA's clandestine training facility expecting to learn how to recruit sources at diplomatic cocktail parties, and finding instead parachute training, resistance-to-interrogation instruction, and — as his old supervisor had warned him — training to kill people.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-powell-telephone-call.title: Curtailment cables
the-powell-telephone-call.summary: The career-ending requests John Kiriakou says he read coming back from the CIA's black sites — officers, doctors, psychologists and nurses asking to end their tours early rather than continue to take part in the interrogation programme — and his conclusion that if that many people were objecting in classified channels, someone would surely go public.

the-pre-interview.title: Suggested responses
the-pre-interview.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-pre-interview.title: The NPR walkout
the-pre-interview.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

the-pre-interview.title: The convicted felon introduction
the-pre-interview.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

the-pre-interview.title: Consulting for royal families
the-pre-interview.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-pre-interview.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-pre-interview.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-pre-interview.title: Signing with CAA
the-pre-interview.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: College tuition as an inducement
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The recruitment inducement John Kiriakou describes as among the CIA's most effective — enrolling a source's child at any American university and paying for it — and the arrangements with universities and corporations he says make it possible.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: Security, finance and medical
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The rule John Kiriakou says CIA recruits were taught in their first week on the job — that there are exactly three offices an officer may never lie to, because those three can end a career — and the reasoning he attaches to each.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: The Indonesian recruitment question
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: A hypothetical put to John Kiriakou and other CIA applicants during the interview process — what to do when a foreign official you have cultivated for a year turns out not to be recruitable — and the answer that Kiriakou later understood had been the point of the exercise: break into the embassy and steal the information.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: Arabic and Greek
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-prostitute-hypothetical.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-prostitute-hypothetical.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Recruitment attempts on Kiriakou
the-reluctant-spy.summary: A series of episodes in which foreign intelligence officers tried to recruit John Kiriakou himself — an over-eager Hungarian during his CIA application, a French counterterrorism officer who staged a car pickup in Islamabad, and a Shin Bet officer at his first liaison briefing.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-reluctant-spy.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
the-reluctant-spy.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

the-reluctant-spy.title: PTSD
the-reluctant-spy.summary: Post-traumatic stress disorder runs through John Kiriakou''s life and worldview — he had it coming out of Greece after an assassination attempt, brought it home from Pakistan alongside his shock at colleagues'' willingness to kill, and was blindsided by a delayed post-prison version that helped end his marriage. For six months after release he dreamed the same dream nightly: that he was out by mistake and had to get back inside before midnight count. He still takes a repurposed blood-pressure drug that stops the dreams, and he extends the diagnosis outward — to secret-site interrogators who came back crying, to drone pilots, and to prisoners released angry and untreated.

the-reluctant-spy.title: Sweat Lodge
the-reluctant-spy.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the federal prison where he was incarcerated had a Native American sweat lodge that was shut down after it was misused for sex rather than religious ceremony; he says he has never personally been in a sweat lodge.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Daniel Hale
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Communications management unit
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Liam O'Grady
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: The Eastern District of Virginia judge who sentenced Daniel Hale, and who in John Kiriakou''s account surprised the courtroom twice: with a sentence of 45 months rather than the far longer term expected, and with a recommendation that Hale serve it in a low-security prison where he could be treated for depression and addiction. The Bureau of Prisons ignored the recommendation and sent him to the communications management unit at Marion instead.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: Daniel Ellsberg
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

the-roadblock-drone-strike.title: The Drone Papers
the-roadblock-drone-strike.summary: The trove of classified documents leaked by Daniel Hale and published by The Intercept — later collected in book form as 'The Assassination Complex' — exposing how the U.S. drone program selected and killed targets; John Kiriakou relied on it in his own writing on the war in Afghanistan.

the-rogue-officer-remark.title: The declination letter
the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-rogue-officer-remark.summary: The detail John Kiriakou uses to compress his argument about interrogation: that the intelligence the CIA''s contractors reported as the fruit of waterboarding had in fact been obtained by an FBI agent who offered Abu Zubaydah a bowl of dates.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: French village LSD bread experiment
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a compartmented MK-Ultra experiment in which CIA operatives broke into the only bakery of a small French village he does not name and dosed the yeast with LSD, sending the entire village on an unwitting trip.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: MK-Ultra
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: Richard Helms
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: CIA director who, per John Kiriakou, ordered the destruction of all MK-Ultra documents on the same day the Church Committee explicitly told him not to destroy them — and who, in Kiriakou's telling, illegally destroyed most of the agency's JFK material as well. He was held in contempt of Congress and fined a nominal sum that colleagues covered by passing a hat down the corridor to his office. Because of the destruction, only about 15% of the MK-Ultra record survives — largely financial records, from which the program had to be pieced back together.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: Operation Midnight Climax
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: Sub-project of the CIA's MK-Ultra program, conducted in San Francisco. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA rented a safe house and paid sex workers to bring men back to it, where agents dosed the men with LSD without their knowledge or consent, then observed their behavior through one-way mirrors. The operation followed an earlier phase in which the CIA had dosed its own employees; when that produced suicides, it moved to using unconsenting members of the public.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: "Our job is to break the law"
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: The line John Kiriakou says CIA instructors repeated in training, and the qualification he attached to it at the time: the job is to break the law over there, not here. He describes participating willingly in break-ins abroad while insisting a warrant is required at home.

the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.title: The war powers resolution vote
the-san-francisco-bacterium-release.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the congressional attempt to take back war powers over the 2026 Iran conflict: a sense-of-the-Congress resolution would have no teeth or authority, and a bill with legal force would simply be vetoed.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: The Fox News military analyst
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: The Syria chemical attack correction
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou's public retraction of what he wrote about the August 2013 chemical attack near Damascus. Asked about the passage in his book on Iran, he said he had written it before United Nations whistleblowers came forward to say they did not believe it was a Syrian government attack, and thanked the questioner for the chance to correct it.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-science-fiction-writer-foia-request.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-second-plane.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-second-plane.summary: The White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001: an attempt to persuade the National Security Advisor to withhold three declassified historical CIA cables that had identified sources who were still alive.

the-second-plane.title: "We''re at war today"
the-second-plane.summary: The short speech John Kiriakou says Cofer Black delivered standing on his desk in the CIA's Counterterrorism Center on the morning of 11 September 2001, telling his officers that not all of them would make it home and that anyone for whom this was not enough could walk out without being thought less of. Nobody moved.

the-second-plane.title: The honey salesman warning
the-second-plane.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

the-second-plane.title: The seventy-two-year-old contractor
the-second-plane.summary: The hallway conversation John Kiriakou says explained why the CIA had not sent him, an Arabic speaker, to interrogate captured al-Qaeda fighters — a returning contractor's answer that he had been in Afghanistan killing people — and the demand Kiriakou made afterwards that got him sent to Pakistan the next day.

He couples the account with an equally explicit statement that he opposes the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

the-sentencing-remark.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

the-sentencing-remark.title: The Loretto camp mix-up
the-sentencing-remark.summary: John Kiriakou's account of turning himself in at the federal work camp at Loretto, Pennsylvania as the court had ordered, being sent across the street to the prison to be processed, and then being handcuffed and walked into the prison itself — with nobody on the outside knowing where he was for five days.

the-sentencing-remark.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

the-sentencing-remark.title: The declination letter
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

the-sentencing-remark.title: Thursday arrests
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The scheduling practice John Kiriakou attributes to the FBI — arresting on a Thursday so that a defendant, unable to be arraigned on a Friday, spends four nights in jail before seeing a judge — and the single sentence that he says kept him out of it.

the-sentencing-remark.title: Arabic and Greek
the-sentencing-remark.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-september-tenth-country.title: The Obama recruitment thesis
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s public explanation of what happened to Barack Obama: not that the CIA created him, but that a first-term senator with no national security experience is exactly the kind of president the agency wants, and that the first briefing several levels above top secret is enough to hook him. Kiriakou supports the reading with two quotations Obama gave to reporters, including that he never had any idea he would be so good at killing people.

the-september-tenth-country.title: The Libya policy reversal
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s verdict on the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi: the United States had a healthy working relationship with a man who hated al-Qaeda as much as it did, and flipping sides at the last minute was a terrible policy error that left the country in anarchy. Told that destabilisation may have been the objective all along, he called that an incredibly shortsighted policy, because power vacuums drag America in and it cannot get back out.

the-september-tenth-country.title: The Benghazi hearings critique
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s complaint about the congressional inquiry into Benghazi, which he watched all the way through: he believes there is some evidence of gun running, doubts anyone will ever establish who was behind it, and objects that the hearings were not trying to find out — having devolved into a political contest that served the American people not at all.

the-september-tenth-country.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-september-tenth-country.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-september-tenth-country.title: False flags are too hard
the-september-tenth-country.summary: John Kiriakou''s practical objection to the idea that governments routinely stage false flag operations: they exist, but they have too many moving parts and require too many people to buy into the conspiracy, so the CIA rarely used them. He couples the objection with the observation that a government which is not transparent has no standing to complain about public suspicion.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001: an attempt to persuade the National Security Advisor to withhold three declassified historical CIA cables that had identified sources who were still alive.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The honey salesman warning
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: The second plane
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: John Kiriakou's account of where he was standing when United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower — in Cofer Black's outer office, mid-sentence, explaining to a secretary why a pilot could not possibly fly into the World Trade Center on so clear a day.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: "We''re at war today"
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The short speech John Kiriakou says Cofer Black delivered standing on his desk in the CIA's Counterterrorism Center on the morning of 11 September 2001, telling his officers that not all of them would make it home and that anyone for whom this was not enough could walk out without being thought less of. Nobody moved.

the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.title: Arabic and Greek
the-seventy-two-year-old-contractor.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Abu Zubaydah as a sounding board
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: The second, longer phase of Abu Zubaydah''s usefulness to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: once the prisoner had given up what he knew about current operations, his value shifted from threat reporting to analysis, with case officers reading him the names of men arrested in European capitals and asking whether the operations attributed to them made sense.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: The German POW chess analogy
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: The reasoning John Kiriakou gave ABC News in December 2007 for why he had believed at the time that waterboarding was necessary: he had heard of Second World War German prisoners who, over months of playing chess with their interrogators, built enough rapport to talk, and he judged that al-Qaeda prisoners were a different order of adversary who would never be seduced into cooperating.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Brian Ross
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-slap-approval-cable.title: Waterboarding
the-slap-approval-cable.summary: Torture technique in which a prisoner is restrained on an inclined board with the head lower than the feet, a cloth placed over the face, and water poured continuously over it to simulate drowning. Per John Kiriakou, waterboarding was treated as a criminal act under U.S. and international law for decades before 2002 — including a post–World War II execution of Japanese soldiers who waterboarded American POWs, and a 1968 court-martial of a U.S. soldier photographed waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner — before the CIA reauthorized it after September 11. Abu Zubaydah was waterboarded 83 times; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed 187 times.

the-snickers-bar.title: Kiriakou's first recruitment
the-snickers-bar.summary: How John Kiriakou made his first CIA recruitment in Athens: by combing 25-year-old Greek police files not for people who had talked but for people who had answered back, finding one such man in a communist neighbourhood coffee shop, and buying his telephone number from a waiter for the price of a fifty.

the-snickers-bar.title: John Kiriakou
the-snickers-bar.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

the-snickers-bar.title: American shoes
the-snickers-bar.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

the-snickers-bar.title: Intelligence peddlers
the-snickers-bar.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

the-snickers-bar.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-snickers-bar.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-snickers-bar.title: There is no such thing as bad food in Athens
the-snickers-bar.summary: The lesson John Kiriakou says he learned at a lorry drivers' stop outside Corinth, where the food was as good as his grandmother's — reached on the three-and-a-half-hour drives he made to meet a source too sensitive to be met in Athens, with a vineyard tour as his cover story.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Vietnam War
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: The war John Kiriakou grew up in the shadow of — his parents marched against it — and the deep precedent for everything he fights: entered on the Gulf of Tonkin lie, prosecuted by generals who knew for a decade they were losing (per the Pentagon Papers), studded with torture whose victims recited the Green Bay Packers'' starting lineup as "intelligence," and ended in part by Daniel Ellsberg, "the godfather of all modern national security whistleblowers." Even Robert McNamara, he notes, understood waterboarding was a bridge too far.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Prison racial segregation
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the rigid racial and ethnic division of American prisons — a cafeteria split like the 1950s South — and his argument that segregating and hardening inmates for years, then releasing them with no skills, makes society less safe.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Whistleblower Protection Act
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: United States statute protecting federal employees who disclose government wrongdoing from retaliation; per John Kiriakou, national security employees — including those at the CIA, Pentagon, FBI, NSA, DEA, White House, and Homeland Security — are explicitly exempt from its protections, leaving them with no legally safe avenue to report illegal activity within their agencies.

the-sociopath-next-door.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-sociopath-next-door.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: The Israeli listening devices ban
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: Why Mossad and Shin Bet representatives were barred from CIA headquarters, per John Kiriakou: the gifts they brought to liaison meetings kept turning up with listening devices and batteries embedded inside, so the agency stopped admitting them and rented meeting space in Virginia instead.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: The Jerusalem harassment campaign
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what happened to a CIA colleague and his wife during a declared two-year State Department rotation in Jerusalem: furniture rearranged after one embassy party, all three toilets in the house defecated in after another, and, before they left, the family dog''s tail cut off and bandaged. Kiriakou presents the three break-ins as routine rather than exceptional.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: Gulf secret prisons for hire
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: Asked whether the CIA knew of Gulf royals operating underground torture facilities and secret prisons, John Kiriakou answered that it did — one hundred per cent — then refused to give details, saying he would risk returning to prison. He described the arrangement instead: the United States sought out these countries precisely because they had no parliament and no free press to answer to, and paid for the use of their cells.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: CIA attention to West Africa
