the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-spell-your-name-briefing.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-spell-your-name-briefing.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-spy-shop.title: Palantir Technologies
the-spy-shop.summary: U.S. data-analytics and intelligence-software company; received its first $1.5 million in seed funding from the CIA's In-Q-Tel venture-capital arm around 2002; characterized by John Kiriakou as functionally inseparable from the CIA in 2025, drawing the majority of its revenue from agency contracts and operating across DARPA, NSA, and the broader U.S. national-security apparatus.

the-spy-shop.title: Spy films John Kiriakou considers accurate
the-spy-shop.summary: Kiriakou's assessment of which espionage films get it right — Argo, The Recruit and Bridge of Spies — and his flat rejection of the action genre's premises, including the hidden weapons stash.

the-spy-shop.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-spy-shop.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-spy-shop.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
the-spy-shop.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

the-spy-shop.title: Bureau of Prisons advisory board
the-spy-shop.summary: The advisory board John Kiriakou joined at the personal invitation of the Director of the Bureau of Prisons, who told him the president had tasked him with tearing the Bureau down and rebuilding it.

the-spy-shop.title: The Green Line in Nicosia
the-spy-shop.summary: The division of Nicosia between the Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-occupied north, which John Kiriakou toured in July 2026 and described as maintained through deliberate humiliation rather than any interest in settlement.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Senate Foreign Relations Committee
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Kiriakou was senior investigator under John Kerry — and still held the post when his own federal prosecution came to a head in January 2012.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Dasht-i-Leili massacre
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Late-November 2001 mass suffocation of approximately 2,000 surrendered Taliban prisoners in unventilated shipping containers in the Afghan desert; the prisoners' surrender was negotiated by the CIA via the Northern Alliance, the transport order was issued by the CIA, and the operation was overseen by Northern Alliance warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum; John Kiriakou in 2009 as Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator attempted to reopen the case under a 2008 Obama campaign promise; the CIA's classified response was, per Kiriakou, "go fuck yourself."

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: General Abdul Rashid Dostum
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: Northern Alliance Afghan warlord; overseer of the November–December 2001 Dasht-i-Leili massacre; characterized by John Kiriakou as a serial defector between the Taliban and the Northern Alliance and as a psychopath.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: Qala-i-Jangi uprising
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: The late-November 2001 prisoner uprising at a fortress in northern Afghanistan during which CIA officer Mike Spann was killed; the event during which the American al-Qaeda figure John Walker Lindh was captured; among the first major firefights of the post-9/11 Afghan campaign.

the-state-department-cover-investigation.title: The Bolivian visa line
the-state-department-cover-investigation.summary: The CIA's interrogation of John Kiriakou's wife, then a serving senior officer, over a single sentence in a Los Angeles Times op-ed her husband had written and had already cleared through the agency's own publications review board. Told the piece was cleared, the security officer replied that one line in it was top secret — the statement that Iranians no longer needed visas to travel to Bolivia. Kiriakou had taken it off the Bolivian foreign ministry's website.

the-stinger.title: Mark Lanzalotti
the-stinger.summary: The prisoner John Kiriakou describes as his closest friend at FCI Loretto and one of the finest human beings he has known — a first-time non-violent drug defendant sentenced to triple life without parole for refusing to inform, the prison's foremost cook and bookie, and the man whose release Kiriakou secured by writing his Second Chance Act petition.

the-stinger.title: FCI Loretto
the-stinger.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

the-stinger.title: Pete Calabrese
the-stinger.summary: The senior Bonanno family member at FCI Loretto, known as Peter the Rabbit, who challenged John Kiriakou over his friendship with the cooperating witness Frank Russo and told him Russo brought dishonour to the Italians.

the-stinger.title: The rat and pedophile table
the-stinger.summary: The cafeteria table at FCI Loretto reserved for cooperating witnesses and sex offenders — a placement that also carried a ban from the television room, and which John Kiriakou describes as an outcome cooperators knew to expect before they agreed to testify.

the-stinger.title: Frank Russo
the-stinger.summary: The former auditor of Cuyahoga County, Ohio, who shared a bunk with John Kiriakou at FCI Loretto — a corruption defendant who cooperated against Jimmy Dimora, was marked in prison as a rat, and whom Kiriakou describes as a sweetheart with a hilarious sense of humour who won everybody over anyway.

the-stinger.title: Kiriakou's FOIA request from prison
the-stinger.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed on himself six weeks into his sentence at FCI Loretto — despite a plea agreement promising he never would — which returned 250 pages including a warden's memorandum warning staff that the incoming prisoner had access to the media.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: Sealing the courtroom
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: The physical measures John Kiriakou describes as accompanying a classified-information trial: plastic sheeting and duct tape over the windows so lasers cannot read the vibrations, white noise in the vestibule, and the clearing of everyone but the judge, jury, bailiff, clerk, lawyers and defendant.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: The jury consultant''s advice
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: What John Kiriakou''s jury consultant told him about a national security trial in the Eastern District of Virginia: that in any other district in America he would say fight and win, but in that one, "buddy, you don''t have a prayer. Take the deal."

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: Assange and the European Court of Human Rights
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: The last legal avenue John Kiriakou identified for Julian Assange in 2022 — three precedents in which the Strasbourg court refused to let Britain extradite mentally ill defendants to American solitary confinement — and the procedural trap that made it useless: Britain said the appeal need not halt the extradition.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: Julian Assange
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: The Istanbul peace talks
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: The early Russia–Ukraine negotiations in Istanbul that John Kiriakou says lasted three days and were never revived — talks the United States neither attended nor encouraged the Ukrainians to attend, and after which, he notes, the words "peace talks" disappeared from American discourse.

the-swimming-pool-substitution.title: The CIPA hearing in Kiriakou's case
the-swimming-pool-substitution.summary: The closed pre-trial proceeding under the Classified Information Procedures Act at which John Kiriakou's defence filed seventy motions to declassify the material it needed to mount a defence, and the judge denied all seventy at once. Kiriakou describes the ruling as the moment the case ended — his lead attorney told him on the way out of the courtroom that they had just lost — and as the point at which plea negotiations began.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: The Fox News military analyst
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: The cable-news commentator John Kiriakou says he identified as a fraud within a single green-room conversation, because the man used movie vocabulary — black ops, wet work — where a real officer would have named a directorate. The man had obtained a Defense Department clearance on the strength of his claimed CIA service, advised generals in Afghanistan, and was later arrested and imprisoned for fraud.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: The Iran–Israel exchange assessment
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement — which he expects to be unpopular — that Iran came out ahead of Israel in their direct missile exchange: the Iron Dome proved fallible, Iranian targeting was selective where Israel''s was not, and the ceasefire came, in his reading, because Israel had run out of missiles.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: The science fiction writer FOIA request
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: The Freedom of Information Act request John Kiriakou filed with the CIA about a 1950s science fiction writer long rumoured to have been an undercover officer — answered only with a letter saying the agency lacked the manpower to meet its statutory ninety-day deadline. Fifteen years later, he says, he is still waiting.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-syria-chemical-attack-correction.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: The ISI as two organizations
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s working model of Pakistan''s Inter-Services Intelligence during his time as CIA chief of counterterrorism operations there: one half made up of British-trained officers he calls great counterterrorism partners, and another half that created, trained, financed and armed the Taliban — a split that left him deciding case by case whom he could trust.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: The cave myth
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: The torture memo signature
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the CIA''s torture programme was authorised: a list of about ten techniques sent from headquarters through the Justice Department, the National Security Council lawyers and Condoleezza Rice to the president — who, to the surprise of the agency''s own leadership, signed it. Kiriakou recalls the deputy director saying three times in one meeting that he could not believe the president had signed the memo.

the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-taliban-lobbyist-in-washington.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-tehran-slip.title: Reading in on the Iraq invasion
the-tehran-slip.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, when he signed six secrecy agreements and was told that the United States would invade Iraq the following March, and that the agencies opposing the war had already lost the argument.

the-tehran-slip.title: Condoleezza Rice
the-tehran-slip.summary: U.S. National Security Advisor on 9/11; John Kiriakou had a meeting booked with her that morning, watched her tell George Tenet to "take one for the team" rather than correct the record on Abu Zubaydah, and offers her failure to act on the CIA's warnings as his alternative to any theory that the attacks were allowed to happen.

the-tehran-slip.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
the-tehran-slip.summary: The White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001: an attempt to persuade the National Security Advisor to withhold three declassified historical CIA cables that had identified sources who were still alive.

the-tehran-slip.title: The Powell telephone call
the-tehran-slip.summary: The morning call John Kiriakou says he took from General Colin Powell, then chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, asking who would have run an Iraqi operation to kill former President George H. W. Bush; Kiriakou named the Iraqi Intelligence Service station in Basra and its headquarters in Baghdad, and eight hours later the United States fired forty-eight cruise missiles at that building.

the-tehran-slip.title: "We''re at war today"
the-tehran-slip.summary: The short speech John Kiriakou says Cofer Black delivered standing on his desk in the CIA's Counterterrorism Center on the morning of 11 September 2001, telling his officers that not all of them would make it home and that anyone for whom this was not enough could walk out without being thought less of. Nobody moved.

the-tehran-slip.title: Arabic and Greek
the-tehran-slip.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: The asset recruitment cycle
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: The four-step career requirement John Kiriakou says governed CIA operations before September 11 — spot, assess, develop and recruit an agent, or do not get promoted — and his description of what the fourth step actually rests on: not money, revenge or ideology, but friendship, real or believed.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: Freemasons and Opus Dei at the CIA
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou's characterisation of the affinity networks at the top of the CIA — a great many senior officers who are Freemasons, and periods in which most of the leadership belonged to Opus Dei and attended the same church in Great Falls, Virginia. He rejects the idea that these are plots, describing them instead as accidental clusters of men who look out for one another.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: CIA–FBI incompatible computer systems
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou's claim that from the CIA's founding in 1947 until 2009 the computer systems of the CIA and the FBI were not compatible with one another — no message could be sent from one to the other and no intelligence shared — which he offers as the material substrate of the interagency hatred that helped make September 11 possible.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: Fake CIA résumés
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of being used as a human authenticator in the private sector: at the consulting firm he joined after leaving the CIA, every job applicant claiming agency service was sent to dinner with him, and by his count fully half of them had never set foot inside the CIA.

the-tier-one-walk-up.title: Forcing Iran toward a bomb
the-tier-one-walk-up.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that Western pressure risks producing the very outcome it claims to prevent: repeated Israeli assassinations of Iranian scientists and generals and strikes on Iranian sites may eventually leave Ayatollah Khamenei with no choice but to permit a defensive weapon — despite the religious prohibition Kiriakou credits him with maintaining, and despite successive American estimates that Iran is not seeking one.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: The 1968 waterboarding conviction
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: The precedent John Kiriakou uses to dispose of the argument that waterboarding was legally uncertain after 2002: a January 1968 Washington Post front page showing an American soldier waterboarding a North Vietnamese prisoner, an investigation ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, and the soldier''s arrest, conviction for torture and imprisonment. The law, Kiriakou points out, never changed in between.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: Abu Zubaydah
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: Bin Laden health rumors
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: John Kiriakou's dismissal of the claim that Osama bin Laden died years before the 2011 raid. He says the CIA received a steady stream of medical rumours about him — kidney failure, dialysis in a cave, a spinal disorder — none of which turned out to be true, and that bin Laden was in fine health apart from arthritis and a hip problem until the day he died.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: SEAL Team Six attrition
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to the claim that the Navy SEALs who killed Osama bin Laden have since been killed off: the dead came from the broader unit rather than the raid party, SEAL Team Six numbers several hundred men rather than the dozen or so people imagine, and losing a high number of them to accidents and combat is, in his phrase, very sadly common.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: The cave myth
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: John Kiriakou's rejection of the popular image of al-Qaeda's leadership living in caves. He says the CIA knew its targets were in major cities, deliberately let them believe the search was concentrated on the tribal areas, and caught them because men who think they are unobserved get sloppy with their phones and email.

the-torture-memo-signature.title: The Taliban lobbyist in Washington
the-torture-memo-signature.summary: A story put to John Kiriakou about a Taliban delegation''s American press conference and the Washington lobbyist who represented them. Kiriakou remembered the episode and the lobbyist''s New Jersey base but not the claim about her parentage, and explained why it caused so little controversy at the time: the United States had no historical quarrel with the Taliban, and had armed and fêted some of its future members during the war against the Soviets.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: The war powers resolution vote
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the congressional attempt to take back war powers over the 2026 Iran conflict: a sense-of-the-Congress resolution would have no teeth or authority, and a bill with legal force would simply be vetoed.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: Bahrain''s naturalisation policy
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: "Iran posed no threat"
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s core objection to the 2026 war, stated as a chain of negatives: Iran had no nuclear weapon, no nuclear weapons programme, no wish for one, a religious ruling against one, and no delivery system if it had had one — findings he says were confirmed twice by the CIA and by the IAEA.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: Marco Rubio and Iran policy
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to who was actually driving American policy toward Iran in 2026: with the Vice President, the Director of National Intelligence and the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs all reported as opposed, and with Marco Rubio holding both the State Department and the National Security Adviser''s job, the policy was Rubio''s.

the-truth-social-announcement.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
the-truth-social-announcement.summary: John Kiriakou''s report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

the-two-tunisians.title: The martyrdom bonus
the-two-tunisians.summary: The recruitment offer John Kiriakou says captured al-Qaeda foot soldiers described to him in Pakistan: three hundred dollars a month to go and fight the Americans in Afghanistan, and five hundred dollars paid to the fighter''s parents if he was killed.

the-two-tunisians.title: The Faisalabad cash run
the-two-tunisians.summary: The drive John Kiriakou made to Faisalabad, Pakistan roughly two weeks before the capture of Abu Zubaydah, with two million dollars in cash in two duffel bags in the van, and the exchange with his colleague about why anyone would cheat the CIA out of twenty dollars.

the-two-tunisians.title: "You were the first person that ever asked me about my children"
the-two-tunisians.summary: The answer John Kiriakou says he received when he asked a mid-level al-Qaeda member he had recruited in Pakistan why he had allowed the recruitment to happen: that in five years of detention Kiriakou had been the first person to ask about his children.

the-two-tunisians.title: The honey salesman warning
the-two-tunisians.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

the-two-tunisians.title: The hooding dispute
the-two-tunisians.summary: The argument John Kiriakou says he had with a subordinate at a CIA safe house in Pakistan on the night of the Abu Zubaydah raid, over hoods placed on captured prisoners; both men reported each other to headquarters, and Kiriakou was the one reprimanded.

the-two-tunisians.title: Arabic and Greek
the-two-tunisians.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

the-underlying-sadness.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

the-underlying-sadness.title: Consulting for royal families
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The work John Kiriakou says he was hired to do by members of two different royal families following the 2026 virality of his interviews — advising on ethics in their own intelligence operations — which he offers as evidence of how far the reversal in his standing had gone.

the-underlying-sadness.title: Signing with CAA
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The representation John Kiriakou says followed the 2026 virality of his podcast clips: a contract with the Creative Artists Agency covering books, film, consulting and licensing, and a run of advertising approaches including one from the maker of the spectacle frames he already wore.

the-underlying-sadness.title: Suggested responses
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The second email John Kiriakou says arrived before his first appearance on Fox News — a list of suggested responses to accompany the questions the producers had already sent him — which he ignored, and which he says was never sent again.

the-underlying-sadness.title: The convicted felon introduction
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The MSNBC appearance John Kiriakou says was his last: booked opposite Daniel Ellsberg, having agreed his on-air identification in advance with the producers, he was introduced instead as "convicted felon John Kiriakou", swore on tape, and began removing his microphone.

the-underlying-sadness.title: The NPR walkout
the-underlying-sadness.summary: The Saturday morning interview John Kiriakou says he ended after five minutes of a scheduled half hour, having been attacked on air over an op-ed about Gina Haspel, and which he closed by asking the host where NPR had been while he was blowing the whistle on the torture programme.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: GeoRisk Solutions
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: The political risk consultancy John Kiriakou founded with the dean of the University of Salamanca's intelligence studies programme, staffed with academics and a former assistant secretary of state, with offices in Salamanca and Washington and a stated business of selling cost-effective country and regional risk analysis to banks, funds and companies.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: Cofer Black
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: Brian Ross
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: American investigative journalist and seven-time Emmy Award winner who was a prominent reporter at ABC News when, in December 2007, he conducted the on-camera interview with John Kiriakou that produced the first public confirmation by a U.S. official that the CIA waterboarded prisoners. Per Kiriakou, Ross called him out of the blue with the assertion that a source said Kiriakou had personally tortured Abu Zubaydah; Kiriakou's decision to give the interview anyway — driven by the conclusion that 'Brian Ross's source is at the White House and they're going to pin this on me' — became the pivot point of his entire post-CIA life.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: The Greek turn toward Israel
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of why Athens abandoned its traditional pro-Arab alignment and embraced Israel — a 180-degree flip he attributes to the collapse of Turkey''s relationship with Israel and, above all, to money: Israeli property buying that he says has tripled Greek house prices, and Cypriot gas fields Greece hopes to develop with Israeli partners.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: Active measures
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: The in-house name John Kiriakou gives to the CIA branch responsible for propaganda and for countering hostile propaganda — a division he describes as running twenty-four hours a day, paired with an opposing anti-active-measures branch, and as the ancestor of the political action group that remains the agency''s clandestine propaganda arm.

the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.title: CIA attention to West Africa
the-university-of-salamanca-professorshi.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

the-walk-in-probe.title: Intelligence peddlers
the-walk-in-probe.summary: John Kiriakou''s breakdown of who actually walks into an American embassy offering information: the overwhelming majority are fabricators or probes, a few per cent are peddlers selling the same nugget to five embassies in a month, and about one per cent are the real thing.

the-walk-in-probe.title: The Athens carjacking
the-walk-in-probe.summary: The motorcyclist who followed John Kiriakou''s car through Athens two months into his posting — leading to a gun drawn on a ten-lane intersection, a shot fired, a disabled motorcycle, and a question asked back in Washington: *is John a hothead?*

the-walk-in-probe.title: Walk-in
the-walk-in-probe.summary: In John Kiriakou's telling, someone who walks into an embassy offering information; 95% are lunatics or liars, some are 'intelligence peddlers' or hostile 'probes,' and about 1% are 'the real McCoy' — a framework he used to see through a supposed 'walk-in' tip during the Abu Zubaydah hunt. A genuine walk-in — a witness to a terrorist assassination — was later hypnotized by CIA psychologists in a London hotel room and read back a stolen van's license plate, verifying his account.

the-walk-in-probe.title: How Kiriakou went armed in Athens
the-walk-in-probe.summary: The load John Kiriakou carried every day during his Athens tour — a 9mm in a tear-away waist pack with three magazines, a snub-nosed .38 on his ankle, about 47 rounds in total, and a buck knife his boss handed him on his first day *"just in case things go to shit"*.

the-walk-in-probe.title: American shoes
the-walk-in-probe.summary: The detail by which the chief of the Greek intelligence service identified John Kiriakou as an American within minutes of meeting him — not his Greek, which was fluent, but his footwear — and which sent Kiriakou straight to a shoe shop before working the anarchist quarters of Athens.

the-walk-in-probe.title: The declared officer
the-walk-in-probe.summary: The CIA officer whose identity is formally disclosed to the host country's intelligence service — as John Kiriakou was in Athens, taken by his chief within days of arrival to be introduced to the head of the Greek service.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: The Truth Social announcement
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: John Kiriakou''s objection to how the 2026 war was announced: at two o''clock in the morning on Truth Social, with no address from the East Room, and with a president shuttling between Washington and Mar-a-Lago rather than explaining to the country why Americans were being sent to fight.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: Bahrain''s naturalisation policy
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: Bombing the Omanis
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: "Iran posed no threat"
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: John Kiriakou''s core objection to the 2026 war, stated as a chain of negatives: Iran had no nuclear weapon, no nuclear weapons programme, no wish for one, a religious ruling against one, and no delivery system if it had had one — findings he says were confirmed twice by the CIA and by the IAEA.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: Iranian strikes on Gulf hotels
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the Iranian drone and missile attacks on hotels in Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Muscat during the 2026 war: not targeted killings, but deliberate strikes at the tourist economies of the Gulf states, aimed at hotels famous enough to empty the country of visitors.

the-war-powers-resolution-vote.title: "Our job is to break the law"
the-war-powers-resolution-vote.summary: The line John Kiriakou says CIA instructors repeated in training, and the qualification he attached to it at the time: the job is to break the law over there, not here. He describes participating willingly in break-ins abroad while insisting a warrant is required at home.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Venezuela regime change (2026)
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: John Kiriakou''s assessment of the American operation that removed Venezuela''s president — a clear violation of international law, since none of the three recognised grounds for one state attacking another applied, but not a violation of US law, which since 1985 has expressly permitted special forces to cross borders and seize people for trial. His reluctant conclusion at the time: "as much as I hate admitting it, this regime change seems to be working right now."

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Venezuelan heavy crude and the refining bottleneck
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: John Kiriakou''s economic explanation for American pressure on Venezuela: the country''s oil is unusually high in sulfur and requires specialty refining, which for years could only be done in Houston. He says sanctions pushed India and China to build refineries capable of processing it, and that a Chinese announcement of a Caribbean refinery for Venezuelan crude left Washington with a policy it could not admit had failed.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Fentanyl and China
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that China declines to stop the flow of fentanyl into the United States for the same reason he says the United States tolerated Afghan heroin reaching Iran and Russia — because an addicted society is a weaker one. He distinguishes Chinese-made illicit fentanyl, largely produced in Mexico, from the medical fentanyl that created the addiction pathway.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: Afghan heroin policy
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: The post-2001 U.S. policy in Afghanistan of protecting, and per John Kiriakou actively encouraging, the cultivation of heroin poppy. Under the Taliban in 2000 Afghanistan produced 0% of the world's heroin; by 2009 under American occupation it produced 93%. Per a DEA officer Kiriakou consulted with on the policy paper he was preparing for Senator Kerry, the strategic rationale was that nearly all of the heroin flowed to Iran and Russia, addiction in those countries was considered desirable as a long-run societal weakener, and the same logic now operates in reverse with Chinese fentanyl flowing into the United States.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: María Corina Machado
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: The Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate whom John Kiriakou rates no higher than Juan Guaidó: a figure in a permanently divided right-wing opposition who commands no armies and no troops. He reads the prize itself as part of the propaganda campaign against Maduro, and expects that if Maduro leaves the next leader of Venezuela will be a senior military officer rather than a civilian politician.

the-west-africa-cocaine-route.title: The Libyan constitution unveiling
the-west-africa-cocaine-route.summary: A launch event John Kiriakou attended in Washington after the fall of Muammar Gaddafi: a new Libyan constitution, commissioned by wealthy exiles from a lobbying firm, unveiled at the lobbying firm''s offices. He calls the document better than the American one — equal rights for everybody, the oil money shared — and notes that nothing whatever was done with it, because nobody in Washington had heard of the people behind it.

there-is-almost-no-upside.title: Frank Serpico
there-is-almost-no-upside.summary: The New York police officer John Kiriakou calls one of the giants of the twentieth century and ranks with Daniel Ellsberg among its greatest whistleblowers — a man shot in the face whose police colleagues did not call an ambulance, and whom Kiriakou counts as a friend.

there-is-almost-no-upside.title: The legal definition of whistleblowing
there-is-almost-no-upside.summary: John Kiriakou''s insistence that whistleblowing is a legally defined act rather than a figure of speech: bringing to light evidence of waste, fraud, abuse, illegality, or threats to public health or public safety — at any level of government.

there-is-almost-no-upside.title: John Brennan
there-is-almost-no-upside.summary: Former Director of the CIA; characterized in KiriPedia's source corpus as the principal architect of the agency's enhanced interrogation program and as having plotted against an elected President

there-is-almost-no-upside.title: Whistleblower psychology
there-is-almost-no-upside.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of what distinguishes people who come forward: psychological studies showing whistleblowers hold a much more sharply defined sense of right and wrong than the general population, weighed against his own claim that there is no whistleblower who has not contemplated suicide in the period after going public.

there-is-almost-no-upside.title: "Whistleblowers die broke"
there-is-almost-no-upside.summary: The observation John Kiriakou attributes to Daniel Ellsberg — that the one thing all whistleblowers have in common is that they die broke — which Kiriakou applies to his own confiscated federal pension and his expectation of working until the day he dies.

there-is-almost-no-upside.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
there-is-almost-no-upside.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

thin-thread.title: Patriot Act
thin-thread.summary: U.S. law passed after the September 11 attacks that vastly expanded domestic surveillance authority. Per John Kiriakou, the Patriot Act ''opened up everything'' — and he disputes the common belief that 9/11 was required to pass it: ''You underestimate Congress. They didn''t need a catastrophe — they would just pass it because they can.'' He ties it to NSA bulk-collection programs that vacuum up every phone call, text, email, and piece of metadata from Americans, in violation of the NSA''s own charter.

thin-thread.title: Edward Snowden
thin-thread.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

thin-thread.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
thin-thread.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

thin-thread.title: Thomas Drake
thin-thread.summary: NSA whistleblower; per John Kiriakou, the source for the statement that on the morning of September 11, 2001, NSA Director Mike Hayden told agency personnel NSA had been 'waiting for a 9/11' to implement the mass-electronic-surveillance program that NSA's founding charter forbids.

thin-thread.title: FISA
thin-thread.summary: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, the U.S. legal framework governing surveillance warrants for foreign-intelligence purposes. Per John Kiriakou, FISA is dangerously easy to abuse — he cites Carter Page, whose life was ruined and who was driven into bankruptcy after the Steele dossier was used to support four FISA applications against him. Kiriakou groups FISA with the Patriot Act and Section 702 as the legal architecture stripping Americans of constitutional protections, opposed by only a handful of legislators.

thin-thread.title: John Kiriakou
thin-thread.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

think-tank-financing.title: Lobbyists writing legislation
think-tank-financing.summary: John Kiriakou''s first-hand account from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee: told that the committee would take part in the carbon offsets debate and protesting that he knew nothing about carbon offsets, he was told not to worry — and the next day strangers came into the office, took over most of the desks, logged on and began writing the bill.

think-tank-financing.title: The Speaker's office as gatekeeper
think-tank-financing.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how legislative power moved in the mid-1990s from committee chairmen and the Rules Committee into the office of the Speaker of the House, where it has stayed because no subsequent Speaker has wanted to give it back — and the member of Congress who explained the death of his own whistleblower bill in four words: ''Nancy said I couldn''t.''

think-tank-financing.title: Progressive taxation
think-tank-financing.summary: John Kiriakou''s argument that the United States abandoned a system it was once proud of: taxation based, in Theodore Roosevelt''s formulation, on a person''s ability to pay. It fell apart under Ronald Reagan, he says, and the regressive substitutes now proposed — a higher gas tax among them — hit the people least able to absorb them.

think-tank-financing.title: The Trumpcare confusion
think-tank-financing.summary: A television interview John Kiriakou says he watched, in which a woman from Arkansas wept with gratitude to President Trump because a website had insured her son's cancer treatment — and, told by the reporter that this was in fact the Affordable Care Act, insisted that Obamacare had been repealed and replaced and that what she had was Trumpcare.

think-tank-financing.title: Concealment of the CIA budget
think-tank-financing.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA hides its spending: there is no publicly available written CIA budget, and individual line items are distributed across unrelated federal departments under invented cover programmes — a practice he says persists unchanged, and which once repeatedly exposed the agency to Senator William Proxmire''s Golden Fleece Award.

think-tank-financing.title: No-bid contracts
think-tank-financing.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of the mechanism he considers the real corruption of American national security: an officer retires on a Friday, returns Monday on a contractor badge at ten times the salary, and is fed no-bid contracts by the friends he left behind — including, in one unnamed case he describes, a tax shelter that became a multi-billion dollar company inside a decade.

thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.title: Freedom of Information Act
thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.summary: The U.S. transparency law that runs through John Kiriakou's story from every direction — his plea agreement banned him from ever filing a FOIA request on himself, so he filed one with the Bureau of Prisons anyway and got back pages stamped "FOIA EXEMPT — DO NOT RELEASE TO INMATE"; a FOIA request exposed the prison commissary skim; Jason Leopold's requests revealed that a detainee's eye was removed under sedation without his knowledge and that NBC's Ken Dilanian sent his stories to the CIA before his own editor; and a FOIA request is how Kiriakou learned Gary Johnson had quietly lobbied for his early release.

thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.title: The buried Senate documents
thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.summary: John Kiriakou's account of a sitting senator who could not obtain a set of documents classified in the 1970s. Long past the point where mandatory declassification should have applied, the CIA disclaimed them as not its own; they turned out to be Senate documents, which no disclosure law reaches, and no authority existed to compel their release.

thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.title: JFK assassination
thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.summary: November 22, 1963 killing of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas, Texas. John Kiriakou's position, drawn from a Pakistan-station encounter with Bay of Pigs commander Jean Gately, an RFK Jr. account of CIA Director John McCone's same-day exchange with Bobby Kennedy Sr., and a White House contact's confirmation that the remaining classified Kennedy documents all contain the word "Israel," is that elements of the CIA were probably involved and that Israeli intelligence was involved as well.

thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.title: Bill Clinton
thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.summary: 42nd U.S. president whom John Kiriakou describes as wholly disinterested in intelligence — briefed by the CIA only twice in eight years, with Vice President Al Gore taking the daily briefing instead and relaying anything important.

thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.title: Charlie Kirk shooting
thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.summary: Kiriakou questions the official account: a court filing says the ATF could not match the autopsy bullet to the rifle tied to the suspect.

thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.title: Congressional intelligence oversight
thirty-year-mandatory-declassification.summary: John Kiriakou''s standing criticism of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee — that unlike the armed services and foreign relations committees, they do not perform oversight at all: "They''re just cheerleaders." His illustration is a sitting committee chairman who summoned him privately, then asked whether Kiriakou would write the criticism publicly on his behalf.

this-desk-kills-fascism.title: FCI Loretto
this-desk-kills-fascism.summary: U.S. Federal Correctional Institution in Loretto, Pennsylvania; the low-medium-security prison at which John Kiriakou served 23 months of a 30-month sentence following his 2013 Espionage Act–era plea deal; the originally ordered "minimum security work camp" placement was countermanded — per Kiriakou, on Brennan's direct intervention — to place him in the actual prison alongside the general population.

this-desk-kills-fascism.title: Diesel Therapy
this-desk-kills-fascism.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a punitive practice within the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons in which an inmate is placed into indefinite transit — moved continuously from facility to facility — for up to six months, with no access to phone, email, or pen and paper, and listed on the BOP website only as 'in transit' with no destination. Kiriakou described it as the one threat at FCI Loretto that actually frightened him.

this-desk-kills-fascism.title: Letter from Loretto
this-desk-kills-fascism.summary: Prison newsletter written by John Kiriakou from FCI Loretto, modeled on Martin Luther King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," which exposed two crimes committed against him by guards and went viral after being relayed to the Huffington Post, drawing national press to the prison.

this-desk-kills-fascism.title: Charles Samuels
this-desk-kills-fascism.summary: Director of the Bureau of Prisons during Kiriakou's incarceration, and the official to whom Kiriakou publicly appealed over the heads of the Loretto staff in a letter from Loretto.

this-desk-kills-fascism.title: Administrative remedy process
this-desk-kills-fascism.summary: The Bureau of Prisons' internal grievance system, which Kiriakou describes as a fig leaf designed to run out the clock on prisoners' complaints rather than resolve them.

this-desk-kills-fascism.title: Bureau of Prisons
this-desk-kills-fascism.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

thomas-drake.title: DARPA LifeLog
thomas-drake.summary: A Pentagon research program meant to track every email, photo, location and purchase of a person; John Kiriakou notes it was killed on February 4, 2004 — one day before Mark Zuckerberg filed the Facebook LLC.

thomas-drake.title: Thin Thread
thomas-drake.summary: Competing NSA programs at the center of the post-9/11 mass-surveillance turn. Per John Kiriakou, on September 11, 2001 NSA Director Michael Hayden implemented Operation Thin Thread — which 'vacuums up every phone call, every text message, every email, every bit of metadata from every American' — and reportedly called 9/11 'the greatest possible gift to NSA.' Three NSA officers (Bill Binney, Kirk Wiebe, and Ed Loomis) had built a competing program, Stellar Wind, that could collect the same data while protecting Americans' identities; Hayden chose to grab everything instead. Kiriakou says it was Tom Drake's effort to report the illegality that destroyed Drake.

thomas-drake.title: David Rockefeller in Bahrain
thomas-drake.summary: Per John Kiriakou — economic officer at the American Embassy in Bahrain, 1994–1996, and control officer for a David Rockefeller visit — Rockefeller''s award from the US-Bahrain Banking Society was a cover stop. After three days of documented public appearances, Rockefeller flew on a military plane to Baghdad to deliver a secret message to Saddam Hussein: stop violating sanctions, or the United States would take military action. Kiriakou cites the trip as a textbook case of how public figures are used as deniable back-channel intermediaries.

thomas-drake.title: Mike Hayden
thomas-drake.summary: Director of the National Security Agency on September 11, 2001; subsequently Director of the Central Intelligence Agency under President George W. Bush. Per John Kiriakou's relay of NSA whistleblower Tom Drake, on the morning of 9/11 Hayden told NSA personnel the agency had been 'waiting for a 9/11 so that they could implement the bigger program and grab everybody's electronics' — despite the agency's founding charter forbidding it from intercepting the communications of U.S. persons.

thomas-drake.title: National Security Agency
thomas-drake.summary: The U.S. signals-intelligence agency. John Kiriakou notes it was never created by an act of Congress and that its own charter forbids collection on Americans — a rule that, when he entered government, meant heads rolled over accidental intercepts, and which he says has since been inverted into total collection stored in Utah for 500 years.

thomas-drake.title: The Panetta bin Laden disclosure
thomas-drake.summary: Leon Panetta's accidental naming of the special forces ground commander of the bin Laden raid in front of a Hollywood screenwriter, which Kiriakou uses as the control case for his argument that Espionage Act enforcement is selective.

thomas-massie.title: AIPAC
thomas-massie.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

thomas-massie.title: Jeffrey Epstein
thomas-massie.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

thomas-massie.title: MOSSAD
thomas-massie.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

thomas-massie.title: Donald Trump
thomas-massie.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

thomas-massie.title: Radio and TV Martí
thomas-massie.summary: U.S. government broadcasters beaming anti-communist programming at Cuba; John Kiriakou uses their accidental reach into Florida to explain why the Obama administration made it legal, in 2015, to propagandize the American people.

thomas-massie.title: Epstein Files Transparency Act
thomas-massie.summary: The law compelling the Justice Department to release the Epstein files by a fixed deadline, passed 419 to 1 in the House and 99 to nothing in the Senate and then, in John Kiriakou's account, simply not complied with.

three-felonies-a-day.title: John Kiriakou
three-felonies-a-day.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

three-felonies-a-day.title: Vault 7
three-felonies-a-day.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

three-felonies-a-day.title: Overcriminalization
three-felonies-a-day.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that the United States criminalizes too much — locking up 25% of the world's prisoners with 5% of its population, and adding roughly 50 new felonies a year — illustrated by a NOAA employee prosecuted for whistling at a whale.

three-felonies-a-day.title: Espionage Act
three-felonies-a-day.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

three-felonies-a-day.title: Arianna Huffington
three-felonies-a-day.summary: Founder of the Huffington Post and the accidental amplifier who turned John Kiriakou's prison writing into a phenomenon. His first Letter from Loretto went to his attorney, then to a friend running Firedoglake who — unknown to Kiriakou — was close to Huffington; she plastered it as a banner headline and it drew over a million hits, bringing CNN and 60 Minutes to the prison gates. She published his open letter to Snowden, ran the diesel-therapy exposé that triggered the "hands off John Kiriakou" campaign, and came to Loretto herself with two young journalists.

three-felonies-a-day.title: CIA Gmail account felony case
three-felonies-a-day.summary: Per John Kiriakou, a CIA colleague working the counterterrorism fusion center night shift was ordered by cable to check a terrorist suspect's Gmail account and password, did so, and was later charged with a felony for illegally accessing a computer — despite having acted only on explicit written instructions from headquarters.

three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.title: The Libertarian Party
three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.summary: The third party a lifelong Democrat joined on release from prison, after its 2016 presidential nominee had written to him in his cell and to the Attorney General on his behalf — the party John Kiriakou says was the only one talking about whistleblowing and the security-versus-liberty trade-off, and the one whose structural problem, he was told, is that it has no benefactor.

three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.title: Iran Nuclear Assessment
three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.summary: Per John Kiriakou's assessment, the US–Israeli military campaign against Iran was a war of choice driven by Israeli political pressure rather than genuine intelligence indicating an Iranian nuclear weapons threat. The CIA produced two National Intelligence Estimates concluding Iran had no nuclear weapons program; Supreme Leader Ayatollah Khamenei issued a fatwa in the 1980s forbidding such a program. The U.S. went to war anyway, in Kiriakou's view, after President Trump replaced the Joint Chiefs of Staff with officers willing to accept Israeli intelligence and proceed.

three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.title: John Kiriakou
three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.title: AIPAC
three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.summary: The American Israel Public Affairs Committee — the U.S. political organization that, in John Kiriakou's framing, ought to be registered as a foreign-lobbying entity but is not, and that wields decisive electoral power against U.S. elected officials who express support for Palestinian human rights.

three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.title: Iran 12-Day War
three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.summary: 2025 Israeli air campaign against Iran during which Israel killed at least fourteen Iranian nuclear scientists by destroying the apartment buildings they lived in; preceded for each scientist by Farsi-language telephone calls from Iranian-Jewish Mossad and Shin Bet officers offering defection in lieu of certain death; characterized by John Kiriakou as a categorical departure from CIA targeting doctrine in its acceptable-civilian-casualty calculus.

three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.title: Iran strike factions (2026)
three-legal-ways-to-enter-a-country.summary: John Kiriakou's reporting, sourced to a former colleague at the White House, that a 2026 decision to strike Iran pitted an anti-war camp of JD Vance and Tulsi Gabbard against a pro-war camp led by Marco Rubio — with the Joint Chiefs newly compliant because Trump had replaced them all.

thursday-arrests.title: Whistleblowers and suicide
thursday-arrests.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, drawn from conversations with some fifty whistleblowers, that every one of them considered suicide in the early stage of their case — and his own account of the family vigil that kept him from the garage.

thursday-arrests.title: "Whistleblowers die broke"
thursday-arrests.summary: The observation John Kiriakou attributes to Daniel Ellsberg — that the one thing all whistleblowers have in common is that they die broke — which Kiriakou applies to his own confiscated federal pension and his expectation of working until the day he dies.

thursday-arrests.title: "It''s about mitigating damage"
thursday-arrests.summary: The sentence John Kiriakou credits with changing his mind about going to trial — one of his own attorneys telling him that his problem was that he thought the case was about justice, when it was about mitigating damage — and the two lawyers who drove to his house after he emailed at six in the morning to refuse the plea.

thursday-arrests.title: Seventy-two denied motions
thursday-arrests.summary: The count John Kiriakou gives of the pretrial motions filed in his case and denied by Judge Leonie Brinkema — seventy-two denied and none granted — which he offers as the mechanism by which a national security defendant in the Eastern District of Virginia is prevented from mounting a defence at all.

thursday-arrests.title: The sentencing remark
thursday-arrests.summary: The comment John Kiriakou says the judge made at his sentencing — that she wished she could give him the maximum, because that is what she would give him — and his reading of it as a performance for the national security reporters filling the gallery.

thursday-arrests.title: Arabic and Greek
thursday-arrests.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

ticking-time-bomb.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
ticking-time-bomb.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

ticking-time-bomb.title: John Kiriakou
ticking-time-bomb.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

ticking-time-bomb.title: Mitchell and Jessen
ticking-time-bomb.summary: The two American psychologists who pitched the CIA's enhanced interrogation program to Director George Tenet at a cocktail party in late October 2001; designers of the program and its theoretical underpinning, "learned helplessness."

ticking-time-bomb.title: Ramzi bin al-Shibh
ticking-time-bomb.summary: Alleged September 11 co-conspirator, captured in Pakistan in the summer of 2002 and taken to a secret prison rather than to trial. John Kiriakou, who is often wrongly credited with his capture, cites him as the clearest demonstration of what torture cost the United States — declared clinically insane by the Pentagon's own psychiatrist as a result of CIA sleep deprivation, and therefore untriable.

ticking-time-bomb.title: Senate Torture Report
ticking-time-bomb.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

ticking-time-bomb.title: Zero Dark Thirty
ticking-time-bomb.summary: 2012 film dramatizing the CIA hunt for Osama bin Laden, criticized on release for suggesting torture produced the intelligence that led to his capture. John Kiriakou surveys the mixed critical reception — praise from Time and the New Yorker for its craft, condemnation from journalist Michael Wolff and director Kathryn Bigelow's critics for what they called pro-torture propaganda — and notes his friend Senator John McCain said the film left him "sick... because it is wrong."

tiffany-stationery.title: The Greek community of Warren, Ohio
tiffany-stationery.summary: The Greek-American community John Kiriakou's mother and first wife both came from — overwhelmingly from the island of Chios, closely enough knit that his divorce started a fistfight in a coffee house between men who had never met him.

tiffany-stationery.title: Double-Agent Capture
tiffany-stationery.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

tiffany-stationery.title: John Kiriakou
tiffany-stationery.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

tiffany-stationery.title: Mary Jane Stevens
tiffany-stationery.summary: The lawyer who represented John Kiriakou through his custody dispute — who told him to wait for Monday and go to court, was ignored, and then got the assurance from a hostile police chief that let him walk into the hearing without being arrested.

tiffany-stationery.title: The propane truck ruse
tiffany-stationery.summary: The improvised environmental emergency John Kiriakou staged to empty a Middle Eastern cul-de-sac so a CIA lock-picking team could search a captured Hezbollah organiser's house — after his liaison partners rejected a gas leak on the ground that the country had no underground gas lines.

tiffany-stationery.title: Training foreign intelligence services
tiffany-stationery.summary: The CIA job John Kiriakou took after returning from Athens — travelling the world to teach foreign services how to carry out counterterrorist raids, break down doors, seize people, conduct interrogations and disrupt cells — and why, he says, those countries asked the Americans rather than the Israelis or the British.

title-10-vs-title-50.title: Executive Order 12333
title-10-vs-title-50.summary: The U.S. presidential directive — in its post-9/11 amended form — that grants the CIA the legal authority to kill any individual anywhere in the world deemed by the agency to pose a "clear and present danger" to the United States; the legal foundation underlying both CIA paramilitary operations and the agency's contractor relationships including with Blackwater.

title-10-vs-title-50.title: Blackwater
title-10-vs-title-50.summary: The private military contractor founded by Erik Prince that ran the CIA's Global Response Staff and, until shut down by Leon Panetta, a global assassination program; staffed at the board level with former CIA officers including Cofer Black as Vice President.

title-10-vs-title-50.title: Ninth Circuit contractor ruling (2025)
title-10-vs-title-50.summary: Approximately July 2025 U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruling, in a case brought by Abu Zubaydah against CIA contractors who had tortured him, holding that contractors operating under a written CIA contract are legally protected as agents of the agency; extends Executive Order 12333 authority to contractor operations including the Blackwater assassination program; received almost no U.S. media coverage.

title-10-vs-title-50.title: Ground Branch
title-10-vs-title-50.summary: The land-operating component of the CIA's Special Activities Division, staffed almost entirely by former Delta Force and SEAL Team 6 operators rather than career officers; per John Kiriakou its job is to kill or kidnap anyone judged a threat to the United States, and its work is so secret that everyone in the office knew what they did and nobody mentioned it.

title-10-vs-title-50.title: Abu Zubaydah
title-10-vs-title-50.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

title-10-vs-title-50.title: Special Activities Division
title-10-vs-title-50.summary: The CIA's paramilitary arm; described by John Kiriakou as having two organizationally distinct components — the pre-9/11 SAD, a covert-action division within the Directorate of Operations, and a post-9/11 special activities group within the Counterterrorism Center, staffed largely by personnel on secondment from Delta Force, SEAL Team 6, and other special-operations units.

todd-blanch.title: Lee Zeldon
todd-blanch.summary: Per Megyn Kelly's opening monologue, the EPA administrator reportedly considered by Trump as a possible replacement for Attorney General Pam Bondi.

todd-blanch.title: Alexa
todd-blanch.summary: Per John Kiriakou, Amazon''s Alexa smart speaker reports directly to the NSA — and he owns one anyway. The device recurs across his interviews as the standing example of the surveillance trade-off in modern smart-home technology, and of his own negotiated exception to it: one speaker, in one room, against the advice of every intelligence officer he has ever known.

todd-blanch.title: Anwar al-Awlaki
todd-blanch.summary: American-born al-Qaeda propagandist; in 1993 the imam of the Falls Church, Virginia mosque visited by John Kiriakou's CIA Arabic-language class on a field trip; in 2001 the cleric at whose mosque the 9/11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks; killed by U.S. drone strike in Yemen in approximately 2011.

todd-blanch.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
todd-blanch.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

todd-blanch.title: Bill Barr
todd-blanch.summary: Per Sean Davis, speaking on the same Megyn Kelly panel as Kiriakou, the attorney general under the first Trump administration, seen as competent but not fully loyal, whose relationship with Trump ended in a "breakup."

todd-blanch.title: CIA Remote Vehicle Control
todd-blanch.summary: John Kiriakou's account, corroborated by Forbes' Andy Greenberg's real-world demonstration, that the CIA can remotely take over a car's systems and cause a fatal crash disguised as an accident.

toll-booth-plan.title: Site 13
toll-booth-plan.summary: The house in Faisalabad, nearest of the thirteen targets to the CIA safe house, where Abu Zubaydah was shot at two o'clock in the morning on the night of the raids — announced to John Kiriakou on the roof a mile away by the sound of a battering ram failing against a steel-reinforced door.

toll-booth-plan.title: Abu Zubaydah
toll-booth-plan.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

toll-booth-plan.title: Faisalabad
toll-booth-plan.summary: The Pakistani textile city of some seven or eight million people where Abu Zubaydah was captured in March 2002 — concrete, mud and corrugated tin in John Kiriakou's description, with a brand-new glass-and-steel McDonald's standing in the middle of it.

toll-booth-plan.title: Magic box
toll-booth-plan.summary: An improvised cell-phone locator that two CIA tech officers built from parts bought in a Pakistani bazaar during the hunt for Abu Zubaydah. It could point toward a phone while a call was live, and did so exactly once — long enough for John Kiriakou to conclude the device was wasted time and to fly in a targeting analyst instead.

toll-booth-plan.title: Mr. Fish
toll-booth-plan.summary: The cover name the CIA used for Abu Zubaydah in Pakistan in 2002 — invented because the Americans would not tell their Pakistani partners who the target was, and derived from the only thing they would say about him: that he was a big fish.

toll-booth-plan.title: John Kiriakou
toll-booth-plan.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

tommy-mchale.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
tommy-mchale.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

tommy-mchale.title: Taliban embassy raid
tommy-mchale.summary: John Kiriakou's account of raiding the last functioning Taliban embassy, in Peshawar, in the middle of the night after 9/11 — a raid that turned up phone bills showing dozens of calls to U.S. cities that stopped on September 10 and resumed on September 16, evidence of possible sleeper cells the FBI never translated.

tommy-mchale.title: Jennifer Keenan
tommy-mchale.summary: FBI agent who partnered with John Kiriakou in Islamabad on the handling of an unreliable walk-in informant who had confessed to firing a rocket at the American embassy in 1996. After the informant's leads to weapons caches in Peshawar and a safe in Multan both turned up empty, Kiriakou and Keenan decided to lure him back to the embassy and arrest him on the strength of his original confession, which carried no statute of limitations.

tommy-mchale.title: Abu Zubaydah
tommy-mchale.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

tommy-mchale.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
tommy-mchale.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

tommy-mchale.title: Bob Grenier
tommy-mchale.summary: Career CIA officer who served as station chief in Islamabad before, during, and after 9/11; later associate deputy director of operations for policy support and Iraq Mission Manager; John Kiriakou's boss and, for one year, his supervisor as executive assistant.

tony-blinken.title: Sergey Lavrov
tony-blinken.summary: Russian foreign minister, and previously Russian ambassador to the United Nations during John Kiriakou's assignment there. Kiriakou describes him as the most admired diplomat at the UN — the most powerful, important and strategic ambassador in the building despite operating with far smaller resources than his American, British, French and Chinese counterparts.

tony-blinken.title: Abu Zubaydah
