waterboarding.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

waterboarding.title: Christopher Hitchens
waterboarding.summary: British-American journalist and author who, at John Kiriakou's telling, argued that CIA waterboarding was 'nothing … not a big deal,' underwent a filmed waterboarding in 2008, tapped out after roughly seventeen seconds, and suffered panic attacks thereafter. Kiriakou knew him and corresponded with him — the experiment happened because Hitchens thought Kiriakou was exaggerating — and remained an admirer of the writer and an opponent of his politics on Iraq.

waterboarding.title: Music as torture
waterboarding.summary: The use of recorded music played on indefinite loop as a coercive interrogation technique. Per John Kiriakou, the CIA's post-9/11 rotation ran to the Bee Gees and the SpongeBob SquarePants theme song, and the practice was not an invention of the war on terror — he places its use throughout the Vietnam War.

waterboarding.title: Learned Helplessness
waterboarding.summary: Psychological concept adapted by the CIA as the theoretical basis for its post-9/11 enhanced interrogation program; per John Kiriakou, the goal of techniques including waterboarding was not primarily to elicit specific information but to render the prisoner so terrified of his captors that he would volunteer confessions on demand. In practice, applied to Abu Zubaydah, it meant a dog cage he would climb into on command, a coffin filled with cockroaches, and a towel whose mere appearance made him crumple — a programme Kiriakou says had far less to do with gathering intelligence than with ruining a man's life.

waterboarding.title: Abu Zubaydah as a sounding board
waterboarding.summary: The second, longer phase of Abu Zubaydah''s usefulness to the CIA, described by John Kiriakou in his December 2007 ABC News interview: once the prisoner had given up what he knew about current operations, his value shifted from threat reporting to analysis, with case officers reading him the names of men arrested in European capitals and asking whether the operations attributed to them made sense.

watergate.title: Dianne Feinstein
watergate.summary: Longtime Democratic U.S. senator from California and chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. Per John Kiriakou, one of the greatest disappointments on Capitol Hill — an unusually friendly chairwoman who exercised no real oversight, good on torture and a cheerleader for the CIA on everything else. She co-authored the 2015 McCain-Feinstein Amendment that reiterated the federal ban on torture, and she blocked Gina Haspel's promotion in 2013 before publicly warming to her in 2018.

watergate.title: Code Pink
watergate.summary: The women-led peace group co-founded by Medea Benjamin. John Kiriakou first saw them as a Senate staffer — a room full of pink t-shirts at a hearing he'd organized for Senator Kerry, where he was caught smiling at their chants and told to keep his opinions to himself. When he was arrested, Code Pink "was right there next to me," threw his going-away party before prison, ran the sustained call campaign that helped stop his diesel-therapy transfer, stood with him through the 2019 Venezuelan embassy siege — and after prison he volunteered as coordinator of Code Pink Congress.

watergate.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
watergate.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

watergate.title: Daniel Ellsberg
watergate.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

watergate.title: Espionage Act
watergate.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

watergate.title: Bureau of Prisons
watergate.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

watermark.title: Fort Gordon
watermark.summary: The U.S. Army installation in Georgia where NSA whistleblower Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, worked as a contractor linguist before her arrest.

watermark.title: Miranda Rights
watermark.summary: Reality Winner, interviewed on Kiriakou's show, says she was never read her Miranda rights during her 2017 arrest by the FBI.

watermark.title: Terry Aubry
watermark.summary: Named by Kiriakou both as an FBI whistleblower who exposed racism at the bureau and as one of two Intercept journalists who sent him to prison.

watermark.title: Afghan Languages
watermark.summary: The three major languages of Afghanistan — Pashto, Dari (a form of Persian), and Arabic — as discussed on John Kiriakou's show with NSA whistleblower and former military linguist Reality Winner.

watermark.title: Edward Snowden
watermark.summary: Former NSA contractor who in 2013 disclosed the scope of U.S. [mass surveillance](/wiki/mass-surveillance), including the Section 702 collection program. Per John Kiriakou — who counts Snowden among the small group of national-security whistleblowers prosecuted under the Espionage Act — Snowden was ''stuck between two awful slippery slopes'': breaking his oath and chain of command on one side, and on the other catching something ''cut and dry against the Constitution'' that no one would act on. Kiriakou notes Snowden could not use his chain of command (as Kiriakou could not, his own chain being Jose Rodriguez), and that Judge Leonie Brinkema had reserved the Snowden case for herself before he fled the country.

watermark.title: FBI Arrest Strategies
watermark.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the FBI deliberately times arrests for Thursdays or Friday evenings because no federal arraignments happen on Fridays, forcing detainees to spend the weekend in jail before facing a judge on Monday — a tactic he says he saw applied to January 6 defendants as well as to himself.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The second plane
we-are-at-war-today.summary: John Kiriakou's account of where he was standing when United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower — in Cofer Black's outer office, mid-sentence, explaining to a secretary why a pilot could not possibly fly into the World Trade Center on so clear a day.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The Condoleezza Rice meeting
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The White House appointment John Kiriakou and Cofer Black never kept on the morning of 11 September 2001: an attempt to persuade the National Security Advisor to withhold three declassified historical CIA cables that had identified sources who were still alive.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The honey salesman warning
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The al-Qaeda briefing Cofer Black delivered unannounced to a visiting delegation of Middle Eastern intelligence officers at CIA headquarters on 6 July 2001, in which he described intercepted code words — a honey salesman arriving with vast quantities of honey, a great wedding, a great football match — as signals of an imminent attack on a massive scale, and begged the visitors for any source inside al-Qaeda.

we-are-at-war-today.title: Reading in on the Iraq invasion
we-are-at-war-today.summary: John Kiriakou's account of his first day as executive assistant to the CIA's deputy director for operations, when he signed six secrecy agreements and was told that the United States would invade Iraq the following March, and that the agencies opposing the war had already lost the argument.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The seventy-two-year-old contractor
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The hallway conversation John Kiriakou says explained why the CIA had not sent him, an Arabic speaker, to interrogate captured al-Qaeda fighters — a returning contractor's answer that he had been in Afghanistan killing people — and the demand Kiriakou made afterwards that got him sent to Pakistan the next day.

we-are-at-war-today.title: The Tehran slip
we-are-at-war-today.summary: The moment John Kiriakou says he witnessed as note-taker in a secure video teleconference a day or two before the 2003 invasion of Iraq, when a briefing general said that if all went as planned American forces could be in Tehran by August, and CIA Director George Tenet turned off his microphone and asked Kiriakou whether the man had said Tehran or Baghdad.

wealth-concentration.title: CIA intelligence failures
wealth-concentration.summary: John Kiriakou's standing position that the CIA has missed every major world event since its founding in 1947 — the building and the fall of the Berlin Wall, the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Iran hostage crisis, 9/11 — and that the remedy is therefore not more money but fewer overseas bases and actual accountability, of which he says there has been none.

wealth-concentration.title: 2028 presidential field
wealth-concentration.summary: John Kiriakou's assessment of the wide-open 2028 presidential race — the first in his life, he says, where he has no idea who either party will nominate. Predictive markets were listing 44 Democrats and 26 Republicans as possible candidates. His own preferred candidate is Tucker Carlson, whom he says he has repeatedly begged to run; his working assumption about anyone who does want the job is that they are "a narcissist and probably a sociopath on top of it."

wealth-concentration.title: Amaryllis Fox Kennedy
wealth-concentration.summary: Former CIA non-official-cover officer who worked under commercial cover as an international art consultant, later a Trump campaign manager and nominee for deputy CIA director. Per John Kiriakou, Senator Tom Cotton threatened to filibuster her appointment; the president responded by naming her deputy national security adviser instead — a job Kiriakou considers more powerful, since the CIA director reports to the national security adviser.

wealth-concentration.title: Andrew Bustamante
wealth-concentration.summary: Former CIA officer who sells CIA-style training online; John Kiriakou identifies him as the lone critic of his work hosting a show on a Russian network, and argues Bustamante's training business — open to anyone who pays — is the more problematic of the two.

wealth-concentration.title: Angry Birds
wealth-concentration.summary: The mobile game John Kiriakou describes as his only vice besides buying art, played every morning for nine consecutive years and cited by his ex-wife as a grievance in their marriage.

wealth-concentration.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
wealth-concentration.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: Church Committee
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: U.S. Senate investigative committee operating in 1975–1976 that examined domestic intelligence abuses by the CIA, FBI, and NSA; per John Kiriakou, the Church Committee — alongside the concurrent Pike Committee in the House — was the last genuine moment of legislative oversight over the intelligence community, born of a national consensus that government had gone dangerously off course. Its work led to the creation of the permanent Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, which Kiriakou says ceased to function as real oversight roughly seven years after its founding.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: COINTELPRO
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: The FBI programme of warrantless surveillance and disruption directed at Americans, and one of the four abuses John Kiriakou names when explaining what the Church Committee actually investigated. He treats it as the historical benchmark for what a real congressional inquiry into the security agencies looks like — and, through the campaign against Martin Luther King, as proof that the state will destroy a citizen it considers a threat.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: MK-Ultra
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: The CIA's mid-twentieth-century umbrella program of mind-control, behavioral-modification, and biological-warfare experimentation, encompassing subprojects such as MK-Chickwit and MK-Seesaw; active 1952–1975; documented practices included LSD dosing of unwitting American citizens in CIA-rented brothels and the aerosolized release of pathogens into the San Francisco fog; 80% of the program's documentation was destroyed by the CIA in defiance of a 1975 preservation order from Senator Frank Church.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: Vault 7
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: The 2017 WikiLeaks disclosure of thousands of pages of CIA Directorate of Science and Technology documents — leaked by agency engineer Joshua Schulte — revealing CIA technical capabilities including remote takeover of internet-connected cars, conversion of smart-TV speakers into covert microphones, and the planting of Russian or Persian language fragments in foreign systems to mislead attribution.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: David Petraeus
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: Retired U.S. Army general and director of the CIA who, per John Kiriakou, confirmed the names of ten covert CIA operatives to his biographer and girlfriend and was never criminally charged — a contrast Kiriakou cites repeatedly as proof that his own prosecution under the Intelligence Identities Protection Act was selective. Kiriakou''s explanation for the disparity: Petraeus had not blown the whistle on the torture program and embarrassed the agency.

weaponization-subcommittee.title: Donald Trump
weaponization-subcommittee.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

weapons-cache-map.title: The propane truck ruse
weapons-cache-map.summary: The improvised environmental emergency John Kiriakou staged to empty a Middle Eastern cul-de-sac so a CIA lock-picking team could search a captured Hezbollah organiser's house — after his liaison partners rejected a gas leak on the ground that the country had no underground gas lines.

weapons-cache-map.title: Double-Agent Capture
weapons-cache-map.summary: Clandestine operation in which an intelligence service, having identified a recruited agent as working simultaneously for a hostile service, arranges a controlled final meeting to apprehend the agent before the agent can carry out orders — which may include killing the handler. Per John Kiriakou, he ran one such operation in the Middle East in the early 2000s after an NSA analyst warned him that his agent had just been ordered to shoot him in the next meeting.

weapons-cache-map.title: Training foreign intelligence services
weapons-cache-map.summary: The CIA job John Kiriakou took after returning from Athens — travelling the world to teach foreign services how to carry out counterterrorist raids, break down doors, seize people, conduct interrogations and disrupt cells — and why, he says, those countries asked the Americans rather than the Israelis or the British.

weapons-cache-map.title: The Greek community of Warren, Ohio
weapons-cache-map.summary: The Greek-American community John Kiriakou's mother and first wife both came from — overwhelmingly from the island of Chios, closely enough knit that his divorce started a fistfight in a coffee house between men who had never met him.

weapons-cache-map.title: John Kiriakou
weapons-cache-map.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

weapons-cache-map.title: The Tiffany stationery letter
weapons-cache-map.summary: The deliberately expensive note John Kiriakou wrote to his first wife on Tiffany & Co. stationery, telling her he was halving her child support on the advice of counsel — a tactic suggested by his divorce lawyer to force her to file, and which worked the next day.

welch-45.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
welch-45.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

welch-45.title: Stephen Saunders
welch-45.summary: British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November in March 2000

welch-45.title: Richard Welch
welch-45.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

welch-45.title: Carlos the Jackal
welch-45.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

welch-45.title: Gust Avrakotos
welch-45.summary: CIA case officer, John Kiriakou's operations mentor, and a central figure in Charlie Wilson's War — the prolific, divisive covert-war veteran Kiriakou credits as the greatest teacher of his adult life.

welch-45.title: Heather Saunders
welch-45.summary: Widow of British Brigadier General Stephen Saunders, the British defense attaché in Athens assassinated by Revolutionary Organization 17 November on April 22, 2000; per John Kiriakou, the person whose post-assassination Greek-television statement — "this organization is not a political organization nor is it a phantom group; it's a gang of criminals" — for the first time since 17 November's 1975 founding turned Greek public opinion against the group.

wesley-clark.title: Donald Trump
wesley-clark.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

wesley-clark.title: George Tenet
wesley-clark.summary: Director of Central Intelligence from 1997 to 2004, spanning the September 11 attacks and the early enhanced-interrogation program; identified by John Kiriakou as John Brennan's institutional patron at the agency; the figure who ordered the Five Eyes intelligence services to "open the files" to each other in the early 2000s.

wesley-clark.title: Iraq WMD intelligence
wesley-clark.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the case for Iraqi weapons of mass destruction was fabricated: the intelligence community''s consensus was that Iraq had no WMD, but the White House had already decided to invade and sought analysis to fit the policy.

wesley-clark.title: Israeli Nuclear Program
wesley-clark.summary: Israel's widely assumed but officially unacknowledged nuclear arsenal; per John Kiriakou, the conventional wisdom within the CIA is that Israel possesses between 120 and 220 nuclear weapons, and the U.S. government's refusal to formally acknowledge this is driven by a specific legal obligation under the Glenn-Symington Act, which would require cutting off all foreign aid to any nuclear-armed country not party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

wesley-clark.title: John Kiriakou
wesley-clark.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

wesley-clark.title: Mary Margaret Graham
wesley-clark.summary: CIA Senior Intelligence Service officer and later Deputy Director of National Intelligence for Collection under John Negroponte — described by John Kiriakou as a career "reports officer" who had never personally recruited a source, and as his difficult chief of station in a later domestic assignment.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Kiriakou's writing process
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how he actually writes — books in waves over roughly nine months, op-eds in forty-five minutes to an hour once an idea has sat for a few days, and a habit of getting up at two in the morning to write one because he cannot sleep. He wrote *Remains of the Day* in six weeks during COVID, losing whole evenings to it: "I look at the clock again, it''s 2:00 in the morning. I''m like, oh my god, what happened?"

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Remains of the Day (book)
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou's book, announced for publication by Simon and Schuster in March 2026, billed as a definitive guide to the historic cemeteries of Washington DC and the first in a planned series; the second installment will cover the Mafia graves of New York City.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Greek death rituals
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: The five-year grave rental, exhumation and ossuary practice of rural Greece as John Kiriakou describes it — bones washed in red wine, blessed, boxed, and eventually laid beneath the foundations of a new church, with cremation strictly forbidden. He visits the ossuary in his ancestral Rhodes village, where the records stop in the nineteenth century because the Ottomans burned everything earlier.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Israel Boyd and the Wonder Bread story
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding the grave of Israel Boyd, one of two brothers forced by their parents into the family bakery business, who went on to invent the first industrial dough mixer and dough-cutting machine, pioneer adding milk to bread dough, and build the largest bakery in America before World War I — before selling the business, whose flagship "Mrs. McGill's Delicious Bread" was renamed Wonder Bread by its buyer.

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: John Kiriakou
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

whispers-in-the-dirt-book.title: Abraham Accords
whispers-in-the-dirt-book.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Abu Zubaydah
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Espionage Act
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: John Kiriakou
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Enhanced interrogation techniques
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: The CIA's post-9/11 interrogation program; described by John Kiriakou as torture and as a euphemism designed to insulate the responsible officials from legal exposure.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Mark MacGann
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: The Uber whistleblower whose case John Kiriakou presented on his own programme: a 52-year-old Irishman who ran the company''s lobbying across Europe, the Middle East and Africa from 2014 to 2016, and who later handed 124,000 pages of internal documents covering 2013 to 2017 to the Guardian. Kiriakou''s account turns on one point — that the opportunity Uber marketed to low-income drivers was never what it claimed, and that the company''s leadership knew it from the beginning.

whistleblower-protection-act.title: Securedrop
whistleblower-protection-act.summary: The encrypted submission tool pioneered by WikiLeaks to let sources hand over documents without exposing themselves.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Daniel Ellsberg
whistleblower-psychology.summary: The Pentagon Papers whistleblower Kiriakou calls 'the Godfather of all national security whistleblowers' — and one of the great mentors of his life.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Julian Assange
whistleblower-psychology.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Death threats against Kiriakou
whistleblower-psychology.summary: The threats John Kiriakou received after going public about the CIA torture program. On FBI advice that at least two of them were credible, he took his wife and children out of the country to Mexico for a fortnight.

whistleblower-psychology.title: CIA media relations
whistleblower-psychology.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA shapes press coverage in the 2020s without needing an Operation Mockingbird-style infiltration program — because corporate media now recites CIA messaging willingly, most journalists simply rewrite emailed statements from the agency's Office of Public Affairs, and the CIA allegedly manipulates algorithms and backs podcasts to spread its point of view.

whistleblower-psychology.title: Frank Serpico
whistleblower-psychology.summary: The New York police officer John Kiriakou calls one of the giants of the twentieth century and ranks with Daniel Ellsberg among its greatest whistleblowers — a man shot in the face whose police colleagues did not call an ambulance, and whom Kiriakou counts as a friend.

whistleblower-psychology.title: "There is almost no upside"
whistleblower-psychology.summary: John Kiriakou''s accounting of what blowing the whistle cost him — pension, friends, freedom and finally family — set against the single thing he says is left: knowing he did the right thing. And his timeline, from the whistle in 2007 to a vindication he says took eleven years.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Kevin Shipp
whistleblower-support-network.summary: Former CIA officer and whistleblower whose case John Kiriakou read about in the Washington Post and who, Kiriakou says, believed he was entirely alone until Kiriakou reached out to tell him he was not — an episode Kiriakou uses to illustrate the isolation that follows a national security disclosure.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Bill Binney
whistleblower-support-network.summary: Former NSA technical director whom John Kiriakou cites as having debunked the DNC hack. Asked by Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity to examine the science, Binney analyzed the speed of the upload and concluded the emails could only have been copied in person to a thumb drive, not taken remotely by Russia — an argument he later made to Donald Trump in the Oval Office. Kiriakou calls him a friend, the most brilliant person he has met on electronics, and a member of the whistleblower circle he belongs to.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Veteran Intelligence Professionals for Sanity
whistleblower-support-network.summary: A group of former U.S. intelligence officials, of which John Kiriakou is a member, that issues the Sam Adams Award for Integrity in Intelligence — which Kiriakou arranged to give to whistleblower-adjacent figure Joe Kent.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Communications management unit
whistleblower-support-network.summary: The two restricted-contact units inside the American federal prison system, at Terre Haute and Marion; built for "the worst of the worst" but, in John Kiriakou's account, used to silence prisoners whose messages are inconvenient — and a practice he groups with solitary confinement as torture. He served part of his own sentence in a modified one.

whistleblower-support-network.title: Daniel Hale
whistleblower-support-network.summary: Per John Kiriakou, drone whistleblower Daniel Hale — an NSA contractor and drone targeting analyst who exposed an 80% civilian death rate in the U.S. drone program, was ordered to fire on two young girls his superior called "goats," and was sentenced to 45 months (of which Kiriakou says he actually served about 18) despite prosecutors seeking nine to eleven years.

whistleblower-support-network.title: John Kiriakou
whistleblower-support-network.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: Thursday arrests
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The scheduling practice John Kiriakou attributes to the FBI — arresting on a Thursday so that a defendant, unable to be arraigned on a Friday, spends four nights in jail before seeing a judge — and the single sentence that he says kept him out of it.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: "Whistleblowers die broke"
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The observation John Kiriakou attributes to Daniel Ellsberg — that the one thing all whistleblowers have in common is that they die broke — which Kiriakou applies to his own confiscated federal pension and his expectation of working until the day he dies.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: "Embrace it and keep telling it"
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The advice John Kiriakou says he was given days after his arrest — that he could not hide from the prosecution but had to embrace it, and had to keep telling his side of the story until it became the side of record, because the government would eventually move on to its next target.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: Assange and solitary confinement
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: John Kiriakou's 2018 argument that Julian Assange's isolation inside the Ecuadorian embassy amounted to solitary confinement — a practice the United Nations classes as torture — and that everybody breaks under it eventually, however strong they are.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: Arabic and Greek
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

whistleblowers-and-suicide.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
whistleblowers-and-suicide.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

whistleblowers-die-broke.title: Whistleblowers and suicide
whistleblowers-die-broke.summary: John Kiriakou's claim, drawn from conversations with some fifty whistleblowers, that every one of them considered suicide in the early stage of their case — and his own account of the family vigil that kept him from the garage.

whistleblowers-die-broke.title: Bankruptcy and the dropped charges
whistleblowers-die-broke.summary: The sequence John Kiriakou places at the centre of his case: that the espionage counts against him were dropped only after his legal fees had bankrupted him, which he presents as evidence that the government''s aim was attrition rather than conviction.

whistleblowers-die-broke.title: Thursday arrests
whistleblowers-die-broke.summary: The scheduling practice John Kiriakou attributes to the FBI — arresting on a Thursday so that a defendant, unable to be arraigned on a Friday, spends four nights in jail before seeing a judge — and the single sentence that he says kept him out of it.

whistleblowers-die-broke.title: The declination letter
whistleblowers-die-broke.summary: The letter the Justice Department sent John Kiriakou's attorneys in December 2008 declining to prosecute him, on the grounds that the torture allegations were already public through human rights organizations and that it is illegal to classify a crime — and the celebration dinner that was followed three weeks later by Barack Obama's inauguration.

whistleblowers-die-broke.title: Arabic and Greek
whistleblowers-die-broke.summary: The qualification John Kiriakou says opened the door to his transfer from CIA analysis to operations: he was, by his account, the only person in the agency fluent in both Arabic and Greek, at a moment when a counterterrorism position was open in Athens.

whistleblowers-die-broke.title: Assange and solitary confinement
whistleblowers-die-broke.summary: John Kiriakou's 2018 argument that Julian Assange's isolation inside the Ecuadorian embassy amounted to solitary confinement — a practice the United Nations classes as torture — and that everybody breaks under it eventually, however strong they are.

why-the-uae-was-targeted.title: Bombing the Omanis
why-the-uae-was-targeted.summary: John Kiriakou''s judgement that Iran''s strikes on the Gulf states — and above all on Oman, which had been trying to broker peace — made enemies Iran did not need to make, of governments that would otherwise have sat the war out.

why-the-uae-was-targeted.title: Dubai as Iran''s window
why-the-uae-was-targeted.summary: John Kiriakou''s explanation of why Iran did not hit Dubai hard during the 2026 war: the city is full of Iranian businessmen and is Iran''s outlet to the Western world and its principal means of evading sanctions.

why-the-uae-was-targeted.title: Iranian strikes on Gulf hotels
why-the-uae-was-targeted.summary: John Kiriakou''s reading of the Iranian drone and missile attacks on hotels in Abu Dhabi, Dubai and Muscat during the 2026 war: not targeted killings, but deliberate strikes at the tourist economies of the Gulf states, aimed at hotels famous enough to empty the country of visitors.

why-the-uae-was-targeted.title: THAAD stocks in the Gulf
why-the-uae-was-targeted.summary: John Kiriakou''s report, during the 2026 war, that the United Arab Emirates were seven days from exhausting their THAAD interceptors and Qatar four days — with American resupply unable to keep pace.

why-the-uae-was-targeted.title: Bahrain''s naturalisation policy
why-the-uae-was-targeted.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of how the Bahraini royal family changed the sectarian arithmetic of the country over thirty years — importing Syrians and naturalising Indian and Pakistani Sunni Muslims until a population that had been two-thirds to three-quarters Shia was closer to half and half.

why-the-uae-was-targeted.title: Chaos as the Israeli objective
why-the-uae-was-targeted.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer to whether Netanyahu''s government actually wanted an American invasion of Iran: what the Israelis want in Iran is what they got in Libya — chaos, civil war, and as many dead Iranians as possible.

wikileaks-as-a-system.title: Julian Assange
wikileaks-as-a-system.summary: Kiriakou — a 15-year friend and former WikiLeaks board member — on why Assange is a publisher owed a journalist's immunity, and a political prisoner.

wikileaks-as-a-system.title: Chelsea Manning
wikileaks-as-a-system.summary: Former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who provided WikiLeaks its 2010 trove of military and diplomatic documents. Per John Kiriakou, Manning meets the legal definition of whistleblower for exposing war crimes, was a torture victim of prolonged solitary confinement with forced nudity, and was sentenced to 35 years in prison before Barack Obama commuted — not pardoned — her sentence. Kiriakou says Manning later refused a grand jury's offer of immunity and chose renewed jail time rather than testify against Julian Assange.

wikileaks-as-a-system.title: John Kiriakou
wikileaks-as-a-system.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

wikileaks-as-a-system.title: The Intercept
wikileaks-as-a-system.summary: The investigative news outlet that published Daniel Hale's drone leak; John Kiriakou notes that the same Intercept reporter, Matthew Cole, was involved in cases that led to the exposure of both Kiriakou himself and NSA leaker Reality Winner — though he insists Hale outed himself rather than being burned by the outlet.

wikileaks-as-a-system.title: Espionage Act
wikileaks-as-a-system.summary: United States federal law enacted in 1917, originally aimed at combating German saboteurs during World War I; per John Kiriakou, never meaningfully updated, does not mention the word 'classified information' anywhere in its text, and has been used disproportionately against national security whistleblowers — particularly under the Obama administration, which prosecuted eight people under the act for speaking to the press, nearly three times the total of all previous presidents combined.

wikileaks-as-a-system.title: Daniel Domscheit-Berg
wikileaks-as-a-system.summary: A WikiLeaks associate discussed on the same panel as John Kiriakou; the anecdote about meeting him via the Chaos Computer Club was told by fellow panelist John Goetz, a Der Spiegel journalist — not by Kiriakou himself.

will-hurd.title: In-Q-Tel
will-hurd.summary: The CIA's openly acknowledged venture capital arm; provided Palantir Technologies its first $1.5 million in seed funding; in John Kiriakou's account the principal vehicle by which the agency finances private-sector development of technologies it intends to use.

will-hurd.title: CIA National Resources Division
will-hurd.summary: The Central Intelligence Agency's domestic intelligence-collection arm, created in the 1980s by Director William J. Casey

will-hurd.title: Abu Zubaydah
will-hurd.summary: Detainee captured by John Kiriakou's CIA team in Pakistan in March 2002; the first subject of the agency's enhanced interrogation techniques program; subjected to both approved and unauthorized techniques including the cockroach-in-coffin treatment exploiting a documented insect phobia.

will-hurd.title: Barack Obama
will-hurd.summary: 44th U.S. president; in John Kiriakou's account, Obama publicly recounted refusing Benjamin Netanyahu's demand to bomb Iran and calling Israel's threat to use nuclear weapons a bluff — a bluff Kiriakou says Donald Trump later believed.

will-hurd.title: Jason Leopold
will-hurd.summary: Bloomberg investigative journalist; characterized by John Kiriakou as the leading practitioner of Freedom of Information Act litigation against U.S. [intelligence agencies](/wiki/intelligence-agencies); broke the Hillary Clinton private-email-server story; whose FOIA suit against the CIA Office of Public Affairs produced documentary evidence that NBC's chief national-security correspondent had been sending articles to the CIA for clearance before sending them to his own editor.

will-hurd.title: Jeffrey Epstein
will-hurd.summary: Convicted sex offender; per John Kiriakou, was "an Israeli access agent" rather than a CIA asset, because the CIA collects foreign intelligence and Epstein's targets — Bill Clinton, Bill Gates, Prince Andrew — were not foreign. Kiriakou further holds that Epstein did die by suicide in federal custody, because in the Bureau of Prisons the cameras never work and the guards are always asleep.

william-donovan.title: Founding of the CIA (1947)
william-donovan.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the CIA's creation under the National Security Act of 1947 — built with British MI6 help after a chaotic 1945-47 interregnum, and opposed by J. Edgar Hoover until Truman falsely promised him the new agency would be part of the FBI.

william-donovan.title: Carlos the Jackal
william-donovan.summary: Venezuelan-born militant (Ilich Ramírez Sánchez) active in the 1970s and 1980s; per John Kiriakou, 'the Osama bin Laden of the 70s and 80s.' Kiriakou spent his Athens posting trying to identify the middleman linking Carlos to the Greek terrorist group 17 November, then six months working the lead with MI5 in London; Carlos was finally run down by CIA contractor Billy Waugh in a Khartoum vegetable market and captured in 1994.

william-donovan.title: Richard Welch
william-donovan.summary: CIA Athens station chief assassinated December 23, 1975; the first victim of [Revolutionary Organization 17 November](/wiki/revolutionary-organization-17-november)

william-donovan.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
william-donovan.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

william-donovan.title: J. Edgar Hoover
william-donovan.summary: The FBI's founding director — 48 years in the chair — whose opposition nearly strangled the CIA at birth. Per John Kiriakou, Truman lifted Hoover's objection to the National Security Act of 1947 by disingenuously assuring him the CIA would be a division of the FBI; the lie seeded the two agencies' permanent mutual hatred. Kiriakou also credits Hoover with perfecting the annual ritual the CIA later copied — scaring Congress witless and demanding budget increases — and with controlling Hollywood's FBI image so tightly that no film could be made without his approval.

william-donovan.title: Revolutionary Organization 17 November
william-donovan.summary: Greek far-left urban guerrilla group active 1975–2002; the deadliest terrorist organization in Greek history

william-friedman.title: Spies of Arlington National Cemetery
william-friedman.summary: On the Walk With History podcast, John Kiriakou — author of Remains of the Day: A Definitive Guide to Washington D.C.''s Historic Cemeteries — toured Arlington National Cemetery and told personal and historical stories about the intelligence figures buried there, including OSS founder William Donovan, deputy CIA director Vernon Walters, codebreakers William and Elizabeth Friedman, slain station chiefs Richard Welch and William Buckley, U-2 pilot Francis Gary Powers, and Mike Spann, the first CIA officer killed after 9/11.

william-friedman.title: Francis Gary Powers
william-friedman.summary: U-2 pilot whose 1960 shoot-down over the Soviet Union and subsequent capture the CIA initially denied any knowledge of, denying not only that he was CIA but that he was U.S. government at all, until trading him in a bridge-of-spies prisoner exchange. Buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Per John Kiriakou, after his U-2 career Powers ended up piloting a Los Angeles traffic helicopter, and was killed when it crashed.

william-friedman.title: Vernon Walters
william-friedman.summary: U.S. Army general who served as Deputy Director of the CIA, Ambassador to Germany, Ambassador to the United Nations, and as Nixon''s occasional secret envoy to foreign leaders. Per John Kiriakou — who met him at an early-career analysts'' dinner — Walters said the only time he was ever afraid for his safety was during a secret Nixon-ordered peace mission to Fidel Castro in Cuba, when it occurred to him that Castro could poison him and no one but Nixon would know he was there: ''I wouldn''t trust Nixon to call my wife.'' Then he looked at Castro and thought: ''I can take this scrawny son of a bitch.''

william-friedman.title: William Donovan
william-friedman.summary: General William "Wild Bill" Donovan — Medal of Honor recipient, decorated World War I veteran, Wall Street figure, and founder of the wartime Office of Strategic Services (OSS). Per John Kiriakou, Donovan had President Truman's ear and insisted the new agency be independent rather than a division of the FBI; he was among the men who sat down with visiting MI6 officers in New York in 1946–47 and sketched out a centralized intelligence service on pads of paper, and he became — in Kiriakou's telling — the first director of the CIA, over the sustained opposition of J. Edgar Hoover.

william-friedman.title: Bill Buckley
william-friedman.summary: CIA station chief in Beirut kidnapped by Palestinian Islamic Jihad in March 1984; tortured at length over fifteen months; killed in captivity; the case from which the agency derived a generation of operational-security lessons including the abandonment of single-point tracking devices in CIA officers' personal kit.

william-friedman.title: Mike Spann
william-friedman.summary: CIA officer; first American killed in combat in Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks; killed during the November 2001 Qala-i-Jangi prison uprising; worked in the Counterterrorism Center bullpen alongside John Kiriakou.

william-proxmire.title: Concealment of the CIA budget
william-proxmire.summary: John Kiriakou''s description of how the CIA hides its spending: there is no publicly available written CIA budget, and individual line items are distributed across unrelated federal departments under invented cover programmes — a practice he says persists unchanged, and which once repeatedly exposed the agency to Senator William Proxmire''s Golden Fleece Award.

william-proxmire.title: USAID as a CIA cover vehicle
william-proxmire.summary: John Kiriakou's account of USAID's use by the CIA as a channel for covert operations and money laundering rather than as an undercover posting for individual officers — including a declassified 1972 exchange in which Henry Kissinger confirmed the CIA had paid Laotian mercenaries through USAID payroll checks.

william-proxmire.title: John Kiriakou
william-proxmire.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

william-proxmire.title: ZunZuneo
william-proxmire.summary: Covert social-media platform built for Cuba through USAID during the George W. Bush administration, intended by John Kiriakou's account to instigate an Arab Spring-style uprising. He says Cubans were indifferent to it, the project died, and its existence became public only when it was leaked by accident to the Guardian.

william-proxmire.title: Bluffdale NSA Data Center
william-proxmire.summary: The NSA's purpose-built facility in the Utah desert, characterized by John Kiriakou as having storage capacity for every phone call, text message, and email of every American for the next 500 years.

william-proxmire.title: Donald Trump
william-proxmire.summary: 45th and 47th U.S. president. Per John Kiriakou, a man genuinely convinced he was doing right by bombing Iran, "duped" by the same Netanyahu nuclear bluff Obama once rejected — and, at the same time, the most blindly pro-Israel president in history, an admirer of autocrats who has never once criticized Vladimir Putin, and prone to gestures — from the Gulf of America to a since-abandoned "Department of War" rename — that test the edges of his actual authority.

william-webster.title: George Habash
william-webster.summary: Co-founder of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine; as a young Lebanese medical student he was the college roommate at the American University of Beirut of Ahmed Khatib, the doctor whom Iraq installed as occupation governor of Kuwait on August 2, 1990 — a connection John Kiriakou carried into the Oval Office that day.

william-webster.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
william-webster.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

william-webster.title: Central Intelligence Agency
william-webster.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

william-webster.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
william-webster.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

william-webster.title: Colin Powell
william-webster.summary: U.S. Secretary of State whose 2003 UN testimony made the case for the Iraq war; John Kiriakou says the white powder in Powell's prop tube was nothing, and that Powell's own chief of staff later told him the presentation was knowingly 'sold.'

william-webster.title: Petra Bank
william-webster.summary: Jordan-based bank founded by Ahmed Chalabi and used by the entire Iraqi refugee community in Jordan; per John Kiriakou, looted of $36 million in a single night when Chalabi transferred every dollar to secret accounts abroad and fled to Syria in the trunk of his secretary's car — bankrupting every Iraqi in the country, driving some to suicide, and earning a death sentence the CIA later had lifted so he could front the Iraqi opposition.

witness-k-case.title: CIA Torture Program Whistleblowing
witness-k-case.summary: In December 2007, John Kiriakou became the first former CIA officer to publicly confirm the agency's post-9/11 torture program, telling ABC's Brian Ross that torture — including waterboarding — was official U.S. government policy personally approved by the president. Per Kiriakou, the decision followed a slow, incremental disillusionment dating back to a hooding incident in the field, years of waiting for someone else to come forward first, and culminated in prosecution under the Espionage Act after the program's congressional overseers publicly denied knowledge of what they had authorized and funded.

witness-k-case.title: Senate Torture Report
witness-k-case.summary: The December 2014 executive summary of the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence's study of the CIA's post-9/11 detention and interrogation program; the first public disclosure of techniques including rectal feeding with hummus, sexual assault with broomsticks, and prolonged sleep deprivation.

witness-k-case.title: Amnesty International
witness-k-case.summary: The human rights organization whose 2006 torture report forms part of John Kiriakou's core defense — the CIA's crimes were already public knowledge before he confirmed them on ABC — and the organization whose silence during his own prosecution he cannot forgive. He begged Amnesty for even a one-sentence statement about his case; the director of Amnesty International USA sent him a New Yorker subscription and a letter saying they wanted nothing to do with it. "After about a year I got tired of begging."

witness-k-case.title: Bahrain Posting (1994–1996)
witness-k-case.summary: John Kiriakou's 1994–1996 assignment to Bahrain under U.S. State Department cover as second secretary for economic affairs — arriving with his wife Joanne and infant son Chris on August 1, 1994, into a tiny Gulf monarchy whose sectarian tensions erupted, two months later, into the first Intifada.

witness-k-case.title: Bureau of Prisons
witness-k-case.summary: The federal agency that ran John Kiriakou's incarceration — and one of his most persistent post-prison targets. The BOP overrode his judge's camp recommendation by deeming him "a threat to the public safety," threatened him with "diesel therapy" until 1,600 logged phone calls and letters from a dozen House members and two senators backed it off, and, per Kiriakou, functions as "an employment agency for unemployable semi-literate rural white men" and "a dumping ground for failed medical professionals" — an agency for which a prisoner's death is cheaper than his treatment.

witness-k-case.title: CIA Training Doctrine
witness-k-case.summary: ''Our job is to break the law'' — Kiriakou on what CIA training actually teaches, why it applies only overseas, and the ethics class that never comes.

wldragnet.title: Mass Surveillance
wldragnet.summary: Kiriakou says the NSA has dropped any pretext of protecting civil liberties, warehousing every call, text and email in the Utah desert.

wldragnet.title: Purchased data as a warrant workaround
wldragnet.summary: John Kiriakou's account of U.S. federal agencies buying Americans' personal data from social-media platforms and data brokers rather than seeking a warrant — a practice he describes as an ethical and legal problem likely to reach the Supreme Court, and one in which no judge is aware a case is being built.

wldragnet.title: Kiriakou on artificial intelligence
wldragnet.summary: John Kiriakou's stated experience with and objections to large language models — a ChatGPT exchange in which the system stated his degrees incorrectly, refused his correction and then cut him off, and a test in which every scholarly citation it produced for his university syllabus turned out to be fabricated. He also describes AI as the flagging layer of contemporary surveillance.

wldragnet.title: Panquake
wldragnet.summary: Open-source, blockchain-based social platform developed by the Iceland-registered company Talk Liberation, for which John Kiriakou has served as brand ambassador since 2020. Kiriakou describes it as advertising-free, subscription-funded, free of back doors, and run on servers powered by Icelandic geothermal steam — a project he frames as a David-and-Goliath fight against banks, big technology and governments.

wldragnet.title: Bluffdale NSA Data Center
wldragnet.summary: The NSA's purpose-built facility in the Utah desert, characterized by John Kiriakou as having storage capacity for every phone call, text message, and email of every American for the next 500 years.

wldragnet.title: Government encryption back-door demands
wldragnet.summary: John Kiriakou's account of state pressure on technology companies for access to encrypted systems — the British government's demand for a back door into Apple's operating system, which he says Apple met with a threat to leave the United Kingdom, and his prediction that the second Trump administration would make the same demand of any new platform under a counterterrorism pretext.

wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.title: The Hersh publishing collapse
wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.summary: John Kiriakou's account of Seymour Hersh's disappearance from mainstream print — from the London Review of Books in 2017, which Hersh told him was already the only outlet that would take his work, to Substack five years later. Kiriakou, who helped give Hersh an award for integrity in intelligence, presents the trajectory as a measure of how bad conditions for American journalism have become.

wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.title: CIA attention to West Africa
wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.summary: John Kiriakou''s answer on whether the CIA is likely to be operating in Burkina Faso: for all the years he was at the agency it cared very little about Africa and especially West Africa, but the presence of al-Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates plus the drug trade makes CIA and special forces involvement probable — and, he adds, the American public will not hear about it.

wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.title: CIA media relations
wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.summary: John Kiriakou's account of how the CIA shapes press coverage in the 2020s without needing an Operation Mockingbird-style infiltration program — because corporate media now recites CIA messaging willingly, most journalists simply rewrite emailed statements from the agency's Office of Public Affairs, and the CIA allegedly manipulates algorithms and backs podcasts to spread its point of view.

wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.title: CIA media revolving door
wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.summary: John Kiriakou's proposed reform to bar CIA officers from becoming paid media personalities without a cooling-off period, and to strip the security clearances of retirees who go straight from the agency to cable-news punditry.

wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.title: Muddling through
wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.summary: An analytic term John Kiriakou says CIA analysts used all the time, and his defence of it: forecasters instinctively reach for either/or outcomes, when what actually happens most often is that the parties to a conflict muddle through and little changes over the medium term. He applies it to Ukraine, and to why he expects Russia not to use nuclear weapons.

wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.title: The African diplomat's remark
wolf-blitzer-at-cia-headquarters.summary: The line John Kiriakou says an African diplomat gave him at a White House summit, and which he uses to explain Chinese success on the continent: you Americans always offer us democracy and military aid, and the Chinese offer us food and new roads. Kiriakou traces the consequence to Chinese bases across Africa and a State Department that did not see it coming.

world-trade-center.title: CIA–FBI interagency rivalry and 9/11
world-trade-center.summary: John Kiriakou's account of the historical CIA–FBI rivalry, dating to J. Edgar Hoover's opposition to the 1947 National Security Act, and how it manifested before September 11 when Cofer Black's Counterterrorism Center withheld from the FBI that hijackers Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar had been granted U.S. visas.

world-trade-center.title: Cofer Black
world-trade-center.summary: Former head of the CIA Counterterrorism Center during and immediately after the September 11 attacks; principal architect of the agency's paramilitary turn on September 12, 2001; later Vice President of Blackwater under Erik Prince.

world-trade-center.title: Kiriakou's transfer to the Directorate of Operations
world-trade-center.summary: John Kiriakou's roughly two-month internal campaign to transfer from the CIA's analytic Directorate of Intelligence to the operational Directorate of Operations, overcoming what he calls a "natural bias in operations against the eggheads on the analytic side," followed by an Athens posting secured because he was the only person in the entire CIA fluent in both Greek and Arabic. Covers his full CIA career arc from 1988/1990 recruitment through analyst years on Iraq, the switch to operations, 9/11, the enhanced-interrogation refusal, executive assistant to the deputy director for operations, and his eventual resignation and post-CIA career.

world-trade-center.title: George H.W. Bush
world-trade-center.summary: The 41st president — and the one John Kiriakou briefed a number of times, finding him "far more worldly" than the others, as befits a former CIA director. Kiriakou credits him with throwing away his presidency by keeping his word and stopping short of Baghdad, faults the ceasefire's helicopter loophole that let Saddam slaughter the Shia, calls him the last president to give the Arabs a fair shake — cutting off loan guarantees until Israel stopped building settlements — and traces the second Iraq war's personal edge to Saddam's 1993 attempt to assassinate him.

world-trade-center.title: Saudi princes and 9/11
world-trade-center.summary: John Kiriakou's account of finding three Saudi princes' personal cell numbers in Abu Zubaydah's seized diary — and how, after the CIA warned the Saudis, all three princes soon died in improbable ways, convincing him the Saudi government was involved in 9/11.

world-trade-center.title: Osama bin Laden
world-trade-center.summary: Founder and leader of al-Qaeda and the central target of the manhunt that shaped John Kiriakou's counterterrorism career. Per Kiriakou, bin Laden came from a billionaire Saudi construction family, was never one of the CIA-funded Afghan mujahideen, overruled subordinates who wanted to attack Israel and insisted the 9/11 attacks hit the United States to crash its economy, escaped Tora Bora dressed as a woman, and spent his final years next to Pakistan's equivalent of West Point — where, Kiriakou says, you would have to be a "mental defective" not to know he was there. Kiriakou believes the United States never intended to capture him alive.

yalta-conference.title: United Food and Commercial Workers
yalta-conference.summary: The huge K Street labor union where a young John Kiriakou — from a family with a long labor history — was working when Dr. Jerrold Post''s class assignment changed his life: shadow your boss for a week and write his psychological profile. Kiriakou''s boss was a mean old-school organizer whose back had been broken by scabs; halfway through the week Kiriakou called him a racist ("which he was"), and the resulting paper diagnosed the man as a sociopath and potentially dangerous. The paper is what put Kiriakou on the CIA''s radar.

yalta-conference.title: 9/11 plea agreements
yalta-conference.summary: The Biden-era plea deals under which Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and co-defendants agreed to plead guilty to murdering 2,976 people in exchange for life without parole and a guarantee against transfer to the Colorado supermax — vacated by the Secretary of Defense after public backlash. Per John Kiriakou, the deals existed because torture had rendered every confession inadmissible, leaving no usable evidence.

yalta-conference.title: AIPAC and foreign-agent registration
yalta-conference.summary: John Kiriakou's argument that AIPAC is the only organization of its kind exempt from registering under the Foreign Agents Registration Act — set against his own experience around 2008, when a contract worth five or six thousand dollars to write four op-eds praising the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce obliged him to register as a foreign agent.

yalta-conference.title: George McGovern
yalta-conference.summary: The 1972 Democratic presidential nominee, whose landslide defeat John Kiriakou identifies as the pretext for creating superdelegates. As a George Washington University sophomore in 1983, Kiriakou wrote to McGovern offering the campus theater for a campaign launch; McGovern telephoned him personally, announced his 1984 candidacy there, and afterwards took him home for tuna sandwiches made by his wife.

yalta-conference.title: Guantánamo Bay detention camp
yalta-conference.summary: Per John Kiriakou — as chief of counterterrorism operations in Pakistan after September 11, 2001 — the Guantanamo detention facility began as a temporary holding measure intended to last two to three weeks while the CIA and Justice Department determined which federal district court should try each prisoner, not as a long-term detention infrastructure. The Rawalpindi jail had reached capacity, Pakistani intelligence demanded the prisoners be removed, and CIA headquarters directed Kiriakou to load them onto a C-12 cargo plane and fly them to Cuba.

yalta-conference.title: Iraq War Israeli tower sabotage
yalta-conference.summary: Per John Kiriakou, after the U.S. rejected Israel's request to join the coalition for the Iraq War in late 2002/early 2003 — fearing the loss of Jordanian, Egyptian, and Saudi cooperation — communications towers across the western Iraqi desert began being toppled by explosives; when the New York Times asked the CIA if Israel was responsible, the agency denied any Israeli involvement.

yasser-arafat.title: Abraham Accords
yasser-arafat.summary: The Trump-brokered normalization deals between Israel and Gulf Arab states — in John Kiriakou's judgment "a terrible idea in the first place," a great victory for Israel and the Gulf Arabs that was "a punch in the throat to the Palestinians." He argues the Accords are how Trump meant to "solve the Middle East in a day" — by screwing the Palestinians — that Hamas read the abandonment correctly, that October 7 shattered the project, and that reviving the Accords (Saudis in, victory declared, Nobel collected) remains the organizing goal of Trump's regional policy.

yasser-arafat.title: Gulf security bargain
yasser-arafat.summary: The decades-old arrangement — traced by John Kiriakou to FDR and the Saudi king, and originally British — under which Gulf Arab monarchies host U.S. bases and sell oil in dollars in exchange for American protection; a bargain Kiriakou says collapsed when those bases failed to shield them during the war on Iran.

yasser-arafat.title: Expulsion of Palestinians from the Gulf
yasser-arafat.summary: The mass expulsion of the Palestinian professional class from the Gulf Arab states in the aftermath of Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, which John Kiriakou witnessed from the region and identifies as the reason Gulf governments are willing to normalise relations with Israel.

yasser-arafat.title: Saddam Hussein
yasser-arafat.summary: President of Iraq from 1979 until the 2003 U.S. invasion; subject of John Kiriakou's CIA portfolio from January 1990 onward, in which capacity Kiriakou became, at age 25, "Saddam Hussein's intelligence community biographer" and the analyst who briefed President George H. W. Bush in the Oval Office on the morning of the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

yasser-arafat.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
yasser-arafat.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

yasser-arafat.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
yasser-arafat.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

yellowcake-niger-forgery.title: Iraqi invasion of Kuwait
yellowcake-niger-forgery.summary: John Kiriakou''s most detailed account of the intelligence process around the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait and its 1991 liberation. As a first-year CIA analyst on a ''training account'' covering Iraq, Kiriakou produced the June 30, 1990 warning paper for the White House; suggested calling the US Defense Attaché in Baghdad to drive to the border and report what he saw (the answer: ''Literally the entire Iraqi military is heading south''); briefed the August 2 Oval Office meeting with Bush; and later took a single phone call from General Colin Powell that led, eight hours later, to 47 cruise missiles striking the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad.

yellowcake-niger-forgery.title: Kuwait oil fires
yellowcake-niger-forgery.summary: The February 1991 sabotage by retreating Iraqi forces of an estimated 600–800 Kuwaiti oil wells; per John Kiriakou's first-person account, the fires blackened the desert and blotted out the sun as far away as Riyadh, vaporized two French journalists who drove onto a sheet of melted-sand glass, and were extinguished only by an international team led by American specialist Red Adair using a Rolls-Royce jet engine to blow the flames out.

yellowcake-niger-forgery.title: Ahmed Chalabi
yellowcake-niger-forgery.summary: Iraqi exile and founder of the Iraqi National Congress; per John Kiriakou, a Shia-Kurdish con man who looted Petra Bank in Jordan of $36 million in the 1980s, was sentenced to death in absentia, was pardoned at CIA request, then pocketed $6 million in CIA seed funding for the INC and bought a Mayfair house in cash; later resurrected by Dick Cheney to feed the Pentagon fabricated WMD intelligence used to justify the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

yellowcake-niger-forgery.title: Kurds
yellowcake-niger-forgery.summary: The stateless people John Kiriakou calls generationally pro-American — he escorted visiting Kurdish delegations around Washington as a young analyst and bristled at officials who talked down to them. In his telling the Kurds were the only genuine opposition inside Saddam's Iraq, the only faction of the exile circus that ever amounted to anything (Jalal Talabani ended up president of Iraq), the victims of Saddam's chemical weapons and of a no-fly zone that forgot to ban helicopters — and the common enemy that actually united Turkey and ISIS.

yellowcake-niger-forgery.title: Petra Bank
yellowcake-niger-forgery.summary: Jordan-based bank founded by Ahmed Chalabi and used by the entire Iraqi refugee community in Jordan; per John Kiriakou, looted of $36 million in a single night when Chalabi transferred every dollar to secret accounts abroad and fled to Syria in the trunk of his secretary's car — bankrupting every Iraqi in the country, driving some to suicide, and earning a death sentence the CIA later had lifted so he could front the Iraqi opposition.

yellowcake-niger-forgery.title: 1993 Bush Kuwait assassination plot
yellowcake-niger-forgery.summary: Iraqi intelligence plot, foiled by Kuwaiti authorities, to assassinate former President George H. W. Bush during his post-liberation "victory lap" visit to Kuwait; the U.S. response, per John Kiriakou's first-person account of his telephone call with Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Colin Powell, was 47 cruise missiles fired into the Iraqi Intelligence Service headquarters in Baghdad eight hours later.

yemen-arrest.title: Central Intelligence Agency
yemen-arrest.summary: U.S. foreign intelligence service; John Kiriakou's employer from 1990 to 2004 and the central institution of KiriPedia

yemen-arrest.title: CIA Drug Facilitation
yemen-arrest.summary: Per John Kiriakou, the CIA''s reported involvement in facilitating the arrival of cocaine into the United States during the era that became the crack epidemic, and his own firsthand discovery — as a Senate Foreign Relations Committee investigator — that under American military control Afghanistan produced 93% of the world''s heroin. A DEA contact told him the report would never be published because ''we want Iran and Russia to be addicted to heroin. It weakens their societies.'' Kiriakou draws a direct parallel to the current fentanyl crisis: China is doing to the US what the US did to Iran and Russia.

yemen-arrest.title: The CIA Insider's Guide to Surveillance and Surveillance Detection
yemen-arrest.summary: Book by John Kiriakou drawing on his experience as a surveillance detection instructor at the CIA and as a private surveillance training consultant. The book covers the techniques used by intelligence professionals to identify whether they are being followed — including the four-phase surveillance detection route, concealment device placement and retrieval, and counter-surveillance strategy — adapted for use by corporate executives, journalists, and others who want to confirm whether they are being followed.

yemen-arrest.title: John Kiriakou
yemen-arrest.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

yemen-arrest.title: NSA
yemen-arrest.summary: Kiriakou on the agency whose Utah facility boasts room to store every American's calls, texts and emails for the next 500 years.

yemen-arrest.title: Patriot Act
yemen-arrest.summary: U.S. law passed after the September 11 attacks that vastly expanded domestic surveillance authority. Per John Kiriakou, the Patriot Act ''opened up everything'' — and he disputes the common belief that 9/11 was required to pass it: ''You underestimate Congress. They didn''t need a catastrophe — they would just pass it because they can.'' He ties it to NSA bulk-collection programs that vacuum up every phone call, text, email, and piece of metadata from Americans, in violation of the NSA''s own charter.

yemen-jazz-radio-plan.title: The Sanaa sewer project
yemen-jazz-radio-plan.summary: The example John Kiriakou uses for what patient foreign assistance looks like: on a visit to Yemen around 2000 he called on the Dutch ambassador and the Italian defence attaché, who were proud because their governments had just finished building a sewer system and water treatment facility for the capital — a project that had taken about fifteen years.

yemen-jazz-radio-plan.title: Fusha and the Gulf dialect
yemen-jazz-radio-plan.summary: John Kiriakou''s account of his own Arabic training — a first year in fusha, high standard Arabic, followed by a second year in khaleeji, the Gulf dialect — and the two consequences he reports: that Yemen is the only place where pure fusha is spoken, and that Saudis asked him why he spoke Arabic like Shakespeare.

yemen-jazz-radio-plan.title: Saudi aid priorities
yemen-jazz-radio-plan.summary: John Kiriakou''s characterisation of Saudi generosity abroad as real but consistently misdirected: instead of building schools they build mosques, instead of building hospitals they send planeloads of Qurans, and instead of water treatment plants or power plants they send money for weapons, ammunition and training.

yemen-jazz-radio-plan.title: The Afghan National Police poisoning
yemen-jazz-radio-plan.summary: An incident John Kiriakou recalls from a 2012 New York Times report and treats as the clearest single illustration of why the American project in Afghanistan failed: at a DynCorp-run training facility that had deliberately mixed recruits from every tribe and region, one recruit poisoned the evening stew and then let four Taliban fighters into the dormitory to stab the survivors in their beds.

yemen-jazz-radio-plan.title: The Afghan police tribal rotation
yemen-jazz-radio-plan.summary: An American anti-corruption scheme in Afghanistan that John Kiriakou describes as achieving the reverse of its purpose: someone in the Pentagon decided that regional chiefs of police should come from other tribes in other parts of the country, so a man from Herat would head the police in Kandahar — which only deepened hatred between tribes and did nothing at all about corruption.

yemen-jazz-radio-plan.title: The al-Qaeda foot soldier
yemen-jazz-radio-plan.summary: What John Kiriakou says he learned from interviewing captured al-Qaeda fighters — not the leaders but the eighteen-, nineteen- and twenty-year-olds, who told essentially the same story: an isolated village, illiteracy, no job skills, a poor relationship with their father, an age at which they wanted to marry, and no father willing to give them a daughter. The local imam offered $300 a month to go to Afghanistan, and $500 to their parents if they were martyred.

yemen.title: Benjamin Netanyahu
yemen.summary: Israeli prime minister, per John Kiriakou an unpopular but politically durable figure whom Kiriakou says has spent decades pressing successive U.S. presidents to bomb Iran, presided over escalating land seizures in the West Bank, and used the October 7 attack and its aftermath to entrench his own political survival.

yemen.title: John Kiriakou
yemen.summary: American former CIA counterterrorism officer, whistleblower, author, and podcast host

yemen.title: MOSSAD
yemen.summary: Israel's primary external intelligence service; characterized by John Kiriakou as universally hostile in his and his CIA colleagues' professional dealings with it ("never had a positive encounter with Mossad"); operates almost exclusively in the operational rather than analytical domain; the CIA is, per Kiriakou, categorically forbidden from spying on it.

yemen.title: Falls Church mosque
yemen.summary: Large mosque on Route 7 in Falls Church, Virginia; the site at which John Kiriakou, in 1993 as a CIA Arabic-language trainee, met then-imam Anwar al-Awlaki on a class field trip; the same mosque at which the September 11 hijackers prayed the night before the attacks.

yemen.title: Prince Muhammad bin Naif
